articles.title: Sundance 2027 In Boulder Unveils Legacy Lineup With ‘Better Luck Tomorrow’, ‘Memento’, ‘Y Tu Mamá También’ & More
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony How ‘Klara And The Sun’ Got Blotted Out At The Box Office ‘Divine Rivals’: Feature Take Of Rebecca Ross Fantasy Romance Bestseller Heads To Disney Searchlight Pictures Marketing EVP Michelle Hooper Leaving Studio View All October 28, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sundance Film Festival 2027 has announced its first lineup for the inaugural Boulder, Colorado edition with the The Legacy Program, formerly known as From the Collection, which includes archival and restored screenings of indie classics that launched at the fest. Cinephile social platform, Letterboxd, is a co-presenter of the Legacy program, and there will be forthcoming details for onsite activations at the Boulder cinema event which takes place Jan. 21-31. The Legacy portion of Sundance will occur during the fest’s second half from Tuesday, Jan. 27-Sunday, Jan. 31. Related Stories Acquisitions Jenna Ortega, Natalie Portman MRC Comedy 'The Gallerist' Heads To Roadside Attractions & Vertical In U.S. Deal Festivals Sundance Film Festival Boulder Expanding Competition Lineup & Making Big Cinema Upgrades For 2027 Event There will still be an online portion of the festival, which will run from Thursday, Jan. 28-Sunday, Jan. 31. The Legacy lineup includes the 2002 Sundance Film Festival version of Better Luck Tomorrow (Justin Lin); a digital 4K restoration of Dogtown and Z-Boys (Stacy Peralta); a 35th anniversary screening of Fool’s Fire (Julie Taymor); Nitrate Kisses (Barbara Hammer), which premiered in the U.S. at the Festival 35 years ago and whose director is at the center of Brydie O’Connor’s 2026 Sundance Film Festival documentary Barbara Forever ; a 25th anniversary screening of Real Women Have Curves (Patricia Cardoso); a 35th anniversary screening of Swoon (Tom Kalin); and a 25th anniversary screening of a 4K restoration of Y tu mamá también (Alfonso Cuarón). Watch on Deadline The Legacy program will also include a two-part session on the final weekend of the Festival called “Sundance Film Festival presents: Cinema Interruptus featuring Memento ” (Christopher Nolan), featuring a 4K restoration and discussion. Legacy screenings will include director appearances and select cast members in attendance, Next reps the 30th anniversary of Sundance Institute and the UCLA Film & Television Archive. Together they established a film preservation initiative, the Sundance Institute Collection at UCLA, to ensure the long-term preservation of independent film. The Collection currently holds material from over 1,000 titles and has participated in restorations of Hoop Dreams , River of Grass , Mysterious Skin , Doom Generation , Just Another Girl on the IRT , High Art , Go Fish , Three Seasons , Paris Is Burning , Superstar , Unzipped , The Hours and Times , SLAM , and, this year, Better Luck Tomorrow and Swoon . “We’re excited to kick off the Festival season in earnest with this first 2027 Sundance Film Festival announcement, revealing some of our Legacy programming,” said Eugene Hernandez, Director, Sundance Film Festival and Public Programming. “Each year we honor the legacy of our founder Robert Redford and the history of the Sundance Film Festival by looking back at just a few of the films and filmmakers who have shaped our history. Our first festival in our new home in Boulder, Colorado will bring change, but as we evolve, we’ll keep at our core what we celebrate: our rich history. Sundance will always uplift independent voices, and our Legacy slate is a beautiful example of that. We are also pleased to announce Letterboxd’s co-partnership for the Legacy category — it’s great to collaborate with organizations that build momentum and excitement for a culture of cinematic discovery, and we look forward to having them at the Festival with us in January.” “Revisiting and becoming newly acquainted with films from our previous lineups in a theatrical setting, in community, and with some of the talent behind the films is a rare treat — even more so when these projects have been restored,” said Kim Yutani, Director of Programming, Sundance Film Festival. “We’re really looking forward to welcoming back these artists and know that audiences will enjoy the opportunity to complement the new films we will soon be announcing with these classics.” “Our Legacy programming at the Sundance Film Festival grew out of a partnership with the UCLA Film & Television Archive and its continued growth is running in parallel to the incredible moment repertory cinema is having across the country right now,” said John Nein, Sundance Film Festival Senior Programmer and Director of Strategic Initiatives. “This program offers a space for brand-new restorations of classic independent films to be discovered or rediscovered by audiences as the creative teams behind these films reunite — it’s an exciting way of celebrating what these artists have brought to independent storytelling.” Below are descriptions of the Legacy lineup: 25th Anniversary of Better Luck Tomorrow / U.S.A. (Director, Screenwriter, and Producer: Justin Lin, Screenwriters: Ernesto Foronda, Fabian Marquez, Producers: Julie Asato, Ernesto Foronda) — To escape the crushing pressure of academic perfection, a group of high-achieving teens lead a secret, thrill-seeking double life of petty crime that quickly spins out of control. Cast: Karin Anna Cheung, John Cho, Roger Fan, Sung Kang, Parry Shen, Jason Tobin. Fiction. Better Luck Tomorrow premiered at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition. It was subsequently released with small changes in the edit. The original 2002 Sundance Film Festival cut of Better Luck Tomorrow was restored by the UCLA Film & Television Archive in collaboration with Sundance Institute and Perfect Storm Entertainment, with funding provided by Chris Quintos Cathcart, co-CEO of Unapologetic Projects. The 4K restoration utilized the original 35 mm camera negatives, 35 mm Sundance Film Festival print, and DA-88 sound materials and was supervised by filmmaker Justin Lin at Resillion and Deluxe Audio Services. Additional lab services by Roundabout Entertainment, Inc. The release version has also been restored and archived. Special thanks to Paramount Pictures for permission to screen the film. 25th Anniversary of Dogtown and Z-Boys / U.S.A (Director and Screenwriter: Stacy Peralta, Screenwriter: Craig Stecyk, Producer: Agi Orsi) — The Z-Boys: outcast surf rats from the run-down Dogtown neighborhood in Venice, California, who revolutionized skateboarding with their innovative style and attitude. The documentary is an exploration of the birth of a cultural phenomenon, narrated by Sean Penn and featuring old-school skating footage, a blistering soundtrack, and interviews with Tony Alva, Jay Adams, and Tony Hawk. Dogtown and Z-Boys premiered at the 2001 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Documentary Competition and won the Audience Award: Documentary and Directing Award: Documentary. 2027 marks the 25th anniversary of its theatrical release. The 4K digital restoration was undertaken from the original 35 mm elements by Sony Pictures Classics. The restoration was approved by the filmmakers. 35th Anniversary of Fool’s Fire / U.S.A. (Director, Screenwriter, and Producer: Julie Taymor, Producer: Kerry Orent) — A captured dwarf, Hopfrog, is forced to become jester to a tyrannical king. But when the King is gifted with another little person, whom the king debases and shames, Hopfrog plots a terrible revenge. Based on the story “Hop-Frog” by Edgar Allan Poe. Cast: Michael J. Anderson, Tom Hewitt, Mireille Mossé. Fiction. Fool’s Fire premiered at the 1992 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition. This new restoration was created by the nonprofit IndieCollect in collaboration with Julie Taymor and with support from the Golden Globe Foundation, using a 6.5K scan of the original 35 mm negative and a soundtrack restored by Endpoint Audio Labs from the optical track negative. Featuring an extended conversation with Julie Taymor and clips from The Making of Fool’s Fire , exploring the film’s artistry and cutting-edge use of high definition. Nitrate Kisses / U.S.A. (Director: Barbara Hammer) — A portrait of queer sexuality that weaves striking images of four lesbian and gay couples with archival footage, interviews, sexual imagery, and queer cinema dating back to the 1930s to unearth forbidden and long-invisible histories. Documentary. Nitrate Kisses had its U.S. premiere at the 1993 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Documentary Competition. Nitrate Kisses was preserved by the Academy Film Archive. The original 16 mm A/B-rolls were scanned at 4K and restored by BB Optics. The mono mix was digitized from the original 16 mm mag track. The restoration was funded by Frameline and supervised by The Estate of Barbara Hammer and Brydie O’Connor. The 25th Anniversary of Real Women Have Curves / U.S.A. (Director: Patricia Cardoso, Screenwriters: George LaVoo, Josefina López, Producers: George Lavoo, Effie Brown) — Ana, a first-generation Mexican American teenager, fights for her independence and her curves in a war of wills with her mother. Based on the play by Josefina López. Cast: America Ferrera, George Lopez, Ingrid Oliu, Lupe Ontiveros, Brian Sites. Real Women Have Curves premiered at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition and took home the Audience Award: Dramatic and the Special Jury Prize for Acting for America Ferrera and Lupe Ontiveros. Supervised by director Patricia Cardoso and director of photography Jim Denault, this new 4K restoration was undertaken by Criterion in collaboration with Warner Bros. Pictures, Sundance Institute, and the Academy Film Archive from the 35 mm original camera negative. The 35th Anniversary of Swoon / U.S.A. (Director and Screenwriter: Tom Kalin, Producers: Christine Vachon) — The true story of Nathan Leopold and Richard Loeb, who kidnapped and brutally murdered 14-year-old Bobby Franks in Chicago in 1924. The revelation that these wealthy Jewish college students had a sexual relationship scandalized the nation. After their arrest and trial, they were sentenced to life plus 99 years. Cast: Craig Chester, Michael Kirby, John A. Mudd, Daniel Schlachet, Natalie Stanford, Michael Stumm, Ron Vawter. Swoon premiered at the 1992 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition and took home the Excellence in Cinematography Award: Dramatic. Swoon was restored by the Academy Film Archive and UCLA Film & Television Archive in collaboration with Frameline, Strand Releasing, and Sundance Institute in 4K from the original 16 mm A/B camera negatives, 35 mm interpositive, 35 mm dupe negative, and 35 mm magnetic track. The restoration was supervised by Tom Kalin and Ellen Kuras at Roundabout Entertainment, Inc. and Deluxe Audio Services. Restoration funding was provided by the Academy Film Archive and UCLA Film & Television Archive with additional support from Frameline, Ellen Kuras, Strand Releasing, and Sundance Institute. The 25th Anniversary of Y tu mamá también / Mexico (Director, Screenwriter and Producer: Alfonso Cuarón, Screenwriter: Carlos Cuarón, Producer: Jorge Vergara) — After their girlfriends jet off for the summer, a pair of Mexico City teenagers become bewitched by an older Spanish woman they meet at a wedding. When she agrees to accompany them on a road trip, the three form an increasingly intense and sensual bond. Cast: Gael García Bernal, Diego Luna, Maribel Verdú. Y tu mamá también screened at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the Special Events category. Newly restored by Esperanto Films in 4K under the supervision of filmmaker Alfonso Cuarón and cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki. The feature is a Janus Films release. MEMENTO, Guy Pearce, 2000 LEGACY SPECIAL EVENTS Memento / U.S.A. (Director: Christopher Nolan) — A former insurance investigator who now suffers from anterograde amnesia uses notes and tattoos to hunt down his wife’s murderer. Fiction. Memento had its U.S. festival premiere at the 2001 Sundance Film Festival in the U.S. Dramatic Competition and it took home the Waldo Salt Screenwriting Award. Restored in 4K from original interpositive materials by Umbrella with approval from director Christopher Nolan. Cinema Interruptus is also part of our Offscreen program, to be announced in its entirety soon. As part of the screening, there will be Sundance Film Festival presents: Cinema Interruptus featuring Memento . A tradition first established by the late Roger Ebert, Cinema Interruptus is communal film criticism in two sessions. As Memento screens, participants can yell “Stop!” at any point to make a comment or ask a question, after which the film will resume. Critic and author Josh Larsen — who hosted Interruptus at the University of Colorado Boulder’s Conference on World Affairs from 2017 to 2024 — will moderate the discussion, with the goal of finishing the entire movie by the end of the second session. articles.title: Netflix Unveils ‘Pride And Prejudice’ Series Trailer Teases Timeless Slow Burn Romance Between Jack Lowden’s Mr. Darcy & Emma Corrin’s Elizabeth Bennett
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi Amy Poehler Leads Young Women Archaeologists Who Make An Important Discovery In Peacock’s ‘Dig’ Trailer Ryan Gosling & Zach Shields Duo Dead Man’s Bones Returns With New Song Plus Music Video Starring Rain Spencer And Noah Jupe ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 Release Schedule: When Do New Episodes Come Out? View All October 28, 2026 8:48am Add us as a Google Preferred Source UPDATED – Oct. 28, 8 a.m. – The full trailer for the Netflix limited series adaptation of Pride and Prejudice has arrived. The series, based on the book by Jane Austen , arrives on the streamer December 3. The clip opens with Emma Corrin’s Elizabeth Bennett and Freya Mavor’s Jane Bennett lying on a rooftop talking of the future. Related Stories Books Jane Austen Adaptations & Where They Are Streaming: ‘Sense And Sensibility’ To ‘Sanditon’ Books Georgia Oakley’s ‘Sense And Sensibility’ Cast Vs. Ang Lee’s 1995 Group: Who Plays Who? “One day, Jane, I shall be either a governess and a spinster, or a wife and a mother,” Corrin’s Lizzie says. “And then finally, we may talk about something else.” Jane and Elizabeth are two of the five Bennett sisters, parented by “a very animated mother” Mrs. Bennett (Olivia Colman) and father Mr. Bennett (Rufus Sewell), a man of few words. Elizabeth comes upon Mr. Darcy (Jack Lowden) skipping rocks on a lake, which curiously echoes George Mackay’s Mr. Edward Ferrars doing the same thing with Daisy Edgar Jones’ Elinor Dashwood in Georgia Oakley’s new film adaptation of Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility , which arrived in theaters earlier this month. Watch on Deadline Fiona Shaw as Lady Catherine de Bourgh in Netflix’s ‘Pride and Prejudice’ Another crossover between the two new adaptation projects is actress Fiona Shaw, who will portray Lady Catherine de Bourgh in the Netflix series. She can be spotted dressed in black in the back of a carriage. “It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife,” Colman says later on. Viewers also get glimpses at Rhea Norwood’s Lydia Bennett, Hopey Parish’s Mary Bennett and Hollie Avery’s Mary Bennett, Louis Partridge’s Mr. George Wickham, Jamie Demetriou’s Mr. Collins and more. The clip ends with Colman questioning why Sewell’s Mr. Bennett, who hasn’t spoken a word in the entire trailer, must make everything so dramatic. PREVIOUS, Feb. 24: The first teaser trailer for Netflix’s Pride & Prejudice series, based on Jane Austen’s classic novel, is here. The clip features Elizabeth Bennet (Emma Corrin) and Mr. Darcy (Jack Lowden). The six-part series will be a faithful, classic adaptation of the novel, written by Dolly Alderton ( Everything I Know About Love, Good Material ) and directed by Euros Lyn ( Heartstopper ). Alongside Corrin ( Nosferatu, Black Mirror ) and Lowden ( Slow Horses, Benediction ), Olivia Colman ( The Favourite, The Crown ) will be Mrs. Bennet, Rufus Sewell ( The Diplomat, Scoop ) will be Mr. Bennet, Freya Mavor ( Industry, La Dame Dans L’Auto ) will be Jane Bennet, Jamie Demetriou ( Stath Lets Flats, Barbie ) will be Mr. Collins and Daryl McCormack ( Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery; Good Luck to You, Leo Grande ) will be Mr. Bingley. Rhea Norwood ( Heartstopper ) will play Lydia Bennett, Hopey Parish and Hollie Avery will play Mary and Kitty Bennett, Siena Kelly will play Caroline Bingley, and Fiona Shaw ( Bad Sisters , Harry Potter ) will play Lady Catherine de Bourgh. When the full cast was revealed during production, writer and executive producer Alderton said: “‘Once in a generation, a group of people get to retell this wonderful story and I feel very lucky that I get to be a part of it. Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice is the blueprint for romantic comedy – it has been a joy to delve back into its pages to find both familiar and fresh ways of bringing this beloved book to life. With Euros Lyn directing our stellar cast, I am so excited to reintroduce these hilarious and complicated characters to those who count Pride and Prejudice as their favourite book, and those who are yet to meet their Lizzie and Mr. Darcy.” Other executive producers include Laura Lankester, Will Johnston and Louise Mutter for Lookout Point, as well as Alderton and Lyn. Corrin is also an executive producer, marking their debut in the role. Austen’s beloved novels have enraptured generations for over 200 years. Her most famous and widely-read novel, Pride and Prejudice has inspired countless writers and filmmakers with its iconic characters, sharp social commentary and timeless love story. In the UK last week, the teaser played on the big screen ahead of Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights starring Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi. Austen’s Sense and Sensibility will get a new adaptation in film form later this year as well from Focus Features starring Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood, Esmé Creed-Miles as Marianne Dashwood, Catríona Balfe as Mrs. Dashwood and more. The 1995 film version of Sense and Sensibility starred Kate Winslet, Emma Thompson, Alan Rickman, Hugh Grant and more.

articles.title: Tokyo: Competition Jury Discusses Event’s ‘A-List’ Status, Fighting Over Favorite Films
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All October 26, 2026 8:29pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tokyo Film Festival competition jury. From left: Oh Jungwan, Rolf de Heer, Watanabe Makiko and Yov Moor. Tokyo International Film Festival A lively discussion about the global standing of the Tokyo International Film Festival — and whether such considerations even matter — was the highlight of a rather genteel competition jury press conference on Tuesday. The 2026 Tokyo competition jury is headed by Dutch-Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer ( Bad Boy Bubby, Charlie’s Country, Ten Canoes and The Tracker ), and he was joined on stage by competition jury members: French film colorist and producer Yov Moor; leading South Korean producer Oh Jungwan; veteran Japanese actress Makiko Watanabe; and Taiwanese-American producer Alex C. Lo. Related Stories Music Macklemore Launches Sold-Out Free Palestine Tour in Dublin With Hozier, Kneecap and Ed Sheeran's Backing Band Business Disney+ to Add Channel 4 Network and On-Demand Content in U.K., Ireland Under "Most Ambitious" EMEA Deal Yet In stark contrast to many recent pressers at the major European and American film festivals, the Tokyo jury conversation was largely politics free, though the event kicked off with an amusingly blunt answer from De Heer as to why there aren’t more Australian and Japanese co-productions. De Heer was asked about the conspicuous lack of co-productions between Australia and Japan , despite both countries having strong state backing to film production. “It makes no sense for a Japanese film to shoot in Australia, or it makes no sense for an Australian film to shoot in Japan,” said De Heer. “Europe is very good at doing co-productions strictly on a financial basis, really. Australia is not so good at that. The sort of co-productions that work out of Australia are ones that are natural—that have a natural story where some things need to be shot in Japan, some things need to be shot in Australia. Those will always be possible if the scripts come and if they’re right.” After the jury members spoke about their great honor at being invited to oversee this year’s competition, the conversation became a touch more animated when they were asked about the standing of Tokyo Film Festival , as compared to other international festivals, and specifically about Tokyo’s recent inclusion as an “A-list” event by the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (FIAPF). “I think Tokyo was… has always been considered one of those festivals by most people who attend festivals,” said De Heer. “Tokyo was effectively an ‘A’ festival. And so in that sense, I don’t think it makes a lot of difference. This sort of categorization seems to be becoming more important in terms of the quality of films available to that festival, and so in that sense it may help that it is officially now again an ‘A’, but I don’t think it changes the festival so much.” “I think Rolf’s answer is… is enough for… is not enough for you?” said Oh to laughter in the room. “Actually, I don’t know about that. I’m not a film festival person, so I don’t know what is A-list or not. Probably A-list means good! But as an audience, we’re not going to the festival because of their A-list or not. We just go to watch film and enjoy the festival feeling.” Asked whether the tier system was somewhat redundant nowadays, De Heer replied cryptically, “It matters a great deal to some people, and not at all to others. And that is as it should be.” From left: Yov Moor, Oh Jungwan, Rolf de Heer, Makiko Watanabe and Alex C. Lo. Tokyo International Film Festival Later in the discussion, Lo returned to the status of Tokyo, suggesting the festival’s reputation was built upon two key operational traits: world-leading festival hospitality and an exceptionally attentive, intellectually curious audience that respects original storytelling. Looking ahead to the competition for the Tokyo Grand Prix, the jury also discussed how they would handle disagreements over the 15 films selected to compete. “It depends entirely on the very specific situation—how much disagreement, how divided is the jury,” said De Heer. “I don’t think there is an answer to that until we get to that point. As far as I understand it, I’m with four other very reasonable people, and I’m sure we can find a way through so that we don’t end up with some sort of lesser compromise film, but a really interesting film that maybe some of us don’t like.” Oh added jokingly that she was ready to fight De Heer over the selection. “Sometimes you want to fight for the film,” she added. “I had an experience where I fought for 7 hours with another jury! Every other jury member hated me. [laughter] But we are grownups and there are so many good films, so we will find a good way to compromise. I hope I don’t fight with him for 7 hours this time!” Elsewhere, Moor spoke of his delight at being invited to sit on the jury, especially given film colorists are often overlooked for such roles. “When I received the invitation I was very surprised, because [with] my job [as a colorist] it [is] quite rare to receive this kind of invitation. And for me… now I’m almost two years in Tokyo… for me it was a very great surprise, and also for people who do the same job as me, to be able to be a jury at a film festival.” Moor added, “For me, it’s like a little dream, and also maybe to try to show more of my job as a colorist—not only me, but people who do the same job as me.” De Heer, in his taciturn manner, also spoke about his future plans. Asked about his next film, the director said, “I don’t know… I am in-between, and I’m trying to make decisions about what to do.” He added, “This is another good reason why I enjoy being here, because it is a punctuation point. It’s not a very good answer for you, but it is the answer.” THR

articles.title: Tokyo: TIFFCOM Market Chief On Riding the Japanese IP Wave as Entertainment Landscape Shifts Due to AI
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Gavin J Blair Plus Icon Gavin J Blair View All October 26, 2026 9:51pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kaori Ikeda TIFFCOM As Tokyo International Film Festival has raised its game and its profile over recent years, its content market TIFFCOM has been carving out its own niche, bolstered by the attractiveness of Japanese IP. On top of attracting more exhibitors and visitors, the market has expanded its seminar offerings, landing bigger industry names to speak at them. In addition to the popularity of anime, the potential of manga and gameshow IP, and the success of Japan -related productions like Shōgun , interest in Japan itself is at an all-time high – nearly 43 million people visited last year. This concatenation of factors is delivering a boost to the fest and the market, acknowledges TIFFCOM managing director Kaori Ikeda. “It definitely is…Tokyo is probably one of the most fascinating cities in the world, and Japan is enjoying a boom. So definitely this supports our activities, because we are dealing with culture,” Ikeda tells The Hollywood Reporter as she and the TIFFCOM team were putting the final touches to preparations a few days before the market opens. Ikeda is in her third year as TIFFCOM managing director following a career with Japanese indie distributor Asmik Ace – where her acquisitions included Trainspotting and Dead Man Walking , “those kinds of good old ones” – a project with DreamWorks and five years at Japanese cable major J:COM. Among the initiatives she points to is the relaunch last year of Tokyo Story Market, which focused on book adaptation with Japanese publishing companies, as Tokyo IP Market: Adaptation & Remake, with a broader remit, this year bringing in remake-rights holders including film companies such as Toei and Shochiku, and toy company Takara Tomy. “This year Japan was the Country of Honour at the Cannes Marché du Film, which we collaborated with and took Tokyo IP Market there to introduce Japanese IP that could be adapted in various ways, into film, games or any other form,” says Ikeda, who emphasizes that it is being backed by major investment from the Japanese government and industry. Ikeda hails the Cannes venture a success that is likely to happen again, saying it brought together international producers and Japanese rights holders, and that she would like to include some smaller publishers which have limited experience in the global marketplace. TIFFCOM logged about 4,600 visitors and 300 exhibitors in 2025, up strongly from previous editions, and is on track to equal or exceed those figures this year. In line with the remake and co-production themes, the ‘Unlocking the Global Potential of Japanese IP’ session will feature producer Shinzo Matsuhashi ( Kokuhō , Kingdom ), Steven Maeda (Netflix’s One Piece ), and Amazon MGM Studios Japan head Buddy Marini. “And this year we are adding AI as a keynote. We have invited the executives from AGBO , Chris Brearton and Dominic Hughes for the Keynote: Technology and Storytelling, which we are very thrilled with,” adds Ikeda. The Association of Japanese Animations will again release its annual industry data at its TIFFCOM session, while TV stations will present case studies of overseas format sales. Another success story that Ikeda points to is the Tokyo Gap-Financing Market, now in its seventh year of linking partially funded projects with production partners. Two now completed productions from last year will be screened in this edition of the festival’s Crosscut Asia + section. Meanwhile, The Violinist , an animation which found an Italian partner at the 2023 event, took home the top award at Annecy this year, reports Ikeda proudly. All the while, the industry is shifting as are viewing habits. Short dramas are winning over audiences – not least in Japan – streamers recently seen as saviors are cutting budgets and AI is disrupting. “There are so many things happening in the market at the moment…So, we’re looking at how to be a better place for the industry to have business meetings and also to network,” adds Ikeda. TIFFCOM runs Oct. 28 to 30 at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center Hamamatsucho-kan. THR

articles.title: The “Sukiyaki” Phenomenon: The Song Behind the Tokyo Film Festival’s Opening Movie
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Gavin Blair Plus Icon Gavin Blair View All October 26, 2026 10:38pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Sukiyaki' Tokyo International Film Festival Opening the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival is Sukiyaki , Takahisa Zeze’s drama charting the backstory of the 1960s song that became a global hit and a symbol of Japan ’s recovery from postwar devastation and humiliation. Centered on composer and jazz pianist Hachidai Nakamura (Junichi Okada), the film tells of his partnership with lyricist Rokusuke Ei (Tori Matsuzaka), and how singer Kyu Sakamoto (Taiga Nakano) turned their combination of a jaunty melody and plaintive lyrics into an unlikely global pop culture phenomenon. Though the tale behind the tune was ripe for onscreen telling, the song’s legacy is perhaps even more remarkable. Related Stories Business Tokyo: TIFFCOM Market Chief On Riding the Japanese IP Wave as Entertainment Landscape Shifts Due to AI Movies Tokyo: Competition Jury Discusses Event's 'A-List' Status, Fighting Over Favorite Films An ill-fated recital left Nakamura struggling with debt and addiction as rockabilly eclipsed jazz. He was saved by forging an unlikely partnership with Ei, a radio writer who had never penned song lyrics, to write a rockabilly score for a 1959 movie from Toho (the company also distributing the 2026 film). In 1961, Nakamura and Ei wrote “ Ue o Muite Aruko “, which translates as ‘I look upwards as I walk,’ for which Nakamura incorporated traditional Japanese scales, jazz chords and U.S. pop influences. Ei’s melancholic lyrics were inspired by the failure of the mass Anpo protests to stop a Tokyo-Washington security treaty that maintained a huge American military presence in Japan, and the looking upwards in the song is to stop tears of sadness falling from his eyes. Singer Sakamoto was brought in on short notice for its premiere at Tokyo’s Sankei Hall on July 21, 1961 – only given the sheet music two hours beforehand. Unrehearsed, Sakamoto went into a minor key on an ad lib, sang the 4-beat song as an 8-beat, and came in a beat late, mimicking Japanese balladeers he had grown up listening to. These quirks added further layers to the song’s distinctiveness. Released as a single, it was the Music Life best domestic song from November 1961 to January 1962, selling 300,000 copies. Kyu Sakamoto on his global tour in 1963. Sjöberg Bildbyrå/ullstein bild via Getty Images It found its way overseas via Louis Benjamin of British label Pye Records visiting Japan in 1962 and falling for its catchy melody. He gave it to Kenny Ball and his Jazzmen to record an instrumental version titled “ Sukiyaki ,” which made the British top ten in February 1963. One story is that Benjamin came up with the name after eating sukiyaki, a hotpot dish, in Tokyo, while another version has Ball picking one of the only Japanese words he knew because he figured the original title was too difficult for listeners. After a U.S. release of Ball’s version, and another instrumental cover by Billy Vaughn, failed to make waves, Capitol US decided to gamble on the original Japanese version — but with the “Sukiyaki” title. It hit record stores on May 3, 1963 and in June topped the Billboard Hot 100 for three weeks. This made Sakamoto the only Japanese artist to ever have a U.S. No.1, and the song the first from Asia to do so. It would not be until BTS’s “Dynamite” in 2020 that another Asian artist would repeat that feat. The appeal of the infectious tune and Sakamoto’s whistling reached far beyond the U.S., with “Sukiyaki” topping rankings from Australia to Norway. The single eventually sold more than 13 million copies worldwide. As the Japanese public began to realize people around the world were whistling along to a song in their native tongue, Toshiba capitalized and reissued the single. The 1963 cover added “Sukiyaki” to the title, rendered in the katakana syllabary for foreign words, along with the packaging legend: “global hit!” Japan’s economy was by then registering double-digit growth as companies like Sony and Toyota were becoming global brands. The worldwide success of “Sukiyaki” was another source of pride for a national psyche still bruised by wartime defeat and occupation. International cover versions of “Sukiyaki” then came thick and fast, with dozens in Chinese languages alone, as well as interpretations in Spanish, German and French. Scores of Japanese artists have also covered the song. Among the U.S. fans of the 1963 release was a nine-year-old Janice-Marie Johnson, who later founded R&B and funk outfit A Taste of Honey. A few years after their No.1 hit Boogie Oogie Oogie , Johnson decided she wanted to do a version of “ Sukiyaki” and contacted lyricist Ei in Japan, who provided her with a rough English translation. She worked these into her own take on the song, but faced stiff opposition from her label and producer, who were convinced R&B audiences had no interest in Japanese-sounding music. Johnson’s persistence was justified when their “Sukiyaki” topped the Billboard R&B chart and reached number three on the Hot 100 in 1981. The band appeared alongside Sakamoto on Japanese TV. Johnson’s lyrics were used in hip-hop duo Doug E. Fresh & Slick Rick’s 1985 classic “ La Di Da Di .” On the evening of August 12, 1985 Sakamoto boarded Japan Air Lines flight 123 from Tokyo to Osaka. Twelve minutes after takeoff the Boeing 747 suffered catastrophic mechanical failure. The pilots managed to keep the plane in the air for around half an hour — enough time for many passengers to write messages to loved ones — before it crashed into a mountainside in central Japan, killing 520 of the 524 onboard, including Sakamoto. It remains the deadliest single-aircraft disaster in aviation history. Sakamoto’s song is played at the annual memorial service. “Sukiyaki” was revived as a symbol of melancholic hope in the wake of the 2011 earthquake, tsunami and nuclear disaster in Japan when it was sung by 71 celebrities in a television commercial. It was also featured in that year’s Ghibli movie From Up on Poppy Hill , leading to a reissue. Tokyo Ska Paradise Orchestra played it at the closing ceremony of the pandemic-delayed Tokyo Olympics in August 2021. Sukiyaki , the film, opens in Japan on Christmas Day, reuniting on screen the trio Sakamoto had said he wanted to bring back together just days before his death. From left: Director Takahisa Zeze, stars Jun’ichi Okada, Tôri Matsuzaka and Nana Seino attend the ‘Sukiyaki’ world premiere at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival . Tokyo International Film Festival THR

articles.title: ‘The One About Matthew Perry’ Review: Netflix’s Intimate and Sincere but Overly Padded Docuseries
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Daniel Fienberg Plus Icon Daniel Fienberg Chief Television Critic TheFienPrint Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 12:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Matthew Perry and Mia Perry Bowick. Netflix Logo text Perhaps it’s most helpful to begin a discussion of Netflix ‘s three-part The One About Matthew Perry with an acknowledgment of the things that it is not. Directed by Mary Robertson ( Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV ), The One About Matthew Perry is not a salacious documentary about Perry’s death and the subsequent criminal investigations. Peacock already did one of those, and if you skipped it, you’re better off. The One About Matthew Perry The Bottom Line A fine feature-length doc unnecessarily extended into a three-hour docuseries. Airdate: Tuesday, October 27 (Netflix) Director: Mary Robertson The One About Matthew Perry also isn’t a definitive celebration of the life and comic genius of Matthew Perry, as related by those who worked with him most closely. Related Stories Business Netflix Hires Former Apple Exec Steve Wilson to Lead Podcast Acquisitions Business Ted Sarandos Swoops Into Seoul as Netflix Celebrates 10 Years in Korea That is to say, it’s not a documentary designed to spawn “10 Fun Things We Learned From…” listicles and — despite the pandering title, with its borrowing of Friends episodic nomenclature — it’s only a documentary about Matthew Perry and his hit NBC sitcom insofar as you can’t tell Perry’s story without reciting nostalgic talking points about Friends . Even if it might be better if you could. Literally none of Perry’s Friends co-stars appear in the documentary — nope, not even Janice or Gunther — nor do any of the key creative forces from the show. Unless you count Warren Littlefield, NBC’s entertainment president at the time, as a creative force from the show. Otherwise, one writer from the first season (Jeff Strauss) is included, but nobody with a high enough profile is there to say anything that might be interpreted as sensational or sensationalistic. The same is roughly true of the rest of the A-listers whom Perry worked with over the years. Fools Rush In is represented by producer Doug Draizin, Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip (and Mr. Sunshine ) by Nate Torrence, The Whole Nine Yards by director Jonathan Lynn. I can’t say whether or not Robertson reached out to the various big names in Perry’s celebrity sphere, but it’s my instinct both that she did not and that none of them would have agreed to participate anyway. The bigger the names you get, the more the focus of the documentary becomes what Lisa Kudrow or David Schwimmer or Aaron Sorkin have to say about Matthew Perry, rather than Matthew Perry. Plus, the truth is that The One About Matthew Perry almost isn’t about Matthew Perry at all, which I don’t really mean as a criticism, though it will leave some viewers disappointed. Yes, it contains a lot of the biographical details and memorable clips that you expect from a documentary about Perry. But The One About Matthew Perry might have been better if it had skipped the basics entirely, because it treats that stuff in a manner that feels perfunctory rather than even remotely inspired. It surely would have been more sharply focused. What, then, is The One About Matthew Perry ? It’s a sincere, generally non-exploitative examination of addiction and celebrity — but not from Perry’s perspective, since Perry wrote a bestselling memoir that covered all of that. Instead, it’s about addiction and celebrity as viewed from slightly outside the celebrity bubble. If Robertson had been able to trim The One About Matthew Perry down to a 100-minute feature-length doc that didn’t find the basics so necessary to include, it probably would have been a better project. I’m not sure I learned anything at all about Perry here, but the documentary’s heart is with the people still struggling with what they did or didn’t know and what they could or couldn’t do when it came to Perry’s life and death. Sure, it would be flashier if Netflix could boast that it had reunited the surviving cast of Friends , but most of The One About Matthew Perry is recounted by people you don’t know, starting with Mia Perry Bowick, Perry’s younger sister. Matthew Perry was 14 when she was born, and she did much of her growing up with an already famous sibling. The latter fact adds poignancy to her decision to become a psychotherapist, inspired by watching Matthew’s decades of struggles. Her memories of learning about Matthew’s first rehab stint from a tabloid headline, or of the day of her brother’s death, are heartbreaking — and not the sort of thing that will get aggregated in entertainment news stories. That’s why they cut through. The same is true of the recollections shared by Roger Castillo and David Pressman, friends going back to Perry’s earliest days struggling as an actor in Hollywood. I don’t know if Robertson reached out to Hank Azaria, part of the same group that hung out at Formosa Cafe and in various cheap Hollywood apartments. But again, it’s savvier to present this chapter of Perry’s life without the distraction of big names. Perry dated plenty of famous women, but the ex-girlfriends featured in the documentary aren’t the Lizzy Caplans or the Julia Robertses, but rather the René Ashtons and the Romes — women who knew Perry intimately but can speak without added distraction. (Actually, this stuff is already close to distracting. Ashton, in particularly, gives the impression that she’s trying to add sizzle to a documentary that doesn’t need it, but I’m glad she and Perry had sex on a private plane.) Instead of offering viewers a line-up of flashy tributes, Robertson wants viewers to come away thinking of Tim Harrington, who met Perry in recovery and ended up living at Perry’s house for a year; or West Huddleston, who worked with Perry on drug court advocacy campaigns. The thing viewers are supposed to take away from The One About Matthew Perry isn’t really that it’s hard to become famous and discover that fame (and $7 million) can’t cure the pernicious demons of addiction, but that it’s hard to do everything you can for a person and love them as best you’re able and still not be able to do enough. It’s hard to watch and painful to listen to, but Robertson handles the documentary’s key moments with subtlety and intimacy. There’s so much good stuff in The One About Matthew Perry that it’s unfortunate how often it’s lost underneath so much less interesting stuff. With all the people telling Perry stories that have never been heard before, do we really need the talk-show footage of Perry telling stories he told repeatedly? Probably not. Does Littlefield add anything that he didn’t say in his own book and that hasn’t been said in various documentaries about Friends ? No. Are the general platitudes about Perry’s talent and why Friends was successful — courtesy of a single cultural critic — really necessary? Maybe in principle, because you don’t want to just approach Perry in terms of his tragic end. But there had to be better ways of approaching the familiar side of things. There’s an original and insightful feature-length documentary that could have been chiseled out from under all the generic padding here. You can’t have the former without the latter, apparently. THR

articles.title: Hilary Rosen Named BAFTA Chair
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 2:58am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Hilary Rosen Courtesy of BAFTA Hilary Rosen has been promoted to BAFTA chair, succeeding Sara Putt. Putt steps down after a three-year term, with her deputy stepping up to fill the role. Rosen will oversee BAFTA’s mission to champion film, games and television talent through its awards, industry leadership and year-round development programs. A BAFTA Television Committee member since 2021 and later its chair, Rosen helped shape the TV and Craft Awards and oversee their juries, according to the British film and TV academy. Outside of BAFTA, Rosen is director of commissioning at UKTV, leading its slate of original scripted and unscripted content. She’ll be supported by Ade Rawcliffe and Andrew Miller as deputy chairs of the Academy. They’ll both serve a two-year term. And after a thorough election process, the following have been appointed to the Board of Trustees: Charu Desodt and Caroline Levy are the new Chairs for BAFTA’s Games and Television Committees, while Nahrein Kemp will take up the role of LIT Committee Chair. Shrina Shah, chair of the governance and appointments committee, will join the BAFTA Board of Trustees. Rosen described the promotion as “a great privilege.” She continued: “I have long been passionate about everything BAFTA does to promote the screen arts and champion talent across the screen industries… I am delighted to be able to do this alongside our newly appointed committee chairs, Charu, Caroline and Nahrein and the rest of the BAFTA Board of Trustees. All are outstanding industry leaders, and with the collective passion and insight we share, I’m confident that this Board of Trustees will continue to build on the important and impactful work that has gone before.” THR

articles.title: HBO’s ‘Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone’ Casts James and Lily Potter, Charlie Weasley
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 5:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source (L-R) Hannah Chinn, Jasper Talbot, Harry Gilby Percy Walker-Smith/Harry Livingstone/Ruth Crafer Logo text Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone has found its James and Lily Potter. Jasper Talbot and Hannah Chinn will play the parents of the titular young wizard in HBO ‘s upcoming TV adaptation of J.K. Rowling’s bestsellers. Their infamous standoff with the Dark Lord sets in motion the events of the books. Harry Gilby ( Tolkien , The Last Kingdom ) has also joined the cast as Charlie Weasley, the second-eldest son of Arthur (Rafe Spall) and Molly Weasley (Katherine Parkinson). Related Stories Business Hilary Rosen Named BAFTA Chair Music The "Sukiyaki" Phenomenon: The Song Behind the Tokyo Film Festival's Opening Movie The series, arriving on our screens Dec. 25, stars Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger, Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley, John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagall, Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape and Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid. Supporting cast members include Rory Wilmot (Neville Longbottom), Lox Pratt (Draco Malfoy), Daniel Rigby (Vernon Dursley), Bel Powley (Petunia Dursley), Luke Thallon (Quirinus Quirrell), Warwick Davis (Filius Flitwick), and Beertie Carvel (Cornelius Fudge). Additions for the previously announced season two — Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets — include Game of Thrones star Kit Harington as Gilderoy Lockhart , Bonnie Hill as Ginny Weasley, Lenny Rush as Dobby, Billy Barratt as Tom Riddle, Molly Hewitt-Richards as Moaning Myrtle, and Jasper Ambrose as Colin Creevey. A logline for the first season reads: “There is nothing special about Harry Potter — or so his Aunt Petunia tells him. But when a mysterious letter of admission to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry arrives, it opens the door to a hidden world of magic, friendship and adventure. Yet behind Hogwarts’ enchanted walls lie dark secrets. Harry must find the courage to prove himself against the darkest wizard of all.” HBO’s Harry Potter is written and executive produced by Francesca Gardiner. Mark Mylod will executive produce and direct multiple episodes of the series for HBO in association with Brontë Film and TV and Warner Bros. Television. The series is executive produced by J.K. Rowling, Neil Blair, and Ruth Kenley-Letts of Brontë Film and TV, David Heyman of Heyday Films, Laura Neal, and Jon Brown. THR

articles.title: David Bowie Returns to Berlin With Immersive Event
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 5:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Bowie JTE Photo ©Blackout David Bowie is coming back to Berlin. Oscar-nominated documentary filmmaker Brett Morgen ( Moonage Daydream , On the Ropes ) will present the world premiere of Stage , his new immersive David Bowie concert experience, at the 2027 Berlinale . Morgen designed the immersive concert around original camera footage from Bowie’s 1978 Isolar II World Tour, which the director discovered while doing research for his 2022 documentary on Bowie, Moonage Daydream . The tour features Bowie performing material from Heroes , the landmark album he wrote and recorded while living in Berlin. Like Moonage Daydream , Stages was created with the cooperation of the David Bowie Estate. Bowie, a genre- and gender-bending icon of pop music , and one of biggest rock stars in history, died in 2016 , aged 69. Related Stories TV HBO's 'Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone' Casts James and Lily Potter, Charlie Weasley Business Hilary Rosen Named BAFTA Chair Stages features a three-screen presentation combining large-scale projections of the recovered and restored footage alongside transparent LED screens and a lighting design from Patrick Woodroffe, who has lit and designed tours for everyone from ABBA and The Police to Adele and Michael Jackson. He also lit Martin Scorsese’s Rolling Stones’ concert documentary Shine a Light , which opened the Berlinale in 2006. Paul Massey, the Academy Award-winning sound mixer of Bohemian Rhapsody (and 11-time Oscar nominee), created a special sound mix for Stages to give the audience the experience of being at the center of a live David Bowie concernt. Stages will have its world premiere at Berlin’s Uber Arena on Feb. 14, on the first weekend of the Berlinale. Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle called the event “a dream come true” for the festival. “The Berlinale is a place where cinema, art, and new forms of storytelling intersect,” she said. “To have this world premiere [of Stages ] in Berlin, a city so closely connected to David Bowie, makes the experience especially meaningful.” Morgen was Oscar-nominated for his 1999 boxing documentary On The Ropes and has directed several acclaimed docs, including Cobain: Montage of Heck (2015), on Kurt Cobain, the Emmy-winning Jane (2017) on the primatologist Jane Goodall, and The Kid Stays in the Picture (2002), on legendary Paramount producer Robert Evans. Morgen will attend the Berlinale and be a headline contributor to the European Film Market’s talks program. The 77 th Berlin International Film Festival runs Feb. 10-21, 2027. THR

articles.title: ‘Babel’: THR’s 2006 Review
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ray Bennett Plus Icon Ray Bennett View All October 27, 2026 6:16am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Brad Pitt in 2006's 'Babel.' Everett On Oct. 27, 2006, Paramount unveiled Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Babel in theaters following its premiere in competition at the Cannes Film Festival in May. The feature, starring Brad Pitt, Cate Blanchett and Gael Garcia Bernal, was nominated for seven Oscars at the 79th Academy Awards, including best picture. It walked away with one win, in the original score category. The Hollywood Reporter’s original review is below: Tense, relentless and difficult to watch at times, Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Babel is an emotionally shattering drama in which a simple act of kindness leads to events that pierce our veneer of civilization and bring on the white noise of terror. Iñárritu and screen writer Guillermo Arriaga involve six families, most of them not known to one another, in four countries on three continents in their story of random fate and the perils of being unable to communicate. Brad Pitt, Cate Blanchett and Gael Garcia Bernal give committed ensemble performances alongside seasoned character performers and nonactors as the story ranges from Morocco to San Diego to Tokyo. The film, which also features exceptional work by director of photography Rodrigo Prieto, production designer Brigitte Broch, editors Stephen Mirrione and Douglas Crise and composer Gustavo Santaolalla, is headed for major prizes and large, appreciative audiences. As with his previous films, Iñárritu tells his story using scenes out of order so that the pieces fall together in a jagged form that heightens the tension. It starts in the Moroccan desert, where a man buys a Winchester rifle from a neighbor to help keep the jackals away from his herd of goats. A Japanese hunter had gifted the neighbor with the rifle in gratitude for his work as a guide. The rifle is entrusted to the goat herder’s two young sons, who end up firing it from a mountainside at a coach filled with Western tourists just to see how far the bullet would go. The bullet, however, strikes an American named Susan (Blanchett) who is traveling with her husband Richard (Pitt) in attempt to patch up their marriage following the death of a child. Four hours from the nearest hospital, the coach takes a detour to a remote village, where a local man offers shelter while the other tourists argue over whether to stay or leave. Desperate, Richard phones the U.S. embassy pleading for help and also calls home in San Diego, where their longtime maid Amelia (Adriana Barraza) is caring for their other two children. With Susan bleeding and near death in the desert, he begs Amelia to remain with the kids as he tries to get help. Amelia’s son, however, is getting married across the border and, having exhausted attempts to find another sitter, she decides to take the kids with her to the wedding in a car driven by her friendly but hot headed nephew Santiago (Bernal). As Richard fights to keep Susan alive with the help of a wise and calm old Moroccan woman and a veterinarian, the shooting escalates into an international incident with security forces believing terrorists to be responsible and hunting for the perpetrators. Meanwhile, in Tokyo, a young deaf-mute woman named Chieko (Rinko Kikuchi) is grappling with the loss of her mother by suicide, fighting with her equally bereft father (Koji Yakusho) and trying to deal with the frustrations of adolescence. The filmmakers succeed brilliantly in weaving these stories together, taking time to explore depth of character and relationships. The suspense builds throughout as everyone involved becomes lost in a place they don’t understand with people they don’t know if they can trust. Several astonishing Tokyo sequences replicate what it might be like to be deaf-mute, and equal imagination is applied to scenes at night in the wasteland of the Mexico-California border and the barren mountains of Morocco. — Ray Bennett, originally published on May 24, 2006. THR

articles.title: The NFL’s Biggest Dramas This Season Are In the Broadcast Booth
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 7:07am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Troy Aikman is in the final year of his ESPN deal. Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images The NFL might be the undisputed king of TV content, but it is off-the-field drama that has dominated much of the conversation around the game this season so far. In particular, it was a widely reported altercation before the Los Angeles Rams-Buffalo Bills game at SoFi Stadium earlier this month … in the ESPN broadcast booth. To recap: ESPN’s lead play-by-play announcer Joe Buck signed a rich new contract with the company, but his longtime analyst partner Troy Aikman has not, resulting in reported bad blood between the boothmates. On-air, of course, viewers would have no clue (Buck and Aikman have continued to deliver a broadcast worthy of their decamillion dollar contracts), but the dispute has become fodder, and Aikman has not been willing to shy away from discussing it. The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback appeared on The Mike Fisher Show on Friday, where he was almost melancholy about what his future holds in media. “I never had any interest in going into television, it was just by happenstance that I even got into it,” Aikman said, recalling the outreach from Fox Sports . “I don’t know that if they hadn’t hired me, I would have gotten an opportunity anywhere else. And here I am, 25 years later, and now as I’m into my last year at ESPN, I’m realizing that this is something that could very well be taken away from me, and so for the first time, I’m realizing how much I really do, and I’ve always enjoyed it. “Until you risk having something taken away from you, I think sometimes you tend to maybe take things for granted,” he continued. “And so for the first time probably in my career, I’m realizing, you know, this is a great profession, it’s been a great ride for me, and I hope that it’s not over.” Joe Buck and Troy Aikman will also lead ESPN’s coverage of the Super Bowl this year. Julio Aguilar/Getty Images As the faces of Fox and ESPN’s NFL coverage, Aikman and Buck have been staples on Sundays (and more recently Mondays) for years. The looming end of that is ripping through sports, media and the league itself. And the situation comes as Disney is set to host its first Super Bowl since 2006, with Buck and Aikman set to lead the game from the booth (they have also been a big part of its marketing). But with their rich deals, nothing can be assured, and in the TV business, any opportunity to get a better deal or sign talent that could make a difference is typically taken fast. At a conference room in the InterContinental Barclay Hotel in Midtown Manhattan last week, NFL executive VP and chief media officer Hans Schroeder was asked about the Buck-Aikman-ESPN impasse. Schroeder, who is responsible for managing the league’s relationships with its media partners, said that it had “no concern” with the situation. “I don’t know if you watched the game on Monday night. It was an incredible game. An incredible game, and incredible coverage by Joe and Troy, just like they always do,” Schroeder told assembled journalists in the room, adding that the league was proud of Disney’s coverage, including its numerous altcasts with the Manning brothers, Pat McAfee and Star Wars , and with all the effort going into next year’s Super Bowl. “I think the fans are deserving of first-class game production, which Joe and Troy have — I think going back to ’02 or something was their first year — a history of doing that as well as anyone, and I think you’ll continue to see them do that as well as anyone.” Suffice it to say, it is not the story that the league or Disney want to be talking about right now. And yet, the ESPN broadcast booth drama underscores what has been perhaps the most tumultuous and uncertain year ever for NFL broadcasters. At CBS, Tony Romo’s preseason arrest for operating a vehicle while intoxicated (OWI) led to his eventual ouster from the network’s broadcast booth. His replacement, JJ Watt, was named the permanent successor last week when he was given a multiyear contract extension, with Skydance Sports chief David Berson praising him as “insightful, entertaining, passionate, meticulous in his preparation, and the ultimate teammate.” Greg Olsen is in the final year of his deal at Fox, and is looking for a new home, while current NFL names like Travis Kelce and Sean McVay have bubbled up as potential TV talent in chats with agents and network execs. A senior NFL source told THR that the league doesn’t micromanage the personnel decisions of its broadcast partners, and that it isn’t involved in the calls being made when it comes to talent. But that doesn’t mean the league doesn’t have any say. Sources at both the league and its rights partners paint the conversation around broadcasting as an ongoing conversation, with the league always interested in improving coverage of the game. More precisely, the league’s NFL deals require a quality of production from its partners that includes an A-team broadcast booth that can deliver a broadcast worthy of the league and its viewers (“first-class production,” as Schroeder said). It might be a mushy benchmark, but it does mean that more out there ideas like the Manningcast, the McAfeecase or animated altcasts remain secondary considerations, and that the main booth needs to have seasoned or otherwise A-list talent (like Tom Brady, who made his broadcast booth debut for Fox). The drama matters, because the NFL matters. While no real fans will turn off their NFL games because of some broadcast booth drama, the entire situation is a rare speed bump for what is otherwise the most reliable bet in all of TV. And yet: The broadcast booths may change, but there’s no reason to think that the NFL will ever become less relevant, or less watched. THR

articles.title: Susan Saint James, ‘Name of the Game,’ ‘McMillan & Wife’ and ‘Kate & Allie’ Star, Dies at 80
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 7:11am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Susan Saint James Susan Saint James Susan Saint James, the Emmy-winning actress who delighted TV viewers with her light-hearted turns on The Name of the Game , McMillan & Wife and Kate & Allie before quitting at the peak of her powers, has died. She was 80. Saint James died Monday of pancreatic cancer, her family announced. Survivors include her third husband, Dick Ebersol, the former Saturday Night Live executive producer and head of NBC Sports whom she married in November 1981. The couple soldiered on after losing their youngest child, 14-year-old son Teddy, in a 2004 plane crash. Related Stories Movies Hubert de la Bouillerie, 'Woodstock' and 'Witches of Eastwick' Film Editor, Dies at 75 TV Alan Dysert, 'All My Children' Actor, Dies at 75 Saint James was someone who was “generous with her time and energy, which she valued more than money, and instinctively drawn to whoever needed lifting up,” her family said. “She taught her children to pause, be kind and look out for other people.” On the big screen, she went on the run with Peter Fonda in Outlaw Blues (1977); played the lustful target of Dracula in Love at First Bite (1979), starring George Hamilton; executed a heist with fellow suburbanites Jessica Lange and Jane Curtin in How to Beat the High Cost of Living (1980); and portrayed George Segal ’s wife in Carbon Copy (1981). A contract player at Universal, Saint James portrayed the frequently kidnapped editorial assistant Peggy Maxwell for three seasons (1968-71) on the stylish 90-minute NBC drama The Name of the Game . ( THR took a look back at the series in 2018). Peggy worked at Howard Publications for all three of the rotating characters on the “wheel” series — Tony Franciosa as hotshot reporter Jeff Dillon, Gene Barry as kingly publisher Glenn Howard and Robert Stack as FBI agent turned magazine editor Dan Farrell. Six months after The Name of the Game ’s final episode, Saint James was back on another 90-minute wheel series, McMillan & Wife , which began in rotation with Columbo and McCloud as part of the NBC Mystery Movie franchise. Like Peggy, Saint James’ Sally McMillan also got into trouble and helped solve crimes, here with her husband, San Francisco police commissioner Stewart “Mac” McMillan ( Rock Hudson ). She appeared on the show for five seasons through 1976, when she left in a contract dispute (Hudson stuck around the final sixth season). Saint James returned to series television in 1984 by reuniting with Curtin for the CBS sitcom Kate & Allie . On that show, two childhoods friends now divorced — Saint James’ free-spirited Kate McArdle and Curtin’s more by-the-books Allie Lowell — raise their kids (three in all) in a Greenwich Village brownstone they share. When Kate & Allie was canceled in 1989 after the sixth season — it was nominated three times for the Emmy for outstanding comedy series — Saint James decided to pretty much shut down her acting career. She told People magazine in 2002 that she was tired of being “one of those people juggling knives and melons and then [saying], ‘Toss me in a razor blade.’” Saint James received an Emmy in 1969 for her work in the first season of The Name of the Game , then added noms in 1970 and ’71. She also was nominated for McMillan & Wif e in 1972, ’73 and ’75 and for Kate & Allie in 1984 and ’85. Susan Saint James (right) and Jane Curtin on a 1984 episode of ‘Kate & Allie.’ Courtesy Everett Collection One of four kids, Susan Jane Miller was born in Los Angeles on Aug. 14, 1946. She and her family moved in 1958 to Rockford, Illinois, after her father, Charles, was named president of The Testor Corp., maker of tools and accessories for model kits, and the Hobby Industry Association of America. Her mother, Constance, was a schoolteacher. Saint James attended the Woodlands Academy of the Sacred Heart for high school and lived and modeled in France for about three years. Inspired by Paula Prentiss, she moved back to California to try acting when she was 20 — she lived at the Hollywood Studio Club — and quickly scored a part alongside Franciosa in the 1966 NBC/Universal TV movie Fame Is the Name of the Game . Directed by Stuart Rosenberg, who would soon helm Cool Hand Luke , it served as the pilot for The Name of the Game . Created by Jennings Lang, the series sported a budget of $400,000 an episode, the largest of its day (Universal’s Black Tower stood in for Howard Publications headquarters). It was canceled after its third season, during which the temperamental Franciosa was fired. In 1967, Saint James appeared in a failed pilot for a crime show called Ready and Willing that starred Jack Weston and Joe Flynn and in the George Peppard feature P.J. A year later, she showed up on the pilot episode of ABC’s It Takes a Thief , starring Robert Wagner, leading to a recurring role as the crook/love interest Charlene “Charlie” Brown. She also made three other films at Universal that were released in 1968: Jigsaw , starring Bradford Dillman ; What’s So Bad About Feeling Good? , starring Peppard and Mary Tyler Moore ; and the sequel Where Angels Go … Trouble Follows! , starring Rosalind Russell. When McMillan & Wife , created by Leonard Stern, bowed in September 1971, Saint James had just turned 25 while Hudson was closing in on 46. In a 1971 interview with Bobbie Wygant, Saint James described Sally McMillan, the daughter of a cop, as “Peggy Maxwell grown up.” “She’s still just as nutty and just as goofy, but she’s married to Rock Hudson, and they live a very sophisticated life, they have a very nice house,” she continued. “She can’t get anything done, she doesn’t do anything right, she gets him involved in all her terrible happenings. It’s kind of a comedy mystery.” Susan Saint James and Rock Hudson, stars of ‘McMillan & Wife.’ Courtesy Everett Collection At the start of the final season, Sally is killed in a plane crash with her and Mac’s never-seen son. Saint James moved to Connecticut in 1983 to star in Kate & Allie , which taped in New York City. The sitcom, created by Sherry Coben , debuted in March 1984 as a six-episode midseason replacement series but was quickly renewed for a full season in the fall. She and Curtin went head to head for outstanding lead actress in a comedy series at the Emmys in 1984 and ’85, with the former SNL star winning both times. As The New York Times wrote in 2007, “Jane Curtin’s Allie, the ex-wife of a cheating Connecticut doctor, is truly miserable, and so the better character.” When the sitcom ended after 122 episodes in March 1989, Saint James was 43 and would soon become pregnant with Teddy. She didn’t quit acting entirely, appearing on episodes of The Drew Carey Show , Law & Order: SVU , Suits and Upload and onstage in Connecticut in The Miracle Worker , but she focused on being an active volunteer with the Special Olympics and launching a business selling baby-gift baskets. Saint James, who had dated rocker Stephen Stills in the late ’70s, got together with Ebersol when she was about to host Saturday Night Live in October 1981. “She comes to New York, we met on a Sunday, I was in love with her by Monday, we were living together in a hotel by Tuesday, and she did the show on Saturday,” Ebersol said in a 2009 interview . “We were married six weeks later.” After she hosted, Ebersol took her out to dinner that night, and their photograph while kissing soon appeared in The New York Daily News with the headline, “When Dick Ebersol Books a Host, He Doesn’t Fool Around … On Second Thought, He Does.” When Kate & Allie became a hit, Ebersol left Saturday Night Live in April 1985 to raise the kids. On Nov. 28, 2004, a private plane carrying Ebersol and he and Saint James’ sons Charlie and Teddy crashed in snow and fog during an attempted takeoff from Montrose Regional Airport in Colorado (the Ebersoles owned a home in nearby Telluride). Charlie pulled his injured dad through a hole in the middle of the plane, but Teddy was killed — his body was discovered underneath the wreckage 24 hours later — as was the pilot and steward. Less than three weeks after the crash, Saint James recorded an interview with Tim Russert for the Today show to thank those who had reached out to her and her family. “If you know anybody that loses somebody, call them on the phone,” she said. “People always say, ‘I know you don’t want to be bothered.’ You can’t be bothered enough. It’s just fantastic, and I just want them to know that.” Her family on Tuesday called what she did in the immediate aftermath of Teddy’s death her “defining act … she delivered his eulogy as a note to each of her other children and her husband, giving them words to heal. Even in the deepest grief of her life, she put everyone else first.” In addition to her husband and Charlie, survivors include another son, William, whom she also had with Ebersol; her son and daughter, Harmony and Sunshine, whom she had with her second husband, makeup artist (and manager) Tom Lucas; her sister, Mercedes; a niece, actress Christa Miller ( Shrinking ); seven grandkids; and her beloved service dog, Lola. Her first husband was screenwriter Richard Neubert; they were married from 1967-68. “She never met a stranger,” her family noted. “Every person she met became the most important person in the room at that moment, from a fellow board member to the clerk at the shoe store, who usually walked away knowing her entire life story.” THR

Maas’s Latest Book 2 days ago Hudson Williams Returns to Screens in Supernatural Thriller ‘Yaga’: How to Watch the New Series Online 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Susan Saint James , the Emmy-winning actress who starred opposite Rock Hudson in “McMillan & Wife” and Jane Curtin in the CBS sitcom “Kate & Allie,” died Monday after being diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. She was 80. Her death was confirmed to People by a representative. In a statement shared with the magazine, Saint James’s family described her as someone “generous with her time and energy, which she valued more than money, and instinctively drawn to whoever needed lifting up. She taught her children to pause, be kind and look out for other people.” Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart “She never met a stranger,” the statement continues. “Every person she met became the most important person in the room at that moment, from a fellow board member to the clerk at the shoe store, who usually walked away knowing her entire life story.” “Her defining act: weeks after losing her youngest son, Teddy, in the November 28, 2004 plane crash, she delivered his eulogy as a note to each of her other children and her husband, giving them words to heal,” the statement concludes. “Even in the deepest grief of her life, she put everyone else first. Days after the crash she sat with Tim Russert to thank the people who had reached out and to tell them the family was okay.” Saint James became a television fixture in the late 1960s with NBC’s “The Name of the Game,” an anthology drama in which she played research assistant Peggy Maxwell. The role earned her three Emmy nominations, including a win for supporting actress in a drama series in 1969. She went on to star alongside Hudon in “McMillan & Wife,” playing Sally McMillan, the wife of a San Francisco police commissioner, from 1971 to 1976. Her performance earned her three additional Emmy nominations. In 1984, Saint James returned to series television in “Kate & Allie,” starring alongside Curtin as two divorced mothers who decide to raise their children together in a Manhattan apartment. The sitcom ran for six seasons on CBS, earning Saint James two more Emmy nominations. Her film credits include “Outlaw Blues” (1977), the vampire comedy “Love at First Bite” (1979) and “How to Beat the High Cost of Living” (1980). Born Susan Jane Miller in Los Angeles on Aug. 14, 1946, Saint James grew up in Rockford, Ill., before pursuing modeling and acting. She largely retired from Hollywood following the conclusion of “Kate & Allie” in 1989, though she made occasional television appearances, including on “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” and “Suits.” Outside acting, she was a longtime advocate for the Special Olympics. She received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2008. She is survived by her husband, former NBC executive Dick Ebersol, four children and seven grandchildren.
