articles.title: Errol Morris Is Sitting on a Secret Elizabeth Holmes Interview (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Larry Busacca/Getty “I have this problem ,” shares Errol Morris , the Oscar-winning documentary filmmaker behind “The Thin Blue Line,” “The Fog of War” and countless other renowned docs. You see, the 78-year-old can’t seem to screen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s docu-phenomenon on Elizabeth Holmes , “You Can See Everything.” He claims to have contacted the appropriate parties but has thus far been rebuffed. “Can you get me a screener?” he pleads. (I cannot.) Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart What Morris did do, however, was finally watch Alex Gibney’s 2019 documentary on Holmes and her sham blood-testing company Theranos — “The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley” — for the very first time. Morris, who’s directed “probably 1,000” commercials for various companies, was hired by Holmes in 2015 to shoot a series of ads for Theranos that depicted the “founder” staring wide-eyed into the camera that have attracted criticism for contributing to her mythmaking . Morris says he doesn’t know how Gibney got ahold of extra footage from the ads to use in “The Inventor,” but that’s not all: Morris exclusively revealed to Variety that he actually conducted a two-hour Interrotron interview with Holmes that he’s contemplating releasing in light of the renewed interest around the infamous grifter. So, I understand you have not seen “You Can See Everything,” but recently watched Alex Gibney’s documentary on Elizabeth Holmes, “The Inventor,” for the very first time. I never really wanted to see it until recently for a variety of different reasons, and I was quite surprised to find out that I was in it. He used outtakes from your Theranos ads, right? Well, what’s really not known about any of this is, yes, I did all the advertising for Theranos, but I did it at a time when Elizabeth Holmes was on the front cover of Forbes and many other magazines. She was riding high, and this was before everything collapsed. Did I have any reason to believe that she was a fraud? I did not. Did that change as time went on? It did. I had tried very hard, over a number of years, to do a documentary on Elizabeth Holmes and it would have happened except that she was under indictment. There was massive litigation going on. You wanted to interview Holmes for a documentary? I asked her, at a certain point, if I could film an interview with her — and this is at the height of her success — and I did film a two-hour interview with her, which is not very well-known if it is known at all. And I just watched that. I am sincerely interested in putting that out as an unedited film. You should. If anything, it gives you a comparison of Elizabeth before and Elizabeth after , which I think is interesting in and of itself. I noticed that the Gibney film begins and ends with my interview with Elizabeth Holmes. This two-hour interview you conducted with Holmes has not been seen by anyone other than yourself? Well, myself and the people in my office, but yes, for all intents and purposes, it has not been seen by anyone. Let me ask you a fast question: Why do you think [“ You Can See Everything ”] has proven so popular? I think it touches on a lot of different things that fascinate the culture — grifters, self-delusion to the point where the person created a persona that incorporated a fake Yoda voice, true crime and Silicon Valley megalomania channeled through the prism of Nathan Fielder’s brand of awkward comedy that pits, to borrow from John Ganz, a neurotic against a psychotic. Well, it’s hard for me to tell you about the film having not yet seen it, but I can tell you what I think about Elizabeth Holmes having spent a considerable amount of time with her. I was interviewed by John Carreyrou recently for an article that subsequently appeared in The New York Times, and he was questioning me about something I’d said to him many, many years ago when I was considering making a documentary about Elizabeth Holmes and had asked him if he would participate in that documentary. Some people see these stories as an on/off switch of she’s innocent or she’s guilty, she’s lying or she’s telling the truth. And when you’re investigating a crime, part of that investigation has to be if the person is guilty or innocent, since the criminal justice system works in such a way that you are looking for some kind of result. But what interests me is: To what extent was she self-deceived? To what extent did she believe in her own bullshit? Carreyrou understandably wants to tell you that she knowingly committed fraud, is guilty, should have been convicted and is in prison, as she should be. I keep wondering about the psychology of self-deception because part of me believes that she believes in Theranos and that she could achieve the results as promised. Aren’t there, say, serial killers who are convinced that what they’re doing is right and just? And isn’t it more about the people you hurt along the way? Yes, it is. You could say that lots of people in Silicon Valley misrepresent or out-and-out lie about what their technology can achieve, but in this case it involved medical results and people whose lives are directly affected by those medical results, and that in itself makes it different. One example of a lie would be that she’d claimed Theranos had a Department of Defense contract and its blood-testing technology was being deployed on the battlefield, none of which was true. Now, we can get into a philosophical discussion of the nature of lying and what is a lie, and did she lie in a very clear sense? Yes. Many, many times. Did she see them as lies? That is of interest to me. I want to ask you about something you’d said during a Reddit Q&A after Holmes’ house of cards collapsed: “When everything fell apart, I was shocked because I believed in Elizabeth Holmes. I feel, rightly or wrongly, that most of the television programs and movies about her have missed the mark. Did she do bad things? Most assuredly. The question remains, why?” You then drew a comparison between her and Joan of Arc. Probably the Robert Bresson “Joan of Arc,” which is one of my very favorite films. But Elizabeth Holmes wasn’t burned at the stake. She’s serving some time in prison for defrauding people. The nature of her punishment is not similar to being burned at the stake, and if you thought that’s what I meant by it, I did not. You were drawing that comparison in regard to their self-deception. One thing I can say about Joan of Arc: Do I think that God was speaking to her? I have a confession to make: I don’t believe in God. Do I think that God exists? No, I don’t! Do I think that God was directly communicating with Joan of Arc? I don’t! Do I think she thought that God was directly communicating with her? She did! She went to the stake on the basis of it. That’s your comparison. Going back to those Theranos promos you shot with her— —Don’t call them promos! I was hired as a commercial director, and I’ve shot probably 1,000 commercials. In the Gibney documentary, it is mentioned that Elizabeth Holmes and Patrick O’Neill, who was her CCO, had hired me because of the many Apple commercials I’d directed for Steve Jobs. If I had known how much of my interview was being used [by Gibney], or even if it was being used at all, I’m not sure what I would have said. I knew it was being used, but I never really wanted to watch [“The Inventor”]. Maybe I’d just had enough of it. How did Gibney get ahold of the footage? This I do not know. I really don’t know. And I’m not being coy or cagey. I do not know. I know the commercials you shot for Holmes and Theranos have garnered quite a bit of criticism for contributing to her mystique, but I found Holmes quite creepy in those commercials. How do you feel about people’s perception of those commercials? People have never seen my long interview that I did with Elizabeth Holmes. I’ve heard that I have been accused of representing a fraud — knowingly — and this is just not true. I’ll join a lot of other people who were on the Theranos board at the time that I was doing this series of commercials. Are you sure you want to join Henry Kissinger? I’m joking. I actually interviewed Henry Kissinger just before he died. Is that going to go anywhere? It might. I have so much stuff that I do nothing with. I’d heard a very funny story about how BP approached you to direct an ad for them following the Deepwater Horizon oil spill and that you proposed a wild idea that they turned down. I believe that’s true! And what was that idea? You tell me and I’ll tell you if it’s real! That Mel Gibson would be standing on a BP oil platform and say something to the effect of, “If anyone knows about a public relations disaster, it’s me.” That’s it! And of course, they said no. Fortunately, enough people have said yes over the years, but I can’t tell you how many people have said no. I once said to my producer for commercials, “You know, I get all these commercials, but I’ve never gotten diarrhea or erectile dysfunction commercials. What’s wrong with me?” I once got a Depend commercial, and my ideas for incontinence/Depend commercials were by and large rejected. What was one of those ideas that you really liked? Thank you for asking. I had just done a long interview with Janis Karpinski, who’d just been demoted in connection with Abu Ghraib — and this interview has never seen the light of day — so there’s this lady general inside a tank in a war zone. Shells are exploding all around. The tank is on maneuvers. We see the face of the lady general inside the tank. She has an enormously pinched expression. She is fidgety, edgy. And then, you hear the sound of running water, and the expression on her face changes to one of total relaxation and pleasure. And then we cut outside and we see the artillery exploding. Depend . That is hilarious. The guy who was producing the commercials to Depend put his face two inches away from mine and said, “THERE IS NOTHING, NOTHING FUNNY ABOUT INCONTINENCE!” And I said, “I guess I beg to differ.” I’m with you on that one. By the way, why did your two-hour Elizabeth Holmes interview never come out? Because the company fell apart and she was prosecuted… but I can’t really answer it. The clearest answer is that I’d moved on. But now I feel pretty strongly that this is an interesting document — not because I’m trying to prove something about Elizabeth Holmes, but it does provide some kind of evidence of what she was like when everything was going her way. And what is your takeaway after watching the interview? That she was a true believer. Loading comments... articles.title: ‘Every Contact Leaves a Trace’ Director on Why She Hired a Detective: ‘I’m Trying to Reconstruct a Life Story’
articles.full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:03am PT ‘Every Contact Leaves a Trace’ Director on Why She Hired a Detective: ‘I’m Trying to Reconstruct a Life Story’ By Will Tizard Plus Icon Will Tizard Contributor @willtizard1 Latest ‘Third Land’ Director on the Risks of Chronicling the Lives of Iranian Refugees in Turkey: It Was ‘Extremely Tense and Frightening’ 2 hours ago Latvian Filmmaker Who Witnessed Last Days of the Soviet Union Portrayed in ‘Podnieks on Podnieks’ 12 months ago Albania’s Soviet-Tinged Propaganda Archives Reveal a Passion for the Cinematic, says Docmaker Roland Sejko 12 months ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "Every Contact Leaves a Trace" (Courtesy of Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival) U.S. artist and documentarian Lynne Sachs has often screened her past films at Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival , but she’s finally made it in person this year, serving on the First Lights jury, which evaluates docu debuts. Sachs says she’s been impressed by Ji.hlava films that span the globe while showcasing the full range of filmmaking approaches and perspectives. “There are about 24 movies to see. It’s kind of revelatory. Already I’ve seen two films here, one from Argentina and one from Congo and they really couldn’t be more different. They make you think about the documentary paradigm.” Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart A case in point, she says: “Positionality.” Whose perspective is an audience seeing and is the filmmaker’s role visible or even known? It’s something Sachs has made crystal clear in her newest film, “Every Contact Leaves a Trace,” screening at Ji.hlava in its Czech premiere. Sachs herself is clearly onscreen, investigating, making connections, doubting herself, and occasionally seeking help from a youthful niece and nephew as she goes through old business cards, some decades old, wondering at who gave them to her and what traces of lives contacting hers can still remain. The film is a kind of detective story that eventually enlists the actual analyses of forensic investigators as Sachs follows leads to track down people whose names remain in her box of hundreds of carefully preserved business cards – a good number she admits have lost all meaning to her. “I actually hired a detective at one point,” she confesses. Some left burning impressions on her and she has always wondered what became of the card giver – such as an artist whose work touched her years ago or a fellow artist filmmaker who was later canceled over allegations of impropriety. One card was from a Syrian woman whose family discouraged her from sitting for an on camera to share her experiences as a refugee – so Sachs settles for filming a tribute to the woman’s cooking skills. Sachs says she is also uneasy about terms that have come into common use for people in docus. Rather than say “protagonists” or “characters,” she much prefers “on camera participants.” Or maybe “visible collaborators who are the people in front of the camera.” “We’re offered the chance to tell our story by the person behind the camera. What I don’t know is, who is the person behind the camera?” In the case of “Every Contact,” it’s clear to all who is filming and inquiring as Sachs visibly, sometimes awkwardly, tracks down people who once met her but certainly never expected her to appear again at their doorstep with a camera. It’s a role she has not always put onscreen so clearly, she says. “I’m trying to reconstruct a life story of life experience from the interactions I’ve had with people…people who left a mark.” Since the film came out, Sachs says, people have offered her their own collections of old business cards. “I say, ‘Oh, no!’ This combination of cards only goes back to one person. You’re the person who had that dentist. You’re the person who met that psychoanalyst. Or potential friend on a bus.” As Sachs investigation progressed, she says, “I was most drawn to the cards that presented the biggest obstacles.” Some card donors may be impossible to find now. And others presented a different challenge: At times figures from your past have made lasting impressions – but that doesn’t always mean that was mutual. The process of recounting past encounters is one fraught with traps, says Sachs, as human minds tend to re-enact them in the mind, often editing, sometimes finding specific moments deeply burned in. As Sachs enlists the help of family on her quest, one suggests that it’s not usually even up to us to choose which memories will stay with us and which we’ll lose. Sachs discovered through her docu detective work that sometimes she did not need to fly across time zones to track down someone she once knew who might not even remember her or feel they shared an important interaction, she says. “I don’t need to prove I did or didn’t,” says Sachs. “I need to deal with the residue.” Jennifer Coolidge to Return for ‘The Watcher’ Season 2 ‘Decision to Leave’ Cinematographer Kim Ji-yong on Chasing Natural Light for Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’: ‘This Is the One Where We Worried, Debated and Planned the Most’ CAA’s Roeg Sutherland Says It’s Too Soon to Predict Fallout From Netflix Firings, Thinks Recent Mergers Represent ‘Opportunity’ for Industry Netflix Says 67% of Surveyed Members Want to Visit Korea as Busan’s Creative Asia Puts Locations in Focus How Netflix’s Messy Transition Will Rock Hollywood: Looking at You, NBCU ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ ‘Squid Game’ Stars Fete Netflix’s Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases ‘Tantara,’ ‘All of Us Are Dead’ Season 2 Loading comments...

articles.title: Billy Bob Thornton Examines Mayflower Voyage in Fox Nation Documentary Series
articles.full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:30am PT Billy Bob Thornton Examines Mayflower Voyage in Fox Nation Documentary Series By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Netflix Grapples With Digital-Ad Squeeze Amid Widening Glut of Streaming Commercials 21 minutes ago Billy Bob Thornton Examines Mayflower Voyage in Fox Nation Documentary Series 31 minutes ago Lisa Ling Signs With CAA 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Emerson Miller/Paramount+ Actor Billy Bob Thornton will host and executive produce “Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower,”a three-part docudrama series that will stream on Fox Nation and examine the voyage of the Mayflower. The series will debut on November 23, just ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday its subject helped spur. “Billy Bob Thornton is a captivating storyteller with a unique ability to bring history to life. ‘The Mayflower ‘offers a fresh and thought-provoking perspective on one of the most familiar chapters in American history, giving viewers a richer understanding of the people, conflicts and events that shaped our nation’s beginnings,” said Lauren Petterson, president of Fox Nation, in a statement. The series traces the Pilgrims’ Atlantic crossing aboard the Mayflower, the alliance forged between English settlers and the Wampanoag people, and the conflict that ultimately pushed what were once colonies of Britain toward forming an an American identity. Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart The team developing the series consulted a range of historical resources and experts, including historians at Plimoth Patuxet Museums, where portions of the series were filmed, as well as acclaimed historian Nathaniel Philbrick, author of “Mayflower: A Story of Courage, Community, and War.” ,“The voyage of the Mayflower set into motion what would become the United States. Kudos to Billy Bob Thornton for helping to bring this vital story from America’s past to life,” said Philbrick in a prepared statement. Thornton joins a growing list of top creatives who have done work for Fox Nation , including Martin Scorsese, Kevin Costner and Kelsey Grammer. Thornton currently stars in the Paramount+ series “Landman,” and has appeared in films including “Bad Santa,” “The Alamo,” “Bandits” and “Monster’s Ball.” He wrote the script for, directed and starred in the film “Sling Blade.” The series is produced by AIRtime Projects and Terminal B, TV with executive producers Billy Bob Thornton, Geyer Kosinski, Tom Forman, David Metzler, Jordan Rosenblum and showrunner and executive producer John Ealer. articles.title: Christina Applegate Tells MS Community ‘I’m Still Your Warrior’ After Being Misdiagnosed: ‘I’m Going to Speak Out on Your Behalf Forever’
articles.full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:31am PT Christina Applegate Tells MS Community ‘I’m Still Your Warrior’ After Being Misdiagnosed: ‘I’m Going to Speak Out on Your Behalf Forever’ By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest Christina Applegate Tells MS Community ‘I’m Still Your Warrior’ After Being Misdiagnosed: ‘I’m Going to Speak Out on Your Behalf Forever’ 30 minutes ago ‘Call of Duty’ Movie Will Be About the ‘Cost of War and Having to Be a Warrior,’ Says Director: ‘These Are Not Comic Books or Cartoon Characters’ 17 hours ago Robert Pattinson Praises Steven Soderbergh for Stepping in to Finish ‘Batman 2’ Filming for Matt Reeves: ‘Completely Selfless’ 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Gilbert Flores/Variety Christina Applegate returned to the “MeSsy” podcast one week after revealing she was misdiagnosed with MS to tell listeners that she will never stop advocating and fighting for those impacted by the disease, even if she does not have it herself. The Emmy winner said people in the MS community are still “my people.” “Even though I don’t have this disease, I’ve fallen in love with everyone that we know, our listeners, our friends that have MS,” Applegate said to podcast co-host on the show Jamie-Lynn Sigler, who was diagnosed with MS in 2001 (via Entertainment Weekly ). “I’m still your warrior, and I’m still going to speak out on your behalf forever and ever. Despite not having MS. I still feel like part of this community. No matter what, I love you.” Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Applegate originally revealed she had been diagnosed with MS in 2021, and retired from acting after the finale of her hit series “Dead to Me” the next year. She then become a fierce advocate for people with the disease — which causes damage to the central nervous system — and co-founded the “MeSsy” podcast as a way to share her experience and spread awareness. On the latest episode, Applegate continued to share the symptoms she faces of a now un-diagnosed illness, explaining: “I actually timed it today, it took me 10 minutes to be able to move off my pillow and get out of the bed and stand up, at which point I almost couldn’t walk to the bathroom, and now a walker is sitting next to my bed because of what’s going on. I don’t know what’s going on. This is what I’m still living with, and I never had that before. I was able to sit up and stuff.” After taking a seven-month break from the podcast, Applegate returned to the program on Oct. 21 and broke down in tears while telling listeners that new technology led to the discovery that she was misdiagnosed with MS . “This may come as great news, but to me, I’m back at square one,” Applegate said. “It’s hard to say that [my doctor] came into my room and she said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS.’ You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I’m better. I haven’t gotten better … If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways. So I’m back at square one, that I don’t know what’s going on with me.” Applegate added that “it’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down” after becoming such a big advocate for the MS community. She said that she’s still in a “state of shock,” adding: “It’s a mindfuck, for sure.” Listen to the latest episode of the “MeSsy” podcast in the video below. ‘Hatchet’ Movie: Netflix and Derek Cianfrance to Adapt Gary Paulsen’s Survival Book (EXCLUSIVE) How Netflix’s Messy Transition Will Rock Hollywood: Looking at You, NBCU Netflix Sets Release Date for Rob Lowe Documentary ‘The Outsider’ ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ ‘Squid Game’ Stars Fete Netflix’s Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases ‘Tantara,’ ‘All of Us Are Dead’ Season 2 Box Office: ‘La Bola Negra’ Scores $277,500 From Four Theaters as Netflix Reports Grosses for First Time Ever Lego’s ‘Heartlake the Musical’ Heads to Peacock in the U.S., Tencent in China Amid Global Sales (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...

articles.title: Netflix Grapples With Digital-Ad Squeeze Amid Widening Glut of Streaming Commercials
articles.full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:40am PT Netflix Grapples With Digital-Ad Squeeze Amid Widening Glut of Streaming Commercials By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Netflix Grapples With Digital-Ad Squeeze Amid Widening Glut of Streaming Commercials 32 minutes ago Billy Bob Thornton Examines Mayflower Voyage in Fox Nation Documentary Series 42 minutes ago Lisa Ling Signs With CAA 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Illustration: Michael Starbuck/Variety VIP+ Netflix blazed a path in the streaming era that many of its media rivals have tried to follow. As it has tried to navigate Madison Avenue, however, the company has found bumps in the road. The streaming giant last week rolled back its projections for advertising revenue, calling for $2.7 billion instead of $3 billion by the end of 2026. At a time when marketers have been moving their dollars from linear TV to streaming video by the millions, the disclosure was surprising. Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters cited “some delays in the rollout and partner integrations” for some of its new advertising products as a primary culprit for the pared-back estimates. Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Media buyers, however, say Netflix has for months held lofty expectations that are out of sync with the general advertising market. These executives say Netflix’s pricing for inventory remains too high, the process for accessing some of its inventory is too removed from the rest of the market, and that the company’s interest in selling ad-supported sports events like Christmas Day games for NFL football has not been matched with a sales executive who is versed in the nuances of such telecasts. “There’s an existing marketplace, and there’s an existing way of working, and a lot of these digital players think that they can just come in and sell, and it’s not that easy,” says one media buying executive with knowledge of the current market. Netflix declined to make executives available for comment. The streamer for years vowed never to sully its viewing experience with commercials, but media economics, and increased competition from services like Amazon’s Prime Video, HBO Max and Disney+ have not let it hold to those convictions. And just as Netflix has made a concentrated foray into ad sales, the market for streaming inventory has been undermined by a glut of supply. Amazon has loads of ads to sell, and traditional media outlets do as well. The sheer tonnage of streaming inventory available has given advertisers the upper hand in negotiations. To be sure, streaming is soaring. The volume of ad commitments put toward streaming in the most recent “upfront” video market rose a whopping 30%, according to consultancy Media Dynamics, hiking to about $17.2 billion, compared with about $13.2 billion in the 2025 market. But a rising swath of digital inventory, spurred by the rise of cheap FAST channels and increased inventory on mainstream streamers, has weakened the media companies’ stance. The cost of reaching 1,000 viewers, a key metric in these annual negotiations that is known as a CPM, is under clear pressure. Streaming CPMs during the upfront fell 4.9%, to $25.90 from $27.75, according to Media Dynamics. This upfront marked the third year in which media companies agreed to what is known as “rollbacks,” or reductions in the rate of change in pricing they seek for the viewers they deliver. “Free ad-supported TV channels are attracting accelerating audiences especially among increasingly challenged lower per capita income households,” says Pivotal Research Group analyst Jeff Wlodarczak in a recent research note. Other media companies are likely to face these pressures. Simply put, more streaming inventory is purchased via programmatic means, or via algorithms that seek out particular audience characteristics, such as expectant mothers or first-time car buyers. This digital automation of advertising inventory has made it harder for media companies to prove that such video opportunities are “premium,” or better than what else is available in the market. Some companies have tried to create new ways to stand out. Before its acquisition by Skydance, Warner Bros. Discovery burnished its ability to help advertisers identify specific settings and emotions present in its programming library. So a marketer might look for a scene set in an airport, grocery store or theme park, or seek out shows that made viewers feel a sense of mystery, curiosity or adrenaline. Paramount had touted a concept called a “streaming fixed unit” that gives advertisers who buy it the same ad placement in the premieres of new episodes of top shows such as “Tulsa King”. When an advertiser buys the unit, it is also buying a guarantee that Paramount will run the ad in a fixed place, such as the first spot in a commercial break, for the first seven days after the episode debuts. Netflix isn’t the first new-tech streaming purveyor to face challenges upon turning to the ad market. Amazon infamously pressed advertisers to pay more for “Thursday Night Football,” then untested as a stand-alone on the Prime Video platform, than they did for Fox’s Sunday-afternoon NFL games, some of the medium’s costliest properties. Media buyers pushed back , and Amazon is believed to have retreated from some of its highest price demands. To be sure, Netflix has something many advertisers want: Programing that gets attention. Blue chip marketers ranging from Coca-Cola to Anheuser-Busch and State Farm have turned logistical somersaults to link their products with programs like “Stranger Things,” “The Gentlemen” and “Running Point,” often with stand-out placements in and commercials liked to the series. The challenge, of course, is that the number of sponsorships available hinges on Netflix’ programming slate. “We’re still growing, our ads business is growing over 80% this year. And I think noting that if you are sufficiently aggressive with your product road map, you’re going to occasionally be behind some milestones,” Peters said, adding: “General demand remains very strong, the breadth of advertisers continues to expand, and ultimately, advertisers want our new products and features, and that’s a big mechanism of growth for us. So we are very focused on getting those out to them as quickly as we possibly can.” Getting more ad dollars into its funnel may require a little savvy. Buyers feel Netflix’ initial decision to focus on creating a stand-alone suite of ad-tech may have crimped some of its efforts. “They were trying to build their own walled garden, their own tech,” says the buying executive. “It is just going to slow down adoption, because you’re making it harder for us to work with you in the ways that we’re used to working.” Perhaps Netflix has heard this complaint. The company has struck deals in recent months to allow its programmatic ad inventory to be purchased via Amazon and Yahoo platforms. Last week, the company unveiled an expansion of its interaction with Trade Desk, a demand-side platform that functions as one of the bigger programmatic marketplaces. With sports the only programming format that truly lures the sizable and simultaneous crowds advertisers covet, Netflix may want to beef up its expertise. Too often, the buying executive notes, Netflix has been slow to reveal pricing terms or inventory packages it sought around sports properties. “There was confusion about even just basic things. Are you requiring a match spend on entertainment? When are you sending out plans? When are we negotiating pricing?” this buyer says. “They’re being too difficult to work with, and it just makes things harder.” Boosting ad sales may come as a distraction as Netflix executives fret about their service’s ability to keep subscribers and boost the number of hours they spend with the platform. Ted Sarandos , Netflix’s co-CEO, described a scenario under which Netflix had to work harder to develop relationships with producers, directors and other members of the creative community. A new executive, Peter Rice, formerly of Fox and Disney, has come aboard to focus on just that. The ad revenue will remain equally important, argues Dan Salmon, an analyst at New Street Research. “We expect mis-execution in the ad business to be added to the investors’ #1 concern about continued slumping engagement,” he says in a recent research note. articles.title: ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama
articles.full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:44am PT ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama Docmaker Jelena Maksimović's first fiction feature is a narratively sparse but atmospherically throbbing exercise, playing in competition at Tokyo following its Venice Orizzonti premiere. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama 30 minutes ago ‘Love Language’ Review: Chloë Grace Moretz Sells Words of Affirmation in an Old-School Romcom With Gen-Z Trappings 3 days ago ‘Clayface’ Review: DC Comics Horror Movie Is Good, Gross Fun, With No Franchise Homework Required 6 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Paul Spengemann Amid the turmoil of mass student protests in the streets of Belgrade, two young people are bonded by a rash act of rebellion, despite their outwardly incompatible ideologies. The premise of Serbian writer-director Jelena Maksimović ‘s “ Until the Day Ends ” portends a tidy political parable — a sort of “why can’t we all get along” homily for an age, and particularly a generation, of vastly polarized beliefs. The execution, thankfully, is flintier and more complicated than that. The film’s teachings, if any, are ambiguous, and learned on the run: Maksimović’s first fiction feature is most memorable for its galloping formal restlessness, moving at the breathless pace of its characters as they evade authority and chase a glimmer of hope in their joint resistance. Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Having made an impression on the docfest circuit with her two nonfiction features “Taurunum Boy” (2019) and “Homelands (2020), Maksimović brings a street-level, vérité -style grit to the lean narrative of “Until the Day Ends” that feels authentically keyed into the reality of current youth unrest in Eastern Europe. The film is set against a surge of real-life anti-government demonstrations in Serbia in early 2025, triggered by the tragic deaths of 16 people the previous year, following the collapse of a train station canopy in Novi Sad. But if the honest performances of a mostly non-professional ensemble contribute to a docudrama spirit, the filmmaker and her DP Paul Spengemann embrace an aesthetic of epic escapism, with roving, kinetic camerawork punctuated with enough bursting lens flare to make Janusz Kaminski blush. It’s an attention-grabbing approach that promises bigger things from Maksimović, and is propelling the film some distance on the international festival circuit. A premiere last month in Venice’s Horizons program has since been followed with berths in Vienna, Hamburg and, now, the main competition in Tokyo. The film opens on a virtuoso long take, roaming through the shadowed, disheveled hallways of a university building that, ahead of the revolution, has become something of a campsite for displaced, rebellious students; insurgent streaks of red disrupt the general gloom of the mise-en-scène. Through this faintly apocalyptic scene, we follow 20-year-old Lena (riveting newcomer Lena Trifunović), a firebrand student activist who is all in on the protests, unwavering in her anti-authoritarian conviction. That may earn her the admiration of her college comrades, but at home, she’s seen as an idealistic naif — mocked, in particular, by her older brother Milan (Miodrag Dragicevic), who is staunchly right-wing in his sympathies. Milan’s similarly inclined friends join in the teasing, but one does so with a little less gusto: 22-year-old Stefan (Andrija Krivokapić) is a working-class punk who goes with the flow of his social group, but doesn’t seem wholehearted in his pro-government stance. Perhaps sensing his lack of commitment, Lena taunts him back. This hint of connection between them is later made concrete when, at the demonstration, the two are complicit in an act of defiance — throwing a cobblestone at a policeman, badly injuring him — and must skip town for the night. As they flee, their mutual attraction deepens, but they must also parse their political differences. There’s no great capitulation or come-to-Jesus moment here, however. “Until the Day Ends” isn’t an outright romance, or a tale of a proud, gathering storm of resistance; rather, it finds human emotions and obligations sometimes messily at odds with social and political ideals. Narratively, the momentum crests at the protest, abetted by Maksimović’s most dynamic cinematic trickery — which extends to a shot from the perspective of the errant, offending stone. As a more intimate two-hander in the second half, the film is less urgent, but kept compelling by the push-pull chemistry between its two punchy young leads, playing characters who are alike in their combative vulnerability, but little more than that. Trifunović, in particular, is a real find, unpredictable in her coiled-up physicality and alternately commanding and petulant presence. Lena bristles with angry, frustrated optimism, recognizable to anyone who has ever, at one point or another, felt alone in trying to change the world. ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama Reviewed at Soho Screening Rooms, London, Aug. 20, 2026. In Venice Film Festival (Orizzonti), Tokyo Film Festival (Competition). Running time: 90 MIN. (Original title: "Do Kraja Dana") Production: (Serbia-Bulgaria-Slovenia-Montenegro-Germany-Croatia) A Taurunum Film production in co-production with PREMIERstudio, Staragara, Kelek Film, Meander Film, Dinaridi Film. (World sales: Heretic, Athens.) Producer: Jelena Angelovski. Co-producers: Nikolay Sotirov Mutafchiev, Miha Černec, Jožko Rutar, Dušan Kasalica, Ivan Salatić, Arda Çiltepe, Steffen Goldkamp, Tena Gojić. Crew: Director: Jelena Maksimović. Screenplay: Maksimović, Ivan Salatić, Olga Dimitrijević. Camera: Paul Spengemann. Editor: Jan Klemsche. Music: Vladimir Živković, Ace Vaptsarov. With: Lena Trifunović, Andrija Krivokapić, Irina Hotomski, Stefan Tarabić, Miodrag Miša Dragičević. articles.full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 8:00am PT Amelia Dimoldenberg’s Final ‘Chicken Shop Date’ Series to Screen in Theaters By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Amelia Dimoldenberg’s Final ‘Chicken Shop Date’ Series to Screen in Theaters 10 minutes ago Meghan Markle to Co-Host ‘Junior MasterChef Australia’ 3 hours ago Macklemore Calls for Unity During First ‘Free Palestine’ Show as Hozier, Kneecap and Mark Ruffalo Support: ‘Those Two Words Are So Threatening to Some People’ 16 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy Chicken Shop Date Amelia Dimoldenberg ‘s “ Chicken Shop Date ” is coming to the big screen. articles.title: Parallax Films Boards Sales On ‘Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting’ Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Rolf de Heer & Fellow Tokyo Jury Members Talk Festival ‘A-List’ Ratings, Co-Production & How To Judge Films Parallax Films Boards Sales On ‘Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting’ Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi Pledges Support For Japanese Film At Tokyo Fest Opening View All October 26, 2026 4:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting Parallax Films EXCLUSIVE: Parallax Films has boarded international sales for Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting , directed by Chinese artist-filmmaker Qiu Jiongjiong, which is receiving its world premiere in the main competition section of Tokyo International Film Festival. Qiu is known internationally for his debut narrative feature A New Old Play , which won the Special Jury Prize at the 2021 Locarno Film Festival. Rooted in the folklore of China’s Sichuan province, Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting unfolds through four separate feasts spanning four millennia, that “bring the living and the dead, gods and ghosts, to the same table”. The word “fuxi” in its title is a Sichuan expression meaning “the joy of the belly”. Related Stories News Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi Pledges Support For Japanese Film At Tokyo Fest Opening News How TIFFCOM Is Building On Cannes Recognition To Strengthen Global Networks, Co-Production & Japanese IP Parallax describes the film as a “handcrafted mythic fantasy” referencing Qiu’s unique style of filmmaking that combines painting, theatre and cinema. “Rather than reproducing reality, Qiu uses hand-painted scenic flats, handmade props and theatrical staging to give physical form to his imagination, creating a cinematic universe entirely his own,” Parallax explains. ( See here for the trailer of the film.) Watch on Deadline The cast includes Lee Kang-sheng, Taiwanese filmmaker Tsai Ming-liang’s longtime leading actor, playing two grandmothers in different chapters of the film, marking his first female roles on screen. He is joined by actor-filmmaker Lee Hong-chi, whose directorial debut Love Is A Gun won the Lion of the Future award at Venice, and Annie Chen, known for her role in Netflix series Born For The Spotlight . Produced by David Tang, Ningyuan Ding and Zhao Jin, Fuxi is a co-production between Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. The project received support from international film funds and project markets including Hong Kong-Asia Film Financing Forum (HAF), MPA APSA Academy Film Fund, Red Sea Fund, Doha Film Institute and Network of Asian Fantastic Films (NAFF) at Korea’s Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival. The film’s visual world also extends beyond the screen in Fuxi: A Feast For The Universe , Qiu’s large-scale solo exhibition at A4 Art Museum in Chengdu. Bringing together paintings, sets, props and installations, the exhibition translates the film’s imagined universe into a new spatial narrative. The deal for world sales on Fuxi extends Parallax’s relationship with Qiu, with the company also representing his seven previous films, which include A New Old Play, experimental documentary shorts and documentary features. Everything We Know About ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 So Far Everything We Know About Universal’s ‘Miami Vice ’85’ Movie So Far View All October 26, 2026 4:44pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Christine Baranski and Cynthia Nixon in 'The Gilded Age' Season 4 Karolina Wojtasik/HBO The turn between the 18th and 19 th centuries draws closer with the next season of The Gilded Age , which will grace the small screen at the end of the year. Season 4 of the period drama, co-showrun by creator Julian Fellowes and Sonja Warfield, the series tackles the results of growth in industry, accumulation of mass wealth and drastic societal changes as well as new inventions that sped civilization along to where it is today. Related Stories News Everything We Know About ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 So Far News ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 Trailer Hints At Tension In Russell Marriage Plus Situation That “Requires” Agnes Van Rhijn “To Take Leave” Of Her Manners For the full release schedule of The Gilded Age Season 4, read on. When does The Gilded Age Season 4 premiere? Watch on Deadline Season 4 of the period drama premieres Sunday, November 1. How many episodes are in Season 4 of The Gilded Age ? Do they arrive weekly or all at once? There will be eight episodes in the fourth season of The Gilded Age . After the first one premieres Sunday, November 1 in the popular 9 p.m. slot on HBO and HBO Max , new episodes will come out one per week through December 20. See the full release schedule below: Sunday, November 1: Episode 1 Sunday, November 8: Episode 2 Sunday, November 15: Episode 3 Sunday, November 22: Episode 4 Sunday, November 29: Episode 5 Sunday, December 6: Episode 6 Sunday, December 13: Episode 7 Sunday, December 20: Episode 8 (FINALE) Who is in the cast of Season 4 of The Gilded Age ? Most of the core ensemble will return for Season 4. Louisa Jacobson portrays Marian Brooke, niece of Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) and Ada Brooke now Forte (Cynthia Nixon, who married the Reverend Luke Forte (Robert Sean Leonard) only to have him pass away from cancer. Carrie Coon and Morgan Spector will be back as the ambitious social climber Bertha Russell and her railroad tycoon husband George Russell, though their relationship hit some rough waters in Season 3. Harry Richardson plays their son Larry Russell, and Taissa Farmiga portrays their daughter Gladys, who married the Duke of Buckingham (Ben Lamb) in Season 3 through arrangement by her mother. L-R: Denée Benton and Jordan Donica in ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 Karolina Wojtasik/HBO Denée Benton stars as Peggy Scott, a journalist and writer who met her match in Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica) last season. Audra McDonald portray’s Peggy’s mother Dorothy, and John Doughlas Thompson portrays her father Arthur Scott. Blake Ritson plays Agnes van Rhijn’s son Oscar. Kelley Curran plays Enid Winterton, formerly known as Turner because she served as Bertha’s maid. Ashlie Atkinson plays Mamie Fish, socialite who is close with Mrs. Astor (Donna Murphy). Ben Ahlers plays Jack Trotter, formerly the van Rhijn footman and now a man of means since his clock invention patent was sold. Also on the van Rhijn household side, Debra Monk plays Agnes’ lady’s maid Ms. Armstrong. Taylor Richardson plays Bridget. Kristine Nielsen plays Mrs. Bauer who cooks for Ada and Agnes. Simon Jones plays the van Rhijn butler, Bannister. Celia Keenan-Bolger plays Mrs. Bruce, housekeeper for the Russell family. Erin Wilhelmi plays Adelheid Weber, Gladys’ lady’s maid. Douglas Sills portrays Chef Borden, who cooks for the Russells. Jack Gilpin is the Russell butler. George Russell’s secretary Richard Clay (Patrick Page) and New York Globe publisher T. Thomas Fortune ( Sullivan Jones ), will not appear in the rotation of Season 4.

articles.title: Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max BAFTA Names New Chair Stephen & Simon Cornwell Take On Chairmen Roles At ‘Night Manager’ Producer The Ink Factory As Michele Wolkoff Upped To President Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK View All October 26, 2026 5:01pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Daisy Haggard and Bella Ramsey in the upcoming 'Maya' Channel 4 Disney and Channel 4 have struck a landmark UK content deal that will also see the Channel 4 linear network become available on Disney+ , a UK first. In one of the biggest deals of its kind in UK TV history, shows like Channel 4 stalwart Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins and upcoming Bella Ramsey-starrer Maya will drop on Disney+ at the start of next year in the UK and Ireland. From there, Disney+ EMEA general manager Karl Holmes told Deadline there will be a “regular tempo” of new Channel 4 shows entering the Mouse House, although he wouldn’t put an exact figure on this. Related Stories Cancellations and Renewals 'Coven Academy' Renewed For Season 2 By Disney News Nicola Coughlan's 'I Am Helen' Trailer Shows Dark Side Of Modern Relationships As Toxic Masculinity Takes Its Toll From the start of next year, Disney+ UK and Ireland subs will be able to watch these shows day-and-date plus hundreds of hours of on-demand content like Russell T. Davies’ Tip Toe and Nicola Coughlan’s Big Mood. And in a UK first, Channel 4’s linear channel will also become available in its entirety on Disney+. Watch on Deadline Speaking alongside Holmes, Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra claimed the Gogglebox network and Disney+ don’t have much overlap in terms of audience and the deal can be complementary. Channel 4 already licenses Disney content like Abbott Elementary , The X Files and Scandal for its VoD player. “From our perspective, people develop viewing habits in different places,” said Dogra. “There are a number of services they may use to discover content, and we need to make sure Channel 4 is available on those platforms.” Holmes said Disney+ viewing skews younger than public service broadcasters like Channel 4, adding that around 40% of Disney+ viewing over the past year has come from 16-34 year olds. “There is a genuinely complementary relationship here,” added Holmes. “We’re not competing with free-to-air partners; we’re helping them reach a broader audience.” The news comes more than a year after Disney+ kicked off a strategy of partnering with local European networks by striking a content-swapping deal with ITV that has seen shows like The Bear and The Kardashians head to ITVX, while Love Island and Mr Bates vs the Post Office went in the opposite direction. This preceded Disney deals with the likes of Germany’s ZDF and Spain’s Atresmedia. Netflix has simultaneously struck a high-profile pact with France’s TF1 that was recently talked up by Ted Sarandos. Holmes said the Disney-Channel 4 pact is broader in scope than Disney-ITV and his team learned from the latter when executing the former. “One clear lesson is that a focus on shows that are current, big, bold and buzzy – and available day-and-date – works particularly well with our audience,” he added. “That’s what we’ve prioritised in this collaboration. We’d like to build on it further in the future.” For Dogra, who has been in post less than a year, the deal is the latest landmark agreement she has helped mastermind following the once-in-a-generation ads deal inked with Paramount (now Skydance) UK network 5 . She has talked up collaboration opportunites including putting Channel 4 shows on BBC iPlayer , while downplaying the idea of a BBC-Channel 4 merger. While the Paramount deal “gives us scale from an advertising perspective,” today’s agreement “allows us to maximise our impact by reaching as many people as possible across the UK and Ireland, including people who may not currently be using Channel 4 services,” Dogra added. “The premise is that we need to lean into the wider ecosystem,” said the CEO, a former Sky and Warner Bros. Discovery executive. “We’re not going to build scale in every area ourselves, so we need to work with like-minded organizations.” More details on the Disney-Channel 4 deal will be incoming in due course. articles.title: Searchlight Pictures Marketing EVP Michelle Hooper Leaving Studio
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony Searchlight Pictures Marketing EVP Michelle Hooper Leaving Studio Steven Paul’s SP Media Creates Joint Venture With Lionsgate To Expand New Businesses, Closes Film Pact ‘Clayface’ Beams $43M WW Opening, Delivers Paramount-Warner Bros. Second No. 1 Weekend Win Since Merger – Global Box Office View All October 26, 2026 5:31pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michelle Hooper Searchlight Pictures EXCLUSIVE: We hear that Searchlight Pictures ‘ EVP of Marketing Michelle Hooper , who delivered the specialty label numerous Oscar nominations and wins during her two-decade tenure, is exiting. Hooper led publicity, awards and creative marketing operations, earning the studio 21 Best Picture Oscar nominations — including Best Picture winners Slumdog Millionaire , 12 Years a Slave , Birdman , The Shape of Water and Nomadland ; a total of 183 Oscar nominations; and 49 wins. Related Stories News Disney Hit By Layoffs, A Couple Hundred Workers Cut News Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK As far as Golden Globes go, her work delivered 32 awards from 133 nominations, including 20 Best Picture noms and eight wins. Hooper, who joined Searchlight in 2006, is respected by her peers for her taste, whip-smart instincts, creativity and ingenuity in marketing, and was internally known as “the closer,” bringing a film’s campaign home in its final stretch. Her campaigns for various Oscar winners often dialed into the cultural zeitgeist, from understanding how Nomadland would resonate in the context of the pandemic, to spotting the cultural relevance of Slumdog Millionaire in the Obama era, and appreciating the historical significance of 12 Years a Slave , which was closely followed by Birdman. This season, Hooper’s awards campaigns include for Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine (93% certified fresh) and Tony Gilroy’s Behemoth! (87% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes). Watch on Deadline Prior to joining Searchlight, Hooper spent four years at Fox Broadcasting where she was VP of Entertainment Publicity. While at Fox, Hooper spearheaded the implementation of national publicity campaigns for multiple series such as launching American Idol , 24 , Arrested Development , Family Guy and The Simpsons . Prior to joining Fox, Hooper was the Director of Entertainment Communications at CBS Entertainment in New York, where she was part of the team that launched and created the publicity campaign for Survivor . After Disney acquired 20th Century Fox in March 2019, Hooper made the jump. I understand that Hooper’s departure is part of the cuts that occurred at the Disney studio earlier this month. Other notable releases during Hooper’s Searchlight administration include James Mangold’s eight-time Oscar-nominated A Complete Unknown, starring Timothée Chalamet as Bob Dylan; Jesse Eisenberg’s A Real Pain , which won an Oscar for Kieran Culkin; Marielle Heller’s Nightbitch starring Amy Adams; Yorgos Lanthimos’ four-time Academy Award winner Poor Things, starring and produced by Emma Stone; Lanthimos’ follow-up Kinds of Kindness , also starring Stone with Jesse Plemons, Hong Chau and Margaret Qualley; and Andrew Haigh’s romantic drama All of Us Strangers starring Andrew Scott, Paul Mescal, Jamie Bell and Claire Foy. She also oversaw the marketing on streaming originals such as Tina Mabry’s The Supremes at Earl’s All-You-Can-Eat starring Uzo Aduba, Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor and Sanaa Lathan; Karrie Crouse and Will Joines’ Hold Your Breath starring Sarah Paulson; and Eva Longoria’s Oscar-nominated Flamin’ Hot , which became the first original film to debut simultaneously on both Hulu and Disney+ and is Searchlight’s most-watched streaming motion picture of all time. Other past successful films during Hooper’s reign include The Favourite, Can You Ever Forgive Me?, Isle of Dogs, Super Troopers 2, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, Gifted, Jackie, Brooklyn, Wild, The Grand Budapest Hotel, Beasts of the Southern Wild, The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel, The Descendants, The Tree of Life, Black Swan, 127 Hours, Crazy Heart, 500 Days of Summer, The Wrestler, Juno, Once, Little Miss Sunshine and The Last King of Scotland. Hooper shared the Publicist Guild of America’s Maxwell Weinberg Showmanship Award for her work on Survivor . She is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and BAFTA. articles.title: Milcho Manchevski Talks ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover’, His Second Feature Of 2026 & Exposing Corruption At Macedonia’s Film Agency — Tokyo
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Bill Kramer Says AMPAS Plans To Expand List Of Festivals That Can Serve As Qualifiers For The International Oscar Category Milcho Manchevski Talks ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover’, His Second Feature Of 2026 & Exposing Corruption At Macedonia’s Film Agency — Tokyo Janus Films Acquires Alfonso Cuarón’s ‘Y Tu Mamá También’ Ahead Of 25th Anniversary 4K Re-Release View All October 26, 2026 5:48pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tokyo Film Festival. This week, Macedonian filmmaker Milcho Manchevski returns with Sister Brother Manhole Cover , his second feature of the year, which screens in competition at the Tokyo Film Festival. Directed by Manchevski from a screenplay he also wrote, Sister Brother Manhole Cover follows siblings Malina and Viktor, who live on the outskirts of post-Communist Macedonia. They make their living stealing bronze busts and manhole covers, which line their city’s streets. When a routine theft goes wrong and Viktor is badly injured, Malina strikes a desperate deal with a corrupt doctor, forcing them into a dangerous journey through Macedonia’s underworld. Their journey leads to an unexpected refuge: the opulent home of the doctor’s blind mother. Related Stories News Parallax Films Boards Sales On 'Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting' Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere News Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi Pledges Support For Japanese Film At Tokyo Fest Opening Sister Brother Manhole Cover is Manchevski’s ninth feature. The filmmaker debuted his first documentary, Good People , earlier this year at the Sarajevo Film Festival. Watch on Deadline “It’s unusual to have two films come out at the same time, but better two than zero,” Manchevski joked in an interview with Deadline ahead of his trip to Tokyo for Sister Brother, adding that he is enjoying this productive period after spending many years being barred from producing films in his home country. Manchevski, who won the Golden Lion at Venice with his debut feature Before the Rain (1994), was blacklisted and had several projects halted by the Macedonian Film Agency after he reported corruption at the organization. Manchevski’s accusations were later upheld by Macedonia’s Anti-Corruption Commission after an investigation. Below, the veteran filmmaker, who lives between New York and Macedonia, speaks with Deadline about the extensive witch hunt he endured after exposing corruption at the Macedonian Film Agency, finally getting to make Sister Brother Manhole Cover, and why he believes the Tokyo Film Festival is the perfect launchpad for movies. Sister Brother Manhole Cover is a Banana Film production, in co-production with Gala Film (Bulgaria), Sense Production (Serbia), Tirana Film Institute (Albania), Berkeley Media Group (UK), Amarcord Production in association with Augustus Color (Italy) with the support of North Macedonia Film Agency, the Bulgarian National Film Center, Film Center Serbia, the Albanian National Center of Cinematography, and Italy’s Direzione Generale Cinema e Audiovisivo – Ministero della Cultura. The Rome-based Coccinelle Film is handling world sales on the title. DEADLINE: Milcho, where did this idea come from? MILCHO MANCHEVSKI: I wanted to make a film about sisterly and brotherly love—something we rarely see in movies or even in literature. It was also partly inspired by Macedonian folk songs and folk literature, which often include the theme of sisterly love. Sometimes it turns shocking and dark, but it is always fully dedicated. That was the initial embryo. Then I wanted to talk about inequality and wealth inequality. I think that’s the premier issue of today. So many problems in the world go back to this sense of unfairness and inequality. That feeling festers in people. But I didn’t want to turn it into an exclusively dark story. I thought it should be told through defiance and humor, because Victor and Marlena don’t see themselves as victims. They see themselves as people with agency—people who do things. Unfortunately, pretty much the only thing they can do is petty crime. DEADLINE: Yeah, I loved the idea of people stealing the busts. It’s so European. MANCHEVSKI: People actually do it. It’s three euros a kilo for the metal. I did a little research. There was an explosion of new monuments in Macedonia in the early 2010s, because the nationalist government decided to reintroduce us to our past. There was plenty of cash just lying around. And the manhole covers, they cover the underground and the septic part of us that we don’t really want to smell or see. Then our heroes take them off, and you can smell the reek. DEADLINE: I read this film was previously titled Leaving Copacabana? MANCHEVSKI: Yes. The title was Leaving Copacabana . Copacabana was their slum, which we constructed for the film. The little shacks you see are leaning on an ancient aqueduct. We got permission from the government to work there because it’s a national monument. We constructed the shacks for two reasons: first, to have full control; and second, so we wouldn’t go into somebody’s home—somebody’s slum—and disrupt their life. The slum was jokingly called Copacabana, as if they were in Brazil. The tagline was “sister, brother, manhole cover.” But that title somehow took over because it’s more irreverent and catchier, and I think it describes the film better. It’s not so much about leaving one place and going to a richer place; it’s about their relationship and society. DEADLINE: Where did you shoot this film? There are a lot of locations. MANCHEVSKI: Everything was done on location. There was no studio. And even on location, we didn’t want to change too much. The exception was the slum, which we constructed based on actual slums in Skopje. Most are inhabited by Roma, but not exclusively. We built it around the aqueduct because I liked the graphic quality, but also because it incorporated the ancient past into the very prosaic present of the characters and the whole community. Everything else was scouted around Skopje. We looked for actual places that had a certain smell, places where you could feel the underbelly, but also places that could give us a cross-section of society. For example, you have the illegal dump, which we had to sanitize so people could work there. DEADLINE: That was a real dump? MANCHEVSKI: That was a real dump. We took over a corner of it, sanitized the area, and brought in our own paper and cloth—things that didn’t stink too much. We had to ward off dogs. We liked that particular dump because you could see the highway below. Again, there was this contrast: here and there, us and them. That’s necessary when you’re telling a drama. The house was a real house, too. We didn’t do much to it; we brought in the piano and the busts, which we created, of course. I’m taking one of the manhole covers to the red carpet in Tokyo next week. DEADLINE: You’ve become a regular at Tokyo Film Festival. Why do you screen your films here? MANCHEVSKI: It’s an old love story. Before the Rain , my first film, played Tokyo. Going there and spending time there was so nice. I like how people in Japan, and especially at the festival, appreciate films. They take special care with them; they create new posters and trailers. It’s not just a run-of-the-mill place or festival. Then Dust played there, and then Kaymak . Now, I want to go there—it is at the top of my list. DEADLINE: This is your second film of the year. You were in Sarajevo with the doc Good People. I read that this was mostly because for years you were unable to produce anything? MANCHEVSKI: Yes, for a while, I wasn’t able to work because I reported corruption at the film agency in Macedonia. I did it twice, and it was eventually confirmed by the Anti-Corruption Commission and the State Audit Office. As retaliation, they blacklisted me, filed criminal charges against me, launched a smear campaign, and blocked my previous films and films in progress. Eventually I won two court cases against the agency, and the dam broke. This film was initially approved in 2022, and then, at the same time, the tragedy in Kočani happened. I felt I should make a documentary about it. The two films are completely different stylistically. There’s a lot of humor in Sister Brother ; there’s no humor in Good People . It’s somber, with a glimmer of hope at the end. The overlap mostly happened in the edit, where you can shuttle between the two. I know it’s unusual to have two films come out at the same time, but better two than zero. DEADLINE: You’ve worked across the United States and Europe and have been able to make many different kinds of things. Many European and American filmmakers now talk about how difficult it is to make work. How do you feel about the industry today? MANCHEVSKI: I’m always an outsider, and I like it that way. I’ve lived in New York since 1985, but recently I’ve mostly been making films in Europe because of the general attitude toward filmmaking and the arts. Financing is always tough. It’s the curse of filmmaking. I’m jealous of painters and poets: you sit down, do your work, and it’s done. Maybe nobody will see it or like it, but at least it’s finished. With film, you first have to sell it and then make it. Filmmaking involves a lot of money, technology, and egos. Working in Europe has advantages, but distribution is not as muscular as in Hollywood. But nobody tells you how to end the film, whom to cast, or whether you need to reshoot a scene. You want feedback and collaboration, but it’s not a situation where the money dictates what the art will look like. That’s why I prefer Europe to Hollywood. I’ve worked in the United States—I worked on The Wire for HBO, made an independent film, developed films with studios, and even started a studio film. But in the last decade or so, there has been pressure to conform ideologically and make films with messages. I think every film has a message by default. The question is whether it offers more: Is there beauty in the film? Is there something profound? Does it talk about a bigger truth rather than just a message? The pressure—from festivals and film funds—to be message-driven and ideological comes at the expense of everything else. Even when I agree with the message, it’s a pity that so much contemporary cinema turns into two-dimensional pamphlets. articles.title: Neil Young Rocks Trump With $10M Suit Over Using That ‘Free World’ Tune Again
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Jay Z & Apple Make It Official! Hova’s Headlining The Super Bowl Halftime Show Neil Young Rocks Trump With $10M Suit Over Using That ‘Free World’ Tune Again ‘Smear’ Campaign: George Clooney, Betty Gilpin, Adam Scott & Laverne Cox Team To Read Clark Gregg-Penned Political Play As Midterms Fundraiser View All October 26, 2026 6:48pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source (L-R) Neil Young, Donald Trump Getty Images Almost no one expects Donald Trump to keep his word, but unlike most, Neil Young ain’t taking any crap from the former Apprentice host. Having repeatedly told Trump to keep his MAGA mitts off his classic Rockin’ in the Free World song, the 80-year-old Grandfather of Grunge took the poll struggling POTUS back to court today with new $10 million copyright infringement suit. And, as Young always does on the guitar, the two time Rock & Roll Hall of Famer let Trump have it. “ Rockin’ in the Free World is a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten,” the short but sharp complaint says. “The lyrics paint vivid street-level portraits – a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity – while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all. In short, the Song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for.” Related Stories News CNN And Politico Again Are Barred From Air Force One Politics 'Smear' Campaign: George Clooney, Betty Gilpin, Adam Scott & Laverne Cox Team To Read Clark Gregg-Penned Political Play As Midterms Fundraiser Trump first used the 1991 hit back at the very start of his first serious (semi-serious?) White House run in 2015. Young told him to back off then and told Trump to back off again in 2020 with legal action. As Young’s critiques of Trump got louder and louder in song and from the stage, it seemed the 45th and now 47th President, or at least his attorneys, got it — until October 12. in Youngstown, Ohio. Watch on Deadline The the five-page filing in federal court in Virginia states: “Just prior to Donald J. Trump taking the stage to speak at the Youngstown Rally, the Committee caused Rockin’ in the Free World to be played. On information and belief, the Committee has caused the Song to be played numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections.” As today made clear, you don’t mess with old Neil and you don’t break your word to him. “Donald J. Trump (‘Trump’) is now and at the time of all rallies this year was personally aware that a license would be required to play the Song at rallies and that Young has not, and would not, grant the required license,” proclaims the complaint. “In 2020 Young sued another corporation formed by Trump, Donald J. Trump For President, Inc., for copyright infringement of Rockin’ in the Free World along with another song written by Young,” the document by lawyers Scott Simmons and Robert Besser against Trump 47 Committee Inc. adds. “Donald J Trump For President, Inc. asserted no defense and immediately settled shortly after it was served, promising that it would never again use Rockin’ in the Free World without a license and permission from Young.” The White House did not respond to Deadline’s request for comment on the complaint. But, with 80-year old Trump posting fast and furiously for struggling GOP candidates, don’t be surprised if the octogenarian barbs starting flying like Tomahawk missiles soon-ish. On the other hand, the Neil Young, or at least his lawyers couldn’t resist a bit of wit, or at least a legalese laugh at Trump’s expense — and maybe even their own. “Young has suffered damage to his reputation and brand as a result of the implication that he supports Donald J. Trump in any way,” the filing says in a statement that literally no one anywhere would ever think. Keep on rockin’ that in the free world. The hip hop icon and Roc Nation founder has picked himself to headline the Super Bowl LXI halftime show in the City of Angels. “From Reasonable Doubt to standing on the Super Bowl Halftime stage, this has been a journey,” the Hard Knock Life rapper stated today, almost a week after Deadline confirmed his role in the February 14 big game at the aforementioned SoFi. Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world’s biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true.” Related Stories News Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK Cancellations and Renewals 'Coven Academy' Renewed For Season 2 By Disney Halftime show sponsor Apple Music posted a to the point video on social media casting the doubters aside. Following in the Roc Nation picked halftime footsteps of Dr. Dre, Eminem, May J Blige, Kendrick Lamar , Snoop Dogg in 2022 , Rihanna in 2023, Usher in 2024, the great (and Drake beefing) Kendrick in 2025, and the show stopping Bad Bunny in 2026 , the league boss had nothing but praise for the man born Shawn Carter: “For several years, we’ve had the privilege of working closely with Jay-Z and Roc Nation, and I’ve seen the extraordinary impact he has had on the Super Bowl Halftime Show,” Goodell declared Monday “When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him,” the Commissioner went on to say, with no small amount of hyperbole. “I couldn’t be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring to the Super Bowl stage.” Now with the marquee act all settled, the real question is who Jay Z’s guest stars will be. Add to that, Jay Z’s London gigs atTottenham Hotspur Stadium featured a mini-Fugees reunion with Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean. Put bluntly, Jay Z may or may not have 99 Problems , but the ESPN and Disney+ shown Super Bowl LXI ain’t one. articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Armando Tinoco Armando Tinoco Staff Writer @armietinoco More Stories By Armando ‘Gilded Age’ Creator Julian Fellowes Calls HBO’s Casey Bloys “Our Protector & Our Defender From Very Early Days” During Season 4 Premiere Netflix Taps Former Apple Exec Steve Wilson To Lead Podcast Acquisitions ‘Star Trek’s George Takei Pays Tribute To Walter Koenig: “My Heart Is Heavy” View All October 26, 2026 8:55pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Julian Fellowes and Casey Bloys Kristina Bumphrey / Getty Images Julian Fellowes attended The Gilded Age ‘s Season 4 premiere at the Plaza Hotel in New York City, where he thanked Casey Bloys for believing in the series from the start. “I have a special place in my heart for Casey Bloys, our protector, our gladiator, our defender from very, very early days,” Fellowes said before the screening. “Anyone who enjoys the show owes him a great deal. I certainly do, and I say that with both pride and happiness.” Related Stories News ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 Red Carpet Photos: Carrie Coon, Morgan Spector, Denée Benton, Cynthia Nixon & More News ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 Release Schedule: When Do New Episodes Come Out? Deadline reported in 2019 that, after NBC ordered the series, the creator’s vision for the period piece proved too ambitious for the constraints of broadcast TV. Universal TV shopped the series, and it landed at HBO in a competitive situation. The series finally premiered in 2022, with Season 4 debuting on Sunday, November 1. During the presentation, Fellowes also gave a shout-out to NBCU’s Pearlena Igbokwe as “one of the first to recognize” the specialness of the series. He also mentioned Bob Greenblatt for not letting it rest and for making the series, and called HBO’s Francesca Orsi “wonderful” for bringing the series home. Watch on Deadline Fellowes said that he had always been interested in the Gilded Age, calling it “a very interesting period of American history,” adding, “I think it was the beginning of modern America, and it was the moment that America decided they didn’t want to copy Europe and have five generations before anyone could be invited for dinner and all that kind of thing.” “Whatever one says about the so-called robber barons, the fact is, within a few years, the century would begin what we would know of as the American century,” he continued. “And in both world wars, the voice of America was the loudest at the peace table, because America had arrived, and it was the big, giant new power of the world.” AMPAS To Expand Festival Qualifier List For International Oscar SAG-AFTRA Faces Reckoning As Few Members Qualify For Streaming Bonus Clooney & Others Set For Read Of Political Play ‘Smear’ As Midterms Fundraiser Keanu Reeves Takes Over From Alan Ritchson As Lead In Netflix Actioner ‘Maelstrom’ Read More About: Comments
