articles.title: Rupert Grint Sets Next Project: Noiser Audiobook Adaptation of ‘Treasure Island’ (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 22, 2026 5:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Rupert Grint Courtesy of Noiser Harry Potter alum Rupert Grint is getting in on the podcast game with a new serialized audiobook of Treasure Island . In an adaptation for podcast network Noiser, Grint is set to play every single character from Robert Louis Stevenson’s classic 1883 novel, including the wide-eyed Jim Hawkins, silver-tongued Long John Silver, the rum-soaked Billy Bones and half-mad castaway Ben Gunn. Episodes will drop weekly starting Dec. 8. “Noiser’s serialised audiobooks now reach over 50 million listens a year, which shows how much appetite there is for great storytelling in this format,” Noiser CEO Pascal Hughes told The Hollywood Reporter . “ Treasure Island is where we bring the whole family in. Rupert is beloved by children and adults alike, and his performance is something truly special. Our hope is that kids fall in love with classic storytelling and grown-ups rediscover it.” Related Stories Business Italy's Movie and TV Spending Drops Amid Tax Incentive Uncertainty Movies Stephen Lang, Uli Edel Reunite on 'Mercy Rider' 30 Years After 'Last Exit to Brooklyn' (Exclusive) Stevenson’s 1883 novel gave the world much of what we now think of as pirate lore — the treasure map marked with an X, the squawking parrot and a deserted island hiding a fortune. When a weathered old sailor arrives at a remote West Country tavern, young Jim Hawkins is swept into the adventure of a lifetime. A treasure map hidden in an old buccaneer’s sea chest takes him from the fog-laden English coast to the sun-scorched shores of a perilous island aboard the Hispaniola. But the crew harbors a dangerous secret, and Long John Silver is not all he seems. Grint is known around the world for his role as Ron Weasley in the film adaptations of Harry Potter and is set to reprise the role from February to May in Broadway’s Harry Potter and the Cursed Child . He’s starred in Cherrybomb , Into the White , Knock at the Cabin and Servant . His most recent movie role was in the Finnish horror Nightborn , which premiered in Berlin earlier this year , and his next is in Ebenezer with Johnny Depp. Noiser is a U.K.-based podcast network reaching millions of listeners every week. With hit shows including Real Vikings, Real Dictators, Short History Of and Real Survival Stories , Noiser prides itself on an immersive approach to audio storytelling and high-quality sound design. Other British stars to have teamed up with Noiser include Dame Julie Andrews, who narrated an adaptation of Emma , and Hugh Bonneville, who narrated some Sherlock Holmes short stories. THR

articles.title: Yes, ‘Heated Rivalry’ Is Really Headed to Movie Theaters

Sabrina Lantos/HBO Have you been hoping to see Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov on the big screen? You’re in luck — Heated Rivalry , the hit Canadian hockey romance series, is officially heading to theaters for limited engagement marathon screenings, distributor Sphere Abacus announced Thursday morning. The Crave original series, which airs on HBO Max in the U.S., is celebrating its one-year anniversary a little early, with screenings of all six episodes of the first season kicking off on Nov. 6. Sphere Abacus, the Bell Media company that helped bring the show international, partnered with Regal Cinemas in the U.S. for the release. Thursday’s announcement comes after speculation on social media throughout the week. Related Stories Lifestyle 'Heated Rivalry' Goes All In on Physical Media Including Special Edition Blu-Ray and DVD TV 'Yaga' Review: Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson Williams in AMC+'s Intriguing but Undercooked Brew of Modern Crime and Ancient Folklore From Nov. 6 through Nov. 30, fans of the show can revisit the series across three paired episode screenings: episodes one and two (“Rookies” and “Olympians”), episodes three and four (“Hunter” and “Rose”) and episodes five and six (“I’ll Believe in Anything” and “The Cottage”). Tickets will run at $9.99 per screening. Regal will show the episodes in over 275 of its own locations in the U.S. The company also serves as the nationwide distributor, bringing the show to 650 theaters including AMC and Cinemark. Regal showings will include welcome content from the cast and director, show creator Jacob Tierney . Participating locations will offer themed, limited-time cocktails: Summer in Montreal and Russians Don’t Blush. “ Heated Rivalry is a global phenomenon creating a rush of social media and press activity wherever it lands. We’re very excited to give audiences the opportunity to watch the drama unfold on big screens in North America, the UK, Australia & New Zealand,” Sphere Abacus’ executive director of global distribution and partnerships Hana Palmer said in a release. Based on Rachel Reid’s novel of the same name, Heated Rivalry focuses on the complicated situationship between Shane Hollander, played by Hudson Williams , and Ilya Rozanov, played by Connor Storrie . The pair are generational talents in the world of professional hockey and sworn on-ice rivals, who meet as teenagers. The first novel of Reid’s book series, Game Changers , which the novel Heated Rivalry hails from, centered on François Arnaud’s character Scott Hunter and Robbie G.K. ’s character Kip Grady; it served as secondary material for the first season. The show’s season one cast was rounded out by Christina Chang, Dylan Walsh, Sophie Nélisse and Ksenia Daniela Kharlamova. Season two of the series is filming in Toronto, and features a slew of new cast members. Williams and Storrie return to front the series, with Justice Smith, Charlie Gillespie, Daniel Diemer and Shaheen Jafargholi joining them in leading roles for the second season. Tickets for Heated Rivalry ‘s theatrical event are available at the box office and Regal’s website and mobile app. THR

articles.title: Italy’s Movie and TV Spending Drops Amid Tax Incentive Uncertainty
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 22, 2026 6:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Rome, Italy. Christopher Furlong/Getty Images Italy’s inward cinema, TV and video-on-demand sectors content investment fell in 2025 for the first time since 2018, the annual APA report released at the MIA Market in Rome indicated. The overall audiovisual content investment dropped 7.4 percent to €2 billion ($2.24 billion) last year, compared with the 2024 stats, according to the APA, the Italian audiovisual producers association. The dropoff came amid a government overhaul of Italy’s tax credit system for indie producers and local audiences shifting from traditional linear TV broadcasters to emerging streaming platforms. The latest APA report also comes against the background of an Italian industry dealing with screens of all sizes and new value placed on original IP as storytellers find new platforms to reach audiences. According to the APA report, Italian scripted productions for TV and VOD platforms saw their inward investment fall to €122 million ($137 million), while fiction production dropped to €740 million ($830 million) last year. “The main factor affecting the sector’s resilience is uncertainty surrounding the public funding framework, from the amount of available resources to eligibility criteria and application timelines. This situation hampers producers’ ability to plan ahead, increases financing costs and reduces margins, placing pressure on all companies, particularly smaller businesses, with consequences for liquidity and investment capacity,” the APA report indicated with commentary. As elsewhere in the global industry the market share of Italian linear free and pay TV channel continues to fall as streaming platform grew to a 43 percent share in 2025. “In the short to medium term, it is expected to surpass linear television in value,” the APA report warned about the continuing dominance of streaming platforms in Italy. European producers at the MIA Market this week heard they no longer compete just with each other but against American studios and streamers, YouTube and social platforms. So they require new public and private financing to maintain their audience share and international revenues. THR

articles.title: A Search for His Biological Father Led to a Top Podcast — and an Endorsement From Ira Glass
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All October 22, 2026 6:31am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sayre Quevedo, host, writer and producer of 'Reaching Out.' Kunjo KR As Sayre Quevedo’s latest podcast premiered, he got a ringing endorsement from Ira Glass, who played some of the show on This American Life and said Quevedo had “invented something completely new.” The podcast, entitled Reaching Out, starts with the premise of Quevedo and his twin brother trying to track down their biological father, whom they had never met and had little information on. This search is interwoven with Quevedo’s diary-like commentary about how he’s feeling about finding his father as well as his own life as he is about to turn 30, and intimate conversations with his brother and mother that delve into how the brothers really feel about each other, and how their paths have diverged. Quevedo is aided in the process by the fact that he has recorded most conversations in his life since his mid-20s, including across the four-year process of finding his birth father. In the end, these conversations, and his own meditations on identity and family, as well as his noted narrative omissions and motives in telling the story, become the main thrust of the podcast. “I don’t know if I’ve heard another podcast that tries to capture a person’s life as completely as this one does, and just what it feels like to be alive right now,” Glass said in describing the show. The six-part series kicked off Sept. 16, from Futuro Studios in partnership with KCRW, and has already won the audio memoir award at the Tribeca Film Festival. The Glass endorsement helped propel the show to the top of Apple Podcast’s series charts that week, with the show still remaining in the top 15. Quevedo, who has previously created podcasts about his family and partners as well as subjects across the world, spoke with The Hollywood Reporter about finding this innovative format, the state of podcasting and how he feels about sharing his life publicly. Why did you start recording your conversations? I have been recording myself consistently. I would say since my mid 20s, but I think the habit probably began when I was a teenager. I think it’s almost a habit at this point. I don’t think about recording or not recording, and a lot of that habit stems from the fact that I grew up without really any documentation of my family. My mom left home when she was very young, and my father obviously was not a part of my life, and so I don’t have really any documents of my family history, and so it just became a way of memorializing, of sort of reminding myself that I exist and that I’m a part of the world and part of history. And in making recordings you’re not necessarily thinking they’ll turn into a podcast or a project? I think, for instance, with searching for my birth father, I’m sure there was some part of my brain that was like, “This is an interesting story. Maybe I’ll turn this into something.” But I think there was another part of my brain that was like, “I would like to remember this. I would like to remember what it felt like to go on this journey. I would like to remember what these conversations sounded like and felt like.” Because I’ve experienced this so often in my life, that I’ve gone through things that I’ve thought, “Oh, I’m never going to forget what it felt like to talk to my father for the first time, or I’m never going to forget how it felt to send that email with my brother,” [reaching out to their father] and then a few months pass or a few years pass, and it’s just a vague notion in my head. And so it does serve that purpose as well as a way to kind of return to these moments. At what point in the process of finding your biological father did you know that this would be a podcast? I think once me and my brother decided to confront my father in person. Because up until that point there was this part of me that, in addition to feeling sort of reticent about looking for him, there was a part of me that felt like it wasn’t going to happen. Though I’m not sure we would have admitted it at the time, I think both of us were so scared of getting that answer and of meeting him that there was some part of me that thought we would never really go through with it. And so after going and confronting him, I was like, something happened. We really did it. And obviously, a lot more happens after that in the series. But I think that was the moment where I was like, I’ve gone through something. I’ve actually done the thing that I was afraid to do. And I think that’s when I knew that there was really a story worth telling, even though I had no idea what was going to happen afterwards. To that point, it seems like the story starts to morph into not just being about your father. When I really began to write the series in earnest, I had this feeling that the search for my father was more of a Trojan horse in some ways. The search for my father was really a way of forcing myself to reflect on my relationship to absence in a lot of ways, and my relationship to desire, and the ways that I had sort of built my life around absences and around yearning and searching for things that I couldn’t have or that were not there. I think that became clear to me as I was listening through all of the conversations that I’d recorded too, not just the conversations but also these minute, quotidian parts of my life. I started to realize I’m doing these same things over and over again. I’m going on these dates and feeling bad about myself. I’m going to the club looking for somebody to go home with. I’m having these conversations with my mother about feeling like I have to to meet this person, and it was through being able to sort of step back and look at the patterns that had sort of cropped up in those recordings, that I was able to see “Oh, I’m actually going through something completely different.” The search for my father is actually helping me see that I was going through something else that I wasn’t able to fully see or recognize in the moment of it. Throughout the podcast, you’re willing to get very personal and be open about yourself, including vulnerable emotional moments as you navigate romantic relationships, as well as others where you acknowledge you’re kind of being a jerk. Were you nervous putting all of that out there? I still feel nervous about it. There’s a lot of me in this work. I mean, it’s personal, obviously, but there’s a lot of me in this work. My philosophy around how I make personal work is that whatever honesty I’m asking of the people that I include in this work, I have to be tenfold more honest because it’s such a big thing to ask, especially my family, my mother and my twin. It’s such a huge thing to ask people to share something so vulnerable with the public, and also to share it with me, and to give me the power to tell that story. And so I’m sharing a lot of parts of myself that frankly, there’s parts of it that I still feel shame about. There’s versions of myself in this story that are extremely judgmental, extremely critical, critical of myself and of others, and parts of myself that are also at odds with how I would like to be in the world or how I’d like to see myself. My hope is that by sharing those parts of myself that are maybe slightly less likable, slightly less relatable, that people can sort of recognize and accept those parts of themselves as well. What did you make of the Ira Glass endorsement, in which he said you’d invented “something completely new,” and are taking the format of his own show and pushing it further? If you say podcasting, that’s the guy people think of, you know, so it was really surreal, and I probably haven’t fully processed what that means. But it was extremely affirming. I’ve worked in audio since I was 15 years old. I’m 33 now, so to receive that kind of feedback from somebody of that stature and who I respect that much really makes it feel worth it to put everything on the line and to make something that where I took some risks both stylistically and personally, to share to share it with the world Were you looking for a new kind of format when you created the show? I try not to repeat myself in terms of the form of the work that I’m making. Maybe this is controversial, but I consider podcasting an art and an art form. I think it’s a documentary form and medium and expression. But there’s also a lot of creativity in the work, and I don’t want to make the same art twice. I want to challenge myself. But I wouldn’t say necessarily the style of the work was done with that in mind as much as in trying to find the right form for it. I wanted to make something that felt reflective of my life in a real way, but that also felt like the kind of art that I enjoy. I wanted to make something literary. I’m a long time reader and grew up reading and love reading and love words as an art form. So I just felt like, at this point, given the state of the industry and the state of where things are at, like why not just take the risk and make something that feels like something I would want to read or something that I would want to watch. Things are so dire in podcasting right now that there’s really nothing to lose in terms of making something that maybe alienates some people because it doesn’t sound like everything that they’ve already heard, and so that was sort of the ethos that I went into making the work. What’s feeling dire for you in the podcasting industry? There has been a little bit less of the resources that so many of us who were in podcasting in the early 2010s and 2020s had. As those resources have gone away, as the Gimlets of the world have gone away, as the Pineapple Streets have gone away, there is a feeling that there’s just a lot less room to make risky creative work that is not meant to engage the broadest possible audience, but is meant for people who just want to listen to something experimental or strange or creative. And so I think that’s the direness, the feeling that there’s less room for this kind of work to exist, and I do hope that the success of the work gives some permission to whoever still has the money and resources to take some risks because people did obviously respond to it in a positive way. But I do think that’s the direness of the moment, alongside the layoffs and everything else. The tightening of the belt also leads to a tightening of what is seen as creatively profitable, or creatively possible or worthy of risk in the moment, and that’s a hard place to be for a lot of my friends and colleagues. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. THR

articles.title: Doc Maker Rocky Mudaliar Signs With Verve (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 22, 2026 6:35am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Rocky Mudaliar Courtesy of Verve Rocky Mudaliar and his Abrupt Entertainment banner has signed with Verve for representation . The move follows Mudaliar producing the true crime documentary Funny Money: The Dane Cook Story, a film that chronicles comedian Dane Cook’s rise to fame and the shocking financial betrayal by his own family. The film about Cook — who at one time was the most successful stand-up anywhere, earning upward of $20 million a tour — debuted earned a Best True Crime Documentary nomination at the Critics’ Choice Documentary Awards on Oct. 13. Brett Harvey directed the Funny Money documentary that will start streaming on Netflix in November. Vancouver-based Abrupt Entertainment specializes in premium documentaries and talent-driven nonfiction programming. The signing with Verve for representation will look to help Abrupt expand its U.S. development and production operations. Other doc credits include the Unbreakable: The Dolph Lundgren Story and Inmate #1: The Rise of Danny Trejo , which was released through Universal Pictures. Mudaliar also co-founded Stage Zero Entertainment alongside music icon Timbaland to bridge traditional entertainment with next-generation music and technology ventures. Mudaliar and his Abrupt banner are currently producing an untitled documentary about a major rock band, with Emmy-nominated and fellow Verve client Sam Lipman-Stern to direct. As a Canadian company, Abrupt has a track record in international co-productions, production financing and tapping tax incentives and other soft money subsidies to get its documentaries made. THR

articles.title: Ben Silverman Still Doesn’t Want a Job — But He’s Busier Than Ever
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All October 22, 2026 6:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ben Silverman Valerie Macon / AFP via Getty Images Ben Silverman has been producing TV since he was 30. Twenty-six years later, the man does not lack for pep. He’s naturally a vibes guy, though the multiple double lattes probably help. On a Monday in late August, Silverman met The Hollywood Reporter at a coffeehouse opposite Manhattan’s Bryant Park to check in on Propagate Content — Silverman’s and his former assistant Howard T. Owens’ production company — but instead golf took over the chat. The Propagate chairman and co-CEO carries an 8.1 handicap and memberships at the ultra-exclusive Riviera and Hillcrest country clubs. As of late, Silverman’s hobby has informed his profession: Propagate has revived the Skins Game at Amazon, is developing an untitled Anthony Kim documentary and will premiere season two of the scripted Owen Wilson golf comedy Stick on Apple TV on Nov. 4. Meyer Silverman (a plus-2 handicap), Ben’s son and the top high school freshman earlier this month in the Colorado Class 3A Boys Golf State Championships, has already eclipsed Dad’s golf game. It’s kind of exactly how Ben built on his own parents’ creative careers. His father, Stanley Silverman, is a composer who has arranged music for Sting and Paul Simon; his mother, Mary (Delson) Silverman,was an opera singer, and his stepmother a violinist. “I kind of grew up in the arts but always seeing that it was a tough life,” Silverman recalls. “I had maggots in my cereal growing up. My dad, when he got divorced from my stepmom, had to move in with me and my mom.” Propagate Content’s Howard T. Owens and Ben Silverman along with Kenya Barris at the ‘Jerry West: The Logo’ premiere at The Culver Theater on April 13, 2026 in Culver City. Phillip Faraone/Getty Images for Prime Video An artist’s upbringing birthed a builder of others’ visions. As the youngest-ever division head at William Morris, Silverman saw the opportunity to repackage overseas formats for U.S. audiences. “That was a quiet business that had a couple of hustling, Willy Loman-type players in it — but otherwise was not a real business,” Silverman says. “I really led the charge in that.” From London, Silverman adapted Queer as Folk for Showtime and later Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? for ABC. Millionaire handed Silverman his Hollywood “I made it” moment. Massive TV ratings brought in phone calls from Disney chief Michael Eisner — “Thanks! What else you got?” — and NBC CEO Bob Wright: “Why didn’t I get Millionaire ?” (He passed on it but soon would buy The Weakest Link from Silverman.) “I’m like, ‘Oh my God, my life just changed,’ ” Silverman recounts. With the backing of Barry Diller, a 29-year-old Silverman left the agency to start Reveille Productions, which brought America The Office and Silverman his “I’ve really made it” moment. “My dad and I are sitting together on an airline… and 95 percent of the plane had chosen to watch The Office ,” Silverman says. “The entire plane was laughing.” “’Oh my gosh,’” he recalls thinking. “’My family’s life just changed.’” At 36, Silverman sold Reveille to the Murdochs for $125 million (who would flip it for seven times that, he says) and became co-chair of NBC Entertainment in 2007. It was the first job Silverman had that didn’t really suit him. The problem was the suit. He lasted two years. The Hollywood Reporter ‘s July 28, 2009 front page story on Silverman’s NBC exit. The Hollywood Reporter “I walked in [Jeff Zucker’s] office and said, “Jeff, this job gives me a stomachache. I do not like it. I feel like a sports car in a parking lot of Tauruses. I don’t enjoy this,”’ Silverman remembers. “’I feel like I’m managing up and managing down without getting to pursue the things I care about. I cannot do this anymore.’” He and Diller next launched Electus, which is now Propagate. Silverman says he won’t join the corporate ranks again. “I get the calls every couple of years, and I’m like, ‘Wait, that sounds like a job. I don’t want a job!’” Silverman says. “I just love being in culture,” he adds. And his own banner now has an undeniably large portfolio of projects — Netflix’s Untold , the CNN doc I’m Chevy Chase and You’re Not , Hulu’s The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives , Amazon’s Jerry West: The Logo , Food Network’s Chopped and scripted fare like The Paper (Peacock) and the upcoming Protective Custody (Apple TV) comedy series starring Ben Stiller and Benicio Del Toro — but Propagate is still seeking its first true society-shaker. That could come as early as November, when its Sam Bankman-Fried doc series The Boy Who Stole Billions? premieres on Amazon. Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM, approvingly screened it a few weeks ago. Hopkins credits Silverman’s “diverse set of relationships” and the “ability to work across a number of dimensions and genres” for his success. “And then he delivers,” Hopkins adds. “We’re a hit-driven business — not everything that every producer does is going to knock it out of the park — but [Silverman has] a really good track record.” Also in the Propagate pipeline is an untitled Mookie Betts scripted comedy from Ramy Youssef and Josh Rabinowitz in development for Apple TV, with an Entourage -like setup for the Dodgers’ star shortstop. (Betts will not personally play himself in the Vincent Chase-role.) The firm is additionally developing a scripted series with Jenny Bicks ( Sex and the City ) and another with Friends co-creator Marta Kauffman; Silverman is in negotiations with Netflix for the latter. Ben Silverman, Liz Tuccillo, Abigail Spencer, Josh Charles, Annie Potts, Cree, Josh Segarra, Rodney Ferrell and Wattson attend an FYC screening and panel for Fox’s “Best Medicine” on the Fox Studio Lot in Los Angeles, California on May 5, 2026. Getty Images For Fox’s Tuesday night hit Best Medicine , an American take on ITV hit Doc Martin , Silverman returned to his roots as an importer of culture. It was wise to pitch it to the British CEO of an American media company. “We had a lunch where we talked about Doc Martin and our shared passion for the series and the possibility of Liz [Meriwether] being involved,” Wade says. “We were both huge fans of the original. Doc Martin was so comedic, and Martin Clunes was known for sitcoms when it launched, and I think Ben’s understanding of really why that show worked helped me and Michael (Thorn, Fox network president) make the decision to buy it.” Josh Charles, who plays the Doc Martin (Clunes) role here, says Silverman charmed the Sports Night and The Good Wife star aboard with one deep pull outside of the TV ecosystem. “When we first spoke on the phone about Best Medicine and were discussing the overall tone of the show, he mentioned an older, more-obscure film I love called Local Hero ,” Charles tells THR, referencing the 1983 British comedy-drama written and directed by Bill Forsyth. “I was surprised he knew of it and I thought it was a perfect example of what the tone of the show could be, and it was in that moment I knew I wanted to be part of it.” Charles adds, “That’s good producing as far as I’m concerned.” Ben Silverman on the set of Apple TV’s ‘Stick’ with golfer Max Homa. Apple TV This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Chuck Lorre Talks David Ellison Optimism, Scientology and the Perks (Really!) of Working for Roseanne Barr
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All October 22, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Chuck Lorre Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images If scathing anecdotes from some of the most popular TV comedies of the last four decades are your thing, perhaps you’ve noticed that Chuck Lorre released a memoir. The showrunner behind Dharma and Greg, Two and a Half Men, The Big Bang Theory, Mom, Young Sheldon and many, many, many other series released Sitcom on Oct. 13. The book include Lorre’s take on Charlie Sheen ’s Two and a Half Men meltdown, a few other sitcom stars who pushed him to the edge (Brett Butler and Cybill Shepherd) and the one who did so while also helping his career ( Roseanne Barr). Related Stories Business David Ellison (Again) Says He Plans to Combine HBO Max and Paramount+ Movies David Ellison Says Skydance Will Make Original Swings Like 'Sinners' Naturally, reviving some of these fraught narratives seem to have irked some mentioned in the book. 20th Century curiosity Tom Arnold shot back at Lorre’s claim that Arnold demanded writers add his name to scripts when he was producing then-wife Roseanne Barr’s hit series. Arnold expressed his displeasure with the accusation on X and then called Lorre “a terrible human, an angry dry drunk who lies every time he opens his mouth.” Speaking to THR days later , Barr agreed with her ex-husband’s claim on writing credits — though not the character assassination. But as I learn over a phone call with Lorre, the super-producer does not seem interested in any more back-and-forth with former colleagues now that everything is on the page. (Those who take issue with any of his recollections, he suggests towards the end of Sitcom, can “write your own book.”) Fully prepared that this book would be full of shit talking, I feared there’d be some damning story about Christine Baranski , who co-starred in the apparently quite problematic Cybill . Thanks for not bursting my bubble. Oh my god. Christine Baranski is one of the great joys of my life — to have been able to work with her, not just on that show, but on The Big Bang Theory . Among the more surprising threads in the book is that, internally at CBS, she was referred to as “the death of comedy” during casting — as were Jon Cryer and Melissa McCarthy. Did these executives ever express any contrition when proven wrong? No. Listen, the big picture is that they’re extraordinarily good at casting dramas, but casting comedies was not their strong suit. You also have to acknowledge that CBS gave me a shot to do a show about quantum physicists. Yes, we disagreed on casting, but it’d be foolish to overlook how many opportunities I had with that company to figure it out and do it right. If a prophet came to you in 1992, the year you were fired from Roseanne , and said that you’d still be publicly battling over the behind the scenes drama of that show 34 years later… how would you have reacted? I don’t know how to answer that. It was a singular, extraordinary opportunity to be on that show. While it was difficult, I also benefited from it. I don’t think anybody who worked there didn’t come out a better writer for having been there. It might have crushed their soul in the process, but we all became better. And that’s because Roseanne insisted on honest, truthful storytelling about this family. She would not suffer any glib sitcom bullshit. You write about your decade in Scientology, sometimes critically and mockingly. In the past, that institution would really go after that kind of criticism. Did you have any discussions about the potential ramifications about how to write about your experience? Because people are rarely this candid about Scientology. The whole book is an effort to tell the truth of my experience and my journey to where I am right now. But at the same time, it was important for me to put in the book that there were benefits regarding that 10-year bubble that I was in. It’d be ridiculous to ignore the fact that for every mistake that I made and every poor choice that I made… surviving it, you can take a step back and go, “Well, here’s what I got from that.” And I made a point of putting that in the book that it’s not all negative. It’s not all just trash talking this organization. I did benefit in some ways that it would be disingenuous to ignore. Have you heard from anyone in that camp? No. I don’t think it’s worth it. I don’t think anybody gives a crap. You talk about a lot of people in here. Who got a heads up? I sent the pages about Charlie [Sheen] to Charlie and he signed off on it. And I ran everything past the ex-wives. I wanted to be careful to not hurt people. There are some passing jokes in the book about Warner Brothers’ many owners since you started there, but one could argue that you’re not just an employee. On the TV side, you’re responsible for a great deal of the studio’s success in the 21st century and arguably a factor in its value. Do you feel a personal stake as it changes hands again? I just know. I’ve been there now going on 28 years. I went in 1999 and they were going through the AOL mistake. But I’ve been the beneficiary and a lot of support from that company, starting with Peter Roth, who was immensely supportive. People tend to speak very kindly about Peter Roth. He loves television. He loves storytelling. He loves to laugh. That’s not always the case with executives. Generally, they’re running scared and they’re trying to figure out how to survive the job. Peter actually loved the job and he loved comedy. He was the one who offered me a job at Fox and that led to Dharma and Greg. He went to Warner Brothers and said, “No, come here.” So I followed him, because there’s an intangible quality that I’ve always gone after — which was to work with people that love what we do. That it’s not just creating content. And I have to say that [Skydance CEO] David Ellison made that very clear to me when I met him. He doesn’t like creating content. He wants to make stories and entertain. And that speaks to me. The idea that it’s content is depressing. “ Content” is a pretty gross term. It’s loathsome. I assume this meeting with David Ellison was quite recent. Maybe a month ago? But when I hear someone in that position say, “I’m not in the content business, I’m in the storytelling business,” that’s meaningful. That’s really meaningful because that’s what I try to do. I keep my job really simple. My job is to make people laugh. It appears to be memoir season for Hollywood’s great white men: Ari Emanuel’s book, the authorized Larry David biography , Bob Iger is releasing another memoir. Is something in the air? I don’t know. ( Laughs ) Serendipity? This was a two-year project for me and I’m glad it’s done. I really am. As I was writing, I was hoping that the book can cause laughter. Otherwise, what’s the point? I’m not in the education business. I’m not in the morality business. I’ve been in the comedy business for a long time and if I’m going to write a book, hopefully it causes laughter, otherwise the book fails. How did you find the experience of recording the audiobook? I was told that it’s difficult. “How tough can it be?” It’s actually really hard because you want to perform the book. You want to make sure that the jokes land and that the stories unfold and that it’s an entirely different experience. I wrote the book to be read, not to be listened to, but audiobooks are a big deal. I actually hadn’t considered it until the book was in, really. I did the very best I could. But you’re a writer of dialogue. Your writing, historically, are spoken. Would you have considered someone else narrating this? You would have had to showrun the recording. There was no chance I was going to let anybody read this. It made no sense to me to have someone read the story of my life. Two stories from your personal life really stood out to me. First, the coincidence of buying a guitar at a bar saved your life. I won’t spoil how. Second, an ex-girlfriend prevented you from having to spend your life with a colostomy bag by helping you change your diet. In recalling these strokes of fortune, did you have any grand realizations? I have a lot of gratitude. I’ve had angels cross my path over and over again. It became very clear in writing this book how lucky I’ve been. Because of the certain people who came along at just the right time to rescue me — sometimes from myself. Are you keeping as busy as usual? Stuart Fails to Save the Universe , Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage , Leanne Morgan’s show… I still go to work every day and try and cause laughter somehow. That’s not a bad gig, right? If you write another book in 20 years… Twenty years!? ( Laughs .) If you write another book in 20 years and reveal that Leanne Morgan ran a really toxic set, it’ll really bum me out. Leanne Morgan is a magnificent human being and that is not hyperbole. Somebody who’s a successful standup comedian, not everybody can make it acting. It’s a difficult transition. And she’s done that, and it’s a very happy set because she sets the tone. That’s Leanne’s nature. THR

articles.title: Jane Krakowski to Reprise ‘Oh, Mary!’ Role on London’s West End
articles.full_text: Oct 22, 2026 4:58am PT Jane Krakowski to Reprise ‘Oh, Mary!’ Role on London’s West End By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Julia Stiles Asked Michelle Williams for Permission to Do Heath Ledger ‘DWTS’ Tribute; David Krumholtz Explains Why He Missed Reunion 2 hours ago Jane Krakowski to Reprise ‘Oh, Mary!’ Role on London’s West End 2 hours ago Mark Ronson, Jessie Reyez, Jorja Smith and More Celebrate Amy Winehouse for the Musical Genius She Was at ‘Back to Black’ 20th Anniversary Show: Concert Review 3 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source EMILIO MADRID Jane Krakowski is heading across the pond to reprise the role of Mary Todd Lincoln in “Oh, Mary!” The Tony and Olivier winner will be back in Mary’s petticoats starting Dec. 7 at London’s Trafalgar Theatre, with her six-week run ending Jan. 16. Krakowski previously played the role on Broadway for a total of 12 weeks after her original eight-week run was extended. Cole Escola’s Tony-winning play has now also extended its London run through June 5, 2027. Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN In a video announcing Krakowski’s return, the “30 Rock” star is seen practicing a British accent, even dropping the c-word. “Wait, is she still American?” Krakowski asks as she turns to the camera. Audiences will have to see the show to find out! Popular on Variety “Ghosts” star Lolly Adefope is currently playing Mary in London, with Lucy Frederick as Mary’s Chaperone, J.R. Ballantyne as Mary’s Husband’s Assistant, Vinnie Heaven as Mary’s Teacher and Syrus Lowe as Mary’s Husband. Other London Marys so far include Escola, who reprised the role for a filmed version that will air on HBO next year, Catherine Tate and Mason Alexander Park. “SNL” alum Bowen Yang is currently playing Mary on Broadway. Sam Pinkleton directs “Oh, Mary!” on the West End . Producers include Kevin McCollum and Lucas McMahon; Mike Lavoie and Carlee Briglia with Bob Boyett; The Council; Jean Doumanian Productions; Nicole Eisenberg; Jay Marcus and George Strus; Irony Point; Richard Batchelder/ Bradley Reynolds; Tyler Mount/Tommy Doyle; Nelson & Tao; Palomares Miller & Rosenberg; ShowTown Productions; Jamie Wilson Productions and Wessex Grove. articles.full_text: Oct 22, 2026 5:00am PT ‘Blippi’ Spinoff ‘Meekah’ Set at Moonbug Entertainment, the Studio Behind ‘Cocomelon’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Selome Hailu Plus Icon Selome Hailu Latest ‘Blippi’ Spinoff ‘Meekah’ Set at Moonbug Entertainment, the Studio Behind ‘Cocomelon’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago ‘Abbott Elementary’ Season 6 Premiere Hits 6.3 Million Viewers in Seven Days (EXCLUSIVE) 17 hours ago ‘Chicago Med’ Season 12 Premiere Hits 8.8 Million Viewers in Seven Days as Dick Wolf’s One Chicago Franchise Leads NBC Lineup (EXCLUSIVE) 19 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Moonbug Entertainment Moonbug Entertainment, the studio that produces popular preschool series “ Cocomelon ” and “ Blippi ,” has set its newest series. “ Meekah ” will premiere on Nov. 7 on its own YouTube channel as a spinoff. A spinoff of “Blippi,” the series stars Lauren Vaz as Blippi’s best friend. Per the official description, “While Blippi loves discovering how things work, Meekah loves jumping in and seeing what she can do, turning everyday play into adventures where kids can bounce like an astronaut, kick like a soccer player, invent new dance moves and more. She is joined on select adventures by her Mini Movers, a group of young kids who move, dance, imagine and play alongside her. Together, they help bring each adventure to life while giving kids at home an easy way to follow along and join in.” Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN On Nov. 2, Moonbug will debut a Meekah-led music video titled “Happy Place.” Then will come the official series premiere on Nov. 7, titled “Superhero Meekah Saves the City.” The episode will see Meekah and the Mini Movers defeat a giant cardboard robot. Moonbug also has plans to release a music video called “Bubble Pop” and a mermaid-themed episode that will help children practice different swim strokes and learn about ocean creatures and sustainability. New episodes will premiere every other Saturday and run for roughly 15 minutes. According to Moonbug, the series focuses on “imaginative storytelling, energetic physical play, games and original music, with adventures spanning fantasy role play, dance, creative challenges and more. Movements are designed to be big, clear and safe for preschoolers to try at home, with Meekah modeling checking for space and getting help from grown-ups.” Popular on Variety Aimed at ages 3-6, “Meekah” utilizes Moonbug’s core learning principles, a UCLA-backed initiative first reported on by Variety in April . In a June interview , the chief creative officer Rich Hickey expanded on the company’s four areas of focus: “navigating real-life moments, modeling positive relationships, promoting learning through play and telling authentically inclusive stories.” “Meekah has an incredible ability to ignite curiosity and make kids feel like they can jump right in with her,” said Lizzy Easterday, Senior Director of Creative at Moonbug Entertainment. “We wanted to build a series around that spirit, where kids aren’t just watching the adventure unfold – they’re part of it. Movement is at the heart of every episode, giving children opportunities to jump, dance, imagine and express themselves in their own way. It’s about inspiring curiosity, celebrating creativity, building confidence and reminding kids that there’s no one right way to play.” See a teaser for “Meekah” below. Rowling Claims Trans Activism in the 21st Century Is ‘Elitist,’ Pens Essay Defending Her Views: They ‘Haven’t Changed’ Despite ‘Death, Rape and Torture Threats’ 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of the TV Festival The TV Festival , previously known as Edinburgh TV Festival , has unveiled the first details of its inaugural event in Manchester. Set to be held for the first time in the northern city next year, the festival will keep its four-day schedule but will take place later in the month than usual. Previously the festival, which has been held in the Scottish city of Edinburgh for fifty years, would traditionally take place in the last week of August. Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN Next year’s edition will take place after the U.K.’s August public holiday, running from Aug. 31 to Sept. 3. Popular on Variety The change of location has had a mixed response, with many citing Edinburgh’s charm and proximity to annual comedy festival the Edinburgh Fringe as reason’s for the festival success. The decision was made by The TV Foundation, a charity that organizes the festival, who believe the move will make the event more accessible to the television community. It will take place at Versa Studios Manchester – formerly the site of the iconic Granada Studios — and Aviva Studios, which is the home of the Manchester International Festival and Factory International. The area has been home to some of Britain’s best-known television shows including “Coronation Street,” “University Challenge” and “The Royle Family.” “With Greater Manchester as our new home, we’re ready to grow and realise the Festival’s full potential over the coming years; whether that’s extending the programme into evening sessions, new creative partnerships or opening the doors to public-facing events or screenings,” said the festival’s CEO, Campbell Glennie. “We have the potential to create a city-wide celebration of the TV and broader creative industries for the next generation.” The advisory chair for next year’s addition will be Sony Pictures Television’s president of international production, Wayne Garvie. Garvie said: “I feel privileged to be bringing the Television Festival to a city I love, a city renowned for innovation, culture, and having a damn good time. We’ll make this an unforgettable event, with emerging voices and global names, argument and laughter, so come and join us to plot the future of our industry.” Sally Field Becomes Oldest Emmy Winner in Her Category and Shades Paramount-Warner Bros. articles.title: JJ Watt Named CBS Sports’ New Lead NFL Analyst in Multiyear Deal
articles.full_text: Oct 22, 2026 5:41am PT JJ Watt Named CBS Sports’ New Lead NFL Analyst in Multiyear Deal By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest JJ Watt Named CBS Sports’ New Lead NFL Analyst in Multiyear Deal 1 hour ago Comcast Q3 Sees Continued Broadband Downturn, Despite Boosts From World Cup, Peacock 3 hours ago Jake Tapper Sketches Work Outside CNN: Graphic Novel Probes Life of ‘Butcher’ Klaus Barbie 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Buckner/Variety/REX/Shutterstock Skydance is handing a pretty big NFL ball to JJ Watt . The former defensive end will take on one of the biggest on-air roles in sports after officially being named the new lead NFL analyst for CBS Sports . He is taking the post on a regular basis following the exit of his predecessor, Tony Romo. Watt will continue to call CBS’ top games alongside Jim Nantz and Tracy Wolfson — including next season when the network telecasts Super Bowl LXII from Atlanta. Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN “I’ve had a front-row seat to JJ’s growth as a top-tier broadcaster, watching him tackle this role just like he did his hall-of-fame playing career,” said David Berson, chairman of the global sports group at Skydance, CBS’ corporate parent, in a statement. “He’s insightful, entertaining, passionate, meticulous in his preparation, and the ultimate teammate. He has a unique ability to see things and communicate to fans of all levels. We are thrilled to have him leading our NFL coverage.” Popular on Variety Watt joined CBS Sports in 2023 as a studio analyst on “The NFL Today.” Last season, Watt moved to the booth to call games with Ian Eagle and Evan Washburn. At the start of the 2026 season, he began calling games with the network’s lead team, working with Nantz and Wolfson. He has been filling in for Romo, who in September pleaded no contest to a charge of operating while intoxicated stemming from an incident that took place in Milwaukee in July . At the time, Romo said he hoped to return. He did not. CBS Sports and the former quarterback said earlier this month that they would split , a move sports-media aficionados attributed to some disillusionment with Romo’s recent on-air performance. Watt also has critical on-the-field experience, having played for the Houston Texans and Arizona Cardinals. He is the only player in NFL history to record multiple seasons with at least 20 sacks. TV-sports outlets have been pouring out money to lure top NFL announcers , with Fox and Disney shelling out top dollar to lure, respectively, Tom Brady and Troy Aikman and Joe Buck. Many top announcers’ contracts are expected to lapse after the end of this season, including not only Aikman’s, but Greg Olsen’s at Fox, and Al Michaels’ at Amazon. ESPN has secured Buck to a new deal — but so far, not Aikman — and Amazon has signed Kirk Herbstreit, who also calls college game at ESPN, to provisional terms. ESPN and Amazon have so far declined to comment on the status of those announcers’ deals. TV networks rushed to line up top talent to call games after the NFL struck a pivotal 11-year rights deal in 2021 . At the time, the thought from many TV sports chiefs was that they had to spend money to make money. Romo carved out new terrain at CBS Sports after revealing a knack for predicting game play — all but forcing CBS to re-sign the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback to a multi-season pact in 2020 valued at around $17 million a year. Since that time, most of CBS’ contemporaries have followed suit. When ESPN signed former Fox Sports mainstays Buck and Aikman to deals in 2022 to call “Monday Night Football, ” it was seen as a critical move that would help the Disney-backed sports-media giant soothe what had become a troubled relationship with the NFL. Amazon lured NBC Sports’ Al Michaels and ESPN’s Herbstreit to serve as the voices for “Thursday Night Football.” And Fox secured the services of none other than Brady , a move that crowded out sportscaster Olsen. People familiar with the market estimate top football-booth personnel can earn between $15 million and $20 million per season. CBS Sports may have other talent issues to juggle in weeks to come. Ian Eagle, a veteran who calls secondary NFL games for CBS Sports, is also believed to have a contract that is set to lapse. articles.full_text: Oct 22, 2026 6:00am PT ‘Heated Rivalry’ to Release in Movie Theaters, Two Episodes at a Time Regal is leading the limited run in more than 650 U.S. theaters. By Marc Malkin Plus Icon Marc Malkin Senior Editor, Culture and Events marcmalkin Latest Alexander Skarsgård on His Wacky ‘Wicker’ Red Carpet Looks: From Clear Shoes and a Multicolored Skirt to a Gray Wig Inspired by Co-Star Olivia Colman 16 hours ago Lea Michele Returning for ‘Glee’ Reboot as Rachel Berry (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago Queer Bodybuilder Drama ‘Test’ Acquired by Dark Star Pictures (EXCLUSIVE) 24 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source HBO Max/Crave Forget about going to the cottage. “ Heated Rivalry ” fans will be going to movie theaters in November. Almost a year after the queer hockey romance series premiered in the U.S., Regal will release all six episodes in more than 650 theaters nationwide for a limited run Nov. 6-30. “When a series connects with audiences the way ‘Heated Rivalry’ has, we look for ways to bring it to the big screen and give fans a reason to experience it together,” Brooks LeBoeuf, senior vice president of U.S. content at Regal, said in a statement Thursday. “Nearly a year after its premiere, we’re proud to work with our partners to turn a season fans have watched again and again into a true theatrical event. It’s a chance to celebrate the story, its creators and its performances before Season 2 arrives in 2027.” Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN Based on Rachel Reid ’s bestselling novels, “Heated Rivalry” follows rival hockey players Shane Hollander ( Hudson Williams ) and Ilya Rozanov ( Connor Storrie ) as they secretly fall in love. The series quickly became a global hit, with Williams and Storrie becoming two of Hollywood’s most sought-after actors. Written and directed by Jacob Tierney, “Heated Rivalry,” currently in production of its second season, also features François Arnaud , Robbie G.K. , Christina Chang , Ksenia Daniela Kharlamova, Sophie Nélisse and Dylan Walsh. Popular on Variety During the theatrical run, which Regal is leading in partnership with Sphere Abacus, moviegoers can revisit the series in order across three paired screenings: Episodes 1 and 2 (“Rookies” and “Olympians”), Episodes 3 and 4 (“Hunter” and “Rose”), and Episodes 5 and 6 (“I’ll Believe in Anything” and “The Cottage”). Tickets for each pairing cost $9.99. “‘Heated Rivalry’ is a global phenomenon creating a rush of social media and press activity wherever it lands,” said Hana Palmer, executive director, global distribution and partnerships at Sphere Abacus. “We’re very excited to give audiences the opportunity to watch the drama unfold on big screens in North America, the U.K., Australia and New Zealand.” Regal screenings will also feature welcome content from the series’ cast and director, while participating locations will offer limited-time themed cocktails: Summer in Montreal and Russians Don’t Blush. In-theater marketing support is provided by PaperAirplane. Advance tickets for “Heated Rivalry” are available now at theater box offices, on mobile apps and through REGmovies.com . articles.title: Egyptian Screenwriter Mariam Naoum on the Struggle for Arab Series to Find Buyers: ‘We’re Suffocating Inside’
articles.full_text: Oct 22, 2026 6:40am PT Egyptian Screenwriter Mariam Naoum on the Struggle for Arab Series to Find Buyers: ‘We’re Suffocating Inside’ CineGouna Series head seeks to clear obstacles that hinder writing talent in the Arab world By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest Sequel to Egyptian Hit ‘Sleepless Nights’ Eyes 2027 Shoot as New Details Revealed (EXCLUSIVE) 20 hours ago Sharjah Film Festival Expands Opportunities for Young Filmmakers: ‘There Is No Shortage of Talent’ 24 hours ago Sharjah Film Festival Unveils Lineup With ‘Gohan,’ ‘Monster Mia,’ Emirati Talent 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of GFF Seasoned Egyptian screenwriter and producer Mariam Naoum sees no shortage of creative talent in Arab television. The harder question is how to give that talent the time, development and routes to market it needs to thrive and build lasting careers. As head of the newly launched CineGouna Series, El Gouna Film Festival ’s first development program dedicated to television, she is trying to tackle some of the obstacles standing in their way. Asked what the industry needs most between time, money and marketing, her answer is clear: “I’ll choose time and marketing.” Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN The move marks El Gouna’s first formal expansion into series, bringing television into CineGouna, the festival’s industry arm. Its inaugural six-week lab, held ahead of the festival, incubated six projects, with writers developing a series bible and pilot before pitching their work at the festival to broadcasters, producers and directors. Popular on Variety The inaugural cohort comprises “Sent From Above,” by Lebanon’s Dareen Shamseddine, Egyptian projects “Marketing for Beginners,” by Shaimaa Gohar, “To the Edge,” by Mamdouh Salah and Muhammed Abd El-Sattar, “There’s Something Wrong,” by Marim Dagher, and “Half an Hour,” by Mohammed Elsayed Taha, as well as Saudi writer Rana Wael Matar’s “Why, Soad?” For Naoum, series require a different development process from films, from the workflow itself to how projects ultimately reach buyers. Streaming has opened new opportunities for Arab television, but she sees too few buyers for the projects being developed. “You have, in the Arab world, maybe three or four platforms. They cannot cater to the whole market, so you have more projects than they can afford to buy,” she observes. “Maybe the thing that we need to work on is to open more markets outside the region, for either those of Arab origins, like the diaspora, or maybe follow the example of Turkey and Latin America, and the way they manage to sell their projects outside.” “So I think this is the time to start this, because we’re suffocating inside.” Author, screenwriter and producer Haitham Dabbour (“ The Tale of Daye’s Family ”), founder of Irth, a regional content development platform and collaborative writers’ room, shares that concern, arguing that fewer owners means less competition and less room to take risks. “The fewer the platforms, the more cautious they tend to be, and the more they rely on safe, proven formulas,” Dabbour contends. “As a result, the ability to develop and launch truly different kinds of projects becomes much more difficult.” He also points to piracy and rights protection as barriers to expanding the market. “The number of platforms will remain limited as long as we do not combat piracy and protect creators’ rights.” Acclaimed Egyptian television and film director Mariam Abou Ouf (”Whose Empire”) shares that unease. “When it comes to the financing and production landscape, I believe we are approaching a deadlock,” she warns. “The increasing monopolization of the industry is creating a difficult environment, one that is neither healthy nor sustainable.” Yet Abou Ouf sees streaming itself as transformative. “For the first time, a television series has a life that extends far beyond its original broadcast,” she notes. “Audiences can discover it years later, revisit it, and watch it again and again.” More broadly, Naoum has seen Arab television open up to a wider range of storytelling. “When I started, we didn’t have horror, we didn’t have a lot of psychodrama, we didn’t have a lot of crime,” she points out. “Now we have more, so it’s changing.” That creative range was only one consideration in selecting projects for CineGouna Series. “We were looking for projects that are producible, so it wasn’t only a creative approach,” Naoum explains. Before making the selections, she consulted platforms about what they were looking for and took those needs into account alongside the creative merits of each project. Once selected, the writers worked with mentors during the six-week lab to develop their projects. “The lab wasn’t for established writers,” Naoum stresses. “It was mainly for young writers who need the networking and this kind of bridging to the industry.” That connection to the wider industry is central to the program. “I tried to cater projects for the platforms, so that they can find good projects that were incubated in this lab, so they have the trust that our lab worked on this,” she continues. “It’s like shortening the process for the platforms to hunt for projects. We become the ‘middle man’ in that sense.” The question of how those projects might eventually travel beyond the region presents another challenge. Naoum argues that culturally rooted stories can travel if they are well executed. “Our problem in traveling, I don’t think it’s either quality or subject,” she stresses. “We still don’t have the know-how of distribution for series. So it’s more a question of marketing than the creative side.” For CineGouna Series, the first test will be whether the six projects make it beyond the lab. “For me, success is that one or more of the projects can be bought by broadcasters or producers,” Naoum concludes. “To find the way for it to be executed from development to broadcast.” Matthew Rhys Makes Emmy History as First Person to Win Two Lead Acting Emmys in One Night and First Man to Win All Three Top Acting Prizes Never Mind the IP, Here’s How Original Ideas Dominated This Year’s Emmy Races Emmys 2026 Party Guide With Katherine LaNasa, Quinta Brunson and Richard Gadd Rob Reiner Wins Posthumous Emmy for ‘The Bear’ Hiro Murai Becomes First Asian Director to Win Emmy for Comedy Directing With ‘Widow’s Bay’ Seven Variety Cover Stars Win 2026 Emmys Loading comments...

articles.full_text: Oct 22, 2026 7:00am PT Lego Unveils Daft Punk Set Based on 2007 ‘Alive’ Tour, Short Film Collab Set to ‘Human After All’ By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest TV Festival Manchester Sets Dates, Venues and Advisory Chair 2 hours ago J.K. Fans of both Daft Punk and Lego are about to get lucky. The electronic music duo and the toy brick brand have partnered for a new multi-platform collaboration spanning product, content and brand experiences. The partnership includes a Lego set based on the stage design from Daft Punk’s 2007 “Alive” tour, submitted on the toy company’s official crowdsourcing platform Lego Ideas. Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN Created by a father-son duo from Belgium, the “Daft Punk Concert” was first entered into a music-themed Lego Ideas competition in 2020, where it was crowned grand prize winner. It has since also reached 10,000 supports on Lego Ideas, meaning it will advance into the next stage of development. Popular on Variety The fan model of Daft Punk’s 2007 ‘Alive’ concert set which will be developed by Lego The set is based on the pyramid stage from the duo’s 2007 tour. “The pyramid stage is one of the most recognisable expressions of Daft Punk’s visual world, so it feels fitting that this fan-created design will be centre stage of this partnership,” said Daft Punk creative director Cédric Hervet. “Fans have always played an important part in Daft Punk’s story, and we are excited to see that creativity reflected through the Lego universe.” To launch the partnership, Lego and Daft Punk have also collaborated on a 48-second film in which the duo appear in Lego Minifigure form, complete with helmets, as they follow a holographic red brick through a mysterious desert landscape. The soundtrack is based on a bassline tribute from the band’s 2001 album “Discovery” as well as the title track from their 2005 album “Human After All.” In a press releases announcing the collaboration, Lego tease more offerings, saying fans will see “the duo brought to life in new ways across the Lego brand, through a mashup of surprising events and content that crosses music, culture and creative spaces.” This isn’t the first time the duo have taken Lego form of course: they also appeared as Minifigures in Pharrell’s 2024 Lego-animated documentary “Piece by Piece,” having collaborated with him and Nile Rodgers on the hit track “Get Lucky.” “What makes this partnership so special is the enduring appeal both brands share. Like the Lego brand, Daft Punk inspires generations through creativity, innovation and a deep connection with fans,” said Julia Goldin, Lego’s chief product and marketing officer. “We’re excited to build on these foundations to reimagine the Daft Punk legacy in a fresh and unexpected way, creating something unique that resonates with fans across all ages. articles.full_text: Oct 22, 2026 7:10am PT Comcast Plans Major Layoffs as It Preps for NBCU Spin-Off, Sees $1 Billion-Plus Restructuring Charge in Q4 By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Comcast Plans Major Layoffs as It Preps for NBCU Spin-Off, Sees $1 Billion-Plus Restructuring Charge in Q4 17 minutes ago Spotify Hums Along in Q3, Reaching 306 Million Paid Subscribers: ‘There Is More Runway Ahead’ 4 hours ago Will Elon Musk Help the Ellisons Pay Down Skydance’s Massive Debt? John Malone Predicts Tech Mogul’s SpaceX Could Invest up to $10 Billion Into Media Company 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images for Comcast Comcast is gearing up for significant job cuts in its cable and telecom business in the coming weeks, as the media conglomerate restructures ahead the expected spin-off of NBCUniversal in 2027. On the company’s third-quarter 2026 earning call, CFO Jason Armstrong said Comcast expects to take a restructuring charge of more than $1 billion in Q4. “We expect to have a significant charge in the fourth quarter related mostly to our transformation efforts, and I would quantify that at over $1 billion,” he told analysts. Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN The scope of Comcast’s layoffs is yet to be determined, with individual teams currently assessing what the impact will be, according to two sources familiar with the situation. For now, the layoffs are expected to affect the Comcast Cable side of the business, not NBCU divisions. Popular on Variety Armstrong said the restructuring “is to get ahead of cost actions that will facilitate sort of a fast start into 2027” and are aimed at “strengthening our competitive position.” He continued: “We don’t look at it as a cost-cutting exercise. This is the ability to simplify in order to move faster, to be more nimble in decision-making, and I think really create capacity, you know, to invest for growth.” Part of Comcast’s growth initiatives involve stepping up its push into wireless services and business services. For the third quarter, revenue in Comcast’s connectivity and platforms business fell 2.7% to $19.66 billion, as it saw continued net losses of broadband and cable TV subscribers. Revenue from NBCU’s TV, film and theme parks operations rose 6.5% to $10.54 billion. Comcast in June announced that it will spin off NBCUniversal (together with Sky) in a tax-free transaction expected to be completed in mid-2027. Execs on the Q3 call reiterated that the spin-off timeline remains on track. The plans for the NBCU spin come after the separation of its cable networks (excluding Bravo) and other businesses into Versant Media, which closed in January of this year. As of Dec. 31, 2025, Comcast has about 179,000 employees. Comcast’s plans to cut jobs in cable TV, broadband and wireless segments were reported Wednesday by Bloomberg. articles.title: Aamir Khan Tears Up About His Family, Shares Updates on ‘3 Idiots 2,’ ‘Andaz Apna Apna 2’ at Singapore Film Fest
articles.full_text: Oct 22, 2026 7:22am PT Aamir Khan Tears Up About His Family, Shares Updates on ‘3 Idiots 2,’ ‘Andaz Apna Apna 2’ at Singapore Film Fest By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘The History Boys’ Returns to London West End After 20 Years, With Nicholas Hytner Back Directing Alan Bennett’s Play 6 hours ago ‘Mother Bhumi,’ ‘Rehana Maryam Noor’ and ‘The Tourist’ Producers Head to Indonesia’s JAFF Market for New Exchange Program 7 hours ago Netflix, Bengali Streamer Hoichoi Partner to Bring Series to Hindi, Tamil and Telugu Audiences 7 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Lim Aamir Khan broke down onstage at the Singapore International Film Festival on Thursday as he recalled realizing, during the COVID-19 lockdown, that three decades of nonstop work had cost him years with his family. The Bollywood superstar, who was handed the festival’s Screen Icon Award by Hong Kong director Peter Chan Ho-sun, also shed light on sequels to “3 Idiots” and “Andaz Apna Apna” during a wide-ranging in-conversation session moderated by Singapore comedian Rishi Budhrani. Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN The emotional moment came late in the evening, when Khan was asked about the weakest point of his journey. He described himself as a lifelong workaholic who ate, slept and dreamed films, and said his family had always been understanding enough to leave him alone. Popular on Variety “When I was sitting in COVID and I was thinking, I said, you know, about 30 years have passed of my life. And it’s okay to work like a madman, completely obsessed with what you’re doing for one year, two years, five years. But if it goes on for 30 years, I mean, you’ve lost your relationships. Your kids have grown up, they’re adults now. So I felt a deep sense of loss,” Khan said. He paused, broke down, apologized and gathered himself as the audience broke into applause. An audience member handed him a box of tissues. Khan, wiping his tears away, said the experience pushed him to make a major change, and that for the last four years he has deliberately carved out time for his family and close friends. “I’m so glad that this thought occurred to me when I was 56 and not when I was 86, when it would be really too late to do anything about it,” he said. On a lighter note, Khan was asked whether a sequel to “3 Idiots,” the 2009 campus comedy directed by Rajkumar Hirani, is in the works. “Well, I’m not allowed to say a lot,” Khan said. “I think I can say this much, that yes, Raju is working on the script. In fact, hopefully once I’m back in the next couple of weeks, he’s going to narrate the final version to me. So, fingers crossed.” According to Budhrani, Khan had phoned Hirani in front of him the previous day to check whether he could share the news, and the filmmaker gave his blessing – though Hirani didn’t pick up the first time, as Khan had changed his number. Khan said he had shut his phone a few weeks earlier and is now off all apps, having found that scrolling could swallow three hours at a stretch. With many fans having shouted out their love for Rajkumar Santoshi’s 1994 cult comedy “Andaz Apna Apna,” Khan was asked whether a sequel is on the cards. “Well, I know that Raj Santoshi is working on something,” he said. “So let’s see what happens.” Asked if there was anything more, he replied: “Yeah, that’s all.” In the same answer about his weakest moments, Khan recounted an earlier low point from the start of his career. After his 1988 debut “Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak” became a hit, he signed nine films within six months, reasoning that if established stars could juggle dozens of projects, he could handle 10. Once shooting began, he realized his mistake and would come home and weep to his then-wife Reena. The films then flopped one after another, and he was branded a “one-film wonder.” “At that time, mentally and emotionally, I felt like I’m in quicksand. I’m sinking slowly, and the more I’m struggling to get out, the deeper I’m going,” Khan said. At that point, Mahesh Bhatt, then riding high on “Saaransh,” “Arth” and “Naam,” offered him a film. Khan had vowed to commit only when he loved the script, the director and the producer, and he didn’t like the script. After a sleepless night, he turned Bhatt down. “If I had compromised with that and I had been practical, and I had, you know, said, ‘Yes, sir, I’m doing the film,’ I think my entire career would have been a series of compromises,” he said. They would go on to work together in “Dil Hai Ke Manta Nahin” and “Hum Hain Rahi Pyar Ke.” Accepting the Screen Icon Award, Khan thanked the festival and said that having Chan present it made the moment special. “Filmmaking is a collective art form, and a lot of people contribute to each other’s work,” he said. Asked why his films have resonated in China, Khan said “3 Idiots” took off there and across the wider region east of India after young viewers began passing it around, prompting them to seek out his other work. “I mean, it’s the truth. For me, my popularity in China is thanks to piracy,” he said, while stressing that he is not an advocate of it. He attributed the deeper connection to what he called a shared “emotional key” between Indian and Chinese audiences, recalling that watching “Dangal” in a Chinese theater felt like watching it in India. Khan also revealed that he holds 50 to 60 test screenings of 25 people each for his films, and that the first test screening of “Taare Zameen Par” was a disaster. For smaller films whose budgets can’t absorb his usual fee, he said he skips the fee and takes a back end instead, so the producer is protected if the film doesn’t work. On artificial intelligence, Khan said he views it as another filmmaking tool, much like VFX, and pointed to a castle set that would once have required 200 carpenters to build. “My common sense is telling me that in the short term, for sure, people are going to lose jobs,” he said. Khan, who last attended the festival nine years ago with “Secret Superstar,” also has a 25th anniversary screening of “Lagaan,” his first film as producer, lined up at the festival on Friday. articles.title: Skydance Nordics & Germany Boss Says “We’re Doing Our Best To Manage The Change” After Mega-Merger
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Andy Burnham Becomes First UK Prime Minister To Join ‘Celebrity Gogglebox’ TV Festival Unveils Dates, Venues & Advisory Chair For First-Ever Greater Manchester Edition Canal+ “Making Progress” In Opposing French VAT Hike That It Says Would Force Subs Increases & Cuts View All October 22, 2026 5:25am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Christina Sulebakk Courtesy of HBO Max “We’re doing our best to manage the change but I’m not naïve.” That was the verdict of Christina Sulebakk , who runs the newly-minted Skydance ‘s operation in the Nordics , Germany and Benelux, over how she is approacing the $110B merger in her territories. Sulebakk, who has been with various iterations of the newly-merged group for 15 years, beginning at HBO Europe, added that “the transformation feels more substantial because the entire media ecosystem is evolving simultaneously.” Speaking at the Munich Media Days conference, Sulebakk was asked about the “elephant in the room” and considered how “some are energized by change and see it as a constant source of opportunity,” while “others naturally worry about what it means for their role, their team, their leaders, their relationships, and the future.” Related Stories Executives Elon Musk & Larry Ellison Will Join Forces To Boost Both Starlink And Skydance, John Malone Predicts Executives Versant Unlikely To Acquire Skydance Cable Networks If They Hit The Market, CEO Mark Lazarus Says Sulebakk is one of the first senior international Skydance executives to speak publicly since the merger closed earlier this month. The majority of Skydance international is being led out of L.A. by JB Perrette, although questions remain over the final shape of the non-U.S. part of David Ellison’s behemoth, including how territories may eventually get divided up. Watch on Deadline “We’re doing our best to manage the change, but I’m not naïve,” said Sulebakk. “I understand that change will have an impact. What may feel even more significant is that the entire industry is changing at the same time. RTL is going through change, ProSieben is going through change, and Netflix is going through change.” She said her approach is about “being present” and communicating. “From a leadership perspective, communication is essential,” she added. “Everything starts with communication: being present, honest, and as transparent as possible. That means sharing as much as you’re allowed to share.” “I’m not here to hold a pen and have a title” Once bedded in, Sulebakk, who took on the German-speaking markets and Benelux territories at the old Warner Bros. Discovery at the start of 2026, stressed that she wants to be an active leader. She pointed to the potential for partnerships with platforms like YouTube and talked up windowing possibilities on the likes of Netflix, Prime Video and Hulu. “I’m not here to hold a pen and have a title,” she added. “I want things to change. I want to look for opportunities in the market.” Skydance Nordics & Germany Boss Spotlights Her Approach Town Hall Takeaways; Are Stock Jitters Valid Or A Market Overreaction? articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac The Lede Company Acquires Lauren Winslade’s London-Based Agency Aisle 8 Charades Boards Juho Kuosmanen’s ‘Dream Come True’ As Production Wraps Across Europe ‘Normal People’ Stars Paul Mescal & Daisy Edgar-Jones Among Signatories Of Open Letter Supporting Sally Rooney After UK Book Ban View All October 22, 2026 5:35am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Lauren Winslade. Lede Company The Lede Company has acquired London-based fashion and lifestyle agency Aisle 8 , Aisle 8 founder Lauren Winslade will join as President of Brand for The Lede Company London, bringing her full team of 21 into the firm. Matthew Avento will continue to oversee the Talent and Strategic Communications divisions at the firm’s London office. Founded in 2014 and based in Farringdon, London, Aisle 8’s current roster includes MERIT, Ferrari, Astrid & Miyu, Our Place, Jigsaw, Dr Dennis Gross, Wonderskin, Bicester Village, Jo Loves, and Ruggable, and UK launch work for Away, Vuori, Kulfi, and Le Monde Gourmand. Related Stories Legal Jonathan Majors & Manager Entertainment 360 Part Ways; Actor Facing Domestic Violence Allegations In NYC News Skydance Nordics & Germany Boss Says "We're Doing Our Best To Manage The Change" After Mega-Merger The agency’s services include brand development, media relations, influencer and talent partnerships, social strategy, and strategic counsel across fashion, beauty, and consumer lifestyle sectors. All of these services will be absorbed into Lede’s operations. Watch on Deadline Winslade’s career spans two decades across agency, in-house, and global corporate roles. She began at luxury agency Aurelia PR working on Versace, Salvatore Ferragamo, and Cîroc Vodka, before moving to Ketchum and later Hill & Knowlton, where she led fashion and beauty strategy for clients including Intel and P&G. In 2007, she joined fashion e-tailer my-wardrobe.com, building the company’s global PR function across the UK, US, Australia, Scandinavia, and the Middle East. She was recruited by Harrods in 2012 to head PR & Communications, where she led a 20-person team shaping the store’s omni-channel presence. She launched Aisle 8 in 2014. “We are so excited to add Lauren, a brilliant brand builder, and her incredible Aisle 8 team to The Lede Company London,” Christine Su, Co-CEO of The Lede Company, said in a statement. “With a rare instinct for turning brands into cultural movements, Lauren has built one of London’s most respected communications agencies. The team’s deep relationships across UK media and their expertise in everyday luxury will both help us better serve our clients and further expand our presence internationally.” Winslade added: “When I launched Aisle 8 in 2014, I saw a gap in the market for an agency built on relationships, commercial focus and a digital-first approach to communications. A decade on, joining Lede brings the scale, talent, expertise, and ambition to take that vision even further. More than an acquisition, this is an opportunity to build something bigger for our clients and our people, and I’m thrilled to be starting this next chapter together.” Skydance Nordics & Germany Boss Spotlights Her Approach Town Hall Takeaways; Are Stock Jitters Valid Or A Market Overreaction?
