articles.title: Space 11 & SK Films Bringing Artemis II To The Big Screen With ‘Return To The Moon: The Story Of Artemis II’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Space 11 & SK Films Bringing Artemis II To The Big Screen With ‘Return To The Moon: The Story Of Artemis II’ Neon Joins Yuval Abraham & Rachel Szor’s Explosive Gaza-Israel Doc ‘NAZA’ ‘Dune: Part Three’ Smashes BFI Imax Record With 33,000 Admissions Sold In First 24 Hours View All October 22, 2026 5:58am Add us as a Google Preferred Source NASA's Artemis II Space Launch System rocket carrying the Orion spacecraft lifts off from Launch Complex 39B at Kennedy Space Center. Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images EXCLUSIVE : Space 11 Corp. and SK Films are behind Return to the Moon: The Story of Artemis II , a new space film with Duncan Copp and Christopher Riley directing. The producers are targeting a PLF rollout for the film, which they say will combine NASA’s real Artemis II mission imagery with the voices of the four astronauts who lived it. Worldwide theatrical release is targeted for summer 2027. The synopsis reads: “Between April 1 and 11, 2026, the crew of the spacecraft Integrity traveled 695,081 miles and reached 252,756 miles from Earth, setting a new record for human spaceflight. The film follows the mission from the launch pad to splashdown in the Pacific.” Related Stories News 'CBS Mornings' To Hold Town Hall With Artemis Mission Astronauts News Artemis II Crew Successfully Splashes Down Off San Diego Coast Space 11 says it is collaborating with NASA under a Space Act Agreement to shoot giant-screen interviews with the Artemis II crew: Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, Mission Specialist Christina Koch and Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency. Watch on Deadline The narrative will be interwoven by the four astronauts in their own words and NASA’s high-resolution photography and footage, reformatted for giant screens. A 45 minute version and a shorter format are being planned to go out via SK’s network of giant-screen and specialty theaters, including IMAX theaters, museums, science-centers, and other institutional venues. The film will also be offered to school groups. Duncan Copp and Christopher Riley have both worked with NASA’s astronauts, engineers and scientists, past and present. Copp and Riley produced Ron Howard-presented In the Shadow of the Moon , winner of the World Cinema Documentary Audience Award at Sundance. Riley, a two-time BAFTA nominee, has worked with the Artemis II crew before, on hit immersive experience The Moonwalkers: A Journey with Tom Hanks , which he co-wrote with Hanks. The film is produced by Andrea Iervolino ( Ferrari ), founder of Space 11. Producer Nicola Allieta will also participate in this production. SK, the natural history and science content specialist, most recently released Ocean Dreams , narrated by Shailene Woodley. Andrea Iervolino, Founder of Space 11, stated: “Artemis II belongs to everyone who looked up at the Moon in April. We are honored to tell this story in collaboration with NASA and alongside the four astronauts who took us there. Our responsibility is to make a film that everyone behind this mission, from the teams at NASA and the Canadian Space Agency to the families who waited at home, will watch with pride. With Duncan Copp and Christopher Riley, who know this crew and this history as few filmmakers do, and with SK Films, we will share that journey with audiences around the world.” Bert Ulrich, Executive Vice President of Production at Space 11 and former NASA Film and Television Liaison, added: “In more than two decades at NASA, I learned that nothing moves people like real imagery and the voices of those who were actually there. This film is built on both: NASA’s own photography and footage, and the Artemis II crew recounting the flight themselves. On a giant screen, it is as close as most of us will ever come to flying aboard Integrity. If it inspires young people to reach for a seat on a future mission, it will have done what the best space documentaries have always done.” “NASA’s Artemis II Mission is the perfect subject for giant screen cinema: it invites audiences to experience a historic accomplishment, with the extraordinarily personal perspective of its astronauts, on a scale unparalleled by any other cinematic experience” said Wendy MacKeigan, CEO of SK Films. “We are excited to be working with Space 11 and the brilliant creative team to bring this film to audiences around the world.” Skydance Nordics & Germany Boss Spotlights Her Approach Town Hall Takeaways; Are Stock Jitters Valid Or A Market Overreaction? articles.title: Investigation Discovery Buys SXSW True-Crime Doc ‘My Brother’s Killer’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Peter White Peter White Executive Editor, Television @peterzwhite More Stories By Peter Investigation Discovery Buys SXSW True-Crime Doc ‘My Brother’s Killer’ Is Competitive Barbecue The Next Big Sport? Wheelhouse & Peyton Manning’s Omaha Put Their Money Where Their Mouths Are Greenwich Entertainment Buys Philip Byron’s ‘Spin Wars’ View All October 22, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source EXCLUSIVE : My Brother’s Killer, the true-crime documentary directed by Circus of Books’ Rachel Mason , has landed at Investigation Discovery . The film, which is exec produced by The Decline of Western Civilization director Penelope Spheeris, will debut on the Skydance-owned cable network on December 3. It comes after the doc premiered at SXSW earlier this year. It followed that up with a festival run that saw it win the Best Documentary Jury Award at the Outshine LGBTQ+ Film Festival and ahead of its launch at the AFI Fest on October 24. Related Stories Legal Dan Schneider's 'Quiet On Set' Defamation Suit Shut Down By Appeal Judges In Big Win For WBD News Octavia Spencer Wins First Emmy After Billy Newton was found murdered on October 29, 1990, his case was forgotten by most but haunted many: from the LAPD detectives first at the scene to his family in Wisconsin, fellow adult performers and LGBQT+ community members in West Hollywood – who were left wondering: who would want to harm someone as beloved as Billy? My Brother’s Killer follows Mason as she investigates his case, partnering with the LAPD, London’s family and friends, as well as authors and podcasters Christopher Rice and Eric Shaw Quinn. The film shows how original assumptions, overlooked evidence, and new theories help find the missing puzzle pieces in order to get to the truth. Watch on Deadline The doc, which features personal archival footage of Newton and interviews with his friends, ultimately leads to the shocking revelation of Newton’s actual killer. Produced by FutureClown Productions, Josh Braun, Ben Braun and James Cude also serve as exec producers, while Dion Labriola serves as producer. “From the moment we saw Rachel Mason’s powerful film and finished processing the stunning revelations of its final moments, we knew we wanted to use our platform to bring this story to the widest possible audience. My Brother’s Killer chronicles how one man’s tragic passing inspired a decades long pursuit of the truth and in doing so delivers a deeply moving portrait of Billy Newton and the underserved community that refused to let him be forgotten,” said Jason Sarlanis, President of ID. From Nov. 6-30, fans can experience all six episodes of Season 1 on a screen befitting of Shane (Hudson Williams) and Ilya’s (Connor Storrie) cinematic love story with a limited theatrical release at more than 275 Regal Cinema locations nationwide, in partnership with Sphere Abacus and Crave . With distribution led by Regal, the show will also be available on the big screen at AMC, Cinemark and other participating theaters, for more than 650 locations total. At $9.99 for the paired-episode screenings, advanced tickets are now available at Regal . Related Stories News What To Expect For ‘Heated Rivalry’ Season 2: Everything We Know So Far News Jacob Tierney Shares ‘Heated Rivalry’ Season 2 Update While Accepting Critics Choice LGBTQ Showrunner Award: “Working Very Hard” Screenings will feature exclusive welcome content from the show’s cast and directors, and participating locations will also have themed cocktails for purchase, including the “Summer in Montreal” and “Russians Don’t Blush.” Watch on Deadline “When a series connects with audiences the way Heated Rivalry has, we look for ways to bring it to the big screen and give fans a reason to experience it together,” said Brooks LeBoeuf, SVP of U.S. content at Regal. “Nearly a year after its premiere, we’re proud to work with our partners to turn a season fans have watched again and again into a true theatrical event. The series is produced by Hearst Media Production Group via a partnership with Epic Entertainment and Media Group and safety equipment maker Kidde. It airs as part of ABC stations’ “Weekend Adventure” educational/informational programming block. Hosted by Art Edmonds, Home for Good is a home renovation series honoring people who make a difference in their communities. Each half-hour episode transforms a room or personal space to better serve people who dedicate their lives to helping others. Season 2 will continue to feature first responders while bringing more community champions and service workers into the spotlight, including educators, mentors and volunteers who serve families in need. articles.title: Apple’s Fleetwood Mac Doc Lands Title & Release Date
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac The Lede Company Acquires Lauren Winslade’s London-Based Agency Aisle 8 Charades Boards Juho Kuosmanen’s ‘Dream Come True’ As Production Wraps Across Europe ‘Normal People’ Stars Paul Mescal & Daisy Edgar-Jones Among Signatories Of Open Letter Supporting Sally Rooney After UK Book Ban View All October 22, 2026 6:31am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Fleetwood Mac Apple Fleetwood Mac : The Chain , the first fully authorized documentary on the legendary rock band, will debut on Apple TV on January 29, 2027. The documentary, directed by Frank Marshall and produced by The Kennedy/Marshall Company and White Horse Pictures, offers fans what Apple has described as a “definitive and unprecedented look at Fleetwood Mac’s story, bringing together voices, memories and perspectives of Grammy Award-winning Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductees Mick Fleetwood, John McVie, Christine McVie, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks.” The doc synopsis reads: Following their fortuitous meeting in 1974, Mick Fleetwood, John McVie, Christine McVie, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks reflect on their uncompromising 50-plus-year history, from their record-breaking recordings and tours — including never-before-seen footage and exclusive new interviews — through to today. articles.title: John Anderson Dies: Country Singer Of Hits ‘Wild And Blue’ & ‘Swingin” Was 71
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘860’ Broadway Review: Billy Crystal Remembers The Stuff Of Life And Loss Tom Cruise To Receive 52nd AFI Life Achievement Award Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Billy Crystal, Bradley Whitford Prove Strong Ticket Draws – Broadway Box Office View All October 22, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source John Anderson (2011) Rick Diamond/Getty Images for BMI John Anderson , one of the “New Traditionalist” country singers of the 1970s who broke into the mainstream with chart-topping hits like “Wild and Blue”, “Swingin'” and “Black Sheep”, died Wednesday, October 21, at his home in Smithville, Tennessee. He was 71. His death was announced by family on social media. A cause of death was not disclosed, but The LA Times reports that the singer died in his sleep. The family statement on Anderson’s Instagram page reads, “It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend. To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special. We are completely heartbroken.” Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries Obituaries Freddie Jackson Dies: R&B Hitmaker Behind “Rock Me Tonight”, “You Are My Lady” & Many More Was 70 The statement continues, “His music will live on, but for us, his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave his family and the memories we will carry with us forever.” Born December 13, 1954 in Apopka, Florida, Anderson moved to Nashville after high school, at first performing as a country duo with his sister before finding some success as a solo singer in the back-to-the-roots “New Traditionalist” movement alongside George Strait, Ricky Skaggs and Waylon Jennings, among others. Anderson, even while maintaining the hard-country, keening vocal style of his traditionalist roots, began a move into mainstream country success in the early 1980s with his rocking, uptempo hit “Swingin'” and, with a nod to the more traditionalist style, the fiddle-heavy title song from his 1982 album “Wild & Blue.” The album brought Anderson to the attention of the wider country radio audience, and earned a slew of Country Music Association award nominations, with “Swingin'” named Single of the Year and Anderson winning the Horizon Award for new artists. The ’90s brought continued success, including with the chart-topping singles “Straight Tequila Night” and “Money in the Bank,” and popular albums including Seminole Wind and Solid Ground . He continued recording well into the 2000s, but with more modest results. His final albums Goldmine and Years were released in 2015 and 2020, respectively. Anderson was inducted to the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame on October 5, 2014, and the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024. Following Anderson’s death, country star and former The Voice coach Blake Shelton paid tribute on Instagram, writing, “There is too much for me to say about @johnanderson in just a statement. I am sick and I am stunned. But I am a very lucky man. I got the opportunity to find out that my hero wasn’t just the guy I hoped he’d be. He was so much more than that. John was my friend. I got to see him last Sunday and I don’t even know why but I told him I loved him. That is what fills my heart in this moment. My love and prayers go out to John’s family. This one really hurts.” Anderson is survived by his wife of more than 40 years, Jamie, and daughters Alexa Kate and Brionna Cheri. articles.title: Brian Selznick’s Rome-Set Queer YA Romance ‘Run Away With Me’ Set For Feature Adaptation With Gianni Nunnari Producing
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman , Diana Lodderhose October 22, 2026 7:17am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Brian Selznick, 'Run Away with Me' and Gianni Nunnari Getty Images EXCLUSIVE : Hollywood vet and Italian native Gianni Nunnari , producer on movies including the 300 franchise , Immortals , and From Dusk Til Dawn , is bringing Brian Selznick ’s ( The Invention of Hugo Cabret ) young adult novel Run Away With Me to the screen, with Selznick adapting his own novel. Rome-born Nunnari, an exec producer on The Departed and Se7en , will produce through his Hollywood Gang Productions banner, with executive producer set as Deborah Belford de Furia. Published by Scholastic in 2025, Run Away With Me marked Selznick’s first novel written specifically for a young adult audience. Set in Rome in the 1980s, the queer coming-of-age romance follows Danny, a 16-year-old American spending the summer in Italy, whose life is transformed when he meets Angelo, a mysterious Italian boy. The novel blends more than 100 pages of Selznick’s signature illustrations with prose. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Hollywood Vet Gianni Nunnari & 'Magazine Dreams' Producer Simon Horsman Launch Film & TV Label Euro Gang With Footprints In London, Rome, Madrid & LA; Company Inks Deal With Warner Music Group For Scripted Slate News ESPN Original Series To Depict Formation Of Premier Lacrosse League Selznick is the Caldecott Medal-winning author and illustrator of The Invention of Hugo Cabret , which was adapted by Martin Scorsese into the five-time Academy Award-winning film Hugo . His novel Wonderstruck was adapted into the Todd Haynes-directed feature starring Julianne Moore, with Selznick writing the screenplay. His other works include The Marvels , Kaleidoscope and Big Tree , the latter originating from an idea developed with Steven Spielberg. Nunnari is expected to draw on his longstanding relationships in Hollywood and the European production community to mount the film on location in Rome. He most recently exec-produced Roland Emmerich’s swords and sandals epic Those About To Die in the city. James Canellos and Michael Ritter will also executive produce. The synopsis continues: “What begins as a chance encounter develops into an intense first love as Danny and Angelo explore the Eternal City together, uncovering stories hidden within its streets, monuments and ruins. Their romance is echoed by other love stories spanning the 17th century, 19th century and 1940s, revealing a history of queer love that has endured even when those relationships were forced into secrecy or erased from the historical record. As the boys grow closer, Angelo’s own secrets begin to emerge, forcing Danny to confront the possibility that their relationship, and the seemingly timeless Roman summer surrounding them, cannot last forever.” “ Run Away With Me is a universal story of love in the Eternal City, set in the 1980s, when I was falling in love with love and with Rome itself,” said Nunnari. “For me, bringing Brian’s story to the screen feels very personal.” Selznick added: “I’m thrilled my book is being brought to life by such an extraordinary team. We’re all eager to tell a story that affirms the importance of love, a message that feels more urgent now than ever.” Executive producer de Furia commented: “ Run Away With Me and Hollywood Gang may seem like an unlikely pairing, but they are a perfect combination. I’ve worked with Gianni for years and have seen firsthand his passion for storytelling, history, love, and Rome, while Brian is one of the most extraordinary creative minds working today and someone I’ve been lucky to know for decades. Run Away With Me pulses with the electricity of first love and the discovery that our own love stories belong to a history much larger than ourselves. And, of course, the Eternal City plays a starring role. Don’t we all want to fall in love in Rome?” Selznick is represented by CAA. articles.title: “Horror Is Now Cool” as the Hunt for the Next ‘Obsession’ and ‘Backrooms’ Is on: Rome’s MIA
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 21, 2026 3:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kane Parsons and Curry Barker Alan Chapman/Dave Benett/Getty Images; Amanda Edwards/Getty Images Horror industry leaders came to Rome to praise Curry Barker and Kane Parsons — the YouTubers-turned-directors behind the breakout Obsession and Backrooms horror movies. “The stigma of horror of the past, that it was niche, is past. Horror is now cool, and that’s great,” Andrea Romeo, founder and CEO of Wonder Pictures, which released Backrooms in Italy, told a panel on the genre at the MIA Market in Rome. Peter Kuplowsky, programmer of the Toronto Film Festival’s thrills and spills Midnight Madness showcase, said the Hollywood box office rebound has helped underpin the resurgence in horror films. Related Stories Movies Seth Rogen Watched Curry Barker's Next Movie, Says It's "Even Better" Than 'Obsession' 'Awards Chatter' Podcast 'Obsession' Star Inde Navarrette on Sudden Fame, Cut Scenes, Relationship Takeaways, a Possible Sequel and Going Rogue for Marvel “The U.S. theatricals have bounded back, and there’s been an excitement to watch a movie with a movie again,” he insisted. So the hunt for Gen Z-tinged horror talent will continue. Including in Italy. Romeo after Backrooms wants more box office success: “We started to look for the next Kane Parsons and Oz Perkins. But we also want to find the Italian Kane Parsons. There’s some screenwriters and directors who want to be the next Kane Parsons. But they want to work in English. So we want to understand how to build an Italian background.” At the same time, the Italian Kane Parsons may be a woman. “A young female director will be my dream,” Romeo added. The horror leaders argued non-traditional horror directors like Parsons and Barker had come out of YouTube to offer fresh, new voices and innovation to the fright-night medium for Gen Z movie-goers. Rachael Labes, manager, acquisitions & productions for IFC’s Shudder, said horror films embracing comedy had also opened up new audiences. “There were 10 years where we were getting harsh movies. Now I can go to see a horror film that scares me, but also offers a fun time,” Labes argued. At the multiplex, Barker’s Obsession grossed over $400 million globally on a $750,000 budget and became Focus Features’ highest-grossing release ever. Meanwhile, Parsons’ Backrooms crossed $350 million in box office globally and is A24’s highest-grossing film in a number of countries. Roberto De Feo, an Italian director and screenwriter, says the breakout success of Obsession and Backrooms has allowed Paolo Strippoli’s campy, fun Italian horror thriller The Spiral , which bowed in Venice and is now potentially up for an Oscar. “It’s important to talk about the fact that the audience were used for 30 years to watch movies form the U.S., which was far from the Italian aesthetic. Now they want to see movies that are connected with Italy,” De Feo said. Jonny Bunning, digital marketing manager for UK-based Signature Entertainment, said horror films from new international filmmakers and exotic countries are having success connecting with audiences. “The genre community is interested to hear from a different community to see the different countries’ interpretation of horror and seeing visuals that you’re not familiar with, and that cuts through and piques that interest,” he told the panel. articles.title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Commish Domingo Corral Touts HBO Max TV Deal: “I’ve Found a Home”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 21, 2026 4:12am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'La Bola Negra' Carla Oset/Netflix Former Moviestar Plus+ fiction and entertainment head Domingo Corral intends to continue being Domingo Corral after striking an overall first-look TV deal with HBO Max. “I found a home,” Corral the former director of original content at Movistar Plus+ until he was fired in 2025 told The Hollywood Reporter on Wednesday while attending the MIA Market in Rome. “It’s like a new home, because I feel fortunate to have found a place where they want to do the same things that I want to do, and that’s amazing,” he added. While at the Spanish pay-TV and streaming giant, Corral gave a green light to Cannes breakout films like Oliver Laxe’s Oscar-nominated drama Sirât , Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo’s La Bola Negra, a epic about gay men in war-torn Spain and the Spanish entry for best international feature film at the Oscars, the Javier Bardem drama The Beloved, from director Rodrigo Sorogoyen, and director Alauda Ruiz de Azua’s Sundays. La Bola Negra was acquired by Netflix out of the Cannes Film Festival for an awards season push. The platform’s long release in theaters started on Oct. 16, ahead of streaming on Dec. 2. With success like that, Corral’s sudden exit from Movistar Plus+ led 144 members of the Spanish creative community, including Bardem, Penélope Cruz and Pedro Almodóvar, to sign an open letter in support of the producer, warning of the damage his exit could have on the Spanish industry. Now with his own indie production banner backed by the Warner Bros. Discovery streamer newly-acquired by Paramount Skydance, Corral said of his exclusive TV series collaboration: ‘I’m very happy I can work with HBO, because it’s very important to work with a commissioner that wants to make the same type of shows that I want to make, and that we share the same vision and the same passion for quality TV.” The first TV series from that overall deal is the 1980s-set El Nani, about a petty criminal from the Spanish slums wrongly arrested amid Spain’s transition from fascism to democracy, and to be written and directed by Alberto Rodríguez and Rafael Cobos ( The Anatomy of a Moment ). Expect few series from a “focused” producer, Corral insisted, and TV shows that bring on board the best Spanish creative talent he often worked with while at MovieStar Plus+. At the same time, now for the first time with a global streamer in HBO Max, Corral understands he will need to make series specific to Spain’s political and cultural reality that also potentially resonate worldwide. “I have an amazing opportunity to work for a streamer that is global and that a show I’m making for Spain can be seen all over the world,” he argued. Of course, for that vision to be realized, HBO Max under Paramount Skydance will need to continue being HBO. Corral has no crystal ball, but the early omens are promising after Casey Bloys signed a new multiyear deal to oversee HBO Max and Paramount+ in a new role at Skydance. “That’s really, really positive… It would have been bad news for HBO if that hadn’t happened. Fortunately it has happened. So I’m optimistic,” Corral told THR . THR

articles.title: Netflix Stock and Price Targets Drop as Wall Street Debates If the Streamer Can Flip the Script
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 21, 2026 4:19am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos Andrew Leyden/Getty Images Netflix ‘s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings report is in, but what does it mean? In co-CEO Ted Sarandos’ telling, it’s all about execution. And how is Wall Street reacting to management commentary about the streaming giant’s outlook and largest layoffs in years, including the exit of film head Dan Lin and the replacement of chief content officer Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice? Sarandos discussed content strategy, with co-CEO Greg Peters addressing a 2026 shortfall in advertising revenue. But the key quote from the call may have been Sarandos’ blunt note about staying the course. Related Stories Movies Camel Racing, a Sect and Workplace Democracy: Tallinn Fest Sets Docs Lineup, Special Screenings Movies Great Lakes Creative Producers Lab Unveils Cohort of 15 Film Producers From Seven African Countries “There is no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy,” he said. “We do need better execution in the U.S.” adding: “It’s just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we’d like. So we had some really solid doubles and triples this year, but the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs so that they’ll travel around the world.” In Wednesday pre-market trading, Netflix’s stock was down more than 6 percent at $64.35, signaling a new 52-week low. As of Tuesday’s market close, that low had been at $65.08. So, what can investors take away from the streamer’s updates? Below, The Hollywood Reporter has compiled analysts’ reactions to Netflix’s latest set of results and outlook. Analyst: Mark Mahaney, Evercore ISI Stock rating and price target: outperform, $90, down from $110 Takeaways: “Is A Better Script Coming?” was the key question that the analyst posed in the headline of his report. “For the third quarter in a row, Netflix shares traded off mid-single-digit to high-single-digit percentages in the aftermarket on soft earnings per share results. And this is now the fourth quarter in a row that Netflix guidance has come in lighter on at least one metric. Growth has clearly slowed at Netflix.” Mahaney reduced his financial estimates and pointed out slowed revenue growth, wondering: “What’s Going Wrong And Is There A Fix?” He then put forward some reasons: “We attribute this to some market maturity, consistent competition from large platforms like YouTube, Amazon, Disney, etc. … potentially a structural challenge from short-form content platforms (TikTok, YouTube again), and content mis-execution (i.e. no major global hits since KPop Demon Hunters ).” What to do? “We believe most of these challenges are addressable, and we view Netflix management as highly capable,” the analyst offered. “By bringing in a new chief content officer, Netflix is at least acknowledging and acting on the challenge. We also believe that Netflix, the global hit machine, will likely have a hit in 2027.” And Mahaney shared an upbeat conclusion. “This along with an improvement in content delivery and some key live events (Women’s World Cup) may well drive growth again in U.S. viewing hours, changing the engagement narrative. We also see live events and the expansion of the ad-supported plan to 15 new markets in 2027 as potentially accelerating sub ads growth,” he wrote. All in all, “we believe the Netflix long thesis is still intact. Or at least, we are more confident than the market is that it is intact.” Analyst: Brian Pitz, BMO Capital Markets Stock rating and price target: outperform, $125 Takeaways: “Advertising faces product delays, but [the] long-term vision [is] still intact,” was the analyst’s post-earnings takeaway, with results leading him to “fine-tune” his financial estimates. Despite ad momentum running behind expectations, the analyst continues to see advertising as a key growth opportunity for Netflix. “We remain positive on the long-term monetization opportunity and see the near-term advertising slowdown as buildout pain rather than a structural growth challenge,” he wrote. Content and subscriber momentum are a mixed bag. “Encouragingly, membership growth remains solid, supported by healthy subscriber retention across regions as churn improved year-over-year,” the analyst noted. “We were encouraged that Netflix’s industry-leading churn improved year-over-year globally and in the U.S., better than management expected. However, management acknowledged that U.S. content execution needs improvement, and the incoming chief content officer Peter Rice will focus on it.” Pitz also addressed the role sports could play in the content strategy. “While Netflix is unlikely to buy expensive season-long premium sports rights, it continues to lean into specific live inventory, adding its first NFL Thanksgiving Eve game,” he said. “Live content accounts for only 1 percent of engagement hours despite representing 5 percent of content spend, but it remains an important lever for improving subscriber acquisition and retention and reducing churn.” Analyst: Michael Morris, Guggenheim Stock rating and price target: buy, $78, down from $80 Takeaways: To explain his stock price target reduction, Morris cited “third-quarter results that met guidance but were paired with an outlook modestly short of expectations,” which led him to lower his 2027 revenue estimate to $56.8 billion from $57.1 billion, with his earnings per share forecast down by 9 cents to $3.80. With Netflix cutting its 2026 advertising revenue target to around $2.7 billion from $3.0 billion also made Morris pare back his 2027 ad estimate to $4.0 billion, which he said compares to a $5.2 billion consensus expectation. Of course, the recent content leadership changes and what it means for its programming strategy also featured in his report. “Co-CEO Ted Sarandos described the company’s strategy as ‘unchanged’ while acknowledging ‘we could do better,'” he wrote. “Peter Rice’s mandate as chief content officer is to find more home runs across formats and genres and strengthen talent relationships. Returning franchises including Emily in Paris , The Diplomat and Wednesday , and feature films including Narnia , provide a bridge to a lineup developed under Mr. Rice, and we consider a more impactful slate non-negotiable for renewed investor interest.” He also called content licensing “a silver lining” in content, citing a recent deal with Disney. Concluded Morris: “Netflix is a top platform for licensed product, and in our view more win-win partnerships with underexposed content at attractive terms would be incremental. Bundling with most other major streamers or launching a free service in the U.S. would not sustainably bolster top-line growth.” Analyst: Ralph Schackart, William Blair Stock rating and price target: outperform, no price target Takeaways: The engagement and content debates featured heavily in Schackart’s report. “The company acknowledged the need to accelerate view-hours growth, highlighting India as an example of successful execution, where view hours increased 24 year-over-year and view hours per member grew in the low- to mid-single digits,” he highlighted. The analyst also weighed in on Rice’s content chief appointment. “Management views the transition as an opportunity to improve content execution, particularly in the United States,” he wrote. “Management stressed that the change does not represent a shift in content strategy, but rather an opportunity to take the slate to the next level.” Schackart summarized his takeaways from the results and outlook this way: “Unfortunately, this quarter did not give the bears a reason to pull back on their growth concerns.” What does this mean for investors? “While it may take patience, we believe investors should benefit from accumulating shares on the pullback, recognizing that there is not a near-term catalyst. We believe the company will solve its near-term content concern at some point in 2027.” Analyst: Laurent Yoon, Bernstein Stock rating and price target: outperform, $80, down from $95 Takeaways: Patience was a recurring theme in Yoon’s report, which is entitled “When Success Starts Looking Mature.” “New content boss, new content strategy?” it asked. “Perhaps, but not anytime soon,” it offered. “Despite new leadership with deep experience across TV, film, and streaming, the messaging remains firmly centered on traditional content, live events, and licensing. Any meaningful strategic shift – if there’s one – could take years, not quarters, to show up in the slate or the numbers.” That may also keep weighing on investor sentiment. “Investors will increasingly focus on the durability of ‘double-digit’ growth and the pace of margin expansion as content investment comes back into focus,” the analyst explained. “The risk is not the near-term fundamentals, but perception. A strategy that continues to lean on traditional content, traditional formats, and traditional engagement risks reminding both consumers and investors of the ‘L’ word – legacy. That alone may be enough to keep the stock range-bound near term, even if the underlying business continues to execute well.” Advertising may not be broken, but also made for a disappointment. “Management discussed slower ad product rollouts rather than demand, suggesting a delay rather than disruption, but it still represents a missed opportunity,” the analyst concluded. All in all, he reduced its forecasts for Netflix, which also pushed down the stock price target. “Changes in earnings per share estimates are due to slower-than-expected advertising revenue growth, domestic subscriber growth and margin expansion slightly offset by accelerated buybacks,” Yoon noted. “We also reduced our valuation multiple to 20 times (from 25 times) to reflect slower growth and ongoing negative investor sentiment without a near-term positive catalyst.” Analyst: Rob Fishman, MoffettNathanson Stock rating and price target: buy, $90, down from $100 Takeaways: MoffettNathanson was among the firms cutting their financial forecasts and Netflix stock price target, in this case by $10, following the latest results and management commentary. Fishman wondered about the outlook for revenue growth, especially given the ad revenue updates, and the outlook for content spending following the recent executive changes. “If revenue is slowing, does Netflix need to reaccelerate content spend?” the analyst asked. And he shared that underlying his forecast is 8 percent content spending growth as “management is clearly focused on reining in expenses to invest in high-impact areas, as evidenced by the recent headcount reductions.” His conclusion is that Netflix can continue to improve the monetization of its reach and scale to grow profits in the future. Wrote Fishman: “After the sell-off, we believe Netflix’s downside is limited, and the stock presents an attractive entry point to capture upside in leveraging the company’s global scale to drive incremental growth above the strength of its core business model.” THR

articles.title: Don’t Stop Believin’: ‘Glee’ Revival a Go at Disney+ and Hulu
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All October 21, 2026 5:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The cast of 'Glee' in the season three finale in 2012. Adam Rose/Fox via Everett Collection Logo text Get your slushies ready: Glee is returning. Disney+ and Hulu have ordered a revival of the high school musical, which ran from 2009-15 on Fox. 20th Television, which produced the original series, is also behind the new show. And that is literally all the public information Disney put out Wednesday morning — no producers or cast are mentioned in the press release announcing the series order. Sources say deals for the the creative team are still being finalized, but it’s an extremely safe bet that co-creator Ryan Murphy is involved. Murphy, after all, told The Hollywood Reporter in August that he was “considering” a Glee -vival: “For many, many people now in their 20s, they grew up on that show and it meant something to them,” he said. “The music meant something. So, let’s kick it around and see what we get.” Related Stories TV Disney+ Sets Japanese Horror Anthology Series 'Night Tales Club' With Kiyoshi Kurosawa, Takayuki Yamada TV 'American Horror Story' Scores Season 14 Renewal at FX In late September, Murphy took the idea further , telling Entertainment Tonight that he had finished a script for a new version with co-creators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan. Glee ran for six seasons on Fox, becoming a cultural phenomenon almost from the moment its pilot debuted. The series followed the members of the show choir at William McKinley High School in Lima, Ohio, through the ups and downs of high school and beyond. The original cast included Lea Michele, Matthew Morrison, Jane Lynch, Cory Monteith, Chris Colfer, Kevin McHale, Dianna Agron, Amber Riley, Jenna Ushkowitz, Heather Morris, Naya Rivera, Mark Salling, Darren Criss, Harry Shum Jr., Jayma Mays, Dot-Marie Jones and Chord Overstreet. Alex Newell, Jacob Artist, Becca Tobin, Blake Jenner and Melissa Benoist joined the series in later seasons. Glee won six Emmys, including a directing win for Murphy for the pilot episode and best supporting actress in a comedy series for Lynch in 2010. The original series streams on Hulu, and songs from Glee draw about 4 million monthly listeners on Spotify. THR

articles.title: Audiovisual Women Leadership Program Unveils Participants, Sets Tallinn Partnership
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 21, 2026 5:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Audiovisual Women participants Courtesy of Erich Pommer Institut Germany’s Erich Pommer Institut (EPI) has unveiled the participants of its fifth edition of Audiovisual Women, its program designed for female professionals in mid- to senior-level management positions across the European audiovisual sector. The cohort includes 15 media professionals from 11 countries. “The program seeks to strengthen participants’ professional networks, unlock new business opportunities and support the sustainable growth of their careers and companies,” the EPI says. “Audiovisual Women helps female leaders navigate industry challenges, develop innovative business models and harness the opportunities of digital transformation.” The offering is open to female leaders working across the entire value chain of the industry. Participants go through a mix of in-person and online training sessions, one-on-one business coaching, exclusive networking events and a self-study phase. The goal is to strengthen leadership skills and explore key topics, including entrepreneurship, innovation, change management, communication and self-promotion. New this year is a partnership with the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event , the industry platform of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF). In mid-November, EPI will take the participants to Tallinn to give them the opportunity to expand their networks beyond their home markets and connect with professionals from across Europe. A distinctive feature of the program is its archery-based learning concept, developed by coach Annette Birkholz, which is designed to allow participants to connect, explore, and reflect on systemic patterns. By also involving participants’ hiring managers and encouraging more diverse, gender-balanced recruitment practices, Audiovisual Women further aims to foster “lasting structural change” across the industry. “With Audiovisual Women, we aim to strengthen female leadership and contribute to a more diverse, innovative and equitable audiovisual industry,” says Gabriela Seidel-Hollaender, project manager international training at EPI. “Investing in female leadership is essential to building a more resilient and forward-looking industry.” Audiovisual Women is funded by Creative Europe MEDIA. Partners of the program are FOCAL, Flanders Audiovisual Fund (VAF), PÖFF – Black Nights Film Festival, Industry@ Tallinn & Baltic Event, EAVE – European Audiovisual Entrepreneurs, EWA – European Women’s Audiovisual Network, and Women in Film & Television International (WIFTI). Check out the complete list of Audiovisual Women participants below. Aurora Alma Bartiromo, Our Films (Italy) Mariam Bitsadze, 17/07 Productions (Georgia) Susa Katz, Zürcher Filmstiftung (Switzerland) Rowena Kelly, Immortal Films (Ireland) Sari Lempiäinen, Elisa Viihde (Finland) Georgiana Maliovski, Vampires in the Sun (Romania) Nicky Onstenk, IJswater Films (The Netherlands) Queralt Pons Serra, MoreThan Films (Spain) Christine Recker (Spain) Mar Sáez Pedrero, Animation in Europe (Spain) Franziska Sonder, Ensemble Film (Switzerland) Daria Stilin, PALMA Artistic Organisation, Vrboska Film Festival (Croatia) Julie Van Den Broeck, Panenka NV (Belgium) Zlata Yefimenko, EF PICTURES (Ukraine) Milena Zajović, Cinehill (Croatia) THR

articles.title: John C. Reilly, Penny Lane Board Short Doc ‘Stalin Boys’ as Executive Producers (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 21, 2026 5:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Stalin Boys' Courtesy of Pipsqueak Productions/Amplify Pictures Nonfiction filmmaker Penny Lane ( Confessions of a Good Samaritan ) and Academy Award-nominated actor John C. Reilly have boarded the short documentary film Stalin Boys as executive producers. Directed by Ora DeKornfeld and Bianca Giaever, the film follows Malachi, a middle school student in Marathon, Texas, who is obsessed with Joseph Stalin . Yes, THAT Joseph Stalin! When he hears about the Texas History Day competition, he writes a play about the late Soviet dictator and enlists his friends Cayden, Lyric and Jurem to play fearful civilians and loyal henchmen. Related Stories Business Audiovisual Women Leadership Program Unveils Participants, Sets Tallinn Partnership Business Netflix Stock and Price Targets Drop as Wall Street Debates If the Streamer Can Flip the Script “In a school of 11 students in a town of about 400, the boys grapple with a dark chapter of history and confront questions of power and legacy in their own lives,” a synopsis teases. The film debuted on The New York Times Op-Docs earlier this month and is eligible for the Academy Award for Documentary Short Film category. Veteran doc director Lane, whose subjects have ranged from Kenny G in Listening to Kenny G to Flaco the owl in Wild Inside , was drawn to what she described as the Little Miss Sunshine -esque blend of whimsy and heart. “I never imagined the words, ‘Screw National History Day!’ could make me laugh so hard and feel as much pain at the same time,” said Lane. “I’d also never thought to ask, ‘What was Stalin’s favorite color?’ but I’m glad to have met Malachi and discover he knows the answer.” Giaever lauded Lane as “a documentary icon,” adding: “Her work taught us that documentaries can be funny, playful, and absurd, while still tackling difficult topics.” Reilly will support the filmmakers’ campaign to bring Stalin Boys to classrooms and audiences nationwide. “I loved this short film,” the star said. “I loved it so much I lent my name to it as an executive producer. It reminded me of my own very imaginative and inspired childhood obsessions as a theater kid. I found the kids to be a wonderful inspiration to us all with their commitment to and enthusiasm for their vision. I also was deeply moved by the teachers who supported and guided them to realizing their visions. It takes caring people like these teachers to shepherd today’s young people if we want a better future for our world.” Concluded Reilly: “I hope everyone watches this film and remembers that big lives always start small and even tiny dusty towns in the middle of nowhere can produce people who can shape a brighter future for us all.” DeKornfeld said about Reilly: “John has spent his career playing people who are funny and heartbreaking in the same breath, which is exactly who these boys are. He immediately understood this film is about what’s possible when teachers encourage kids to follow their interests, as weird as they may be. We could not have asked for a better champion to help us get it in front of the audiences who need it most.” The filmmakers learned about the story while visiting their friend Crawford Hunt, who had been recruited to teach history at the school. They spent a week with the boys and their teachers during rehearsals for the state competition. Stalin Boys , which you can watch here, premiered at the Big Sky Documentary Film Festival and won the Audience Award and a Special Jury Award at the 2 026 SXSW Film & TV Festival. In July, the film also won the Academy Award-qualifying Documentary Grand Prize at Indy Shorts. It screens later this month at AFI Fest in Los Angeles. Stalin Boys was edited by Natalie Ancona, with an original score by Elori Saxl. The Pipsqueak Productions film was produced by Alejandra Vasquez and Amplify Pictures. For Op-Docs, Alexandra Garcia is the executive producer and Yvonne Ashley Kouadjo the producer. The short was supported by Southern Methodist University’s Narrative Now Initiative, Mountainfilm and The Economic Hardship Reporting Project. DeKornfeld directed the Emmy-nominated short USA v SCOTT , The Grandfather Puzzle and several episodes of the Netflix original series Explained . She is currently in production on a feature documentary about journalistic fixers in Mexico. Giaever is an independent filmmaker, radio journalist and the creator and host of the podcast Constellation Prize . Her upcoming documentary series Free Help premiered at the Tribeca Film Festival and will be available next year. THR

articles.title: Interscope Unveils Exec Promotions Following Shake Up
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All October 21, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michelle An, Laura Carter and Ramon Alvarez-Smikle. courtesy of Interscope Interscope revealed a suite of promotions on Tuesday, a week after the record label and parent company Universal Music Group underwent a round of layoffs and executive departures as part of UMG’s previously-announced cost-savings measure that started in 2024. Longtime Interscope exec Michelle An has been named president and Chief Creative Officer at the label, Interscope said, adding that An would both IGA’s pop/rock division as well as have a broader role across the whole roster to help artists “shape the worlds around their music, from visual identity and storytelling to brand development and long-term career strategy.” “IGA has always been defined by original voices and by the teams who back those voices with taste, conviction and care,” John Janick, Chairman and CEO of Interscope Capitol, said in a statement. “Michelle has one of the clearest creative instincts in the business. She helps artists make the world around their music feel bold, fully realized and unmistakably their own.” Laura Carter and Ramon Alvarez-Smikle, meanwhile, have been named co-presidents of Urban at the label. The two are well-respected hip-hop marketing executives, and Interscope said the duo “will bring A&R, marketing innovation, digital strategy and audience development closer together for IGA Urban’s artists.” “Laura and Ramon bring complementary strengths to IGA Urban,” Janick said. “Laura has earned deep trust through her artist relationships, creative judgment and commitment to developing talent. Ramon brings cultural instinct, deep digital expertise and a sharp understanding of how artists build audiences and communities. Together, they will connect A&R, marketing and digital strategy around each artist’s vision, helping IGA Urban artists move with more clarity, momentum, and impact.” Interscope’s pop/rock and urban divisions were impacted by last week’s restructuring as Sam Riback, Interscope’s co-president and head of pop/rock A&R, as well as Nicole Wyskoarko, the label’s head of urban A&R, both departed. THR

articles.title: Sacha Baron Cohen Gets Real About Backlash, Death Threats and Resurrecting Ali G
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Sacha Baron Cohen was photographed Oct. 14 at PMC Studios Los Angeles. Styling by Artistic & Fashion Director Alison Edmond Paul Smith sweater; Ali G’s jewelry. Paul Smith sweater; Ali G’s jewelry. Photographed By Beau Grealy Sacha Baron Cohen insists his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I? , is the last guerrilla comedy of its kind that he’ll make. He’s adamant. No more Borat. No more Bruno. No more Ali G. They’re too hard, he says, too risky. He’s tired of hoodwinking people to expose their prejudices, and he’s even more tired of the death threats that periodically follow. There are easier ways to make money in this business, and eventually his luck will run out. The trouble with his declaration, however impassioned, is that he has been making it for years. He’d routinely say he was done before he made the 2020 Borat sequel, which, incidentally, earned two Oscar nominations, and he was even more insistent afterward. And each time he says it, he believes it to be true. He wants it to be true, he tells me. So, why are we here, I ask, discussing an Ali G revival? “Because I’m terrified of where our society is headed, and the way I can comment on that is through my comedy,” he says. “I wanted to show the extremism on both sides of the political spectrum and the danger of virtuous violence.” There’s a level of seriousness that belies the 90-minute comedy film he’s made, which features an imbecilic white rapper who speaks in Caribbean-British slang and a contraption that shoots bullets out of one’s rear end. Recognizing this, he adds: “And obviously we wanted to make the funniest film that’s ever been made.” His longtime collaborators have other theories about his return. Anthony “Ant” Hines, who’s been working with Baron Cohen since The 11 O’Clock Show , where the Ali G character originated, believes his pal had missed the adrenaline rush, just as he had. “It’s a visceral buzz you get from making a movie this way,” Hines says, “and nothing comes close to it.” Dan Mazer, whose friendship with Baron Cohen dates back to secondary school in the U.K., wasn’t particularly surprised to get the call about dusting off Ali G, in part because they’ve never stopped talking about the character. In fact, whenever they got together, they’d often slip into Ali G’s voice, he says, and imagine what patently absurd things he would be saying or doing in different situations. “I also think it’s a knowledge that Sacha is the Michael Jordan of this sort of filmmaking,” says Mazer. “And yeah, Michael Jordan went off and tried to play baseball, and you go, ‘OK, you’re a pretty good baseball player,’ but he’s not the Michael Jordan of baseball. And Sacha is the Michael Jordan of this, and to an extent, we all are. We invented this genre, and nobody else has matched what we’ve done.” Whatever the reasoning may be, Ali G is back, rolling into theaters Oct. 23 before landing on Amazon Prime Video soon after. And like plenty else that Baron Cohen has done, it’s already prompted a full-blown meta-outrage cycle, complete with a campaign to boycott the film. With each new trailer or PR stunt posted to social media come fresh accusations of an outdated caricature and of cultural appropriation — the latter a central plot point in the film, in which Ali G’s progressive nemesis (also played by Baron Cohen) attempts to cancel him on those very grounds. Some in his camp have speculated that it’s more of a coordinated attack by pro-Palestinians who are critical of Baron Cohen’s past support of Israel. (Though he’s been quiet about Israeli politics and the conflict in Gaza in recent years, Baron Cohen is a prominent Jew who has sounded the alarm about the surge of antisemitism on social media, reportedly telling TikTok executives in 2023 that what was happening on their platform was “creating the biggest antisemitic movement since the Nazis.”) Colton Dunn, an Emmy-winning Ali G superfan and one of three Black writers hired on the film, is aware of the cultural appropriation claims. “But we knew where we were coming from, and we dealt with it all in the movie,” he says, “and at the heart of it, Sacha and the movie want to defeat evil and hate. That’s the intention behind it.” Still, the internet has suggested the backlash has Amazon spooked. Courtenay Valenti, Amazon MGM Studios’ head of film, streaming and theatrical, offers this: “We want to be in business with exceptional storytellers who have distinctive creative visions, and Sacha is exactly that. He has always been fearless in his comedy, with a unique ability to tap into the cultural conversation in ways that are both provocative and entertaining.” Over cappuccinos in the garden of the Chateau Marmont, Baron Cohen lets loose on the mounting backlash, his battles with studios and the $3 million day that nearly derailed his film. Paul Smith robe; Wander socks; stylist’s own slippers; Ali G’s own jewelry, glasses, hat. Photographed By Beau Grealy In 2021, you allegedly performed as Ali G at The Comedy Store in Australia. How soon after did you explore the idea of another film, and what did those early conversations entail? During the pandemic, our family moves to Australia, and when they lock down in Australia, you cannot leave where you are. My ex [Isla Fisher] is from Perth, so we applied to go there. She’s rejected. I find out that you have to show that there’s a financial benefit to Western Australia to be allowed in. You have to apply to the police. So I say, “Listen, I’m doing a stand-up tour. It’s going to create 300 jobs. It’s going to bring tens of millions of dollars into Western Australia.” Obviously I had no intention of doing it. But then the police accept me. We spent 14 days in lockdown, and at the end, a police car turns up, an inspector comes out, and she says, “I am in charge of your stand-up tour.” So, you had to do a stand-up tour. I did, and I had the police watching me. I ended up doing a 90-minute show, and what was interesting was that people really loved seeing Borat and Bruno, but when Ali G came out, there was a different response. It was as if people believed he was real. There’s going to be a lot of amateur psychology in this interview, but my observation was that because Ali G existed before I existed as a public figure — for five or six years, I didn’t give an interview [as myself] — people thought Ali was real and therefore there was this different response to him. So, I felt, “Hold on, is there a movie in this character?” I came back to America at the end of 2021 and started talking with the team about it. We all felt Ali by himself wouldn’t be a satirical movie because he was from a bygone era — this relic from another period who’s unaware that he is deeply problematic. But what if we brought in another character, an ultraprogressive extremist [also played by Baron Cohen] who’s his rival and make it a thriller like The Fugitive ? We had in our mind this line that goes, “We have a cultural appropriator on the loose,” from that famous speech in The Fugitive . That felt funny to me. In the revisionist history of the film, you had ended Da Ali G Show because you couldn’t come to financial terms with HBO. It left me wondering if there were any conversations or interest, from either side, about doing more? Oh, yes. HBO wanted to carry on. I said no because at that time, in Britain, I think a lot of comedians were snobs about doing multiple seasons. So, there was no expectation or desire to do 15 seasons — to do the American way. I’m very friendly with Larry David, and I’m jealous of him that he can do Curb again and again. I probably would’ve had a much easier life if I just carried on doing Da Ali G Show . Paul Smith sweater, pants; Wander socks; Doucal’s boots; Ali G’s own jewelry, glasses. A decade ago, you said of this type of filmmaking: “It’s a young man’s game. You have to be prepared for a small amount of risk, and my philosophy was always: ‘Well, if something bad happens, I’m single and everyone’s going to be all right if I end up in hospital for two weeks.’ Now that I’m married with kids, it’s more difficult to justify.” So, did you find a way to do it differently, or did you just say, “Fuck it”? I’m never cavalier. These movies are dangerous to make, but we try to limit the risks and keep everybody safe. But even physically, they’re incredibly demanding. So, the final scene of this film is an eight-hour continuous scene that takes place over 12 locations. It’s a continual shot. There’s gunfire in it. There’s a medical procedure. There are drones, there are explosions, and it’s taking place in the desert. On the way to shooting it, I bumped into one of the great stuntmen and he said, “You will go to hospital if you make this movie,” because I explained I’m wearing a prosthetic head in a fat suit. He said, “You’ll be so dehydrated you’ll be in hospital for two weeks.” You hear that and think what? That I have to fix the problem. So, I had an endurance specialist who does the Tour de France be by my side during the scene and they’re measuring my weight. I think I had 11 liters of Pedialyte. And listen, a number of people went to the hospital for dehydration, including the bodyguard. There were dangers in the scene as well. One of the people grabbed a gun and almost did something very dangerous. These really are the hardest movies to make, but I suppose I made it because I’m scared of this world of conspiracies and lies that are spread by social media and now by AI. If we don’t have these shared facts, then democracies crumble and we can’t have a tolerant society. And to make people laugh is therapy. As I read your own quote back to you just now, you were laughing. Why? Because I’m always surprised at my own idiocy. I’m very bad at looking into the future and imagining how I will feel. So, for example, the naked fight in Borat 1 , we get to set and Ken Davitian, who’s not conventionally attractive, is naked, and he’s going to sit on my face. And I say, “I’m not going to do this!” At that point, Larry Charles, the director, said, “So why did you write it?!” I continually make these decisions that are very bad for my own health and sanity. You are making this film in a very different moment, culturally and comedically. Do you derive some masochistic pleasure from that kind of challenge? I’ll tell you, in the script, there was a moment where Ali G is canceled, and the way we wanted to do that was that I, Sacha, should be canceled in the real world and the idea was to use the footage of me being canceled and stick it into the movie. And we did actually get some of the second bit, but we didn’t have the money to open up the movie and put the footage in. That was the intention, though. I’m told you get a fair number of death threats, which now come from both the left and the right. When have you decided something wasn’t worth it? I was about to do a scene [in Borat 1 ] and we had a cop who had his gun on his thigh and I said, “Why is your gun on your thigh?” He goes, “Well, I need to be really fast to draw in this area.” I said, “Well, how close are you to me?” And he said, “I’ll be with you within three minutes.” I realized that was not a good thing to do, so I pulled that scene. I will never do a scene if I think I’m actually going to die. Thom Sweeney shirt; Ali G’s ring, sunglasses. Photographed By Beau Grealy You’ve filmed in a bulletproof vest, so you’ve clearly anticipated the possibility of being shot? Yes, on Borat 2 , there was a scene at a gun rights rally that I knew there was a risk of getting shot. But I felt it was an important film to be made. Is there anyone who says to you, “Hey, Sacha, I know this seems noble to you, but maybe it’s not necessary”? Yes. Who? Your children? I don’t talk about my children. But my brothers tell me that. And my mom and some of my team as well, because there are much easier options. I made a movie called Ladies First . I shot it in three months. It came out. A lot of people saw it [on Netflix]. And it’s as financially beneficial as making something that takes years, and there’s absolutely zero risk. There must be some masochistic nature to me, but I don’t think it’s just that. I want to give the fans who’ve been loyal for the last 28 years something that they’ve never seen before. I want to give them the most ambitious movie I’ve ever made, which is a three-character movie. [Baron Cohen also plays a former Mossad agent.] It is my version of the Avengers. I’ve always assumed that you were like Tom Cruise, after the same adrenaline rush that he is as he jumps out of planes. I don’t think that’s the reason I do it. You don’t? Your collaborators seem to … No. The first [for-hire] movie I did, Talladega Nights , I walked into my trailer and there was a bed there. I realized I’d never been in a trailer before, and I go, “Hold on, this is a paid job where I can go to sleep?!” I couldn’t comprehend how relatively easy it was, and it was great fun. But as you’ll probably deduce from this interview, I’m not very self-aware. Paul Smith sweater; Ali G’s jewelry. Photographed By Beau Grealy I don’t know that I buy that. OK. Do I enjoy it when something works? Yes. Am I upset when something doesn’t work? Yes. So, for example, this final scene is an eight-hour continuous shot over multiple locations and no one had ever done that before. Normally we shoot a scene or two scenes a day. Here, we put probably 40 scenes together and shot them continuously. I had a variety of line producers and assistant directors refuse to schedule it. And there are 400 or so beats that must all go perfectly, because you’re dealing with real people and if anything doesn’t feel quite right, they will stop and say, “Hold on, this isn’t real.” Of course. So gunfire, the squibs have to go off perfectly. A medical procedure happens. That body that we use has to be believable. Then a fire breaks out during the first part of the scene. As we’re driving to the second location to kidnap somebody with these real people, I find out that location four is surrounded by fire, and it’s being evacuated, and we have to pull the scene. And each time we run it, it’s $4 million and we’re insured for $1 million, and I personally have to pay $3 million. So, we shut down production and we have a discussion, which is that it’s completely idiotic that we’re trying this. And everyone is telling you it’s not possible? Yes, and I’ve lost $3 million that day. Obviously it was my money, which is a very stupid idea. But you ultimately got it? We got it. We had some of the team that worked on the Oscars because I was like, “What is a movie or a TV show where nothing can go wrong? It’s the Oscars.” And even there, sometimes something’s going wrong! I said to them, “OK, this is the Oscars, it’s just taking place over 50 miles in 12 locations. And it has gunfire and blood.” But at the end of all of it, if you look at the behind-the-scenes footage, I’m not jumping up and down. I’m content. The Ali G film, which has Baron Cohen playing three different characters, suffered multiple shutdowns and a change of studios. Michael Legato © 2026 Amazon Content Services With 2020’s Borat 2 , you’ve said that several of the places you pitched were concerned by the political content and the idea of running it before the election. How did this pitch compare? Well, the desire was always to have this come out a few days before either a presidential election or the midterms. A lot of my movies have come out around those times. Borat 1 came out almost 20 years to the day, on November 3, 2006, just before the midterms. It’s a time for people to think about the choices that they’re about to make. But this movie is more about the dangers of extremism on both sides. I get that, but you’re also operating in an extremely risk-averse climate. I can’t imagine there weren’t any concerns … Well, Hollywood is a superficial place. Noooo. I know. ( Laughter. ) But I pitched this after Borat 2 had won two Golden Globes and had Oscar nominations and was the most watched movie ever on Amazon. That’s enough to convince studio heads to buy it. And everyone tried. It was somewhere else first, no? Yes. Amazon and Universal were the final contenders. We ended up going with Universal but, in the end, the movie took so long that we went back to Amazon. And it was actually great because we’d had an incredible experience there with the last one. We really did. And that movie [ Borat 2 ] also was at Universal and ended up at Amazon. So, this one moved because — It was taking too long. You have to understand the basis of this kind of movie is that we have to find people who don’t know who I am, which becomes harder and harder. I think our research department interviewed 5,000 doctors to get one [for a single scene]. Then we had a number of other things that kept on shutting it down. The fire. The writers strike. I ended up doing another movie in the middle. Baron Cohen was joined by 300 Ali G look-alikes who followed him around London for a viral promo stunt Oct. 11. Jeff Spicer/Getty Images Amazon came aboard a third of the way through. What did their notes look like? For better or worse, maybe for worse, I’m a final-cut producer and director. So, you’re saying it didn’t much matter what their notes were? Well, executives can have really fantastic notes. And they can have terrible notes. But I always listen to the audience and I’m really guided by that. You were once asked about comparisons between you and Andy Kaufman, to which you said, “In a way, he’s more of an artist than I am in that I don’t think he cared what the audience thought — and deep down, I really want to make the audience laugh. And that’s why I fight to get jokes to be funny … I’ll go to war with whatever studio has been stupid enough to pay me money to make a movie.” Again, you’re laughing … I can’t believe how honest I was. What did those fights look like on a film like this? If something is funny, then I will go to war for it. And the studios know that because I make it clear when we do these movies, which makes me not very studio-friendly in some ways because my allegiance is to the audience. And I go to every single screening and I record the laughter and I grade the jokes and I have a few people that I’ve trained to grade them too, and then I cut the jokes within a frame. It’s obsessive and very intricate, but it’s designed to deliver really funny movies. Some people find me incredibly arrogant because they’ll come up and say, “You know that movie, Borat 2 , wasn’t funny.” And I’ll say, “You’re entitled to your opinion, but you’re wrong. I have 5,000 people laughing at these jokes and I can show you they are empirically funny.” While the vast majority of the Ali G cast are unsuspecting nonactors, Baron Cohen and his onscreen partner, played by Morgana Robinson, are the exceptions. Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios You said that you’re not studio-friendly, but, as you noted, this is a superficial business and if your model can put butts in seats … Yes, it’s about money. But I’m also a great supporter of the Oscars and other awards ceremonies because, however absurd they are, it creates another incentive for studio heads to make quality projects. Because studio heads do want to win Oscars and they want to get nominated. And we’ve been very lucky in that the Academy and the Globes and some other organizations have recognized our work. In fact, I was sitting at that table [pointing to another table in the Chateau garden] in 2006 having done Borat , and Sean Penn came and sat at the table and he said, “Why don’t you do an Oscar campaign for your performance in Borat ?” I said, “That’s absurd. They’ll never give me an Oscar nomination.” And he said, “They will.” So, we went to Fox at the time and they said, “Listen, we’ll pay for one Oscar campaign, but it’s either writing or acting.” At the time, I was actually winning some of the acting awards, to my great surprise, but I spoke to the team and we decided to push the writing. [The 2006 film was nominated for best adapted screenplay.] So, we gave up the acting campaign. Also, I was about to make Bruno and I didn’t want to go on a baby-kissing tour, which would destroy my next movie. Me doing this kind of stuff [an interview as himself] destroys the ability to make another one. I know, I know. I’m sorry. There we go. Look what you’ve done. You’ve ruined me. As you anticipated, it didn’t take long for people to start lodging complaints. One criticism, which mirrors a plotline in the film, is that Ali G uses the character as a cover for enforcing racial stereotypes. What do you say to that? Well, I’ll repeat what I’ve said for many years, which is that Ali G is a white cultural appropriator who steals from the musical artists that he admires. The reason Ali G says “West Side” is not because the Afro-Caribbean community in London was saying “West Side.” Nobody there was. It’s because Tupac Shakur, who he admires, is saying “West Side.” And so he is funny because he is delusional. He lives this boring, white middle-class life in a suburban town, and he deludes himself that he’s living in Compton, and that is the absurdity of Ali G. The core joke is that a white moron, possibly the stupidest man in the world, is interviewing a white expert or high-status politician, and that white expert or high-status politician believes that this imbecile played by me is real and that leads to comedy. And in my belief, it slightly undermines the power of the establishment. So it was fundamentally an anti-establishment character where we’re pricking the assuredness of the establishment by saying, “Listen, these people aren’t that smart. They believe that Channel 4 or HBO could have sent one of the most stupid people in the world to interview them.” Baron Cohen as Bruno in 2009 in Berlin. Sean Gallup/Getty Images What do you make of the argument that not everybody recognizes the absurdity and so the stereotypes being presented can have dangerous ramifications? Everyone is entitled to their own view. And a lot of the stuff on social media is orchestrated, and not necessarily orchestrated by people who really believe in what they’re saying. We’ll get to that. But when I did Da Ali G Show in America, the first people who gravitated to it were the Black hip-hop community. The first GQ Award that I was given was given to me by Method Man and Redman. I did a series of adverts for the NBA directed by Spike Lee, who’s not naive about racial issues. They recognized these characters, these white cultural appropriators, and they found them funny. So, this notion of it being problematic hadn’t been raised for 20 years. OK, but you seemed to know it would be this time around? Yes. I knew, and I wanted to make sure that this was an anti-racist movie, which is why we were so concerned with having absolutely brilliant Black writers on board and consulting with brilliant Black cultural commentators. As I believe you were referencing, there was a pretty sizable social media campaign to boycott the movie, and some have speculated that the campaign is tied to your pro-Israel stance — Well, I haven’t said anything about Israel. [Baron Cohen voiced his support for Israel and the hostages immediately after the Oct. 7 attacks but has been quiet on the Gaza war and Israeli politics in the years since.] I think people are being portrayed as things that they are not on social media and it’s problematic. We are in a world where people can’t distinguish between facts and lies, and that’s something that I’ve spent a lot of the last few years trying to fix. For example, I co-founded a group called Stop Hate for Profit with the NAACP and Color of Change and the ADL and certain other civil rights groups to stop the misinformation and incitement of racism on social media. So, I’m not surprised that prominent Jews are being targeted. I knew that this was going to happen. The level of organization is surprising, but this is a trend of Jews being portrayed in certain ways and trying to be silenced. You’ve been vocal about the rise of antisemitism, broadly speaking. Have you felt any difference in your own Hollywood career after Oct. 7? No, not really. I mean, maybe it’s because I don’t do much, but I haven’t. Well, you’re about to make your West End debut in a Quentin Tarantino play, which feels like a big leap, going from this film, in which you’re in complete control as the writer, director and star, to being a puppet in Tarantino’s theater. How did that come together? I’ve never had a career plan, but I have this kind of no-brainer rule, which is if one of the best directors in the world asks me to do something, I’ll say yes, even if it’s instinctively the wrong project. So when Martin Scorsese says, “I’m doing a kid’s film, will Sacha play the villain in it?” And I read the book and the character’s not that interesting. I actually had a lot of arguments with [screenwriter John] Logan about it [ Hugo ]. But I say yes because I want to learn how to make better films. And so if Quentin comes along and says, “I want to do a play,” I say yes. Then I actually read the play and I thought it was fantastic. And I felt, why not? So currently, I’m doing nine hours of sword-fighting training a week. And I would just clarify, rather than be a puppet, Quentin did suggest that there would be some element of collaboration. As Borat, sporting a mankini in Cannes in 2006. Anthony Harvey – PA Images/PA Images via Getty Images Have you seen it yet? A little bit, yes. But Quentin and I have been talking about doing a project for at least 20 years. We talked about doing The Scarlet Pimpernel about 20 years ago. Borat came out and Quentin and I would have dinner monthly and I almost did a part in [his 2012 Western] Django Unchained . In the end, I had to drop out because I ended up doing Les Misérables . But I came very close to doing a scene with Kerry Washington. I even had a prosthetic chin made because Quentin was very adamant that I would resemble this character he’d liked from the ’40s. Ant Hines, one of your longtime collaborators, suggested you’ve tussled with Amazon in the promotion of this new film. “We’re giving Amazon panic attacks on the daily,” he told me. “They’re used to Timothée Chalamet eating some chicken wings; they’re not used to 300 Timothée Chalamets attempting to take part in the London Marathon, which is a thing they shut down.” This is why it’s best not to talk to somebody like Ant. ( Laughs. ) You know, they’ve actually been great in terms of the marketing. But it’s not a traditional process when you work with me and you’re marketing a movie. You did end up with 300 Ali G look-alikes following you around London. That had to be validating, if a little overwhelming. The really concerning thing was that these fans were coming out with catchphrases that I’d completely forgotten. I was like, “Wait a minute. I recognize that … What is that from?” And they’d go, “It’s you!” And some of them were doing better Ali G impressions than me. There was one guy there, an Ali G impersonator, and I had to explain, like, “Listen, you’ve been doing this at weddings and bar mitzvahs every week for the last 20 years. I haven’t been doing this.” I’ve actually had that happen before. We did a movie called Bruno , and Jonah Hill was one of the writers. And in the writers room, he was doing impressions of Bruno, and they were better than Bruno. Then when I started shooting the movie, I realized that I was doing an impression of Jonah Hill doing an impression of me. In any genre, there’s always an “It” person, and at various points, you’ve employed those people shortly before they reached that status: Jonah, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg and, most recently, Nathan Fielder, who worked on your Showtime series, Who Is America? What do you think of what Nathan has done in the eight years since you worked together? Oh, I think he’s a comic genius and he reinvented the genre that I, I suppose, created or developed. And he had a rule, really, which was to not do anything that I had done. But he’s a brilliant, brilliant mind, and absolutely hilarious. I think his documentary [ You Can See Everything ] is going to be huge, so I’m very excited for him. But it’s been an honor to have all of these incredible people come and work with me. Seth and Evan, the story with them was, it was the Ali G Show , and they came in with an idea for Bruno — instead of Girls Gone Wild , it was Boys Gone Wild . I said, “OK, you’re hired, but I’ve only got enough money for one writer, so unless you want to share a hotel room and a bed and a wage, I can only hire one of you and it’s going to be Seth.” They came back and said, “We’ll split the wage.” And basically they would write in a double bed in the Best Western hotel we were in. They had beers all around them. They were smoking and they’d write in bed. That’s fantastic. For you, what do the incoming calls look like these days? I think they’re kind of what comes in to everyone. I get the traditional comedies, kernels of comedy ideas, and then dramas. Is one genre more appealing than the other right now? No. I want to do stuff that challenges me. So again, I’m not doing Borat 3 , which also would be incredibly challenging.
