Again, this movie I just did is the most challenging movie I’ve ever done, but I’m not doing more. Until the next one … No, no, I really have had enough. I know you don’t believe me. I do not. Oh, I really pray that in six years’ time, you don’t come to me and quote me to myself. This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Disney and Netflix Are Courting Creators. YouTube Is Playing Hardball to Keep Them
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 21, 2026 6:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Texas-based sports creators Dude Perfect inked a wide-ranging partnership with Disney that will span entertainment, sports, consumer products and experiences. Illustrated by Neil Jamieson On Sept. 23, YouTube gathered a couple hundred of its top creators at Pier 57 in New York City for its annual “Made on YouTube” event. The showcase is where YouTube reveals new initiatives for its creator community, giving attendees a sneak peek at what the video platform has been cooking up in its Skunk Works, like new AI video editing tools. But this year, YouTube wasn’t the only platform on their minds. Netflix, Disney+, Tubi and others are aggressively cutting deals for top creators, in some cases securing wholly original programming or day-and-date releases with YouTube, offering millions of dollars in the process. The Google-owned video platform is not taking it lying down, launching a carrot-and-stick approach to try and keep its place as the primary home for top talent. “It’s a very good time to be in the creator business,” says Adam Wescott, CEO of Home Game Studios, noting the demand for their work. With creator-owned studios proliferating nationwide, it’s a battle that could portend the future of streaming entertainment. It started with kids and family content. Netflix, seeking to bolster its kids programming, inked deals for YouTube native content from CoComelon , Ms. Rachel and Mark Rober. It worked, with all three becoming among the most watched programs in the category. The streamer subsequently ordered originals from them and began to reach out to creators in other genres, spanning food (Nick DiGiovanni), talk ( Good Mythical Morning with Rhett & Link) and teen content (Alan Chikin Chow). Rich Greenfield, the LightShed analyst, believes Netflix has committed upward of $1 billion on creator and podcast programming over the next three years (still, admittedly, a very small slice of its $20 billion annual content budget). But Netflix only started the current war. Disney has long worked with creators, but recent months have seen wide-ranging deals with the likes of Dhar Mann, Dude Perfect and Like Nastya as it seeks out family-friendly and on-brand creators who can live on Disney+. And the company recently hosted a creator event at the El Capitan Theater and Disney Studios Lot, with some 350 creators to further forge those relationships. Tubi, the Fox-owned streaming service, has inked deals with dozens of creators for both originals and library fare. YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Dhar Mann at YouTube Brandcast at David Geffen Hall on May 14, 2025 in New York City. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for YouTube There’s already hope in the creator community that Skydance is about to follow them, with new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz having served as the CEO of Maker Studios. But why are these other streamers so eager to get in the creator business? Multiple sources paint a picture built around audience, money and speed. The larger studio platforms and streamers desperately want to have a product that appeals to the younger, digitally native audience that religiously watches creator content on YouTube. “I think creators really do value, in the right circumstances, the elevation and amplification of being on a main channel platform like a traditional media company,” says Akshay Mehta, the CEO of Lighthouse Studios, a creator entertainment studio. “Creators are creatives fundamentally. They just discovered that in the last 15 years, for a lot of people, the best way to be creative is to go make stuff on YouTube.” The money certainly helps. Multiple sources on the creator side stress that they need funding to help pursue some of the ideas they have, and such places as Netflix, Tubi and Disney are helping them do that. The big streamers are funding original shows and offering help to break into areas like consumer products or live experiences (that was a key piece of Disney’s Dude Perfect deal). Streamers also are banking that creators can not only bring their audience with them but fill their libraries with content that is, frankly, dramatically less expensive than traditional fare and that is produced at a more rapid clip. “These platforms have seen this shift, and they can’t ignore it,” says Nic Paul, the president of the creator services company Spotter. “They all have subscriptions, they all have ad-supported products, even at Netflix, the ad-supported product is becoming a lot more of the focus. There’s a lot of churn. Everyone is like, how do I create enough content fast to keep audiences engaged? Because if you think about it, Stranger Things on Netflix, I’ve got to wait a year plus for a season, and creators are obviously very fast at putting out IP.” Indeed, one top creator who has a deal with a streaming platform says they told their new partner that they can produce an hour’s worth of programming at perhaps 10 percent of the cost (or less!) of a traditional comedy, drama or unscripted concept, all at a faster pace. But what has surprised creators more than anything is how hard YouTube is fighting back. The platform is a juggernaut, and it would be just fine if it lost top creators to other places. But it is waging a multipronged effort — with both incentives and threats — to try and convince creators to make YouTube their primary home. Many of the incentives focus on brand deals, with YouTube significantly increasing its resources in the space. Some creators see YouTube’s brand deals as a way to subsidize or pay for content that they want to make, given that YouTube does not pay to license content in the same way platforms like Netflix do. “Given the cultural phenomenon that YouTube creators are, and this sort of juggernaut that they are in the culture out there, of course other streaming platform services have taken note,” YouTube CEO Neal Mohan told the Big Technology podcast after Made on YouTube when pressed on the dispute, adding that even as MrBeast produces his Beast Games for Prime Video, he still keeps YouTube as his home base. “And, frankly, I think that’s flattering to our creators.” But YouTube also has played hardball, with one creator telling THR that they were “shocked” at the platform’s approach. On the one hand, some of the threats are reasonable: YouTube selects a handful of creators to appear onstage at its annual Brandcast upfront event, a high-profile stage that can lead to major deals. And it has supported Emmy campaigns for creators in certain categories. Those would stop for creators who shift their allegiances to other platforms. (Netflix and Disney already have promised to bring creators to their own upfronts next year and fund some Emmy efforts, according to sources.) And they have even suggested that creators may not be eligible for YouTube Select, an ad program for its very top creators. That caught some creators off guard, as it was seen as an objective program based on reach and scale and is built around videos on YouTube. “That was never their approach in the past,” says Wescott. “It was always about supporting creators and reminding them why YouTube was their home.” Lilly Singh has spoken out candidly about the difference between working in the traditional Hollywood system vs. the creator-driven YouTube economy. Mathew Tsang/Getty Images The platform still plays that game, though even there the tone has become somewhat combative, as one creator notes to THR . Earlier in October, comedian Lilly Singh returned to YouTube after a years-long hiatus, once again creating original content after working in Hollywood. In an interview YouTube posted to its blog , she did not hold back. “Hollywood has real systemic issues, especially for women and people of color. Over the past few years, I received countless notes that weren’t about improving the project, but about making it ‘more palatable,” ‘more marketable,’ or ‘less niche.’ That is fundamentally anti-creative. Our job is to tell our stories unapologetically,” Singh said. “On YouTube, there are no gatekeepers demanding I make my brain baby more palatable for the masses. That authenticity is why my channel worked in the first place.” Message received. But why is YouTube seem so interested in keeping creators on-platform? Especially because, as Mohan notes, it’s a good thing for the ecosystem when others are interested? “On the surface, YouTube should not care. Creators are not launching their careers on Netflix or Disney+,” LightShed analyst Greenfield wrote on Oct. 9. “We suspect YouTube is concerned because the top 20-50 creators have an outsized importance to its major brand advertising commitments each year. Most brands only know a select group of high-profile creators. If brands start to see those creators appearing on Netflix… does a brand start to ask why it is paying YouTube for creators it can find in a curated, brand-safe environment elsewhere?” Advertising is at the heart of the battle, with the ad-supported Tubi competing with Netflix and Disney (each of which is leaning into ads) for creator deals. Creators, of course, are used to working with brands. “A dirty little secret of our space is 90 percent of the revenue is brand endorsements, influencer marketing,” Wescott notes. Still, none of the creators (or those who worked with top creators) suggest that they will completely leave YouTube, even if they may still cut deals to develop original ideas elsewhere. And it isn’t just out of loyalty to the platform that made them or that funds them (Instagram and TikTok, they note, pay basically nothing). “I think you’ll be hard pressed to find a successful YouTube creator who’s willing to walk away from that platform, because it’s what they know, it’s where their audience is, it’s where they grew their business, and it’s where they have the most direct control,” says Wescott. “You’re still playing on someone else’s playground, but YouTube is not telling you what to post on your channel. The other guys are going to have some sort of opinion on what you create on the original side.” For an ambitious creator, it may mean taking a more strategic approach to how, when, and where they choose to produce content. “I’m distributing on [YouTube], I’m paying for everything, I’m getting paid, which is amazing, but now I’ve got to start thinking like a CEO and be like, wait, hold on, strategically, what is my distribution? Where is my next thing coming from?” says Paul. It’s a question that will be felt across the entertainment world. This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: The Emancipation of Charli D’Amelio: How the TikTok Queen Took Back Her Life
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nancy Jo Sales Plus Icon Nancy Jo Sales View All October 21, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Charli D’Amelio was photographed Oct. 5 at PMC Studios in Los Angeles. Artisitic & Fashion Director Alison Edmond Prada dress, top, jewelry. Photographed by Emman Montalvan Charli D‘Amelio — the reigning queen of TikTok — loves to dance. Whenever a new song comes on at this photography studio in L.A., Charli is shimmying her shoulders, shaking her hips. Now she stamps and turns like a flamenco dancer, swishing the skirt of her ruffly black gown. “So pretty, stunning,” says Emman Montalvan, the photographer snapping her. “Gorg!” With her glossy black hair and sparkly smile, Charli is gorg. She’s the girl next door drawn by Disney; she’s the bright and shiny face of social media , making it all seem benign. “This is her before she becomes jaded,” Montalvan observes. “Nothing calculated. Natural. She reminds me of when Britney Spears was young.” Related Stories THR Cover Story Sacha Baron Cohen Gets Real About Backlash, Death Threats and Resurrecting Ali G Business Instagram Lines Up Donatella Versace, A$AP Rocky, Finneas, Chloé Zhao as This Year's Creator Awards Judges (Exclusive) Rihanna’s “Breakin’ Dishes” begins to play. Charli mouths the words: “I don’t know who you think I am —” “Are you having fun?” I ask, finding myself smiling. Because when Charli is happy, you feel happy — which is no doubt part of her appeal. You want to believe that a life spent dancing around in fabulous clothes and opening yourself up to a dizzying 160 million-plus followers (the second most on TikTok) really is as wonderful as it looks. But a flicker of annoyance crosses Charli’s brow, as if the question touches a nerve. Maybe that’s because of how the algorithms are always demanding she offer up the semblance of a perfect life, the performance of joy, no matter the reality. “Are you having fun?” she asks, flashing her diamond bracelet smile. Then she’s running gleefully down the hallway of the studio, followed by her social media manager, Alexa Davis, who films her nearly constantly with a DJI Osmo Pocket. When Charli’s having fun, there’s someone there to capture it. *** Coming off a 10-month run in Broadway’s & Juliet — in which she sang and danced in the ensemble cast, earning some good reviews — Charli moved into a house in Valley Village, California, all by herself, earlier this year. The place represents something more than just a first home: At 22, Charli has separated herself professionally and financially from the family with whom she built her extraordinary career. “I’m figuring out who I want to be,” she tells me, “and that’s what I’m really excited for.” Photographed by Emman Montalvan For years, Charli and her parents, Marc and Heidi D’Amelio, and her older sister, Dixie, seemed inseparable. They moved to L.A. together, signed with the same talent agency, started businesses, starred in a Hulu reality show. Charli was always the main attraction, the engine of an empire — consisting of brand partnerships, media ventures, a clothing line and more — all built on the image of a close-knit family. Now, amid public speculation that her parents mismanaged her money — which her father has denied — she’s trying to find out who she is apart from them. (None of the D’Amelios responded to requests for comment.) The new place is her first house of her own. It doesn’t quite look like what you’d expect of a young woman who earns an estimated $18 million a year annually, according to Forbes . It’s a modest, almost nondescript two-story house on a tree-lined street, with a gate and security door, but nothing that screams “TikTok star.” But then you get to the secluded backyard with its shimmering pool, immaculate lawn and big stone grill, and you see the dance studio with the neon sign: RED BULL DANCE YOUR STYLE. Red Bull, one of Charli’s sponsors, built it for her. She grew up promoting brands; now even her backyard comes with one. “This is a very much a home,” Charli says, her voice soft and gentle as ASMR. She’s sitting cross-legged on the oversized wraparound couch in her big, open living room — her “safe space,” she tells me. She’s wearing Levi’s and a long-sleeved black Prada top (she’s an official friend of the house, so there’s Prada, Prada everywhere around her). Seventeen silver studs and hoops glint at her ears. “Sometimes I just fall asleep here,” she says sleepily. “It’s so comfy, it’s a slippery slope.” She spends a lot of time alone, just being on her phone or watching her giant, wall-mounted TV. On the couch, there’s a pillow that says: JUST A GIRL WHO LOVES ORCAS. Charli says she likes the way they always win in a fight with sharks. “Lame of a life as it may be sometimes, I love just to be at home and do nothing,” she says. “I’m surrounded by a lot of peace, which is something it took me a long time to realize I need to be comfortable.” She’s been a bit of a “hermit” over the past year, she says, retreating from a life in which almost everything she did was potentially something to be shared. “I took my first break off of social media” between October and February, “which was a really tough decision — I was always told, ‘If you take a break, you can never come back’ — but I think mentally I was just in a place where I needed to stop working and figure out who I was. Photographed by Emman Montalvan “I started working full-time when I was 15,” she continues, “and once I started, it was, ‘OK, this is my life now.’ But the other side of it was, ‘This is all I’ve ever known.’ And I think it took me, really for the first time, taking a step back and being like, ‘Who am I? What am I? Do I have a favorite color? Do I have a favorite anything?’ I realized I didn’t really know anything about myself, and so I had to sit with the hard truth of like, ‘Who am I at night when everyone leaves and no one cares that I’m Charli D’Amelio,’ you know?” Her dog, Rebel, a 12-year-old chocolate lab, stares up at her worshipfully. The bloodshot eyes of the internet noticed, of course, when Charli took a break — not just from social media but seemingly from the family that had been so central to her identity. She hasn’t appeared publicly with her parents or her sister for about a year, adding to speculation of a rift. In May, the gossip website Deuxmoi published allegations that Marc and Heidi had mismanaged Charli’s money. In June, Marc took to TikTok to deny these claims. “So a website said … we took money and put it offshore,” said Marc, sounding frustrated. “I wouldn’t even know how to do that. Come on, dude. This was never about money, it was about having this crazy, awesome experience with my family.” And then in September, appearing on creator Quenlin Blackwell’s YouTube cooking show, Feeding Starving Celebrities, Charli was asked how much money she had made from a certain item of merch. “Mmm, ain’t that the question,” she responded, deadpan. “Wouldn’t I like to know.” The moment went viral, becoming a GIF. “Charli D’Amelio family drama” trended on TikTok. *** Photographed by Emman Montalvan Charli was just your average upper-middle-class girl, growing up in Norwalk, Connecticut, when TikTok made her famous overnight. She’d been dancing competitively for nearly a decade when, in May 2019, at age 15, she began posting videos of herself doing popular routines, “just like everybody else was doing.” “My dream in life was to be a backup dancer,” she says. “I was like, ‘I want to go to the University of Nevada at Las Vegas and join their dance team,’ because they’d won nationals. I’m a very type A person. I had a vision board — I had a whole plan. But then the plan went sideways.” Five months after she started posting on TikTok, she had a million followers. By November 2020, she’d become the first TikTok creator to reach 100 million. Why her? Even Charli can’t explain it. “I think it was a mix of things,” she says. “Happy accident.” People watched her videos repeatedly to learn the choreography. “Also, when I started, I got just as much hate as I got love, so people were talking, arguing with each other.” Enragement, as they say, drove engagement. People argued about Charli’s looks, her dancing, whether she deserved her fame. In 2019, she drew criticism for performing the viral “Renegade” dance to K Camp’s song “Lottery” without crediting its 14-year-old Black creator, Jalaiah Harmon. (Charli and pop star Addison Rae later performed the original choreography with Harmon, giving her proper credit.) Then COVID-19 drove young people inside, where they were more often on their phones, and what better way to distract oneself from a pandemic than watching pretty Charli D’Amelio dance? For a generation of girls, Charli represented the ultimate social media success story. You didn’t need a Hollywood agent — you could become famous in your bedroom, just by being yourself. The catch: Once being yourself became your job, you might never get to stop working. Charli was about to become one of the most famous teenagers in the world while remaining remarkably powerless over her own life, she says: “I was a child, which I didn’t really get the significance of at the time, but I can see it very clearly now.” In summer 2020, Charli moved with her family into a rented mansion in the Hollywood Hills. The relocation was her idea; she felt “there was a lot more I could be doing,” though she’d already appeared in a Super Bowl commercial and an ABC special. She and her family signed with UTA as a package. Marc came from the apparel industry and had an unsuccessful run as a Republican candidate for the Connecticut State Senate in 2018; Heidi was a former model and personal trainer; and Dixie, three years older than Charli, was an aspiring singer. The family seemed to envision a Kardashian-esque enterprise, with Charli as its teenage Kim. Marc and Dixie launched their own TikTok accounts after Charli went viral. Everyone had a part to play in Charli’s newfound fame. Photographed by Emman Montalvan There’s a family story here that predates TikTok: A gifted child gets flooded with opportunities, and the adults around her see ways to capitalize on her appeal. Their involvement in her career, no matter how well-meaning, also gives them a say in her image and her decisions. In the pilot episode of The D’Amelio Show (2021-2023), the family sits down to hear the business plan for the upcoming year. Greg Goodfried, a former UTA agent who became their manager, holds forth enthusiastically. On the floor are 23 binders — 23! — containing proposals for a slew of new business ventures. Charli looks scared. “Where is the binder where she gets to be a kid?” Heidi asks. “I still have those binders,” Charli tells me wryly. “Twenty-three major projects in a year were agreed to. I had just turned 16.” (Goodfried did not respond to requests for comment.) Photographed by Emman Montalvan *** “I’m always grateful. I know I’m very lucky,” Charli says. “I don’t know what doing this without them would have looked like; I don’t know if I would have had this life.” It’s a refrain she returns to, almost as if she fears that questioning what happened will be mistaken for ingratitude. One of the peculiar cruelties of fame for young women is that they must be grateful for it, no matter how much it hurts. But lately she’s been reassessing what it meant to be a working child in the entertainment industry. “I was the youngest in every room I was in,” she says. “I was surrounded by people who were the best in the business, so you trust because that’s all you have — these people who are supposed to be guiding and helping you. But people are selfish, and that’s the sad reality. “And people have bad intentions, too,” she adds. “You can’t be a trusting person. I’ve learned that the hard way.” Rebel presses her nose against Charli’s knee. Charli pats it. “There are not a lot of rules and regulations when it comes to people who do what I do,” says Charli. “I didn’t start learning about and getting involved in my financials until I was about 21. I’m very fortunate to be able to be living the life that I am, but I’ve also been working nonstop since I was 15, so I should have stuff to show for it.” The laws protecting children in film and television evolved over decades in response to cases of exploitation. But the business of children making money on social media has grown faster than the rules protecting them. When parents are also business partners, who is looking out for the child? Are the rumors true, I ask, about her parents mishandling her money? “No, they’re not true,” Charli says. “I wouldn’t say that they stole my money.” There’s a long pause. “I think we did a lot of things as a family,” she says carefully. Photographed by Emman Montalvan *** Recently, Charli has been watching The D’Amelio Show for the first time. “It’s kind of like watching something I never lived,” she says. “It’s almost as if I’m figuring out what has happened in my life over these last few years. I was so disconnected in so many ways.” I mention how flat and monotone she seems onscreen, nothing like the person talking to me now. “I was like that. For years,” she says. “I kind of stopped talking. I stopped having a personality. I stopped doing much of anything because I had so much scrutiny from the outside world. It’s taken me to now to realize maybe I was dissociating through a lot of it.” All 28 episodes of The D’Amelio Show come with mental health trigger warnings. Charli and Dixie are seen struggling with the unceasing abuse that comes with online fame. At one point, a viral post predicts Charli’s death. Grown men make vulgar, sexualized videos about her when she’s still a teenager. “It’s a scary world, and it was hard on me,” she says. Her experience wasn’t so different from that of millions of girls negotiating a world of constant comparison and judgment — it was just on a much larger scale. Charli was the smiling face of a platform that amplified those pressures, twerking and twirling like the girl in The Red Shoes who couldn’t stop dancing. To many of her fans, she represented the fantasy: beauty, popularity, incredible clothes, a seemingly perfect family, wealth that came from doing what she loved. Behind it was a girl overwhelmed by scrutiny. Adolescent girls had always been judged on their looks and popularity; what was new was the technology that could make the judgment relentless, public and profitable. Charli was both a victim of social media culture and one of its most effective advertisements. “Have you ever seen The Matrix ?” I ask. “Is that the one where Keanu Reeves goes like this?” she says, doing the move where he dodges bullets in slow motion. I tell her about the main character, Neo, who discovers his world is a simulation controlled by machines. “And then when he wakes up, he starts fighting back. You should watch it.” “I love that, you’re giving me homework,” she says with a little laugh. Charli had suffered from anxiety even before TikTok. “I was a kid when I started having severe anxiety,” she says. In third grade, bullies pulled her hair and shoved her into a bathroom stall, breaking two of her fingers. “That was the same age I started having anxiety, so maybe they are connected,” she says. “I never really thought about that before.” On her reality show, her anxiety becomes a storyline. She describes having up to 15 panic attacks a day; viewers see her sob and break down in response to online hate. “But then I would get hate for showing my feelings,” she says. “You’re not allowed to be upset, you’re not allowed to cry, you’re not allowed to have any emotion, you can’t be angry.” Part of the concept of the show was to expose the dark side of influencer fame — even as it made its underage star more famous. But while the show urged viewers who were struggling to seek treatment for their mental health, Charli feels she didn’t always get the help she needed. “I went untreated for most of my life,” she says. “I had a life coach” from ages 16 to 19, “but I didn’t have a therapist. I probably should have had a therapist. I wasn’t medicated at all, even though I had ADHD, which I didn’t get diagnosed with until I was 18.” She was later also diagnosed with OCD and trichotillomania, a hair-pulling disorder associated with OCD and anxiety. Her life was work. Due to her professional commitments, she dropped out of high school at 16, though friends back home in Connecticut made sure she went to prom. Meanwhile, she was having experiences some kids dream of, such as winning season 31 of Dancing With the Stars (along with her dance partner Mark Ballas) in 2022, when she was 18. Her mother, Heidi, also competed that year. She came in eighth place. *** Matt Winkelmeyer/Kca2021/Getty Images for Nickelodeon/Tyler Golden/Hulu Charli has been seeing a therapist lately. “I told my therapist,” she says, “one thing I don’t want to be is another statistic. I don’t want to be another kid who got thrown into Hollywood and let that ruin their life.” The cautionary tales of child stardom, from Judy Garland to Britney Spears, have found a new breeding ground online. Charli’s generation doesn’t need studio executives to make them famous anymore, but the disappearance of the old gatekeepers hasn’t made children any less vulnerable to exploitation. I ask what finally made her reconsider how she wanted to move forward? “This is probably going to sound really crazy,” Charli says, “but I was doing Broadway” — & Juliet, a gig she’d chosen herself — “and it was the easiest thing I had ever done. And I did a good job. I showed up every day with a smile on my face, and I loved every second of it. And it reignited something in me, this love that I used to have” for dancing, performing. She had moved to New York — without her family — and was living in Columbus Circle to be near the theater. After years of being the star, it felt like a “relief” to be part of an ensemble of dancers, some of whom became friends. For the first time in her life, she was on her own, and it felt good. But then, when her run ended in September 2025, she says she became “the most depressed I’d ever been.” She rarely left her apartment and “didn’t see another human for a few months.” She went off social media and decided it was time to “take a look at myself.” Her team continued pitching projects that felt uncomfortably familiar. She started saying no. In December, she parted ways with Goodfried, her former manager. She doesn’t have a replacement manager yet, “but I’m OK with that,” she says. “I like it. I’m in charge. Now I say what I’m doing and not doing.” She sits up a little as she says this, her drowsy voice suddenly more alive. She also separated herself from the D’Amelio family business. Now, she oversees her own finances. For most 22-year-olds, independence means getting a job and supporting oneself; for Charli, it has meant taking command of an empire she helped build before she was old enough to vote. The internet took note again when she and her parents unfollowed one another on Instagram. Marc said on TikTok that he now communicates with Charli “through her lawyer.” As for Dixie, Charli says, “I mean, that’s my sister. I’m going to love her till the day I die. But there are times where you’re figuring stuff out.” Charli’s still making TikToks, still dancing around, smiling, in cool clothes; and she’s vlogging more on her YouTube channel, which has around 9 million followers. “Sometimes I want to record my entire day,” she says. “And sometimes I talk about whatever people are asking for. People like to feel included.” She’s still looking for ways to monetize her platform, still promoting Dunkin’, which has named two drinks after her: The Charli (2020) and The Charli Cold Foam (2021). Charli isn’t trying to bring down TikTok or renounce the fortune that brought her here. She isn’t trying to escape the machine. She just wants to be the one at the controls. “I’m taking the last few months of 2026 to work on getting to a place where I’m doing things I’m really proud of,” she says. She has a major project to announce in November, something that “I hold dear to my heart.” She continues: “Because of being told so often I didn’t deserve where I was, I felt that way for a really long time. But I’m at the point now where I can see that, like, I’ve lived a pretty amazing life, and I’m getting what I feel is like my second chance to do this the way that I want to do it. “I love what I do,” she says. “I love the person that I’m turning out to be.” Charli’s publicist, Nicole Perez-Krueger, comes in the room and says it’s time to stop. Charli’s dinner guests are arriving — her social media manager, Davis; her day-to-day manager, Alison Scoon; her stylist, Carlee Barrow; her agent, Ali Berman, and Berman’s 7-year-old daughter, June. They really are her friends, Charli says. They bring the sides. Charli’s going to grill them steak. “How do you do your TikToks and stuff?” June asks. “I just dance what I feel and say what I feel,” Charli says with a smile. Her social media manager is filming again. This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Noel Clarke Pleads Not Guilty to Sexual Offense Charges
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 3:19am PT Noel Clarke Pleads Not Guilty to Sexual Offense Charges By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest Noel Clarke Pleads Not Guilty to Sexual Offense Charges 4 hours ago Sacha Baron Cohen Defends Bringing Back ‘Problematic’ Ali G Amid Controversy: He’s ‘Designed to Expose’ Prejudice 21 hours ago BBC Three Among Linear Services Set to Close as Broadcaster Looks for Savings 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images Noel Clarke has pleaded not guilty to six sexual offense charges. Appearing at Westminster Magistrates Court in London on Wednesday morning, the actor, writer and director entered not guilty pleas in relation to all the charges, which include two charges of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism and one charge of exposure. The charges relate to alleged offenses that took place between 2007 and 2016 involving five women. Related Stories CMA's 'Celebration of Dolly Parton' Special Slates 20 Performers, Including Ella Langley, Lainey Wilson, Molly Tuttle and Reba McEntire As well as a long-running role on “Doctor Who” as dimension-hopping hero Mickey Smith, Clarke won critical acclaim for his teen dramas “Kidulthood,” “Adulthood” and “Brotherhood.” Popular on Variety He also co-wrote Sky drama “Bulletproof” with Ashley Walters, which ran for three seasons. It was cancelled in spring 2021 after The Guardian published an article containing multiple sexual misconduct allegations, which Clarke denied at the time. Clarke eventually brought a libel claim against the newspaper, which he lost last year after the judge, finding in favor of The Guardian, held that the paper’s reporting was “substantially true.” Justice Steyn also found Clarke to lack credibility as a witness. The actor was ordered to pay £3 million ($4 million) of the paper’s legal costs. Last month, Clarke was charged by London’s Metropolitan Police after the U.K.’s Crown Prosecution Service (similar to a D.A.) gave authorization having reviewed a file of evidence. He will next appear in court on Nov. 18. articles.title: ‘When I Existed,’ a Cannes Market Standout, Swooped On for World Sales by M-Appeal and Now Bound for Tallinn Black Nights (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 4:04am PT ‘When I Existed,’ a Cannes Market Standout, Swooped On for World Sales by M-Appeal and Now Bound for Tallinn Black Nights (EXCLUSIVE) By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest ‘When I Existed,’ a Cannes Market Standout, Swooped On for World Sales by M-Appeal and Now Bound for Tallinn Black Nights (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom 6 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source When I Existed (Courtesy of M-Appeal) Berlin-based M-Appeal has boarded “ When I Existed ,” a buzzy, feel-good second-chance drama comedy and Kafkian social satire which proved a standout at the Cannes Market’s Ventana Sur Goes to Cannes showcase, marking an auspicious debut for Uruguay’s Alejandro Damiani and Martin Avdolov. A select but discerning sales agent of Latin American movies, M-Appeal has picked up international sales on “When I Existed” (“Cuando yo existía”) just weeks before the feature’s world premiere in the Critics’ Picks Competition at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival . Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately The feature debut of writer-directors by Damiani and Martin Avdolov, “When I Existed” unfolds its humane modern parable when Silvio Bertolini retires after spending 40 years building Uruguay’s foremost gates construction company. Popular on Variety Attempting to draw his pension, and with his credit cards frozen, he discovers that the National Pension and Retirement Fund, also his bank, register him as deceased. Sent from pillar to post – to the bank’s Accounts, Payments and Claims treading dark puddled basement corridors and joining seemingly interminable lines. He meanwhile reconnects with old friends from his sculling boat club of youth, and re-awakes – but is it too late? – to what it really means to be alive: Spending time with his wife who hopes retirement will open a new chapter in their life together. Driving “When I Existed” is a notably modulated performance from César Troncoso, star of “The Pope’s Toilet” and “The Eternaut,” as Silvio, ranging from smiling containment of a reasonable man to outraged anger, paralysis from anxiety, wistful regret and lovelorn solitude. Silvia Kutica (“Avellaneda’s Moon,” “Argentina, Land of Love and Revenge”) plays Silvio’s now increasingly estranged wife of 40 years. “When I Existed” is lead produced by Federico Cetta for Uruguay’s El Cielo Cine who describes as “a story of reinvention built around the things that truly matter.” Structured as near any film of ambition these days an as international co-production, “When I Existed” is co-produced by David Matamoros at Barcelona’s Doce Entertainment and Andrés Rosenblatt at Montevideo’s Metropolis Films as co-producers. Matías Burgos at Moon Ideas, also based out of Montevideo, serves as associate producer. “This story speaks to us in a world where we have the constant feeling that time is slipping away between obligations we don’t always choose,” said Avdolov. “What do we do with the time we have? Today we need small acts of resistance against a logic that tends to make everything increasingly automatic and artificial. For me, making this film has something of that.” “What won us over about ‘When I Existed’ was its rare mix of humor and humanity,” said M-Appeal founder Maren Kroymann. She added: “Silvio is a charming man who struggles to accept retirement, while his wife has been waiting for this moment, hoping they can finally enjoy life together. Their story is both touching and deeply relatable, reminding us how easily we can get caught up in our habits and lose sight of what matters most. It’s a film that makes you laugh, moves you, and reminds us that it’s never too late to reconnect with the people we love.” ‘When I Existed,’ Broken Down by Damiani and Avdolov “When I Existed” is shot with unusual elegance but sense of humor by Manuel Branaa, a camera operator on J.A. Bayona’s Netflix smash-hit “Society of the Snow.” This is caught in the the lateral tracking shot with which it opens, crossing a dark granite stone tomb taking in the red and yellows of flowers left on it. Asethetically, it’s a highly pleasing composition, but the flowers are wilting. Drawing a counterpoint between the open expanses of marshlands, where Silvio catches up with his boat club best friends of youth, the charcoal grey and black corridors and barred doors and windows of the National Pension and Retirement Fund’s labyrinthine office conveys a sense of claustrophobia – that of a man caught not only in a bureaucratic system but his own self-absorption. “When I Existed” delves into “the nature of the system, the ego, bureaucracy, technological trends, the dangers of alienation, and the erosion of humanity,” said Damiani and Avdolov. “We poured our souls into even the smallest details – things that might go unnoticed by others, but which, to us, made the work feel complete and purposeful,” they added. Damiani has worked for years in advertising, as a copywriter and designer, wining Uruguay’s fist Golden Lion, then in VFX rising to Creative Director at top Uruguayan VFX house Aparato. Avdolov has transitioned to filmmaking from a career as a novelist (“Violeta Corazón,” “Camba”), short-story writer and author of the non-fiction “El Corazón Creativo” (“The Creative Heart”). “When I Existed” is born from the deepest fear any human being can have: how are we supposed to live? No one teaches you that,” Damiani told Variety . It is also semi-autobiographical. “Working on ‘When I Existed’ made us realize how much of ourselves we poured into the film’s protagonist,” they added. “For many years, we had channeled our energy and creativity into other people’s projects. Following the pandemic – and having passed the age of 40– we decided to commit ourselves to our own meaningful projects. We see this film as a reminder that we are not here to live someone else’s life; Damiani’s 2016 short, “M.A.M.O.N. (Monitor Against Mexicans Over Nationwide),” went viral, hitting over 13 million views on YouTube. El Cielo Cine Of features, “El Cielo Cine” has produced with Argentina 2025’s well-received adopted son drama “Emi,” directed by Ezequiel Erríquez, and Santiago Giralt’s 2023 “Norma,” a later-life self-discovery tale starring and co-written by Mercedes Morán (“Neruda,” “My Sad Dead”) which scored a best comedy Platino Award nomination. articles.title: Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 4:05am PT Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says 3 hours ago ‘Deadstream’ Directors Joseph and Vanessa Winter to Helm Horror Movie ‘Future Me’ as Longevity Pictures, Spooky Pictures and Image Nation Studios Ink Multi-Picture Deal (EXCLUSIVE) 22 hours ago Raj Singh and Italy’s RP1 Holding Launch €100 Million Film Fund to Boost Country’s Struggling Indie Ecosystem 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "The Monster of Florence" (Courtesy of Emanuela Scarpa/Netflix) Investment in content production destined for Italy’s film TV and streaming industries dropped 7.4% to €2 billion ($2.24 billion) in 2025, compared with the previous year, with the scripted sphere suffering most amid uncertainty over government support of the country’s tax credits and the ongoing transition in viewership from linear to streaming. That is the main takeaway from a report issued on Wed. by Italian TV producers’ association APA during Rome’s MIA market, which is dedicated to international TV series, animation, feature films and documentaries. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately After reaping the rewards of a protracted growth spurt, Italian producers in 2025 faced a forced slowdown as the country’s right-wing government dithered with ongoing regulatory modifications to tax incentives for domestic film and TV production. The domestic tax credit modifications impasse did not impact Italy’s international production rebates which remained firmly in place. Popular on Variety “This situation hinders producers’ ability to plan, increases financial burdens, and shrinks profit margins,” the report pointed out. “It negatively impacts all companies — especially smaller ones — by straining liquidity and limiting their capacity for future investment,” is added. Hopefully, there is some relief in sight with the new tax credit now in place. The so-called application “window” to apply has been reopened. The report underlined that unscripted content remains the backbone of Italian broadcasting programming, with an output of over 17,000 hours of original, first-run content, being churned out by Italian producers last year. Independent production accounts for 59% of these titles. Unscripted offerings from streaming platforms in Italy have also expanded, with a 51% increase in the number of titles and a 30% rise in total hours. Within Italy’s unscripted sphere, the factual genre has seen the most significant growth, up 36% in terms of number of hours, with the number of domestic factual titles adapted from international formats doubling. Game shows are also gaining ground on linear networks, both in early evening and prime time slots. As for scripted originals, the number of titles in 2025 grew 9% to a total 101 shows produced for the current season. But this growth is driven primarily by 74 smaller domestic series for linear networks, that don’t tend to travel, while the number of Italian originals served up by streamers last year stands the same as 2024 with 27 titles, most of which are, similarly, “local for local” product. The report underlined that Italian scripted content continues to reach broad and demographically diverse audiences. In the linear broadcasting sphere, Lux Vide’s “Sandokan,” a modern take on the classic pirate tale adapted from Italian author Emilio Salgari’s iconic book series, and BiBiFilm’s “La Preside,” about a feisty female principal of a school in a crime-ridden Naples neighbourhood, both drew a hefty average of over 4.6 million viewers per episode. In the streaming space, Picomedia’s Naples-set prison drama “The Sea Beyond” is still a big hit on state broadcaster RAI’s streaming and linear outlets, as is Aurora TV’s period drama “Il Paradiso delle Signore.” The standout Italian original on Netflix is serial killer series “ The Monster of Florence ,” pictured above, directed by genre specialist Stefano Sollima that launched from the 2025 Venice Film Festival and garnered 9.7 million global views in its first week in October 2025. Meanwhile, as in the rest of the world, the market share for linear television (both free-to-air and pay-TV) is steadily shrinking in Italy while global platforms continue to grow. The streaming segment, which accounted for 21% of the market in 2020, has now reached 43% in the Italian market and “is set to surpass linear television in value in the short-to-medium term,” the report said. Also in line with global TV trends, microdramas are starting to gain traction in Italy with ReelShort, DramaBox, NetShort, and DramaWave already among the country’s top fifteen entertainment apps in terms of user spend, the report said. And the first original Italian microdrama production has been released, titled “Tutto in una notte,” produced by Fascino PGT, with its 54 episodes distributed on Italian platform WittyTV and on social media. articles.title: ‘Glee’ Reboot Officially Set at Disney+ and Hulu
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 5:00am PT ‘Glee’ Reboot Officially Set at Disney+ and Hulu By Selome Hailu Plus Icon Selome Hailu Latest ‘American Horror Story’ Renewed for Season 14 18 hours ago Elizabeth Holmes Mania: ‘You Can See Everything’ Drives 186% Viewership Spike for Amanda Seyfried’s ‘The Dropout’ (EXCLUSIVE) 19 hours ago ‘Lioness’ Season 3 Closes With 9.7 Million Viewers in Seven Days, a Series High and the No. 5 Paramount+ Finale Ever (EXCLUSIVE) 19 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Everett Collection To quote Finn Hudson, “The show must go all over the place, or something.” He was right: “ Glee ” is back. Disney+ and Hulu have greenlit a reboot of Ryan Murphy ‘s famous (and infamous) musical dramedy series. “Glee” premiered on Fox in 2009 concluded in 2015 after six seasons of following a group of show choir members from Lima, Ohio as they dealt with the highs and lows of high school and beyond. It was a massive cultural phenomenon that is especially remembered for the blunt, sometimes controversial ways it tackled topics such as sexuality, race, disability, mental health and more — as well as its covers of songs like “Don’t Stop Believin’,” “Teenage Dream,” “River Deep, Mountain High” and “Smooth Criminal,” among others. The series remains popular today, as does its music, which averages 4.1 million monthly listeners on Spotify. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately The original cast included Lea Michelle, Cory Monteith, Matthew Morrison, Jane Lynch, Dianna Agron, Chris Colfer, Darren Criss, Amber Riley, Naya Rivera, Heather Morris, Kevin McHale, Jenna Ushkowitz, Harry Shum Jr., Chord Overstreet, Mark Salling and more. Popular on Variety Details about the new “Glee” are scant; Disney shared nothing aside from the fact that the series is being produced by 20th Television and will air on Hulu and Disney+. Casting information is not yet known, though it can safely be assumed that several of the original stars will return. “I’ve been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members,” Murphy recently said in an interview with Entertainment Tonight, in which he confirmed that he’d just written a reboot script with collaborators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan. “It’s very sweet, and they all had a lot of questions, but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea.” Murphy’s comments came weeks after Michele expressed to E! News that she’d be happy to join a “Glee” reboot: “I love ‘Glee.’ I will always love ‘Glee.’ I love Ryan Murphy. It just holds such a special place in my heart for me… I will follow Ryan wherever he goes.” Speaking to Bustle recently, Colfer pointed out that rebooting “Glee” would be complicated following Rivera’s death, but that he would consider it: “It was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya [Rivera] is gone. But I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no. So I don’t know, but hopefully I’ll have more information and I can actually think about it.” Rivera died in 2020 at age 33, tragically drowning in a lake while saving her young son who had fallen into the water. She was the third death among the “Glee” cast: Monteith died from an overdose in 2013, while the show was still on the air, and Salling died by suicide in 2018 after pleading guilty to possession of child pornography. articles.title: Netflix Stock Deflates to Two-Year Low. What Will It Take to Revive Revenue Growth?
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 5:06am PT Netflix Stock Deflates to Two-Year Low. What Will It Take to Revive Revenue Growth? By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Netflix Stock Deflates to Two-Year Low. What Will It Take to Revive Revenue Growth? 2 hours ago Ted Sarandos Addresses Netflix Content Exec Purge: ‘I Know That We Could Do Better’ 17 hours ago Netflix Q3 Revenue Meets Wall Street Estimates, Forecasts Q4 Slowdown and Says It Will Miss Ad Sales Target for the Year 18 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Netflix Shares of Netflix hit a two-year low after the streamer’s Q3 2026 earnings report revealed an ongoing softening in top-line growth and a miss on advertising revenue for the full year. The stock was down -7% in premarket trading Wednesday, to under $64/share, a decline of nearly 30% year-to-date to the lowest point since August 2024. Netflix’s Q4 revenue guidance was slightly below Wall Street expectations, and the company said ad sales for 2026 are now expected to be $2.7 billion, $300 million lighter than previously forecast, because of the slower-than-expected rollout of “some ad product capabilities.” Related Stories CMA's 'Celebration of Dolly Parton' Special Slates 20 Performers, Including Ella Langley, Lainey Wilson, Molly Tuttle and Reba McEntire So how does Netflix recharge audience engagement (and therefore keep revenue pointed up) after a drop-off in viewing, particularly in the U.S. ? Popular on Variety To Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, the answer is better execution on its core model — that the company needs to crank up its buffet of buzzy, must-watch TV shows and movies. Last week he dismissed content chief Bela Bajaria, who’s being replaced by Peter Rice, as part of a larger overhaul of content leadership . On the Q3 earnings call, Sarandos praised Bajaria but said “I know that we could do better.” Ahead of its Q3 earnings, Netflix also laid off 1,000 workers , 6% of its headcount, which execs have framed as giving it the ability to invest more into growth areas. But some on Wall Street believe Netflix needs to do more than churn out TV and movie hits — that it needs a strategy to capture viewing of short-form video content, which is being soaked up by platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram. “[W[e think the Street should remain skeptical of a long-term strategy that simply sees NFLX double down on its legacy core strength (premium TV, films, and increasingly, live events), while NFLX remains largely absent from the fastest areas video entertainment growth (e.g., mobile, short-form),” New Street Research analyst Dan Salmon wrote in an Oct. 20 research note. YouTube continues to make significant viewing share gains with an “all content types, all formats” approach on connected TV, Salmon wrote. While it doesn’t make sense for Netflix to adopt a straight user-generated content approach, he said, “we believe bold thinking is increasingly needed to address these long-term threats to NFLX mindshare with younger audiences.” Pivotal Research Group’s Jeff Wlodarczak similarly cited concerns for Netflix that short-form entertainment “is doing to streaming what streaming has done to traditional Pay TV,” as younger consumers spend an ever-increasing amount of time on social media platforms. Following Netflix’s Q3 earnings report, Wlodarczak reduced his subscriber forecasts and increased programming cost forecasts, leading to a $5 reduction in his year-end 2026 target price on the stock to $65. Meanwhile, Netflix once touted the addition of videogames as an extension of its core service as a promising growth driver — but games weren’t mentioned at all in its Q3 earnings, except that the company noted in its shareholder letter that it teamed up with Take-Two Interactive to unveil a sneak peek in August of highly anticipated title “Grand Theft Auto VI.” But all of that said, with over 325 million global subscribers, Netflix remains well positioned to keep its core streaming business humming along nicely, albeit at a somewhat less rapid clip, according to MoffettNathanson analyst Robert Fishman. “We continue to believe Netflix has significant headspace to push monetization of its leading SVOD scale, which should lead to compounding profits for years to come,” Fishman wrote in a research note. MoffettNathanson forecasts Netflix earnings per share to reach $3.85 in 2027 (down from $4.00 previously), growing by 21% in 2028 to $4.65 (vs. $4.80 previously). The analyst reiterated a “buy” rating on Netflix stock but lowered his 12-month price target by $10 to $90/share. Also bullish on the long-term strategy was Wedbush Securities analyst Alicia Reese, who wrote in a note that “the details suggest Netflix isn’t beholden to industry headwinds; it is in control.” She noted, “Churn and pricing held up, ad demand is intact, Netflix is expanding its valuable live-events inventory, and it plans to preserve its content strategy rather than duking it out with YouTube on short-form.” “Importantly, management’s tone underscored its intent to shift toward a platform model as it broadens its licensing partnerships and add-on deals, in addition to reaccelerating its ad rollout,” Reese wrote. Because Netflix still has “significant potential” to expand ad revenue, Wedbush analysts reiterated their “outperform” rating on Netflix but lowered the price target on the stock from $90 to $80/share. articles.title: Neiman Marcus’s Luxe 2026 Holiday Offerings Include $180,000 ‘Star Wars’ Experience
articles.full_text: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. For “ Star Wars ” fans with $180,000 to spare, Neiman Marcus is offering something even harder to come by than a vintage lightsaber: a look inside the famously guarded world of Lucasfilm. The luxury department store has unveiled its annual Fantasy Gifts collection , headlined by a one-of-a-kind “Star Wars” experience that includes private access to Lucasfilm and Industrial Light & Magic, custom lightsabers and four VIP tickets to an upcoming “Star Wars” world premiere and afterparty. The six-figure package arrives ahead of the franchise’s 50th anniversary in 2027, when Disney and Lucasfilm will release Shawn Levy’s highly anticipated “Star Wars: Starfighter.” Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately Des Willie The experience begins at One Letterman in San Francisco’s Presidio, home to Lucasfilm and Industrial Light & Magic, the visual effects company George Lucas founded in 1975. Guests will receive private, behind-the-scenes access to the studios where some of Hollywood’s most recognizable cinematic worlds have been brought to life, along with a visit to an active Lucasfilm production. Also included is a one-of-one replica of an “Ahsoka” Season 2 lightsaber hilt prop signed by Lucasfilm president and chief creative officer Dave Filoni, as well as a private consultation to design a pair of custom-assembled lightsabers. The experience culminates in four VIP tickets to an upcoming Star Wars world premiere and afterparty, offering the opportunity to celebrate alongside the franchise’s cast and creators. Lucasfilm also prepares to celebrate half a century since the release of George Lucas’s original 1977 film. The anniversary comes amid a new theatrical chapter for the franchise, with “The Mandalorian & Grogu” slated for May 2026 and Levy’s “Starfighter,” starring Ryan Gosling, set to arrive in theaters in May 2027. The “Star Wars” package is the centerpiece of Neiman Marcus’ 2026 Holiday Book, which is celebrating its own milestone: 100 years since the retailer introduced its now-famous holiday catalog. This year’s edition, titled “Grand Gestures,” continues the Fantasy Gifts tradition that began in 1959, when Stanley Marcus started offering customers elaborate, sometimes outrageous presents that money could buy — provided they had enough of it. And while a $180,000 trip inside the “Star Wars” universe may be the most obvious draw for Hollywood obsessives, the rest of this year’s lineup is similarly ambitious. For fashion and jewelry collectors, Neiman Marcus is offering a six-day trip through Venice, Florence and Milan hosted by the Buccellati family, featuring private museum and atelier visits and a design session with Andrea Buccellati to create a bespoke piece of high jewelry. Another package, offered in partnership with Verdura, takes guests to New York City for a private tour of the jeweler’s historical collection and a fitting for a custom Maltese Cross cuff set with emeralds, sapphires and diamonds, followed by dinner at Orso and producer house seats to a Broadway show. Dolce & Gabbana is contributing a Carretto Siciliano foosball table, complete with hand-painted Sicilian artwork, solid wood construction and a screen-printed glass playing field. A fragrance experience with Saujet and Lalique includes a trip to Alsace, France, where guests will stay at Villa René Lalique, participate in a perfume masterclass and receive an exclusive first-edition crystal fragrance trunk. For those who prefer being on the water, another gift includes a fully loaded electric Arc Sport wake boat, personalized equipment and private lessons with world champion wakesurfer Austin Keen. And in perhaps the most sentimental offering of the bunch, customers can work with Neiman Marcus’ corporate chef to refine a cherished family recipe, which will then appear on the retailer’s restaurant menus nationwide for a full year. “The 2026 Fantasy Gifts continue to redefine extraordinary luxury through one-in-a-lifetime experiences, unparalleled access, and boundless imagination,” Darcy Penick, president and chief commercial officer of Exemplar Luxury Group, Neiman Marcus’ parent company, said in a statement. This year’s holiday campaign, dubbed “Holiday Fantasy,” also features supermodel Natasha Poly in imagery shot by director and photographer Alexandre Bassard at Neiman Marcus’ Beverly Hills store. The retailer is rolling out additional in-store events, holiday dining experiences and gift guides across its locations and digital channels. A portion of every Fantasy Gift purchase will benefit the Heart of Neiman Marcus Foundation through a corporate donation. The retailer is also continuing its seasonal fundraising campaign for Boys & Girls Clubs of America. Loading comments...

articles.title: Jake Tapper Sketches Work Outside CNN: Graphic Novel Probes Life of ‘Butcher’ Klaus Barbie
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 6:00am PT Jake Tapper Sketches Work Outside CNN: Graphic Novel Probes Life of ‘Butcher’ Klaus Barbie By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Starz Gets Back on Verizon Fios After New Carriage Pact 20 hours ago Atlanta Hawks Strike Streaming Alliance With Amazon’s Prime Video 23 hours ago Meet Kate DePetro, Fox News’ Social-Media Ambassador to Younger Viewers 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Top Shelf/Elliott O'Donovan Many of the stories, interviews and analyses Jake Tapper presents to his followers on CNN rely heavily on moving pictures, courtesy of his employer. A new project from the anchor and author will substitute still images — that Tapper drew himself. Tapper has spent the past three years working on a graphic novel, and much of his time was spent drawing every panel. “ The Butcher : The Decades-Long Hunt for Klaus Barbie, One of the World’s Most Notorious Killers,” will publish on June 1, 2027, from Top Shelf Productions. The illustrated novel examines the story of Klaus Barbie, the Nazi figure known as the “Butcher of Lyon” who escaped Germany and avoided capture for decades, until Nazi hunters and journalists tracked him down. Tapper, who first became interested in the story while visiting France with his family, used source material in four different languages to chronicle the pursuit for Barbie in excruciating detail. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately “It’s just this fascinating story about this young Nazi who comes to Leon, France, terrorizes the city, and then pops up years later in South America in Bolivia,” says the CNN anchor during a recent interview. “He also helped support a right-wing government in South America before eventually being captured.” In what may be a surprising twist, the journalist presents eyebrow-raising information about who helped Barbie escape Europe. Popular on Variety Graphic novels are a favored medium of younger readers who not only read coming-of-age tales or longer stories involving fictional characters, but also memoirs that deeply probe cultures or perspectives that may not turn up in more mainstream media formats. Top Shelf, Tapper’s publisher, has released graphic novels such as “From Hell” by Alan Moore and Eddie Campbell, “They Called Us Enemy” by actor George Takei, and the “March” trilogy co-written by Congressman John Lewis. Tapper may best be known for anchoring “The Lead” and “ State of the Union ” on CNN as well as some special news events, but he has long juggled his news job with a suite of other activities. He has written eight books, including three novels. What people may not know about him is that he has been drawn to comics and cartooning for most of his life. As a child, he avidly read Charles Schulz’ “Peanuts” and Walt Kelly’s “Pogo,” as well as super-heroes like Batman and Superman. His home office contains strips of “Little Orphan Annie,” “Doonesbury” and “Zippy the Pinhead.” Some of his work has been seen in Roll Call, the college paper at Dartmouth when he attended, and even in a local paper, The South Street Star, where he grew up. For a period of time, he drew a fresh piece for CNN’s “State of the Union” “It’s a very American art form,” he says of the medium. “There’s just a brilliance. It’s not filmed, but it’s not written. It’s somewhere in between.” Still, CNN viewers haven’t seen the end-of-show political cartoons he once drew in several years. “The truth of the matter is that I stopped doing it because the best political cartoons are really hard hitting, and I just, as an anchor, I just couldn’t do cartooning the way that it deserves to be done,” Tapper says. “I had to hold back. I had to pull punches. I had to run towards silly and inoffensive as opposed to hard hitting and brutal. And it just wasn’t as good. I wasn’t happy with it.” He’s had a lot of time to work on “The Butcher.” Tapper, who says he draws less frequently now, has been tough on himself. “After I finished the 250th page, I went back and redrew 100 pages because I’m like, those are awful. And I need to redraw them.” The recent practice has helped him regain some of his skill, he says, but “I’m still going back and tweaking.” One reason he embraced Top Shelf as his publisher is because he admired other graphic novels they have produced and he liked the fact that the editors there challenged him, with notes that could be “absolutely brutal.” Tapper embraced them. “I didn’t want it to be fast,” he says of the project. “I wanted it to be good.” He hopes the new graphic novel will have appeal. “It’s obviously a very serious topic, but it’s kind of a suspenseful book about how they track down this mass murderer who’d gotten away with it,” he says. “And then it gets into the politics of it, but in a very accessible way, about all the people that let this guy get away. I think anybody who’s interested in in a mystery, anybody who’s interested in World War II, anybody who’s interested in just a good yarn” will find something in the project. Tapper even worked with the daughter of Allan Ryan a former U.S. Department of Justice official who investigated how Barbie was able to avoid punishment for so long. He places Ryan in the graphic novel, where he serves as a sort of narrator. Tapper knows that some people may be surprised by his work in the medium, but believes the tale will win them over. “It’s not about 2026 politics at all,” he says. “It’s just a true story.” NFL on Sling TV 2026: Here’s How to Watch Minnesota Vikings vs. Chicago Bears Game Live Online Disney and NFL Team Up on Apparel Collection, Pairing Each of the League’s 32 Teams With Beloved Franchise Characters NFL Season 2026-2027 Livestream: Here’s Where to Watch Pro Football Games Online X Launches ‘NFL Gametime,’ a Football Feed Placed Alongside ‘For You’ and ‘Following’ Tony Romo Suggests He’d Like to Return to CBS’ NFL Coverage After No Contest Plea Netflix Taps ‘Friday Night Lights’ Director Peter Berg for NFL Gameday Openers, the First Narrated by Kyle Chandler Loading comments...

articles.title: Young Audiences Want to Redefine Modern Storytelling, New Study Shows
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 6:30am PT Young Audiences Want to Redefine Modern Storytelling, New Study Shows By Mya Copeland Plus Icon Mya Copeland Latest Young Audiences Want to Redefine Modern Storytelling, New Study Shows 33 minutes ago ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Screenwriter on Book-to-Screen Changes and Why Jane Austen Is So Adaptable: ‘She’s Almost Like Shakespeare’ 2 days ago Betty McGuire, ‘Growing Pains’ Actress, Dies at 100 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy Everett Collection Begone the days of 30-year-olds playing high schoolers! Gen Z and Gen Alpha want to see themselves depicted accurately on screen. A study from the Center for Scholars & Storytellers at UCLA found that young viewers are often not consulted about what they want to see on screen — even in projects about and for them. Over the past five years, CSS’s annual Teens and Screens Report has worked to change that by providing data about what young people really want to see. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately The 2026 report reveals a broad definition of what a “story” is and where to find it, coupled with an appetite for traditional media and in-person experiences. This year’s study surveyed more than 1,500 adolescents aged 10-24. Popular on Variety Among the interesting findings: YouTube (72.9%) ranked as the top medium for storytelling, with nearly four out of five respondents saying that short-term videos can tell a story. 16.8% said they would not cast an influencer in a project, while almost 40% said they would most prefer to cast an unknown actor. Gen Alpha and Gen Z are split on AI: 27.4% of respondents at age 19 identified “doom” as their dominant emotion toward its portrayals in media, while 44.2% of 10 to 13-year-olds described it as “fascinating.” 55% want to see more neurodivergent characters on screen. Friendship is key: 57.3% want to see more platonic relationships represented. “Adults are making stories that they think are going to resonate with young people, but they’re not really talking to a lot of young people to do it,” CSS founder and CEO Yalda T. Uhls, Ph.D., tells Variety about the findings. Uhls is a professor in UCLA’s psychology department who spent nearly two decades as a senior executive at studios like MGM and Sony before pivoting to psychology research of media and young adults. Since launching the Teens and Screens Report, Uhls has seen industry executives and researchers make a concerted effort to integrate the study’s findings. Uhls highlights that individuals from across the industry at CAA, Disney and UTA will attend a summit on Oct. 22 to listen and inform their work. “Our assumptions based on what we thought were stories when we were younger can’t hold,” Uhls says. “They’re not holding, and we need to really talk to young people, do research like this to make sure that these stories are everywhere and they’re consuming it all the time. Make sure that hopefully, if the people we work with that are in the industry — who have the real cultural power, they’re the ones making content that goes all over the world — if they’re really paying attention to our work about what young people need and want and care about, they’re gonna not only probably make content that will resonate and that these young people will see more, but also, it’ll just hopefully create a more empathetic and kind world.” In her work with CSS and the study, Uhls challenges her gut instincts on young people’s take on entertainment. She was surprised to hear participants say they think short-form content like Instagram Reels can tell stories. “So many adults look down on this medium,” Uhls says, but younger audiences “see stories everywhere. They see media. They’re looking for something that they can relate to that resonates with them. And if they don’t see it in a traditional piece of content storytelling in TV, books or movies, they’re going to go elsewhere, and they are going elsewhere.” Uhls describes these young audiences as “way more discerning” than executives might realize. “They like to discover someone new, but yet at the same time, with ‘Obsession’ and ‘Backrooms,’ there’s a different kind of storytelling that’s learned on YouTube really, and maybe TikTok and other things too. So, from a filmmaker perspective, it’s not that they want the stories on those platforms to be translated into mainstream content, but certainly the style and the thinking of their issues and what they do seems to be something Gen Z loves.” But this group Uhls surveys isn’t monolithic, something she stresses is important to remember. She recalls working on her dissertation and realizing that assumptions based only on Los Angeles teens did not ring true across the country. She has two things she hopes executives take away from the study’s findings: “Listening to young people and diverse young people from all over the country is one. And then the second thing is they’re way more nuanced than we give them credit for. They’re way more sophisticated than we give them credit for. Sometimes they say really wise and brilliant things.” CSS will host its sixth annual Teens & Screens Summit on Oct. 22 at the UCLA Meyer and Renee Luskin Conference Center. The event features panels and discussions with industry leaders, researchers and youth activists. Barack and Michelle Obama’s production company Higher Ground Productions will be honored with CSS’s second annual Greg Berlanti Social Impact Award at the event. articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 6:51am PT Sharjah Film Festival Unveils Lineup With ‘Gohan,’ ‘Monster Mia,’ Emirati Talent By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest ‘Big Boys Don’t Cry’ Director Muhammad Mustapha Talks Masculinity Ahead of El Gouna Premiere: ‘The Only Emotion Men Are Allowed to Express Is Anger’ 1 day ago Egyptian Star Mona Zaki Reflects on Three Decades of Reinvention as El Gouna Honors Her Career: ‘Art Is About Freedom’ 2 days ago 10 Films to Track at El Gouna, From Cannes and Berlin Standouts to Rising Arab Filmmakers 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "Monster Mia" (Courtesy of Arx Anima, Peng! Boom! Tschak!, Arxlight Pictures, Arx Anima MD) The Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth will bring films from Thailand, Brazil, India, Italy and across the Arab world to the UAE for its 13th edition, with a lineup featuring international festival titles, emerging filmmakers and Emirati talent. Running Oct. 26-Oct. 31, SIFF’s Green Carpet program includes Chayanop Bunprakob, Baz Poonpiriya and Atta Hemwadee’s Thai drama “ Gohan ,” Fabrizio Cattani’s Italian feature “Forever With You” and Verena Fels’ Austrian-German animated film “ Monster Mia ,” all receiving their Middle East premieres. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately “Gohan” follows a stray dog as he passes through the lives of three owners over more than a decade, while “Forever With You” follows two friends whose search for a missing dog leads them deep into the woods and into unexpected danger. “Monster Mia” follows a 12-year-old girl who finds herself at a school full of monsters. Poonpiriya previously directed Thai box-office hit “Bad Genius” and Sundance prize winner “One for the Road.” Popular on Variety Elsewhere in the lineup, Juan Cabral’s Argentine feature “Risa and the Wind Phone” receives its Gulf premiere. Cabral’s previous feature, “ Two/One ,” premiered at Tribeca and was released by Mubi across select international territories. Indian filmmaker Ravi Nimbalkar’s “87 Rupees Ink Pen” also receives its Middle East premiere, while Brazilian director Celia Catunda’s animated feature “My Grandfather Is a Nihonjin” arrives in Sharjah after premiering at Annecy in 2025. The animation selection extends to David Súkup, Patrik Pašš, Leon Vidmar and Jean-Claude Rozec’s Czech-French-Slovak-Slovenian stop-motion feature “ Tales From the Magic Garden ,” another 2025 Annecy selection. Local talent features in the shorts program. Abdulrahman Al Madani’s “Oug,” part of the Arabic short-film competition, follows an Emirati couple facing family and social pressure to have children. The film received the Gulf Capital-ADMAF Visual Arts Award in 2025 and has since screened at Denmark’s Odense Intl. Film Festival. Young filmmakers also get their own space through SIFF’s Child & Youth Made Films and student competitions, with selections spanning live-action and animation. The wider festival program counts 71 films from 38 countries selected from a pool of 1,802 submissions representing 72 countries, with a further eight films screening out of competition. Morning screenings at VOX Cinemas City Centre Al Zahia are reserved for school-aged and university students, while evening screenings are open to the public. Workshops introduce young participants to stop-motion and flipbook animation, alongside workshops on cinematography, production management and content creation. Italy, this year’s country of honor, is represented in the workshop program with “The Italian Eye – Photography Through Light, Color & Composition” and “Tell a Story in Five Shots – Inspired by Italian Cinema.” The festival’s panel lineup turns to what happens once filmmakers have industry-ready work. “Film Festivals Decoded: What Happens After You Press Submit?” brings together festival programmers and directors to discuss the selection process, submissions and how festivals build their programs. Moderated by Saudi Cinema Assn. CEO Hani Al Mulla, the panel features Rotterdam Arab Film Festival artistic director Rosh Abdelfattah, American Intl. University Kuwait executive director of alumni affairs and strategic events Alia Al Azzeh, and Alexandria Short Film Festival head Mohamed Mahmoud. Another panel, “How Do I Get My Next Film Made? From Idea to Financing,” will focus on pitching materials, development labs, producers, financing and co-production opportunities. The festival’s Industry Hub and pitching sessions will run alongside the public program, giving emerging filmmakers opportunities to present projects and connect with industry professionals. SIFF opens Oct. 25, with screenings beginning Oct. 26 and continuing through Oct. 31, ahead of the closing ceremony on Nov. 1.
