articles.title: LuckyChap International Hires Experienced Searchlight Exec Katie Goodson-Thomas as President of Film
articles.full_text: Oct 20, 2026 6:00am PT LuckyChap International Hires Experienced Searchlight Exec Katie Goodson-Thomas as President of Film At Searchlight, Goodson-Thomas oversaw film including "The Favourite," "Poor Things," "Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri," "The Banshees of Inishirin" and "Wild Horse Nine" By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest LuckyChap International Hires Experienced Searchlight Exec Katie Goodson-Thomas as President of Film 1 hour ago Prince Harry Opens Up About Move Back to England and Wanting to ‘Work It Out’ With King Charles and Prince William: ‘The Most Important Thing Is to Reconcile’ 2 hours ago Emily Watson Joins ‘The Drive,’ Inspired by JFK Assassination, as Exec Producer (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Debbie Zhou LuckyChap International, the London-based joint venture between LuckyChap and Mediawan that was unveiled in late 2025, has given its filmmaking ambitions a shot in the arm with a significant new hire. Katie Goodson-Thomas , a hugely respected and experienced exec who has spent more than a decade at Searchlight Pictures , is set to leave the studio to join the LuckyChap International team in the new role of president of film. Related Stories Laika Submits Original Song From 'Wildwood' for Oscars, 'The Better Part of Bravery,' Performed by The Decemberists (EXCLUSIVE) Oscars: Rwanda Selects 'Ben'Imana' as First-Ever Entry to International Feature Race Working in close partnership with co-managing directors Mona Qureshi and Tanya Qureshi, who joined earlier this year, Goodson-Thomas will spearhead the film slate, with the LuckyChap International leadership trio working in collaboration with LuckyChap partners Margot Robbie, Tom Ackerley, Josey McNamara and Milan Popelka, alongside the broader U.S. team. Popular on Variety At Searchlight, where she was most recently executive vice president, co-head of production and development, Goodson-Thomas played a key role in expanding the studio’s U.K. presence, overseeing numerous award-winning films such as Yorgos Lanthimos’ “The Favourite” and “Poor Things,” Martin McDonagh’s “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri,” “The Banshees of Inisherin” and the upcoming “Wild Horse Nine,” as well as “All of Us Strangers,” “The Roses” and Alice Birch’s forthcoming directorial debut “Sweetsick,” starring Cate Blanchett. “We’re thrilled to welcome Katie to LuckyChap International,” said Mona Qureshi and Tanya Qureshi. “Her career embodies the kind of independent spirit and big-heartedness that inspires us, and her ambition, taste and creative instinct make her a natural fit for what we are building. We can’t wait to have her alongside us as a fellow journeywoman!” Added Goodson-Thomas: “The LuckyChap team has exceptional taste, fearlessness and a creative identity entirely its own, as well as an infectious sense of possibility about what the company can achieve. Searchlight has been such an incredible creative home for me that I always knew it would take somewhere truly special to tempt me away. The opportunity to join that alongside Mona, Tanya and such a brilliant team was simply too exciting to resist. The U.K. and Europe are full of remarkable talent, and I’m hugely ambitious about what we can find, back and get made together.” Goodson-Thomas will officially join LuckyChap International in the new year. “We’re in awe of everything Katie has accomplished throughout her career, and we all feel extraordinarily privileged that she is bringing her undeniable creative talents, vision and depth of experience to LuckyChap International,” said LuckyChap’s US partners Robbie, Ackerley, McNamara and Popelka. “She’s such a kindred spirit culturally, and we’ve long admired her ability to spot exceptional filmmaking talent and champion their projects from the very beginning all the way through. We genuinely couldn’t be more excited to have her join us on this adventure, and to forge a killer slate together that we can all be incredibly proud of!” Added Searchlight president Matthew Greenfield: “Katie has been a wonderful colleague all of these years and LuckyChap International is getting an exceptional and passionate advocate for filmmakers. We couldn’t be happier for her as she takes on this next chapter, and we’re excited to see all that she and the team will accomplish together.” Charlize Theron on ‘The Odyssey’ Becoming Universal’s Highest-Grossing Movie and Raising Millions to Fight Femicide in Africa With CTAOP Loading comments...

articles.title: Hulu’s Mother-Son Mystery ‘Phony’ Mutes Connie Britton’s Charisma Under Visual Effects: TV Review
articles.full_text: Oct 20, 2026 6:15am PT Hulu’s Mother-Son Mystery ‘Phony’ Mutes Connie Britton’s Charisma Under Visual Effects: TV Review By Alison Herman Plus Icon Alison Herman TV Critic aherman2006 Latest For the Love of Television, Please Watch ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2: TV Review 6 days ago Like Its Hero, Marvel’s ‘VisionQuest’ Struggles to Connect Emotionally: TV Review 1 week ago ‘Avatar: Seven Havens’ Takes the Franchise in an Intriguing, Postapocalyptic New Direction: TV Review 2 weeks ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Hulu It’s a shame Hulu shared only half the first season of the streamer’s new comedy-mystery series “ Phony ” with critics in advance, because so much depends on how the show resolves its central source of suspense. The premise is what one character calls a “reverse cuckoo situation,” or at least a potential one: When Sonny (Sam Nivola), a high-school student in the Pacific Northwest, gets into a nasty car crash, he wakes up a week later to a surreal nightmare. His mother, Ellen ( Connie Britton ), has been replaced by someone else, and nobody around him seems to notice. Is he crazy, or is everyone else blind? Related Stories Oscars: Syria Selects Doc 'The Other Side of the Sun' for International Feature Race, Marking First Entry Since Fall of Assad Regime Oscar Predictions: Best Original Screenplay — 'Club Kid' and 'Josephine' Lead a Field of Personal, Timely Stories At first, “Phony” creator Nick Paley, who directed half the season and penned the first couple of episodes, plays into the ambiguity of Sonny’s possible delusion. Obviously, a child who recently suffered a serious head trauma is far from a reliable narrator, and in the premiere, Paley leans into the subjectivity with distorted sound and imagery. When the camera inhabits Sonny’s point of view, as it does almost constantly in the beginning, Ellen does, in fact, look different: thanks to the magic of visual effects, Britton’s eyebrows, nose and other features are all subtly altered, and the changes played up with side-by-side comparisons. Popular on Variety The distortions are especially striking given the actor’s pre-existing place in the pantheon of TV moms. (Britton also serves as an executive producer here.) Ellen is also the principal of Sonny’s high school, and a warm-but-firm educator naturally evokes Tami Taylor, even if Oregon is thousands of miles and metaphorical light-years away from West Texas. Subtly tweaking Britton’s face and voice is effectively uncanny, because viewers have such a deep knowledge of her mannerisms from “Friday Night Lights” and other shows. But for “Phony,” depriving itself of Britton’s full expressive powers cuts both ways. We’re supposed to feel their absence, and do. And yet when it comes to understanding Sonny and Ellen’s relationship, particularly while we don’t understand what actually happened to Ellen and why, the audience is met with just that: an absence. Before the crash, we get a few scenes that establish the status quo of Ellen and Sonny’s relationship. As a single mom and her only child, they’re a tightly knit pair, with Ellen respectful yet wary of Sonny’s growing autonomy. Not that Sonny knows what to do with that independence: He’s an inveterate people-pleaser, insistently upbeat in a way his peers know is “a little full of shit” but unable to stop himself from adapting to suit whoever’s in front of him. Ellen and Sonny’s maybe-final fight goes down when she finds the sex toy he bought in anticipation of sleeping with his girlfriend Chloe (Mahaela Park), because he thinks that’s what he’s supposed to do. Given that so much about Ellen (or is it “Ellen”?) is physically and figuratively obscured, Nivola — Britton’s fellow “The White Lotus” alum, though the two appeared on separate seasons — ends up shouldering the lion’s share of the show. He’s up to the task, giving Sonny a sweetly nervous energy and even some slapstick as he runs around in search of the truth. The tone of “Phony” is lighter and more comedic than one would expect of the horror-adjacent premise, if reflective of Paley’s CV, which includes credits for co-writing “Marcel the Shell with Shoes On” and directing on “Broad City.” Episodes are a zippy half-hour, and unfold in a world where a teen spotting a corpse in the woods is an occasion for a “dead body party” with a massage line. With its evergreen forests and ominous shots of beavers subbing in for owls, “Twin Peaks” is a clear influence, but the predominant vibe is less eerie than benignly kooky. Too insecure to confide in Chloe or his best friend Vogel (Maliq Johnson), Sonny instead finds investigative partners in cousins Mallory (Grace Brennan) and Weldon (Colter Lee), social outcasts — she’s an ex-homeschooler from an evangelical family, he’s just a weirdo — who prove open to his theories. A sympathetic ear is always nice, but the trio doesn’t accomplish much in the season’s first half besides hiring Sharla (Meera Syal), a “private investigator” whose chief qualification is her enthusiastic posts in conspiracy forums. “Phony” nonetheless starts offering hints that Sonny may be onto something. Circumstantial evidence (this Ellen doesn’t return Sonny’s customary triple squeeze) gives way to more objective indicators. Even in scenes outside Sonny’s perspective, Ellen still looks like not-quite-Connie Britton, fielding suspicious phone calls and making covert trips to the bank. “Phony” probably couldn’t draw out the question of whether Sonny is imagining things or not for eight entire episodes, but by the point the screeners stopped, the show is in an awkward lull: too far in to be intriguingly open-ended, not far in enough to judge the journey by its destination. Without knowing not-Ellen’s origins, MO or motivations (or what happened to actual Ellen!), it’s hard to tell what “Phony” is even about, and therefore how well it executes a self-assigned brief. Is the show a coming-of-age story about Sonny learning to listen to his instincts? Is it a family story about how adolescence turns parents and kids into strangers? Is it something much weirder altogether? “Phony” provokes a mild curiosity, rather than a burning urgency, to find out which. Partially handicapping Britton turns out to be a big sacrifice. The first two episodes of “Phony” are now streaming on Hulu, with new episodes airing weekly on Tuesdays. articles.title: BBC Three Among Linear Services Set to Close as Broadcaster Looks for Savings
articles.full_text: Oct 20, 2026 6:20am PT BBC Three Among Linear Services Set to Close as Broadcaster Looks for Savings By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest BBC Three Among Linear Services Set to Close as Broadcaster Looks for Savings 29 minutes ago Merged Banijay, All3Media Entity Sets Top Brass Comprised of Banijay Execs 6 hours ago ‘Slow Horses’ Season 7 Taps ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Star Varada Sethu, ‘Mank’s’ Tuppence Middleton 24 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images The BBC has confirmed it will shut down a host of linear broadcast services next year. Among those impacted are BBC Three, BBC Scotland and BBC Radio 4 Extra. The decision was made as the beleaguered corporation seeks to make cuts across the board in a bit to save £500 million by 2028. “We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world,” said BBC director-general Matt Brittin. “We all know that means tough choices.” Related Stories Ava DuVernay’s Doc ‘14th’ to Submit New Original Song by Brittany Howard and Robert Glasper for Oscars Consideration (EXCLUSIVE) Why 'You Can See Everything' Could Make Oscars History as First Doc Nominated for Best Picture “Much of the great content they currently carry will still be found where audiences already enjoy it on iPlayer and Sounds,” he said specifically of the shuttering linear services. “While this follows media speculation, I recognise the confirmation of this news will be hard for audiences and colleagues.” Popular on Variety Content from BBC Scotland, BBC Three and Radio 4 Extra will still be available digitally, via iPlayer, BBC Sounds and YouTube. BBC Scotland will also continue as a standalone channel on iPlayer while some of its content will be available on local broadcasts of BBC One and BBC Two. News director Rachel Jupp will also be making changes within the BBC News division. In response to the news, Directors U.K. CEO Andy Harrower, said: “The removal of BBC Three and BBC Scotland from linear broadcast must not lead to a reduction in the number or range of programmes commissioned for their audiences. For many directors, commissions on BBC Three and BBC Scotland provide essential opportunities for them to develop their craft, take creative risks and progress towards larger productions.” “Directors U.K. is therefore calling on the BBC to guarantee that these changes will not reduce the volume or breadth of commissioning, or opportunities behind the camera. Any new model must protect investment in emerging directors and production across the nations and regions, and ensure that audiences are still able to easily find these programmes online.” Rough Seas: A War-Torn Middle East Isn’t the Only Reason the Red Sea Film Festival Was Abruptly Canceled Paul Walker’s Brother Says AI Could Bring Actor Back for Final ‘Fast and Furious’ Movie but ‘I Would Not Be Interested in Doing That’ Red Sea Film Festival Cancels 2026 Edition, Will Return Next Year Loading comments...

articles.title: Meet Kate DePetro, Fox News’ Social-Media Ambassador to Younger Viewers
articles.full_text: Oct 20, 2026 6:30am PT Meet Kate DePetro, Fox News’ Social-Media Ambassador to Younger Viewers By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Meet Kate DePetro, Fox News’ Social-Media Ambassador to Younger Viewers 34 minutes ago ‘Star Wars’ Comes to 2027 Super Bowl With Animated ‘Alterna-Cast’ for Disney Channel, XD, Disney+ 12 hours ago Christiane Amanpour to Exit CNN in June After 43 Years in TV News 23 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Fox News Media Aficionados of Fox News may not know Kate DePetro as well as they do mainstays like Harris Faulkner, Sean Hannity or Bret Baier. Give them some time. Fox News Media has hired DePetro, a former production assistant, for a new role that may prove to be extremely important to the cable-news mainstay as it seeks broader audiences beyond its traditional TV connections. DePetro will serve as a sort of in-house creator, developing original content and programming aimed at offering a behind-the-scenes look at the goings-on at Fox News Channel , Fox Business Network, Fox Nation, and other properties that are part of the Fox Corp. unit. DePetro will appear primarily on Fox News Now, a social-media platform that launched in June to help forge connections between viewers and Fox News shows and figures. Related Stories ‘You Can See Everything’ Sets Oscar Campaigns for Best Picture, Supporting Actress and More Categories Amanda Seyfried Rejects Sex Scenes and Turned Down a TV Series Where 'I'd Have to Have Sex All the Time': I Don't Want to Be 'Naked With a Stranger' “I’ll have the opportunity to create original content, introduce audiences to familiar faces in a more personal way and share experiences across Fox News Media platforms,” DePetro says in a statement provided via email. “It’s a dream opportunity and I can’t wait to get started.” Popular on Variety Like other TV networks, Fox News Channel is paying more attention to the younger viewers who don’t rely on cable subscriptions for news, information and entertainment. Executives at Fox, for example, have noticed that Fox News has proven a popular option on Fox One, the streaming subscription service that was originally intended as a way to get Fox Sports in front of the digital generation. And Fox News has seen its audience on TikTok, which stood at around 25,000 followers in 2024, rise to 12.2 million as of October of this year. DePetro is “kind of like the ultimate insider,” says David Eccleston, Fox News Media’s senior vice president of brand strategy and consumer experience, during a recent interview. Many of the company’s top personalities have come to interact with her during her five years with the company, he says, and “know who she is and trust what she is about.” Elevating DePetro, who recently worked as an assistant to Dana Perino , the daytime anchor and panelist on “The Five,” spotlights the growing affinity younger viewers have for so-called “creators ” and other figures who find connections on social and digital media platforms. One-fifth of U.S. adults regularly get news on TikTok, according to a Pew Research Center survey from August, 2026 — a statistic that is the same as in 2025 but up from a mere 3% in 2020. Pew also recently found that the share of Americans who say they prefer to get news from television decreased to 28% in 2026 from 34% in 2025, while the share who prefer to get news from social media increased to 19% from 14% in that same time period. Fox News has been paying more attention to creators , podcasters and digital experts. The company’s alliance with the conservative “Ruthless” podcast, for example, continues to expand. On Election Night, “Ruthless” will host a three-hour livestream from a Washington, D.C. bar, airing between 8 p.m. and 11 p.m. eastern on both Fox Nation and Fox News Digital. Brett Cooper, who gained a profile with a YouTube show from The Daily Wire, is now a Fox News contributor who also leads her own digital program via Fox Corp. sibling Red Seat Ventures. Sports-TV powerhouse ESPN has also tapped young, digital savants in a bid to find younger audiences. The Disney sports-media outlet hired Omar Raja, creator of the popular “House of Highlights” account on Instagram in 2020. Since that time, he has even made appearances on ABC’s pre-Oscars red carpet show. Katie Feeney, who developed her own popular sports-focused social-media accounts while in college, joined ESPN in 2025. “There is definitely an opportunity to reach a new audience” for Fox News’ properties, says Eccleston. “We know we can do that on digital and social.” DePetro knows how to get behind the scenes at Fox News because she has worked there. She logged stints as an overnight production assistant for “Fox & Friends,” and later helped supervise the show’s green room, where guests and personalities stay until the time arrives to go on air. As part of her job, she has met athletes, entertainers and world leaders. DePetro met Fox News’ Perino in the green room after reading the anchor’s book, “Everything Will Be Okay.” After a mentoring session, Perino offered her a position as her assistant. Over two years, DePetro helped Perino build a presence on social media. Perino has “been an incredible mentor, advocate and friend who saw something in me before I saw it in myself,” says DePetro. DePetro will juggle other tasks as well. She is also working on “The Vow,” a Fox Nation dating series hosted by Chris Harrison, who once led “The Bachelor” on ABC. She is also the co-founder of Pizza to Pews, an initiative that encourages young people across the country to come to church and make friends. Her new role is aimed at helping Fox News create new bonds as well. l. articles.title: Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’
articles.full_text: Oct 20, 2026 6:30am PT Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’ Guillermo del Toro, at the 24th Morelia Film Festival to present the 3D re-Release of his Oscar-winning “Pan’s Labyrinth,” Del Toro reflected on the 20 years that have passed since his anti-fascist fable was first released By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest ‘Leap Year’ Director Michael Rowe’s Cross Border Drama ‘Last Weekend’ Boarded by Mexico’s Paloma Negra 19 hours ago Caos Cine, a New Mexican Distributor, Launches at Morelia Fest With ‘The Huntress,’ Picked Up From Edher Campos and Gabriela Maire’s Zafiro (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s ‘Jengira’s Magnificent Dream,’ With Tilda Swinton, Boarded by ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Mexican Co-Producer Piano 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source (l-r) Daniela Michel, Guillermo del Toro, UNAM's Jorge Martínez Micher and Hugo Alejandro Concha. Courtesy of the Morelia Film Festival Mexico’s beloved Guillermo del Toro descended on the 24 th Morelia Film Festival like the rockstar he is, greeted by hordes of shrieking fans that impressed even the most jaded in the crowd. In town to present the much-anticipated 3D Re-Release of “Pan’s Labyrinth,” he was everywhere all at once, holding a masterclass where tickets were as elusive as a seat at Cannes that went on for nearly three hours and a free-wheeling press conference that extended past its time limit. Related Stories Andrew Garfield Could Win an Oscar for 'Artificial' and His Norman Bates-Inspired Turn as Sam Altman Oscars: Pakistan Selects Documentary 'Hanging by a Wire' for International Feature Race (EXCLUSIVE) It was his third time at the fest, 20 years after his multi-Oscar winning “Pan’s Labyrinth’ first played there and years later with his 2018 best picture Academy Award winner “The Shape of Water.” Popular on Variety Before the presser kicked off, Del Toro, an Honorary Doctorate recipient from the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), received the Filmoteca UNAM Medal, an honor also bestowed on Alfonso Cuarón, in town to support his son Jonas Cuarón’s opening night film, “Campeón Gabacho,” which he produced. Alongside Del Toro were festival director Daniela Michel, “Pan’s Labyrinth” producer Bertha Navarro, his then young lead Ivana Baquero and DP Guillermo Navarro, who took home the cinematography Oscar for his stunning work on the anti-fascist fable. Reflecting on a question posed midway through the press conference about what has stayed the same and what has changed over the 20 years since “Pan’s Labyrinth,” del Toro responded with tears. “The state of our species and society today goes beyond anything we could have imagined back then. But I recognize the same sadness and despair. It pains me deeply to see one, two, or three generations fail the next. We’re handing down a world in ruins, morally, socially and spiritually fractured, with the very fabric that once allowed us to tell fables and parables falling apart.” Asked whether he knew beforehand if “Pan’s Labyrinth” would be well received, Del Toro recounted how his collaborations with both Navarros sustained him through all the challenges they faced. “We embarked on an adventure that was financially horrifying but cinematically beautiful,” he said. “You never know how a film will be received. We only found out when we screened it for the first time at Cannes. We got that famous standing ovation that lasted more than 22 minutes, and from that moment on, everything changed. It changed our lives.” “I think ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ marked a before and after for me. In terms of creative freedom, possibilities and everything else, I’m where I am today because of that film. But none of it would have been possible without the faith of my immediate family, Bertha and Guillermo.” Said DP Navarro: “Guillermo and I share the belief that cinematic language is storytelling through images that convey emotion and narrative. ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ is the ultimate expression of that. The camera is constantly searching, discovering and communicating.” “It was also an incredibly difficult shoot. We had a limited budget, had to find unconventional solutions and took risks that could easily have failed. But we gambled and we won. Without a doubt, it’s my best film, and I hold that experience close to my heart. I hope new generations will continue to discover and appreciate it. And now, 20 years later, it returns. Olé!” Producer Navarro, who also backed Del Toro’s career-launching feature debut “Cronos” and his much-lauded “The Devil’s Backbone,” said: “When he gave me the screenplay for ‘Cronos,’ I was absolutely fascinated. Talent shines, and you have to know how to recognize that light. That’s what I saw in Guillermo.” “It’s been an incredible privilege to have made those three great films with Guillermo. I’ve produced many films throughout my life, but those three hold a much deeper significance for me. They changed my life.” Baquero concurred: “’Pan’s Labyrinth’ undoubtedly opened doors for me, both into the genre and in my career. We’ve talked this afternoon about how much the film changed our lives, professionally and personally. For me, acting went from being a hobby – I had worked before ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ – to becoming my profession. Without that film, I might not be here today. It unquestionably marked a turning point in my career.” Reflecting on its impact on young audiences. Del Toro noted: “There’s an urgency and a fragility and ferocity that coexist in ‘Pan’s Labyrinth.’ And somehow, I think it’s an urgent moment to speak, for the film to speak to a new audience.” Local politics also crept into the conference, with a journalist asking him what he would say to the young people protesting in his hometown of Guadalajara over its current issues of contaminated water, repression and the alleged kidnapping of protesters on Oct. 11. He responded: “This morning at my masterclass, I gave young people the floor to speak about these issues. It’s terrifying that something so fundamental should have to be fought for instead of being resolved through basic humanity and responsible leadership.” “I said it clearly: “Their voices must be heard, and I stand with them 100%. It’s unacceptable that this remains unresolved or that anyone would try to silence them. Speaking out, protesting, and demanding a solution are fundamental rights – anytime, anywhere.” The Morelia Film Festival began on Oct. 16 and wraps Oct. 25. articles.title: Palestinian Filmmaker Rakan Mayasi on His Search for Unconventional Stories and Portraying ‘Communities That Have Not Been on Film Before’
articles.full_text: Oct 20, 2026 6:31am PT Palestinian Filmmaker Rakan Mayasi on His Search for Unconventional Stories and Portraying ‘Communities That Have Not Been on Film Before’ By Jay Weissberg Plus Icon Jay Weissberg Latest Palestinian Filmmaker Rakan Mayasi on His Search for Unconventional Stories and Portraying ‘Communities That Have Not Been on Film Before’ 31 minutes ago ‘Safe Exit’ Director Mohammed Hammad on Staying True to His Vision: ‘I Need to Be Free as a Filmmaker’ 4 days ago ‘Back to Buenos Aires’ Review: Marco Bechis’ Return to the Screen Covers Similar Ground to Earlier Works but is Only Fitfully Effective 1 month ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Atata and Rakan Mayasi Iconoclastic Palestinian filmmaker Rakan Mayasi ’s debut feature “ Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep ” made a splash in this year’s Un Certain Regard in Cannes with its powerful, poetic treatment of a Bedouin community in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley. This week it plays in a competition slot at the El Gouna Film Festival , where Variety spoke to the director. Inspired by Mayasi’s grandmother, it’s a story of two women who become pawns in a tribal blood feud, played out in a visionary style that owes much to Mayasi’s mentor Abbas Kiarostami, yet has its own rhythm and sensorial, at times almost feverish, point of view. Following its Cannes premiere the film has been warmly received at other festivals, and will be screening at Montpellier’s CineMed followed immediately by the Rome Film Festival, in their Best First Feature section. International sales are being handled by Salaud Morisset . Popular on Variety Related Stories Pedro Pascal in 'Behemoth!': The Oscar-Worthy Role That He (and Latinos) Have Been Waiting For Oscars: Pakistan Selects Documentary 'Hanging by a Wire' for International Feature Race (EXCLUSIVE) The film has several exceptional set pieces: it opens with a car in flames, in the middle there’s a stunningly hallucinatory wedding sequence, and it ends with an evocative longshot that plays with visual space. When you and your cinematographer Pôl Seif were conceiving the film, did you have these already in mind? Some of it was already set and ready in our minds. Some of it, no. For example, for sure the fire, it was there since the beginning. I’m interested in metaphors and how to translate that visually, so with Pôl we had the idea that we zoom in so you feel that the car is getting closer to you and the fire is spreading. We were trying to translate what the metaphor could possibly look like. Whereas the end was rewritten, by the two of us, because it’s a very visual scene. So we blocked it again three days before the shoot ended, and we rewrote it entirely. The wedding scene has been singled out by many critics for its visual beauty and the emotional shift it conveys. In that scene I allowed myself to get out of the narrative, so to speak, to change the rhythm and play with a kind of psychedelic approach. It’s never really stated that this was the actual wedding, and when the one sister, Jawahir, is revealed as a bride, it is very theatrical. The idea was kind of like zooming into her subconscious, into her imagination of a celebration. It allowed me to play around. For example, the whole scene was improvised. I never met any of these dancers before. We made a call for the biggest number of people to join, and we were very lucky because a lot of people came and they were very, very energetic. My job was to just have a microphone and make them more energetic. The scene also allows the community to be seen in a more three-dimensional light. The idea was to juxtapose two emotions and then make the audience feel guilty afterwards. I want to enjoy watching this pleasing, psychedelically shot dance sequence, but then afterwards I will ask myself, what the fuck did I just watch and why did I enjoy that? This was the idea. Is that something that you enjoy in film in general? Do you like that idea of sort of thinking, what the fuck did I just watch? Yes! My next film will be entirely like this. Speaking of things that are unexpected, we’re used to a particular kind of Lebanese cinema that deals primarily with the Civil War and subsequent crises. Yet you’ve chosen something completely different. You’ve gone into the Bekaa Valley and focused on a community that probably hasn’t been seen before in a feature film. I don’t like formulaic films. I don’t like the way we are seen outside, with every film having to talk about the Civil War, or the post-Civil War. I want to go to communities that have not been on film before, mainly because there’s much more depth in plots and characters and life there. This is why I wanted to work with non-professional actors. I could have gotten actors and put them in there in this context, but I prefer not to because this fragile authenticity has to be kept. Also, don’t forget that I’m Palestinian. I lived in Lebanon 20 years, and though I don’t have Lebanese nationality, I also feel Lebanese somehow because I became a filmmaker in Lebanon. But I don’t like the mainstream, so to speak. I like to dig in and see much more into life, basically. Is your next project also set in Lebanon? Half of it happens in Gaza. It was supposed to be my first feature, but it’s a dark comedy, so I had to stop it when the Israeli genocide began in Palestine. Now I’m returning to it a bit slowly; it’s an absurdist, deadpan dark comedy, very different from “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep.” It’s more staged, in a more controlled environment. And it’s about life and death. and the bureaucracy of life, basically. It’s called “The Passport” and I’m in late development/early pre-production. May Odeh, who’s associate producer on “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep,” is producing that film. What’s next for “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep”? After Cannes, it was selected in 50 festivals, which is fantastic, and it’s doing quite well at the festival circuit. I’m doing a tour of eight festivals in October, including Rome, the Viennale, Valladolid and in Bucharest, Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes Reprise. It will also be in Geneva in early November. articles.title: Spotify Inks Licensing Deal With Believe Music for AI Remixing Tool
articles.full_text: Oct 20, 2026 7:00am PT Spotify Inks Licensing Deal With Believe Music for AI Remixing Tool By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Collage, a New Management and Investment Company, Launches as a Bridge Between AI-First Studios and Hollywood (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago Ticketmaster Goes All-In on AI, Names Ex-Amazon Exec as Chief Technology Officer 22 hours ago Diddy Moved to New Prison Days After Being Hospitalized for Alleged Head Injury 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Spotify/Believe Spotify has struck a content licensing deal with the France-based independent music company Believe ahead of its forthcoming AI-powered remixing tool, an agreement that also covers Believe’s digital distribution division TuneCore. The deal is the latest in Spotify’s stable of agreements with music companies for the tool, following agreements with Universal Music Group , Merlin and Kobalt. The platform envisions the tool as a paid add-on to Spotify Premium, letting fans remix or cover songs by their favorite artists on a platform the company controls while creating an additional revenue stream for musicians and companies. The service — still unnamed, with no release date — is meant to combat the swarm of unauthorized AI-generated adaptations of songs that have littered social media platforms. Related Stories Oscar Predictions: Best Actress — How Obsessed Will the Academy Become With Inde Navarrette? Elizabeth Holmes Exposé Book 'Bad Blood' Returns to Bestseller Lists Following Nathan Fielder Doc Believe and Spotify had been discussing a partnership for a year, Believe said in a statement, and its artists’ participation is voluntary. Artists can first choose whether to participate in an AI service and then, after that, decide whether to permit Spotify to use their work for the tool. Popular on Variety “Together, we are turning an already widespread fan remixing activity into a licensed experience that will enhance fan remix creation within Spotify’s controlled platform and generate revenues for artists,” Believe CEO and founder Denis Ladegaillerie said in the statement. “This is how our four principles – consent, control, compensation and transparency – translate into tangible benefits for artists. Equally importantly, we share a commitment to protecting artists, reflected in Spotify’s strengthened safeguards against AI-generated spam and low-value content, and Believe’s ongoing work to further reinforce its GenAI music content framework. These efforts illustrate how we are working together to eradicate AI slop and make AI a value creator for music fans, artists and right-holders.” Charlie Hellman, Spotify’s senior vice president and global head of music, claimed the remixing tool can “deepen the connection between fans and the artists they love” while “creating new value for artists and driving attention back to the original music.” “Getting there takes partners across the industry, and Believe and independent artists have helped move the industry forward at every major turning point,” he said. “I’m encouraged that their participation now strengthens the momentum toward artist consent, compensation and credit.” The partnership came hours after Spotify revealed it removed 50 million AI slop tracks from users’ recommendations this year, a new figure it shared as part of its insights into how it’s navigating the AI era. The deal also came just over a month after Believe Music inked a partnership with Suno, the AI music generation platform, to help power its label-backed model “v6.” Charlize Theron on ‘The Odyssey’ Becoming Universal’s Highest-Grossing Movie and Raising Millions to Fight Femicide in Africa With CTAOP Loading comments...

articles.title: Deadline first revealed last month that BBC Three
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake BBC Three To Be Switched Off For Second Time, As BBC Confirms TV & Radio Network Closures BBC News Slashing 100 Jobs: “This Will Be Very Difficult For Those Affected” Ex-MTV Worker Didn’t Report Alleged Russell Brand Rape Because “Media Industry Protects Its Own” View All September 23, 2026 10:32am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'RuPaul's Drag Race UK' airs on BBC Three BBC/World of Wonder EXCLUSIVE : The BBC is preparing to announce the closure of TV and radio services, with speculation rife that youth network BBC Three is at risk of being unplugged for a second time. Deadline hears that the BBC is expected to unveil what one source described as “audience-facing” closures as early as next week, as the UK broadcaster ramps up efforts to save £500 million ($660M) over the coming years. BBC sources said director general Matt Brittin is attempting to juggle the cuts with futureproofing the corporation. Brittin has spent his early months in the job interrogating whether the broadcaster’s output is properly meeting audience needs and is said to be clear-eyed about shifting resources away from services that are dwindling in influence. Related Stories Legal BBC Seeks Deposition Of Jack Smith As Network Defends Itself From Donald Trump's Defamation Lawsuit News 'Grey's Anatomy' Star Kevin McKidd & Laura Fraser Cast In BBC's 'The Young Team' From Director Paul McGuigan BBC insiders and industry sources, who were not at liberty to speak on the record, believe that BBC Three is vulnerable, while there has been press speculation about BBC Scotland’s future. The corporation is also expected to announce changes to radio services. Nothing is confirmed at this stage. Watch on Deadline A BBC spokesperson declined to comment, but senior leaders have consistently said nothing is off the table. Brittin told staff in June that the BBC will slash commissioning spend across its TV, radio, and news divisions by £80M, necessitating a review of its “broadcast TV channels and radio network portfolio as audiences move online.” Internal announcements are being made over the coming days, with the BBC telling Manchester-based staff on Wednesday about plans to axe sports bulletins on its news channel. BBC boss Matt Brittin BBC If BBC Three were closed, it would be the second time the TV network has been taken off air in a decade. It was originally moved online in 2016 before former director general Tim Davie reversed the decision and the channel was restored to television in 2022. Although BBC Three’s move to iPlayer was ahead of its time (a fact that was acknowledged by the BBC at the time), Davie’s U-turn bemused many — particularly as the network enjoyed a purple patch creatively online, launching series including beloved comedies Fleabag and This Country . A source said Davie came close to acknowledging that this was a mistake in a March 2024 speech, when he said that the BBC would “deliver more value for younger audiences” by focusing commissioning and marketing power on iPlayer rather than BBC Three’s linear channel. BBC Three is home to shows including RuPaul’s Drag Race UK , which was recently canceled by the BBC , and comedies including Things You Should Have Done and Smoggie Queens . One person pointed out that switching off BBC Three would not actually save a great deal of money because it occupies the same TV real estate (known as spectrum) as children’s channel CBBC. It would be more radical for the BBC to consolidate its children’s channels, CBBC and CBeebies, into a single network, but insiders think that this would prompt political backlash. The BBC’s £500M target expands on a previous savings goal worth £1.5 billion. The bigger picture behind the cuts is that 94% of the UK population use the BBC every month, but fewer than 80% pay the £180 annual licence fee. The BBC is attempting to bridge this gap. Up to 2,000 jobs are at risk under the savings strategy, while the BBC is also involved in tense negotiations with unions over employee pay rises . Unions have rejected two BBC offers, meaning the risk of industrial action is increasing. The drumbeat of BBC cuts is playing at the same time as executives are locked in talks with the government over renewing the corporation’s operating agreement, known as its charter. Weekly meetings are now taking place between government officials and BBC policy staff as they thrash out the broadcaster’s future funding arrangements. articles.title: Christie Brinkley Opens Personal Archive With Never-Before-Seen Home Movies For ‘Uptown Girl’ Docuseries
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Netflix’s Jinny Howe Restructures U.S.-Canada Scripted Operation By Genre, Ups Cole Galvin To VP Read the full story By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart Christie Brinkley Opens Personal Archive With Never-Before-Seen Home Movies For ‘Uptown Girl’ Docuseries Netflix Strikes Deal With Globo For Brazilian Fare Including ‘I’m Still Here’ & ‘India – A Love Story’ ‘Tall Tales & Murder’ Scores New International Deals As Season 2 Takes Shape View All October 20, 2026 4:37am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Christie Brinkley Kristina Bumphrey/PMC via Getty Images Before social media even existed, Christie Brinkley was documenting her life through letters, journals and home movies. The star has opened up this trove for Uptown Girl: The Christie Brinkley Story , the upcoming doc series about her life. Brinkley has previously let some of the material be used in HBO doc Billy Joel: And So It Goes about her ex-husband Joel, but held plenty back for her own film. She asked the HBO filmmakers to send thumbnails of the footage they wanted and when she wanted to keep it back, the message to the producers was, ‘Nope, that’s for me.” Related Stories News 'Grey's Anatomy' Star Kevin McKidd & Laura Fraser Cast In BBC's 'The Young Team' From Director Paul McGuigan News Rafe Spall On Playing An Amnesiac Super Sleuth In 'The Death Of Sherlock Holmes': "This Is A Clean Slate" “These are films never before seen,” Brinkley told Deadline about the archive used in the new series, which is produced by Lionsgate Alternative Television. The doc was greenlit by streamer Fox Nation and will bow in 2027. Over three parts it will take in Brinkley’s early years as an artist before fame, life on the road with Billy Joel, and marriage, motherhood and private heartbreak, as well as the helicopter crash that nearly claimed her life. Watch on Deadline In addition to the intimate personal records and archive, there will be present-day vérité footage in the doc series, which Larissa Bills directs. Brinkley started out as an artist before becoming a supermodel, actor and author. Along the way she wrote and illustrated letters and journals, and when she got together with Joel, started capturing moving images too. “I started doing a lot of video when I hooked up with Billy,” she said. “There’s so many joyous videos there. We are on the road, there’s honeymoon footage. We used to love to just get in the car and drive. In the car we’d become a million different personalities playing around, and you know, singing songs and having fun.” The three-part doc will take in Brinkley’s time as an artist in Paris and Europe. Sitting down with Deadline in the Majestic Hotel in Cannes while in town to talk about her doc and leave her handprint on the City’s walk of fame, she remembered writing home as her modelling career started to take shape after being spotted by a photographer. “I have the letter where I say, ‘breaking news, I was discovered today,’ and I put ‘a man came up to me and asked me if I was a model.’” “Looking back, these are little capsules of time and so incredible. We all live such fast-paced lives, and we cram so much in. When we take time to actually read the way we were, we see that, ‘Oh, there’s certain parts of me that have always been the same.’ I’ve always had a certain enthusiasm, a joie de vivre.” Digging into the letters and videos from years gone by was illuminating, she added. “Some of the things I can’t even believe that I did. I was like, ‘Whoa!’ And some of the parts of my life, I’m like, ‘What was I thinking?’ And you get to see this perspective from where you are now.” Fox Entertainment Global is distributing. Uptown Girl: The Christie Brinkley Story was a key title on its MIPCOM slate in Cannes. Brinkley, meanwhile, made a mark on Cannes, literally, with the handprint on the city’s Chemin des Étoiles, its walk of fame. As the ceremony took place, ‘Uptown Girl’ was the soundtrack. The star’s appearance in the video for the 1983 hit is firmly part of pop history. “I always say to Billy, you know, ‘Thank you for my theme song,’” she said. “It was everything that I dreamt of and it was like I had manifested this,’ she said of the Cannes ceremony. “It was incredible, and to think that the decisions that I made, and I made some good ones and I made some bad ones, but it all led me here, where I’m standing on the [Cannes] steps. “I hope that it gives other people chasing their dreams the desire to stay with it. I was told I’d be chewed up and spat out by the time I was 30 by this business, this industry. But I’m 72 and I feel like I’m peaking.” ‘Fleabag’ Network BBC Three Closing Again; 100 Layoffs Coming In News Division Tilda Swinton Sets New York Stage Debut In ‘Man To Man’ This Winter U2 Set For Halftime Performance During Netflix’s Thanksgiving Eve NFL Show Banijay’s Bassetti On Europe Vs Studios Battle; Edward Berger On Netflix Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Patrick Brammall On Apple TV Thriller ‘Last Seen’, Letting Go Of ‘Colin From Accounts’ & His ‘Devil Wears Prada 2’ Role
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Italian Prioduction Shoots Get U.S. Backing With $112M One Media Capital Fund Patrick Brammall On Apple TV Thriller ‘Last Seen’, Letting Go Of ‘Colin From Accounts’ & His ‘Devil Wears Prada 2’ Role Domingo Corral Urges Commissioners To Ditch Conservative Thinking Or Risk Missing Next ‘La Bola Negra’: “You Cannot Reject The Other Way” View All October 20, 2026 5:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Patrick Brammall in 'Last Seen' Apple TV Colin From Accounts actor Patrick Brammall has changed speeds with his latest series, Apple TV mystery drama Last Seen . The drama, which rolled out its final episode on October 7 to good reviews, came after Brammall and his on-screen partner and real-life wife Harriet Dyer brought their much-loved Australian comedy Colin From Accounts to a close after three seasons. Brammall said switching to a dramatic role of a father desperately searching for his-long lost daughter was “a bit scary and attractive at the same time,” as he paid tribute to Apple pushing into Australian originals for the first time and director Christian Schwochow, known for work on the likes of The Crown and feature film Munich ’38 . Related Stories Casting Mary-Louise Parker Joins Julia Garner, Lewis Pullman & Maddie Hasson In Apple TV's 'Guilty Creatures' Casting 'Slow Horses' Adds 5 To Season 7 Cast Of Apple TV Series “Apple has the resources, so we had time to shoot,” he added. “We were not struggling to shoot nine or 12 minutes a day, or constantly facing the light. We had a 100-day shoot, and you can see it. The production value is there. It looks fantastic.” Watch on Deadline He also reflected on the end of Colin , which was ordered out of Australia at the ABC and played in the U.S. on Paramount+ and in the UK on the BBC. “I am starting to feel the legacy of it,” said the writer and actor, while also explaining on the decision to stop after three seasons. He also revealed the much-loved, feel-good show was almost not centered on a mismatched couple attempting to nurse an injured dog back to health. Instead, Brammall and Dyer came close to substituting Colin with an elderly lady, before reverting to their original premise. “We talked about making a statement about how we treat older people,” he said. Elsewhere in the interview, Brammall spoke about his role as Andy’s (Anne Hathaway) love interest Peter in The Devil Wears Prada 2 . “Even though it was a massive movie, the set was often very relaxed,” he said. “There were a couple of days when people gathered in the street to watch, which was strange.” Deadline spoke to Brammall during a recent trip to London. DEADLINE: The success of Colin will have opened up new avenues for you and Harriet. Last Seen like Colin is about family, although in a completely different way. What attracted you to it? Patrick Brammall: The first thing I knew was that it was a big Apple show and their first major foray into Australia. I knew they had big resources and a broad scope, and that they followed through on that. Then I read the scripts and a synopsis of the second and third episodes. I thought it was interesting and it was something I was not really known for. I did a supernatural drama called Glitch more than 10 years ago, but people do not necessarily know me for dramatic acting. That was a bit scary and attractive at the same time. It is a thriller, and the setup — a desperate father searching for a missing child — is a trope we have seen before. But when I met Christian, the director, and we worked on it more, it became clear that it was very character-driven. DEADLINE: Given the premise has been done many times before, what do you think sets this apart? PB: You get the entertainment of the thriller, but you also get a study of the intergenerational trauma affecting two families. It is not simply about heroes and villains. Ian, my character, is not entirely good, and Henry, the ostensibly villainous character played by Brendan Cowell, is not purely dark either. The moral ambiguity is interesting. Then there is Sarah [Chloe Jean Lourdes], the young girl. When you meet her in the second episode, she does not seem imperilled – she seems quite happy in this family unit. You think you know what the show is going to be, but it becomes something else. DEADLINE: I wanted to ask you about Colin . In an interview back in July, you were talking about how you were not quite ready to process what the whole show meant. Have you had more time to reflect on what it has done for you and your family? PB: Being here in the UK helps because the show had an impact here that we did not anticipate at all… So many people saw it on the BBC. I have had a bit more time to reflect and I am starting to feel the legacy of it. ‘Legacy’ is a big word, but there is a feeling that we stopped it at the right time. People were asking, “Are you sure? It is going well. Why would you do that?” But I feel that it was right for various reasons, politically and creatively. I am really proud of it. The reach has been breathtaking. Harry and I are seeing people responding to the third season and the ending on social media, and it has been received incredibly well. We were nervous because it has been so important to us. We put everything into it and wanted to land the plane well. DEADLINE: It is a very British thing to end a comedy after two or three seasons, Patrick. INTERVIEWEE: Absolutely. I understand why. In America, writers’ rooms can keep a show going for a long time. With us, Harry and I write everything, and it is exhausting. That is why I understand shows such as The Office and Fawlty Towers ending when they did. Catastrophe went for four seasons, I think, and its creators were exhausted by the end. You want to continue because you love the show so much, but there is a limit. DEADLINE: Looking ahead, would you want to write something as closely entwined with your personal life as Colin ? PB: Colin emerged organically. It is definitely a fictionalised version of us, although the setup is pure fiction. In the writing of the three seasons, we stole elements from our own lives and from other people — friends, stories we had heard. It became a patchwork. I do not think we would write something exactly like this again. The success of the show is not just that Harry and I write it; it is the setup. It is about a relationship, comedy and love. We will not write another romantic comedy because we have done that, and we would just be trying to repeat ourselves. Every story arises organically once you inhabit it, and this is where we found this one. We got lucky, really. Patrick Brammall as Gordon and Harriet Dyer as Ashley in ‘Colin From Accounts’ Season 3 John Platt/Paramount+ DEADLINE: The dog being hit by the car is such an immediate device. You instantly understand what kind of world the show is in. PB: Comedy is hard to set up, and that was a very helpful device. When we were writing the first season, Harry came in one morning and said, “We do not need a dog. We will get an old lady.” She had been allergic to the idea of making a cute dog show. She said, “It is an old lady. She has dementia. She does not know where she is.” We talked about making a statement about how we treat older people. We told our long-suffering producers, Rob [Gibson] and Ian [Collie]. A couple of days later they came back and said, “We trust you guys. If that is what it is, let us go for it.” Then we said, “No, we have let it go. That was a stupid idea.” For a day and a half, we were making a show in which an old lady, rather than a dog, was hit by a car. It would have been a very different show. Rob and Ian must have gone home wondering what on earth was happening. DEADLINE: What was the experience of working with Apple compared with Colin ? PB: It was very different for me. I am across everything on Colin . On Last Seen , I had the luxury of just being an actor. I was responsible for my own character, and that is all. It was decadent for me. Apple has the resources, so we had time to shoot. We were not struggling to shoot nine or 12 minutes a day, or constantly facing the light. We had a 100-day shoot, and you can see it. The production value is there. It looks fantastic. Bonnie Elliott, the director of photography, has a great eye, and Christian is passionate about the show and deserves a lot of credit for balancing an art-house sensibility with the psychological and emotional realism of the story. He grounds what could have been a juggernaut. DEADLINE: Australia is fascinating as a production community. Some of the best producers in the world are working there, and unsurprising, distinctive shows are emerging, but it is still often seen as a production location. How do you feel about the state of the Australian industry? INTERVIEWEE: I think we are in a pretty good spot, although there is never enough work to go around. I have worked on many sets in America, and they are very good at what they do. But there is a sense of “another day, another dollar” — a workaday mentality. In Australia, it is more like, “We are making this thing. Let us all muck in.” That is why Australian crews are the best in the world. Nothing is a problem. Even when there are clearly many problems, we will solve them. If the new Apple show goes well, hopefully Apple will invest in more Australian stories. There are quotas for streamers, which is a good thing, although I do not think the same quotas are in place for local broadcasters. Streamers may end up carrying the lion’s share of Australian content. Hollywood productions coming in are good for the industry because the crews get work, but the stories are not Australian and the vernacular is not Australian. That is what I love about Colin : Harry and were are committed to making it genuinely Australian. We do not want to gild the lily. That is how we talk, and people should know that. DEADLINE: What is next for you? Is it more acting, writing or both? PB: Ideally, both. I am not great at planning. Harry and I have a film that we are writing for a British production company, but it is early days and I cannot say much about it. That is all we have on the books at the moment. We have two little girls under five, so our family is the priority. We have to make everything work around that. DEADLINE: What was the experience of making Devil Wears Prada 2 like? Patrick Brammall at the world premiere of ‘The Devil Wears Prada 2’ at Lincoln Center in New York in April Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images for 20th Century Studios PB: I had a lot of pressure around it because it was an iconic property and people had a strong connection with the original film and those characters. My approach was to stay relaxed and present, and the character was not especially complicated or a huge stretch, so I enjoyed it. Even though it was a massive movie, the set was often very relaxed. There were a couple of days when people gathered in the street to watch, which was strange. DEADLINE: With the success of Colin and Last Seen , are you still talking to Australian broadcasters, or are global streamers now the main folk competing for your time? INTERVIEWEE: Harry and I live in Los Angeles, so we are exposed to global opportunities. That is part of the reason we are there. We are still talking about smaller shows, but we ask whether they will travel and whether they have global distributors. I do not want to make something that only goes on a local broadcaster and then sits there. Shows such as Fisk demonstrate that Australian work can travel. It is ultimately about the quality of the material. When we were pitching Colin , we knocked on every door — although at the time that meant about four doors. The ABC developed it for a short time and then passed. A few other places did the same. Then Binge launched. We saw that it had bought the HBO catalogue and had shows such as The White Lotus and Game of Thrones . Beggars cannot be choosers, and nobody else wanted us, and Binge picked us up. We were very grateful. They were incredible because they gave us the space to make the show we wanted to make. A lot of credit goes to Brian Walsh, one of the commissioners [who passed away in 2023 ]. He is a legend and a person who genuinely loved what he did. DEADLINE: Brian was one of the most generous executives when I was a young reporter , happy to explain how the international distribution system worked and how Australian television was received around the world. PB: He was incredibly generous. He was not trying to get to the next thing. He was present in his work and loved what he did. He was the real deal. It is interesting that Alison [Hurbert-Burns, Walsh’s former colleague at Binge] and Bruna [Papandrea] have now set up a company focused on Australian stories . I am delighted for them. Bruna is fantastic, and Alison is a wonderful producer with a great eye. DEADLINE: How do you see the future of Australian television, particularly with local-content quotas? PB: Apple, Netflix and the other streamers would prefer quotas not to exist. That is their position around the world, but having quotas is good because it forces them to decide whether they are in or out, and most of them have said they are in. It anchors the industry and gives people some sense of what will happen several years from now. The same is true culturally. It allows Apple, Netflix and Prime Video to have local offices with Australians working in them. If you do not anchor people in a territory, you get a purely hyper-capitalist model in which the bottom line leads everything. An American executive may say they want something from Australia and send Americans to make an Australian show. You end up with a red-dirt kangaroo version of Australia rather than something genuine. This interview was edited for clarity and length. articles.title: Lin-Manuel Miranda’s ‘Warriors’ Broadway Cast To Include Casey Likes, Amber Gray & Jasmine Cephas Jones; Opening Date, Venue Announced
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Tilda Swinton Sets New York Stage Debut In ‘Man To Man’ This Winter Lin-Manuel Miranda’s ‘Warriors’ Broadway Cast To Include Casey Likes, Amber Gray & Jasmine Cephas Jones; Opening Date, Venue Announced Controversial ‘Downstate’ Again Delays Broadway Previews Due To Illness View All October 20, 2026 5:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Casey Likes, Amber Gray, Jasmine Cephas Jones Getty Images Warriors , the upcoming Lin-Manuel Miranda Broadway musical based on the 1979 film and the Sol Yurick novel, will feature a cast including, among others, Casey Likes ( Back to the Future, Almost Famous ), Amber Gray ( The Rocky Horror Show, Hadestown ) and Jasmine Cephas Jones (TV’s Lanterns ), and will begin performances on March 9, 2027, at the the Lunt-Fontanne Theatre . The official opening night will be April 8, 2027. The announcements were made today by the show’s producers Miranda, Thomas Kail, Luis A. Miranda, Jr. and Jeffrey Seller. In addition to Likes, Gray and Jones, the initial casting also includes Jaci Calderon, Aneesa Folds, Julia Harriman, Sasha Hutchings, Gizel Jiménez, Kenita R. Miller, Sasha Allen and, from Apple TV’s Severance , Donald Webber Jr. Related Stories News Controversial 'Downstate' Again Delays Broadway Previews Due To Illness News 'Other Desert Cities' Review: Julia Louis-Dreyfus Gets Seriously Funny For Broadway Debut As previously announced, the musical features book, music and lyrics by Miranda and Eisa Davis, with direction by Jenny Koons and co-direction and choreography by Andy Blankenbuehler. Watch on Deadline Based on the Paramount Pictures motion picture The Warriors , directed by Walter Hill, as well as Yurick’s 1965 novel, the production is described by producers as “a boundary-pushing adrenaline shot of a musical that tells a story of loyalty, friendship, a search for peace, strength, and survival over one tumultuous night in New York. When the Warriors, a fictitious gang from Coney Island, are framed for the shocking murder of a respected leader, Cyrus, at a summit in the Bronx, they must race to get home to Coney Island to prove their innocence and save Cyrus’ hope for peace in a perilous city.” Likes has been cast as Luther, a gang leader who in the movie was played by David Patrick Kelly and uttered the film’s famous line, “Warriors – come out to play-ee-eh…” Gray will play Ajax (portrayed in the film by actor James Remar) and Jones will play Swan (Michael Beck in the movie). The musical reimagines the original story by, among other things, changing the male gangs to female gangs. “We’re having the time of our lives making Warriors ,” said Miranda and Davis in a statement. “It’s a rollercoaster like the Coney Island Cyclone, with all the action of Walter Hill’s classic film. It’s a New York story to the bone, with music steeped in all the genres that were born and revolutionized here, from hip-hop to salsa to ska and metal and everything in between. It’s an edge-of-your-seat journey from Brooklyn to the Bronx and back again. It’s a dream of a more peaceful city where we all come home alive. This is the sound of something being born.” Other cast and characters announced today are Calderon, who will play Fox; Folds (Cleon); Harriman (Mercy); Hutchings (Cowgirl, who was Cowboy in the movie); Jiménez (Rembrandt); Miller (Cochise); Allen (Cyrus); and Webber (Masai). The production’s creative team includes scenic design by David Korins, costume design by Dede Ayite, lighting design by Natasha Katz, sound design by Jason Crystal, projection design by Hana S. Kim, fight direction by Drew Leary, music supervision by Kurt Crowley, orchestrations by Kurt Crowley, Mike Elizondo, and Scott Wasserman, and wig, hair and makeup design by Nikiya Mathis. ‘Fleabag’ Network BBC Three Closing Again; 100 Layoffs Coming In News Division Tilda Swinton Sets New York Stage Debut In ‘Man To Man’ This Winter U2 Set For Halftime Performance During Netflix’s Thanksgiving Eve NFL Show Banijay’s Bassetti On Europe Vs Studios Battle; Edward Berger On Netflix Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Tilda Swinton Sets New York Stage Debut In ‘Man To Man’ This Winter
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Lin-Manuel Miranda’s ‘Warriors’ Broadway Cast To Include Casey Likes, Amber Gray & Jasmine Cephas Jones; Opening Date, Venue Announced Controversial ‘Downstate’ Again Delays Broadway Previews Due To Illness ‘Other Desert Cities’ Review: Julia Louis-Dreyfus Gets Seriously Funny For Broadway Debut View All October 20, 2026 5:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tilda Swinton in 'Man To Man', London Ruediger Glatz EXCLUSIVE: Oscar winner Tilda Swinton will make her New York stage debut this winter in an Off Broadway revival of Manfred Karge’s Man to Man at the Lucille Lortel Theatre. Previews for the limited 8-week engagement begin February 21, 2027, with an official opening night set for February 28, 2027. Swinton originated the role in an acclaimed 1987 UK premiere at the Traverse Theatre, which first commissioned the original production before it transferred in 1988 to the Royal Court. The revival, now in performances at London’s Royal Court Theatre, reunites the multi-award-winning creative team, including director Stephen Unwin and designer Bunny Christie with translation by Anthony Vivis and revisions by Unwin, and marks Swinton’s return to the stage for the first time in four decades. The London engagement sold out in two hours and maintains a waitlist of over 30,000 people. Related Stories News Carla Gugino, Fred Hechinger, Tom Pecinka & Riley Prior Join Off Broadway's 'A View From The Bridge' News Wayne Brady Withdraws From Off Broadway Production On Doctor's Orders; Ato Blankson-Wood Joins 'Ms. Blakk For President' The Off Broadway announcement was made today by producers Brian and Dayna Lee, The Royal Court Theatre, Berliner Ensemble, and Madison Wells Live. Man to Man will have limited runs in Scotland at the Traverse Theatre and in Germany with the Berliner Ensemble before arriving in New York. Watch on Deadline The synopsis: “In 1930s Germany, a woman puts on her dead husband’s trousers and never takes them off. As the world around her changes, she endures war and dictatorship, hunger and humiliation – always fighting to stay alive.” The creative team for Man to Man includes Bunny Christie (Design), Ben Ormerod (Lighting Design), Elena Peña (Sound Design), and Matt Powell (Projection Design). Swinton won the the Academy Award in 2007 for her supporting role in Michael Clayton , and her many other credits include Orlando, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, Moonrise Kingdom, Uncut Gems and many others. articles.title: Italian Prioduction Shoots Get U.S. Backing With $112M One Media Capital Fund
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Netflix’s Jinny Howe Restructures UCAN Scripted Operation By Genre, Ups Cole Galvin To VP Read the full story By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Italian Prioduction Shoots Get U.S. Backing With $112M One Media Capital Fund Patrick Brammall On Apple TV Thriller ‘Last Seen’, Letting Go Of ‘Colin From Accounts’ & His ‘Devil Wears Prada 2’ Role Domingo Corral Urges Commissioners To Ditch Conservative Thinking Or Risk Missing Next ‘La Bola Negra’: “You Cannot Reject The Other Way” View All October 20, 2026 5:44am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mauro Martani, Stephen Saltzman and Raj Singh MIA A €100M ($112M) fund for TV and film projects shooting in Italy launched today at the MIA Market . Raj Singh ‘s Media Capital Technologies and Italy’s RP1 Holding have team to create the One Media Capital Fund , which will be used to back productions and help finance distribution. It was announced at the European Investment Hub, which launched at this year’s MIA Market in Rome, Italy. Mauro Martani, CEO of RP1 Holding, and Raj Singh, CEO of MCT Credit Solutions, unveiled the fund during a conference panel titled ‘New Capital, New Opportunities’ that also featured Stephen Saltzman, Partner & Head of the International Entertainment Group at FieldFisher, who is also investing. Related Stories News Domingo Corral Urges Commissioners To Ditch Conservative Thinking Or Risk Missing Next 'La Bola Negra': "You Cannot Reject The Other Way" News Marco Bassetti Says Banijay Has Spent $1.1B On "Creativity" In Four Years But Warns U.S. Giants Must Reward European Producers The idea is to support the industry by offering companies financing tools geared towards production that are “complementary to traditional bank lending” and to create a system that efficiently capitalizes producers and frees up resource elsewhere. Adding this to European soft money sources will, in theory, attract more content makers to use Italy as a production base and maybe even get more Italian stories on screen. Watch on Deadline RP1 Group companies – Start One Media Funding , +One and PayOne – devised the idea through their work on on audiovisual production, industry consulting and the management of incentive schemes, including film tax credits. The fund launched to a backdrop of calls from the European Commissioners and other major figures in the European production financing sector for more inward investment to help the continent’s producers compete against the primarily American global players. Meanwhile, Italy’s Directorate-General for Cinema and Audiovisual Media of the Italian Ministry of Culture and France’s CNC officially announced a joint Italian-French group of experts, who will dedicate their time to European policy for the film and audiovisual sectors. The group was set up under a Cooperation Programme signed by the two countries’ Ministries of Culture in Antibes, France on June 25. ‘Fleabag’ Network BBC Three Closing Again; 100 Layoffs Coming In News Division Tilda Swinton Sets New York Stage Debut In ‘Man To Man’ This Winter U2 Set For Halftime Performance During Netflix’s Thanksgiving Eve NFL Show Banijay’s Bassetti On Europe Vs Studios Battle; Edward Berger On Netflix Read More About: Comments

articles.title: BBC News Slashing 100 Jobs: “This Will Be Very Difficult For Those Affected”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake BBC Three To Be Switched Off For Second Time, As BBC Confirms TV & Radio Network Closures BBC News Slashing 100 Jobs: “This Will Be Very Difficult For Those Affected” Ex-MTV Worker Didn’t Report Alleged Russell Brand Rape Because “Media Industry Protects Its Own” View All October 20, 2026 5:53am Add us as a Google Preferred Source BBC News presenter Clive Myrie BBC The cuts keep coming at the BBC . BBC News told staff on Tuesday that the division will close more than 100 roles over the coming months, saving £5.5 million ($7.4M). Rachel Jupp, the BBC’s new director of news, announced the savings plan in an internal email, telling staff: “I know this will be very difficult news for those affected.” She added: “We will continue to work closely with colleagues and trade unions throughout the consultation process and will do everything we can to minimise the need for compulsory redundancies.” Related Stories Legal BBC Seeks Deposition Of Jack Smith As Network Defends Itself From Donald Trump's Defamation Lawsuit News 'Grey's Anatomy' Star Kevin McKidd & Laura Fraser Cast In BBC's 'The Young Team' From Director Paul McGuigan Jupp warned that more is to come. BBC News has previously announced that it must contribute £51M of savings to the corporation’s overall target of £500M. Watch on Deadline The £5.5M takes its running total contribution to £30.5M, meaning at least further £20M will need to be saved, though it could be more. “These proposals are necessary, but they are not sufficient to meet our funding reduction,” Jupp said. “Given the BBC’s financial pressures, the savings requirement for News could increase.” The former Panorama editor said she will disclose further details in early 2027 after “looking at costs across BBC News to have the fullest possible financial picture.” She added that BBC News will examine how “we use our presenters” across video, audio and digital, as well as “how to get as much value as we can from our great long-form journalism, planning and commissioning.” Other BBC divisions have announced layoffs in recent weeks, including 110 role closures in BBC Media Tech , the division that powers online services like iPlayer. The BBC’s £500M target expands on a previous savings goal worth £1.5 billion. The bigger picture behind the cuts is that 94% of the UK population use the BBC every month, but fewer than 80% pay the £180 annual licence fee. The BBC is attempting to bridge this gap. articles.title: BBC Three To Be Switched Off For Second Time, As BBC Confirms TV & Radio Network Closures
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake BBC Three To Be Switched Off For Second Time, As BBC Confirms TV & Radio Network Closures BBC News Slashing 100 Jobs: “This Will Be Very Difficult For Those Affected” Ex-MTV Worker Didn’t Report Alleged Russell Brand Rape Because “Media Industry Protects Its Own” View All October 20, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Fleabag' launched on BBC Three Bye bye BBC Three — again. The BBC will pull the plug on BBC Three for the second time in a decade in spring 2027, as the UK broadcaster confirmed network closures under plans to save £500 million ($666M). Deadline first revealed last month that BBC Three , the youth network that has given rise to beloved British series including Fleabag and Gavin & Stacey , was in serious jeopardy. The BBC originally planned to reveal the closures in late September, but the corporation delayed confirmation as it managed the timing of various cuts announcements across the organization. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News 'This City Is Ours' Renewed For Season 3 At BBC Legal BBC Seeks Deposition Of Jack Smith As Network Defends Itself From Donald Trump's Defamation Lawsuit The BBC has confirmed that BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra will also close as linear networks in spring next year. Deadline first reported that Radio 4 Extra was at risk earlier this month. It marks another brutal day for the British broadcaster, which also announced 100 layoffs in its news division over the coming months, saving £5.5M. BBC Three will remain a brand on iPlayer, and the BBC has committed to increasing investment for younger audiences. BBC Scotland will also be retained on iPlayer. In a memo to staff setting out the changes, BBC director-general Matt Brittin said: “We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. We all know that means tough choices.” He added: “Much of the great content they currently carry will still be found where audiences already enjoy them on iPlayer and Sounds. While this follows media speculation, I recognise the confirmation of this news will be hard for audiences and colleagues.” The BBC’s decision marks the second time BBC Three has been taken off air in the past 10 years. It was originally moved online in 2016 before former director general Tim Davie reversed the decision and the channel was restored to television in 2022. Although BBC Three’s move to iPlayer was ahead of its time (a fact that was acknowledged by the BBC at the time), Davie’s U-turn bemused many — particularly as the network enjoyed a purple patch creatively online, launching series including beloved comedies Fleabag and This Country . BBC Three is now home to shows like RuPaul’s Drag Race UK , which was recently canceled by the BBC , and comedies including Things You Should Have Done and Smoggie Queens . BBC Three falls under the remit of Kate Phillips, the corporation’s chief content officer. Fiona Campbell was the controller of the network until earlier this year, when she was promoted to director of factual content. The BBC’s £500M target expands on a previous savings goal worth £1.5 billion. The bigger picture behind the cuts is that 94% of the UK population use the BBC every month, but fewer than 80% pay the £180 annual licence fee. The BBC is attempting to bridge this gap. Up to 2,000 jobs are at risk under the savings strategy, while the BBC is also involved in tense negotiations with unions over employee pay rises . Unions have rejected two BBC offers, increasing the threat of industrial action. The drumbeat of BBC cuts has been playing for weeks, with the broadcaster canceling shows including Radio 4’s You and Yours ; axing sports bulletins; and making 110 layoffs in BBC Media Tech , the division that powers online services like iPlayer. BBC commissioners have also been asked to consider applying for voluntary redundancy, per an email seen by Deadline. The BBC is slashing costs at the same time as executives are locked in talks with the government over renewing the corporation’s charter. Weekly meetings are taking place between government officials and BBC policy staff as they thrash out the broadcaster’s future funding arrangements.
