articles.title: Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 7:00am PT Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE) Kicking in from December, the deal sees 18 wide-ranging Globo titles, including International Emmy Winner 'India – A Love Story,' hitting Netflix in Brazil or worldwide By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom 4 days ago ‘The Castle’ Shapes Up as Another Hit From ‘La Bola Negra’ Producer Movistar Plus 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Credit: Alile Dara Onawale - Globoplay When the going gets tough, the tough get together: Brazil’s Globo , Latin America’s biggest media company, has struck an 18-title licensing deal with Netflix , led by one jewel in Globo’s crown, Walter Salles ’ Academy Award winner “ I’m Still Here .” Kicking in from December, the agreement sees titles rolling out on Netflix through mid-2027. The wide-ranging deal also takes in “India – A Love Story,” created by Glória Perez, the doyenne of Brazilian telenovela writers, and directed by Marcos Schechtman, which won the 2009 International Emmy for Best Telenovela. Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Todd Rundgren Slams Taylor Swift, Says She ‘Ruined Music’ and Is ‘the Apotheosis of Mediocrity’ Also in the mix is “Vitória,” directed by notable film-TV helmer Andrucha Waddington (“Under Pressure,” “Emergency 53”) and starring Academy Award nominee Fernanda Montenegro (“Central Station”) in a lauded central performance as an 80-year-old battling to expose a drug racket on Copacabana. Popular on Variety Rights details vary. Sold worldwide by Goodfellas in theatrical deals, “I’m Still Here” has been licensed just for Brazil. Netflix has closed the U.S. and Latin America, a telenovela heartland, on “India – A Love Story.” Created by Leandro Soares and directed by João Fonseca and Regis Faria, seven seasons of “Vai Que Cola,” Brazil’s biggest pay TV comedy series hits, running over 2013-26, has been acquired by Netflix in Brazil. “Vitória,” in contrast has been bought for the world. The Globo original productions will be made available on Netflix, dubbed and subtitled in multiple languages. The package is comprised by 14 films, three telenovelas and a series. “We hope this agreement is just the first step in a long partnership between two companies that share the ambition, creative craftsmanship and commitment to take Brazilian culture even further”, said Elisabetta Zenatti, VP of Content at Netflix Brazil. “It makes us proud to see interest in Brazilian productions growing across different markets,” said Pedro Garcia, Globo’s Director of Rights. “For decades, we have been dedicated to sharing the richness of our culture with the world. By combining that experience with Netflix’s global scale, we take another step toward bringing Brazilian creativity to new audiences, expanding the presence and strengthening the recognition of Brazilian film and television abroad.” Several broader market trends are also at work. “The deal is a reflection of a wider trend in streaming,” said Guy Bisson, Ampere Analysis executive director. “Licensing spend is growing while original production spend is flat,” he added. “Content owners can no longer afford to keep their own content in long windows of exclusivity or in perpetuity given the challenge of customer acquisition in a saturated market so we’re seeing more content enter the market again and windows shortening. Courtesy of Netflix Why Globo Is Important to Netflix? “Both companies say the move underscores the power of Brazilian content to entertain audiences around the world,” Globo and Netflix noted in a press statement Monday. Globoplay co-produced “I’m Still Here” and saw it gross a remarkable $36.5 million worldwide, racking up $17 million in box office gross outside Brazil, including $6.2 million for Sony Pictures Classics in the U.S. Globo announced at Mipcom that Globoplay Original “Red Blood,” a teen werewolf-vampire love triangle thriller, has sold at the BBC. Equally, Netflix has seen a surge in international audiences’ passion for Brazilian fiction, movie “Caramelo” reigning s Netflix No. 1 non-English film in the world over Oct. 6-19 last year. “Rulers of Fortune,” and “Radioactive Emergency,” also hit the Netflix Global No. 1, Non-English show spot, over Nov. 3-9, 2025 and March 23-29 this year. As a streaming service , Netflix reigns supreme in Latin America, where it has 63.8 million subscriptions forecast for 2026, which will increasing to 73.7 million by 2031, María Rúa Aguete, Head of Media and Entertainment at Omdia, announced at Mipcom. Brazil is said to have more Netflix subscribers than any other country in the world outside the U.S. at a time when international revenue growth is increasingly vital to Netflix’s fortunes. Globo can supply some of its drivers. articles.title: Nathan Fielder Says Elizabeth Holmes Called Him From Prison Right Before ‘You Can See Everything’ Release to Tell Him Repeatedly: ‘I Trust You’
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 7:20am PT Nathan Fielder Says Elizabeth Holmes Called Him From Prison Right Before ‘You Can See Everything’ Release to Tell Him Repeatedly: ‘I Trust You’ By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest Nathan Fielder Says Elizabeth Holmes Called Him From Prison Right Before ‘You Can See Everything’ Release to Tell Him Repeatedly: ‘I Trust You’ 2 hours ago Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Billy Evans Admits ‘She Looks Insane’ in ‘You Can See Everything’ Trailer but Defends Making the Doc: ‘Make Up Your Own Mind’ 3 days ago Ben Affleck Says Bullying ‘Digger’ Will Only Lead Studios to Make More ‘S—ty Homogenized Movies’: Don’t ‘Punish Movies That Take Risks’ 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jc Olivera / Justin Sullivan Nathan Fielder revealed in a new interview with Wired magazine that Elizabeth Holmes called him from prison right before the theatrical release of his new documentary, “ You Can See Everything .” The call marked the first time the director and his documentary subject had spoken in half a year. Ex-Theranos CEO Holmes is currently in federal prison after being convicted for fraud. “She had not called me in over six months. I had not heard from her in any way… she asked how I was doing,” Fielder said about their conversation. “I asked her if she had seen any stuff about the film coming out and how she felt about it. She told me she had seen some stuff, but most things she just isn’t seeing, so she’s heard things, but she hasn’t really read anything. And then, at the end, she said to me – ‘I trust you.’ I said, ‘OK, thanks.’” Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'The Life of a Showgirl' Spends 15th Week at No. 1 on Albums Chart Olivia vs. Olivia: Predicting the Grammys' Album of the Year Contenders... and Why Rodrigo and Dean Are at the Front of the Race Fielder continued, “We talked about some other stuff. She talked about her kids, and then some updates that are not really my place to share. But then after that, she said again, at the end of the call— ‘I trust you.’ And I don’t know what she meant by that.” Popular on Variety “You Can See Everything,” directed by Fielder and “Primetime” helmer Lance Oppenheim, follows Holmes and her partner Billy Evans in their final weeks before Homes’ 11-year prison sentence begins. The filmmakers moved in with the couple 34 days before Holmes went to prison. Fielder told Wired that he got involved with the project after hearing that Holmes and Evans had tried and failed to pitch a documentary about them to A24, explaining: “Months later, I heard that that had happened. So I called A24 and said, ‘Well, could I meet her?’ That was the start of it all.” But why would Holmes allow Fielder to come into her home? That’s a question that still has Fielder puzzled considering his previous work, be it “Nathan for You” or “The Rehearsal,” should’ve made it clear to Holmes that bringing Fielder on board would not produce anything straightforward or conventional. “This is part of the mystery that, like, doesn’t make sense to me,” Fielder said. “I asked her that on, I think, one of the first days we shot. I still don’t fully understand it. That really messed with my head. Also, I got the sense very early that she hadn’t seen a lot, but she had seen some of what I did, and she had talked to people who had seen what I did. Billy had seen more. I think she found the clip that she said she saw funny. But you know, her relationship to that … to what’s funny? I don’t even know. She said her favorite movie is ‘Elf,’ the Will Ferrell movie.” Evans appeared on the “All-In” podcast the day before “You Can See Everything” opened in theaters and explained the couple’s rationale behind letting Fielder and Oppenheim into their home. Mainly, they wanted people to get to know Holmes up close and personal so they could decide for themselves if she is a bad person or not. “It was to have people see who she is,” Evans said. “I have gone through this consistent experience with the people who love me most, from my grandmother to my best friends. They’d hear I knew [Elizabeth Holmes] or I was falling for this person and now we’re going to have a kid… in the beginning, every single one of these people thought I was crazy. ‘Do you know who she is?’ I would tell them, ‘I understand why you feel that way but just meet her.’ And they would meet her and spend time with her and see her in a totally natural environment, like going on a hike or helping a friend. Every opinion of her would radically shift. That was the intention of the film. To help scale that up and allow other people to sit with her and make up their own minds.” The decision is backfiring for Holmes, however, since “You Can See Everything” is only amplifying the backlash against her. Even before the movie screened for press, A24 dropped a chilling teaser trailer that had many viewers disturbed by Holmes’ demeanor and claims that she did not do anything wrong at Theronos. The movie has since turned into a box office hit by grossing $15 million in its domestic debut, which is the biggest launch for a documentary in decades. “You Can See Everything” is now playing in theaters nationwide. Head over to Wired’s website to read Fielder’s interview in its entirety. articles.title: ‘Smallville’ at 25: Tom Welling and Michael Rosenbaum on Clark Kent and Lex Luthor’s Origin Story, the Journey to Superman and That Final Moment
articles.full_text: Dan Doperalski for Variety A little more than 25 years ago, on Oct. 16, 2021, “ Smallville ” premiered on The WB. Created by Alfred Gough and Miles Millar, and based on the DC Comics character, the show set out to do something that’s now common practice but was then novel: tell the origin story of an iconic character, enriching the character’s mythology along the way. On the show, an immediate hit for the network, Tom Welling and Michael Rosenbaum played, respectively, a high-school-aged Clark Kent and his eventual nemesis Lex Luthor in the fictional town of Smallville, Kansas. One of the inventions of “Smallville” is that Clark (who yearns to be ordinary) and Lex (who lives under the thumb of his controlling zillionaire father) are, for a time, best friends, before the inevitable happens, as Lex succumbs to his darker instincts. “I felt like I had the liberty to just do what I wanted to do, and be real, and grounded,” Rosenbaum said in a recent interview. “I mean, seeing Lex and Clark as friends — and then obviously we know what happens with the relationship, but I thought it was really fascinating. It had never been done.” As opposed to their characters, Welling and Rosenbaum remain close: They host a “Smallville” rewatch podcast called “TalkVille,” and the night before they came to the Variety office, Welling, who doesn’t live in Los Angeles, had stayed at Rosenbaum’s house. They’ve been celebrating the show’s 25th anniversary, and in their most extensive conversation together about the show’s legacy, they filmed a “How Well Do They Know Each Other?” video, answering questions about one another and about “Smallville.” During the game, they flopped on things like the show’s premiere date (somehow, Welling’s first answer was Oct. 14 , 1992 , before he switched it to that same date in 2002) and its ratings, which broke records for The WB. The correct answer was that 8.4 million total viewers tuned in live, but Rosenbaum wrote “12 million, Beeyotch,” and Welling wrote “1 trillion,” then trying to explain by saying, “Well, I mean, worldwide.” Rosenbaum harangued him. “You know how much a trillion is? A trillion is like, a lot of billions,” he said. “Dude, if we had those ratings, we’d still be on the air. Good lord.” As they reminisced, they talked about the guest stars who’d appeared on “Smallville” over its 10 seasons, some already well known, others new to the business. One of them, in a loving tribute to Superman ’s long history, was Christopher Reeve, who appeared twice on the show as billionaire scientist Dr. Virgil Swann, Clark’s mentor. Well before superhero movies became ubiquitous, Reeve had his breakthrough role as Clark Kent in the 1978 “Superman” film, a blockbuster, and played him three more times in its sequels. In 1995, however, Reeve, a competitive equestrian, had a devastating accident, breaking his spine while riding, and becoming paralyzed for the rest of his life. (He died in 2004.) Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Bumps 'Choosin' Texas' Out of No. 1 on Hot 100; 'Encore' Tracks Fill Four Out of Five Top Slots Taylor Swift to Perform at Academy Museum Gala Dan Doperalski for Variety Welling said he’d filmed the scenes with Reeve in New York, and they bonded. “We talked a lot about what it meant to play the character,” he said. “He said he was really happy that they chose me to play the role, which I thought was cool.” Popular on Variety The “Smallville” production wanted to make things easy for Reeve, Welling said, with him filming his part of the scene and then leaving. “But he wanted to stay for my coverage, where they filmed me speaking — I mean, he totally didn’t need to do that,” Welling said. “We laughed a lot; he was very funny, and it got to the point where he was being told to leave. And he wouldn’t leave! His nurse was like, ‘If you don’t leave, I’m going to call the police, and I’m going to take you out of here.’ And he turned to me, and he goes, ‘They’re always telling me what to do,’ which is really funny, just considering the whole situation.” In “Smallville” lore, Clark landed on Earth as a toddler from the planet Krypton during a meteor shower that took a toll on the town, and he had super-strength, super-speed, X-ray vision, and was growing into all the abilities we associate with the character of Superman. The meteor rocks also infected Smallville and its population, which gave the show its engine for the case-of-the week format of its early seasons — and brought in a lot of guest stars, one of whom was Amy Adams in Season 1. Dan Doperalski for Variety Welling picked Brian Austin Green as his favorite (“because I watched ‘Beverly Hills, 90210’”), and Rosenbaum selected Adams “because it’s memorable and she became a big movie star, and she was really cool,” writing her name in cursive on the game’s whiteboard. “That’s respect,” Welling told Rosenbaum. “You’re an elegant man, Michael.” “TalkVille” has re-familiarized them with the show, so they had no problem remembering Adams’ episode. “‘Crave’ — she was a girl who craved to get thinner, right?” Rosenbaum asked. Welling replied, “She took kryptonite to get skinnier. And she took it too far.” Rosenbaum: “Yeah. She devoured people.” As the show’s central character, Welling appeared in every episode of “Smallville.” But Rosenbaum left after Season 7, following a contract dispute with Warner Bros. Television, the show’s producer. “I mean, do I get into it?” Rosenbaum wondered, looking to Welling, who then backed him up. “There’s a point in the show where the actor’s contract comes up for renewal, and the idea is that, based on the success of the show, the contract will be increased,” Welling said. “And that wasn’t happening.” Rosenbaum said he was already itching to do other things when the impasse occurred. “It was like, ‘Hey, we want you to come back for three years — we want you to sign a three-year deal, and give you no increase in pay,’” he recalled. “And anybody who works in any business, it’s like, ‘Oh, I’m an integral part of this show, or this business,’ or whether you work at Kmart or whatever. And you’re like, ‘I’m part of the success, and don’t I need to get rewarded?’ So I said, ‘Yeah, no thanks.’ And that was it.” Dan Doperalski for Variety Rosenbaum did return for the “Smallville” series finale, though, which aired on May 11, 2011 — with a full head of hair they had to cover with a bald cap. (He shaved his head to play Lex for the seven seasons he was on the show.) He’d called the then-showrunners Brian Peterson and Kelly Souders (Gough and Millar had also left after the seventh season) to say he wanted to come back one last time. Rosenbaum remembered thinking to himself, “You should come back and wrap it up for the fans — I think the fans will love it. And I didn’t realize how much I would love it, and I’m glad I did it.” Lex was a last-minute addition, and they had Rosenbaum for only one day, so Peterson and Souders had to scramble to explain where Lex had been for all those years, filming one last scene in the Luthor Mansion. (Additionally, in a flash-forward, Lex becomes president, portending ominous showdowns between Lex and Clark far in the future.) For Rosenbaum, it was an emotional return. “I was in the makeup trailer with Natalie, our makeup artist, who was like a mother to me,” he said. “I go, ‘All right, well, that’s it!” And I gave her a hug, and I just go, ‘Oh man. Oh, shoot. Here I go!’ I just started crying, and she cried, and we hugged it out, and that was it. It was bittersweet.” Throughout “Smallville,” Gough and Millar had a “no flights, no tights” ethos about the character, which Welling felt so strongly about that he had it in his contract. “We toed the line a few times, don’t get me wrong, but they couldn’t do it without me saying, ‘All right, this one will be all right.’” But in the finale’s last shot, after he’s been alerted to yet another crisis, Clark bounds up to the Daily Planet rooftop. As he prepares to take off, he rips open his shirt — revealing the classic imagery of the Superman suit. Welling remembers it well. “We didn’t even do a rehearsal on it, because we didn’t want anyone to see it if it wasn’t right,” he said. He’d wanted assurance that there wouldn’t be a full suit, and the head of wardrobe told him, “No, no, no — it’s too expensive.” “We got to set that day, and they had given me just a T-shirt, with no sleeves to wear underneath the shirt. Because they didn’t have the money to put the suit on, and they weren’t going to see it anyway.” Welling had been inspired by the conclusion of Kiefer Sutherland’s “24,” when Jack Bauer goes on the run and says his final goodbyes to his closest colleagues. Welling pitched that idea to the writers, he said, because he liked the idea of it as an ending to Clark’s story. “We can’t go with him,” Welling said. “But he’s out there.” As they reflected on “Smallville,” both Welling and Rosenbaum said they wished they’d appreciated it more at the time. “You’re on a hit show, and you’re doing all these things,” Rosenbaum said. “And sometimes you should really enjoy it, and embrace it. And I did; I think we both did. But if I could go back and do it again, I would’ve just been like, ‘Remember, this is fun . We’re getting paid to do this!'” Welling feels the same way. “I didn’t really have anybody who I knew to be like, ‘Hey buddy, you know this is cool, right?’” On Rosenbaum’s popular podcast “Inside of You,” “we talk about mental health, facing adversity, loss, all those things,” he said. He thinks a number of its listeners are “Smallville” fans. “The fans have stood by me, I think, for almost everything we do,” he said, crediting Gough and Millar — who’ve gone on to, among other projects, create “Wednesday” for Netflix – for how good the show was, and for creating the “family atmosphere” among the cast and crew. “Al and Miles,” Rosenbaum said, “it came down to them, and they chose us.” “I mean, we’re lucky,” he added. “People are like, ‘Well, do you think you’ll ever do anything as big as “Smallville?”’ I’m like, ‘Probably not!’” “But we were on one of the biggest shows ever, and isn’t that enough? It’s always, ‘What’s next? What are you doing?’ It’s like, ‘Hey dude, I’m content. I’m happy. And we kicked some ass for a while.” ©CW Network/Courtesy Everett Collection Loading comments... articles.title: Christiane Amanpour to Exit CNN in June After 43 Years
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 8:16am PT Christiane Amanpour to Exit CNN in June After 43 Years By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Christiane Amanpour to Exit CNN in June After 43 Years 46 minutes ago CBS News Correspondent Jan Crawford Apologizes for Post on Abdul El-Sayed That Sparked Social-Media Ire 22 hours ago Odell Beckham Jr. Taps Range Sports for Off-Field Opportunities 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Vintiner for Variety Christiane Amanpour , who parlayed a job as a news assistant on CNN ‘s foreign desk into a years-long globe-trotting assignment for the news giant, plans to step away from the media company in June. “After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said in a statement Monday. She added that she “looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.” Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Graham Norton Shoots Down ‘Conspiracy Theory’ That Taylor Swift’s ‘Opalite’ Video Was Shot Before She Came on His Show Amanpour’s exit is announced just as CNN comes under the control of a new owner, Skydance , which is grappling with billions of dollars in debt and perceptions that it may want to skew its news operations toward a particular view on politics and other issues. Popular on Variety Amanpour, 68 years old, has hosted both an evening program for CNN’s international channel since 2009 and a show for PBS, “Amanpour & Company,” since 2017. She left CNN briefly for an ill-fated run at ABC News, where she was named moderator of the Sunday program, “The Week,” in 2010. Low ratings undermined her efforts there, and she returned to CNN in 2012. “Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” said Mark Thompson, CEO of CNN, in a statement. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.” CNN employs many journalists, correspondents and anchors, but few of them are as tied to the news outlet’s overall brand as Amanpour. Perhaps only Wolf Blitzer and Anderson Cooper enjoy similar status among present staffers. After securing a role in eastern Europe in 1986, she made a reputation for herself by covering conflicts in Bosnia, Iraq and Afghanistan. From 1992 to 2010, she worked as CNN’s chief international correspondent. “I will end my daily shows across CNN and PBS at the end of this year, while continuing to maintain a weekly show on CNN through May and working on a smooth transition through June,” Amanpour said in her note Monday. She indicated that she expects to continue working on an independent podcast, “Ex-Files,” which she leads along with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, former official at the U.S. State Department. Even if expected, it’s a significant shoe to drop following a layoff bloodbath last week at the streamer. Roughly 1,000 employees got the chop, capped by the shock firing of chief content Bela Bajaria. Lin was let go at the start of the weekend, two sources added, and will address his teams throughout the day on Monday. The executive attended Saturday’s Academy Gala, and was spotted Sunday evening at a tastemaker screening for “La Bola Negra” on the Netflix campus. It’s unclear who will replace Lin, though an announcement is expected in the coming days. Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, the former heads of the Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group, have been widely speculated to be speaking with the streamer about a possible role at the company. Popular on Variety Netflix is embarking on a major creative restructuring after months of headlines citing engagement problems and stock stagnation — all in the aftermath of its defeated bid for Warner Bros. — namely in hiring the seasoned film and TV executive Peter Rice to replace Bajaria. In the days leading up to his ouster, Lin watched as layoffs claimed his right hand Doug Belgrad and the film vertical’s indie head Sheroum Kim. Lin’s ascension to the top Netflix film job turned heads in 2024. The accomplished producer sat atop a thriving self-made business in Rideback. That production house is best known for building the animated “Lego” film franchise, Stephen King’s “It” adaptations and the “Sherlock Holmes” movies. He departed Rideback to replace longtime film lead Scott Stuber. articles.title: Egyptian Star Mona Zaki Reflects on Three Decades of Reinvention as El Gouna Honors Her Career: ‘Art Is About Freedom’
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 9:00am PT Egyptian Star Mona Zaki Reflects on Three Decades of Reinvention as El Gouna Honors Her Career: ‘Art Is About Freedom’ By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest 10 Films to Track at El Gouna, From Cannes and Berlin Standouts to Rising Arab Filmmakers 3 days ago El Gouna’s Amr Mansi on CineGouna Expansion, New Partnerships and Making ‘the Industry Our Hero’ 3 days ago El Gouna Artistic Director Andrew Mohsen Puts ‘Discovery’ First: ‘We’re Trying to Draw Attention’ to Overlooked Films 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Alia Rady The 9th edition of El Gouna Film Festival (Oct. 15-23) may be celebrating Mona Zaki ’s past, but the Egyptian film star is far more interested in what she’s yet to do. Honored with the festival’s Career Achievement Award at the opening ceremony, Zaki, who has already built a career spanning more than three decades, hasn’t even turned 50. Sitting down with Variety on the shores of the Red Sea, she speaks about that prolific career less as a completed body of work than a continuous process of reinvention. That ongoing transformation has required her to repeatedly shed audiences’ expectations of who Mona Zaki should be. “I get bored easily with myself,” she shares. Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Bumps 'Choosin' Texas' Out of No. 1 on Hot 100; 'Encore' Tracks Fill Four Out of Five Top Slots Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Looking back, Zaki says two lessons in particular stand out: learning the power of saying “no” and finding the confidence and willingness to express herself, both personally and emotionally. The latter, she confides, was something acting itself helped teach her. Popular on Variety “You just have to open up,” she reflects. “Your emotions are important to be heard, and it’s okay. Part of your healing is saying what you feel.” Zaki entered the industry young, first in theater, before moving into television and, ultimately, the silver screen. Early on, she became closely associated with the “girl next door,” an image that increasingly felt at odds with both the woman she was becoming and the kinds of characters she wanted to explore. “I started to kind of feel like I’m going there doing the same thing in every different project,” she recalls. “How boring is that? I needed to shift.” That turning point came with Yousry Nasrallah’s 2009 drama “ Scheherazade, Tell Me a Story ” (Ehky Ya Shahrazad), written by the late Wahid Hamed, which saw Zaki take on the role of a television host whose program examines the experiences of women navigating romance, health, everyday life, and the expectations placed upon them by Egyptian society. The departure from Zaki’s familiar screen persona drew intense backlash, with audiences questioning what had happened to the “girl next door” they had come to know. The response shook her enough that she turned to Hamed with concerns about facing the film’s promotional tour. He encouraged her to stand behind a choice she had made out of love for the work, advice that helped Zaki confront the resistance to seeing her move beyond the roles that had defined her early career. For Zaki, the experience marked the beginning of a struggle that has followed her throughout her career, that of finding roles that allow women to address subjects Egyptian cinema has historically treated as difficult or off-limits. “Censorship, talking about taboos, things that are not okay most of the time, especially for women to talk about,” remain among the challenges she continues to face. “I’m still living in that struggle even now. It can be very difficult to find a meaningful script.” While she believes the landscape has advanced over more than 30 years, Zaki remains deeply frustrated by the gap between the talent of Egypt’s actresses and the opportunities afforded them. “It breaks my heart that most of them are not taking the chances they deserve and the topics they would love to talk about and the rights they want to stand for.” Her own connection with audiences is something she has learned to negotiate over time. “It’s a relationship. You work on it like any other relationship in your life,” she explains. Part of that relationship, she believes, means establishing boundaries around her freedom to evolve as an artist. “I have the right not to feel bored and sick of myself doing the same thing because I’m not corporate, I’m an artist,” she stresses. “Art is about freedom, it’s about change, it’s about trial and error.” With each role, Zaki starts by building a life for the character beyond what exists in the script. She works with an acting coach on every project, drawing on different techniques to construct the character’s history. One of the most important parts of that process, she explains, is imagining a character’s life before the audience ever meets her. Zaki might close her eyes and picture the woman she’s playing at seven years old, in her childhood home with her mother, building memories and emotional associations that will never appear on screen but are critical to the performance. “I don’t have to say it, but I can make people feel it the way I felt it.” That method was put to a different test with “ El Sett ,” Marwan Hamed’s biopic of Umm Kulthum. This time, Zaki was building a character from the life of one of the Arab world’s most revered cultural figures, with decades of history and public memory with which to contend. She plunged into what she calls “crazy research,” watching every piece of footage she could find and repeatedly listening to a rare two-hour radio interview that became one of her most important references. “The whole internal emotions are the imagination of the writer and me.” While the facts of Umm Kulthum’s life are immutable, Zaki still had to find the woman behind them. To bridge that gap, Zaki imagined the parts of Kulthum’s life no archive could relate: the emotions, relationships and private struggles that might have shaped her from childhood. The character stayed with Zaki long after cameras stopped rolling, and she found it difficult to sever that connection after filming wrapped. “I came out of the project feeling that I’m a 70-year-old woman. I’m serious, this was not a joke.” For months, she had taken on not only the physical transformation into Kulthum, but also the emotions and experiences of a woman decades older than herself. Fully returning to Mona Zaki proved disorienting. “I think my whole face changed after that,” she recalls. “I couldn’t accept myself in the mirror.” Some of Kulthum has proven difficult to shake. “I’m trying to get rid of her,” Zaki muses. “I only have a few leftovers, gladly. Honestly, I don’t want to feel like I’m 70 and I’m not there yet.” Asked what she looks for in a role now, after more than three decades of acting, Zaki doesn’t hesitate. “Reality. Honesty. That would just take my heart.” Charlamagne tha God on Mental Health, Social Media and Prioritizing Real-Life Connection: ‘You Got to Constantly Weed Out Your Garden’ Loading comments...

articles.title: Ticketmaster Goes All-In on AI, Names Ex-Amazon Exec as Chief Technology Officer
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 9:00am PT Ticketmaster Goes All-In on AI, Names Ex-Amazon Exec as Chief Technology Officer By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Anna Faris Says ‘It Hurts’ After ‘Mom’ Creator Chuck Lorre Admits His ‘Reluctance to Hire’ Her Was Proven ‘Correct’ After She Exited the Show 3 days ago CNN and Google Strike Multiyear Partnership to Embrace Generative AI 4 days ago Trump Says Execution of Fort Hood Shooter by Firing Squad Will Not Be Livestreamed 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Ticketmaster Bot attacks have plagued Ticketmaster for years, so to combat it, the ticketing service is shaking up its executive ranks and going all-in on AI. Ticketmaster has hired Jim Freeman as its chief technology officer, filling a slot left vacant since February after its London-based chief technology officer, Carlos Alvarez-Coch, departed ahead of a deposition in the U.S. government’s antitrust trial against parent company Live Nation. It has also appointed Rachel Smith, a veteran of Block (owner of music service Tidal), to be its first senior vice president of data science and machine learning, and Disney and Stripe product veteran Chuck Mortimore as its next senior vice president of product. The team will boost Ticketmaster’s adoption of AI tools across the company while also building out the platform’s AI infrastructure. Popular on Variety “Reliable, secure and personalized experiences depend on how effectively we use technology and data,” Saumil Mehta, Ticketmaster’s global president, said in a statement. “Jim, Rachel, Chuck and the Ragie.ai team will help us move faster, build better tools and deliver better outcomes for fans, artists, venues and clients.” Freeman’s remit as chief technology officer will tackle all things AI: building AI tools, using the technology to power fan experiences and ensuring its adoption across Ticketmaster’s organization. Freeman joined the company after a stint as senior adviser at Permira, though he formerly worked as a vice president at Amazon to build and launch Prime Video and its respective device and distribution partnerships. Smith’s work will include an expanded focus on data science and analytics, including tightening integration between data and the company’s broader product development, while Mortimore will help lead product strategy to help combat the company’s bot issues and ensure fans have easier access to both their accounts and their tickets. articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Jesse Eisenberg TV Series Produced By Peter Rice To Be Taken Out By A24 Prime Video Orders Julie Plec YA Tennis Drama Series ‘Rally’ Executive Produced By Andre Agassi ‘Cupertino’ Creators Robert & Michelle King On Episode 2’s Shocking AGI Twist & Predicting The Future Again With AI Guardrails Storyline View All July 20, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa, 'Afterlife with Archie' and Greg Berlanti Courtesy/Getty Disney+ has given a green light to Afterlife with Archie , an hourlong drama series based on the best-selling Archie comic book series by Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa and Francesco Francavilla . It will have a Halloween 2027 premiere on the streamer. The order comes nine months after the project landed at Disney+ with a big script-to-series commitment . Afterlife with Archie comes from the same auspices as the CW’s Riverdale and Netflix’s Chilling Adventures of Sabrina : writer Aguirre-Sacasa, Greg Berlanti ‘s Berlanti Productions and Warner Bros. Television where Aguirre-Sacasa and Berlanti are under overall deals. Related Stories News KJ Apa Asked 'Riverdale' Showrunner Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa For 'Afterlife with Archie' Cameo: "I Don't Know Who I'd Play" News Disney+ And Hulu To Stream Pave Studios True-Crime Podcasts 'Clues' And 'Mother Knows Murder' Penned by Aguirre-Sacasa based on the Archie Comics characters, Afterlife with Archie turns the all-American town of Riverdale into a zombie-overrun apocalypse — where the only thing scarier than the undead is trying to survive your teenage years. When a supernatural spell from a certain teen-witch backfires, unleashing an army of the possessed dead upon Riverdale, Archie and his friends must fight to stay alive, testing the friendships, romances, and loyalties that have always held them together. Watch on Deadline Afterlife with Archie is executive produced by Aguirre-Sacasa and Jimmy Gibbons via Muckle Man; Greg Berlanti, Sarah Schechter, Leigh London Redman via Berlanti Productions; and Jon Goldwater via Archie Comics Studios. “ Afterlife with Archie has always been about more than just zombies — it’s about the friendships, loyalty and humanity that make Riverdale worth fighting for,” said Ayo Davis, president, Disney Kids & Family. “Roberto, Greg, Sarah and Jon have such a deep appreciation for these characters, and they’ve built something that’s equal parts thrilling and heartfelt. Fans are going to fall hard for this new version of the gang … and maybe scream a little too.” This is Aguirre-Sacasa, Berlanti Prods. and Warner Bros. TV’s third live-action Archie Comics series adaptation — and the first to launch on the outlet it was originally sold to. Riverdale was initially set up at Fox before moving to the CW, Chilling Adventures of Sabrina started at the CW before relocating to Netflix. Riverdale spawned a short-lived spinoff series on the CW, Katy Keene. Afterlife with Archie also marks Warner Bros. TV’s first series for Disney+, which has been increasingly opening up its slate to outside studios. “The world of ‘Archie’ and Riverdale is the gift that keeps on giving,” said Channing Dungey, Chairman and CEO, Warner Bros. Television Group and WBD US Networks. “To bring Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa’s incredible story to life with our partners at Berlanti Productions, ArchieComics and Disney+ is a thrill for all of us at WBTVG.” Aguirre-Sacasa, a film, TV and comic book writer, had written Archie Comics’ two best-selling horror series, Afterlife With Archie and Chilling Adventures Of Sabrina , when he was named the publisher’s Chief Creative Officer in March 2014. Twelve years later, he continues in his role while also expanding his TV footprint — and the Archie TV universe which launched with the 2017 Riverdale. “This was the comic book that started it all. Before there was a Riverdale, before there was a Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, there was Afterlife with Archie , which I collaborated on with the best horror artist in the business, Francesco Francavilla,” Aguirre-Sacasa said. “Getting to turn Afterlife into a TV series for the amazing team at Disney+ with our incredible partners at Berlanti Productions, WB and, of course, Jon (Goldwater) and his Archie family is truly a full-circle moment — and the ultimate dream project for me. Time to say a prayer for Archie, Betty, Veronica and the whole gang, ‘cause THE ZOMBIES ARE COMING!!!!” Berlanti Prods. and WBTV also have the upcoming Scooby-Doo! live-action series at Netflix, the HBO drama pilot How To Survive Without Me , Stillwater , based on the Skybound comic books, which has a series commitment at Amazon , as well as All American , which just launched its eighth and final season on the CW. “We are so happy to reunite with Roberto on this exciting series that takes us back into the Riverdale world that we so love, and we are thankful to Disney+ and WBTV for giving us the opportunity to revisit some of our favorite characters in a unique and thrilling way,” Berlanti and Schechter said. “A special thank you to Jon Goldwater for letting us continue to play within the beloved ‘Archie’ universe and trusting us to bring Archie’s various stories to life.” Aguirre-Sacasa is repped by WME and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern. Berlanti is repped by CAA and Felker McGinnis & Ryan. Schechter and Goldwater are repped by CAA. articles.title: Christiane Amanpour To Leave CNN In 2027 After 43 Years With Network
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Jon Ossoff Makes L.A. Fundraising Swing In Midterm Final Stretch Christiane Amanpour To Leave CNN In 2027 After 43 Years With Network CBS News Correspondent Jan Crawford Apologizes For X Comment On Michigan U.S. Senate Candidate Abdul El-Sayed View All October 19, 2026 8:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Christiane Amanpour David Buchan/PMC Christiane Amanpour will depart CNN next year, with plans to scale back her schedule at the end of this year before exiting in June. The network’s chief international anchor on Monday wrote in a memo to staffers, “After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” She added, “From my very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much, as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor.” (Read her full memo below.) Related Stories News Jon Ossoff Makes L.A. Fundraising Swing In Midterm Final Stretch Politics CBS News Correspondent Jan Crawford Apologizes For X Comment On Michigan U.S. Senate Candidate Abdul El-Sayed Amanpour also said that she would end her PBS show, Amanpour & Company , by the end of this year, along with her daily CNN International series. She will maintain a weekly CNN show through May, she said, and will continue to do a podcast, The Ex Files , a Global production. Watch on Deadline Mark Thompson , chairman and editor in chief of CNN, wrote in his own memo, “Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months. Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.” (Read his full memo below.) Amanpour’s departure comes amid the closing earlier this month of Skydance Paramount’s deal to acquire CNN’s parent company, Warner Bros Discovery. Thompson is remaining in place as leader of the news network, while Skydance CEO David Ellison has promised editorial independence. Amanpour has been outspoken about coverage of Donald Trump. In 2023, she publicly criticized the network’s town hall with Trump as he was campaigning for a return to the White House. Amanpour said that she shared her views with then-CEO Chris Licht. In her note to staffers on Monday, she wrote, “Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.” Here is Amanpour’s complete memo: “After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years! I will end my daily shows across CNN and PBS at the end of this year, while continuing to maintain a weekly show on CNN through May and working on a smooth transition through June. I want to thank all the amazingly talented people I’ve worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews. From my very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much, as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor. I will be continuing my successful podcast the Ex-Files with Global and look forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.” Here is Thompson’s note to staffers: Dear all, I’m writing today with news about a CNN icon – and our dear friend and colleague – Christiane Amanpour. After more than 43 years at CNN, Christiane has decided that the time is right to begin a new chapter. Early in 2027, she will scale back her CNN International show, Amanpour , to once a week. The program will conclude in May, and she will leave CNN at the end of June. Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months. Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally. Christiane has been a household name around the world for decades. Yet she began more than 40 years ago not as one of the biggest stars in CNN’s history, but as a news desk assistant in our Atlanta newsroom. Famously, one of her bosses told her back then that she didn’t have what it took to become a foreign correspondent – or to hold any on-air role at all. Boy, did she prove him wrong! It would be impossible to list all of her reporting triumphs, exclusive interviews, awards and broadcasting firsts, or the many other accomplishments that have made her one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere. We will make sure to share and celebrate them all before she departs next year. In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship. articles.title: Lance Armstrong On Schwinn Bicycles Documentary ‘No Hands’: “It’s An Incredible American Story”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart ‘Tall Tales & Murder’ Scores New International Deals As Season 2 Takes Shape Cineverse Boards Genre-Bending Holiday Film ‘Ralph’s Perfekt Christmas’ From ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ To Scottish Indie Boss: Kevin McKidd On Ferryman Films & His New Show ‘The Only Suspect’ View All October 19, 2026 8:37am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Lance Armstrong narrates 'No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company' Schwinn Doc LLC EXCLUSIVE: No Hands : The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company documents the extraordinary tale of the titular bike brand with Lance Armstrong serving as both an interview subject and narrator. Armstrong tells Deadline about this rags-to-riches-to-bankruptcy tale and how things could have been different for the iconic brand if he had been on board a Schwinn as he raced the Tour de France , in turn creating a boom in the U.S. market for road bicycles. “It doesn’t have the greatest ending for the family, but it’s an incredible American story,” he says of the feature documentary. “It’s the story of an immigrant. It’s the story of starting from scratch. It’s also the story – and I love thinking about this – of the importance of the bicycle on American culture, and I think sometimes that’s lost on people.” Related Stories News Tour De France: Tadej Pogacar Dominates Race For Record-Tying Fifth Win News Paramount's 5 Pacts With WBD's TNT Sports For Tour De France Highlights Unfeatured Films founder Daniel Clarke directs the film, which comes from the people behind The Lego Brickumentary , narrated by Jason Bateman, and Loopers: The Caddie’s Long Walk , which was narrated by Bill Murray. Watch on Deadline “There are a few brands in the history of whatever that have really owned the category, or, said another way, have named the category,” Armstrong says of Schwinn. And the feature doc duly shows how ingrained in U.S. culture Schwinn became as it got to a point of making over a million bikes a year. “Schwinn equals bike, bike equals Schwinn,” Armstrong said of its glory years. He got involved in No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company via Jim Packer , the Lionsgate exec who is an EP on the documentary, which uses AI to bring historical pictures and sequences to life. Deadline has a first look at the trailer (see below) as the film embarks on a festival run. No Hands recounts how Ignaz Schwinn traveled from Germany to the U.S. and, in 1895, he and Adolph Arnold launched the iconic bike brand, setting a manufacturing base in Chicago. Different generations will get misty-eyed over various models Schwinn produced, from the humble safety bike to the Sting-Ray, which took its design cues from American muscle cars, to sleek race bikes such as the Paramount. Armstrong, a veteran of the world’s biggest bike races, has his own memories: “I did the [1989] Junior World Champs on a Paramount, and to this day, for whatever reason, I still think that’s the best riding bike that I’ve ever ridden.” The film shows how Schwinn was cutting edge in many ways. The brand leaned into what would now be called influencer marketing, with the likes of Roy Rogers, Frank Sinatra and Joan Crawford seen aboard their bikes. It pioneered having its own stores – nowadays the A-list bike brands have their own concept stores – and it had groundbreaking designs and detailing. Having gotten generations of people onto two wheels, it had huge influence on BMX, mountain biking and cutting-edge design, but did not capitalize on these trends as they changed the face of cycling. Armstrong’s succinct take captures it: “They were innovative until they weren’t.” He rode a Trek bicycle in multiple editions of the Tour de France and cycling’s other blue ribband events. As U.S. audiences saw their man in the Yellow Jersey, sales at the likes of Trek and Specialized exploded. But Schwinn had been left in their dust, filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 1992. The Schwinn brand continued under new ownership after the bankruptcy and the No Hands filmmakers said they have no relationship with the current Schwinn Bicycle Company. “There’s a world where, somehow, they had agreed to offshore production, or got into the carbon game, and if they had done that in those early years…if that was a Schwinn instead of a Trek [I was riding], we would 100% be having a very different conversation,” Armstrong says. Sadly for Schwinn, that was not the case, but the rise and fall story takes in how a family business became a cultural icon. No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company opens with scenes from film and TV that reference Schwinn, underlining how it became shorthand for cycling. Director Clarke says his film “is the love letter to Schwinn that generations of kids deserve.” He adds: “The documentary feature explores Schwinn’s storied history, from the iconic Sting-Ray to its widespread influence in the worlds of BMX and mountain biking. “Through the accounts of fans, collectors, cycling pioneers and the Schwinn family themselves, No Hands tells the story of a brand that changed cycling forever and survived through the struggles of American manufacturing, family drama, fads and business forces that ultimately led to its bankruptcy.” Armstrong was keen to get involved. “I watch probably an unhealthy amount of documentaries, so there’s just my general interest in the category, and then obviously I had a touchpoint here, I have a lot of history with this brand.” Having been the subject of numerous docs, this was new for Armstrong in that here, he is narrating and being interviewed, and the doc isn’t focused on him. “I thought it was a fun thing to try. You hope the audience appreciates it. I think the film is great. I enjoyed the hell out of being a little bit involved in the process, obviously sitting for the interview, but then just getting in the studio and recording the narration.” While No Hands is a family story, a business story, a sports story and a story about moments in history, ultimately, it taps into the simple and timeless joy of riding bicycles, with which Schwinn is synonymous. The simple premise is: you never forget your first bike. In the film, Armstrong talks about the excitement and freedom that a first bike can bring. Decades later, the fire lit by his first steed, a brown Schwinn Mag Scrambler, still burns bright. “It’s not lost on anybody, my history with the bicycle, with the sport, with all of the races, with the Tour, all of the things associated with it,” he says. “Still to this day, at 55 years old, if I can wake up and go for a bike ride … and it borders on sounding a little corny, but when I talk about how that makes me feel, how that is still an escape for me, in many ways, it is like church.” No Hands comes from Tiburon Productions and Gem Pictures in association with Brookwell McNamara Entertainment and KSQD Media, and is produced by Human Design. Packer is an EP alongside Chris Brown, David Brookwell, Carl Cramer, Khristian A. Howell and George K. Howell. articles.title: Dan Lin Axed As Netflix Film Boss; Stock Slumping Streamer Set To Unveil Earnings Tuesday
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony How A24 Spurred A Meme Craze & Got The Many To Watch ‘You Can See Everything’; Documentary Opens To $15M Milestone ‘Street Fighter’ Rings Up No. 1 $51M+ WW Opening, Largely Driven By Fans – Global Box Office Update ‘Street Fighter’ Socks $31M, ‘You Can See Everything’ Has 2,000+ Sellouts With $15M Docu Milestone – Sunday Update View All October 19, 2026 8:38am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Dan Lin Getty Images Dan Lin is out as film boss at Netflix in what has been largely speculated for weeks. Insiders at the streamer have denied that Dan Lin and even Bela Bajaria were on the chopping block, but here we are. At Saturday night’s Academy Museum Gala cocktails, we caught up with Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos and asked if more cuts were coming. In what seemed like a polite dodge, he just winked and stepped away. Interpret that as you may. Lin’s firing comes in the wake of Netflix making 1,000 pink-slips given their recent slow growth, and minimal overall viewership spike. Wall Street is bracing for what is expected to be a downer quarter from the OTT service. At the time of this post, Netflix shares were trading at $69.76, -1% at the time of this report. The 52-week share high on Netflix was $124.86. Related Stories Acquisitions Netflix Strikes Deal With Globo For Brazilian Fare Including 'I'm Still Here' & 'India - A Love Story' Cancellations and Renewals Ju Ji-hoon & Choo Young-woo Return To 'The Trauma Code: Heroes On Call' With Seasons 2 & 3 In Production At Netflix Many were shocked when the ax swung last week and it missed Lin’s head, landing on his lieutenant co-head of film, Doug Belgrad. It was seen that Belgrad was an extra layer at the top of Netflix’s film brass that could easily be let go, dollar wise. Lin was expected to be safe until Bajaria’s replacement arrived on Oct. 26, Peter Rice. It was at that point in time that the exec was going to assess the situation. Watch on Deadline All of this boils down to: Netflix, what is it you exactly want? All of streaming has turned into basic cable as we get farther away from Covid. They looked to Lin in April 2024 post Scott Stuber in order to ratchet down the quantity of features and at a lower cost. Lin did exactly what they asked, steering away from overpriced $200M-plus, non downstream features like Red Notice, The Irishman and The Electric State . However, he had a no-nonsense approach to filmmakers. He had no problem reportedly pushing back on prestige content creators like Greta Gerwig and Ben Affleck. During the Lin regime, one source told us that relationships with filmmakers were fraying. Recently, The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth filmmaker David Fincher opted not to renew his longtime exclusive contract with the streamer. During Lin’s run Netflix saw their most viewed movie of all-time, Sony’s Kpop Demon Hunters (325.1M global views). However, that was greenlit under the previous Stuber administration. Lin and Belgrad’s bragging rights include War Machine ($80M production cost, 147M views), animated movie Swapped (144.9M views, which broke into the streamer’s top 10 of all-time), The Rip ($100M production cost, 136M views), Happy Gilmore 2 (135.1M), Apex (129M), Thrash (100M views) and People We Meet on Vacation ($14M production cost, 77.1M). Still there wasn’t a consistent reseeding of the Top 10 Most Popular list like there was during the Stuber era. The Mike and Pam Of It All After being passed over by Skydance for top jobs at the new Paramount Warner Bros. post-merger, we hear that former WB Motion Picture Bosses Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy are in the home stretch this week of finalizing the payout of their WB contracts by David Ellison. Until they’re closed, they can’t entertain any job offers. Those close to De Luca tell us he’d have no problems reporting into Rice if offered the job, however, Netflix would need to make a fire-breathing commitment to theatrical. The notion of a 45-day theatrical window to streaming isn’t a prospect that De Luca (and Abdy) could make to the filmmakers they’ve worked with, i.e. Ryan Coogler, Paul Thomas Anderson, Ridley Scott. The notion that the duo are bound to raise capital for their own feature operation seems like the more practical future for them. All this smoke over De Luca and Abdy heading to Netflix came about due to a friendly lunch with Sarandos. This has morphed into gossip that Sarandos was full-on courting the duo. If Sarandos and Rice bring the filmmaker-friendly duo in, the question is whether they’ll put any guardrails on them. When it came to De Luca and Abdy justifying the lofty costs for Anderson’s One Battle After Another, Coogler’s Sinners, Tom Cruise’s Digger and so on, David Zaslav didn’t blink an eye. Will Sarandos allow them the same greenlight independence he granted Stuber? Or will he expect them to count coins like Lin? Riddle us that, Mr. Sarandos. “Netflix isn’t a place where they talk about film,” says one creator who has worked with them, “They’re all about the process, the algorithm and breaking the code, which still makes Lin a good workhorse for them as he’s also about process.” There’s a rumor out there, and that is despite the notion that De Luca and Abdy are always joined at the hip, historically they haven’t been. Some believe there’s a world that Abdy could entertain an offer sans De Luca from Netflix once her WB contract is paid out. “Sure, there is a world where that could happen,” says one source with knowledge of the situation. Still, there’s no solid definite word out there as to who might fill Lin’s vacancy. No interview process going on as of yet. A rival studio boss complimented over the weekend, “I think you’ll be surprised as to who Peter Rice selects.” But still, no matter how the greenlight process is improved at Netflix, there’s a new sign of the times for the streamer. “If you want to know where the young crowd is looking, Meta just introduced Muse. People are heading back to cinemas, and streaming has become basic cable,” said one Netflix vet, “They can change shuffle as many executives as they want, and it still won’t make a difference.” Sources in the know have confirmed Lin’s firing to us. articles.title: Edward Berger Says Movie Biz “Needed Netflix To Wake Up” But Studios Can Now “Inspire” The Streamer
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Ju Ji-hoon & Choo Young-woo Return To ‘The Trauma Code: Heroes On Call’ With Seasons 2 & 3 In Production At Netflix Rafe Spall On Playing An Amnesiac Super Sleuth In ‘The Death Of Sherlock Holmes’: “This Is A Clean Slate” Hudson Williams, Zach Galifianakis & Jay Baruchel Set For ‘The Assembly’ Season 2 At Canada’s CBC View All October 19, 2026 8:48am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Edward Berger Violeta Sofia The movie business “needed Netflix to wake up”, according to Edward Berger , but the Oscar-winning All Quiet on the Western Front director predicted it could be the Hollywood studios inspiring the streaming service in years to come. Related Stories News Netflix Dismisses Dan Lin As Film Boss Before Peter Rice Arrives Executives Netflix Names Peter Rice As Chief Content Officer Speaking today during a fireside chat at the MIA Market in Rome, Berger offered an assessment of how Netflix, which greenlit Oscar winner All Quiet , had impacted Hollywood with its global streaming model. “The movie business needed Netflix to wake up,” he said. “They needed a real disruptor. They had probably become complacent and thought, ‘Okay, let’s do this because it was successful [before]’.” Netflix last week underwent its largest round of layoffs since 2022 – around 1,000 – incidentally the same year World War II pic All Quiet released. With Paramount and Warner Bros. recently becoming one under the Skydance banner and David Ellison promising to make 30 films a year, the wheel could be turning the other way. Watch on Deadline Berger didn’t comment directly on the market, but noted: “Maybe we are now entering a period where the relationship works the other way around, with Netflix being inspired by the movie business. I think the two worlds are additive.” Berger recalled how Sasha Bühler, Netflix’s Director of Film for German-speaking Europe at the time All Quiet was on the market, gave him a simple assessment of how the streamer would handle the film . “She said, ‘If the movie’s great, we’ll support it. If it’s not, we won’t.’ That’s so scary, but I really love that,” he added. Berger called his experience with All Quiet and Netflix “singularly great, with no stress at all.” He praised the streamer for giving “a considerable amount of money for a German film – money we could not have raised in that environment through local or international sales,” coming just as the Covid-19 outbreak was beginning. “Without that support, we might not have been able to make the movie,” he added. The film ultimately won the Best International Film category at the 2023 Oscars. Bühler, who helmed it for Netflix, exited the streamer in August this year, as we revealed at the time. How an Italian actor changed ‘ Conclave ‘ Conclave director Berger charmed a room of Italian delegates today at the MIA Market with a humorous tale from the set of the Oscar-nominated pic, which filmed in Rome. He and his team were searching for a male Italian actor over the age of 65 who spoke English. “The list was very short,” he recalled to laughs from the room. Sergio Castellitto was recommended to play Cardinal Tedesco, and soon given the role. It quickly became clear that Castellitto’s English was limited, but this led to an unexpected change of direction for the movie. Castellitto began changing lines from English into Italian, and with just days to go before filming, the decision was made to add the language. “We had an all-English cast and Sergio was speaking basically only Italian,” he laughed. Ralph Fiennes, who was leading the cast as Cardinal Thomas Lawrence, then decided he would need to quickly learn Italian, so he could respond naturally. “No one was going to go and say, ‘We’re going to stop the film,'” said Berger. It has been a busy few years for Berger, with another bustling period coming up. We were first with the news that Berger had given the World War Z sequel impetus by being attached as director, with Brad Pitt returning to star. The original film, released in 2013, was based on Max Brooks’ bestselling 2006 novel World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War . Pitt, Dede Gardner and Jeremy Kleiner are producing the sequel on behalf of Plan B Entertainment. Berger will also executive produce. Dennis Kelly will write the script. Berger is also attached to direct the untitled Lance Armstrong movie package starring Austin Butler as the disgraced cyclist, with Apple winning a heated auction . He will also direct Itamar Moses’ Netflix pic Stradivarius . Berger is headlining this year’s MIA Market in Rome alongside the likes of Jane Tranter. The event begins today and runs through October 23. articles.title: ‘Abbott Elementary’s Janelle James Sets Debut Hour Stand-Up Special With Netflix

articles.title: Patrick Schwarzenegger & Leslie Grace To Star In AGC Crime-Thriller ‘The Journeyman’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Andreas Wiseman , Matt Grobar October 19, 2026 9:05am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Patrick Schwarzenegger and Leslie Grace Getty/Melissa Isabel Quiñones EXCLUSIVE : Patrick Schwarzenegger ( The White Lotus ) will star as a down-on-his-luck tennis pro who is drawn into the dark world of match-fixing to make ends meet for his family in crime-thriller The Journeyman . Leslie Grace ( In the Heights ) will co-star as his fiercely loyal fiancée. Ángel Manuel Soto ( Wrecking Crew ) will direct from a script by husband-wife duo The Roberts with revisions by Bill Dubuque ( Ozark ). AGC Studios will fully finance and produce the crime-thriller. Stuart Ford will produce alongside Bryan Haas ( The Order ), Mason Eways, and Scott Franklin ( Black Swan ), with AGC’s Miguel A. Palos, Jr., Zach Garrett and Anant Tamirisa executive-producing. Related Stories News New AFM Summit To Explore Federal Production Tax Incentive News Ridley Scott & Doug Liman Collaborator Alexander Witt To Direct High-Speed Youth Sailboat Racing Feature 'Feathering The Wind' Pic will begin shooting on November 30th in San Juan, Puerto Rico, with The Pimienta Film Company providing production services. Watch on Deadline The White Lotus and Love of Your Life star Schwarzenegger is currently filming Mike Birbiglia’s Focus Features comedy Old Friends New Friend s. In the Heights star Grace recently released album Amor Quien Eres? through Sony Music Latin. Puerto Rican filmmaker Manuel Soto’s latest feature was the Amazon MGM action-comedy The Wrecking Crew starring Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista. He previously directed Blue Beetle (Warner Bros./DC), the first Latino-led superhero film from a major studio, and Charm City Kings , which premiered at Sundance and won a U.S. Dramatic Special Jury Award for its ensemble cast. AGC International reps the film’s international rights and will continue shopping the project at next month’s American Film Market. UTA and WME are co-repping domestic sales with AGC. The film has been in the works a little while and a couple years back had Dev Patel aboard to star with Tarsem Singh directing. Ángel Manuel Soto is repped by WME and Redefine Entertainment; Patrick Schwarzenegger is repped by UTA, Entertainment 360, and Goodman, Genow; Leslie Grace is repped by CAA and 641 Meridian; The Roberts are repped by Gersh Agency and LBI Entertainment; and Anant Tamirisa is representing AGC Studios. articles.title: Sony Wins Rights In Host Of International Territories To A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ & ‘Primetime’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Cineverse Wins North American Rights To Thriller-Horror ‘The Night Driver’ With Josh Lucas, Alyssa Milano & David Arquette Indonesian Star & ‘Reacher’ Actress Agnez Mo Joins Nicolas Cage & Michael Sheen In Cyber-Thriller ‘C.L.A.Y.’ Daylight Adds Deuxmoi Podcast Deux U To Network View All October 19, 2026 9:16am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'You Can See Everything' and 'Primetime' A24 EXCLUSIVE : In a competitive situation, Sony Pictures Worldwide Acquisitions has acquired rights in a host of international markets to A24 ’s awards season movies You Can See Everything and Primetime . Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything made its North American debut this weekend with a historic opening, ranking among the largest limited-release openings of the century and marking the biggest documentary opening in more than 20 years. The film, a mind-bending fly on the wall doc in which Theranos founder Holmes invites Fielder and Oppenheim into her home before she is sent to prison, has scored sky high ratings on Letterboxd, Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic. Related Stories News Jesse Eisenberg TV Series Produced By Peter Rice To Be Taken Out By A24 News How A24 Spurred A Meme Craze & Got The Many To Watch 'You Can See Everything'; Documentary Opens To $15M Milestone Sony Pictures has picked up rights in Germany & Austria, Latin America, Scandinavia, Greece, the Middle East, Israel, India, South Africa, South Korea, and Southeast Asia. Watch on Deadline Directed by Lance Oppenheim, Venice drama Primetime is currently playing in North American theaters and select international markets, where it has grossed more than $50M to date. Robert Pattinson stars as Chris Hansen, the Dateline NBC journalist who hosted controversial but popular show To Catch a Predator . Sony Pictures has taken rights for Primetime in Middle East, Indonesia, Israel, Singapore, Switzerland, South Korea, South Africa, Thailand, and Vietnam, with theatrical releases currently being planned across those regions. The deals reunite Sony Pictures Worldwide Acquisitions with A24 following Materialists , which earned north of $70M internationally for Sony Pictures and brought the film’s worldwide total past $100M. The A24 deal was negotiated on behalf of the studio by Joe Matukewicz, President, Sony Pictures Worldwide Acquisitions; Virginia Longmuir, EVP, Business Affairs; and Elan Kovo, VP, Business Development & FP&A. articles.title: Carrot Top Breaks Silence After Suicide Attempt and Hospitalization as Comedian Preps Return to Stage
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 17, 2026 12:41pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Carrot Top at the premiere of FilmDistrict's 'Parker' at Planet Hollywood Resort and Casino in Las Vegas on Jan. 24, 2013. David Becker/Getty Images Carrot Top returned to Instagram Saturday with a message for his fans, marking the comedian’s first comments after a Sept. 18 suicide attempt and hospitalization. “I’m truly overwhelmed by the outpouring of love, support, prayers, and well wishes I’ve received over the past couple of weeks. Every message, text, and kind thought has meant more to me than you know,” posted the 61-year-old comedian, whose real name is Scott Thompson. “While I haven’t been able to respond to everyone individually, please know that I’ve felt your love and appreciate each and every one of you from the bottom of my heart. Thank you for being there for me during this time. It truly means the world to me!” Related Stories Music Metallica Thrashes Las Vegas With Five Decades of Monumental Metal Music Donnie Wahlberg Says NKOTB's Final Las Vegas Shows Will Be "Super Emotional," Teases New Elements and Shares What's Next He closed the caption with an orange heart, and by some news that he will return to the stage at Luxor Hotel & Casino on Oct. 19 for the 8 p.m. show. He has a residency at the MGM property. Notable names flooded the comments section with words of support, including stand-up superstar Jay Mohr who wrote “LOVE LOVE LOVE.” Emmy winner Hannah Einbinder wrote, “Love you Scott,” while songwriter Sarah Hudson also wrote, “Love you.” The post comes after two public appearances alongside his mother at a local Las Vegas church, on both Oct. 4 and Oct. 11. Paparazzi images surfaced from the outings but he had not yet made any statements regarding his health or what happened amid the mental health crisis beyond what his publicist had shared with media outlets including TMZ. “Mr. Thompson is currently recovering, surrounded by his family and those closest to him. His focus is on his health and recovery, and we ask that his privacy be respected at this time,” his rep told TMZ as part of a published report by the outlet that included allegations of extortion over sexually explicit content featuring Carrot Top. Per TMZ , a rep for Carrot Top alleged that a man named Brian Evans had threatened to file a “sexually explicit recording on a USB drive depicting the comedian into a court’s legal docket…unless he was paid $500,000 as a settlement.” View this post on Instagram THR

articles.title: Ari Emanuel Pitches Brother Rahm as Centrist Democratic President and Says He Isn’t Too Worried About AI: “It Doesn’t Have Taste”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 17, 2026 1:44pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ari Emanuel Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC/Getty Images Ari Emanuel , TKO Group executive chair and CEO and executive chairman of WME Group , was in London on Saturday to discuss his memoir , entitled Roll the Calls , published by Penguin Random House. And to no one’s surprise, he didn’t hold back, including on issues like AI, politics in the age of Donald Trump — and his brother Rahm’s potential White House run. In a conversation with Tina Brown , former editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair and The New Yorker , which was organized by Intelligence Squared, he also touched on such details as his early days in the CAA mailroom all the way to the super-agent and Hollywood power broker he is today. The title of the event: “An Evening With the Dealmaker Who Reshaped Hollywood.” Related Stories TV 'The Diplomat' U.K. Prime Minister on the Operatic Way He Learned of His "Shocking" Season 4 Storyline TV Patrick Brammall Is Poised to Join the Ranks of Australia's Great Exports Emanuel, who has represented the likes of Larry David, Martin Scorsese and Oprah Win­frey, famously also served as the inspiration for Ari Gold, portrayed by Jeremy Piven, in the TV drama Entourage . Asked about his work as the agent to big names, he said: “What I say to people is: ‘You pay me 10 percent for my opinion. You’ll listen to my opinion. You don’t want to follow it, don’t follow it! Now I have gotten fired for giving my 10 percent. I’m OK with that. I’ve re-signed the people that have fired me, a couple of them, but you’re paying me for my opinion.” Emanuel connected that to the rise of AI. “In this day of AI, that’s more important than anything — your opinion, your taste,” he offered. “AI doesn’t have taste, and taste only comes with time and knowledge of situations.” Curiosity and ideas matter more than ever in the age of AI, he argued. “AI is just an average, a very good average,” Emanuel said. “There is something so important that people are missing here. It is not the answer. Curiosity is important, judgment is important, taste is very important. It has no taste. As much as there are scary things about AI, those are qualities that you own that are only human.” Will AI enhance creativity? “Yeah, it will,” the agent offered. “It will add [for] a great creative mind, such as Marty Scorsese. They will be able to implement taste and creativity. My wife’s a fashion designer. She works with AI, but she’s the one who has the taste, and she’s giving it the ideas.” Brown asked if he was concerned about AI’s “absence of morality.” His take: “It’s something that has to come into it. I’m not sure how,” or how that will be possible without stifling technological opportunities. Which of his many deals of the past gave him the biggest headache? “The hardest deal was probably the UFC deal,” Emanuel told the London crowd. “I had been representing UFC for 25 years. It was on Fox. …. We thought Fox was going to buy it – easy.” Another option, Warner, was downsizing at the time. “So those two were out, and then it was us against the Chinese because they had a lot of money coming into the entertainment space,” the super-agent recalled. “But [UFC boss] Dana [White] didn’t want to go to them, and then all of a sudden something horrible happened. I blame all of you from Britain because you guys didn’t elect the right person at the time. Brexit happened, and the banking system fell apart, and so we had to buy the business [when] the banking system kind of went haywire.” In short, “it was just one headache after another, but we got it done,” he concluded. Emanuel also described UFC and other sports and live experiences as events that can bring a politically divided world together. “I’d rather talk to the other side,” as a Democrat, he said. “Sports is a common ground.” Continuing the talk about politics, Brown asked if MAGA wasn’t “the biggest cult going.” Emanuel replied: “I don’t want to be in MAGA. And I don’t want to be in the DSA [Democratic Socialists of America]. When the moderator suggested that UFC may have become the biggest sport associated with the Trump era, asking if it could last beyond it, Emanuel offered: “Yeah, I think it’s going to outlast me.” The agent didn’t let Brown drag him into speculating about Trump’s political future and future directions. “I talked to him about four weeks ago,” he said. “This Ukraine [policy] thing is upsetting.” And he added: “I think after Congress is back, I’m going to call him because I got some stuff I have to talk to him about. I plan on having a conversation.” Asked about his hopes for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Emanuel said: “Let’s hopefully get the Senate and the House.” He also expressed support for his brother, Rahm Emanuel, as the centrist Democratic candidate in the next presidential election. He said: “All kidding aside, I don’t think there’s a better candidate in the world who could be president and cares more about the world, the United States, helping kids and will fight the fight.” THR
