articles.title: ‘The Diplomat’ U.K. Prime Minister on the Operatic Way He Learned of His “Shocking” Season 4 Storyline
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All October 17, 2026 4:11pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Rory Kinnear in 'The Diplomat.' Idris Solomon/Netflix Logo text [The following story contains spoilers from the first four episodes of The Diplomat season four, through “Pagliacci.”] Rory Kinnear couldn’t leave The Diplomat without one more surprise. The actor, who has spent the past four seasons playing wild-card British prime minister Nicol Trowbridge, resigns midway through the Netflix political thriller’s latest season, announcing the move in a shocking moment at the end of episode four. Trowbridge steps down after an unusually surreal episode for The Diplomat , in which he imagines that former adviser Margaret Roylin (Celia Imrie), who dies early in season three, is still alive and chiming in on his latest actions. He also hallucinates that the U.S. officials with whom he’s meeting are laughing at and mocking him and sings an aria as he thinks of himself as both a king and a clown (donning both costumes). Related Stories Business Ari Emanuel Pitches Brother Rahm as Centrist Democratic President and Says He Isn't Too Worried About AI: "It Doesn't Have Taste" TV Patrick Brammall Is Poised to Join the Ranks of Australia's Great Exports Despite the trippy scenes leading up to Kinnear’s final scene, which comes just one episode after viewers learn that U.K. foreign secretary Austin Dennison (David Gyasi) has died in a helicopter crash, Diplomat showrunner Debora Cahn says there were grounded, real-life reasons for this season’s shake-up in the British government. “By the time we got to this season, Rory had been prime minister for a period of time where the actual U.K. had like five different people at 10 Downing Street,” Cahn tells The Hollywood Reporter . “And it felt like there was this essential part of being a diplomat, which is that you’re always learning the cast of characters from scratch. You either outlast the people that you’re working with, or you’re sent to a different country. And I wanted to see our team going through the struggle of just when you think you know where the ground is under your feet, it completely changes. You’ve built all these relationships, and suddenly you have nothing.” Cahn was also interested in showing what it would mean for Keri Russell ‘s American ambassador to the U.K. to no longer have to work with someone like Trowbridge. “I also really wanted to play with the dynamic of like, you think you’re working with somebody who’s difficult and they’re the problem, and then they leave, and it turns out you were the problem or both of you were the problem,” she says. Cahn gave Kinnear a heads-up that his character would be resigning at some point in season four, but the specifics around his departure didn’t emerge until the actor received an unusual request while he was boarding a flight to Lithuania. “I got a message from Deb saying, ‘Do you think you’d be able to sing this?’ And she sent me the aria,” Kinnear recalls. “And I thought, ‘Why on earth would I be required to do that?’ And I said, ‘I think I could, but how did you know I could sing?’ And she said, “Do you remember it? I think it was at the beginning of season two, there was a funeral in St Paul’s Cathedral, and the whole congregation was asked to sing a hymn and I could hear your voice.’ I thought, ‘Interesting.’ And she’d obviously held on to that for two and a half seasons and brought it back. So I thought, ‘OK, how does that fit into why he might be resigning?'” Trowbridge’s resignation is immediately preceded by Russell’s Kate blackmailing him by telling the newly appointed British foreign secretary Robyn Palmer (Abigail Marlowe), as Trowbridge looks on, about Roylin’s involvement in the carrier ship attack that kicked off the series and how Trowbridge “tried to kill” Roylin when he learned what she’d done. The risky move is, unsurprisingly, Hal’s (Rufus Sewell) idea and though Kate initially resists his “mafioso”-like approach to foreign policy, she ends up doing what he suggested. “I just think [Trowbridge] makes her crazy. I think he pushed her buttons,” Russell says of why Kate threatens him after he said, in part, that she and Hal won’t be invited to Dennison’s funeral. “He knew how to get her riled up and make it personal, and it’s too fresh. She’s doing something she doesn’t want to do anyway. She doesn’t believe in it, and then he’s attacking her when she hasn’t processed something.” The shake-up also meant Gyasi and Kinnear would be leaving the Netflix series on which they’d been central castmembers for the past few years, a disappointing development for Cahn and the show’s remaining cast. “We wanted to keep Dave Gyasi and Rory Kinnear forever,” Cahn says. “I wish I could see them every day. It’s a bummer when the company shifts in some way. We’ve had the luxury of bringing a lot of people in, and sometimes the story is ejecting people out on the other end, and it sucks.” Sewell adds that Dennison’s death and Trowbridge resigning are “tremendously shocking.” For Kate, though, Russell says the loss of Dennison, with whom she had a close relationship (the show teased the possibility of a romance early on, culminating in a passionate kiss in season three) is “really hard.” “I think what that does to Kate is really hard, especially at this moment when her morals are being put to the test because he was such a moral character, so I think that fuels all of those doubts,” she says. “And then you have Hal on the other line going, ‘This is what you got to do. You got to do this.’ It’s an enormous loss for the show, for a lot of people who loved him, too. But it’s good storytelling ultimately.” Kinnear, while sad that he won’t get to keep working with his Diplomat colleagues, is confident the bonds he’s forged with them will continue after he’s left the show. And he’d be happy to return in a guest capacity. “I’d be fascinated to see where Trowbridge does end up,” he says. “There are so many different roles that a retired politician finds themselves in, and I’m sure he wouldn’t spend the rest of his life lying low.” Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter , Kinnear opens up about why Trowbridge resigns; how his character feels about Dennison’s death, as the two had a complicated relationship; and the experience of filming his final episode. What was your reaction when you found out that this is what would be unfolding for your character? I got a heads up from Deb that at some point during the series, Trowbridge will be resigning, and I’ve already felt pretty lucky to have stayed on for as long as I have, given the nature of British politics over the last six or seven years. To finally receive the script, to see, as is typical of Debora’s writing, the psychological acuity she was going to bring to it, and how much she wanted to explore his inner life at the point of his greatest crisis. I sort of knew then that it was going to be a real gift for me as as an actor to be able to to bring that to life. How do you feel about about having to leave the show and the people that you were working with for a number of seasons? Well, luckily, when you do a job for as long as this has been — a lot of the time we were hosting our American friends in London, and then luckily they got to return the favor when we were filming in New York — we’re in and out of each other’s lives to such an extent that we knew that we had formed these lifelong friendships. So while it’s obviously sad that I won’t be able to get to go to work with them. I know that I’ll still be able to hang out with them whenever they’re in town or I’m in their town. To have been able to be part of a series that is so smart, so funny, so dramatic, so psychologically aware and so incredibly well-written and -cast is one thing. But to have left with a load of lifelong friends is far too great. What was it like filming that very surreal episode in which Trowbridge resigns, with the Margaret Roylin hallucinations? That’s such a different approach for this show. What was exciting about it was that you knew that it was a new flavor. Shows like this, they constantly have to reinvent themselves or show new aspects of themselves, and a character that has loomed as large as Trowbridge has over the four seasons, to be able to get into what really sort of drives him, what makes him tick and to see what what it meant to him to be prime minister, to see what losing that meant to him, what destruction it wreaked him, and how he thought he might be seen both as a king and as a clown and that he’d sort of straddled both roles in his prime ministership, and that we get to see them played out for for real, as it were, within this kind of wild dream life. We never really get a concrete explanation from Trowbridge about why he resigned. How much do you think Kate’s blackmail threat prompted his resignation? What do you think it was really due to? Well, I mean, I do think that most politicians have a sort of self-awareness about how they how they can present themselves or how they can operate and what constitutes a line in the sand for something they wouldn’t be able to to go on with. And I think knowing how compromised he would be, particularly in his relationship with America, and how complicated he had been with that, with this new information in their hands, I think he knew: There’s nothing I can do without feeling I’ll be limping on. I won’t be able to do it with the gusto that I feel like I’ve been able to operate for as long as he has been prime minister. I also think events catch up with people, and it caught up with him what happened with Roylin and at the very beginning of season one, and sometimes people’s appetite goes for the the hurly burly of politics, and I think everyone knows that you’re a long time retired and resigned once you leave it so you keep on going, keep on going because there’s nothing quite like it in terms of the status that you’re afforded, in terms of the decisions you get to make, in terms of just the day-to-day excitement of it, but when it’s time to to step away, it must be sort of crashingly obvious, and I think that’s why he leaps to resignation. We also find out at the end of the previous episode that Austin Dennison (David Gyasi) has died. How does Trowbridge feel about that? He and Dennison had a complicated relationship. That’s, I think, definitely another reason that pushes him towards the resignation. They had come up together. They had been adversaries together, but they had found a use for each other as well in the highest echelons of politics. So, to have lost Roylin, to then lose Dennison. Those were the good cop and bad cop on his shoulder, or the devil and the angel on his shoulder, throughout his time. So, I think he felt completely settled as to where he would turn. Lydia obviously provides some support, ballast and encouragement, determination for him. But without Dennison and without Roylin, there was there was an instability to how he saw himself. Do you have a favorite memory or scene from playing Nicol Trowbridge in The Diplomat ? Driving up in that Jag outside the big country house, in the first [season], you thought, oh yeah, this is going to be fun. This show’s got something about it. Getting to film in St Paul’s Cathedral, getting to film in all those amazing locations. We’re up in the foreign office, and there were times where you felt — I see why people in the top echelons of power try and cling on because traveling in big motorcades or helicopters, all the ceremony of it, you can see how it can go to people’s heads and become quite addicted. I’ve made sure that I kept my feet on the ground, but you could see, particularly with a Netflix-style budget affording you. I’m sure it’s not all as quite as grand and as glamorous, being prime minister, but it certainly felt it at times. And I always remember turning the corner dressed in full crown and coronation robes and singing an aria straight down the camera, and I don’t think the crew had any idea what was going on or why I was doing that or dressed like that. THR

articles.title: Miley Cyrus Returns to the Stage With Emotional and Cathartic Hollywood Bowl Show
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All October 17, 2026 4:17pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Miley Cyrus performs at the Hollywood Bowl. Kevin Mazur / Getty Images Fans of all ages packed in close at the Hollywood Bowl Friday to witness a rare experience in today’s music landscape: A full-fledged Miley Cyrus solo concert. The 33-year-old pop star, going by just Miley these days, has been open about the tolls that performing live takes on her mental health and wellness. As a result, it’s been a near-decade since her last large-scale world tour, and four years since her last major concert. Even during Friday’s performance, the singer was honest about the fact she wasn’t sure if she’d ever do a show of this scale again, attributing her desire to do these shows in part due to her late godmother, country music icon Dolly Parton, who died earlier this this year. Related Stories Music Harry Styles Debuts Unreleased Song at MSG to Honor Liam Payne on Second Death Anniversary Music Miley Cyrus Tearfully Pays Tribute to Dolly Parton With "Jolene" Performance at Hollywood Bowl: "Me and Dolly, We Are Eternal" “For me, performance can’t be everything because the curtain closes and the lights go down, and I have to go back home and be happy with who I am,” the pop star told the crowd. “I really appreciate you all honoring that and respecting and celebrating and supporting and encouraging me, finding this balance in my life where I can really have everything that I’ve ever wanted.” Dubbed Bass Persuades Live at the Hollywood Bowl, Friday’s concert, the first of two this weekend, was held in support of her latest album Bass Persuades . Her fans have been patiently waiting for the day she’d return — the 1.5 million people that joined the queue for the roughly 36,000 tickets across the two nights are serving as proof. Miley Cyrus performs at the Hollywood Bowl. Kevin Mazur / Getty Images The singer kicked off the night with material from Bass Persuades , unsurprisingly, given the show’s name. She took the stage after one of what would be several pre-recorded, black-and-white videos of the star spoke directly to the crowd. “‘Hello.’ A voice greets me that sounds more like a mirror. ‘Make a record.’ Oh, that’s very specific for an angel,” pre-recorded Cyrus said to the crowd. “You will stand on that same stage held by the people, the sound and the desire that’s carried you all the way to your destiny. And sitting behind you is the rest of your life, but nothing waits forever.” Cyrus reiterated many times that she was grateful to her fans for being understanding about where she’s at in her career. “I didn’t know that if live performance was going to be a part of my future, if this was something that I wanted to dedicate and devote myself to, because that’s what it really is,” she said. “Tonight, it isn’t just the night for us, but it’s all the preparation of everyone that is behind the scenes that you’ll never get to see that make this show possible.” The 18-song set — which included two surprise guests in the form of The Flaming Lips’ frontman Wayne Coyne, a collaborator of the pop star, and her fiance Maxx Morando, another collaborator — included both new and old hits, but the experience was admittedly different for each. Miley Cyrus performs at the Hollywood Bowl. Kevin Mazur / Getty Images Cyrus clearly felt the most passionate about the newer material, belting the words to the songs from Bass Persuades , while tending to let the backtrack and the crowd lead on some of her older hits like “Party in the USA” and “We Can’t Stop.” Her Hannah Montana movie track “The Climb” received one of the biggest reactions of the night, with the entire crowd singing along. Her 2013 hit single “Wrecking Ball” took on a new arrangement for the show, skipping the iconic shift into the chorus. Sure, the hits were lighter on Cyrus’ live vocals, but they were still endlessly enjoyable and emotional for both the singer and the crowd. Cyrus could have stood onstage with a laptop playing music videos, a la Justin Bieber’s Coachella headlining set, and the sold-out crowd, would’ve still likely counted the night as a success. The most emotional moment of the evening came in the form of a tribute to Parton, who Cyrus has often referred to as Aunt Dolly. As the pop star’s godmother, Parton has been close with Cyrus her entire life. The singer broke down in tears speaking about the country music pioneer as the intro to Parton’s iconic song “Jolene” played in the background. She told a story of her experience seeing Parton at the Hollywood Bowl before covering “Jolene.” Later in the show, during “Wrecking Ball,” her Aunt Dolly’s favorite song, she clutched a small photo of Parton in a heart-shaped frame to her chest. Miley Cyrus performs at the Hollywood Bowl. Kevin Mazur / Getty Images Friday’s performance was cathartic for the audience, and clearly for Cyrus, who’s seemingly found the balance for her life as a pop star that she’s been looking for. She told the crowd she was excited to perform at the iconic venue all day, but she’d been equally excited to have acquired a new fish that day. These Hollywood Bowl performances were as much for Cyrus as they were for the crowd. “Being able to create a life that I get to wake up every day and have those joys that give me meaning and purpose — I’m proud to be a person that those kinds of things bring me just as much joy as performing for almost 18,000 people here tonight,” she told the crowd midway through the show. “Being able to live a life in true harmony and have everything that I’ve ever wanted… Every dream that I’ve been able to conjure and make a reality, I’m experiencing here today. October 16th. This is like a new holiday in my life.” She didn’t, of course, forget the fans. “It’s been 20 years of us on this journey, this evolution and this metamorphosis. You all, you have not skipped a beat. I am so, so appreciative of your support,” she said. “It’s been steadfast, and it’s been deeply felt. The appreciation I have for you is never forgotten on show days.” Cyrus, preparing to launch into her 2013 anthem “We Can’t Stop,” finished her speech with more gratitude. “Because of you, I get to have the life that is everything I could have ever imagined. I have love, I have animals, I have all of you, I have music, I have creativity. I have someone else, and I just love my life. It’s the most beautiful. Thank you all for making it that way.” Cyrus returns for the second and final night of Bass Persuades Live at the Hollywood Bowl on Sunday, Oct. 18. THR

articles.title: Gene Schwam, Hollywood Publicist to Elvis Presley, Judy Garland and Julie Andrews, Dies at 96
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 17, 2026 4:35pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Gene Schwam Courtesy of the Schwam family. Gene Schwam, the veteran Hollywood publicist who worked with the likes of Elvis Presley , Judy Garland , Julie Andrews , Barbara Eden and Blake Edwards , has died. He was 96. Schwam died Friday in Los Angeles following a brief illness. In 1954, he was working with fellow publicist Stanley Cowan making $35 per week, when he decided to leave the company and found his own agency. Alongside Adeline Hanson, they opened Hanson & Schwam Public Relations in 1955. The firm began by representing restaurants and musicians, though their roster quickly expanded into the wider entertainment industry. Nancy Wilson and Lou Rawls were among those represented by the agency, which additionally handled publicity for the Cocoanut Grove nightclub. Related Stories Movies Michael Forest, Actor in Roger Corman Movies and 'Star Trek,' Dies at 97 Music Mark Pucci, Longtime Music Publicist and Blues Advocate, Dies at 79 Schwam also worked with Lenny Bruce, Cyd Charisse and Gene Barry. His work with Andrews and Eden were central to his career as a publicist, and he formed a close friendship with Edwards; the publicist character in his 1981 film S.O.B. was inspired by Schwam. He is also the creator of Humanity 101, an initiative of Arizona State University’s Project Humanities that promotes compassion, empathy, forgiveness, integrity, kindness, respect and self-reflection. The veteran publicist reflected on his career in conversation with The Hollywood Reporter ‘s Chris Gardner in April 2021, noting, “There’s a mistake people make when they think it’s about who you know in Hollywood, but it isn’t about that — it’s about who knows you.” He also shared some secrets to success: “Begin with the end of the game and work your way backward,” Schwam said. “Figure out what it is that we want to do, such as win an Oscar, then we figure out how to get there.” Schwam added, “I’ve always felt that success of the personal service business is referrals. It’s not getting on the phone or going online. It’s always been someone saying, ‘Hey, Gene, I have a friend who is writing a book, would you be interested in working with them?’” He is survived by his wife, Myrna Schwam; his daughter, Stephanie Schwam Adams; his stepchildren, Adam London, Greg London and Linda London; and four grandchildren. THR

articles.title: South Africa’s Oscar Entry ‘Variations on a Theme’ Was Written With Microsoft Excel
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 18, 2026 12:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Variations on a Theme' Courtesy of IFFR Ouma Hettie is an octogenarian goat herder in South Africa’s Kamiesberge. When she falls victim to a scam promising reparation for her father’s unpaid service during World War II, her family becomes more involved than she would like them to. Welcome to the world of Variations on a Theme ( Variasies op ‘n Tem ) from writers/directors Devon Delmar and Jason Jacobs ( Carissa ), which won the Tiger Award at this year’s International Film Festival Rotterdam and just screened at the 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival (LFF). Related Stories TV 'The Diplomat' U.K. Prime Minister on the Operatic Way He Learned of His "Shocking" Season 4 Storyline Business Ari Emanuel Pitches Brother Rahm as Centrist Democratic President and Says He Isn't Too Worried About AI: "It Doesn't Have Taste" “A poetic and distinctive visual style infuses playfulness into this insightful study of a woman’s resilience and a community that exists close to the land,” the LFF website said about the film. Delmar, who also edited the film, came to London for LFF snd talked to THR about the musicalness of Variations on a Theme and how it may well be the only movie ever to be written on Microsoft Excel. The film has a rhythmic dance vibe, a sense of an underlying choreography that you just feel while experiencing it – without necessarily being able to explain that feeling. And that is all by design. “It all starts with Jason being a very perceptive and observant person,” Delmar tells THR . “He is from this village you see in the film. He was born there, went to school there, and then came back after living in Cape Town to live with his grandmother.” The duo actually made a short film there a few years ago, ”and I have become part of this community in some way as well,” he explains. And the place has its own pace. “Anyone would be able to observe the routine, the rhythm of this space,” Delmar says. “If you sit in a corner for long enough, you’ll start to notice the routines and the rhythms that occur naturally. ‘Here comes Mr. So and So with his goats when the sun is setting,’ and so on. The routines are very ingrained into the space, and it’s very beautiful to observe the musicality of the space within that rhythm.” That’s also where the title Variations on a Theme comes from. The repetition of everyday life also “harmonized, to use a musical term again, with the awareness that the exploitation that’s happening there in 2026 is merely history repeating itself,” the filmmaker tells THR . “What’s happening with villagers being scammed out of money is exactly what happened in the 1940s to [the protagonist’s] father, who was being exploited by the government at the time, which is exactly what happened to the people who were colonized going back several generations.” Highlights Delmar: “So this idea of repetition became very important to our way of thinking, and then it was very natural to incorporate that into the structure of the film to show this repetition and the cycle of violence, and the daily routines of this woman.” One possibly surprising tool to map out shots for the film to ensure the visual representation of this repetition and cycle was Microsoft Excel. Yeah, really! “I’ve joked that it’s the only film ever, potentially, to be written on Microsoft Excel,” says Delmar. “Because we have five story days, so we has five columns and then 30 shots that repeat like clockwork.” And the filmmaker keeps the surprises coming. “We were borrowing from an Estonian composer called Arvo Pärt,” Delmar explains. He’s the big guy in Tallinn in terms of music, and he wrote music very formulaically. He came up with these almost formulas or equations for his music. He would work on a very small kernel of an idea or a seed, but once he unleashes that little seed, it manifests the most unbelievably beautiful and spiritual music.” That served as an inspiration for Variations on a Theme . “We were interested in how we could contain the film into one core idea, and then almost press play on it and let it unfold,” Delmar explains. “It’s like an origami thing you do, and then a pop-up book appears.” THR

articles.title: ‘What Belongs to Others’ Wins Top Warsaw Film Festival Award
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 18, 2026 2:10am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'What Belongs to Others' Courtesy of Warsaw International Film Festival The 42nd edition of the Warsaw International Film Festival is wrapping up on Sunday after its winners were unveiled during a Saturday night awards ceremony. The top honor, the Warsaw Grand Prix in the international competition of the Polish fest, went to Grzegorz Dębowski for What Belongs to Others . The film follows a Polish burglar who assumes the identity of a dead stranger’s girlfriend, with unexpected results. The jury said it awarded the top honor to the film “for its precise and delicate storytelling, its exceptional performances, and its complex portrait, devoid of judgment, of a flawed and elusive woman who undergoes a transformation as she slips into a stranger’s identity and life, and therein finds the possibility of her own.” Related Stories Movies South Africa's Oscar Entry 'Variations on a Theme' Was Written With Microsoft Excel TV 'The Diplomat' U.K. Prime Minister on the Operatic Way He Learned of His "Shocking" Season 4 Storyline The Warsaw best director award went to Chinese filmmaker Cai Chengjie for Suzhou Quartet , which the jury lauded as “an original and ambitious concept brought to life through striking cinematography and daring experimentation with narrative form.” The “visually captivating and richly layered meditation on life and mortality” tells the story of four people who meet by chance in a small noodle shop, only to find they are long-lost acquaintances. Meanwhile, the Warsaw festival also gave a special jury award to Maria Dębska for her performance in Through the Wall , directed by Maciej Sobieszczański, about two young political prisoners during the Stalinist terror in Poland who fall in love The jury lauded the actress for “a remarkably precise and emotionally truthful portrayal [and] for creating a complex character with great sensitivity and without exaggeration.” It added that the honor is also “for a role that stays with the audience long after the film ends.” Meanwhile, a special jury mention went to Bloody Men , directed by Jens Sjögren, with the jury saying it “captures with remarkable authenticity the chaos caused by domestic violence and the challenges faced by children growing up with a single parent struggling with personal difficulties and making decisions that repeatedly put the entire family’s safety at risk.” Also at Warsaw, the main award in the Competition 1–2 program, dedicated to directors’ first and second fiction features, went to Lorin Terezi’s Agia . “It is rare for a fiction feature debut to feel so complete,” the jury said. “Its structure recalls a Greek tragedy, offering a glimpse into a disappearing world. A subtle story of a young woman rebelling against patriarchal tradition and a world in which family honor is valued above life itself. Agia wants to live on her own terms and make her own decisions.” A special mention in the 1-2 program went to Urša Menart’s Everything That’s Wrong With You , “a touching portrait of a young woman desperately trying to find an honest human connection in a world full of emotional uncertainty, white lies and cheating German boyfriends.” The Warsaw documentary competition saw the award go to Jonas Spriestersbach’s Meanwhile in Namibia , which explores how the German government, instead of paying reparations for its occupation of Namibia in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, offers development cooperation programs. “The director demonstrates an amazing ability to frame reality with extraordinary precision, letting the images slowly unfold and reveal the unsettling and absurd contradictions of human behavior,” the jury said. “The film addresses moral complexity without simple judgments, allowing viewers to construct their own meaning.” María Molina Peiró’s Like Any Other Mortal received a special mention in the doc program. Check out further Warsaw film festival awards below. Short Grand Prix Meteorit , directed by Elisabeth Werchosin Best Live-Action Short Film Award Meteorit , directed by Elisabeth Werchosin Best Animated Short Film Award Knowing Gaze , directed by Dylan Glynn Best Documentary Short Film Award A Letter to Home , directed by Sina Aghazadeh Ecumenical Jury Award The Child , directed by Linda Olte FIPRESCI Award Through the Wall , directed by Maciej Sobieszczański NETPAC Award Mentor , directed by Keisuke Yoshida Young FIPRESCI Award Lover, Not a Fighter , directed by Martina Buchelová Polish Film Institute Award Josephine , directed by Beth de Araújo Orlen Award for the Best Polish Short Film Dying of the Young Deer , directed by Angelika Cygal Speakers’ Avenue Film School Award The Death of a Bird , directed by Felipe Sánchez García KIPA Award for Best Producing Debut from the Polish Producers Alliance (KIPA) Dagmara Piasecka for Pixie. The New Beginning THR

articles.title: ‘Imperium,’ ‘Concrete Land’ and ‘9 Temples to Heaven’ Win BFI London Film Festival Awards
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 18, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Imperium' Courtesy of BFI London Film Festival The 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival (LFF) is wrapping up Sunday night with the U.K. premiere of Jesse Eisenberg ’s star-studded The Debut , following the afternoon unveiling of this year’s award winners. The 2026 honors were led by Sergei Loznitsa ‘s Imperium , which won the best film award in the official competition, and Asmahan Bkerat’s Concrete Land , which was named the winner of the Grierson Award in the LFF documentary competition. Imperium brings together Italian footage from the early 1970s that was shot across what was then the USSR. The result is a look at the diversity of the country in contrast with official Soviet portrayals and productions from the same era. Related Stories Movies South Africa's Oscar Entry 'Variations on a Theme' Was Written With Microsoft Excel TV 'The Diplomat' U.K. Prime Minister on the Operatic Way He Learned of His "Shocking" Season 4 Storyline “ Imperium is an extraordinary film that explores the Soviet Union in the early 1970s from a rich archive with a wide-ranging perspective that looks at life in a country with an extraordinary social and cultural landscape that has rarely been seen,” the LFF jury said. “The film is richly evocative and emotionally engaging on all levels, giving us a visually arresting perspective of life before the Soviet Union was broken apart.” Palestinian-Jordanian director Bkerat’s Concrete Land tells the story of a Palestinian Bedouin family displaced in Jordan. The young filmmaker told THR in a recent interview that the family featured in the film helped her discover her love for documentary filmmaking. ‘Concrete Land’ Courtesy of Asmahan Bkerat “This was a beautifully observed portrait filmed with mastery and confidence,” highlighted the LFF jury. “In image creation, sound design, scene building and, most importantly, the deep and trusting relationship with the films’ characters, the filmmaker proved themselves a worthy recipient of the Grierson award. It takes a tremendous cinematic skill and maturity to bring the audience to feel so close to each and every character of this remarkable family, across generations and in a very different part of the world, yet the warmth we feel for each is profound. In a noisy and often polemical world, it was refreshing, humbling and deeply relevant to see the quiet resilience and dignity of this family in the face of the erasure of their culture and traditions. This is filmmaking which never gets in the way of itself and will surely take its place in the annals of observational greats.” A special mention in the doc competition was awarded to Queer Edward II from director Theo Rollason , who recently discussed their archival look behind the scenes of Derek Jarman’s Edward II film set, against the backdrop of anti-LGBTQIA+ legislation in 1980s Britain, with THR . “This was a spirited and tightly constructed portrait of Jarman as both an artist and an activist,” the jury noted. “Along with the luscious making-of footage, the integration of wider political archive was skilfully and heart-fully done, making it a fitting and timely tribute to Jarman in its defiant call for tolerance and against prejudice.” Meanwhile, 9 Temples to Heaven , directed by Sompot Chidgasornpongse, won the Sutherland Award in the first feature competition. In the road movie, which is Thailand’s international Oscar feature film submission, a prophecy prompts an aging grandmother to embark on a nine-temple pilgrimage with her children and grandchildren. “An accomplished first feature paving his own path in the well-established tradition of filmmaking in the Southeast Asian region,” said the jury about the winning project. “The film is visually outstanding, spiritual, and meditative, where a story about life and death transcends borders and generations.” ‘9 Temples to Heaven’ Cannes A special mention in the first feature program went to Bertil Nilsson’s MASC , following Robin as he moves through temporary jobs and tentative relationships in search of a place to belong. The jury called the filmmaker “a strikingly original new voice in British cinema, using innovative storytelling, notable performances, and artistically crafted scenes. We were impressed by Bertil’s highly unique concept coupled with capable new talent and a humorous script.” Finally, Aman , from director Rahul Roye, received the Short Film Award in the LFF short film competition. It follows a trans man whose journey takes an unexpected turn on the eve of his gender-affirming surgery, when he discovers that he is pregnant. “We were deeply impressed by Aman ’s accomplished filmmaking, tackling knotty themes through authentic and nuanced characters we felt compelled to follow,” shared the LFF jury. “We were struck by the film’s painterly cinematography and expansive and assured storytelling, which guided us through the world with care. Aman ’s finely drawn narrative is made all the more engrossing by the film’s refusal to provide easy answers to the complexities it presents us with.” ‘Aman’ Elizabeth Hobbs’ Daughters of the Late Colonel received the short film special mention. The film sees two middle-aged sisters finding themselves at a loss after the death of their ill-tempered and controlling father. Said the Short Film Competition jury: “We would like to give a special mention to Daughters of the Late Colonel for its singular and inventive visual style, and its deft balance of humor, pathos and provocation.” Voting for the LFF Audience Awards closes on Wednesday. THR

articles.title: James McAvoy Says ‘Split’ Is The Only Film That ‘Really Consistently Pays Me’
articles.full_text: Oct 17, 2026 4:21pm PT James McAvoy Says ‘Split’ Is The Only Film That ‘Really Consistently Pays Me’ By Payton Turkeltaub Plus Icon Payton Turkeltaub Latest Quentin Tarantino Confirms He’s ‘Written a Script’ for His Tenth Film, But Won’t Pursue It Yet Because He Wants to ‘Live a Little’ 13 hours ago James McAvoy Says ‘Split’ Is The Only Film That ‘Really Consistently Pays Me’ 14 hours ago ‘Musk’ TikTok Ad Account Permanently Suspended Ahead of Documentary’s Wide Release 19 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source ©Universal/courtesy Everett / Everett Collection James McAvoy has starred in films including “Speak No Evil,” “Atonement” and “X-Men: First Class,” but he recently revealed the “only” film he still consistently receives residuals from is M. Night Shyamalan’s 2016 horror “ Split .” “You get the odd check for, you know, a couple 100 quid here or sometimes you get checks for, like, 25 cents and you’re like, ‘It literally costs more to post this than it did for me to cash it,’” McAvoy said during a recent episode of the Happy Sad Confused podcast. “But the only one that really consistently pays me is ‘Split.’” “I think it was made for like $6 million or something like that? And let’s say they spent 30 advertising it. In our first weekend, we made 40, so we were in profit,” McAvoy continued. “Our first residual check came at the end of the first weekend. It was bonkers.” Popular on Variety In “Split,” three girls are kidnapped by a man with a diagnosed 23 distinct personalities (McAvoy). “They must try to escape before the apparent emergence of a frightful new 24th,” per the film’s official description. Anya Taylor-Joy, Haley Lu Richardson and Jessica Sula starred alongside McAvoy. The film, which cost just $6 million to make, went on to gross $138.29 million domestically and $140.16 million internationally for a $278.45 million worldwide total. McAvoy also spoke about Shyamalan and his experience working with the director. “I very consciously took from many of the directors that I worked with, and subconsciously as well, but the thing I took away from him is his preparedness,” McAvoy said. “He made that film, and [sequel] ‘Glass,’ on incredibly modest budgets, and very focused on how he would maximize his day and maximize his shots and maximize what he got out of the story by just being incredibly well-prepared and being able to share that and communicate that with the crew.” ‘Beast in Me’ Renewed for Season 2 With Claire Danes Returning Produced by J.A. articles.title: Quentin Tarantino Confirms He’s ‘Written a Script’ for His Tenth Film, But Won’t Pursue It Yet Because He Wants to ‘Live a Little’
articles.full_text: Oct 17, 2026 4:59pm PT Quentin Tarantino Confirms He’s ‘Written a Script’ for His Tenth Film, But Won’t Pursue It Yet Because He Wants to ‘Live a Little’ By Payton Turkeltaub Plus Icon Payton Turkeltaub Latest Quentin Tarantino Confirms He’s ‘Written a Script’ for His Tenth Film, But Won’t Pursue It Yet Because He Wants to ‘Live a Little’ 13 hours ago James McAvoy Says ‘Split’ Is The Only Film That ‘Really Consistently Pays Me’ 14 hours ago ‘Musk’ TikTok Ad Account Permanently Suspended Ahead of Documentary’s Wide Release 18 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images Quentin Tarantino has long said he’ll be retiring after his tenth feature film, but fans shouldn’t worry yet. While the “Pulp Fiction” director confirmed he’d finished penning the script for his final project, he won’t be getting much further with it until his newly opened play, “The Popinjay Cavalier,” closes. Tarantino made the statement on a recent episode of “The Graham Norton Show,” where he joined the host alongside fellow guests Ellen DeGeneres, Colin Farrell and Gemma Chan. It was his first appearance on the show in more than a decade. “I’ve written a script that I really like, but I want to do the play and see who I am; then I’ll then go back and spend time with my family and live a little and then see what I want to do,” Tarantino said. Popular on Variety He also gave audiences more insight into “The Popinjay Cavalier,” which he said started as a screenplay before the director realized “it really worked as a play.” “I think it will be thrilling,” he said. Starring Sacha Baron Cohen, “The Popinjay Cavalier” will open at London’s Phoenix Theatre next March, following previews in late Feb. The play, described as a “swashbuckling comedy,” is set to run for three months, closing on June 13. “I’m keen with anticipation to give the West End a great night out,” Tarantino said in a statement when the show was announced. Tarantino’s most recent release remains “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which came out in 2019 and starred Brad Pitt, Leonardo DiCaprio, Margot Robbie, Margaret Qualley and more. Pitt won the Oscar for best supporting actor that year, as did Barbara Ling and Nancy Haigh for best production design. Tarantino was also nominated for best picture and best director, while DiCaprio was nominated for best actor. ‘A Different World’ Renewed for Season 2 at Netflix How AI Is Used by Netflix at Its VFX Eyeline Studios, Revealed by VP Mohsen Mousavi at View Conference Madrid’s Iberseries & Platino Industria Pivots Toward More B2B Activities Where the Hot Button Issues of AI and Microdramas Also Take Center Stage Netflix TV Layoffs Include Director of Original Series Carolina Garcia, Who Exits After 10 Years ‘East of Eden’ Hits 6.5 Million Views in Four Days on Netflix Netflix Film VP Doug Belgrad Is Out Amid Layoffs Loading comments...

articles.full_text: Gilbert Flores / Michael Buckner The red carpet at the Academy Museum Gala is now open. Once again, the event is proving to be one of Hollywood’s most glamorous A-list nights of the year. Among those expected to walk the carpet are Taylor Swift, Connor Storrie, Jessica Biel and Justin Timberlake, Kim Kardashian, Jacob Elordi, Kendall Jenner, Eva Longoria, Salma Hayek, Inde Navarrette, Nia Long, McKenna Grace, Rosé, Sabrina Carpenter, Drew Starkey, Janelle Monáe, Pamela Anderson, Charles Melton, Alexander Skarsgård, Tom Ford and many others. articles.title: Ryan Gosling’s Zero-G Stunts on ‘Project Hail Mary’ Broken Down by the Space Epic’s VFX Supervisors
articles.full_text: Oct 18, 2026 12:28am PT Ryan Gosling’s Zero-G Stunts on ‘Project Hail Mary’ Broken Down by the Space Epic’s VFX Supervisors Oscar-winning supervisor Paul Lambert and co-supervisor Mag Sarnowska also talked at Turin’s View Conference about how ESA star maps, Greig Fraser’s cinematography and puppetry shaped the Ryan Gosling space epic By Davide Abbatescianni Plus Icon Davide Abbatescianni Latest ‘The Angry Birds Movie 3’ Unpacked by VFX Supervisor, Including Red’s Redesign and Character-Effects Automation: ’He’s Similar by Choice’ 23 hours ago ‘Toy Story 5’ Co-Director Kenna Harris on Going From Jessie Superfan to Pixar Filmmaker — and the Two-Week Rewrite That Reshaped the Sequel 2 days ago ‘The Mandalorian and Grogu’ VFX Veteran Hal Hickel on Rotta’s Redesign, Phil Tippett and Jon Favreau’s ‘Less James Bond, More Jackass’ Approach 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ryan Goslng's zero-G stunts in 'Project Hail Mary' explained at View Conference, Oct. 16, 2026 Courtesy of View Conference For Oscar-winning VFX supervisor Paul Lambert Lambert, of all the huge challenges presented by Ryan Gosling space epic “ Project Hail Mary ,” the most daunting was creating convincing zero gravity. “Zero-G was probably my personal biggest concern going into the movie,” he said at View Conference in Turin, Italy, drilling down on its VFX. “We tried very hard to convince the production to use the vomit comet,” he added, referring to aircraft maneuvers that briefly generate weightlessness. But the spacecraft sets were too elaborate to recreate onboard, so Gosling performed on wire rigs, including a rotating harness. Removing the wires was only the beginning. When a suspended body still appeared to be hanging rather than floating, VFX artists adjusted the position of Gosling’s legs, arms or torso and added drifting objects to reinforce the illusion. Lambert said the actor was committed to performing his own stunt work, including demanding spacewalk material. Popular on Variety Other experiments were deliberately hands-on. Fraser used an infrared-modified camera, programmable IR lights and water running in front of the lens to develop some of the film’s stranger imagery. “It was literally a mad science lab,” Lambert recalled. Burning fireballs, liquids, lasers and ferrofluid were also filmed to provide starting points for the microscopic effects. The DP returned during postproduction to work with ILM’s Helios virtual-camera system on the sequence near Adrian. Artists tracked Gosling’s on-set performance and recreated it within digital environments, allowing Fraser to choose new camera positions without discarding the original acting. Across those techniques, the supervisors’ ambition remained consistent: to make even the most elaborate effects obey a recognizable physical logic while ensuring Rocky felt as present beside Gosling as any human scene partner. The visual effects team behind “Project Hail Mary” started its journey through space, however, by making an unexpected discovery: much of the sky would look surprisingly familiar. Rather than fill Ryan Gosling’s interstellar adventure with colorful nebulae, Lambert and co-supervisor Mag Sarnowska used astronomical data, practical puppetry and carefully controlled cinematography to keep its science-fiction imagery grounded in reality. “We had visions of all these beautiful nebulae, but in the end, the skies were pretty much as we see them today, from Earth,” Lambert told View Conference in Turin on Friday, describing research conducted for directors Phil Lord and Christopher Miller ’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s novel. The team drew on data from the European Space Agency’s Gaia mission to map the stars between Earth and Tau Ceti, some 11.9 light-years away, while studying NASA footage and raw images from the International Space Station to establish how cameras behave in orbit. Exposure became a guiding principle. “If you were to take a movie camera up to space and try to shoot something, you wouldn’t see the stars,” Lambert explained. Near the brightly illuminated planet Adrian, background stars were therefore largely absent. Farther from Tau Ceti, where the light was weaker, a hypothetical high-sensitivity camera could reveal them. “Rather than simply choosing when to show stars with dramatic effects, we wanted their visibility to follow the actual lighting and exposure conditions,” Lambert said. DP Greig Fraser extended that philosophy into the film’s texture. Digitally captured footage was printed onto Kodak film and scanned back: 5254, with silver retention, for a relatively smooth, subdued Earth, and grainier 5203 for space. Two months of virtual-production exploration before filming also allowed Fraser and the directors to test lighting, camera movements and the scale of spacecraft interiors. Rather than dictate final shots, those sessions let the filmmakers experiment with digital environments and camera positions early, with the resulting camera data helping guide the physical shoot and subsequent VFX work. Rocky, the alien companion performed by James Ortiz and a team of puppeteers, posed a different problem: making a physically present character indistinguishable from his digital counterpart. Sarnowska described three practical versions, including an animatronic and a smaller reference puppet. Framestore scanned the physical creation and studied hours of performance footage, reproducing the puppeteers’ movement when the cramped spaceship sets made practical operation impossible. “Our full CG Rocky got really good at mimicking the puppeteers,” Sarnowska said. “In the end, half of the Rocky shots were puppet and the other half CG.” She added that the team sometimes struggled to distinguish the versions during internal reviews. The effects crew also rebuilt Rocky’s transparent xenonite barriers digitally to remove reflections, hide operators and maintain the complicated play of light through the set. For Rocky’s sonar-based point of view, the filmmakers also experimented with printing the images onto different film formats, ultimately using 10mm and 16mm for selected shots to give them a more organic texture, to bring a larger credibility to a moving tale of interstellar friendship which proved one of this year’s box office hits. articles.title: Roger Deakins on Instinct, Experience and Not Knowing What Is a Cinematographer: ‘I Still Can’t Answer That’
articles.full_text: Oct 18, 2026 1:38am PT Roger Deakins on Instinct, Experience and Not Knowing What Is a Cinematographer: ‘I Still Can’t Answer That’ By Callum McLennan Plus Icon Callum McLennan Latest Roger Deakins on Instinct, Experience and Not Knowing What Is a Cinematographer: ‘I Still Can’t Answer That’ 4 hours ago A Cyclops on Strings and Samantha Morton Reshaping Faces by Hand: How Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ Made Its Monsters Real 5 days ago Sony Pictures Imageworks’ Michelle Grady and ILM’s Janet Lewin on Bad Bosses and Changing Studio Culture: ‘Culture Is What You Tolerate’ 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Roger Deakins Courtesy of Lionsgate Walking through Turin with his wife and creative partner James Ellis Deakins, Roger Deakins found himself thinking about Giorgio de Chirico. The Italian painter, one of his favorites, had drawn inspiration from the city’s vast squares, long arcades and unusual arrangements of light and shadow. Deakins was noticing the relationship for himself. It’s characteristic of a man who has spent much of his life looking at the world, yet remains somewhat at a loss to explain precisely how he sees it. “Somebody asked the other day, what is a cinematographer? I mean, I still can’t answer that,” he says. Popular on Variety It’s an uncommon admission from someone whose images have helped define contemporary cinema, from “No Country for Old Men” to “Blade Runner 2049” and “1917.” But for Deakins, the work is too dependent on the circumstances of a story, and the people telling it, to be reduced to any one method. “It’s your emotional reaction to things that’s important,” he says. Technical considerations can be discussed, but the decisions that shape an image ultimately arise from something inexplicable. Perhaps his relationship with looking began as something more personal. As a young man, Deakins, born in the southern English resort of Torquay, discovered that the camera offered a kind of confidence, a way of approaching a world in which he hadn’t always felt comfortable. “I was kind of hiding behind the camera to a certain degree,” he recalls. “I had confidence because there was something between me and reality.” He could scarcely have imagined where that camera would take him. Only in retrospect has he come to appreciate the significance of experiences whose importance wasn’t apparent at the time. “If you don’t experience things, then what have you got to contribute?” It’s a conviction he shares with Ellis Deakins, his wife and essential collaborator on every project since they met on Michael Apted’s “Thunderheart.” For her, experience gives a filmmaker more than a collection of visual references. It provides different ways of understanding the people and specifics of a story. “If you’re going to tell a story, having had many different experiences gives you many different points of view,” she says. “You’re able to actually add more to the story.” Deakins worries that cinema can become too inward-looking, with filmmakers drawing inspiration primarily from other films. “I rarely, if ever, do that,” he says of referencing earlier movies. “You bring all the things that you experienced in your life to something.” Their Team Deakins podcast often explores the myriad routes people have taken into filmmaking. There is no repeatable path, just as there is no formula for a good image. James encourages the aspiring to experiment, examine their photographs and footage, and ask themselves why something works or doesn’t. It’s how they develop an eye, or what Roger calls a personal sensibility. Deakins, however, is less inclined to analyze his own. When asked about the relationship of shapes and forms in his still photography, he struggles to explain what draws him to a composition. He tends to see the whole image, he says, rather than its individual elements. Ellis Deakins is more definite. Looking at his photographs, she notices how shapes intersect and contrast. “You may not be aware of it, but you are interconnecting shapes,” she tells him. “But I know it’s instinctual.” The distinction between conscious intention and instinct becomes more intriguing when we discuss Andrew Dominik ’s “The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford.” Much of the film contrasts light and dark, yet the scene depicting Robert Ford’s murder takes place in a bar housed in a tent, surrounded by snow, its interior swathed in flat, even light. The violence, and Casey Affleck’s Robert Ford, seem jarringly exposed. Was the contrast deliberate? Deakins considers the question. The appearance arose partly from the circumstances of the set: the tent, the snow outside, the whiteness of the surroundings. Whether the scene had been staged there for its visual effect or because of its historical circumstances, he cannot entirely say. But there were choices to be made. They could have introduced stronger shadows, allowing the light to fall on only part of the tent. Instead, they chose to preserve the evenness of the illumination. “I think it was a very conscious decision to have almost a sort of documentary feel about it, as opposed to the rest of the film.” He thinks the scene is stronger for it. How much is planned varies from one director to the next. With Sam Mendes on “Jarhead,” he worked largely handheld, responding to actors as they performed. With Joel and Ethan Coen, the process was often meticulously planned. Different ways, he suggests, of reaching the same place. The common concern is what matters in the scene, and where the audience should be as that part of the story unfolds. For James, that requires entering someone else’s imagination. She recalls her early work as a script supervisor, when understanding what a director wanted meant learning to see through another person’s eyes. It is a reminder that, however personal Deakins’ instincts may be, the images are not made in isolation. His way of seeing must always attempt to meet the director’s vision, the actors’ performances and the needs of the film. Harrison Ford once described what it feels like to work with Deakins. Discussing “Blade Runner 2049” alongside Ryan Gosling, Ford observed that Deakins’ approach to lighting proceeds from the story, leaving an actor feeling supported. It’s a quality Deakins himself describes as the product of collaboration. He particularly misses the intimacy of operating a camera with a director standing beside him, rather than watching from a monitor elsewhere. After a take, the director might turn and ask, “How was that for you?” “Then there was that sense of trust,” he remembers. He misses, he says, that “intense collaboration and trust.” He and Ellis Deakins are careful to distinguish digital technology from the working habits it can encourage. They have always embraced whatever technology best serves the storytelling, and have a long and fruitful history of shooting digitally. But Roger remembers the particular discipline of working on low-budget film productions, when stock and time were precious and rolling the camera was consequential. “You kind of had to figure out what was the essence of the scene and what was the shot that was going to give you that.” Finding the essence of a scene does not always mean moving closer or showing more. Ellis Deakins points out that holding back from an actor can itself create a feeling, leaving the audience uneasy because they want a closer view. Deakins recalls admiring Andrei Tarkovsky’s long takes. “They would hold shots, and the shot would become something else. It would be saying something else.” He finds another kind of patience in his still photography, where a single image can hold the viewer’s attention indefinitely. And he has spent a lifetime fishing. A couple of days before our conversation, he had been out in his boat off the Devon coast catching mackerel. Enough for supper, anyway. “You never know what might happen,” he says, “and you’ve got to sort of change your approach constantly to adapt to the sort of tide and the weather and the way the fish are running.” He acknowledges the parallels with filmmaking, without wanting to make too much of them. Both involve waiting, observation and a willingness to respond to the world as it is rather than impose a fixed plan. At View Conference in Turin, I later spot the partners attending a number of technical talks themselves. For all their insistence that filmmaking depends on instinct and experience rather than formulas, they remain curious about what others are making and discovering. There is something fitting about seeing Deakins, whose work is so often studied and dissected by others, sitting among the audience, still looking and listening. During our conversation, he had recalled a remark by the photographer Raymond Depardon: if he knew how to take a good photograph, every photograph he took would be good. I had also mentioned “Moby-Dick,” the novel Deakins chose to take to the island on a recent episode of “Desert Island Discs.” Did he identify more with Ishmael, the observer, or Captain Ahab, the obsessive pursuer? “I’m definitely Ahab,” he replied. “Isn’t Ahab the captain?” Ellis Deakins asked. “Yeah, he goes down with a whale.” “A crazy captain,” she said. “Searching for something he doesn’t really understand, fighting something he doesn’t really understand,” Deakins replied. “I’ve always felt an affinity with Ahab for sure.” Netflix Says 67% of Surveyed Members Want to Visit Korea as Busan’s Creative Asia Puts Locations in Focus What’s New on Netflix in October 2026 ‘Bridgerton’ Spinoff, Centered on Lady Violet, Ordered by Netflix Netflix Lays Off 6% of Employees, Eliminating About 1,000 Jobs in Biggest Cutbacks to Date Madrid’s Iberseries & Platino Industria Pivots Toward More B2B Activities Where the Hot Button Issues of AI and Microdramas Also Take Center Stage Netflix Film VP Doug Belgrad Is Out Amid Layoffs Loading comments...

articles.title: James Austin Johnson’s Trump Stops by ‘SNL U.K.’ for Meeting With Burnham and Zelenskyy: ‘You Don’t Have One Guy Who Can Play Trump?’
articles.full_text: Oct 18, 2026 2:23am PT James Austin Johnson’s Trump Stops by ‘SNL U.K.’ for Meeting With Burnham and Zelenskyy: ‘You Don’t Have One Guy Who Can Play Trump?’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest ‘SNL U.K.’ Weekend Update Takes Jab at Shane Gillis: ‘You Stupid F—ing C—’ 4 hours ago ‘I Play Rocky’ Surprise Screens at London Film Festival 2 days ago Russell Brand Trial: Second Woman Alleges He Was a ‘Wild-Eyed Maniac’ as He Tried to Pull Her Into Bathroom 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Screenshot courtesy Sky/SNL UK Donald Trump made his first appearance on “ SNL U.K.,” courtesy of “SNL” cast member James Austin Johnson . Saturday night’s cold open recreated U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham (George Fouracres) meeting with Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy (Freddie Meredith) to reaffirm Britain’s support in their war with Russia. “We need America to restore the Starlink internet. Without it, we are vulnerable to drone strikes,” Meredith’s Zelenskyy said. “Also, it is very difficult to stream ‘Celebrity Traitors.’ I’m very behind, no spoilers, but I think Richard E. Grant is going to go all the way.” Replied Fouracres as Burnham, “Well, I can promise you now that I’ll raise all of this with President Trump at the first opportunity.” Popular on Variety Johnson then appeared with his spot-on Trump impression, marking the first crossover between the “SNL U.K.” and “SNL” casts. “Did somebody say Richard E. Grant?” he said. “President Trump?!” Fouracres’ Burnham exclaimed. “That’s right, you say my name and I appear,” Johnson’s Trump sad. “I got the idea from my very close friend Beetlejuice, the late, great Beetlejuice. It’s one of the two ways I am like him, the other is sex pest — alleged, they can’t prove he did that stuff.” When asked why he’s in the U.K., Johnson as Trump said he’s been in town “to see my favorite comedian” who is “performing live at high court in the role of defendant,” referencing the Russell Brand trial. Johnson’s Trump then explained that he is hoping to do a job swap with Burnham. “I take over the U.K., you take over America,” he said. “I tell ya, that place is a real mess, you’re going to hate it. It’s an awful, awful job. It’s a terrible place full of disgusting people, I don’t know what the hell happened. C’mon, job swap with me!” Fouracres as Burnham replied, “I can’t swap jobs with you now, cocker! I’ve barely gotten started. People don’t even hate me yet!” Johnson’s Trump then went on a rant about things he could fix in Britain, including that M&S have too many variations of Percy Pigs. “And how about British comedy, folks? What a bad situation, it’s not doing well,” he continued. “‘SNL U.K.,’ you’re telling me you don’t have a guy — the whole cast, you don’t have one guy who can play Trump? What an awful situation. Some of these people went to RADA! What is that, the Royal Academy of Dogshit Actors? Ooh, you can say shit on this one! That felt really good.” Johnson as Trump finally gave up on the job swap, saying: “Fine, I’ll go home. And Zelenskyy, let me know if you need anything, anything at all. Provided it’s not help with war.” Added Fouracres as Burnham, “Sorry Zelenskyy, me old mocker. But as dire as things might be, what matters most is that we all be nice to this insane man.” Watch the full sketch below. articles.title: Sergei Loznitsa’s ‘Imperium’ Wins Best Film at BFI London Film Festival
articles.full_text: Oct 18, 2026 6:00am PT Sergei Loznitsa’s ‘Imperium’ Wins Best Film at BFI London Film Festival ‘9 Temples to Heaven,’ ‘Concrete Land’ and ‘Aman’ also take top prizes as the festival wraps its 70th edition. By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Mahershala Ali Cries Recalling ‘Moonlight’ Scene, Keeps Quiet on ‘Spider-Verse’ at London Talk: ‘I’ve Got to Be Careful’ 23 hours ago ‘Renoir’ Producers Join Asia-Europe Co-Production Panel at Tokyo Market as Japanese Accelerator Atmovie Global Track Partners With Ties That Bind 1 day ago Indonesian Zombie Franchise ‘Zona Merah: Dead City’ Unveils Teaser, Takes Outbreak Into the City 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim Sergei Loznitsa’s “Imperium,” which revisits the Soviet Union of the early 1970s through footage shot by Italian cameramen, has won the best film award at the 70th BFI London Film Festival competition. The prizes were unveiled Sunday as the festival drew to a close. The competition jury was led by filmmaker Sam Pollard, whose credits include “MLK/FBI” and “Citizen Ashe,” and also featured “Life of Jorge Luis Borges” filmmaker Mariano Llinás and DDA chief strategy officer Julie La Bassiere. “The film is richly evocative and emotionally engaging on all levels giving us a visually arresting perspective of life before the Soviet Union was broken apart,” the jury said. Popular on Variety In the first feature competition, the Sutherland Award went to Thailand’s Oscar submission “9 Temples to Heaven,” the first fiction feature from Sompot Chidgasornpongse. The film reflects on faith, kinship and the passage from life to death. Actor Amir El-Masry (“Giant,” “Limbo”) presided over that jury, joined by “Moonglow” producer Alemberg Ang and sales, distribution and awards strategist Rosa Bosch. “An accomplished first feature paving his own path in the well-established tradition of filmmaking in the Southeast Asian region,” the jury said. Bertil Nilsson’s “Masc” received a special mention in the same section. The debut tracks Robin, who drifts between short-term jobs and uncertain relationships while looking for somewhere he fits. The jury singled out Nilsson as a fresh British talent with an unusual concept and a funny script. The Grierson Award for documentary went to Asmahan Bkerat’s feature directorial debut “Concrete Land,” which spends time with several generations of a mixed-race family in Jordan as they resist displacement and hostility. “Santosh” director Sandhya Suri headed the documentary jury, alongside Melbourne International Film Festival senior programmer Kate Fitzpatrick and BAFTA and Emmy-winning producer Andee Ryder. “In a noisy and often polemical world it was refreshing, humbling and deeply relevant to see the quiet resilience and dignity of this family in the face of the erasure of their culture and traditions,” the jury said. Theo Rollason’s “Queer Edward II,” assembled entirely from archive material, earned a special mention. It goes behind the scenes of Derek Jarman’s “Edward II,” set against the anti-LGBTQIA+ laws Britain passed in the 1980s, and the jury praised it as a portrait of Jarman the artist and Jarman the activist. Rahul Roye’s “Aman” won the Short Film Award. The film centers on a trans man who learns he is pregnant the night before his gender-affirming surgery, upending his sense of who he is as a man and as a father. It is streaming free on BFI Player until Oct. 25. Writer-producer Helen Simmons (“100 Nights of Hero”) led the shorts jury, which also included comedian Leo Reich and script editor Jack Casey. “We were struck by the film’s painterly cinematography, and expansive and assured storytelling, which guided us through the world with care,” the jury said. Elizabeth Hobbs’ “Daughters of the Late Colonel,” about two middle-aged sisters left adrift after the death of their domineering father, took a special mention for its inventive visual style. Audience voting for the festival’s best feature film and best British discovery prizes closes Oct. 21, with winners to be named later. Last year, Chloé Zhao’s “Hamnet” took the audience prize for best feature, while Yemi Bamiro’s “Black Is Beautiful: The Kwame Brathwaite Story” won British discovery. ‘The Monster of Florence’ Director Stefano Sollima on ‘Completely Different’ Second Chapter of Netflix’s Hit Serial Killer Series: ‘A Very Complex Story to Tell’ (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Icebreaker’ Netflix Series Casts Daisy Jelley, Connor Simos in Lead Roles (EXCLUSIVE) Bela Bajaria on Netflix’s Epic TV Trek Into Local Language Production: ‘There’s No Roadmap for This’ Netflix Content Chief Bela Bajaria on Overseeing Global Storytelling: ‘My Super Power Is I Hire Really Great People and I Let Them Do Their Job’ ‘Under Siege,’ Netflix’s Second Most Ambitious Colombian Series – a ‘Huge Undertaking Even by Our Standards’ – Bows Nov. 6 John Steinbeck’s ‘East of Eden’ Returns to Top of Book Charts Following Netflix Adaptation’s Release Loading comments...

He was 97. Sparks most recently resided at an assisted living facility in Sparks, Nevada. His death was announced on Facebook by his friend James A. Brown. Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries Obituaries Bernie Orenstein Dies: Writer-Producer On ‘Sanford & Son,’ ‘That Girl,’ ‘Kate & Allie’ & More Was 95 Among the actor’s numerous TV roles was a favorite among Star Trek fans: Forest played the giant Greek god Apollo in the memorable 1967 episode “Who Mourns for Adonais?” Watch on Deadline Other notable TV roles include a former boyfriend of The Dick Van Dyke Show ‘s Laura Petrie (Mary Tyler Moore) who gets set up for a date with Rose Marie’s ever-single Sally Rogers (Laura doesn’t know he has become a priest. That same year – 1964 – Forest played a member of an alien biker gangs in The Twilight Zone episode “Black Leather Jackets.” Just a sampling of his many other TV credits in the 1950s, ’60s and ’70s includes appearances on episodes of Z orro, Have Gun – Will Travel, Maverick, Ben Casey, The Outer Limits, Gunsmoke, Gomer Pyle: USMC, I Spy, Mission: Impossible, Gilligan’s Island, Get Smart, The Rookies and Who’s The Boss. Forest also was a busy voice and dubbing actor, appearing in hundreds of animated films lending his skills to hundreds of The 1990s and 2000s saw Forest largely pivoting to voice work and dubbing for animated series and video games including entries in the Power Rangers and Dynasty Warriors franchises, World of Warcraft and various anime projects. Michael Forest as Apollo in 1967 Star Trek episode ‘Who Mourns for Adonais?’ On the big screen, Forest appeared in such drive-in notables as 1959’s Beast From Haunted Cave and Roger Corman’s The Saga of the Viking Women and Their Voyage to the Waters of the Great Sea Serpent (1958), Ski Troop Attack (1960) and sword-and-sandal adventure Atlas (1961). Decades later he played a pilot in the Tom Hanks 2000 film Cast Away, among other late career appearances. Over the years he appeared in the soaps As The World Turns, Days of Our Lives and The Young and the Restless. In 2013, Forest reprised his Apollo role for the fan-made web series Star Trek Continues . Born Gerald Michael Charlebois on April 17, 1929, in Harvey, North Dakota, Forest moved to Los Angeles in 1955 and met director Corman through an acting class, leading to their collaborations that began in the late 1950s. Forest was preceded in death by his wife, the actress Diana Hale, who passed away in 2022. The death was classified as natural. The cause of death was first reported by The New York Post and has been confirmed by other media outlets. Satterley, who over the years wrestled for AEW and WWE under various names including Pac, Bastard, Adrian Neville and Neville, died September 27, one day after he was featured (as Pac) at AEW’s All Out pay-per-view from Chicago. He had lost the AEW National Championship to Andrade El Idolo. Related Stories Obituaries Wrestler Benjamin Satterley Dies One Day After Match: AEW Star Known As “Pac” Was 40 News Michael Forest Dies: Actor In Roger Corman B-Movies, ‘Star Trek’s Apollo Was 97 His death was announced by AEW in a statement reading, “A native of Newcastle upon Tyne, England, Satterley began his wrestling career in 2004 and went on to perform for wrestling organizations all over the world, captivating fans with innovative high-flying moves and incredible in-ring ability. Pac signed with All Elite Wrestling in 2019 and held multiple AEW Championships and competed in some of the most memorable matches in AEW history. Our condolences go out to Satterley’s family, friends and fans.” Watch on Deadline Satterley was known as “The Man that Gravity Forgot” for his signature finishing move, a corkscrew shooting star press off a top rope. He won multiple championships throughout his career. Bronchial asthma, or simply asthma, is, according to the Cleveland Clinic, a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways that causes the breathing tubes in the lungs to swell, narrow, and produce extra mucus. articles.title: ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Suspends Val Chmerkovskiy For TikTok Referencing Will Smith Oscar Moment; Dancer Responds, “Instinct Was To Defend My Wife”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Miley Cyrus Tearfully Remembers Dolly Parton At Hollywood Bowl Concert, Performs ‘Jolene’ Harry Styles Pays Tribute To Liam Payne With New Song At Madison Square Garden Concert Pro Wrestler Benjamin Satterley Cause Of Death Determined View All October 17, 2026 12:30pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Val Chmerkovskiy and Jenna Dewan Greg Doherty/Getty Images for iHeartRadio UDPATED with Chmerkovskiy response: Val Chmerkovskiy is being suspended from Dancing with the Stars for a week after he posted a controversial TikTok message that seemed to reference Will Smith’s 2022 Oscar slap. In a statement released today, producer BBC Studios said, “The well-being of everyone who works on Dancing with the Stars is non-negotiable. Val’s social media post was inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show. As a result, he will not participate in next week’s show.” Chmerkovskiy sparked the controversy the day after the show’s first “Super Bowl Night,” during which judge Carrie Ann Inaba offered a withering critique of the performance of Chmerkovskiy’s wife, DWTS dance pro Jenna Johnson. Wrote Chmerkovskiy in the since-deleted post, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night.” Related Stories News 'Dancing With The Stars' Scores 9-Year Ratings High Among Adults 18-49 On Super Bowl Night News 'Dancing With The Stars' Recap: Super Bowl Night Sends Home A Fan Favorite In a response to the suspension, Chmerkovskiy issued a statement through his rep, acknowledging his “poor decision” and “bad judgment,” saying he hadn’t thought through his TikTok comment before posting. Watch on Deadline Chmerkovskiy’s statement reads: “Hi everyone. As you may have seen in the news, I won’t be in the ballroom this week. “In a moment where my instinct was to defend my wife, I made a poor decision to reference a meme to ‘keep my wife’s name’ out of the conversation, without stopping to think through what else that reference could imply, which was genuinely never my intention. Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was. “The last thing I want is to become a distraction from an important week or from the incredible work my dance partner Jenna Dewan is putting in. “Please send Carrie Ann, Jenna, and the whole DWTS family lots of love during Dedication Night. I’ll be watching and cheering everyone on!!” Chmerkovskiy’s scrutinized post came in response to Inaba’s on-air critique of a lift move made by Johnson, in which she read the definition of a lift and suggested Johnson should know better. The Fresh Prince comment referred, unintentionally or not, to the infamous 2022 Oscar-night moment when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock across the face after the latter made a joke about Smith’s wife Jada Pinkett Smith. Chmerkovskiy’s TikTok comment was widely interpreted to suggest, however jokingly, that he had considered taking action similar to Smith’s, though the dancer later said he hadn’t thought that far. In any case, the joke was apparently lost on Inaba, who on Thursday posted a since-deleted message on Instagram saying, “So this is what we are doing now?” Her post showed photos of Chmerkovskiy and Smith, and in the text of her message she thanked the New York Post and Entertainment Weekly “for bringing this to my attention.” After he posted the TikTok, Chmerkovskiy apologized, writing on Instagram, “I want to apologize from the bottom of my heart for my recent post. I have reached out to Carrie Ann to apologize directly and personally, and I also want to apologize publicly as I understand my words affect so many outside of our internal DWTS family. I should have never made the reference that I did and I deeply regret it. I recognize that I am in a fortunate position to have a platform and to be a role model to some, and I need to treat that with more care by actively pausing to think before I post to ensure what I am sharing aligns with who I am, and who I want to be for you all.” Chmerkovskiy’s celebrity partner Jenna Dewan is apparently aware of the pro’s temporary suspension and will dance with pro Alan Bersten next week in a performance dedicated to her mother. Bersten had been paired with Giada De Laurentiis this season; the duo were eliminated in Week 3. ‘Street Fighter’ Slays $31M; Elizabeth Holmes Doc Milestone $12M+ J.K. Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection/Michael Buckner/PMC More than 30 years later after she blew away Street Fighter fans as bazooka-toting Cammy, Kylie Minogue nearly returned for a cameo in the latest feature adaptation. The 2x Grammy-winning Australian pop icon’s friend and collaborator Orville Peck , who stars as Vega in the newly released Paramount video game movie, revealed that he “was trying to orchestrate” her return, but scheduling conflicts ultimately stood in the way. “They were trying to get Kylie to do a cameo in our Street Fighter,” he told Queerty . “They were having a hard time getting ahold of her or whatever, and I was like, ‘Guys, I can text her.’ So, I was trying to orchestrate this whole thing, and it didn’t work out with timing. But he’s not the first icon of music to do so: Back in 1994, his friend & collaborator Kylie Minogue starred in the original big-screen adaptation of the video game, and he says he texted her immediately when he got the part. And he’s got some tea, too: Apparently they tried to get Kylie to make a cameo in this Street Fighter! While Orville reveals she was “so down to do it,” timing just didn’t align, but he’s still hoping to orchestrate a photo op with his movie’s Cammy—actress Mel Jarnson—or maybe leave the door open for something in a potential sequel. Regardless, Kylie told Orville filming the ‘94 Street Fighter was “one of the most fun experiences of her life,” and it sounds like he felt the same this go-around, especially because he was emboldened to bring his full self to the project, leaning into queer energy to his portrayal of the masked character Vega. The Beatles alum said he was concerned that Paul Mescal looks “markedly shorter” compared to his co-stars, and he even reached out to Mendes about it, but doesn’t know how the director is “gonna deal with it” in the four-film cinematic event. “Yeah, and guess what? He’s smaller than the guy who’s playing John [Lennon],” explained McCartney on the Good Hang with Amy Poehler podcast. “Sam Mendes is making the film. I heard Sam Mendes is making the film.
