articles.title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Directing Duo Los Javis Reveal How Spanish Sensation Became “The Journey Of Our Lives”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Baz Bamigboye Baz Bamigboye Columnist/International Editor At Large @BazBam More Stories By Baz Sacha Baron Cohen Confirmed To Star In Quentin Tarantino’s ‘The Popinjay Cavalier’ West End Stage Play With Dates & On Sale Window Announced Breaking Baz: Why LFF Opener ‘Elsinore’ Is A Triumphant Epitaph For An Extraordinary Man Breaking Baz: Anthony Mackie Returning To Broadway To Play Macbeth After 16-Year Absence From The Stage View All October 16, 2026 3:15pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Penelope Cruz in ‘La Bola Negra’ Carla Oset/Netflix Penélope Cruz had been a muse to Los Javis — the moniker for Spanish filmmakers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo — for years before they met for lunch to persuade her to play a singer (more a force of nature, really) in La Bola Negra , an electrifying sensation at Cannes that’s now Spain’s entry for best international feature film Oscar . “I saw her in a clip of Jamón Jamón ,” says Ambrossi, referring to Bigas Luna’s 1992 picture, in which Cruz appeared for the first time opposite her now-husband Javier Bardem. “I was young, and I thought, ‘Who is she ?!’ ” Related Stories Reviews ‘La Bola Negra’ Review: Spain’s Javier Calvo And Javier Ambrossi Capture Hearts With Their Unashamedly Romantic Decades-Spanning Drama – Cannes Film Festival Festivals Penélope Cruz’s ‘La Bola Negra’ Lands 20-Minute Ovation From Overjoyed Audience At Cannes Calvo was similarly enchanted when he saw Cruz in Pedro Almodóvar’s 1999 Oscar winner All About My Mother . “She’s got that material of the stars,” he says. “When you put a camera in front of her, she can do anything, and she doesn’t even realize what she’s doing. There’s a power , there’s a force guiding her, and that’s amazing to see first-hand.” Watch on Deadline Los Javis wanted Cruz for a small but pivotal role in their epic tale La Bola Negra , the intertwined story of three gay men who exist in three different time periods in Spain. In 1932, Carlos (Milo Quifes) is a young man in Grenada at a time when Spain is lurching uncomfortably towards an ever-increasing spiteful intolerance of homosexuality. In 1937, against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War, Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) and Rafael ( Miguel Bernardeau ) are soldiers from opposing political divides brought closer by the conflict. And in 2017, Alberto (Carlos González) is a playwright from Madrid who engages with an eminent Federico Garcia Lorca scholar (played by another Hollywood star, Glenn Close , speaking fluent Spanish) in a storyline that links the characters in the prior timelines.

articles.title: How ‘Whalefall’s Director & Author Wove The Closure Of A Father-Son Relationship Into A Survival Tale
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi How ‘Whalefall’s Director & Author Wove The Closure Of A Father-Son Relationship Into A Survival Tale The Smashing Pumpkins Release Latest ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Album Track, ‘Black Stars’ Everything We Know About ‘The Housemaid’s Secret’ Film So Far View All October 16, 2026 4:20pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Director Brian Duffield and Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in 20th Century Studios' WHALEFALL Jennifer Clasen/20th Century Studios SPOILER ALERT: This story spoils the plot of the film Whalefall , now out in theaters, based on Daniel Kraus ‘ novel. A running joke Whalefall director Brian Duffield had going to summarize the film hailing from 20 th Century Studios and Imagine Entertainment and hitting theaters this week was that “men would rather get swallowed by a sperm whale than go to therapy.” Just as Austin Abrams ’ Jay Gardiner finds himself in quite the harrowing predicament trapped in a whale’s stomach after a tangle with a squid, the cast, crew and filmmakers of Whalefall also found themselves in the tricky situation of bringing the premise of Daniel Kraus’ novel to the big screen. Related Stories Reviews ‘Whalefall’ Review: Austin Abrams Wrestles With Grief, Toxic Masculinity & Grotesque Whale Innards In Emotionally Gutsy Body Horror News 20th Century’s ‘Whalefall’ Producers Reflect On Shooting In California: “The Best Creative Teams Are Here” To back up, Jay’s decision to seek out the remains of his dead father Mitt Gardiner ( Josh Brolin ), who has committed suicide by drowning in the Pacific Ocean following a diagnosis of mesothelioma, is what really landed him in this situation. Just as he has to get scrappy and use anything he can find to escape, those behind the making of the movie had to be in constant communication about what it would take to pull off such intense scenes, many of which took place inside a life-sized whale stomach built specifically for the film. Watch on Deadline “It takes a village to build a whale, and I think it takes a really great village to survive it. And that’s been really one of the most gratifying parts of [production],” Duffield said when Deadline visited the set of the movie at Radford Studios in L.A. in September, during an early tank scene where Abrams encountered the whale for the first time. “It’s such a new and unique challenge that I think we hired the right people, because it was a lot of us all banging our heads together trying to figure out how to shoot every day.” Multiple whale stomach models were built by Weta Workshop in New Zealand, with the head, throat, esophagus and larynx constructed in California because they were too big to ship to set on time. The 12-foot-tall, 18-foot-long whale head was manufactured by StudioArt & Technology. Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in 20th Century Studios’ ‘Whalefall’ 20th Century Studios “It’s such an interlocked set. I’ve never made a movie, and I can’t imagine ever making a movie where every single department really has to be talking to each other every step of the way,” Duffield said. “For the stomach, Ramsey [Avery] our production designer [had] to figure out how to build it, and then we [had] to figure out how to put cameras in it, but then also we had to figure out how to light it, and then the lights become bioluminescence. Visual effects supervisor Guillaume Rocheron, who worked on Jordan Peele’s Nope , rigged the LED lighting in the stomach to eventually render as the bioluminescence that then helps illuminate Jay’s environment. “Some colors do not show up the same color in LED lights. So, our costume designer had to build Austin’s costume around what the LEDs would show up with,” Duffield added. “So we would take neoprene samples to New Zealand, where we built the stomachs, to show them under the lights, against the whale skin, to see what colors show up.” Cameras and lenses were broken “nonstop” during filming; the crew ultimately constructed scenes around the one spot the camera could actually fit into the cramped space and worked backwards from that vantage point. If that weren’t claustrophobic enough, Abrams also faced the added challenge of emoting behind a facemask and the diving equipment Jay uses. “We redesigned the regulator to make it as small as possible, because regulators are not really meant to be worn outside of water. And yet, the air inside the whale stomach is toxic. It won’t kill him, necessarily, but it’s full of methane and things that make him a little high,” Duffield said. “So we redesigned the regulator to give him as much mouth shape as possible. He actually does talk throughout the movie to himself or to other characters in the stomach. That has been a challenging learning curve.” Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner 20th Century Studios These formidable aspects of the film’s creation echoe Kraus’ general approach to writing books; he now has 30-plus under his belt. “I like to create new problems and have to fight through the solutions — I try to start with an impossible [conceit] where I just throw hurdles in front of me of things that I don’t know,” Kraus told Deadline on set. “So I have to relearn how to write a book every time.” The impetus for Whalefall came from a viral video in which a kayaker ended up in the mouth of a whale. Once Kraus heard about the clip, it spawned discussions with friends about whether it could actually happen. He could not stop thinking about it. Following an email to author friend Mary Roach, author of Gulp: Adventures on the Alimentary Canal (2013), and correspondence with three whale experts she recommended, Kraus had found the “high concept” hook for the book, which hit shelves in 2023. “I didn’t want to do it if it couldn’t really happen — being swallowed by a whale has been treated like a fable and Biblical stories forever. My interest was, could you do it scientifically accurately?” Kraus said. “And by the end of the day, I was all systems go. All the whale experts were super-excited to help, and they think about whales all day, but never in this context. We were off to the races.” Both Duffield and Kraus drew connections to the science fiction genre in different ways, with Kraus developing an interest in whales during the frontloaded research process for the book, which took about three months. “I became more and more … obsessed, you might say, with whales,” he said. “There’s a lot of what I was doing with this biology of a whale, but I also unexpectedly started to get really enamored of whales as a being, as a force of nature. “Sperm whales are extraordinarily intelligent. They’re one of the most mysterious animals on the planet. Everything about them is strange. They really feel like aliens. Even in the deep ocean, which is filled with alien-like creatures, the whales almost feel like a master alien. They’re not aggressors. They’re very peaceful animals. Sperm whales have been witnessed helping humans many, many times, like divers in trouble.” Experiencing a whale from the inside out adds complicated layers to Whalefall ‘s story, even when it comes to the father-son relationship at its heart. “How do you fall in love with a character through its guts, basically? It’s definitely gross, but what are the ways that we can fall in love with this animal, because Austin is in such a unique situation, and I think there’s something interesting about his character, who is very fond of of animals and nature,” Duffield said. “One of the things that differentiates his character and Josh’s character is Josh is very hard and Austin’s very soft. But they both have this love of nature, and so giving Austin moments that he can really, for lack of a better way to put it, appreciate how cool the situation is — while also being scared sh*tless and thinking he’s going to die pretty much at any given moment — that was part of the craft of it, too.” Duffield evidently shared a similar awe. For him, the trick with the stomach being the setting for a majority of the movie was balancing the claustrophobic feeling of Jay’s plight with breaks from the cramped space. “It’s challenging for a couple reasons. One, it’s such a long stretch of the movie, and quite a lot happens while he’s in in the stomach, but it was also about keeping it fresh and interesting so [that] after 30 minutes, people weren’t just like, ‘Alright, I’m sick of this stomach,’” Duffield said. “[Jay] does have different little side adventures. He spends some time in the second stomach, which is very visually different, and then in the esophagus of the whale as well. Different animals that are also in the stomachs, and different problems he has to MacGyver his way out of, so it’s just trying to figure out how to keep it fresh visually, which Daniel honestly just did a lot of in the book.” Whalefall executive prodcuer Doug Merrifield, whose credits include the Free Willy films, joined Duffield, Kraus and Imagine Entertainment’s Allen Mandelbaum in emphasizing that the whale is not the villain in the movie. It’s orcas that attack Jay’s sperm whale that ultimately provide the antagonists and the catalyst for the film’s climax. “The whale is not a bad guy. The whale is just an animal that’s doing what it’s meant to be doing. The whale is not interested in [Jay]. It’s trying to get a squid, and Austin is in the way,” Duffield said. “The movie makes a very direct correlation, eventually, between Josh Brolin and and the whale, and part of Austin’s journey is making peace with his dad, who is dead at the start of the movie.” L-R: Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner and Josh Brolin as Mitt Gardiner 20th Century Studios One of the main threads of the book that drew Duffield to directing the adaptation was the father-son relationship at its core; his own son was 4 at the time of the set visit. In Whalefall , Mitt and Jay didn’t always know how best to communicate with each other; the ocean is where they find common ground. “The miracle of the book and hopefully of the movie is, when it ends, you primarily are talking about the relationships, and then the whale is third or fourth build, which for a movie that’s set almost entirely inside of a whale feels impossible, but somehow [Kraus] pulls it off,” Duffield said. “As you age up, you start viewing things from different perspectives. I think before I was a dad, I probably would have been firmly in Jay’s point of view, and then now being on the other side of it and having a son — granted, my son just turned 4, so it’s a very different than the relationship between [Jay] and [Mitt] — [I’m] really starting to feel for Brolin’s character, and understand him to some extent.” Kraus, who grew up in conservative small-town Iowa, leaned into the personal when it came to building the tension of Mitt and Jay’s relationship. His father was a hunter, not as extreme as Mitt, but still an inspiration for the character. “I’m a product of [where I grew up], which is to say, I have avoided getting therapy. I’m a product of that culture where you don’t express yourself and you don’t show your feelings when it comes to interpersonal things,” Kraus said. “Mitt is a very emotional guy when it comes to the ocean, like he will fight tooth and nail for every living creature in there. He’ll do whatever it takes to protect the ocean. But when it comes to dealing with his son, he’s absolutely clueless. He would be much better at interacting with a whale than he would be his son. And ultimately, Mitt becomes the whale, in a sense, and through the whale, they are able to have the conversation.” As Jay fights nitrogen narcosis — a condition in divers in which certain gases take on an anesthetic effect in the nervous system, resulting in a kind of high — and the methane in the whale’s stomach, he has flashbacks that help him piece together info he needs for his survival. The memories often involve his father imparting pearls of wisdom, regardless of whether Jay though of them that way at the time. “The challenge really was, the book has probably 50 flashbacks where it’s constantly hopping back and forth. In the movie, [we had] to take all that information that Jay needs to know scattered across all those flashbacks, and find ways to pack them into vastly fewer flashbacks,” Kraus said. “That was really the biggest challenge.” A small creative detail further merges Mitt and the whale, who speak as one character in Kraus’ book. “The whale’s heart is beating, and the stomach is reacting to the beats of the whale’s heart. So that’s sound puppeteering the stomach. There’s water in it, which is moving from that. And then, on top of all of that, just to show how full circle it starts to go, the whale’s heart is Josh Brolin’s heartbeat,” explained Duffield, who came up with the idea. “We’ve recorded Josh’s heartbeat, and then our sound guys made it a whale heartbeat that is playing.” L-R: Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner and Josh Brolin as Mitt Gardiner 20th Century Studios This detail also fits in with Kraus’ thematic vision. “When I came across the concept of a whalefall, which is when a whale dies and its corpse sinks to the bottom of the ocean, and its body, as it decomposes, sets off a shock wave of life, generations of life are born from its remains,” Kraus said. “ I found that very emotional and touching to the idea that when a whale dies, or somebody we know and love dies, that their death sort of begets life, the memory of them, the influence of them. It goes on, and it goes on for generations, and even when I talk about it now, I get goosebumps, it’s just such a beautiful thought.” Sometimes it takes getting stuck inside a whale to provide some perspective. ‘Street Fighter’ Socking Away $30M; A24’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc Eyes $12M J.K. articles.title: Diablo Cody Teases ‘Jennifer’s Body 2’ Explores A More “Sympathetic” Side Of Megan Fox’s Character
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn KJ Apa Asked ‘Riverdale’ Showrunner Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa For ‘Afterlife with Archie’ Cameo: “I Don’t Know Who I’d Play” Brad Caleb Kane Teases ‘It: Welcome to Derry’ Is “Bigger” In Season 2 With “A Different Kind Of Pennywise” Diablo Cody Teases ‘Jennifer’s Body 2’ Explores A More “Sympathetic” Side Of Megan Fox’s Character View All October 16, 2026 6:01pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Megan Fox in 'Jennifer's Body' (2009) Doane Gregory/Fox Atomic/Courtesy Everett Collection As Diablo Cody prepares to resurrect Megan Fox ‘s teen succubus one more time, she’s adding a more human element to the demonic role. While discussing the “imminent” sequel Jennifer’s Body 2 , the Oscar-winning writer explained that the followup will “explore even more about why Jennifer is sympathetic and what she’s been through” after she was sacrificed in a satanic ritual in the 2009 horror comedy, which turned her into the boy-eating entity. “Jennifer is a sympathetic character for me, before and after the transformation,” she explained on the Petticoat Revolution podcast. “I mean, she is very isolated, she’s very lonely, she’s very insecure. Everybody remembers Jennifer when she’s like, ‘I am a god,’ or when she’s at her most radiant and at her most powerful. But people forget about these moments in the movie where she’s like a shell of herself, she’s just exsanguinated almost. And to me, Megan played both of those sides of Jennifer so well.” Related Stories News ‘Jennifer’s Body’ Director Karyn Kusama Teases Diablo Cody’s “Fun & Crazy” Sequel, Recalls Pete Wentz’s Audition, Says Cult Status “Tickles Me” News Amanda Seyfried Teases ‘Jennifer’s Body’ Sequel: “I Didn’t Confirm It!” Cody continued, “And one fun thing—I can’t talk about it too much—but you know we’re doing a sequel to this movie, like imminently, and I felt like in the new movie, I was able to explore even more about why Jennifer is sympathetic and what she’s been through. And there is absolutely, to me, a loneliness and a poignancy to that character that people don’t always recognize.” Watch on Deadline Deadline previously confirmed that Cody is developing the sequel for 20th Century Studios, with the movie’s original director Karyn Kusama teasing that she’s “very excited to hear what comes” of the follow-up, for which Megan Fox and Amanda Seyfried have both expressed interest in returning. View this post on Instagram “I know some of the bones of it, so I’m not going to give anything away, but it sounds fun and crazy like the first film,” Kusama told Deadline last year. “And I have no doubt that Diablo will do something absolutely incredible with it.” In Jennifer’s Body , Needy (Seyfried) is BFFs with the titular mean girl played by Fox, whose body becomes possessed by a succubus with a taste for teen boys after a botched sacrifice by a devil-worshipping boy band (led by Adam Brody). ‘Street Fighter’ Socking Away $30M; A24’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc Eyes $12M J.K. articles.title: Brad Caleb Kane Teases ‘It: Welcome to Derry’ Is “Bigger” In Season 2 With “A Different Kind Of Pennywise”

The showrunner teased to Deadline that the killer clown (played by Bill Skarsgård) is depicted in a “way you’ve never seen that character before,” with the sophomore season being “bigger” than Season 1 of the HBO series. “We’re writing the scripts. We’re about halfway through the writing of the scripts,” said Kane. “We have a production schedule, we’re greenlit for a Season 2, and Andy Muschietti’s out there casting.” Related Stories Cancellations and Renewals ‘It: Welcome To Derry’ Renewed For Season 2 By HBO; Brad Caleb Kane Now Sole Showrunner News Brad Caleb Kane On Making ‘Crystal Lake’ A “Small-Town Show” In Same N.J. Locations Where ‘Friday The 13th’ Filmed, “Faithfully” Re-Creating An Iconic Scene & “Twin Peaks-y” Plans For Season 2 Set amid the Great Depression in 1935, Season 2 revolves around the bloody massacre of the Bradley Gang, a group of bank robbers who stop in Derry to buy ammo and end up facing unimaginable horror, another piece of morbid town history depicted in King’s 1986 novel. Watch on Deadline Kane added, “I don’t think it’s a big secret. I think it’s a little bit out there, but it’s 1935, it’s a Warner Bros. gangster movie. It’s bank robbers and Hoovervilles and street urchins riding the rails religious fundamentalism. And a different kind of Pennywise, Pennywise the way you’ve never seen that character before. So, it’s very exciting what we’re building, and it’s gonna be a big challenge because it’s a bigger season than Season 1, but we’ll see what happens.” As he flies solo to take the reins on Season 2 of 'It: Welcome to Derry', Brad Caleb Kane is ready to give fans a whole new version of Pennywise. articles.title: KJ Apa Asked ‘Riverdale’ Showrunner Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa For ‘Afterlife with Archie’ Cameo: “I Don’t Know Who I’d Play”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn KJ Apa Asked ‘Riverdale’ Showrunner Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa For ‘Afterlife with Archie’ Cameo: “I Don’t Know Who I’d Play” Brad Caleb Kane Teases ‘It: Welcome to Derry’ Is “Bigger” In Season 2 With “A Different Kind Of Pennywise” Diablo Cody Teases ‘Jennifer’s Body 2’ Explores A More “Sympathetic” Side Of Megan Fox’s Character View All October 16, 2026 7:50pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source KJ Apa as Archie in 'Riverdale' Dean Buscher/The CW Network/Courtesy Everett Collection As KJ Apa navigates life after Riverdale , he’s up for a return to the upcoming Afterlife with Archie series adaptation. Following his performance as Archie on the CW series for its seven-season run from 2017-’23, the actor expressed his excitement for series creator Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa , the Archie Comics chief creative officer who also co-wrote the Afterlife with Archie comics. “I spoke to Roberto, who was our showrunner for Riverdale , who’s also showrunning that show,” he told Entertainment Weekly . “And I’m really excited. I can’t wait to see who they cast as Archie and the gang.” Related Stories News ‘Afterlife With Archie’ Series Based On Comic Ordered By Disney+, Gets Halloween 2027 Premiere News ‘Afterlife With Archie’ Series Based On Comic In Works At Disney+ From Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa & Berlanti Prods. With Big Commitment Apa admitted it would “be cool if we could do some cameos or something,” noting, “I asked him!” Watch on Deadline “I would think that would be really fun if I could come in for a scene,” added Apa. “Maybe I’m not even [Archie], I don’t know who I’d play, but it’d be fun to do it.” View this post on Instagram Set for a Halloween 2027 premiere on Disney+ , Afterlife with Archie received a script-to-series order from the streamer last October, with Berlanti Productions ( Riverdale , The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina ) and Warner Bros. TV producing. articles.title: Ben Affleck Warns ‘Digger’ Box Office Bomb Will Lead to “A Bunch of Sh***y Homogenized Movies”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 15, 2026 5:18pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ben Affleck waves during the red carpet and fan event of the movie 'Animals' at Centro Comercial Mitikah. Toya Sarno Jordan/Getty Images Logo text Amid Digger ‘s box office bomb, Ben Affleck is warning that those who are celebrating the film’s poor performance could instead lead to “a bunch of shitty homogenized movies.” During an appearance on the Happy Sad Confused podcast this Monday, the Animals actor addressed the poor performance of Tom Cruise ‘s latest movie. He argued that criticizing a “big swing” movie could result in studios later opting to take a safer approach with future projects. “It’s a little bit like the high-school bullying thing, with people who hadn’t even seen movies. You see it happening now, frankly, with Digger . Everybody wants to celebrate this bomb as if it’s the most exciting thing to happen, and you think like, it’s a pretty ambitious, interesting movie made by interesting people that have talent,” Affleck said. Related Stories Movies Ben Affleck Calls Filming 'Justice League' a "Low Point" in His Career: "About as Gross as It Gets" Movies Theo James, Hoyeon, Christian Slater Thriller 'The Hole' Lands Summer 2027 Release From Orion (Exclusive) “Everybody wants to count the money, what it lost or whatever. To me, I just think, like, if you punish movies that take risks, guess what you’re going to get? A bunch of shitty, homogenized movies,” he explained. “You cannot do something interesting without taking a big swing, and that means you’re going to sometimes look bad.” In The Hollywood Reporter ‘s review of Digger , chief film critic David Rooney wrote, “ Digger is basically what happens when you put two outsize egos together with nobody holding the reins to keep their most self-indulgent impulses in check. Piloted by a spectacularly obnoxious Tom Cruise, who evidently spent hours in the makeup chair each day to look his age, Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s wannabe Dr. Strangelove is a heavy-handed cataclysm scenario built around the blunt point that any attempt to halt global warming this late in the game is pure political theater.” Digger opened with $8 million domestically, totaling $12 million internationally. The film’s box office performance has sparked many conversations and led to many celebrities speaking out in support of the movie directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu. Among those were Anne Hathaway , who topped Digger at the box office with Verity in their opening weekends, giving the film a perfect score. She wrote on Letterboxd, “I loved this brilliant movie. It’s smart and trippy and aggressive and funny and ambitious. It’s worth making the time see and decide for yourself what you make of it. For me? 10/10.” THR

articles.title: ‘Street Fighter’ Eyes Box Office Victory as Buzzy Elizabeth Holmes Doc Heads for Strong Launch
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All October 15, 2026 5:27pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Callina Liang in 'Street Fighter.' Paramount Pictures Logo text Street Fighter is hoping for a muscular opening weekend at the box office as it faces competition from a number of newcomers, including A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything . Paramount Pictures releases video game adaptation Street Fighter in more than 3,500 North American theaters on Friday, with the studio projecting a range of mid-$30 millions domestically and another sum of mid-$30 millions internationally. Director Kitao Sakurai’s feature carries an $82 million production budget that is split evenly between producers Legendary Pictures and Capcom . Paramount sees only upside for the film that marks the first release in its distribution deal with Legendary. Related Stories Movies Ben Affleck Warns 'Digger' Box Office Bomb Will Lead to "A Bunch of Sh***y Homogenized Movies" Movies Prepare to Fall in Love With 'Sense and Sensibility' Star Herbert Nordrum Critics have not been blown away, with Street Fighter holding a 43 percent approval rating from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , critic Frank Scheck called the film a “jumbled tonal mess” and “only sporadically entertaining.” Noah Centineo , Andrew Koji and Callina Liang star in the movie that centers on a combat tournament. Street Fighter marks the third feature in the franchise adapting the Capcom video game that launched in 1987. Austin Abrams in Whalefall . 20th Century Studios Also hitting theaters is Whalefall , with 20th Century Studios releasing director Brian Duffield’s survival thriller in 3,065 North American locations. The studio projects an opening between $10 million and $12 million for the $60 million-budgeted feature that adapts author Daniel Kraus’ 2023 novel. After leading last month’s Resident Evil , Austin Abrams stars as a scuba diver who, while searching for the remains of his late father (Josh Brolin), is swallowed by a sperm whale. Whalefall holds a 70 percent critics approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review , THR chief film critic David Rooney wrote that the movie is “just not batshit crazy enough to be much fun.” You Can See Everything A24 A24 has high hopes for You Can See Everything , the documentary following infamous Theranos founder Holmes in the lead-up to the start of her prison sentence. The studio releases the feature in around 800 North American theaters, with projections coming in around $7 million for the $5 million-budgeted doc from directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim . Earlier this year, Melania opened to $7 million from 1,700 domestic theaters, marking the highest-grossing non-music doc launch in over a decade. You Can See Everything boasts a superlative 100 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes. In her review for THR , critic Angie Han deems it “smart, funny and full of surprises.” Daisy Edgar-Jones in Sense and Sensibility . Courtesy of Focus Features Also making its debut this weekend is Focus Features’ Sense and Sensibilit y, which opens in 2,436 North American locations. Focus projects an $8 million domestic haul for filmmaker Georgia Oakley’s adaptation of Jane Austen’s classic work, with the movie carrying a budget in the mid-$20 millions. Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles star as the Dashwood sisters as they grapple with their father’s death. Ang Lee helmed 1995’s Oscar-winning version that starred Emma Thompson and remains well-regarded. The new Sense and Sensibility stands at 77 approval from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes. Rooney writes that the film “seldom steps out from the long shadow of Ang Lee’s enchanting 1995 retelling.” THR

articles.title: ‘DWTS’ Pro Val Chmerkovskiy Apologizes to Carrie Ann Inaba for “Careless” Will Smith Oscars Slap Reference: “I Will Do Better”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 15, 2026 6:18pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Val Chmerkovskiy and Carrie Ann Inaba. Ethan Miller/Getty Images, Disney/Eric McCandless Logo text Dancing With the Stars professional dancer Val Chmerkovskiy has apologized to Carrie Ann Inaba for his “careless” reference to Will Smith’s infamous Oscars slap in a since-deleted TikTok Story post. “I want to apologize from the bottom of my heart for my recent post,” the pro wrote on his Instagram Story Thursday. “I have reached out to Carrie Ann to apologize directly and personally, and I also want to apologize publicly as I understand my words affect so many outside of our internal DWTS family. I should have never made the reference that I did and I deeply regret it. I recognize that I am in a fortunate position to have a platform and to be a role model to some, and I need to treat that with more care by actively pausing to think before I post to ensure what I am sharing aligns with who I am, and who I want to be for you all.” Related Stories TV 'DWTS': Val Chmerkovskiy References Will Smith's Oscars Slap While Defending Wife Jenna Johnson Amid Carrie Ann Inaba Criticism TV Justin Baldoni Makes Rare Public Appearance on 'Dancing With the Stars' Following Blake Lively Legal Battle Chmerkovskiy concluded, “I am truly sorry to Carrie Ann, and everyone who I hurt with my careless post. I will do better moving forward.” The three-time DWTS winner had been defending his wife, fellow pro Jenna Johnson, online following criticism the judge shared for her samba performance with Harry Shum Jr. on Tuesday’s Super Bowl Night. Chmerkovskiy particularly received backlash for a TikTok Story he posted on Wednesday that read, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night,” a comment many took as a reference to Smith slapping Chris Rock at the 2022 Oscars. Inaba responded to his remarks earlier on Instagram Thursday, writing “So this is what we are doing now?” while resharing a screenshot of a Page Six post featuring the dancer’s “Fresh Prince” comment, alongside a split image of Smith and Chmerkovskiy. After Johnson and her celebrity partner Harry Shum Jr. performed a samba to Usher’s “Yeah!,” the judge told the mirrorball champion, “I think you need to put more content in your dances. Especially because [Harry’s] so good, I want to see you challenge yourself a little bit more in the vein of what we’re looking for. And there was a lift.” Johnson responded to Inaba’s comments by asking, “A lift?” Inaba brought out a piece of paper with the definition of lift, which she read during the live episode: “A lift is — I just need to say it — any movement during which one of the dancers has both feet off the floor at the same time with the assistance or support of their partner. Yeah, lift.” Chmerkovskiy’s Fresh Prince TikTok Story was posted on Wednesday and was live for at least six hours. One Reddit thread was flooded with theories that Chmerkovskiy’s post was “likely referring to when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock for making a comment about his wife,” adding that they took his comment as he allegedly “wanted to slap Carrie Ann for telling Jenna to step it up.” The story was subsequently deleted. Smith walked onto the Oscars stage while Rock was hosting in 2022 after he made a joke about his wife, Jada Pinkett Smith, starring in a G.I. Jane sequel. “Keep my wife’s name out of your fucking mouth!” Smith infamously yelled from the crowd after he returned to his seat following the slap. THR

articles.title: ‘SNL’ Star Michael Che Reacts to Shane Gillis’ Controversial Monologue: “That’s Comedy”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All October 15, 2026 6:27pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Che Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images Logo text Michael Che has been preparing for potential questions about Shane Gillis’ controversial monologue on Saturday Night Live last weekend, and the moment has arrived. “I gotta do more press this week to promote the special. Wonder what every fucking question’s gonna be about,” Che wrote on his Instagram earlier this week, regarding the press tour for his new Netflix stand-up special, Michael Che: Shot in Minnesota . “Thanks a lot Shane.” For context, after hosting the NBC sketch comedy program on Saturday, Gillis drew heat over his joke about women working out. Related Stories TV Druski Becomes First Online Creator to Host 'SNL' TV Former 'SNL' Star Ego Nwodim Reacts to Shane Gillis' Controversial Joke About Women “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now,” Gillis said to the live audience. “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts? Have you seen the shorts? They’re neon, like, artificial bait-colored? And the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look. You’re not allowed to look. For real, don’t look, because they are filming. I’m in the background of like 10 TikToks right now.” Despite being adamant about not being interested in weighing in on the discourse, Che, who anchors “Weekend Update” with Colin Jost on SNL , was asked on the Today show Thursday about the controversy. “That’s comedy,” he said. “It’s like, you think it’s funny and some people don’t.” He was later asked if he laughed at Gillis’ joke about women, to which Che replied, “I was at cue cards actually, thinking about what I was gonna say that was gonna make people upset. I didn’t even see it until the next day.” Che isn’t a stranger to controversial jokes, especially during his bi-annual joke swap with Jost on SNL , where the jokes can get quite dicey. “That’s why I can’t criticize anybody for swinging and missing because I’ve definitely swung and missed too,” the comedian said on Today . “I try to keep that heat off of me.” After drawing some backlash for his remarks on the NBC morning program, Che responded to a fan on Instagram who asked why he had no problem calling Kanye “Ye” West out in the past, but not Gillis. “That’s a fair question. Especially since when I called Kanye out, I did so privately. I had no idea he was filming. Point being, when I have a problem with someone I address them in person. Not thru the media. I’m not gonna drag someone on the Today show, when I can just text them. It’s a courtesy that’s been extended to me in the past, and I like to pay that forward.” Following Gillis’ monologue, Dan Levy was among some celebrities who slammed the comedian over his joke about women at the gym. “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists. There’s a difference there,” the Schitt’s Creek co-creator and star wrote in part. Levy added in his Instagram post, “I’m speechless that something like that can exist on live national television. And to be perfectly honest, more men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it’s complacency that has created the environment in which women are sexually assaulted and it’s a ‘conversation’ as opposed to a ‘crime.’” Former SNL castmember Ego Nwodim also responded with a photo of herself at the gym with the caption, “Whore reporting for duty.” THR

articles.title: Daisy Edgar-Jones Reveals She Might Be “Slightly Deaf” in One Ear After Filming ‘Twisters’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All October 15, 2026 6:58pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Daisy Edgar-Jones in 'Twisters.' Everett Collection Twisters has had a lasting impact on Daisy Edgar-Jones , but not necessarily in the way that she wanted. During a recent episode of Jake Shane ‘s Therapuss podcast , the actress revealed that she might be “slightly deaf” in one ear after shooting the 2024 action-adventure thriller, directed by Lee Isaac Chung. “I think I still am slightly deaf in my left ear because there was so much debris and wind that was entering from a sharp left,” she said. “It was a windy shoot. It was quite ironic because we were shooting in Oklahoma and often would have to shut down filming because of an actual wind storm, to then recreate a wind storm once it’s passed. It was a wild experience.” Related Stories Movies 'Street Fighter' Eyes Box Office Victory as Buzzy Elizabeth Holmes Doc Heads for Strong Launch Movies Prepare to Fall in Love With 'Sense and Sensibility' Star Herbert Nordrum Twisters , which served as a standalone sequel, came nearly two decades after 1996’s Twister . The film followed Kate Carter (Edgar-Jones), a retired tornado-chaser and meteorologist who is persuaded to return to Oklahoma to work with a new team and new technologies. There, she meets Tyler Owens (played by Glen Powell), a content creator who posts his storm-chasing adventures. The Sense and Sensibility star definitely wasn’t afraid to get in on the action, previously telling The Hollywood Reporter that she got “a bit addicted” to doing stunts after filming Twisters . “It was so stunt heavy and I’d never done really proper stunts, so I was so curious to see how they were going to achieve a lot of the action sequences, but I’m a bit addicted now, I’ve got the bug,” Edgar-Jones said in 2024. “It was so much fun. I mean we had a phenomenal stunt department who really just helped to immerse us in it, also keep us safe. Most of the stunts were sort of being battered by wind, rain and debris so it was definitely an interesting filming experience.” THR

articles.title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ Boss Meg Marinis on Texas Spinoff, Ellen Pompeo and Season 23 Premiere Cliffhangers
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Ellen Pompeo in the season 23 premiere. Disney/Raymond Liu Logo text [This story contains some spoilers from the Grey’s Anatomy season 23 premiere, “Collide.”] Twenty-three seasons in and Grey’s Anatomy is not going anywhere. “No one has said anything to me about when the last season of Grey’s is going to be,” showrunner Meg Marinis tells The Hollywood Reporter when chatting about the new season, which returned Thursday night. That doesn’t mean she doesn’t ask. As the person charged with running ABC ‘s long-running, hit medical drama, Marinis wants to be prepared for whenever that day comes. “But it really seems like they want it to be a collaborative decision with Shonda,” she says of show creator Rhimes. “The series has done so much for the studio and network, they [would] want to do it right. And they’re not ready.” Related Stories TV 'DWTS' Pro Val Chmerkovskiy Apologizes to Carrie Ann Inaba for "Careless" Will Smith Oscars Slap Reference: "I Will Do Better" TV Where to Watch 'Grey's Anatomy' Season 23 Premiere They are in expansion mode, instead. Grey’s , whose previous spinoffs were Private Practice and Station 19 , is getting a new spinoff this 2026-2027 season that will be set at a rural West Texas medical center. Marinis co-created and is writing the untitled series with Rhimes, and Grey’s star/executive producer Ellen Pompeo is also exec producing the new show. “It’s related to Grey’s , but its stories are going to be different,” teases Marinis, who counts Texas as her home state. She’s always wanted to explore “what’s happening in medical deserts,” as well as “the disparity between people who can afford excellent healthcare and the people who can’t.” The latter comes up in the season 23 premiere of Grey’s , “Collide,” which welcomed Pompeo’s Meredith back to the hospital after the season 22 ending that sparked wedding bells for her and Nick (Scott Speedman). When Grey’s returned, one month had passed since the exits of beloved doctors Teddy (Kim Raver) and Owen (Kevin McKidd) , and the episode’s ending sets up more than enough threads to follow in coming weeks. Below, Marinis talks about all of it, including more on the spinoff, how she really feels about medical show competition (we’re looking at you, The Pitt ) and how much Pompeo will be on screen this season. *** Congrats on the news about the Grey’s spinoff ! We know that the series (which doesn’t yet have a name) will premiere sometime in the 2026-2027 season and that it’s set at a rural West Texas medical center — “the last chance for care before miles of nowhere.” You and Grey’s creator Shonda Rhimes are co-creating and writing the show, and Ellen Pompeo is executive producing. How has it been working on this second show amid the Grey’s schedule? ( Laughs .) I have a great team here at Grey’s that I lean on, and Shonda’s doing the new one with me so it’s easier when there’s two of us! Where are you in your work on the spinoff? Is there a timeline? We are working away. I can’t say much, but we’re far enough along where I’m really, really excited. We’re digging into the actual communities and true stories of what happens out in rural West Texas. There’s so much going on there that I haven’t seen on TV. I’m thrilled to be able to dive into that world. It’s so different from Grey’s . It’s related to Grey’s , but its stories are going to be different. Previous Grey’s spinoffs were Private Practice and Station 19 , but this feels a world away from Grey’s ‘ Seattle hospital. Were there lessons learned from those two shows that you are applying now? The only lessons are good lessons from those two. They were very successful spinoffs with hardcore fan followings. I loved both of them. This one is something dear to my heart [ Marinis is from Houston, Texas ] and being on a medical show like Grey’s , and hearing a lot about what’s happening in medical deserts, it’s hard to show that in Seattle. I’ve always been really interested in showing it, and in doing a small town show in Texas. Will Grey’s launch the Texas show in-show this season? We have thoughts based on airing schedule and things like that, but we’re still working it out, also because there are so many things going on on Grey’s , I want to make sure to do it where it’s servicing both shows equally. How do you view this within the larger Grey’s franchise? Does it signal anything about the flagship? It’s just expanding the flagship. No one has said anything to me about when the last season of Grey’s is going to be. I think it’s never! I always ask and they’re like, “Not now!” You always want to be prepared, as a showrunner of a season 23 show, that you’re aware of when that decision is going to happen. But it really seems like they want it to be a collaborative decision with Shonda. Because the series has done so much for the studio network, they want to do it right. And they’re not ready. We last spoke after last season’s finale and the exits of Kim Raver and Kevin McKidd’s Teddy and Owen, respectively, which you said was a difficult decision and related to the budget, which is something shows are experiencing across the industry. How did you approach season 23 with your very large ensemble? Will there be characters we see more or less of? Are you still feeling those constraints? Not yet. I mean, you always feel the general constraints of a large ensemble and what’s going on in the industry, so I’m mindful of how many times we go out on location and things like that. So the general constraints, yes. But no, those conversations usually are when they approach me later in the season — to drop that news on me! We’re in a positive place right now. On the show, the hospital is having some budget issues as well, but that’s mainly continuing on what we started last year about what’s happening to research funding and funding for healthcare in general. Now Grey Sloan is just feeling more of it. How much time has passed since the finale to start this premiere, and how is the hospital rebounding from losing veteran doctors, Teddy and Owen? It’s been about a month. We did that for a couple of reasons. I’ve done direct pickups for the past couple of seasons and I wanted to do something different, to start stories in different places. Also, I didn’t have Nick [Scott Speedman] available to me at the beginning of this season — he was left in the hospital in the finale, and he was busy on [his ABC show] R.J. Decker. That played into the decision. And I really wanted time for this VIP floor to come into play. We didn’t see that floor when we left the season last year. We don’t mention Teddy and Owen a ton in the premiere, because it’s been a month, and I didn’t want to start on such a down note. But we’re definitely feeling, and I’m feeling, the loss of Teddy and Owen. I’m searching for them in the scripts. We have to get a new chief. We don’t have a head of trauma right now. And it’s just leading to how busy the hospital is, maybe how our ER is not functioning as well as it should be. Winston [Anthony Hill] can do what he can, but he’s not a military trauma surgeon. James Wolk in the season 23 premiere. Disney/Ser Baffo James Wolk is a new character who was announced with a four-episode arc. Now we know his role — he’s the new chief. Will that arc extend? And how extensive was your search for the new chief? I love having him, but, you know, chiefs can come and go quickly on this show! But he’s a great character. He’s very fun to write for. He is also just a delightful human being and he seems to really enjoy his time here. We always have a long list of options [of actors] that people are sending us. He fit that suave look we wanted. He really seems like a villain you learn to love. Even when he’s being snarky about money, he’s still fascinating to watch. You say you got a long list of actors who want to come and play on Grey’s , a network show in its 23 rd season. How does that make you feel as showrunner about how appealing the show still is in the streaming era? It makes me feel great. I credit it to our show filming in L.A. If you have your family here, it’s really appealing to get to do an arc in L.A. I think there’s a reason we’re in season 23. It works, and I think a lot of people are fans of the show and curious about the show because it’s been going on for so long. And also, we’re really nice over here! People tell me all the time. Guest actors will write me emails and say, “This is the nicest set I’ve ever been on.” This episode had a line that Debbie Allen’s Catherine said to Ellen Pompeo, when she tells Meredith about hiring a new chief, “Well, you’re not here all the time” — which also could apply to Pompeo’s lesser onscreen role. Did those two have fun doing that scene? Yeah, they really enjoyed it! Sometimes we write stuff like that and we don’t even really think about it, and then when you watch it on set, you’re like, “I didn’t mean it that way!” ( Laughs .) But you know Debbie threw some sass into it and they were they were laughing; the two of them together laughed really hard. How much will we see Ellen Pompeo on screen this season? I ask you every year, but is it more or less? The same? [ Pompeo is also working as an EP on the Texas spinoff .] Like I say, every year, we take her as much as we can get. I know she has a couple of things going on in the mix, but we’re scheduling around that and she really lets me know ahead of time the days she is around, and it’s the same thing with Scott [Speedman]. It’s a logistics game, right? You want everybody to be able to do all their other projects, because work is work and it’s important right now to keep working in the industry. She and I have a good relationship. We’ll plan things out, and I’m more than happy to schedule around her. Will you be building towards Meredith and Nick’s wedding this season? We will definitely see Scott later in the season. In the premiere, we couldn’t work it out. But we’ll see Scott and we’ll definitely tag that engagement. So engagement , but you’re not confirming a wedding this season… [ Shrugs in coy silence .] Meredith’s storyline in this premiere highlights the upstairs-downstairs of Grey Sloan. Meredith is fighting back against tiered treatment and Catherine is approaching this as a plan to help with their financials. How is this a larger story you want to tell this season, and why did that interest Ellen for this to be Meredith’s fight, at least for now? I’m interested in telling that story because I’m seeing it so much now across healthcare. The disparity is growing even wider between people who can afford excellent healthcare and the people who can’t. I think it’s also really interesting because, historically, Grey Sloan has always provided VIP care, the way we’ve told it on the show. So now, are they dividing care into tiers? A lot of our doctors are going to question it. But these floors are popping up all over the country. Obviously, they’ve had them in L.A. for a while, but also in New York, and even when I went to see my dad and Houston. When he had pneumonia, there was a VIP floor there. I saw the signs and I was like, “What’s the difference between what my dad’s getting and what they’re getting?” I find it fascinating. There are a lot of stories where sometimes you don’t want to be on the VIP floor because they don’t have all the tools you need if something catastrophic happens. But also, if I had a very chronically ill family member and I had the means, why wouldn’t I throw every dollar I had at helping? It’s an interesting debate to sink our teeth into. Meredith, especially, is an owner of the hospital, so she understands the business. But her whole career, she has fought for the have-nots. So it’s like, do you keep the hospital doors open? What side do you choose? Will Ellen be appearing in batches, like a five-episode arc to tell storylines? Or will she pop in and out in a less structured way? I would love for it to be structured like that, but schedules aren’t working! ( Laughs .) But there are runs where she’s in for more than one episode. Do you have an episode count for her this season? Not yet. Are there any other returns you can tease? Probably not. Obviously, she’s been in the picture, so people know that Jen Landon is returning [as Toni]. But as for old cast series regulars, I can’t tease any of that right now. The Grey’s social account teased a Cristina Yang (Sandra Oh) return, and the fans went wild. They were speculating Yang would maybe come back for Meredith’s wedding to Nick. Anything you can say about that? She is welcome to walk in these doors anytime! I would love for her to. At one point, she was doing some theater in London, but it would be a dream come true to have her back. You also kicked this season off with a classic disaster episode, and one that picks up on a lot of relationship threads that were unfinished at the end of last season, taking a backseat to Teddy and Owen’s big goodbye. Did this premiere feel more nostalgic to you — chaos and romance? You’re right that a lot of stories had to take up smaller real estate in the last couple of episodes at the end of last season, rightfully so, because we were writing off two long-term, beloved characters. I love when people have relationship issues with each other, and you have to throw them on a medical case together. There’s nothing more Grey’s than that. I love all those looks between Amelia and Toni and them having to come together; and Simone [Alexis Floyd] and Lucas [Niko Terho] and West [Trevor Jackson]; Jules [Adelaide Kane] and Winston having to operate with Bailey (Chandra Wilson). It’s quintessential Grey’s when there’s the bubbling underneath it as they’re trying to save someone’s life. Caterina Scorsone and Jen Landon as Amelia and Toni in the season 23 premiere. Disney/Raymond Liu You have a pregnancy reveal at the end of this premiere with Simone. We do. Grey’s has tackled pregnancy and abortion storylines before. How will this one be different? It is different. We’ve never done it this way before. It’s going to take a couple of episodes to play out. I also think this one is different because Simone was just told that she probably wouldn’t be able to have children; to be able to conceive and get pregnant. So that’s going to be top of mind for her. That’s a struggle. She’s someone who’s put career first and she’s worked really hard to get where she is. I think that’s what a lot of us struggle with, right? Do you put the career on pause for a second and start a family? It’s something so many people relate to, so we’ll show that. But it is different. We’ve never done it this way before. The other bomb at the end of the premiere is Jo (Camilla Luddington) quitting the hospital, as Link (Chris Carmack) is still being secretive about his pills. This couple is always tested! I know, what can I do? I love torturing them! Sometimes they’ll be like, “ Really ?!” They have such talent to play funny stories, and we played them very light and funny for a long time. Then I kind of tapped into this talent that I did not know they both had, and it’s amazing to watch. Their performances are so great. Even Jo watching that thing in the elevator? Camilla’s performance is exquisite. So yeah — we’re putting them through it again. ( Laughs .) Blue got fired at the end of last season, and now Harry Shum Jr. is on Dancing With the Stars . Did he come to you for approval to be on that series, and is that impacting his story and all? Obviously, he’s back as a series regular. It did not impact his story. It just happened to be that he was the character who was quitting, and then he, ABC and his team came to me after and I was like, “Oh, this really worked out, because now people are going to think once he’s announced on DWTS that maybe we went through with [firing him off the show].” But I think there’s been so much social media of him in his scrubs that his return is spoiled! We’re so happy for him. He’s so talented. A lot of us have gotten to go see the live taping of DWTS . You’ll see him and Jenna Johnson just rehearsing outside in between setups for Grey’s . On Tuesdays, Harry’s not here because Dancing With the Stars films. But other than Tuesdays, he’s really been able to schedule rehearsals around the show. I’m sure he’s exhausted! Grey’s remains the longest-running medical drama on TV. But more medical shows are popping up on streaming; there’s The Pitt. You could compare that to ER , which was on at the beginning of Grey’s . Does that sharpen what you’re trying to do? Do you ever worry about overlap? How do you feel about medical show competition? I don’t worry too much about it because I feel like what’s good for one medical show is good for all. It’s trending again. Anytime that it can trend, I think it’s a great thing. We’re so different than The Pitt that I don’t worry about that one. I was a huge ER fan. It had a huge influence on me wanting to be a TV writer. I love medical shows. I love the better ones more. ( Laughs .) And then I’m excited to introduce this new [the Texas spinoff] into the fold. Grey’s is a streaming show too now, on Netflix, courting new generations of viewers. But 23 seasons in, what are your tricks to keeping the show fresh and keeping the cast engaged? It has been a long time and it can be difficult. It can be tricky, but I also think that medicine has changed so much and the world has changed so much. Between AI and climate change and where money goes toward research, there are always new things that we haven’t explored. Often, we have an overwhelming amount of stories we want to tell and we don’t get to tell all of them, so we have a huge bank of things we’re interested in. Also, knowing that we have a 23-year history of characters who have come and gone and bringing them back. And, you can always introduce new interns! You have three series originals stars who are still on the show: Ellen, Chandra Wilson and James Pickens Jr. Are you never letting them go? Yes, I will say, I am never letting those three go! I mean, I hope they never go. It’s not gonna be me who writes it! *** Grey’s Anatomy releases new episodes Thursdays at 10 p.m. on ABC, releasing on Hulu the next day. THR

articles.title: James McAvoy Reveals Which Film Paid Him “Bonkers” Residuals
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All October 15, 2026 8:12pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source James McAvoy in 'Split.' Everett Collection James McAvoy is getting candid about pay, including which project paid him “bonkers” residuals. During a recent interview on the Happy Sad Confused podcast , the actor admitted that while his residual income typically isn’t consistent, he can’t say that about director M. Night Shyamalan ‘s 2016 film Split . “The only one that really consistently pays me is Split ,” he told host Josh Horowitz. “Well, I think it was made for like $6 million or something like that. And let’s say they spent $30 [million] advertising it, and in our first weekend, we made $40 [million].” Related Stories Business BBC Asks Judge to Force Trump to Sit for Deposition in His Own Lawsuit Against Broadcaster Movies Prepare to Fall in Love With 'Sense and Sensibility' Star Herbert Nordrum “So, we were in profit. So our first residual check came at the end of the first weekend. It was bonkers,” McAvoy added. Split follows three girls who try to escape after being kidnapped by a man (McAvoy) with a diagnosed 23 distinct personalities. He also reprised the role in 2016’s Glass . The Atonement actor went on to praise Shyamalan, saying he’s “super smart in so many ways.” “The thing that I took away from him was his preparedness because you know he made that film and Glass on incredibly modest budgets and was very focused,” he said, adding that the filmmaker maximized his shooting time by “being incredibly well-prepared” and “communicat[ing] with the crew.” While McAvoy has enjoyed the residuals from Split , he also admitted that he doesn’t “get too much money from [2008’s] Wanted .” “You’ve always got a good back end and there’s some in your contract, you get back end here and back end there. I very rarely see anything from anything,” he added. “You get the odd check for like a couple hundred quid here or sometimes you get checks for like 25 cents, and you’re like it literally costs more to post this than it did for me to check it.” THR

articles.title: ‘Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald’ Review: Judd Apatow’s Latest Comedy Doc Sends Viewers Down a Laugh-Filled Rabbit Hole
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Daniel Fienberg Plus Icon Daniel Fienberg Chief Television Critic TheFienPrint Follow Sign Up View All October 16, 2026 12:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald' Netflix Logo text As much as I adore Freaks and Geeks and Undeclared and The 40-Year-Old Virgin and Knocked Up , it’s becoming increasingly clear that Judd Apatow ‘s greatest legacy may be the documentary project he started fairly late in his career. In the past decade, Apatow has directed or co-directed multi-part documentaries on Garry Shandling , George Carlin and Mel Brooks , as well as feature-length documentaries on Maria Bamford and Norm Macdonald , with the Brooks, Bamford and Macdonald projects all hitting streaming this year alone. In a documentary landscape wildly oversaturated with the stories of certain kinds of comics from a certain generation (or two), Apatow’s films stand out as the most thoughtful and thoughtfully made, puzzle pieces that will eventually come together as an indispensable record of a genre and its key artisans. Related Stories TV 'SNL' Star Michael Che Reacts to Shane Gillis' Controversial Monologue: "That's Comedy" TV 'Lupin' Is (Nearly) Back! Star Omar Sy Shares How Season 4 Is Bigger and Bolder Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald The Bottom Line A greatest-hits approach that suits its subject fairly well. Airdate: Friday, October 16 (Netflix) Director: Judd Apatow 2 hours 7 minutes Hitting Netflix one week ahead of Apatow and Neil Berkeley’s Paralyzed by Hope: The Maria Bamford Story (and one week after the Berkeley-co-directed documentary about Marin Mull), Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald finds Apatow continuing to experiment formally. If Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man! was driven by the remarkable gift of Brooks’ ongoing presence in our cultural lives and The Zen Diaries of Garry Shandling was driven by Shandling’s unreleased diaries, Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald defies the notion of documentary as a path toward intimacy. This is the first of the Apatow docs that feels more like an opportunity to point and laugh at favorite one-liners and late-night appearances than to learn anything deeper and more personal about its subject, which is simultaneously a limitation and the purpose here. Macdonald, who died in 2021 , is and was revered in comedy circles. He was a respected stand-up, an all-time great talk show and podcast guest and, depending on your age, the Platonic ideal of a Weekend Update anchor on Saturday Night Live . The latter was a three-and-a-half year run that made him both a truth-telling god and, ultimately, a martyr to corporate interference when he was abruptly fired for his refusal to back down from punchlines related to O.J. Simpson and murder. Macdonald was also, for much of his career, intentionally unknowable. When he disclosed autobiographical details, they often deviated wildly from recounting to recounting. When he penned a memoir, he explicitly argued that it should be treated as fiction. Only in the last few years of his life, when he became a popular presence on Twitter and Instagram, did he give the impression that he was letting audiences into the “real” Norm. But when it was revealed after his death that he had been fighting cancer for eight years, it was a detail he’d somehow never mentioned in all of those posts and reels. He was unknowable, but Apatow treats that as the path to knowing him. The conceit in Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald is that it’s the documentary version of a YouTube rabbit hole, building a portrait of Macdonald primarily through assembled clips, many quite familiar to anybody who has, on their own, gone down a rabbit hole of Norm Macdonald clips. So that means a lot of footage from Macdonald’s stand-up, his regular appearances with David Letterman and Conan O’Brien, his run on Saturday Night Live and his subsequent career arcs, which included a very brief tenure as a movie star and a run as an adored streaming talk show host. Instead of bringing Macdonald’s contemporaries in for original sit-downs, Apatow goes to the clips from countless podcasts and video shows in which those contemporaries reflected on and celebrated Macdonald. Sometimes Apatow and editor Jake Hostetter utilize those “commentary” clips to show the love and admiration that Macdonald’s fellow comics had for him, and sometimes they use those clips to show how even those closest to Macdonald didn’t necessarily know his real age, his real educational history, his real romantic interests. There’s a suggestion that something more honestly revelatory came out of Macdonald’s last few years on social media, but a lot of the clips from the end of Macdonald’s life come from unexplained and uncited sources, which makes them somehow both more and less trustworthy as a result. Not every comic would benefit from this treatment. I’d venture to say most comics wouldn’t benefit and, honestly, I’m not sure that a more traditional approach would have allowed Apatow more insight. Part of why we do documentaries at all, rather than just letting people tell their life stories exclusively in five-minute late-night interviews, is the opportunity for depth and reflection that a filmmaker can evoke. That’s lost here. But if the ironic remove of his comic voice was part of what allowed Macdonald to speak so many uncomfortable truths, Apatow creating a remove of his own is justifiable. Going back to the idea that these documentaries are pieces in a far larger project, it’s appropriate the the Macdonald film is premiering a week before the documentary about Bamford, whose unique gift has always been using absurdity and even surrealism as a way to strip away all boundaries between an artist and her truth. Bamford digs deep and Paralyzed by Hope digs deep. By design, Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald flits like a moth around a porch light. It doesn’t cover or include every O.J. joke or every conversation with O’Brien or Letterman, but if you sit around for over an hour waiting patiently for the indelible Courtney Thorne-Smith appearance , it will eventually pop up, good for a big laugh as ever. It’s all accompanied by visualizations of various search engine queries and whatnot, giving the impression that you could have made this documentary in your own head but Apatow has saved you several steps. Of course, if you did your own searching and curated your own favorite clips, you’d get to watch the entire conversation with Thorne-Smith, but it might take you many hours. So it’s a service that Apatow and Hostetter have kept this film to 127 minutes. Some of the limitations of the documentary illustrate, without comment, the limitations of a generation of standup comedy. For most of its running time, Norm features no women at all and no people of color, a suggestion of restrictions to Macdonald’s appeal and voice that I wouldn’t think was necessarily accurate. Then in the closing segment, nearing and after Macdonald’s death, we briefly see Lori Joe Hoekstra, his longtime producing partner (and a producer on this documentary), and Molly Shannon, whom Macdonald once credited as the only SNL co-star to have his back in the immediate aftermath of his firing, as well as Dave Chappelle, whose presence will serve as a distraction to some viewers. Still, I wish there had been some way to get those voices integrated earlier, since it’s not like the world had any doubt what David Letterman and Conan O’Brien thought about Norm Macdonald. Actually, I wish somebody would make a docuseries about the insularity of stand-up comedy, the voices who rise to a status deemed worthy of documentary treatment and those who are deemed too niche. I respect this current run of comic-centric documentaries, but it’s hard not to notice that the same people are making and appearing in all of them — that it’s self-fulfilling that those people represent, and become representative of, the entire industry. That probably isn’t a documentary Apatow should make — though perhaps he could produce it on behalf of a woman or person of color. Meanwhile, I’ll just wait patiently to see whom Apatow chronicles next. Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald isn’t his best, but Apatow remains very good at this thing he’s found himself doing. Full credits Airdate: Friday, October 16 (Netflix) Director: Judd Apatow Producers: Judd Apatow, Ross Dinerstein, Amanda Rohlke, Lori Joe Hoekstra Executive producers: Ross Girad, Josh Church, Zoe Rogovin, Mark McCune, Jon Liebman, Nicaury Santana Editor: Jake Hostetter 2 hours 7 minutes THR

articles.title: Comics Accuse Hot AI Fakes of Stealing Their Jokes Word for Word to Push OnlyFans Pages
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All October 16, 2026 5:32am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The real George Brett Olson is at left. AI is coming for your jokes — and its armed with double Ds. Two comics have posted videos within the past couple of weeks showing sexy AI “comedians” on social media racking up views by performing their exact routines. First was comic and content creator, George Brett Olson, who did a breakdown (watch it below) accusing an AI Instagram account with 300,000 followers of seemingly ripped off his joke word for word. The fake comic was a highly realistic-looking female character that even had the same venue background and wore clothing similar to his own. The avatar also, he noted, has an OnlyFans page. Related Stories Business Disney Circles Character.ai as Chatbot Company Files For Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Business Netflix Has Used AI on About 300 Titles, but "Human Touch Is Critical," Exec Says in Busan “AI stole my joke and my outfit,” Olson said. “You might be saying, ‘I’ve heard comedians talk about this already,’ but this is new — very new.” Adding to the surreal nature of the incident, Olson’s joke was about AI’s threat to jobs and how billionaires like Instagram’s parent company co-founder Mark Zuckerberg are complicit. “This is the most ironic thing that’s ever happened to me,” Olson said. A few days ago, stand-up comic Julia Jasunas ( Comics Unleashed ) took to Instagram to show a similar side-by-side example of an AI account with 250,000 followers ripping off one of her jokes verbatim (below). The fake comic even made the same random aside that Jasunas said to a member of her audience. “So another AI bot just stole my joke,” Jasunas said. “I’ve seen a couple other videos of other comedians posting about the exact same problem, and the thing that’s the most concerning is these AI bots are going viral, and people think that they’re real people.” The AI version was seemingly crafted to look like a stand-up comic version of Lara Croft. “Who does comedy in Daisy Duke shorts?” Jasunas quipped. UK comedy news site Chortle found several other examples of stolen jokes on the same account that knocked off Jasunas — including content by Char Ramtin, Olivia Carter and Hannah Berner. “It’s incredibly unsettling that someone is using scantily clad AI-generated women to perform stolen jokes and generate profit from views and engagement, then funnel people toward an OnlyFans account for additional profit, all for a woman who doesn’t even exist!” Jasunas told the site. “No wonder there’s a male loneliness epidemic.” (Neither AI Instagram account cited by the comics replied to a request for comment). Two of the AI-generated comedians Olson and Jasunas said they have received no support from Meta regarding the issue and Olson blasted the platform for not doing more to protect original content. “The craziest thing is that there’s no terms of service violation here,” he said. “We’re watching [social media leaders] in real time say, ‘Hey, we’re building something that’s going to destroy everything,’ and then watching them protect no one [and] not anything that makes us human — songs, laughter … Maybe [Meta] should realize the reason we like the internet is that low key we like each other … and now you’re going to exponentially flood the internet with things that are not us.” In response to an inquiry by The Hollywood Reporter , Instagram chief Adam Mosseri said in a statement, “I don’t think it’s practical for us to try and ban AI content from the platform. It’s gonna be harder and harder to identify, and it’s not all bad content (though yes, there is plenty of slop). But we are very invested in trying to drive more traffic to original content creators, and if an AI creator is ripping off content wholesale, it would be good for us to work out what we can do about that. I’m not sure what it would be, but I’ll make sure to talk to the team and look into it.” A Meta spokesperson added the problem has cropped up on other platforms (such as YouTube and Tiktok) as well. Jasunas, meanwhile, urged those watching her video to support comics by going to see live shows instead of scrolling for clips “Comedians post their stand-up clips online to get you to come out and see live comedy,” Jasunas added. “Live comedy is meant to be experienced in the flesh, and if you’re watching these videos and you’re not realizing that these are computers regurgitating our jokes that we’ve crafted over time on stage and honed and whittled down into a punchy bit. Then you need to get out and take a walk and go see a live show.” View this post on Instagram View this post on Instagram THR

articles.title: ‘Clayface’ Director James Watkins on Why He “Auditioned the Hell” Out of Star Tom Rhys Harries
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 16, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tom Rhys Harries attends the world premiere of Warner Bros. 'Clayface' at Hollywood Legion Theater in Los Angeles on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Kevin Winter/Getty Images) Clayface , the new DC Studios film, centers on a Hollywood movie star named Tom Hagen who is left grossly disfigured following a violent attack orchestrated by a Gotham mob boss. Desperate to get that handsome life back, Hagen undergoes an experimental procedure that initially works only to give way to a scary new reality with shape-shifting skin. Enter Clayface. Because it’s a dual role in a body horror thriller, the casting process to find a leading man up to the task was a real beast. “I auditioned the hell out of him,” filmmaker James Watkins told The Hollywood Reporter of finding Mr. Hagen/Clayface in Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries . “He came in, and I thought he really had something but I wanted to explore it. So we spent time exploring it.” Related Stories Movies DC Studios' 'Clayface': First Reactions Business Barbie's New Boss: Mattel Taps a Warner Bros. Exec to Be Its New Head of Dolls Watkins, speaking at the film’s world premiere on Tuesday night at Hollywood Legion Theater, said he brought in a host of actors but Harries had something special. “I don’t think I’ve ever auditioned anyone that much,” he added. “There was just a sense that Tom had something and [the audition process helped] me explore the character and understand the character.” Harries, who had worked across film and television with credits on such projects as Suspicion, White Lines, The Return, Chewing Gum, Jekyll and Hyde and Unforgotten , had no issues with the lengthy process. “It was spread out over three months and I did two fairly long screen tests with James,” he recalled. “But I’m untested in this space, so I was glad he did it with me really because it meant that we’d had time to workshop the thing before he got onto set.” Harries as Matt Hagen in DC Studios’ Clayface Parisa Taghizadeh/Warner Bros. Pictures Tom Rhys Harries as Matt Hagen and Naomi Ackie as Caitlyn Corr in DC Studios’ Clayface Parisa Taghizadeh/Warner Bros. Pictures Naomi Ackie, who plays the scientist charged with Hagen’s experimental procedure, praised how her co-star shouldered what was a very challenging role. “He’s awesome. He’s hardworking. He comes into the room with so much enthusiasm, but like a lightness. And for this role, it’s actually really hard what he’s doing. I feel like people, when they see it, will understand why,” said Ackie, who also had a front row seat working with another DC star, Robert Pattinson, when they filmed Mickey 17. “He has to go through so many changes, transformations, and he has to track that emotion all the way through and make people kind of love him and want him to win in a way. And he did it with so much grace, so much attention to detail whilst being a really funny, nice guy.” Producer Lynn Harris, who works as Matt Reeves’ producing partner, also touched on the delicate balance Harries had to walk in order to pull off the role. “The idea was to examine a story from Matt Hagen’s perspective with the empathy you might have for this guy who’s just a regular guy that makes a terrible, terrible choice that affects him for the rest of his life. Doing that from a very, very grounded emotional place was an exciting journey to me and to Matt,” she said of the project, which initially came in as a pitch and first draft from horror maestro Mike Flanagan, who eventually had to depart for all of the projects he was juggling from Carrie to the upcoming The Exorcist: Martyrs. Hossein Amini did another draft and Watkins filled in to direct. “Watkins came in and had a great take, and he saw it in the same way that we did in terms of it being super grounded, very emotional, very character driven. It sort of got the core tragedy of the character,” Harries added. Watkins for one can’t wait to see how the film plays when it goes wide because from what he’s seen so far, preview audiences and critics alike are digging it. “It’s a rollercoaster ride. It’s got a lot of horror, a lot of heart, and a lot of humor. It’s a full meal,” he teased. “Look for me, I like horror that gets under people’s skin. I like horror that isn’t just jump scares or mechanical or clockwork. I like horror that’s relatable. And what’s more relatable than our fears for what can happen to our bodies, how they can betray us, all those sorts of things.” So what was the hardest scene for Harries to pull off? “Oh man. The hardest scene was a scene right at the end of the film where I’m lying in a lot of gook and gunk and I was on my last legs,” he said with a smile. “Hopefully it aided the performance.” See for yourself when Clayface opens on Oct. 23.
