articles.title: Boo Junfeng’s ‘Trinity,’ Sidharta Tata’s ‘Slaughterground’ Among JAFF Market 2026 Selections
articles.full_text: Oct 16, 2026 4:50am PT Boo Junfeng’s ‘Trinity,’ Sidharta Tata’s ‘Slaughterground’ Among JAFF Market 2026 Selections By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Indonesian Zombie Franchise ‘Zona Merah: Dead City’ Unveils Teaser, Takes Outbreak Into the City 8 minutes ago Boo Junfeng’s ‘Trinity,’ Sidharta Tata’s ‘Slaughterground’ Among JAFF Market 2026 Selections 2 hours ago Singapore Media Festival Launches Creator Summit as Asia TV Forum Adds AI Zone, Microdrama Focus 5 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Trinity Boo Junfeng ’s “ Trinity ” and Sidharta Tata’s “Slaughterground” are among 11 feature projects picked for JAFF Future Project (JFP), the film development strand of Indonesia’s JAFF Market , which has also chosen 10 intellectual properties for its adaptation-focused JAFF IP Connection (JIPCon) program. The third edition of JAFF Market, powered by Amar Bank, will run Nov. 28–30 at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta, during the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (Nov. 28–Dec. 5). One of the film projects comes from Australia through a partnership with the Adelaide Film Festival and mylab, while two Korean IPs join via a tie-up with the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM). Related Stories White House's New AI Website Confirms Trump Lost the 2020 Presidential Election Mayor Zohran Mamdani Refuses Jimmy Kimmel’s Request to Text Trump a Selfie of Them “Trinity” (original title “Tsai Kuang Chih Chien”) is one of two works in progress in the selection and lists the widest spread of production countries: Taiwan, France, Singapore, Poland, Greece, Germany, Japan, Brazil, South Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines. Peanut Pictures is the production company, with Raymond Phathanavirangoon, Sophie Erbs, Aileen Li, Huang Junxiang and Boo producing. Popular on Variety The other work in progress is Tata’s “Slaughterground” (“Hujan Kematian”), produced by Ajish Dibyo, Pramudya Andika, Annisa Adjam and Sunny Gho for Aftersun Creative. The remaining nine projects are in development. Among them is M. Raihan Halim’s Singapore project “The Smuggler,” produced by Asra Aman for Papahan Films. Two Indonesian women directors are at work on what will be their first features: Ninndi Raras with “A Quiet Sunshine” (“Perempuan di Pulau Lea”), produced by Giovanni Rahmadeva and Siera Tamihardja for QUN Films, and Dian Tamara with “Somewhere Between” (“Titik Temu”), from Gambar Gerak and Pancaran Sinema with Arya Ibrahim and Moch. As’ad Azwin producing. Also from Indonesia are Dhiwangkara Seta’s “αLPα (Absence),” from Lune Features; Timoteus Anggawan Kusno’s “Orphaned Atlas” (“Sampar”), an Indonesia, France and Netherlands project from Forka Films produced by Ifa Isfansyah and Agustiya Herdwiyanto; and Rein Maychaelson’s “Primal,” a Studio Rumah Kedua project listing Indonesia, Singapore and South Korea as production countries. Yudhatama Fajar Nugroho’s “Pupus: The Orchid of Merapi” (“Pupus: Anggrek Merapi”) from Manimonki Studio is the only animated title. Glenn Barit’s “Luz and Flor” (“Luzonensis and Floresiensis”), produced by Kristine De Leon and Tanveer Hossain for Katalog, represents the Philippines. Taken together, the films deal with family, faith, memory, identity and migration, in forms that range from close-quarters drama to genre work. The Australian entry is Rosie Lourde’s “Wreck and Ruin,” which Lourde is producing with Katharine McPhee for In Cahoots Creations. “Our partnership with JAFF Market and mylab gives Australian filmmakers an opportunity to engage with the region’s creative and production networks while their projects are still taking shape,” said Mat Kesting, CEO and creative director of the Adelaide Film Festival. “We want these exchanges to build a stronger foundation for collaboration, connecting teams with partners who can contribute to development, financing and the international journey of their films.” Lorna Tee, founder of mylab, said international collaboration starts with understanding a filmmaker’s vision and what each partner can bring. “Through our collaboration with JAFF Market and Adelaide Film Festival, we want to connect Australian filmmaking teams with producers in Indonesia and across Asia, building relationships that can shape their films and continue beyond the market,” she said. On the IP side, six of the 10 selections are Indonesian. They are “Komarong,” represented by Gilang Bhagaskara; the board game “Mantra,” represented by Sigit Ezra Prayoga; the comics “Darah di Atas Salju” (“Blood Upon the Snow”), represented by Dedy, “Lao Sam 1892,” represented by Toni Masdiono, and “Yuuko’s Gloomy Days,” represented by Anwita Citriya; and the novel “Hati-Hati Ada Dua Hati,” represented by Ario Tamat. The selection also takes in two IPs from Hong Kong and Taiwan: the comic “Disposable Dolly,” represented by Ben Liu, and the book “Cat Rental Company,” represented by Maka (Zhou Lishu). The ACFM pair are the book “My Upstairs Neighbors,” represented by Clayhouse Inc., and webtoon “Friend Request,” represented by Ryoung Studio. Both slates will also feed into JAFF Market’s first Producers Exchange, which will set up meetings between participating producers and the JFP teams, JIPCon representatives, exhibitors and other delegates. “We want producers to come to JAFF Market knowing they can discover films taking shape and original IP with potential for the screen,” said Linda Gozali, market director of JAFF Market. “JFP and JIPCon bring filmmakers and IP representatives into conversation with partners who can contribute creatively, help structure financing and connect stories with audiences. Our ambition is to turn that discovery into lasting collaboration and strengthen Indonesia’s role as a creative and production partner.” The Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival was founded in 2006. ‘A Different World’ Renewed for Season 2 at Netflix ‘The Hunting Wives’ Renewed for Season 3 at Netflix Ahead of Season 2 Premiere Netflix Romance ‘Love Untangled’ Director Namkoong Sun on Netflix Freedom and the Funding and Distribution Gap in Korean Indie Film Bela Bajaria on Netflix’s Epic TV Trek Into Local Language Production: ‘There’s No Roadmap for This’ John Steinbeck’s ‘East of Eden’ Returns to Top of Book Charts Following Netflix Adaptation’s Release Netflix Scores Exclusive 2030 FIFA World Cup Rights in Spain and Andorra in Landmark Deal Loading comments...

articles.title: Netflix Is Profitable and Still Growing. Why Did It Just Make a Huge Round of Layoffs and Oust Its Top Content Exec?
articles.full_text: Oct 16, 2026 5:15am PT Netflix Is Profitable and Still Growing. Why Did It Just Make a Huge Round of Layoffs and Oust Its Top Content Exec? By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Netflix Is Profitable and Still Growing. Why Did It Just Make a Huge Round of Layoffs and Oust Its Top Content Exec? 2 hours ago Skydance’s Market Value Is Currently Less Than Half What Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Combined Were Worth 18 hours ago Comcast Donated $7.5 Million for Donald Trump’s Lavish New White House Ballroom 20 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Haddad for Variety In 2025, Netflix notched a net profit of $11 billion on a 16% increase in revenue, to $46.6 billion. It expects revenue growth to cool off this year, projecting an increase of 13%-14%, while the streamer is aiming to boost operating margin by 200 basis points, to 31.5%. It has a healthy balance sheet, with $9.1 billion in cash and equivalents and very manageable total debt of $14.4 billion as of June 30. So why did Netflix, which is still throwing off a good chunk of change, this week lay off around 1,000 employees — its biggest cutback to date? Related Stories Pro-Trump Ads Funded With Taxpayer Dollars Air on CNN and MS NOW; White House Has Spent $2.9 Million on the TV Spots to Date 'SNL' Opens Season With Mamdani Hanging Out With BFF Trump, Natalie Harp Going 'Obsession' Over President Companies often make layoffs in crisis mode, such as when they’re facing near-term revenue shortfalls and they simply can’t make payroll. That’s not the case here. But Netflix faces a festering pain point. Popular on Variety Specifically, investors are worried about the slowdown in its U.S./Canada region — which has raised questions about its long-term growth trajectory. For the second quarter of 2026, Netflix’s UCAN revenue decelerated from 14% the prior quarter to 10% (partially due to its recent price hikes ). The company also issued Q3 revenue guidance below analyst expectations. Shares of Netflix are down 20% year-to-date on fears the streamer’s days of double-digit gains are coming to an end. Netflix’s 6% reduction in force and the move to boot chief content officer Bela Bajaria — replacing her with well-regarded industry veteran Peter Rice, who hails from Disney and 21st Century Fox — signal its attempts to get in front of the issue. Multiple industry sources told Variety they think Bajaria is being made the scapegoat for Netflix’s larger problems. But content is the main engine that powers Netflix’s financials. As Variety ’s analysis of Bajaria’s exit noted, Netflix hasn’t produced a “culture-defining hit in the vein of ‘Stranger Things’ in quite some time.” Back to the all-important UCAN region: Total viewing hours in the U.S. and Canada declined in Q2, according to BMO Capital Markets analyst Brian Pitz. Netflix’s parting ways with Bajaria and hiring Rice “suggest[s] to us that engagement trends may have softened further in 3Q26E,” Pitz said in a research note Friday. The change in content leadership prompted the Wall Street firm to lower revenue estimates for Netflix’s Q3 and Q4 by around 1% each and to also reduce its 2027 revenue forecast by 1.5%. BMO’s model, Pitz added, “conservatively does not assume a UCAN revenue acceleration” until 2029. Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, in a memo to staff Thursday about the executive shake-up, seemed to acknowledge that the company needs a more robust content lineup in the U.S./Canada region. Sarandos wrote that he sees “an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in UCAN where we have an outsize impact in creating big, buzzy hits that our members love and drive conversation around the world.” And what about the tranche of 1,000 employees being laid off? Sarandos and co-chief Greg Peters told staffers in a companywide memo the job cuts are part of giving it the means to “invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation.” Note that Netflix isn’t alone in handing out pink slips. Disney — also profitable — has made three rounds of layoffs in 2026 across different parts of the business. Unlike Netflix, Disney is wrestling with the ongoing deterioration of linear TV. But echoing Netflix’s explanation for its RIF, CEO Josh D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston have told the Street they’re looking to cut costs, including through layoffs, to “create incremental capacity to invest for growth.” Netflix’s top brass will surely be asked for more detail on the restructuring (and their decision to swap out Bajaria for Rice) when it reports Q3 earnings next Tuesday, Oct. 20. That will be the kickoff to an intriguing quarterly earnings season for the entertainment sector, which will include the first print from David Ellison’s freshly minted Skydance — poised to ax thousands of staffers after the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. articles.title: ‘Toy Story 5’ Co-Director Kenna Harris on Going From Jessie Superfan to Pixar Filmmaker — and the Two-Week Rewrite That Reshaped the Sequel
articles.full_text: Oct 16, 2026 5:17am PT ‘Toy Story 5’ Co-Director Kenna Harris on Going From Jessie Superfan to Pixar Filmmaker — and the Two-Week Rewrite That Reshaped the Sequel By Davide Abbatescianni Plus Icon Davide Abbatescianni Latest ‘Toy Story 5’ Co-Director Kenna Harris on Going From Jessie Superfan to Pixar Filmmaker — and the Two-Week Rewrite That Reshaped the Sequel 1 hour ago ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ VFX Boss Jerome Chen on Hulk’s Redesign, Finishing 445 Shots in a Week 1 day ago Laika’s ‘Wildwood’ VFX Supervisor Steve Emerson Details the Making of Travis Knight’s Stop-Motion Epic 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kenna Harris walking an audience through 'Toy Story 5' at View Conference, Oct. 16, 2026 Long before co-directing Pixar’s “ Toy Story 5 ,” Kenna Harris spent childhood afternoons drawing Jessie, painstakingly reproducing details from “Toy Story 2” and even imagining Woody offering the cowgirl a flower. Decades later, the character helped Harris navigate a daunting first feature — including a two-week production pause to overhaul a story that was not yet working. “She was my cowgirl through and through,” Harris said at View Conference in Turin on Friday, displaying childhood fan art and explaining how Jessie’s boldness became a guiding principle while making the film with director Andrew Stanton . Related Stories 'SNL U.K.' Mocks Donald Trump and Andy Burnham's First Meeting, Harvey Weinstein, Sam Altman and More in Wild Weekend Update Mayor Zohran Mamdani Refuses Jimmy Kimmel’s Request to Text Trump a Selfie of Them Stanton invited Harris to co-direct in late 2022, after work on “Luca,” “Ciao Alberto” and “Inside Out 2.” Harris accepted, then asked to co-write the screenplay despite never having tackled a feature script. “Who was I to put myself in a position this precarious, where I could very well fail in front of the man who wrote my entire childhood?” Harris recalled. The collaboration ultimately earned Harris a screenwriting credit alongside Stanton. Popular on Variety That willingness to take risks extended to campaigning for Jessie and Buzz to kiss amid a perilous action sequence. “I just think there should be a ton of action, and it should be perilous, and then they should kiss super duper hard,” Harris remembered telling Stanton, who agreed. Another image — Jessie riding a real horse — helped inspire the ranch setting and a new character, Blaze. Harris, production designer Bob Pauley and the story team visited BreyerFest, a Kentucky convention devoted to model horses, for research. The filmmakers also had to find the right approach to Lilypad, the tablet threatening Bonnie’s attachment to traditional toys. Harris rejected the notion of an irredeemably evil device: the story needed to acknowledge how difficult it is for children and adults alike to escape technology’s grip. But the early versions still failed to deliver an emotionally compelling journey. “We stopped production for two weeks, and focused on the film’s core issue at the time,” Harris said. “Our act one was not working.” The first week was devoted to diagnosing the problem; during the second, Harris and Stanton raced to rewrite. Initially, Jessie’s overriding goal was simply to win back playtime with Bonnie, especially after becoming separated from her during a dance class. But early screenings showed that audiences were unmoved by a conflict that echoed the first film’s competition for a child’s attention. “The stakes of losing playtime felt too soft,” Harris explained. The breakthrough was to make Bonnie’s loneliness the emotional engine. Jessie, whose painful history with her former owner Emily was already established, would instead strive to help the shy girl make a real friend. Blaze, previously more peripheral to the adventure, became essential. “This was the moment that turned an okay movie into a good one,” Harris said, recalling a noticeable improvement in reactions at internal screenings. Another discarded approach had Jessie meet an elderly Emily at her former home. Harris felt it resolved the character’s pain too neatly. The filmmakers instead returned to the tire-swing tree from “Toy Story 2,” building a more understated climax around a time capsule. Harris recalled seeing the revised ending at a screening and realizing, “There’s no way we’re changing it.” The decision to put Jessie front and center was itself contested. “Part of the risk of this film was having Jessie as the protagonist,” Harris revealed, recalling questions about whether audiences would rather watch Woody and Buzz. The filmmakers held firm: those characters would remain important, but Jessie’s emotional history gave the sequel its purpose. Harris also helped shape the movie’s imagination sequences, pushing Pixar’s artists toward more spontaneous, painterly images rather than the studio’s usual meticulous realism. “We wanted to lean into something that felt more ephemeral and fleeting,” Harris said. Rapid experiments in lighting, movement and effects became part of a process the crew called “playtime weeklies.” The approach reflected a larger lesson in directing: learning to delegate, invite others into difficult decisions and leave space for play. Stanton’s guiding idea for the film was that “our limited time with others can impact a lifetime,” a theme that spoke both to Jessie’s journey and to Harris’ own time at Pixar. “I wanted people to know that I was here,” Harris said of the desire to leave a personal imprint on a beloved franchise. By the end of production, that fear had given way to confidence. “I look back now, and I can see that I was here.” Why Netflix, Amazon and Other Streamers Have Not Proved Saviors for the Kids Content Industry ‘The Monster of Florence’ Director Stefano Sollima on ‘Completely Different’ Second Chapter of Netflix’s Hit Serial Killer Series: ‘A Very Complex Story to Tell’ (EXCLUSIVE) Netflix Film VP Doug Belgrad Is Out Amid Layoffs ‘Bridgerton’ Spinoff, Centered on Lady Violet, Ordered by Netflix ‘East of Eden’ Hits 6.5 Million Views in Four Days on Netflix ‘A Different World’ Renewed for Season 2 at Netflix Loading comments...

articles.title: Omar Sy on Taking Creative Control of Netflix’s ‘Lupin’ and Why ‘Black Dumas’ Will Spark Political Debate in France
articles.full_text: Oct 16, 2026 5:22am PT Omar Sy on Taking Creative Control of Netflix’s ‘Lupin’ and Why ‘Black Dumas’ Will Spark Political Debate in France By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest Omar Sy on Taking Creative Control of Netflix’s ‘Lupin’ and Why ‘Black Dumas’ Will Spark Political Debate in France 1 hour ago YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom 1 day ago Mediawan’s Pierre-Antoine Capton on Buying Reese Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine and Doubling Down on Hollywood Amid Consolidation (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Selly Sy/Netflix Netflix ‘s smash hit heist series “ Lupin ” is back bigger and bolder after three years, and its French star Omar Sy , who plays French gentleman thief Assane Diop, has something to do with it. Sy, who served as artistic producer on previous installments, makes his debut as co-showrunner alongside Louis Leterrier for the show’s fourth part, on top of co-producing it through their joint banner Carrousel Studios. Related Stories Trump Says Execution of Fort Hood Shooter by Firing Squad Will Not Be Livestreamed Judge Extends Block on Trump's White House Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico Speaking in an interview with Variety ahead of the Oct. 23 launch, Sy revealed he made greater creative control a condition of his return on the show. Popular on Variety “There were quite a few moments in previous seasons when I felt frustrated because things I wanted didn’t necessarily end up on screen. So my condition for continuing was that I would have a little more say in the decisions. They gave me that role, and it allowed me to change things,” Sy said during the zoom interview, sitting against a red backdrop of “Lupin” featuring an animated silhouette of Diop and the Eiffel Tower. The new season picks up four years after the events of Part 3, with Assane behind bars before finding himself targeted by a mysterious copycat who pulls off a string of elaborate heists in his name. With a bigger budget from Netflix, Sy and Leterrier leaned further into the show’s superhero-like qualities, expanding its universe beyond the novels of Maurice Leblanc and weaving some futuristic elements. “We’re moving a little further away from Maurice Leblanc…. We brought it more into our own universe,” said Sy. “That’s why we’re going further into the prison setting, introducing new technologies and all these different elements. We’re embracing modernity, whether it’s through the prison itself or all the technology that the copycat uses to trap Assane.” Emmanuel Guimier/Netflix The challenge, Sy says, was to preserve what made “Lupin” a global hit while making the new season feel fresh enough to draw in viewers who have never watched the series. The new role also allowed Sy to bring in rising French actor Théo Christine and explore more emotional side of Assane’s story, Sy, who’s currently shooting Bradley Cooper’s Ocean prequel alongside Margot Robbie, has carved out a career in Hollywood and in European cinema, often serving as a producer on projects exploring social and political issues. He starred in and produced Mathieu Vadepied’s “Father & Soldier,” which shed light on the largely overlooked history of Senegalese soldiers who fought for France during WWI. His upcoming French projects include Ladj Ly’s “Dumas: Diable Noir” (“Black Dumas”), which reunites him with Christine and tells the story of Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, the formerly enslaved man who became France’s first Black general and whose son would go on to become one of the country’s most celebrated writers. Slated for release in October 2027, “Black Dumas” will arrive just months after France’s presidential election, which is shaping up to be one of the country’s most divisive in decades, with the far right leading polls and political tensions running high. “One thing I’m sure of is that ‘Dumas’ is going to generate a lot of debate and discussion,” said Sy, who’s lived in Los Angeles for years but still votes in France. “We need conversations right now. I just hope they can be calm, thoughtful conversations rather than heated ones.” While he had broken through with his first leading role in the French comedy “Intouchables,” it’s his part as Assane Diop in “Lupin” which turned Sy into an international star in 2021. Like “Emily in Paris,” “Lupin” has contributed to boosting tourism in the French capital, and has been hugely successful internationally on Netflix, although the latter has even more merit, being in French. You’re co-showrunner on this season. What made you want to get more involved creatively, and how did that change the way you worked on the series? The truth is, I’ve been involved in the same way from the very beginning. My involvement hasn’t changed. I’ve always been part of all the conversations, from the first to the last. The difference is that before, I was allowed to participate and make suggestions, but I couldn’t make the decisions or necessarily see those ideas through. There were quite a few moments in previous seasons when I felt frustrated because things I wanted didn’t necessarily end up on screen. So my condition for continuing was that I would have a little more say in the decisions. They gave me that role, and it allowed me to change things. For example, bringing in Théo Christine was something we wanted to do, and we went after him. There are decisions like that which might seem quite radical but can take the show somewhere different. That’s what this new role has allowed me to do. But in terms of my involvement, it’s been the same from the start. I just have a little more decision-making power now. Emmanuel Guimier/Netflix I found the father-son relationship with Théo Christine in the first episode incredibly moving. You also worked together with this young actor on Ladj Ly’s “Dumas: Diable Noir,” didn’t you? What’s funny is that actually happened afterward. We approached Théo for “Lupin,” and he said yes. Then, while we were working on the series, he got the role in “Dumas.” The first episode feels more dramatic than previous seasons, especially with the father-son relationship. Was that something you particularly wanted to explore? What’s great about this series is that you have a bit of everything. There’s drama, but there’s also comedy, lighter moments, flamboyant characters and all the action that comes with it. It’s really a place where you can put so many different things. That’s why I always say that “Lupin” is my favorite toy. You can turn it in every direction, you can do all sorts of things in the same universe and with the same character. Were you also interested in exploring the prison setting more extensively this season? Yes, because ultimately we’re dealing with a thief, and prison is part of that world. It’s something we hadn’t really explored before. In the first season, there’s a short sequence where he’s in prison, and we also touch on that world through his father, but we’d never really gone into it in depth. This time, we wanted to explore it further, and we also filmed it a little differently. The prison almost has a futuristic, science-fiction quality. It feels quite stylized. We brought it more into our own universe. That’s really what this season does. We’re fully embracing the world we’ve created. That’s why we’re going further into the prison setting, introducing new technologies and all these different elements. We’re moving a little further away from Maurice Leblanc and bringing more of our own ideas into it. We’re embracing modernity, whether it’s through the prison itself or all the technology that the copycat uses to trap Assane. The production looks bigger and more ambitious. Did you have a significantly larger budget this time? We definitely had more resources. And we have to acknowledge that, because Netflix would be very upset if we said otherwise! They gave us the means to make this season, and it was important to us that you could see and feel that on screen. There’s almost a superhero quality to this season, particularly with the idea of Lupin versus Lupin. It feels a little like a Marvel movie. Yes, but actually, when I say we’re moving away from Maurice Leblanc, that’s one area where we’re not. He did that several times himself. He brought in Sherlock Holmes, and at one point Lupin even faces another Lupin. Maurice Leblanc had already done that. I think it’s Marvel that copied Maurice Leblanc! But seriously, from the very beginning, when we decided to bring Lupin back and make this series, that’s how we imagined the character. Louis [Leterrier] decided to film him using those codes. That’s why his coat is like a cape. We really conceived this character as a superhero. It’s also why you have those shots of him on the rooftops of Paris, with his silhouette against the skyline, almost like a shadow. That superhero dimension has always been part of our vision of the character, and we fully embrace it. I’ve only seen the first episode, but I already suspect that Assane’s best friend might have something to do with what’s going on. Is betrayal one of the central themes of this season? With “Lupin,” there’s always betrayal somewhere. It’s a battle of wits, a game of intelligence, and we need those twists. Very often, betrayal is part of that. One of the things I love about this series is that we established something in the first season that continues to work today: speculation. Everyone is trying to figure out who’s behind everything. It’s like a game of Cluedo, trying to guess who the killer is. I love that. It’s one of my favorite aspects of the series. That whole whodunit element is something we deliberately work on. It’s part of the pleasure of “Lupin,” both for us and for the audience. I feel that quite a few films and series have tried to copy “Lupin” in recent years. I’m not the one saying it! You said it, not me! Has the success of “Lupin” made you want to become more involved in creating other films and series, beyond acting and producing? Yes, absolutely. That’s exactly what we’re working on with Thomas [Benski], Louis [Leterrier] and Carrousel Studios. We’re developing projects that I hope we’ll be able to announce soon. Carrousel really came out of everything we experienced together on “Lupin.” Louis and I discovered each other artistically through this series. At a certain point, we reached another level in our collaboration, and we realized that together we were capable of creating these kinds of projects. Carrousel is really about taking that collaboration further and doing it on a much bigger scale. We’re working on things, and I hope we’ll soon be able to come out with an idea that is still cooking at the moment. What’s also remarkable about this new season of “Lupin” is that someone who has never seen the series could start watching with Part 4 and still get into it. Was making it accessible to new audiences important to you? Thank you, because that’s exactly what we wanted to achieve. That’s also why we took our time. Obviously, we’re continuing a series that has been watched by a lot of people, so there are things we had to preserve. But at the same time, we had to bring something new. Finding that balance was really the challenge, and it’s something we worked on enormously. So hearing you say that is very satisfying, because it’s exactly what we were trying to do. You’ve had a busy year. You starred in “Dumas: Diable Noir,” and you’re also shooting the new “Ocean’s” movie. Have you finished filming that? No, we’re still filming. Can you tell me anything about your character? I can’t! You know how these things work. You can’t really talk about anything until someone tells you exactly what you can say. And since we’re still shooting, I’m keeping quiet. You know what you know, and I can’t tell you anything more. But I can tell you we’re still working on it. We shot over the summer, and we’re now finishing it. It’s great. What’s Bradley Cooper like as a director? Bradley is someone who’s incredibly inspired. He’s very involved, very passionate. He’s completely immersed in what he’s doing. He really enjoys his work and throws himself into it. And because he’s also an actor, he has a way of communicating what he wants that makes it very easy for another actor to understand and deliver. I’d already worked with him as an actor on “Burnt.” Even back then, he was someone who shared a lot with the people around him. Now that he’s also behind the camera, it’s a real pleasure. It’s incredibly inspiring to watch him work. And because I’m also interested in exploring what’s happening behind the camera, particularly as a producer, seeing the way he approaches and invests himself in every aspect of a project is very inspiring for me. You’ve been working in Hollywood for several years now. Are there still things you’re particularly eager to do in the U.S. that you haven’t had the chance to do yet? I don’t really think that way. I don’t approach my career by telling myself that there’s a particular box I still need to tick. That’s not how I function at all. I started in this business with a certain momentum, and I’ve tried to keep moving without making too many plans or calculations. There are encounters, opportunities, things that inspire you. I see it as a movement that continues rather than something that needs to be planned out. Take Carrousel, for example. It started with my meeting Louis, then Thomas, and that led to Carrousel. It’s the same with Bradley. We met on “Burnt,” we got along really well, and today he’s calling me to work with him on this new project. That’s how things happen for me. I don’t sit down and think that I need to do this or that next. It’s not my way of working. The things I do come more from my gut than from my head. What’s interesting about the U.S. industry right now is that alongside all the consolidation, with Paramount and Warner Bros., there are also a lot of independent companies and extraordinary creative talent. That’s what I believe in more. I believe in what’s being created a little on the margins, with lighter, more flexible structures that are more focused on creativity and on bringing something new. Because on the other side, the studios are becoming bigger and bigger. But the more they merge, the more they become fixed and rigid. What’s exciting about creating things is that sense of freedom, that lightness and the ability to adapt. And coming back to Carrousel, that’s exactly what we want to preserve: the ability to move quickly and adapt quickly. You also have Ladj Ly’s “Dumas: Diable Noir” coming out next year, possibly around the time of the French elections. Given the political climate, do you think a film like that could have a particular resonance? What role can cinema play in these debates? One thing I’m sure of is that “Dumas” is going to generate a lot of debate and discussion. For me, that’s also one of the things cinema can do. It’s not its only purpose, obviously, but it can create conversations. When you make a film like “Dumas,” that’s also something you hope to provoke. And given the current political context, I do think a film like this will generate discussion. We need conversations right now. I just hope they can be calm, thoughtful conversations rather than heated ones. You’re still based in Los Angeles, right? Yes, I’m still in the United States. So you’re watching what’s happening in France from a distance? No, I’m not watching from a distance. I’m here, I’m right in the middle of it, and I feel what’s happening. Although you have plenty of problems in the U.S. as well. The thing is, the problems in the United States aren’t my problems. My problems are here. So your heart is still in Paris? Obviously. articles.full_text: Oct 16, 2026 6:06am PT Russell Brand Trial: Second Woman Alleges He Was a ‘Wild-Eyed Maniac’ as He Tried to Pull Her Into Bathroom By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Russell Brand Trial: Second Woman Alleges He Was a ‘Wild-Eyed Maniac’ as He Tried to Pull Her Into Bathroom 39 minutes ago Jenna Ortega Says She Hopes ‘Klara and the Sun’ Encourages People to ‘Put Down the Computers and Phones’ as Dystopian Film World Premieres in London 15 hours ago Jack O’Connell, Sandra Hüller, Taron Egerton, George MacKay, Rosalind Eleazar, Florian Zeller and More Celebrate London Film Festival at Variety Dinner 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source PA Images via Getty Images Russell Brand ‘s criminal trial in London continued on Friday, with his second accuser alleging that Brand was a “wild-eyed maniac” as he tried to pull her into a bathroom. The actor and comedian has been charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault relating to incidents with six women spanning from 1999 to 2009. He has pleaded not guilty and denied all allegations against him. Related Stories ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Brutally Mocks Trump for Losing Nobel Peace Prize White House's New AI Website Confirms Trump Lost the 2020 Presidential Election Arriving to Southwark Crown Court, Brand wore a grey suit, white shirt and grey skinny tie. His wife, Laura Gallacher, was by his side again after not attending court on Thursday. He told reporters outside the courthouse that the trial has been an “extraordinary and stressful situation,” according to Sky News . Popular on Variety “But it is also an exploration of truth and justice. As I’ve said before, I pray for everybody involved,” he continued. “It’s in a way very, very sad but hopefully it can bring about some conclusions that are beneficial.” On Friday afternoon, the second alleged victim testified in person from behind a blue screen to protect her identity. In the U.K., all complainants in sexual assault cases are granted automatic lifelong anonymity if they so choose. She said she met Brand while working at MTV in 2001 and complimented his T-shirt, which read “I Am Spartacus,” referencing Stanley Kubrick’s 1960 film. It was “jovial and cheerful banter,” she said, according to Sky News. He then asked her where the bathroom was, and she agreed to show him as she was going that direction anyway. Once they got to the bathroom, “his demeanor changed,” she claimed. He allegedly grabbed her arm “hard” and pleaded with her to “come in, come in, come in,” she added. The woman tried to pull herself away, and said at this point Brand had a “wild look in his eye.” Once she broke free, she called him an “idiot” and then he “gave up” and went into the toilet. After the incident, she questioned how Brand “went from jovial and friendly to this wild-eyed maniac,” according to Sky News. She proceeded to tell two colleagues but not her managers as Brand, who hosted several programs for MTV at the time, was a huge “asset” to MTV and she thought she wouldn’t be believed. Following the Channel 4 documentary that investigated Brand in 2023, she reached out to the police. “I decided I thought it was the right thing to come forward,” she said. The woman was then cross-examined by Brand’s defense lawyer, Ian Winter KC, who claimed that Brand was not pulling her into the bathroom to assault her but rather to have a “consensual” sexual encounter. “Why would you try to drag someone into a toilet unless you wanted to assault them?” she replied. “I was there, I know what happened.” When Winter suggested that her memory of the alleged incident could have been altered by the 2023 media circus surrounding Brand, she said “I knew it was wrong,” adding that the documentary and press coverage “did not change my view of the situation.” On Thursday, the court heard from the first alleged victim via her police video interview. She described in detail an alleged rape by Brand that occurred at the Labour Party conference in 1999 after she met Brand at a cabaret show he was performing in. The woman was then cross-examined in person by Winter, again from behind a screen. The first complainant alleged on Thursday that after talking to Brand at the show, she invited him to come back to her hotel room. She said she thought he was gay at first and felt “sexually safe” with him. However, after she went to the bathroom, the complainant alleges that she emerged to find Brand partially undressed. He demanded that she take photos of him topless — which the court then viewed — and then allegedly raped her. “I was frightened. I remember feeling ‘what on earth have I got myself into’ — and then he did rape me,” she alleged. She claimed that she did say no, but struggled to get him off of her as he was “really heavy.” “I did say no,” she said. “I didn’t want his dirty penis inside me. articles.title: How Creators Make Money: Digital-Native Leaders on What Drives Audiences and Brands in the Attention Economy
articles.full_text: Oct 16, 2026 6:15am PT How Creators Make Money: Digital-Native Leaders on What Drives Audiences and Brands in the Attention Economy Variety's 'Strictly Business' podcast features conversations with industry leaders about the business of media and entertainment By Cynthia Littleton Plus Icon Cynthia Littleton Business Editor @Variety_Cynthia Latest FlyDubai Hijacking Incident Set for Development as an Inspirational Movie by Dori Media Group and India’s Sphereorigin 1 day ago YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom 1 day ago From Bob Hope to Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to ‘Wicked: One Wonderful Night’: How NBC Became America’s Home for TV Specials 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Variety via Getty Images On the latest episode of Variety ’s “ Strictly Business ” podcast, leaders of top digital-native firms discuss the factors that are funneling viewership, fan engagement and brand deals in the creator economy. Aaron Doades, senior VP of product management for Comscore , Zach Miller, president of JesserCo., Jarret Myer, CEO of Uproxx Studios, and Shaun Newsum, CEO of Culture Genesis, gathered in Los Angeles in September for a session held as part of Variety ‘s annual Entertainment and Technology Summit. This session, and much of the day, was devoted to examining how creators and social video platforms are rewiring our world, especially when it comes to marketing and advertising. Related Stories Trump Taps 'Devoted Fan' Katie Zacharia, a Fox News and CNN Commentator, as White House Press Secretary White House Has Spent More Than $440,000 on Pro-Trump TV Ads Paid for by U.S. Government; Administration Defends 'Unapologetically American' Spots and Denies They're Campaign Ads Myer, a digital media veteran, argues that the rise of superpowers in the creator economy (including sports influencers such as Jesser and IShowSpeed) is a movement back toward a monoculture environment. That’s a counterintuitive take given that the disintermediation of media is driving the upheaval across traditional Hollywood (exhibit A: the newly created Skydance colossus). Popular on Variety Listen to the podcast: “The idea that a creator, an event, a movie, a song can have a moment in culture that everyone’s talking about is happening more and more,” Myer says. “The creator economy is bigger than most people assume it is. They think it’s maybe someone who started a channel in their bedroom, but it’s studios, it’s artists, it’s creators that are all happening outside of the traditional Hollywood formation. More and more, these people are creating the monoculture moments that everyone is talking about. Missing out on that is missing out on the point of entertainment and culture.” Newsum, who leads a creator talent management firm, echoed Myer’s sentiment. “These moments of collective mass consciousness. At Culture Genesis, we call them mini-Super Bowls and they’re happening all the time. And you just don’t know about it,” Newsum says. “The creator economy is always on. There’s content being produced all the time.” Comscore’s Doades pointed to data showing that YouTube is becoming a preferred spot for marketers to find “pockets” of younger viewers who are increasingly hard to find on linear channels, outside of sports. “A lot of folks consume content almost exclusively on creator media. Now, when you’re looking at TV versus creator, the incrementality is massive,” Doades said. “We know that in March of 2026, Jesser had a greater unique reach than 14 live NBA games and the incrementality was 99% — meaning 99% of that audience did not tune in to those NBA games.” Miller in his role helps lead the charge for Jesser, the sports influencer who has enormous cachet with young NBA fans and the league itself. Miller has deep roots in traditional media but he sees no turning back for the content marketplace. “If you’re a marketer and you’re trying to reach a younger audience, you’re going to have a really hard time finding them on television. They’re just not watching TV unless they’re watching live sports,” he says. “But on YouTube, you can find these pockets of audience. The question for advertisers becomes, do you want to spend the money on the traditional media channel that has always been the place to spend it and cross your fingers and hope to find younger audiences there? Or do you need to broaden your strategy, swapping some of that spend on TV for digital channels that will allow you to reach that audience. Or at least expand the spend so that you reach your core audience that you’ve been historically reaching on TV.” (Pictured above, l. to r.: JesserCo.’s Zach Miller, Culture Genius’ Shaun Newsum, Uproxx Studios’ Jarret Myer and Comscore’s Aaron Doades) “Strictly Business” is Variety ’s podcast featuring conversations with industry leaders about the business of media and entertainment. articles.title: El Gouna Artistic Director Andrew Mohsen Puts ‘Discovery’ First: ‘We’re Trying to Draw Attention’ to Overlooked Films
articles.full_text: Oct 16, 2026 6:34am PT El Gouna Artistic Director Andrew Mohsen Puts ‘Discovery’ First: ‘We’re Trying to Draw Attention’ to Overlooked Films By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest 5 Fribourg Film Festival Takeaways, From Audience-Driven Programming to Political Cinema 7 months ago Leon Le on Reframing Vietnam Beyond the Western Gaze: ‘Vietnamese Stories Have Been Told Through a Dated, Disrespectful, Ignorant Lens’ 7 months ago Ukrainian Director Zhanna Ozirna Explores Intimacy Under Siege in ‘Honeymoon’ 7 months ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of El Gouna Film Festival For his first edition at the helm of Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival , artistic director Andrew Mohsen wants to widen the scope of what, and who, audiences discover on the shores of the Red Sea. “Discovery,” Mohsen asserts, sits at the heart of that vision, which builds on the festival’s established place as a showcase for prize winners and standout titles from Cannes, Venice and Berlin, while expanding the emphasis on emerging filmmakers and films that might otherwise escape the spotlight. Related Stories 'SNL' Opens Season With Mamdani Hanging Out With BFF Trump, Natalie Harp Going 'Obsession' Over President Hillary Clinton to Co-Host Podcast on 2026 Midterm Elections With Kara Swisher for Vox Media, Owned by James Murdoch It’s an evolution rather than a break with El Gouna’s past. Succeeding Marianne Khoury, Mohsen, a Cairo International Film Festival vet, who joined the El Gouna programming team in 2023 and later served as head of programming, is looking to deepen the festival’s ties to Arab filmmakers still developing an international profile and to forge stronger connections with filmmakers across Africa, in particular, where the relatively small pool of titles reaching the international festival circuit makes competition for projects particularly intense. Popular on Variety “We are trying to draw attention to the films that didn’t have the same coverage, or the films we feel our audiences need to see,” he tells Variety . Major festivals can screen around a hundred films in a given year, Mohsen notes, yet it is often the prize winners and established directors that remain in the international conversation, while others disappear. A former film critic, Mohsen has attended El Gouna since its 2017 launch. He wants to establish the festival as a go-to meeting point between Arab filmmakers and the international industry and more closely integrate its film selection with CineGouna , its industry and talent-development arm. Internally, that means getting the festival’s various branches working more closely together. Mohsen describes an “open kitchen between us,” with teams exchanging information about filmmakers, projects and guests who could connect with different parts of an increasingly well-established El Gouna network. That effort has become particularly important for Arab cinema . Mohsen says last year El Gouna had just one non-Egyptian Arab film in its narrative competition and one in documentary, its lowest showing for regional cinema since the festival began. Industry-wide competition for films, especially world or regional premieres, is part of the challenge. “We are trying our best to knock on all doors to see how we can expand our connection with the filmmakers,” Mohsen says. Projects backed by other festivals and funds can come with premiere commitments, so El Gouna has responded by investing through its own funding program and approaching filmmakers earlier. Mohsen is also widening the programming scope. Genre cinema has a larger presence this year, a choice he says reflects its growing prominence at major international festivals. Another current emerged across the selection, though not by any explicit design: fear, be it within families, under political regimes, or through anxieties and difficult realities characters themselves struggle to identify. Mohsen points to Miroslav Terzić’s “ Three Weeks After ,” a study of Serbian students confronting the aftermath of a classmate’s death by suicide, as one film in which that unease builds gradually. “You feel you are not really comfortable when you’re watching the film, that there’s something happening, but you cannot put your hand on,” he says. “I find this resonates with what’s happening in the world today.” Another addition is CineGouna Series, led by Egyptian screenwriter Mariam Naoum, an extension of the industry program into an ever more popular medium, both across the region and the wider international entertainment industry. Mohsen sees the move as a natural fit for Egypt, whose television industry has long supplied audiences across the Arab world with on-screen entertainment. “Series, they’re always happening. They’re always selling,” he says. “So we are very strong.” For Mohsen, that strength gives El Gouna an opportunity to invest in a field that remains relatively underrepresented at film festivals in the region. The expansion into series is part of a broader effort to make El Gouna useful to creators beyond simply screening their work. For Mohsen, that means making a case for what the festival can offer filmmakers navigating an increasingly crowded international circuit. “You want exposure, you want connections, you want audiences to react to your film? We can offer all of that.” Asked about the filmmakers he would most like to bring to El Gouna, Mohsen has two names on his wish list: Guillermo del Toro and Park Chan-wook on a festival jury, leading a master class, or simply taking part in the festival. “My two dreams,” he shares. articles.title: Chris Pratt and Pope Leo Explore St. Peter’s Tomb in Trailer for Vatican Documentary ‘Discovering the Origins’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Oct 16, 2026 6:35am PT Chris Pratt and Pope Leo Explore St. Peter’s Tomb in Trailer for Vatican Documentary ‘Discovering the Origins’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Guillermo del Toro Pays Tribute to Late ‘E.T.’ Designer Carlo Rambaldi Ahead of Hollywood Walk of Fame Honor: ‘A Worldwide Maestro of Magic’ (EXCLUSIVE) 23 hours ago Joanna Hogg to Preside Over El Gouna Film Festival Jury 2 days ago Qatar to Bow Domestic Feature Productions at Upcoming Doha Film Festival in ‘Watershed Moment’ 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source A new documentary pairs Pope Leo and Hollywood star Chris Pratt to delve into the history, religious passion and archaeological discoveries surrounding the tomb of St. Peter at the Vatican. Titled “Pétros Ení — Discovering the Origins,” the doc — which launches from the Rome Film Festival on Friday ahead of its international rollout — marks the 400th anniversary, on Nov. 18, of the consecration of St. Peter’s. Variety can reveal its trailer exclusively above. Related Stories Mark Ruffalo Tells Trump 'Hands Off Our F---ing Vote' or 'I'm Gonna Hulk Out': 'You Won't Like Me When I'm Angry' 'SNL U.K.' Mocks Donald Trump and Andy Burnham's First Meeting, Harvey Weinstein, Sam Altman and More in Wild Weekend Update Featuring footage rarely seen by the general public, it “explores how Peter’s burial place became a center of devotion for early Christians and, eventually, the foundation for the first great basilica built under Emperor Constantine,” as the synopsis puts it. The words “Pétros Ení,” in the title, refer to a Greek inscription than means “Peter is here” found near the apostle’s burial grounds. Pratt, who is best known to audiences for starring in the “Guardians of the Galaxy” and “Jurassic World” franchises, guides viewers on a journey beneath the basilica to discover the history and archaeology of one of Christianity’s most important sites. “The journey culminates with the special participation of Pope Leo XIV, who appears in the film’s final scenes to reflect on Peter and the meaning of his tomb beneath the Basilica,” the synopsis says. “It was an incredible honor to collaborate with Pope Leo and the Vatican on this project,” Pratt said in a statement. “The story of St. Peter is foundational to the Christian faith, and I am deeply grateful for the trust and access I was given to bring his legacy to the screen.” Pope Leo in “Pétros Ení — Discovering the Origins.” Courtesy AF Films, Vatican Media “Pétros Ení — Discovering the Origins” is directed by Spanish filmmaker Paula Ortiz and written by Andrea Tornielli. The doc is produced by AF Films, led by Frank Ariza and Manu Vega, together with Vatican Media and La Fabbrica di San Pietro. The high-profile doc is scheduled to start its international theatrical rollout in February 2027 during the opening weeks of Lent, the Christian season of prayer, reflection and preparation for Easter and the central celebration of the Christian calendar, according to the statement. The rollout will bring together regional distribution partners, with Hallow Studios handling U.S. and Canada distribution; Bosco Films releasing the documentary in Spain; and Cinépolis +Que Cine overseeing its theatrical release in Mexico, Brazil and Colombia. articles.title: Indonesian Zombie Franchise ‘Zona Merah: Dead City’ Unveils Teaser, Takes Outbreak Into the City
articles.full_text: Oct 16, 2026 6:41am PT Indonesian Zombie Franchise ‘Zona Merah: Dead City’ Unveils Teaser, Takes Outbreak Into the City By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Boo Junfeng’s ‘Trinity,’ Sidharta Tata’s ‘Slaughterground’ Among JAFF Market 2026 Selections 2 hours ago Singapore Media Festival Launches Creator Summit as Asia TV Forum Adds AI Zone, Microdrama Focus 5 hours ago Busan Takeaways: Record Crowds Meet a Political Storm as Asia’s Producers Close Ranks 6 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Screenplay Films The first teaser for “ Zona Merah : Dead City,” the big-screen adaptation of Indonesian zombie series “Zona Merah,” has landed ahead of the film’s Jan. 14, 2027, release in Indonesian cinemas. Screenplay Films, which unveiled the trailer on Friday, is billing the feature as the largest zombie production Indonesia has ever mounted. The source series, a Vidio original, has racked up more than 34 million views on the streamer. The film follows survivors struggling to outlast an undead threat that grows far beyond anything the show attempted. Related Stories Judge Extends Block on Trump's White House Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi and Daniel Brühl Lead a Star-Studded Lumière Fest Opening With Haynes Teasing ‘De Noche,’ Starring Pedro Pascal “As one of the most ambitious projects we’ve ever undertaken, we want to deliver an extraordinary cinematic experience for everyone, not just fans of the ‘Zona Merah’ series,” said Screenplay Films producer Wicky V. Olindo. Popular on Variety The teaser shows where that ambition has gone. The series stayed mostly in the countryside, among villages and quarantine sites. The film moves the outbreak onto city streets and into malls, with action also staged at an airport. Sidharta Tata returns to direct and shares duties on the feature with co-director Fajar Martha Santosa. “From day one, we knew we had to go all out for ‘Zona Merah: Dead City.’ We filmed across three cities in Indonesia, worked with hundreds of extras, and built incredible set pieces,” Tata said. Several faces from the series are back, including Aghni Haque, Andri Mashadi, Devano, Maria Theodore and Lukman Sardi. Joining the franchise for the first time are Bryan Domani, Shindy Huang, Myesha Lin, Derby Romero and Luna Maya. Maya is also an executive producer on the film. articles.title: Anna Faris Was “Hurt” By Chuck Lorre’s Comments About Her ‘Mom’ Exit: “Yikes”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff & Catherine Tate Join ‘Bad Fairies’ Cast With Cynthia Erivo ‘The Beekeeper 2’ Teaser: Jason Statham Kicks Rogue Govt. Agent Butt To Metallica In First Look At Sequel Anna Faris Was “Hurt” By Chuck Lorre’s Comments About Her ‘Mom’ Exit: “Yikes” View All October 15, 2026 4:38pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Anna Faris responds to Chuck Lorre's comments about her 'Mom' exit. Robert Voets/Warner Bros./Christopher Polk/Deadline Six years after announcing her departure from CBS ‘s Mom , Anna Faris has reacted to Chuck Lorre ‘s comments about her exit. On Thursday, the actress shared a statement explaining that she “never took a day of [the show] for granted” after series co-creator Lorre wrote in his new memoir Sitcom that he “was, in fact, correct” about his initial reluctance to cast her as Christy Plunkett in the sitcom. Related Stories Books Chuck Lorre Q&A On The Care & Feeding Of Sitcom Stars & Why A WGA Strike Doomed Democracy Casting ‘Mom’ Star Anna Faris Exits CBS Comedy Series After Seven Seasons “Yikes. Yes, I read a few things. I really didn’t see that coming. Of course it hurts,” she began in a statement on Instagram . “Chuck gave me a job I loved, and for seven years I never took a day of it for granted. I’m proud of what we made together, and nothing changes how grateful I am for those people and those years.” Faris continued: “I’ve been sober for a year and a half. I was on a show about recovery, and then I lived it. Now I’m healthy, I’m working, and I’m happier than I’ve been in a long time. If anyone reading this is where I was, I hope that’s useful. It gets better. I’m proof.” Watch on Deadline Premiering in 2013, Faris starred in the first seven seasons of Mom as Christy, a recovering alcoholic who struggles to maintain a job, her family and her sobriety as her mom Bonnie (Allison Janney), who’s also in recovery, moves in with her. View this post on Instagram Faris left the show in 2020 to “pursue new opportunities,” leaving Janney as the sole lead for the eighth and final season, which ended in 2021. In an excerpt from Sitcom , Lorre wrote: “I wasn’t sure Anna would be appropriate for this kind of material. Then I thought about how badly I’d bungled my working relationship with Charlie Sheen.” After his experience with Charlie Sheen on Two and a Half Men , Lorre recalled conceding, “Someone’s personal life is none of my business. The mom in Mom would be, and should be, Anna Faris.” Lorre added: “As the years went by, it became apparent that my initial reluctance to hire Anna was, in fact, correct. After six years, she left the show for mysterious reasons that were not mysterious to anyone on the show.” Netflix Shakeup: Bajaria’s Exit Signals Changes To Come As Rice Hire Elicits Praise Steven Soderbergh To Work With Matt Reeves On Final Weeks Of ‘The Batman II’ Shoot Tim Burton And ‘Klara And The Sun’ Author Kazuo Ishiguro’s Secret Project ‘Street Fighter’ $4M Previews, A24 Holmes Doc Draws $2M Read More About: 13 Comments

articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt ‘Seeker’ Writer-Producer Michael Learner Inks With WME & Untitled Lauren Cohan, Mark O’Brien & Mia Tomlinson Join Prime Video’s ‘Stillwater’ As Series Regulars Talia Ryder, Elizabeth Marvel & Bill Camp Join STX & Aggregate’s True-Crime Thriller ‘PRƎPPY’ View All January 6, 2026 8:12am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sydney Sweeney in 'The Housemaid Daniel McFadden/Lionsgate Amid big box office success for The Housemaid , its Freida McFadden thriller starring Sydney Sweeney , Amanda Seyfried and Brandon Sklenar, Lionsgate is moving toward a 2026 production start for a sequel, The Housemaid’s Secret , based on the second novel in McFadden’s bestselling trilogy. The project has been in development for the past few months, with Sweeney eyeing to return to star and exec produce, and co-star Michele Morrone also looking to reprise. The Housemaid’s Secret is another wildly thrilling book in Freida’s series that has captivated readers worldwide, and we look forward to translating it into a similarly rousing and riotous moviegoing experience.” Said Hidden Pictures’ Lieberman, a producer on both Housemaid films, “We’re thrilled with the reception and incredibly proud of this entire team from Freida McFadden to our partners at Lionsgate, and the outstanding work of Paul and Laura. Most rewarding has been seeing how strongly audiences are connecting with the film.”

articles.title: ‘Law & Order’ Season 26, Episode 2 Recap: What Happened To Det. Vincent Riley In Reid Scott’s Final Episode?
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Armando Tinoco Armando Tinoco Staff Writer @armietinoco More Stories By Armando ‘Law & Order’ Season 26, Episode 2 Recap: What Happened To Det. Vincent Riley In Reid Scott’s Final Episode? Aaron Paul Mourns ‘Breaking Bad’ Co-Star RJ Mitte: “I Am So Sorry You Were Hurting, My Friend” Aaron Sorkin On ‘The West Wing’ Revival: “It Would Be Very, Very Tricky To Do In The Current Environment” View All October 15, 2026 8:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Reid Scott NBC SPOILER ALERT: This post contains details on Law & Order Season 26, Episode 2, which aired on NBC on Thursday, October 15. Earlier this year, Deadline reported that Reid Scott , who plays Senior Detective Vincent Riley, was leaving the NBC procedural. Scott’s exit finally aired in the second episode of Season 26 titled “Into the Mystic.” The episode opens with Riley sitting at his work desk, and something prompts him to look for Ray Biller. When he arrives at Ray’s apartment, the person who answers the door says Ray isn’t there. Riley orders the guy to call Ray to find out where he is. Related Stories News 'Newlyweds': Bruce Helford Tapped As New Showrunner In 'Anything But Love' Reunion With Jamie Lee Curtis, Production Hiatus Extended News 'Friends' Returning To Channel 4 After 15 Years Moments later, Riley calls Nolan Price (Hugh Dancy) and tells him, “Need to talk to you right away. Call me back.” Watch on Deadline Riley then calls Theo Walker (David Ajala) and tells him he’s headed to a bar as “something is cooking.” After heading to the bar, Riley gets a text from Walker saying he’s on his way. As Riley approaches the bar, he notices Ray exiting the establishment. Riley follows Ray, who tells him he needs to talk. However, when he turns around, he shoots Riley twice in the chest and runs off. Walker arrives at the scene and notices a man running away with a gun in hand. However, by the bar, there’s a lot of commotion as Riley bleeds from the gunshot wounds. Walker calls for help, applies pressure, and yells, “Vince, stay with me, come on!” Lieutenant Jessica Brady (Maura Tierney) arrives at the hospital, and Walker fills her in on what happened, leaving her shocked and without words. At the hospital, the doctor tells Walker they couldn’t save Riley, leaving all his colleagues in despair. Robert Calvino, played by James Badge Dale, is introduced to help investigate Riley’s death. Riley’s wife shows up at the police station and tells them that he had been withdrawing “lots of cash” recently. Although Riley’s wife didn’t know what the money was for, she did note that he was a drinker. Jessica Brady and Robert Calvino visit a woman who Riley had been arguing with hours earlier on the day that he died. The pregnant woman tells officers that Riley was giving her cash as he “felt guilty” for killing her husband years before. Brady and Calvino find out Riley was at Ray Biller’s apartment and talk to his friend, who corroborates what Riley was doing there the night he was killed. When they get back to the office, Nolan tells them that Ray Biller’s brother, Wayne, whom he found for murder, was killed in prison. The police find Ray Biller, who was attending his brother’s Wayne funeral, and arrest him as the prime suspect in Riley’s death. Actor Ryan Eggold made an appearance reprising his role as Matt Riley, the troubled brother of Detective Vincent Riley, showing up in court and wanting justice for his brother’s death. The prosecution runs into a problem when Ray Biller’s defense argues that they can’t prove he was the one who killed Riley, as they didn’t recover a weapon. DA Nicholas Baxter (Tony Goldwyn) is determined to put Walker on the stand, but Nolan pushes back as he doesn’t believe Walker actually saw Ray Biller as the man who killed Riley. On the day of the verdict, Ray Biller was found guilty on the charge of first-degree murder. Although it was a victory for the prosecution, doubt remains over whether Walker told the truth, and Nolan remains skeptical about whether they did the right thing. In July, Deadline first reported that Reid Scott was leaving Law & Order , after joining in Season 23. He reportedly decided to exit the NBC procedural due to the strain of the cross-country commute to New York City, where the series is filmed.
