articles.title: From ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ To Scottish Indie Boss: Kevin McKidd On Ferryman Films & His New Show ‘The Only Suspect’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart BBC Studios’ Boss Says Streaming Is The Future But Linear Still Pays The Bills MIPCOM 2026 Takeaways: Surfing The New Wave Of TV With YouTube, ‘Baywatch’, Skydance, Banijay & More How Matthew Gray Gubler Went Back To The Drawing Board For ‘Einstein’ View All October 16, 2026 5:33am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kevin McKidd in 'The Only Suspect' Red Planet Pictures, David Hindley Scottish multi-hyphenate Kevin McKidd has launched an indie on home turf, and says he’s using his Hollywood experience to make it work. When Deadline speaks with him in his New York hotel, McKidd is in the throes of filming Conviction , the Elisabeth Moss-starring Hulu legal drama from House creator David Shore. After that, he’s headed to L.A. to direct some episodes of ABC’s Grey’s Anatomy , the show in which he starred as Dr. Owen Hunt before he said goodbye to the role in 2026 after almost two decades. Meanwhile, he’s recently wrapped on UK drama The Only Suspect . Related Stories News Sky-ITV: UK Culture Secretary "Minded To Intervene" Over $2.1B Merger News ITV Buys 'The Galway Bay Murders' Thriller Starring Kate Mulgrew & Colm Meaney In Conviction McKidd plays the husband of Moss’ Neve Harper, a confident lawyer who finally has her shot at a career-making case: a high-profile murder where the husband is accused of killing his wife by setting their home on fire. Watch on Deadline The conversation, however, quickly turns to his native Scotland. McKidd is using the smarts he learned in the U.S. business to power up Ferryman Films , his indie label out of Edinburgh. “I’ve got access to this American skillset and these people who’ve been showrunners on big shows,” he says, “and then there are these Scottish writers with all this potential. It’s really been fun to see that cross-pollination.” One project he’s working on but keeping mum about is Troubadour. “We’re developing that with Bruno Heller ( Rome ) who is the chieftain of it, but Kieran Hurley, who’s quite an accomplished Scottish playwright, is co-writing with him,” McKidd says. His new indie banner has partnered with STV Studios, the production and distribution arm of Scottish broadcaster STV run by former NBCUniversal exec David Mortimer. An adaptation of William Shaw detective novel The Red Shore is the first collaboration resulting from the deal. There’s also Friends Like These for the BBC in the works, a female-led show about a group of 30-something friends. Gillian McCormack ( Counsels ) is writing. A Guilty Secret One thing that has wrapped is psychological drama The Only Suspect , adapted by Simon Ashdown ( Trigger Point ) from the novel by Louise Candlish . It is for ITV in the U.K., with Farren Blackburn directing. Moving between the present day and mid-1990s London, it follows Alex (McKidd) and his wife, Beth, played by Amaka Okafor ( Black Rabbit ). The devoted couple’s seemingly picture-perfect suburban life hides a devastating truth linked to a dead body—Alex, it transpires, is the man who buried that body, and has been harboring the dark secret ever since. The Only Suspect Red Planet Pictures, David Hindley “He’s very much a kind of antihero,” McKidd says of his character. “That’s a really delicious challenge—to have an audience root for a character while also having major mixed feelings about them. I find those characters a fantastic knot to untie.” The setting for the 1990s part of the series is Camden, London, which was very much the epicenter of the U.K.’s Cool Britannia movement. It struck a chord with McKidd, given he was one of the stars of Trainspotting , a defining movie of that era. He played the memorable and tragic character of Tommy in the Danny Boyle film and recently attended a 30 th anniversary screening of the film in Edinburgh. “I spent my formative years exactly in the period of time in which we see the younger versions of these characters,” McKidd says. “I didn’t kill anyone, thankfully,” he quips. “But there are those mistakes that you make in your twenties as you’re figuring out life, which is what this show is all about. I was able to get into that character because it weirdly reflected my own life, going back to this place in the same way as Alex as he has to go back and face what happened in the 90s.” McKidd says viewers should buckle up for twists and turns. “Every episode keeps you guessing. Just when you think you know what’s happening, they pull the rug from under you. It has quite a dark psychology, but there’s a lot of humor in it too.” Red Planet Pictures is producing. The venerable U.K. label is majority-owned by Fremantle, which is handling international sales and will be pushing at MIPCOM. It is Red Planet’s second Candlish adaptation after Our House, one of ITV’s biggest new drama launches back in 2022. Explaining why McKidd was such a good fit for The Only Suspect , Red Planet’s Tom Mullens, who is an exec producer on the show, says: “He’s such a clever actor with great dramatic range and a chameleon-like versatility, which was essential for the part of Alex, a deeply complex character who goes on a cathartic journey across the four episodes. “Not only do we see a charming and manipulative Alex as he protects his secret, but we also see a man who loves his wife and is faced with an impossible choice, knowing that by confronting his guilt and telling the truth, he might also destroy his life and marriage.” Heading Home McKidd starred in several U.K.-produced shows during his time on Grey’ s Anatomy but still noticed a change when it came to filming The Only Suspect . Grey’s Anatomy ABC, Scott Everett White “On [ Grey’s Anatomy ] we have three cameras rolling all the time, every take. But with The Only Suspect it was a single camera, which is pretty much where I started, in indie films in the ’90s and the early 2000s. “With three cameras, it can dilute what you’re doing. [Director] Farren Blackburn and the DP did such a good job at using that one camera and always placing it in the optimal position to get the most intense version of that setup.” McKidd’s own directing work has made him more of a team player. “Before, I was probably a bit of a pain in the arse. I was like ‘You know, my character wouldn’t do that.’ Now I’m much more accommodating. I know what it is like to sit in that director’s chair.” With experience in front of and behind the camera, he says he’s also happy to relinquish control when an acting gig comes up. “When I worked with Ben Williams, who was brilliant [as the director of Hideo Yokoyama adaptation Six Four ], and Farren, the first thing I said to them was, ‘I’m not going to come in as this actor-director who’s going to be rolling his eyes at your choices. I can take that chip in my brain out and just focus on being an actor. I’m just going to put my complete trust in you.’” Being an indie boss, meanwhile, is another skillset. It requires patience as the options are picked up, writers are attached and pitches made to buyers. “I’ve got this underpinning of being a theater actor, really, who fell into all this TV and film,” McKidd says. “Then I was plugged into the Hollywood system, having come from very independent grassroots. I’ve got one foot in both camps, and that can benefit my acting, but also the company.” With Conviction calling, McKidd signs off: “I’m always trying to be a moving target. That’s what I want for the company. I want to keep people guessing.” Netflix Shakeup: Bajaria’s Exit Signals Changes To Come As Rice Hire Elicits Praise Steven Soderbergh To Work With Matt Reeves On Final Weeks Of ‘The Batman II’ Shoot Tim Burton And ‘Klara And The Sun’ Author Kazuo Ishiguro’s Secret Project ‘Street Fighter’ $4M Previews, A24 Holmes Doc Draws $2M Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Russell Brand Accuser Argues He Wanted To Assault Her When Trying To Drag Her Into A Toilet: “The Intent Was There”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Russell Brand Accuser Argues He Wanted To Assault Her When Trying To Drag Her Into A Toilet: “The Intent Was There” International Insider: Surfing To MIPCOM Cannes; Russell Brand Trial Begins; Nicole Wallace Interview UK’s Bectu Union Unveils New Chief View All October 16, 2026 5:44am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand Getty Russell Brand ‘s second accuser in his trial has argued “intent was there” to assault her when the presenter allegedly tried to drag her into a toilet at the MTV offices in London 25 years ago. The accuser, who we are calling C2, said Brand went from “affable, jovial and friendly” to “suddenly turning into a wild-eyed maniac, trying to pull me into the toilet.” She was working for MTV in London at the time and had been showing Brand where the toilet was, she said. Once she showed him, C2 alleged Brand “was trying to pull me into the bathroom.” Related Stories Legal Russell Brand Trial: Woman Alleges She Was Raped By Star In Hotel Room After He Posed For Semi-Nude Photos News Russell Brand's Accusers: Prosecutors Claim 'Despicable Me' Star Preyed On Women In TV Industry During "Frenzied" & "Wild-Eyed" Incidents “I said, ‘What are you doing? Are you mad? Let me go’, and then he started to plead almost, saying, ‘Go on, go on, come in,'” added C2. “He had hold of my arm hard in a grip and I’m pulling back out towards the corridor.” Watch on Deadline After about 20 seconds, C2, who described herself as “physically stronger than the average woman,” said she was able to “wrench herself away.” She added that she subsequently told two colleagues but didn’t tell her employers as she was “scared” and thought it would be “my word against his.” Brand faces seven charges, encompassing three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault, and one of indecent assault. The charges pertain to allegations made by six women, spanning a decade from 1999 to 2009. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges and has consistently denied wrongdoing. Under cross-examination from Brand’s lawyer, Ian Winter, C2 was questioned over whether at the time she could have actually felt that Brand wanted consensual sex, and it was only after she watched the 2023 documentary Russell Brand: In Plain Sight that she changed her view. C2 denied this. “Why would you drag someone into a toilet if you didn’t want to assault them?,” she added. “You don’t drag someone by the arm. You don’t grip someone and try and pull them. That’s not consensual. The intent was there. It could have been very different.” As they were walking towards the toilet before the incident, C2 said “nothing was suggested about romance, not a word.” She added that even though he was one of the flagship MTV presenters at the time, she did not see Brand again while working at the network. She did not come forward before seeing the documentary because “in 2001, it would have been my word against his,” C2 said, adding: “I had a job to consider, [and] came away relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me, and I managed to get myself out the situation. I just wanted a quiet life. I didn’t need this.” “Sex was a huge preoccupation for him” Yesterday, a police interview was played to the court from complainant C1, who alleged Brand raped her in his hotel room during the 1999 Labour Party conference in Bournemouth after he posed for semi-nude photos from her. He was appearing in a play at the time on the fringes of the conference. Today, a number of witnesses gave evidence supporting C1. John Rogers, who wrote a play Brand appeared in at the Labour conference, said the presenter had told him he had had an “encounter” with a woman that week. Brand’s “reaction was a bit odd” and “he was a bit flustered” when telling the story, according to Rogers. A flatmate of Brand’s during the Bournemouth conference, Andrew Dobson, alleged Brand wanted to leave hurriedly the morning after the alleged assault took place. “He came in and there was suddenly an urgency,” added Dobson. “It felt tense and confusing. I didn’t understand why.” Dobson said “sex was a huge preoccupation” for the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star. Before finding fame, he described Brand as “vibrant, egotistical, lively, demanding, persuasive and erratic.” Two acquaintances of C1’s also told the court via witness statement that she had told them about her alleged rape after watching the Brand documentary in 2023. One said C1 had told her she had been raped previously by her husband “and felt as if she were reliving this and completely froze” during the alleged assault. C1 told her she was worried about backlash from her community if she reported Brand at the time, this acquaintance said. The other said she was told by C1 over WhatsApp after C1 had reported Brand to the police. The police had told her she should only share the information with “trusted persons,” this witness said, via a pre-written statement. The trial continues. articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac ‘Dear William:’ Film Adaptation Of David D. Magee’s Memoir Underway Rita Coburn & Jeffrey Wright To Bring Their Feature Doc ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel With A Cause’ To London BFI & Chanel Filmmaker Award: ‘Ish’ Director Imran Perretta Among 2026 Winners View All October 16, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Matt Passmore, Hudson Macread, Gabriel Nagy and Emily Rose. EXCLUSIVE: A big-screen adaptation of David D. Magee’s memoir Dear William : A Father’s Memoir of Addiction, Recovery, Love, and Loss has been greenlit, with production underway in Mississippi, and Andrew Hyatt ( The Blind and Paul ) directing. Hyatt has also written the film’s screenplay. Matt Passmore, Emily Rose, Gabriel Nagy and Hudson Macready star in the film, which tells the true story of a family confronting addiction and loss while finding its way back to one another. Magee is also producing the film, alongside Cory Pyke. Passmore plays David, a divorced, broke, and unraveling father who sets out for California with his oldest son, William (Nagy), on a two-thousand-mile drive. Along the way, he discovers that they are both struggling with addiction. The synopsis continues: With Rose portraying Kent and Macready playing Hudson, the story expands beyond father and son to follow a family reckoning with the truths it has kept hidden, navigating marriage, loss, and faith, and discovering the possibility of hope and joy on the other side. At its heart is a son’s final request that gives his father a lifelong purpose. articles.title: Rafe Spall On Playing An Amnesiac Super Sleuth In ‘The Death Of Sherlock Holmes’: “This Is A Clean Slate”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Hudson Williams, Zach Galifianakis & Jay Baruchel Set For ‘The Assembly’ Season 2 At Canada’s CBC ‘Down Cemetery Road’: Apple TV Detective Drama Adds 12 To Season 2 Radial Entertainment Completes Busy MIPCOM Week With ‘Making A Serial Killer’ Season 3 Order View All October 16, 2026 6:37am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'The Death of Sherlock Holmes' Fabienne Berchtold, Silver Reel Rafe Spall was one of the biggest names at MIPCOM Cannes this week where he gave Deadline his take on playing super sleuth Sherlock Holmes. The Trying star is leading The Death of Sherlock Holmes , which fills the gap between the detective’s apparent death at the Reichenbach Falls in 1891 and his reappearance in The Adventure of the Empty House three years later. Set against the Swiss Alps, the story follows an Englishman (Spall) found barely alive in an icy mountain stream by local woman Alma ( Deleila Piasko ) and her young son, Franz. When the village doctor is found murdered, villagers turn on the boy – leaving the amnesiac stranger, who is experiencing flashbacks to a previous life in England, as his only hope as his powers of deduction return. Related Stories News International Insider: Surfing To MIPCOM Cannes; Russell Brand Trial Begins; Nicole Wallace Interview Executives BBC Studios' Boss Says Streaming Is The Future But Linear Still Pays The Bills “What makes it original is the fact that he’s someone who has no idea who he is,” Spall told us at the Majestic Hotel on the Croisette. “He gets these flashes of brilliant deduction that lead him toward understanding what kind of person he is, and eventually perhaps figuring out that he’s the most famous detective in the world.” Watch on Deadline Piasko said the relationship between Holmes and Alma is central to the story. “What’s very special is that this Englishman doesn’t judge her,” she added. “She’s a single mother living in a small village, and she’s treated with contempt, experiencing a kind of exclusion. With him, it’s different.” Spall said these circumstances of amnesia allowed him to create a fresh take on the character and freed him from comparison to other Sherlocks. “It’s a clean slate in a way. I didn’t feel like I was following in a long line of great actors who have played him in the past — Benedict Cumberbatch, Jeremy Brett, Basil Rathbone, Robert Downey Jr. and all these amazing people.” The show is a co-production between Sky and SRF in Switzerland, Germany’s ARD Degeto and the Bell Media-owned Sphere Abacus, which brought Spall to Cannes this week. The series will broadcast on Sky in the U.K. and Ireland and also goes out on Sky in Switzerland and Germany. FFF Bayern from Germany and Italy’s IDM Film Commission are supporting the series. Spall’s face was all over town given he’s also starring in Channel 4 drama Number 10 , which ITV Studios has been shopping. He talked about playing a British Prime Minister – revealing he actually met one in the research phase – and addressed his role as Arthur Weasley in the upcoming HBO TV series Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone – chuckling as he compared his role with that of his dad, Timothy Spall, in the movie series. Here’s the full interview with Spall and Piasko. DEADLINE: Rafe, There are lots of different versions of Sherlock coming through at any one time. This one is slightly unique in that he is suffering from amnesia and doesn’t know who he is. How did that color what you wanted to bring to the character? What did you think was the core of this version of Sherlock? RAFE SPALL: What makes it original is the fact that he’s someone who has no idea who he is. He gets these flashes of brilliant deduction that lead him toward understanding what kind of person he is, and eventually perhaps figuring out that he’s the most famous detective in the world. It’s a clean slate in a way. I didn’t feel like I was following in a long line of great actors who have played him in the past — Benedict Cumberbatch, Jeremy Brett, Basil Rathbone, Robert Downey Jr. and all these amazing people. The comparison is somewhat taken away by the fact that I can say, if people think I’m rubbish in it, that it’s a different Sherlock Holmes. It was completely different. I would have been much more frightened if it had been one of the Conan Doyle novels, which is what Steven Moffat adapted. But the great characters in the modern Western canon are always ripe for interpretation. Hamlet gets done every year, and so does Sherlock Holmes, because they’re great pieces of work and great characters that can sustain different shapes and approaches. DEADLINE: Deleila, when Sherlock — or whoever he is at the start of the show — comes into Alma’s life, what does she make of this man who seems to have come from nowhere? He could be helpful, or he could be a disaster for her. DELEILA PIASKO: They are strangers, and they become partners in crime. We tell the story of them getting to know each other. They are both lost in the world, so their relationship is really at the core of the show. It’s about the relationship between the Englishman and Alma. It’s a journey with them. Alma realizes that she needs him. She’s a lone wolf, but at one point she needs a partner — somebody to help her. What’s very special is that this Englishman doesn’t judge her. She’s a single mother living in a small village, and she’s treated with contempt. She’s experiencing a kind of exclusion. With him, it’s different. It’s the beginning of a friendship — or whatever it becomes. DEADLINE: Most Sherlock Holmes stories are mysteries – intricate, complex and brilliantly written. Would you describe this series as a mystery, or does it fit somewhere else tonally? SPALL: Fans of the genre will be satisfied by the whodunit – the question of how something happened and the mysterious nature of it. They’ll also get a thrill from seeing flashes of this famous character’s powers of deduction. What’s interesting is that Conan Doyle got sick of writing Sherlock Holmes. He killed him off, with Holmes and Moriarty falling off the Reichenbach Falls. Then, I think, he missed the money, so three years later he brought him back. This is the first attempt I can think of to fill in the gap of what happened, so it isn’t based on a Conan Doyle novel. It’s a new story that, hopefully, fulfils people’s expectations of a Sherlock Holmes story. There’s a lot of mystery and a classic Holmes whodunit at its heart. DEADLINE: When did you first hear about the project, and what drew you to it? SPALL: My agent called and said they were doing a new version of Sherlock Holmes and asked if I’d like to speak to the people making it. I found it very charming and nice, and I thought it was really original. I was asked, I said yes, and here we are. It was probably about a year ago that it came to me, although I think the project had been around for a while and was then pulled together quite rapidly. DEADLINE: Deleila, was it a similar process for you? PIASKO: Yes, pretty much the same time. I read the script and thought it was fantastic. I was very lucky. SPALL: We had a fun time because we were filming in some pretty rough-and-ready places — the Swiss Alps, the Italian Alps and a great town called Regensburg in Bavaria. We were in fairly remote locations, so it was very important to be surrounded by nice people. We really got on with each other and had a good time making it. DEADLINE: With European co-productions, different parties can sometimes pull in different directions to serve their respective audiences. Did this feel more holistic and complete? PIASKO: There were many different approaches. Our show is about cultural clashes, and of course there are different experiences. It’s also a multilingual show, so behind the scenes you have to communicate somehow, but I think that’s the beauty of it. It makes the world bigger and fleshes it out, especially when you have different languages. It was very free creatively. We were very welcome to bring our nerves and our ideas into it. SPALL: From a trade point of view, it’s an interesting example of a new way of putting together big television in Europe. The bottom has fallen out of the American co-production market and a new way needed to be found. I can only speak from an English point of view, or as someone who predominantly makes British film and television, but I think there have been some very successful examples of this new model. This series is an example of the way the industry has changed and evolved. When it came to me, I knew Sky Switzerland and Sky Germany were putting up the initial money, and it was then acquired by Sky UK, which I had previously worked with. I was the only English person involved, which felt appropriate because Sherlock Holmes is in the Swiss Alps. DEADLINE: Rafe, you’re doing a lot of work at the moment. What does the next year or two look like for you? SPALL: I’m doing Harry Potter at the moment. If people like it, I’ll be doing that for a long time. Then I’m going to do Under Salt Marsh Season 2 next year. I’ve got Number 10 , which I think is coming soon, and ITV Studios is selling that. Maybe there’ll be another season of Trying — we’ll see. Who knows? I’m very lucky to be paid to do a job I love. It’s the only skill I could possibly exchange for cash. No one else would accept money for anything else I could offer. DEADLINE: And what does the next couple of years look like for you, Deleila? PIASKO: There are some things in the pipeline, but I can’t share them yet. Maybe there will be in a second season of The Death of Sherlock Holmes — we’ll see. There are also some other projects, including the German TV show Zweifel , which won Best Series at the Cannes Series festival in 2024. The second season will air next January. DEADLINE: Are you nervous about Harry Potter , Rafe? We’re hearing the sets are looking amazing, like nothing else. SPALL: I’ve never seen production values like it. I’ve been lucky enough to do things such as Prometheus and Jurassic World , big franchise projects, but I’ve never seen sets like these. Kate Hall, who does the hair and make up and worked on The Crown , is extraordinary. Holly Waddington, who won an Oscar for Poor Things , is doing the costumes. I’ve never come out of costume fittings feeling so excited. I was around true genius — a costume designer who just blows my mind. So I’m not nervous about it. I’m just really enjoying it. It’s funny that my dad played Ron’s rat and now I’m playing Arthur Weasley. The other day I was on set and Ron’s rat was there. I took a photograph next to it. If I had social media, I would post it. DEADLINE: Talking of which, do you worry about the social media reaction, given the controversy surrounding J.K. Rowling? SPALL: I’m mercifully not on any form of social media, and I don’t feel I have anything further to contribute to that debate. I’m just feeling really lucky to be part of something full of amazingly creative, brilliant people, all working at the top of their game. There are fabulous actors involved. Katherine Parkinson and I play the Weasley parents, and to my mind, she’s one of the best actors in the world. She’s phenomenal. The other day it was me, her, Kit Harington and Johnny Flynn. It was just fun. DEADLINE: You’ve said you’re hoping for a second season of The Death of Sherlock Holmes … SPALL: If people like it, we’ll do more of it. There are more stories to tell. WHITTOCK: I also wanted to ask you about Number 10 . The British prime minister is obviously never just one person and can be whoever you want him to be. But there is a picture in people’s minds of what the prime minister is. What was your take on playing that character? SPALL: It was pretty thrilling. It was one of the most challenging things I’ve ever done because Steven Moffat writes 10-page scenes, which is rare in modern television. And for a writer of Stephen’s quality, every comma needs to be observed. If it isn’t, you soon get reminded where it needs to be. It was technically pretty full-on, but wonderful. We built the entirety of the downstairs of Number 10, and it became one of my favourite things I’ve ever done. I’m playing a fictional prime minister. I was lucky enough to meet a real former prime minister to talk about who he could be. In a way, it could be anyone — practically anyone you meet on the street these days. They were very charming and generous. I loved doing it, and I hope people enjoy it. Stephen and Sue — his producing partner and wife — are powerhouses. Sue is one of the best producers the country has ever produced, and Stephen is one of the best writers. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. articles.title: ‘7 Miles Out,’ Starring Lucy Halliday, Tells a Coming-of-Age Story Full of Grief, Music and Friendship
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 15, 2026 2:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source '7 Miles Out' film still Courtesy of BFI London Film Festival British writer-director Carol Morley ( Dreams of a Life , The Falling ) has adapted her moving semi-autobiographical novel 7 Miles Out , about her adolescence in Stockport, near Manchester, during the 1970s and 1980s, into a coming-of-age journey for the big screen. Lucy Halliday ( Blue Jean , The Testaments ) stars as Ann, who struggles with grief after the death of her beloved father, portrayed by Aidan Gillen ( Game of Thrones, Peaky Blinders, Queer as Folk ), and finds escapism in the new-wave punk movement and her friendship with Hel. Gemma Whelan ( Game of Thrones, Killing Eve ) stars as her mother in the movie, which features a soundtrack fit for the era, full of Joy Division, New Order, The Raincoats and more. 7 Miles Out is as much a story about finding one’s own voice and creativity as it is an ode to friendship. Related Stories Business CNN Targets Cord-Cutters In Canada With Streaming Launch Lifestyle Sally Rooney's Books Pulled From U.K. Shelves Amid Controversy Over Palestine Action Support When local band Joy Division’s frontman Ian Curtis kills himself, and Hel leaves town, everything collapses for Ann, who turns to alcohol and casual sex. But a rekindling of the past and a rediscovered cassette tape may provide a pathway to a new beginning. Original songs performed in the film are written by Morley and Carly Paradis, who also handled the score. The cinematographer is Morley’s frequent collaborator Agnès Godard ( The Falling, Beau Travail ), with editing by Raluca Petre. (Time) travel to England a few decades ago with a clip for the film right here. 7 Miles Out world premieres in the official competition of the LFF on Saturday. Morley talked to THR about the challenges and joys of adapting one’s own novel, finding the right person to play Ann, and why, despite suicide, grief and other darkness, 7 Miles Out also features so much joy and hope. When did you know or decide that you would adapt your book into a film? When I was making Dreams of a Life , I wrote the book because we were finding it hard to finance that film, and I got quite frustrated. So I wrote the book, and I felt it was complete – in the sense of putting that away after having looked at that part of my life and made something creative out of it. During COVID, Michael Winterbottom interviewed me for a book he did about British filmmakers. And he said, “I read 7 Miles Out . You should turn it into a film.” And that made me begin to think about that possibility. How do you approach adaptations? I adapted Martin Amis’ Night Train into Out of Blue , and what I realized doing that adaptation is how much you move away from the original source. I think you have to transpose literary things for the screen. With 7 Miles Out , I did think it would be easier because it’s my own book, but it wasn’t. It was harder in a sense, and in some ways, it was easier because I just looked at other events that had occurred, so it was very authentic. But you still have to shape it into a screenplay and not have as many characters or as many episodes. You’re really trying to create a throughline. What’s beautiful, compared to a book, is that with the film you have sound and music and actual dialog. And you have actors, performances, and locations. So you’re not imagining it in the same way. In terms of my book and the film, the themes are the same, but the episodes change. I want to know what Courtesy of BFI London Film Festival Let’s talk a bit more about the themes and your take on them. Grief and community are central themes of 7 Miles Out … Yes, with grief, it’s that idea that grieving isn’t instantaneous. I don’t think you get over it. You incorporate it into your life. So I really wanted to make a film where tragedy and grieving were not something that you get over, but something that you live with. It can make you think more deeply about the world and lead to creative actions, like the music in the film. I really wanted to look at it in a way that was much more complex, possibly, than it is looked at in other places. And in terms of community, I remember early on, I was really interested in looking at different generations as well. Young people’s tendency is to think about themselves as the center of the world. But they’re surrounded by these other people that they relate to. So it’s about that sense of community in a small town as well. Yes, the film feels like a smaller version of the bigger universe… Yes, it’s like a microcosm of the world, and what goes on within this community is reflecting the larger world. How did you think about mixing the darker sides with the lighter sides and hope? I often look at quite dark subject matters. For example, Dreams of a Life is about a woman that lay dead in her flat for three years. And I remember people at the time saying it was awfully optimistic. I felt oddly happy, and they couldn’t understand why. I think they thought it would be grim only. But it celebrated a life. And it also made people think about friendship and how they could make a difference in the world. With 7 Miles Out , I wanted people to feel the light at the end. The film particularly talks about suicide, which was very taboo back then. Even now it’s very hard to talk about. So I wanted to make a film that addressed that. Suicide is one of the biggest causes of death of young men under 50 globally. So I wanted to look at suicide in a way that people afterwards could talk about, but not feel completely disempowered. The young woman in the film making music and writing songs and becoming able to express herself in a different way was, to be very obvious, about her finding her voice, which was very important. Rather than you feeling very down at the end, I hope that you feel like you’ve been through a lot of emotions, and at the end you feel lighter and enlightened, and you feel like you can go and process some of your own feelings. It was more about catharsis. Carol Morley, courtesy of Paul Marc Mitchell 7 Miles Out is based on my dad and his suicide. When I was growing up and when he saw a psychiatrist, he would be okay because he could present himself. In my research into suicide, [I found] that people who are going to kill themselves often make that decision a few weeks before, and they start to seem happy because they have resolved something. So people go, “I saw him the day before, and he seemed happy, so I couldn’t believe it.” That’s why I think I make films about the idea of what people represent to the world and who they really are inside, which you cannot always tell. How did you find your amazing cast? I cast with casting director Shaheen Baig, and we decided to do a massive open casting call in Stockport, and 450 people came to that. With the younger cast, they sent videos. A lot of the cast are first-timers. They’ve never done anything, and I find that enormously exciting. I’d seen Lucy Halliday in Blue Jean . We did a Zoom interview because she was filming in Canada, and we really got on. But for me, it’s all about meeting them. So we met at Shaheen’s offices and spoke for about two hours. Shaheen came in at one point and went, “Is everything all right?” I just felt this energy she had and ability to just [express various layers]. So, as soon as I met her, she was Ann for me. Aidan, I actually had briefly once, and [at another event,] I went over to him and said: “I met you once. Would you be in a film for 10 minutes?” I said we’d send the script to his agent. And then his friend got in touch and said, “Aidan wants to be in touch.” So I ended up meeting Aidan the next week, and he had read it and wanted to be in. Aidan had a conversation with my brother, and my brother afterwards said that was the best conversation he’d ever had in his life. Aidan wanted to talk to my brother about my dad because my brother’s nine years older than me, so Aidan really wanted that perspective, And weirdly, with Gemma Whelan, what I found out was that the very first thing she did was my short film The Madness of the Dance [in which she appeared as a nun]. So, I keep going: “I discovered you.” And she goes: “I launched you.” So, we had the core of the cast. And then Kasper Hilton-Hille ( Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man , Outrageous ) is brilliant as Ann’s brother. ‘7 Miles Out,’ courtesy of BFI London Film Festival Where did you film, and were any scenes particularly difficult to shoot? We were on a very stringent budget, so I knew I couldn’t ever do reshoots or pick-ups. I had to get it all at the time. So if it rained, we were filming in the rain. Now, rain never shows up as much on film as it really is. So the filming in the rain was really hard because you’re having to protect the equipment, and the actors are just getting more drenched than they look. We filmed everything within a 15-minute radius in Stockport. Agnès Godard had never been to Stockport, so I love that. She was seeing it through a different lens, and so the combination of us was good. I love working with Agnès. She calls me “dangerous girl” because I like to be in the moment. I have a plan, but change it at the last minute if I notice something. And all the songs that you see people sing are all sung live. I wanted that live feeling, which was very challenging but we did a lot of prep. None of those girls could play. Leila [Entwistle who plays Hel] picked up the bass and looked like she could play it. And she did because it was quite simple as the punk idea was that anyone can play. And they all went for it. 7 Miles Out is set in a very specific time and location but feels like people in other parts of the world will quite easily connect with the core themes and emotions. What do you think? A filmmaker said you could make a film about a village that’s universal. If you make a film where you are primarily conveying emotion, that will connect with everybody. I’m personally not interested in nostalgia. I’m interested in authenticity. So it’s really a great thing to look at things that have happened to you personally to draw out that authenticity. When I made a film a long time ago called The Alcohol Years , which was a documentary about Manchester, I discovered people in Melbourne and America were writing. People in Australia said it was just like Melbourne, and people from the U.S. said it was just like New York. I think that music has that ability to really transcend place. Do you know what you will do next? I really want to work within a genre I’ve not worked in yet. I definitely have got something in mind that would be cross-generational, working with young people and old people, set in a time I’ve never worked in before and a place I’ve never worked in before. I never want to repeat myself. THR

articles.title: Christian Slater, Trine Dyrholm,  Dree Hemingway Join Dogma25 Feature ‘Incidents of Intimacy’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All October 15, 2026 2:38am Add us as a Google Preferred Source (R to L): Christian Slater, Trine Dyrholm Anders-Overgaard Christian Slater ( Mr. Robot ), Dree Hemingway ( Starlet ), and Danish star Trine Dyrholm ( Queen of Hearts ) have signed on to star in Incidents of Intimacy , from director Jasper Just. Johannes Lilleøre, Julie Agnete Vang, Laura Drasbæk and Michael Moritzen will co-star. The low-budget feature will mark Just’s directorial debut, and be the second in the new Dogma25 slate of ambitious arthouse features from producer Zentropa. Dyrholm, whose credits include Susanne Bier’s Oscar-winner In a Better World , Magnus von Horn’s The Girl With The Needle and Nikolaj Arcel’s A Royal Affair , will play Linda, an intimacy coordinator who struggles to form intimate connections. Unable to acknowledge or access her own feelings, she steals objects from people instead of getting close to them, filing her loot in an archive of intimacy in her cupboard. Related Stories General News Iranian Filmmaker Majid Majidi Denounces U.S. War as 'Midday Meal' Emerges as Busan Fest Standout Lifestyle Alan Mandell, Esteemed Actor and Interpreter of Samuel Beckett Plays, Dies at 98 The project will see Slater return to Danish cinema after co-starring Lars von Trier’s Nymphomaniac . Just is best known as a visual artist. He represented Denmark at the 2013 Venice Biennale and has presented solo exhibitions around the world. Much of his work deconstructs conventional representations of gender, love, social norms in mainstream cinema. Incidents of Intimacy will be his first feature as a director. Just co-wrote the script together with Sissel Dalsgaard Thomsen ( The Quiet Migration ). The film will be the second produced under the Dogma25 label, a slate of arthouse features to be made under a strict “vow of chastity” that requires the directors to comply with several enforced restrictions, including keeping the crew to a maximum of ten people, having at least half of the film be dialogue-free, and a ban on using the Internet for research or development. The films each have a maximum budget of 10 million Danish Krone (around $1.5 million) with backing from Zentropa, Danish public broadcaster DR, and Nordisk Film Distribution. All the movies will be released theatrically in Denmark via Nordisk Film, with Netflix taking streaming rights in the Nordics. TrustNordisk is handling world sales. Zentropa unveiled the Dogma25 concept at the Cannes Film Festival last year together with the group’s five directors: Just, May el-Toukhy ( Queen of Hearts ), Milad Alami ( Opponent ), Annika Berg ( Team Hurricane ), and Isabella Eklöf ( Kalak ). The group takes its name from the Dogme 95 movement, started by Danish directors Lars Von Trier, Thomas Vinterberg ( The Celebration ) Kristian Levring ( The King is Alive ) and Søren Kragh-Jacobsen ( Mifune ), another back-to-basics film movement that is credited with revitalizing indie cinema in the late ’90s.T The movement has already inspired a similar project in Germany , with director Tom Tykwer ( Run Lola Run ), Ilker Çatak ( The Teacher’s Lounge ), Nora Fingscheidt ( The Outrun ), Helene Hegemann ( Axolotl Overkill ) and Kurdwin Ayub ( Mond ) announcing their own Dogma 25 slate. THR

articles.title: The Academy’s Bill Kramer and Lynette Howell Taylor to Attend Tokyo Film Festival
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All October 15, 2026 3:48am Add us as a Google Preferred Source From left: Bill Kramer, Lynette Howell Taylor, Meredith Shea and Hiro Matsuoka. Courtesy of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and the Tokyo International Film Festival A trio of Hollywood heavyweights are set to feature in panel discussions at the fast-approaching 39th Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF). Bill Kramer , CEO of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences ( AMPAS ) as well as the Academy’s President Lynette Howell Taylor and chief membership, impact and industry officer Meredith Shea will be in Japan for a host of events. On Oct. 28, the Kramer, Taylor and Shea will participate in a panel discussion (details below), followed by the presentation of a leadership award to Kramer and a gathering for Academy members. And on Oct. 29, Kramer will take part in a conversation with Hiro Matsuoka, President and CEO of Japanese production giant Toho. Related Stories Movies Christian Slater, Trine Dyrholm, Dree Hemingway Join Dogma25 Feature 'Incidents of Intimacy' Movies '7 Miles Out,' Starring Lucy Halliday, Tells a Coming-of-Age Story Full of Grief, Music and Friendship As well as the above named trio, the Academy will have several additional senior executives in attendance at the festival and member reception, including Amy Homma, Director and President, Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and Academy Collection; Jenny Galante, chief revenue and business development officer; and Jennifer Davidson, chief marketing, communications and content officer. The events the Academy trio are set to be involved in include: Academy in Tokyo: Festival Panel Set for Oct. 28, this panel will “offer a behind-the-scenes look at the Oscars as well as insights into the Academy’s global initiatives and membership programs. The discussion will also explore the Academy’s perspective on the current state and future of international cinema.” Speakers from AMPAS include Bill Kramer, Lynette Howell Taylor and Meredith Shea, with Takeo Hisamatsu, TIFF Festival Director, moderating. Special Award to Be Presented to Bill Kramer Following the panel discussion on Oct. 28, Kramer, making his first visit to Asia , will receive the Global Cinema Leadership Special Award in “recognition of his significant contributions to the development of the global film industry and the advancement of film culture.” Kramer is being recognized for his work since becoming Academy CEO in 2022, including his push to further diversify and globalize the Academy’s membership, and overseeing all of the Academy’s global operations and programs, including the Oscars, the Academy Foundation, and services for the organization’s 11,000 global members. Academy in Tokyo: Member Gathering The final event on Oct. 28 will be a private reception for Academy members from around the world, will take place. Members of the Academy’s global film community will come together at TIFF for an opportunity to connect and exchange ideas. Academy in Tokyo: Special Talk Session On Oct. 29, Kramer will participate in a wide-ranging dialogue with Toho President and CEO Hiro Matsuoka. The two will discuss the “global cinematic landscape, the future of theatrical and streaming distribution, and next steps for international collaboration.” THR

articles.title: Zendaya to Star in Alex Garland’s New Sci-Fi Movie for A24
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All October 15, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Zendaya Randy Shropshire/NBC Logo text Zendaya has joined a new project as her memorable year winds down. The actress is set to star in an untitled sci-fi movie that filmmaker Alex Garland will direct from his own script for A24 . Plot details have not yet been disclosed for the feature that is expected to shoot in 2027. This movie marks the latest collaboration between Zendaya and A24 following her hit HBO series Euphoria , which counted A24 as a producer, and this year’s feature The Drama . Garland has a long history with A24 that includes Ex Machina , Civil War , Men , Warfare and his forthcoming video game adaptation Elden Ring , set for theatrical release in 2028. Related Stories Movies Nobody Would Read His Script, Then He Got the Call From Robert Pattinson Movies Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes Doc Sets U.K. Release Date The current year has been filled with notable projects and moments for Zendaya, who co-starred with Tom Holland in Sony Pictures’ summer blockbuster Spider-Man: Brand New Day , which now stands as the highest-grossing film in domestic box office history. She and Holland, who recently confirmed that they secretly tied the knot , also co-starred in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , which became Universal’s highest-grossing release ever and is expected to garner plenty of attention during awards season. Zendaya starred opposite Robert Pattinson in A24’s spring hit The Drama and can soon be seen reprising her role as Chani in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three , which Warner Bros. releases theatrically in December. Additionally, she earned an Emmy Award nomination this year for starring as Rue in the third and final season of HBO’s acclaimed Euphoria . Among the actress’ other forthcoming films, Zendaya is attached to star as late singer Ronnie Spector in Barry Jenkins’ biopic Be My Baby for A24. She will also voice the daughter of Shrek and Princess Fiona in DreamWorks Animation’s Shrek 5 , hitting theaters next summer. THR

articles.title: Doja Cat to Debut Doc Short Recorded on Ma Vie World Tour Using Ray-Ban Meta Glasses
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 15, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Doja Cat is pictured on a stop amid her Tour Ma Vie while wearing Ray-Ban Meta. Courtesy of Ray-Ban Meta Tour documentaries are nothing new. But shooting one — even a short — on Ray-Ban Meta glasses is a new way to do it. On Oct. 23, the day after she takes the stage at Kia Forum in Los Angeles, Doja Cat will drop Ma Vie World Tour in partnership with Ray-Ban Meta. It’s a roughly 12-minute short filmed almost entirely on Ray-Ban Meta glasses and shot from the perspective of Doja Cat and members of her crew on the current tour. It was helmed by noted director Quinn Whitney Wilson, who previously directed the forthcoming feature doc Jean-Michel Basquiat about the iconic artist, shows like Ziwe, Your Attention Please and MPower and music videos for artists like Lizzo and Baby Ariel. The footage captured finds Doja revealing what it’s like to hit the stage on tour with all the behind-the-scenes shots that fans have come to love from these types of tour documentaries, like waiting in the wings before showtime and backstage with members of her inner circle. Related Stories News BET Awards Nominations Revealed: Cardi B Leads With Six Lifestyle Inside LACMA's Art+Film Gala With Moguls, Gucci-Clad A-Listers and a Reflective Ryan Coogler “Doja leaves everything on that stage for her fans, and getting to build a doc style piece around that energy was a dream. We shot on Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which let us capture the tour from the inside, through Doja’s eyes and through the eyes of the team that makes it all happen. It’s an intimate, unfiltered look at Tour Ma Vie that drops you right into the chaos, the craft, and the love she pours into every single show,” said Wilson in a statement provided to The Hollywood Reporter. The short will debut on Doja Cat’s YouTube , a channel that counts north of 14 million subscribers. But wait there’s more: Ray-Ban Meta is also an official partner of the Tour Ma Vie, and she’s been sporting five custom Ray-Ban Meta glasses which were designed by her creative director Brett Alan Nelson, who helped curate the spectacles into her looks and show choreography. Fans who can’t get to Kia Forum, or even those who can, will be able to check out the custom frames on display with three tour looks at Meta Lab Los Angeles on Melrose Avenue next week. articles.title: Jennie to Headline Soundtrack for Netflix’s Upcoming Animated Film ‘Steps’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All October 15, 2026 6:02am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jennie is set to headline the soundtrack for 'Steps.' The Chosunilbo JNS/Imazins via Getty Images; Netflix Jennie is set to headline the soundtrack for Netflix ‘s upcoming animated film Steps with a new song. Netflix announced the soundtrack, which is entirely written and produced by prolific songwriter Justin Tranter, for the animated comedy adventure Thursday. Global pop star and Blackpink member Jennie will lead the soundtrack with a new track “Someone to Hold.” There will be four original songs on the album, with additional vocals from Academy Award nominee Amanda Seyfried, Rose Gray and Emei and a score by Kris Bowers. “I am so excited to join the Steps family and it was really fun making my first song for an animated film,” Jennie said in a statement. “I love how much heart and personality the characters have, and I’m so happy I got to be a little part of their world. I hope you enjoy ‘Steps’ and ‘Someone to Hold’ as much as I do and I can’t wait for you guys to hear it.” Related Stories Business Netflix TV Executives Lisa Lang McMullen, James Oh, Carolina Garcia and Andrew McQuinn Among Layoffs TV Netflix's 'Untold' to Tackle Daejon Love (Exclusive) Tranter describes Jennie’s track as “pure danceable joy” inspired by vintage dance pop, while Emei’s track “The Understudy” was described as “an underdog anthem.” Gray’s track, “Meet Me on the Dance Floor,” is an electro dance pop villain song. Seyfried’s track “Smile and a Song” is more of an “old school musical theater banger,” according to the songwriter. Adds Tranter, “The story in Steps lends itself beautifully to a variety of voices and sonics, and the main throughline in the soundtrack is dance music.” The announcement comes alongside the trailer for the film, released Thursday morning. A preview of “Someone to Hold” is included in trailer. Centering around Cinderella’s stepsisters, the logline for Steps reads, “Think you know Cinderella’s ‘evil’ stepsisters? Think again. Tired of living in Cinderella’s shadow, Lilith (Ali Wong) steals the Fairy Godmother (Bette Midler)’s magic wand and hijacks the Royal Ball with her sister Margot (Stephanie Hsu), breaking the Cinderella story as we know it and dooming the kingdom to the tyrannical rule of Priscilla (Nikki Glaser), a villainous schemer who swoops in and snatches the throne. Now, Lilith must team up with Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) to fight biker trolls, outrun evil henchmen and escape the Screaming Woods on an epic quest to save the kingdom, but most importantly, their relationship.” Steps and its companion soundtrack are set to be released on Nov. 20. articles.title: Sky’s $2.1 Billion ITV Megadeal: U.K. Government Eyes Intervention
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 15, 2026 6:10am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport Lisa Nandy on her way to a weekly cabinet meeting at 10 Downing Street earlier this year. Peter Nicholls/Getty Images The U.K. government is “minded to intervene” in the planned $2.1 billion takeover of ITV ’s TV networks and streaming assets by Comcast ‘s Sky , U.K. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said on Thursday. The ITV-Sky deal promises to bring together Britain’s largest pay-TV operator with its largest commercial free-to-air broadcaster. Sky CEO Dana Strong called it “ a defining moment for British media .” ITV CEO Carolyn McCall touted it as the creation of “a U.K. champion with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms.” But critics have expressed concerns about the merged entity’s market power. And now, the Labour Party government in the U.K. has also cited concentration worries. During an appearance in the London parliament, she mentioned “public interest considerations,” such as “the need for free expression of opinion in news media” and “the need for a sufficient plurality of views in news media in each market.” Nandy also highlighted “the need for the availability throughout the United Kingdom of a wide range of broadcasting, on-demand programs or both.” ITV agreed to sell its media and entertainment arm to Sky for £1.6 billion in July. The deal covers ITV’s terrestrial TV channels and streaming service ITVX. Production arm ITV Studios would continue operating as a separate company. Sky is led by CEO Dana Strong. It not only operates pay-TV and streaming businesses in the U.K., Ireland and Italy but also has been growing its telecom offerings, such as broadband and mobile phone operations. Sky also owns the production arm Sky Studios, which is led by Cécile Frot-Coutaz and has been growing its investment in original content creation. Recent Sky Studios productions have included the likes of Mary & George , starring Julianne Moore; The Tattooist of Auschwitz , starring Harvey Keitel; and The Day of the Jackal , starring Eddie Redmayne. Comcast acquired Sky in 2018. THR

articles.title: Iranian Drama ‘Midday Meal’ Wins Busan Film Festival’s Top Prize, Qualifying for Oscar Consideration
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All October 15, 2026 6:50am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Majid Majidi's 'Midday Meal' BIFF Iranian director Majid Majidi’s Midday Meal won the best film prize at the Busan International Film Festival Thursday, giving the acclaimed drama about a teacher struggling to feed his pupils a route into the Oscars ’ best international feature race. Busan’s seven-member jury, led by Chinese filmmaking legend Zhang Yimou, said its decision was unanimous. Buzz around Majidi’s movie had been building on the ground in Busan all week, with many predicting — correctly — that it would take home the top prize. Accepting the honor at the Busan Cinema Center, Majidi dedicated his victory to the people of Iran and used portions of his speech to condemn the civilian toll of the U.S.-led war on his country. Related Stories Business Sky's $2.1 Billion ITV Megadeal: U.K. Government Eyes Intervention Movies The Academy's Bill Kramer and Lynette Howell Taylor to Attend Tokyo Film Festival “I would like to dedicate this prize to the brave heroes of Iran — the people of Iran, who have stood firm through all these years and are still resisting oppression,” he said. “On the very first day of this war in Iran, a school in Minab was hit, and 120 innocent students were killed. Even now, some of the bodies have not been found,” he later added. “What crime have our people committed? There is nothing except that our people want to be independent. They will stand firm until the end.” He concluded: “I wish for a world where there is no more war, full of peace, love and brotherhood. I’m praying for that future.” Midday Meal dazzled critics in Busan with its powerful, parable-like storytelling and assured visual style. The film follows Davoud Soulan (Mohammad Rahimi), a contract teacher in a remote village in southeastern Iran whose hopes of securing a permanent government job are jeopardized when a wealthy benefactor dies and the free lunches that keep his impoverished pupils coming to school disappear. Determined to save both his school and his future, Soulan resorts to increasingly desperate measures, including dangerous cross-border fuel smuggling, as his natural decency comes into conflict with his modest ambitions. The film continues Majidi’s longstanding thematic preoccupation with the moral pressures faced by people on society’s margins, as seen in earlier festival-winning works like The Color of Paradise (1999) and Baran (2001). For Midday Meal , he assembled an entirely nonprofessional cast through street casting in the region, setting their performances against the stark, otherworldly landscape of Iran’s so-called Martian Mountains. Earlier in the festival, Majidi spoke at length at a press conference about how he had nearly declined the invitation to travel to South Korea because he felt depressed and exhausted by the dire situation at home. He ultimately decided that the trip would allow him and his film to convey “some kind of small message from my people to the people of other nations and other places.” Majidi’s victory on Thursday night also gives Midday Meal an instantaneous jolt of Oscars buzz. The Busan festival introduced its main competition just last year, bringing its awards structure closer to those of Europe’s leading cinema events. Under rules introduced by the Film Academy, Busan’s best film winner can be submitted for international feature consideration without being selected by its country’s Oscar committee (Busan joins Cannes, Venice, Berlin, Sundance and Toronto on the Academy’s list of festivals whose designated awards offer such consideration). Iran has already chosen Babak Khajehpasha’s Land of Angels , a drama about children enduring the war in Gaza, as its official submission for the 99th Academy Awards. But Midday Meal now has an open, alternate route to the race. Majidi previously made Oscar history with Children of Heaven (1997), which became the first Iranian film nominated in the international category, then known as best foreign-language film. Among the other main competition winners, Indonesian director Eddie Cahyono received the special jury prize for Ibuku . The film stars veteran screen actress Christine Hakim as a widow whose late husband’s gambling debts force her to arrange a marriage for her only daughter, setting in motion an anguished mother-daughter drama. Taiwan’s Lee Yun Chan won best director for To Be Ordinary , about a family whose strained relationships are tested by a devastating accident. The award marks a return to the Busan spotlight for Lee, whose debut feature, The Shoe Fairy , screened in the festival’s New Currents section in 2005. The two best actor awards went to Chinese star Zhou Xun and Japanese newcomer Kashun Himeno. Zhou was recognized for Gu You’s The First Taste of Loneliness , which follows three generations of women navigating grief after the death of the family’s patriarch. The film also earned the artistic contribution award for Li Danfeng’s sound work. Himeno won for her screen debut in Shuichi Okita’s Satoko Always . She plays the youngest of three women who share a name but occupy different stages of life, each turning to writing to make sense of her experiences. India’s Shashank Walia earlier won the New Currents Award for Birds in the Dark , a black-and-white Punjabi-language drama exploring caste, labor and love in rural Punjab. The film, backed by filmmaker Hansal Mehta, had already collected the Songwon Vision Audience Award for an Asian title the previous evening. And a New Currents special mention went to South Korean director Lim Hayeon’s debut feature Beach Fictions , about a young woman whose escape to a seaside town brings enigmatic encounters with a novelist, a magician and a fortune teller. Zhang’s jury assessed 13 competition titles. Joining him on the panel were Chinese director Bi Gan, Korean actress Moon Choi, Japanese filmmaker Kei Ishikawa, Korean director July Jung, Vietnamese producer Tran Thi Bich Ngoc and Kazakh actress Samal Yeslyamova. Busan organizers reported total attendance at the festival of more than 200,000 moviegoers this year, the event’s biggest crowd since 2015. Other programs and special events drew an additional 77,000 attendees, they said. The festival linked the growth to changes in its opening schedule and an expanded screening program. The accompanying Asian Contents & Film Market, held Oct. 10-13, attracted 30,484 participants and 339 companies from 32 countries. In other starry moments, BIFF’s 31st edition, which ran Oct. 6-15, welcomed Alfonso Cuarón on his first visit to South Korea, alongside guests including Charlotte Gainsbourg, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Fan Bingbing, Hirokazu Koreeda, Lee Chang-dong, Na Hong-jin, Lav Diaz and anime veteran Rintaro. Michelle Yeoh received the Asian Filmmaker of the Year award at the opening ceremony, while Hong Kong director Ann Hui accepted the Camellia Award. The full list of this year’s BIFF award winners follows. Best film: Midday Meal — Majid Majidi Special jury prize: Ibuku — Eddie Cahyono Best director: Lee Yun Chan — To Be Ordinary Best actor: Zhou Xun — The First Taste of Loneliness Best actor: Kashun Himeno — Satoko Always Artistic contribution: Li Danfeng, sound — The First Taste of Loneliness New Currents New Currents Award: Birds in the Dark — Shashank Walia Special mention: Beach Fictions — Lim Hayeon THR

Related Stories Russell Brand Was 'Ruthless and Calculated' With a 'Voracious' Desire for 'Sexual Contact,' Prosecution Alleges in Rape Trial Opening Statement Russell Brand Trial: Woman Details Alleged Rape After Asking Her to Take Photos of Him Half-Naked “I was a kid and the female lead on ‘Even Stevens.’ I was paid half of what Shia was paid; we were co-leads and had the same screen time,” Romano said, adding that while penning her memoir, she found a handwritten letter her mother wrote her agent in 2000 “asking for equal pay and admitting we were deep in debt.” Popular on Variety A photo of the letter is included in the post. It reads: “Shia receives $12,000 per episode and Christy $6,000. With 30% going into trust, we can’t make it here financially. This show also holds her up from other work that pays more. articles.title: Russell Brand Trial: Woman Details Alleged Rape After Asking Her to Take Photos of Him Half-Naked
articles.full_text: Oct 15, 2026 5:07am PT Russell Brand Trial: Woman Details Alleged Rape After Asking Her to Take Photos of Him Half-Naked By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Christy Carlson Romano Says Her Salary Was Half of Shia LaBeouf’s on ‘Even Stevens’: ‘We Were Co-Leads and Had the Same Screen Time’ 2 hours ago ‘Clayface’ First Reactions Praise DC Body Horror as ‘Freakishly Awesome’ and ‘Loaded With Brutal Scenes’ 1 day ago Aaron Sorkin Thinks About Reviving ‘The West Wing’ for a ‘Couple of Seconds Every Day’: ‘I Miss It’ 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source PA Images via Getty Images The second day of Russell Brand ‘s criminal trial is underway in London, with the first complainant detailing an alleged rape at the 1999 Labour Party conference in Bournemouth. Arriving to Southwark Crown Court on Thursday, Brand sported a grey suit, white shirt and black-and-white polka dot tie, with his hair tied back in a half-up bun. His wife Laura Gallacher, who has been by his side for the first two days of the trial, was not present. Related Stories Russell Brand Was 'Ruthless and Calculated' With a 'Voracious' Desire for 'Sexual Contact,' Prosecution Alleges in Rape Trial Opening Statement Russell Brand Trial: Woman Details Alleged Rape After Asking Her to Take Photos of Him Half-Naked The jury, consisting of eight men and four women, was shown video of the first complainant’s police interview, according to Sky News . She alleges that Brand raped her in her hotel room at the Labour Party conference in 1999. “I second-guessed myself if it was rape because it was so normal,” she said in the video. “Sorry… he raped me basically — I know that happened.” Popular on Variety The woman said Channel 4’s 2023 “Dispatches” documentary, in which allegations against Brand were first brought to light, “triggered” her to go to the police. At the start of the proceedings on Thursday, Sky News reported judge Mr Justice Bennathan told the jury that the allegations in the documentary have “never been tested in any court,” but it is relevant to the case since it spurred many of the alleged victims to come forward. He said the defense may suggest that the documentary caused the complainants to “twist” their memory of events, and said he thinks the doc is “one-sided and dramatic in manner,” so it will not be shown to the jury. In the police interview video, the woman said that she met Brand at a cabaret event he was performing in at the Labour Party conference. Brand was “gentlemanly” at first and she thought he was gay, saying: “It didn’t feel like he was trying it on with me.” She suggested that they go back to her hotel room to continue their conversation. Once there, she went to the toilet and emerged to find Brand half-naked and “prancing” around the room “like an ostrich,” she said. He forced her to take photos of him, she alleged — at which point she became “frightened” — and then pushed her onto the bed and took off her clothes. She tried to push him off, she said, but he was “really heavy.” She then “drifted out of her head … but I know I said no,” the woman said. “I was frightened. I remember feeling ‘what on earth have I got myself into’ — and then he did rape me,” the woman alleged as she became tearful, according to Sky News. Afterwards, she claimed that Brand behaved like nothing was wrong and left her his email address. She didn’t tell anyone about the alleged rape out of shame, she said, until she told a friend in 2023. It was her friend who first reported the incident before the alleged victim came forward to the police herself. On Wednesday, the prosecution laid out its opening statement , alleging that Brand was “ruthless and calculated” and a “sexual predator.” The actor and comedian has been charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault relating to incidents with six women spanning from 1999 to 2009. He has pleaded not guilty and denied all allegations against him. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones outlined the six claims against Brand in her opening statement. The first woman alleged that Brand raped her in her hotel room at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. The second alleged incident involves a woman who was working at MTV in 2001, where she claims Brand grabbed her and tried to pull her into a toilet. The third woman alleges that Brand squeezed her breasts at a party in Soho in 2004 and then orally raped her in a toilet. The fourth allegation occurred at Capital Radio in 2004/2005, where Brand allegedly pushed a woman against a wall and “aggressively” kissed her while grabbing “her body, at her breasts, sides and buttocks,” the prosecution said. The fifth woman alleges that Brand anally raped her in 2009 after they had consensual vaginal sex. The sixth claim comes from a woman who alleges Brand demanded a massage from her while she was on a work assignment in 2009. Several of the allegations received the same response from Brand when he was questioned about them by the police, the prosecution claimed. “He set out that he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that any accounts had been reinvented or imagined after a defamatory documentary and subsequent press reporting,” Karmy-Jones said. In 2023, Brand was the subject of a joint investigation by The Sunday Times of London and Channel 4 documentary “Dispatches,” which published allegations against him of rape, sexual assault and emotional abuse. Brand strongly denied the allegations. The Metropolitan Police then began their own investigation into him, with the Crown Prosecution Service formally bringing charges against him in April and December of last year. Brand’s trial is expected to last six weeks. articles.title: British Government ‘Minded to Intervene’ in Sky’s Proposed $2 Billion Takeover of ITV
articles.full_text: Oct 15, 2026 5:34am PT British Government ‘Minded to Intervene’ in Sky’s Proposed $2 Billion Takeover of ITV By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom 6 hours ago Ben Frow Stepping Down as Chief Content Officer of 5, Skydance’s U.K. Network, After 14 Years 1 day ago Stephen Amell Says Putting on the ‘Baywatch’ Red Trunks Felt ‘So Familiar’ Because ‘It’s a Superhero Show’ 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source ITV U.K. culture minister Lisa Nandy has signalled she is “minded to intervene” in Sky ’s proposed $2 billion takeover of ITV , citing concerns about maintaining media plurality, particularly with regard to news. Nandy confirmed in a statement she may intervene if she has “reasonable grounds to suspect” that public interest considerations are at play. These include the “need for free expression of opinion in news media,” “a sufficient plurality of views in news media” and “a sufficient plurality of persons with control of the media enterprises” serving a variety of areas around the U.K. (in effect, local news). Related Stories Russell Brand's Criminal Trial Begins in London as He Faces Rape and Sexual Assault Charges Russell Brand Trial: Woman Details Alleged Rape After Asking Her to Take Photos of Him Half-Naked Comcast-owned Sky struck a deal with ITV back in July to acquire the broadcaster and its streaming platform ITVX for £1.6 billion ($2.1 billion) subject to regulatory and legal processes. If the acquisition goes ahead, the network’s production arm, ITV Studios, will be carved away to form a standalone listed company. Popular on Variety Sir Peter Bazalgette, former chair of ITV, told Variety earlier this year he thinks government policy is now more favourable to media consolidation because it’s the only way for public service broadcasters to survive in the current climate. “Domestic broadcasters across Europe are under considerable pressure from not just the streamers, but also from YouTube,” he said, pointing out that with broadcasters now competing with YouTube, Meta, TikTok and other platforms for video advertising, Sky and ITV jointly represents only a 20 to 30% market share. Bazalgette was, however, speaking under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s administration. While Starmer’s government was understood to be more pragmatic about M&A activity, it remains to be seen whether his replacement Andy Burnham feels the same. Although, notably, Nandy — who’d previously said she was “minded to intervene” on Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery — ultimately let the deal go through , just a few weeks into Burnham’s premiership. If Nandy does go ahead and issue an intervention notice to Sky and ITV, the Competition and Markets Authority as well as the media regulator Ofcom would need to assess the deal and its impact and report back to the minister. The CMA would then carry out a more detailed investigation. Nandy said she has written to Sky and ITV to inform them of her intention to further scrutinize the process. The companies will have until Oct. 20 to make representations. articles.title: Spike Lee and Mick Jagger’s Favorite Eyewear Brand Unveils First Collection From New Creative Directors John Juniper and Jeff Solorio
articles.full_text: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. Spike Lee, LeBron James and Mick Jagger have all been spotted in Morgenthal Frederics eyewear, helping make the century-old New York label a favorite among celebrities. Now, the luxury eyewear house is getting a refresh courtesy of John Juniper and Jeff Solorio, the design duo who founded DITA and helped turn high-end spectacles into a fashion category of their own. Their debut Fall/Winter 2026 collection , launching Oct. 15, brings a new design direction to a brand best known for its handcrafted buffalo horn frames. The lineup expands on Morgenthal Frederics’ Japanese acetate and titanium offerings, with sculptural silhouettes, intricate metalwork and subtle new signatures, including purple temple tips. Related Stories Russell Brand's Criminal Trial Begins in London as He Faces Rape and Sexual Assault Charges Russell Brand Was 'Ruthless and Calculated' With a 'Voracious' Desire for 'Sexual Contact,' Prosecution Alleges in Rape Trial Opening Statement Morgenthal Fredericks SHOP ONLINE The appointment brings two familiar names in luxury eyewear to one of the category’s oldest players. Childhood friends who founded DITA in Los Angeles in the mid-1990s, Juniper and Solorio built the label around Japanese craftsmanship and vintage-inspired silhouettes. Their influence eventually extended into the designer eyewear business, most notably through DITA’s collaboration with Thom Browne, which launched in 2011. Morgenthal’s history, meanwhile, dates back to 1913, when it began as Frederics Opticians in Manhattan, before adopting its current name under optician Richard Morgenthal in 1986. Its natural buffalo horn eyewear, introduced in 2006, helped distinguish it from competitors. But the brand’s celebrity following is what really helped sustain its reputation. Lee, whose oversized, brightly colored glasses have become nearly as recognizable as his Knicks fandom, has commissioned custom orange frames from Morgenthal Frederics. Norman Reedus has also previously appeared in a campaign for the label. Juniper and Solorio aren’t abandoning the buffalo horn designs that made Morgenthal Frederics distinctive. Instead, they’re bringing a similar attention to materials and construction to acetate and titanium, with Japanese artisans producing frames featuring hand-etched surfaces, custom metal accents and detailing on the lenses and nose pads. “What draws us to Morgenthal Frederics is that it has nearly a hundred years of history, yet creatively it still feels like a clean slate,” the designers said in a joint statement. “There’s a great team around the brand, a lot of support, and no unnecessary guardrails. That gives us the freedom to build something beautiful at the highest level—and that’s what excites us.” The collection is accompanied by a campaign titled “Heritage in Motion,” photographed by London-based photographer Darren Gwynn. The Fall/Winter 2026 collection will be available beginning Oct. 15 at Morgenthal Frederics boutiques and online , with prices ranging from $795 to $2,995. Loading comments...

The star has boarded a new untitled sci-fi to be written and directed Alex Garland for A24 . Plot details are being kept under wraps, but the feature is set to shoot in 2027. The project marks the latest collaboration between Zendaya and A24 following hit series “Euphoria,” which concluded after three seasons earlier this year, and the pitch-black dramedy “The Drama” alongside Robert Pattinson, which became a box office hit, earning almost $135 million worldwide. Shooting on “The Elden Ring” wrapped on July 30, with the film set to be released in March 2028. But the news could also dent hopes for a third “28 Years Later.” Garland wrote “28 Days Later,” later reuniting with Danny Boyle for last year’s “28 Years Later” and its quick-fire sequel “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple.” Speaking recently at the London Film Festival, Boyle said Garland had written a “fantastic script” for the third “28 Years Later” but noted he was now busy working on “Elden Ring.” “So it’s on the back burner at the moment,” he said.
