articles.title: Fox Entertainment & Kevin Hart’s Hartbeat Strike Microdrama Deal
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Fox Entertainment & Kevin Hart’s Hartbeat Strike Microdrama Deal Fox Boss Rob Wade Commits Long Term To Creator Studios: “We’re Not Here To Flip A House” Channel 4 Unveils First-Ever Microdrama: Female Friendship Series Stars ‘You’s Jadesola Odunjo View All October 13, 2026 9:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kevin Hart Christopher Polk/Variety via Getty Fox Entertainment and Kevin Hart ‘s Hartbeat are getting into business on microdrama. Fox Entertainment Studios will have a first look at feature film and television series projects developed from vertical series released under a trio of Hartbeat brands, while distributor Fox Entertainment Global sells them worldwide following their first run. The pipeline launches with a slate of 25 live-action titles, spanning thriller, drama, and faith-based storytelling. They will be release under the Codeblack, Essence and Revolt brands, and hosted on My Drama, which is run by microdrama behemoth Holywater Tech . Fox invested in Holywater last year. Codeblack will become the first dedicated branded channel on My Drama. articles.title: Steve Stark’s Toluca Pictures Extends MGM TV Overall Deal, Expands Amazon MGM Studios First-Look Pact & Taps Max Kisbye As President
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Steve Stark’s Toluca Pictures Extends MGM TV Overall Deal, Expands Amazon MGM Studios First-Look Pact & Taps Max Kisbye As President ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ EP On How Harry Shum Jr. Juggles Medical Drama & ‘Dancing With The Stars’ & If It Affects His Presence On ABC Show ‘High Potential’ Gets Post-Super Bowl Slot, Eyes ‘Grey’s Anatomy’-Style 2-Parter On ABC & Disney+ View All October 13, 2026 9:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Steve Stark and Max Kisbye Gene Reed/Courtesy EXCLUSIVE : Steve Stark has extended and expanded his relationship with Amazon MGM Studios and its MGM Television division. His production company Toluca Pictures has signed a multi-year extension of its exclusive overall deal with MGM Television. Once again, it will include a first-look deal with Amazon MGM Studios, which is now being expanded beyond scripted TV to also include feature films and documentaries. Former MGM Television President Stark has named longtime MGM television executive Max Kisbye as President of Television & Film at Toluca Pictures. Kisbye succeeds Stacey Levin who recently left the company. Related Stories News 'Project Hail Mary' DoP Greig Fraser Says The Film Was The "Most Complicated" He's Ever Shot - Contenders London News 'Stargate' Series From 'WandaVision' Creator Jac Schaeffer In Works At Amazon Kisbye will work with Stark overseeing Toluca Pictures’ development and production operations. Additionally, the company has promoted longtime development executives Jessica Farrelly and Elan Fingles, along with creative executive Mia Stelling. Watch on Deadline “I am thrilled to have Max joining Toluca Pictures,” Stark said. “He is an exceptional executive with tremendous creative instincts, a go-getter with an incredible understanding of the business and, most importantly, a friend with a real passion for great storytelling. We have an incredibly ambitious slate ahead of us, and I couldn’t be more excited to have him alongside me. I’m equally excited to be expanding the roles of Jessica, Elan and Mia, who have been such an important part of building Toluca.” Stark and Kisbye have been friends for more than 20 years. Kisbye was a TV lit agent at CAA when Stark, then President of MGM Television TV, hired him as VP of Television Production in 2012. Kisbye most recently served as Senior Manager of Creative Development in MGM’s TV Scripted group. “I’ve always admired Steve’s instincts and his fearlessness in following them—whether that leads to a historical epic, a dark comedy, a documentary or something no one expects,” Kisbye said. “That spirit is what makes Toluca so exciting to me.” Stark launched Toluca Pictures in 2021 with a five-year overall deal at MGM Television after a nine-year stint as president of the TV studio. Toluca’s current slate includes flagship Netflix series Wednesday , which recently wrapped principal photography on its third season. The company also has coming up Nordic historical epic Bloodaxe , which is slated to premiere in January on Prime Video, as well as Mexican superhero series El Gato Negro, also for Prime Video. The company is in production on the second season of Hulu’s The Testaments and is set to begin production in 2027 on Fear Not , a true-story thriller starring Anne Hathaway for Paramount+. “Steve and I have been creative partners for years, and what he’s built at Toluca is a testament to his extraordinary taste and drive to make great content,” said Lindsay Sloane, Head of MGM Television. “From Wednesday to Bloodaxe to The Testaments , the range and ambition of what Toluca delivers is remarkable. And having worked closely with Max, I’ve seen his talent and passion firsthand.” Stark was under a producing deal with Universal Television in 2011 when he was recruited by Gary Barber, Roger Birnbaum and Roma Khanna to relaunch MGM Television following the studio’s 2010 bankruptcy. Some of the series he launched during his tenure building up the division include The Handmaid’s Tale for Hulu, Fargo for FX, and Vikings for History. Since he launched Toluca in 2021, the company has also produced the series The Consultant , starring Oscar winner Christoph Waltz for Amazon Prime Video, Vikings: Valhalla for Netflix, and The Bombing of Pan Am 103 , which recently premiered on Netflix and BBC, as well as the documentary The Devil’s Confession: The Lost Eichmann Tapes. “I’m incredibly grateful to Lindsay Sloane and my friends and colleagues at MGM Television, who have been extraordinary partners throughout this journey,” Stark said. “I’m also thankful for the continued support of Mike Hopkins, Peter Friedlander, and Kara Smith at Amazon MGM Studios.” Stark is repped by CAA and attorney Greg Slewett at JSSK. Kisbye is repped by David Matlof of Hirsch, Wallerstien, Hayum, Matlof and Fishman. articles.title: Dan Levy Slams Shane Gillis’ ‘SNL’ Joke About Women at the Gym: “Speechless That Can Exist”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All October 12, 2026 8:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Shane Gillis on 'Saturday Night Live.' Screenshot. Logo text A joke from Shane Gillis ‘ Saturday Night Live monologue is drawing fire from Schitt’s Creek co-creator and star Dan Levy . Gillis — the popular stand-up comedian who also stars in Netflix’s Tires — hosted SNL this weekend and delivered this joke during his opening set (watch it below): “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now. Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts? Have you seen the shorts? They’re neon, like, artificial bait-colored? And the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look. You’re not allowed to look. For real, don’t look, because they are filming. I’m in the background of like 10 TikToks right now.” Related Stories TV 'SNL': Shane Gillis Shares "Gas Station Egg" Nickname From Joe Rogan, Pete Hegseth Celebrates USS Lincoln San Diego Homecoming TV Taylor Swift Crashes Dakota Johnson's 'Saturday Night Live' Hosting Stint: "My Literal Therapist!" In response, Levy posted the following on Instagram on Sunday: “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists. There’s a difference there. By the way, I’ve seen more men’s nipples at the gym than I’ve ever seen women showing their bodies off.” Continued the Canadian actor: “But I’m speechless that something like that can exist on live national television. And to be perfectly honest, more men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it’s complacency that has created the environment in which women are sexually assaulted and it’s a ‘conversation’ as opposed to a ‘crime.'” “Men need to be defending women more. This is not a women’s issue, this is an everybody issue. Because the more that men objectify women in the media, the more that other men see them as objects and treat them as objects. They are not objects. They are superior human beings to men, OK? And I’m sorry if this gets me in trouble with the internet, but fuck.” Gillis also drew some criticism for unintentionally saying the F-word during a sketch on SNL , and Gillis subsequently apologized. The stand-up has a long and unique history with the NBC series, having been hired as a cast member in 2019 then quickly fired before he could start the season due to resurfaced comments he made on podcasts. Gillis’ stand-up career then took off, and he hosted the series in 2024 and 2025. THR

articles.title: ‘Beatles’ Films Release Details: A Mega-Month of Movie-Going, Producers Hope
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 12, 2026 8:53am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Paul Mescal as Paul McCartney in Sony's Beatles biopics. Courtesy of Sony More intel on Sony ‘s distribution plan for Sam Mendes ‘ hotly anticipated Beatles films has arrived. Paul Mescal , Harris Dickinson , Joseph Quinn and Barry Keoghan will play Paul McCartney, John Lennon, George Harrison and Ringo Starr , respectively, with the four features currently slated to release in the same month in 2028. Internet-savvy fans will have noticed a swathe of social media videos of the actors in costume filming around London over the last few months. For example, in August, they were spotted re-creating the group’s iconic Abbey Road album cover . The original photo, taken on Aug. 8, 1969, features the Fab Four walking in single file across a crosswalk outside EMI Studios in London. Related Stories Movies Ava DuVernay Says That '14th' Saved Her and "Hollywood Is Over" TV Rakuten TV Launching in U.S., Japan, Middle East (Exclusive) On Monday, Mendes’ long-time producing partner, co-founder of the pair’s Neal Street Productions, Pippa Harris , sat for a keynote session at the BFI London Film Festival’s Industry Forum. She provided a coy update on the rollout, currently described as a “four-film cinematic event” across the month of April. Harris — who came from set to make her Industry Forum appearance for just an hour before heading back — said the team is currently on day 180 of the shoot. She responded later in the session when asked for more details on the distribution plan: “The idea at the moment is the films will come out in 2028, and we want people to be able to experience them in the cinema during the same period.” She clarified: “That doesn’t necessarily mean we’re thinking that people will go and see all four films on the same day. But within the same month, you might see one a week, or you might see one on a weekend, two the next one. However you see it, I think our hope is that people will see all four films,” she continued. “They stand alone as individual stories of each of those four men, but they have a cumulative power, which I think is greater than the sum of their parts. The Beatles are, I think, the greatest band in history, and we’re trying to do our best to do them justice. Hence the four films. I don’t think there’s probably another band that you could legitimately say you wanted to see four films for,” she added. Earlier in the session, she jokingly revealed that the cast members have been explicitly told not to talk about the top-secret movies on various red carpets. “It’s a big endeavor,” said Harris. Also in the Beatles films, Mia McKenna-Bruce stars as Maureen Cox, the wife of Ringo Starr; Anna Sawai will be Yoko Ono, John Lennon’s wife; and Aimee Lou Wood will be Pattie Boyd, who married George Harrison. Saoirse Ronan plays Linda (Eastman) McCartney. Prolific producer Harris is a titan of the British film and TV industry and has worked for decades on some of the most popular shows and films the country has ever produced. Among them are Hamnet , 1917 and Call the Midwife . She went into depth about her wide-ranging career with radio presenter Edith Bowman on Monday, where she reflected on an array of iconic projects, her advice for aspiring producers in the room and why she hasn’t picked up that well-earned Oscar yet. The 70th BFI London Film Festival runs Oct. 7-18. THR

articles.title: John Stamos Voices Concerns About The Beach Boys’ Mike Love’s “Health Challenges”: “We Don’t Know What the Future Holds”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All October 12, 2026 9:05am Add us as a Google Preferred Source From left: Mike Love and John Stamos at the Songwriters Hall of Fame gala in June in New York. Photo by Joy Malone/Getty Images) Beach Boys frontman Mike Love is “facing serious health challenges,” longtime friend John Stamos revealed Sunday in a lengthy post on social media as he prepared to join the band for a Sunday concert at Nashville’s Ryman Auditorium. “We hope he’ll be doing what he loves for years to come, but we don’t know what the future holds,” Stamos said of Love, who he called in part his “father figure, musical hero and mentor” and admitted he was “struggling to put [his] feelings into words.” “Mike is a fighter. Despite doctors, family and friends urging him to focus on his health, he insists on being on stage,” Stamos added on Instagram . “He says he needs his band, the audience, his friends and drummer surrounding him to lift him up. I’ve played with Mike for 41 years. I never imagined how deeply it would affect me to see someone larger than life face something so human and fragile.” Related Stories Movies 'Drag' Review: Lizzy Caplan Headlines a Twisted, Tongue-in-Cheek Robbery Thriller That Overstays Its Welcome Music Mike Love Pays Tribute to Brian Wilson at Songwriters Hall of Fame Induction: "I Do Feel His Presence" He tried to prepare fans, who had expressed concerns after seeing Love look weaker during a Cincinnati, Ohio show on Saturday, for the Nashville performance: “The Mike Love we see tonight may not be exactly the Mike we’ve always known. But he’s still every bit the Mike we love. His lyrics, optimism, unforgettable hooks and more than 7,000 concerts have brought joy to generations. What he’s given me personally is immeasurable.” Stamos went on to talk about what Love had meant to him personally, as a friend, musician and entertainer and reflected on their 41-year bond. And he said he wanted to be “completely present” for his performance with Love and the band in Nashville. Stamos elaborated further in a longer post on Facebook. The previous night, in Cincinnati, the Beach Boys ‘ first show since July, apart from a private performance in Dana Point, California, Love appeared somewhat frail, according to a fan video . Stamos walked him to a chair at the beginning of the show where he remained seated for the performance, barely moving apart from a few hand gestures, before triumphantly being helped to stand, to the Rocky theme. The group had canceled some dates before the Cincinnati concert amid Love’s health concerns. Stamos addressed the crowd prior to the Cincinnati show, saying, according to a fan video, that while Love was there, he has “been going through some health issues.” “He’s had to cancel some shows. But he would not miss tonight. We sort of said ‘stay home,’ but he was like, ‘No, I’m going to Cincinnati,'” Stamos said. “It’s what he loves the most. He loves the audience. He loves the music. He knows how important it is to all of you. We’re all here to support him and give him as much love as we can. So ladies and gentlemen, please welcome the Beach Boys.” Onstage in Nashville, according to reports, Love briefly mentioned that he had “been going through health challenges, but I had to make it to the Ryman.” The Beach Boys’ next show is set for Nov. 11 at Disney World, followed by a Bristol, Virginia show on Nov. 13. THR

articles.title: Amanda Seyfried Passed on a TV Role Because She’d “Have to Have Sex All the Time”: “I’m Uncomfortable With It”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexy Perez Plus Icon Lexy Perez Senior Digital Editor and Producer View All October 12, 2026 9:53am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Amanda Seyfried Dominik Bindl/Getty Images Amanda Seyfried is opening up about passing on a role in a television series due to its sex scenes. While speaking on a panel hosted by Alec Baldwin at the Hamptons International Film Festival in East Hampton, N.Y., on Oct. 4, according to People magazine , the actress reportedly discussed the reason for her discomfort with an offered role. She did not share which television series the role was for. “I passed on a show where I would have to have sex all the time because of the sex,” she said. “Doesn’t matter [who it’s with] … I don’t wanna do it. I’m uncomfortable with it. I’m not into it right now.” Related Stories Movies 'The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd' Review: Amanda Seyfried and Scoot McNairy Bring Raw Intensity to Tim Blake Nelson's Death Row Drama Lifestyle Amanda Seyfried Splits From Thomas Sadoski After Nearly 10 Years of Marriage She explained that her thoughts may change when she‘s in a “different space“ in life. “Maybe if [the project] came along again [at a later point], maybe I’d be in a different space. But I don’t wanna deal with being naked with a stranger,” she said. A mom to two, Seyfried referenced her kids and them “paying attention to what I do“ as a motivating factor. “And so I have to be less of a pushover,” she said. “The other day — this is so silly — but Nina, my daughter, and I were walking across the street [in Manhattan] … and a person on our side of the street asked for a picture, and I looked at my daughter, and I said, ‘No, I’m sorry.’ And then we walked across the street and I was like, ‘How was that for you, Nina? Was that okay?’ ” “She’s like, ‘I’m very proud of you, mama,’ ” Seyfried shared. She also recalled her daughter telling her that she was “proud“ of her for saying no when someone asked for a photo while they were at a coffee shop. “[If] I’m with my kids, I say no … whatever [they are] going through is more important than what I’m going through,“ she said. Also during the panel, Seyfried further reflected on how things get “weirder“ the older you get while being an actor and portraying passion onscreen. “Our jobs are weird,” she said. “And as I get older, it gets weirder. We have to be romantic with people that we’re not romantic with.” “Sometimes it’s great,“ she added. “Sometimes it’s really uncomfortable. But I can’t believe back in the day I was just like, ‘We gotta make out. Great! This is awesome. I know how to make out. And it used to be so fun. It was a non-thing. It was like, ‘I get to make out with a hot person today … And they’re paying me.’ ” Seyfried‘s comments are not the first time an actor has spoken out about onscreen sex scenes. In 2023, Penn Badgley had opened up about his request to have no more intimacy scenes ahead of You season four. “This is actually a decision I’d made before I took the show,” Badgley said on his podcast Podcrushed at the time. “I don’t think I’ve ever mentioned it publicly, but one of the main things is like, ‘Do I wanna put myself back on a career path where I’m just always a romantic lead?’” He continued, “It’s really important to me … Fidelity in every relationship — and especially my marriage — is important to me, and it just got to a point where I didn’t wanna do that. Then, of course, before I took the show is there a question of, ‘Do I have a career if I don’t?’ I mean, you know, think about every male lead you’ve loved. Are they kissing someone? Are they doing a lot more than that? It’s really not my desire to.” THR

articles.title: Getty Images to File for Bankruptcy, Go Private In Restructuring Deal
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All October 12, 2026 10:40am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images After abandoning a $3.7 billion merger with rival Shutterstock in late June over a regulatory roadblock, Getty Images now plans to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and go private in partnership with Charles Koch’s investment firm. As the company plots an overhaul, it says that there will be no impact on operations, employees, partners and vendors. It plans to undergo a prepackaged Chapter 11 process shortly and emerge from restructuring by the end of the year. Getty provides wire service photography and video to news outlets and businesses globally, including most red carpets and film festival premieres. In June, Getty CEO Craig Peters said that its board of directors decided to scrap the deal to merge with Shutterstock after the top regulator in the U.K., the Competition and Markets Authority, required the sale of Shutterstock’s editorial business. Getty, which is focused on growing its core editorial business, viewed that as a non-starter. During its latest earnings call in August, Peters said the company had spent “more than $100 million across professional fees and financing costs in pursuit of what we believe will be a strategic transaction” with Shutterstock that ultimately didn’t go through. At the time, Getty had hired Guggenheim Securities to seek strategic financing alternatives in its standalone path. That now has resulted in the Koch team arriving to provide financing. The company disclosed in an investor presentation on Monday that its iStock eCommerce business has seen “declining agency demand and disruption,” presumably due to the rapid adoption of AI tools and products that have made stock image creation easy. Yet Getty projects growth in its core editorial image unit, forecasting that the division that’s powered by news images (i.e. real photos of actual events that have occurred), will grow from $369 million to $400 million by 2029. Getty CFO Jennifer Leyden had said in August that annual subscribers fell from 321,000 to 241,000 over the prior year due to a “deliberate strategy to deemphasize lower-value acquisition channels, including the discontinuation of our iStock free trial program.” Now it will be leaning even further into its archive and news photography-driven business. “This transformational transaction is underpinned by the strength of the business and the significant growth potential we see ahead,” said Mark Getty, co-founder and chairman of the Board. “I am pleased to continue our strong partnership with Koch Equity Development and the lender groups to provide capital structure improvements that will enable us to build on our solid foundation and seize new growth opportunities.” Affiliates of Koch Equity Development have pledged up to $533 million of new equity to help the image provider go from a publicly traded firm to setting itself up as a private company. CEO Peters said of the deal, “Core pillars of our success are the longstanding commitment of our customers and partners, the deep expertise and creativity of our team and content contributors, and the uniqueness of our archive.” Mike Harris, senior managing director and co-head at Koch Equity, added: “We remain confident in the company’s future and fully support this transaction alongside the Getty family. This equity investment will provide Getty Images with a firm financial foundation and greater flexibility to continue investing in its employees, customers, contributors, and future growth.” THR

articles.title: Cynthia Erivo Hopes ‘Prima Facie’ Will Lead to Debate About “How Lack of Consent Is Received”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 12, 2026 10:41am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Cynthia Erivo in 'Prima Facie.' Courtesy of Nicole Dove Cynthia Erivo knows when to say “yes” and “no” to roles, and she hopes her new film will cause a debate about how the word “no” is received in human relationships and society. That was one of the takeaways from the star’s jam-packed Monday Screen Talk during the 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival (LFF), which runs through Oct. 18. In a wide-ranging chat, the Emmy, Tony and two-time Grammy winner and three-time Academy Award nominee discussed her career, including her latest film, Prima Facie , in which she plays a lawyer who becomes a rape victim. Erivo previously told THR that the work on the film would make her “feel sick and angry.” Related Stories Movies 'Beatles' Films Release Details: A Mega-Month of Movie-Going, Producers Hope Movies Ava DuVernay Says That '14th' Saved Her and "Hollywood Is Over" The star hopes that the film can help start a debate about “preconceived notions about how Black women particularly experience pain” and consent more generally, along with how we hear and accept a “no” in a broader sense. “We expect more violence for her to feel the pain. We expect her to be more in pain than we see,” Erivo shared. “And hopefully, when people watch this movie, you will understand that it’s a violent act.” She also said: “Consent is sometimes hard for all of us to comprehend. That it’s a big complex thing that is more to do with the way we receive ‘no’ than the way we see a ‘yes.’ Now we can have a conversation about that more than about the rape. It really is about the consent and the way her lack of consent is received.” During her appearance, Erivo also lauded the intimacy coordinator and her co-star Daniel Ings. About Ings she said that he, “from the beginning, was very, very kind and immediately wanted to have a conversation about how we could be protective of one another and how we could be helpful in those places, at those moments, so that we could go as far as we needed to go, and then come back again.” And she argued: “I think not enough credit is given to intimacy coordinators. They’re often given a hard time for the work that they have to do on the set. But the work that they do is really important, and it isn’t just about choreographing a scene, a sex scene, a love scene, romantic scene — it’s about sometimes having to not just choreograph these really hard, harrowing scenes but also making sure that everybody comes back to their bodies safely.” Erivo on Monday also mentioned sharing a “no” quite regularly when she is offered roles, highlighting: “I feel like I have an internal metronome that tells me when something is right for me, and when something is not.” As a result, “I say no to a lot of things,” the actress explained. When portraying real people, she said she is “playing these women who brought wonderful things into the world, probably because I care about these women very deeply, and I want the world to see them as they were — in all their complexity and all their greatness, and some of their failings, because they’re human. What I love about these women, I guess, is the deep humanity that each of them holds and carries.” When Erivo was approached about Prima Facie , “I just knew immediately that I wanted to do this because I knew how important it was,” the star recalled. “I also I had this feeling that it was more important than I was even aware of, and I wanted to be part of it.” With her production company, she is looking to tell complex stories with complex characters, including vehicles for great young actors. Erivo mentioned, for example; that she wants to find something interesting for Demi Singleton. Questioned about her own mentors, she shared that Michelle Yeoh is among the great stars who are checking in with her and “looking out for me.” Erivo even recalled, to audience laughter, that Yeoh asked her in between Wicked scenes when she would direct for the first time. And she shared: “She asks me the question every time I see her.” THR

articles.title: Ynon Kreiz,  the Intense CEO Who Thrives When His Back Is Against the Wall
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin , Borys Kit , Mia Galuppo October 12, 2026 11:03am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ynon Kreiz Jesse Grant/Variety/Getty Images On Thursday morning, shortly after 9:30 a.m., Ynon Kreiz , David Ellison and the entire senior leadership team at Skydance walked across the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in lower Manhattan to the booth operated by Citadel Securities, where a large gold bell had been set up. They were there for the first trade, a ceremony that the NYSE holds whenever a public company rings the opening bell, a made-for-the-cameras moment. Citadel trader Peter Giacchi called out the trade. “I’ve got $9 on 519,000 shares!” he shouted, as Ellison held a wooden mallet, striking the bell as the group burst into applause. Related Stories TV John Oliver Says 'Last Week Tonight' Is "Never Gonna Change" Following Skydance Acquisition Business Barbie's New Boss: Mattel Taps a Warner Bros. Exec to Be Its New Head of Dolls Then Kreiz took the mallet and landed a cannon-shot ring on the bell that was so loud that one of the Citadel traders turned around in shock, and even Wall Street veteran Gerry Cardinale’s eyebrows were raised. As anyone who has ever had a handshake with Kreiz will tell you, he projects strength and operates with force and with little hesitation. Kriez is an avid kite surfer whose post-college job was as an instructor at a Club Med and is fond of recalling the story of delivering his baby daughter in the back of a car in front of Paddington Station in London. He is, as one person said, a “bundle of energy,” who seemed to thrive most when his (and the company’s) back was against the wall. The COVID-19 pandemic, President Trump’s tariffs, the risky push into entertainment via the Barbie movie. Whenever the stakes were highest, he rose to the occasion, becoming the leader that the moment required, which has ranged from unemotional cost-cutting to to pivoting when business and political winds changed. Now he is bringing that energy to some of Hollywood’s most venerable assets, swapping dolls for DC and board games for backlots. “There are some questions about David leading a company of that size,” says a former Warners executive. “Ynon is there to make investors feel better.” According to people who worked with Kreiz at Mattel , he was a visionary leader, centering the toy company around individual brands like Barbie, Hot Wheels and American Girl. One of his first orders of business was to build out an in-house entertainment division. After all, why license its toy chest’s worth of IP, when Mattel could reap a part of the financial reward themselves? The business model seemed foolproof: Take toys with built-in audience appeal and make a movie that would appeal to that audience, all of which would in turn sell more toys. At he time, the Lego movie was a massive success story, and spawned a film franchise with spin-off movies, series and video games. And Disney was cashing in big time on nostalgia-laced remakes of their classic animated movies a la Aladdin and Beauty and the Beast. “We look at Marvel as a very good analogy,” Kreiz told Time in 2022 before Mattel has released a single feature film but had an entire slate in development. “That is directionally what we believe we can achieve in terms of the strength, appeal and built-in fan base of our franchises.” Kriez, who previously served as the chairman of Fox Kids Europe, joined the company in 2018 and started his search for an entertainment chief. He made what many saw as an unconventional choice in Robbie Brenner, a veteran independent producer with studio executive bona fides, who was an Oscar nominee thanks to the 2013 drama Dallas Buyers Club . The slate that emerged was filmmaker-focused, with seemingly Mad Libs-esque pairings of directors and talent like M. Night Shyamalan, Clea DuVall and Ayo Edebiri with well-known toys like Magic 8 Ball, Polly Pocket and Barney. The first project out of the gate just so happened to center on Mattel’s biggest property: Barbie . And many people, including the film’s top creatives, credit Kriez with being a hands-on supporter of the film Greta Gerwig film starring Margot Robbie. “The Mattel board was being skittish and was scared the concept was too subversive. But he supported Robbie and he supported Greta,” says one source. The movie includes the Mattel logo placed over swear words and a Mattel executive getting shot with a (fake!) arrow, not to mention Will Ferrell playing the film’s villain as a bumbling CEO, all choices that could have been shut down. Says the source, “[Ynon] got the company comfortable about being uncomfortable about it.” “Ynon has a great sense of humor, and I think he thought it was funny,” Brenner told THR in 2023. “To be inside the joke and to be part of it and to be able to laugh at yourself, we all just had to encourage each other that it’s funny. If you’re not laughing at yourself, someone else is.” In a quote that possibly best encapsulates Kriez’ unique ability to walk the delicate line between corporate-minded and creative-friendly that is required as the leader of an entertainment company, Kriez said of Ferrell’s CEO skewering, “We take our brands very seriously. We take what we do very seriously. But we don’t take ourselves too seriously.” Not all of Mattel’s movies have been major hits or earned critical acclaim like Barbie. Masters of the Universe was a bomb for Amazon MGM Studios this summer, while the new Matchbox movie — made with Skydance and on Apple TV+ today, was skewered by critics. But Barbie proved to be a resounding success, grossing over $1.4 billion at the global box office, with sales of the doll jumping 16 percent in the fiscal quarter that followed the film’s release. It was also during Barbie ’s rollout that the ground shifted under the entirety of Hollywood. The Barbie premiere took place on July 9 in Los Angeles, and less than a week later, SAG joined the WGA in its labor strikes, which slow-rolled directly into our current moment of M&A and consolidation. Just as Kriez proved adept at leading a company through a Hollywood boom cycle, he quickly got to work at navigating the bust, in addition to a shifting political climate. Mattel went through several rounds of layoffs over the course of 2025 and into 2026, ultimately affecting nearly 300 employees at the company’s El Segundo headquarters. Additionally, last year, as the incoming second Trump administration started to wage a federal battle against anything it deemed as falling under the umbrella of diversity, equity and inclusion, Mattel, like larger entertainment companies, including Disney, Warner Bros. Discovery and Amazon, pulled back on these efforts. The company dispensed with its DEI disclosures to investors, scrubbing any references to goals and resources aimed at boosting diversity at the company. It is these more austere moments of leadership that Kriez will have to call upon as he assumes the co-CEO mantle at Skydance. That axe will have to come to Skydance soon, though Kirez insisted Thursday that most of the $6 billion in synergies will not come from staff reductions. “When it comes to making those decisions, of course, we’re thinking of our people,” Kreiz said on the NYSE floor, a few minutes before ringing the bell, speaking to CNBC’s David Faber.” We’re going to do it in the right way, respectfully, transparently, and communicate our plans. This will be part of the plan.” THR

articles.title: Selma Blair Taken Into Custody at New York’s JFK Airport After Allegedly Punching, Biting Delta Staffers
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 12, 2026 11:46am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Selma Blair attends 35th Environmental Media Association in Los Angeles on Oct. 11, 2025. (Photo by Presley Ann/Getty Images) Selma Blair was taken into custody at New York’s JFK Airport on Sunday after allegedly assaulting Delta Airlines flight attendants on board flight 938 from Los Angeles. Around 11 p.m. ET last night, the New York Port Authority Police Department responded to a call regarding a physically abusive passenger identified as Blair, 54, after she had allegedly assaulted Delta staffers. As first reported by TMZ and confirmed by The Hollywood Reporter , Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant and bit another. She also reportedly attempted to open the aircraft door at some point during the flight. Related Stories General News Selma Blair Reveals Extent of Fallout After Anti-Extremist Instagram Comment: "I Didn't Have a Career at All" Movies Selma Blair Set for Bridget Stokes' Mystical Coming of Age Film 'Schmoolie The Deathwatcher' Blair was taken into custody by the Port Authority Police Department and transported to the hospital for evaluation. The two Delta staffers also reported injuries, with one serious enough that they, too, were taken to the hospital for further evaluation. The matter has been taken over by the FBI, which is said to be currently investigating the incident. It’s unclear what charges Blair is currently facing. THR has reached out to the FBI for additional comment and will update when more information becomes available. A representative for Delta tells THR , “Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first.” The incident did not have any operational impact on the flight as it landed ahead of schedule at JFK. As for Blair, her publicist confirmed the incident, saying, “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition.” It’s not Blair’s first incident on board a flight. In June 2016, Blair, who was returning to Los Angeles from a vacation in Cancun, Mexico, began screaming uncontrollably and causing chaos on the flight. Two nurses on board helped subdue the actress, who was then taken to the hospital for evaluation. As reported at the time by THR , Blair apologized and claimed she had blacked out after mixing prescription medication and alcohol. “I made a big mistake yesterday. After a lovely trip with my son and his dad, I mixed alcohol with medication, and that caused me to black out and led me to say and do things that I deeply regret,” Blair said in a statement. “My son was with his dad asleep with his headphones on, so there is that saving grace. I take this very seriously, and I apologize to all of the passengers and crew that I disturbed and am thankful to all of the people who helped me in the aftermath. I am a flawed human being who makes mistakes and am filled with shame over this incident. I am truly very sorry.” More to come. THR

articles.title: ‘Merry the Christmas Witch’ Director Estimated Movie Would Cost $80 Million — but Says With AI, He Made It for $1.5 Million (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Oct 12, 2026 9:37am PT ‘Merry the Christmas Witch’ Director Estimated Movie Would Cost $80 Million — but Says With AI, He Made It for $1.5 Million (EXCLUSIVE) By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest ‘Merry the Christmas Witch’ Director Estimated Movie Would Cost $80 Million — but Says With AI, He Made It for $1.5 Million (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Antonio Banderas to Star in AI-Powered Feature ‘Cortes’ From Utopai Studios 4 hours ago An AI-Generated Trailer Won the Inaugural $2.5 Million Future Vision XPRIZE — and Its Director Hopes It’ll Change Minds About AI 3 days ago See All TW3 Entertainment AI has come for docudramas , for summer blockbusters , even for adaptations of books about farts . What’s left other than holiday films? Enter “ Merry the Christmas Witch .” The film focuses on Merry, the first witch born on Christmas Day, who must defeat a coven of evil witches that has kidnapped Santa Claus in a bid to destroy Christmas. The project is based on a 2012 children’s book by Bobbi Hess, a 70-year-old New Orleans-based technical writer who, in her own words, called the adaptation “a perfect marriage” of subject and technology. Related Stories 'Dungeon Crawler Carl' Live-Action TV Series to Begin Shooting in 2027, More Details Coming 'Very Soon' Marvel's 'VisionQuest' Surprise Premieres at NYCC and Earns Glowing First Reactions: 'A Worthy Successor' to 'WandaVision' “AI enhanced the whole idea,” Hess tells Variety . “It was created by a human — the character Merry was created by me — but then Tom, with his amazing imagination and his wonderful ability to create wonderful creatures, it just came together.” The “Tom” in question is Tom Walsh, the CEO of the independent production company TW3 Entertainment, who directed and co-wrote the adaptation. Walsh came across Hess’ book in 2014 during a Los Angeles meeting with her late husband, who gave Walsh a copy of her book. Walsh tells Variety he loved the idea of a Christmas witch and was eager to adapt the title. But when he sat down to figure out the budget, the total cost seemed unwieldy: $80 million, a cost studios would balk at for “an unknown property,” Walsh said. Instead, using AI, he managed to produce the final two-hour film for $1.5 million, perhaps serving as a test case for the types of projects AI can help make. “We were kind of stuck,” he says. “The doors are not very open to new kind[s] of ideas and new kind[s] of stories and everything, and that makes it a little tough for independent filmmakers, so that’s where AI came in.” Walsh recruited a team of production professionals — including foley artists, editors, sound designers, a composer and other roles commonplace in a film’s production — to help craft “Merry” in the vein of a traditional movie. Human actors were hired to record the script and help guide how the characters should move and sound, but Walsh ultimately opted for AI-generated voices due to syncing issues with the technology. Instead, Walsh — with the help of the AI studio Phatty Acid, which worked on the film — used tools such as ElevenLabs’ voice generator and video generators Seedance and Nanobanana to bring them to life. With roughly 50 different people working on the film throughout its 10-month production cycle, the film resembled a “hybrid AI production,” Walsh said, one he believes could be a new standard of making projects traditionally hampered by large budgets. “The quality of your AI production depends on the quality of your traditional production staff,” he says. “If you have inexperienced people who don’t know production…and timing and how shots should look, it’s going to look like garbage.” But whether general audiences will want to watch any AI film — much less a two-hour holiday film already competing for time with the dozens that came before it — is questionable. Even as AI films like “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” try to compete for attention at cinemas, outrage continues to swirl whenever a film or studio reveals the technology was used at any level. (The film currently has no distributor, though a spokesperson said “optimistic” conversations were underway with “a few different companies.”) In Walsh’s view, there’s room for everything, and he’s hopeful people can look beyond the technology’s use. “They should really just be looking at the story and the characters,” he says. “They shouldn’t really be getting down to, well, ‘are these human or not human? It’s almost like when you’re watching animation, you’re not thinking you’re watching animated characters on that kind of basis.” Even if audiences do reject it and distributors pass on picking up the film, Walsh remains undeterred. He is already working on another AI-generated picture, and he said he and Hess — who says she has “no issues at all with AI” — have remained in touch for future stories centered around the Christmas witch. “AI can again continue to help to create those adventures that children will love,” Hess says. “It’s a little scary on taking those chances, but I think you have to take it in order to hit,” Walsh adds about finding distribution. “We would never have gotten a movie like ‘Merry’ made if we didn’t take that chance. It would have just sat in a screenplay never made, and so I have no regrets of taking that chance.” Cynthia Erivo Says ‘Not Enough Credit Is Given to Intimacy Coordinators’: ‘They’re Often Given a Hard Time’ but ‘What They Do Is Important’ Loading comments...

articles.title: Out With the New, in With the Old?: How the Grammys Should Recognize Revived Hits
articles.full_text: Oct 12, 2026 10:06am PT Out With the New, in With the Old?: How the Grammys Should Recognize Revived Hits By Steven J. Horowitz Plus Icon Steven J. Horowitz Senior Music Writer speriod Latest Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart 1 hour ago Out With the New, in With the Old?: How the Grammys Should Recognize Revived Hits 1 hour ago Adéla Brings Sass, Vocals and Razor-Sharp Moves to Los Angeles’ Fonda Theatre 3 days ago See All picture alliance via Getty Image Earlier this year, Goo Goo Dolls ’ “Iris” had another sudden resurgence — one of many since its release in 1998 — after social media users and celebrities spanning Drew Barrymore to Kevin Bacon used the song to showcase photos of what they looked like in the 1990s. By late September, the melancholy ballad had become a staple in the top 10 of the Spotify Global 50 chart, ranking ahead of freshly released singles from Ariana Grande and BTS. “Iris” is one of several songs that have had second (or third, or fourth) lives decades after their original release, joining tracks like Fleetwood Mac’s “Dreams” and the Killers ’ “Mr. Brightside” in a new school of hits from older eras. But as catalog tunes have become commonplace in contemporary culture (nearly half the songs on Global 50 were released before 2025), the question of what the Recording Academy could — or should? — do to honor popular songs outside of the eligibility cycle has become a sticking point for artists with this type of renewed success. Related Stories Charlie Brooker's New Netflix Series Gets Title, 'Blackmere,' as Rory Kinnear Joins Cast and First-Look Photos Revealed The Grammys have long honored achievements in audio restoration with the best historical album award, while the Academy has celebrated classics and artists through the Grammy Hall of Fame and Lifetime Achievement Award. But as TikTok has democratized music consumption and listeners care less about how old a song might be, some think that the Grammys could reconsider its eligibility rules for older songs, or perhaps offer a new category that reflects the shift in modern music. Popular on Variety “I think it’d be an amazing idea, especially if something is culturally happening now. Why not?” says Pat Magnarella, who has managed Goo Goo Dolls for the past 36 years. “Iris” was initially nominated for record of the year and pop performance by a duo or group in 1999, but its resurgence cannot currently be acknowledged by the Grammys unless it’s submitted through a loophole, like with a cover, a live recording or new remix. “There’s this whole new generation that’s discovering ‘Iris,’ and the great thing now is with new music, there’s no more genre. So as a 14-year-old kid hears ‘Iris,’ it’s not like, ‘Oh, that’s an old song’ — it’s a new song to them.” “There’s got to be some kind of recognition for that kind of thing,” adds Robert Reynolds, who has managed the Killers since the start of their recording career. “Mr. Brightside,” which was first released in 2003, had a surge similar to “Iris” over the past year, hitting No. 1 on Billboard’s Rock Streaming Songs chart in early August. “It feels like it is in the ballpark of the Academy. They already accept that the recording’s life extends beyond the release year [with] the Hall of Fame, historical categories. I think this just applies the same logic to the living streaming culture.” (A representative for the Recording Academy declined to comment on the issue.) Across the industry, music-listening habits have gradually shifted in favor of older music over the past few years, particularly because of the nostalgia surrounding it. According to Luminate’s 2026 midyear report, 60% of Gen Z consumers favor music from the 1990s or earlier, a whopping escalation from 18% in 2021. The report credits nostalgia as a significant contributing factor, as 54% of Gen X and 49% of Gen Z cite it as a motivating factor when buying vinyl. Adapting to the times, says Reynolds, is crucial for an institution like the Grammys to reflect the shifting tastes of consumers. “You have to stay relevant to the younger generations — they need to recognize this,” he adds. “It’s definitely time for them to look at this gap between what they’re rewarding and what’s actually happening. Focusing only on what’s come out within the last 12 months doesn’t jibe with how music is being consumed anymore.” Cynthia Erivo Says ‘Not Enough Credit Is Given to Intimacy Coordinators’: ‘They’re Often Given a Hard Time’ but ‘What They Do Is Important’ Loading comments...

articles.title: Cynthia Erivo Says ‘Not Enough Credit Is Given to Intimacy Coordinators’: ‘They’re Often Given a Hard Time’ but ‘What They Do Is Important’
articles.full_text: Oct 12, 2026 10:24am PT Cynthia Erivo Says ‘Not Enough Credit Is Given to Intimacy Coordinators’: ‘They’re Often Given a Hard Time’ but ‘What They Do Is Important’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Dan Levy Calls Out Shane Gillis’ ‘SNL’ Monologue and Says ‘More Men Need to Be Standing Up’: ‘Speechless That Something Like That Can Exist on Live National Television’ 9 hours ago Andrew Garfield Reacts to Oscar Buzz as ‘Artificial’ Gets Resounding London Reception: ‘So Flattered That Anyone Is Going to See This Film in the First Place’ 18 hours ago Quentin Tarantino Play ‘The Popinjay Cavalier,’ Starring Sacha Baron Cohen, to Open on West End in March 20 hours ago See All Getty Images for BFI Cynthia Erivo spoke candidly about the importance of working with an intimacy coordinator on her new movie “ Prima Facie ” at a London Film Festival screen talk on Monday, saying that often “not enough credit is given” to them. In her first film role post “ Wicked ,” Erivo leads “Prima Facie” as Tessa Ensler, a successful defense lawyer who finds herself at the center of a trial when she is sexually assaulted by a colleague. Based on Suzie Miller’s acclaimed stage play, the film premiered last month at Toronto Film Festival and has its U.K. debut at London Film Fest on Tuesday. Related Stories LaKeith Stanfield Previews 'Molepeople' Movie From Paramount Primal, Blumhouse Atomic Monster at New York Comic-Con Jason Blum on How ‘Other Mommy’ Got That Controversial Title, Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ and More From Blumhouse at NYCC Erivo said she “knew immediately” that she wanted to sign on to the film, which she also produced. “I just had this feeling that it was more important than I was even aware of and I wanted to be apart of it,” she said. Popular on Variety She readily admitted that the intense legal drama was “really hard” to film, especially the scene involving the assault. This is where the film’s intimacy coordinator, Lizzy Talbot, came in. “Lizzy, our intimacy coordinator, was really helpful with creating a space that felt very safe,” Erivo said. “I had to understand what it was like to be in your body but not there, so finding what that looked like for me, where you’re there but you have to check out to stay safe. And that was the thing that we had to figure out — how to do that and come back safely.” She continued, “A lot of this was really hard to film, but the hardest thing was actually coming back from filming it. Getting your feet back on the ground, getting back into your body and finding the safest place again.” Erivo said that she and Daniel Ings, who plays the lawyer who assaults Tessa, had many discussions about how to handle the scene in a way that made them both feel safe. “He from the beginning was very, very kind and immediately wanted to have a conversation about how we could be protective of one another, and how we could be helpful in those moments so that we could go as far as we needed to go and then come back again,” she said. “I think not enough credit is given to intimacy coordinators and they’re often given a hard time for the work they have to do on a set,” Erivo added, earning applause in the room. “But the work that they do is incredibly important. And it isn’t just about choreographing a sex scene, a love scene, it’s sometimes about how to not just choreograph these really hard, harrowing scenes, but make sure everyone comes back to their bodies safely.” Erivo said she hopes the film sparks a wider conversation about consent, as well as about how Black women are often overlooked when it comes to discussions about sexual assault. “We already have preconceived notions about how Black women, particularly, experience pain. And so what this does is it puts us in the eye of the beholder — we’re sort of front and center to have the discussion of what it looks like when this happens to us as well. It’s more often than you would realize, more than we discuss at all. It’s often not reported,” Erivo said. “Rarely do you see films where a Black woman has experienced this in this way, and I think now we can have a conversation about that as a whole because we’re often left out of that conversation.” Of course, Erivo also spoke a bit about both “Wicked” films, the first of which earned her an Oscar nomination for her performance as Elphaba, who she said she “so loved playing.” When asked about how she first got into the character, Erivo said she sought to find the similarities between them. “I know that the two of us are very different. I know that the two of us have strange relationships with fathers. I know that the two of us can get frustrated and can be stubborn. I know that the two of us also have a joy in us that no one really realizes and hasn’t been able to see. I knew all those things and I could start from there,” she said. “But I also knew, I’m not trying to make her different, but just trying to make her as true as possible. So when the words are on the page, how would I say them so that they mean something? So that they are connected to me, not connected to her or how I’ve heard them said before.” She added, “The more I started to understand who this person was, I realized that, I think for a lot of people it’s like, ‘Oh, the green girl. The makeup is on.’ But for me it was like, no this is her DNA, this is the way she was born.” As for what’s next for Erivo, she teased that it could be time for her villain era. “I keep saying I’m in my villain era and it keeps coming up,” she said with a laugh. “I want to find those stories where we get to see faces that are different in leading roles that are complicated and not necessarily the hero, but are gritty and in the gray area and fun to play. I think I’m sort of seeking them out for myself, and I want to seek them out for other people.” Cynthia Erivo Says ‘Not Enough Credit Is Given to Intimacy Coordinators’: ‘They’re Often Given a Hard Time’ but ‘What They Do Is Important’ Loading comments...

articles.title: Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart
articles.full_text: Oct 12, 2026 10:34am PT Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart By Steven J. Horowitz Plus Icon Steven J. Horowitz Senior Music Writer speriod Latest Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart 1 hour ago Out With the New, in With the Old?: How the Grammys Should Recognize Revived Hits 2 hours ago Adéla Brings Sass, Vocals and Razor-Sharp Moves to Los Angeles’ Fonda Theatre 3 days ago See All TAS Artists Rights Management Taylor Swift has scored a second week atop the Billboard Hot 100 with “Patient Zero,” the lead single off of “The Life of Showgirl: The Encore.” “Patient Zero” is one of four new Swift songs included on “Encore,” which, just yesterday, earned her a 100th week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 for all of her albums combined. The track earned 17.4 million official streams, down 50 percent week over week, and on the Streaming Songs chart, it slips from No. 1 to 2. “Patient Zero” is Swift’s 51st career week at No. 1 on the Hot 100, giving her the fifth-highest total in chart history for weeks at No. 1 behind Mariah Carey (101), Rihanna (60), the Beatles (59) and Drake (58). Related Stories Charlie Brooker's New Netflix Series Gets Title, 'Blackmere,' as Rory Kinnear Joins Cast and First-Look Photos Revealed Speaking of Drake, the Toronto rapper bowed at No. 5 on the Hot 100 with “Solar Eclipse,” his collaboration with Don Toliver that puts a spin on Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas,” which itself holds at No. 2 following a record 24 weeks at No. 1. “Solar Eclipse” first debuted as part of Drake’s “Fear of Missing Out” film that he aired on YouTube in mid-September, and was subsequently released to streaming services as part of his “Habibti (FOMO)” edition along with three other new songs. Popular on Variety The other notable debut on the Hot 100 this week came from Slovakian pop newcomer Adéla , whose swaggery “Nicole Kidman” jumped from No. 12 to 9. The track became her first Hot 100 entry last month, while her other single, “Ain’t in LA,” remains in the top 30. Her chart presence continues to grow following the release of her debut album “Prima” in early September, bolstered by her “Red Bottoms” tour that’s currently working its way through North America. articles.title: What Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Reveals About Media’s Future (Guest Column)
articles.full_text: Oct 12, 2026 11:00am PT What Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Reveals About Media’s Future (Guest Column) 'You can’t consolidate your way out of disruption,' writes Accenture's John Peters By John Peters Plus Icon John Peters Latest See All Getty Images Paramount Skydance ‘s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery to form Skydance Corp. , which pushes the combined company to second place in Nielsen’s U.S. TV audience share and brings together two major Hollywood studios, has reignited debate about consolidation in media. But the bigger story is what the merger highlights about the pressures reshaping the media industry and the race to reinvent a market where audiences are more fragmented, competition for attention is intensifying and technology is changing how content is created, distributed and monetized. Related Stories Charlie Brooker's New Netflix Series Gets Title, 'Blackmere,' as Rory Kinnear Joins Cast and First-Look Photos Revealed The most interesting thing about this acquisition isn’t merely the consolidation itself. It’s what companies do with the scale after they consolidate. Combining two companies can create scale, but scale alone doesn’t automatically create relevance — much less long-term survival. Media companies now are being forced to take a harder look at their portfolios and determine which assets, brands and capabilities will drive future growth. The real test is whether that scale can be turned into stronger audience affinity, better experiences and new sources of growth. Popular on Variety Competition in an M&A climate Hollywood may be consolidating, but attention is not. There may be fewer traditional media companies today, but there are dramatically more competitors for consumers’ attention. Media companies are chasing the same things: consumer attention, subscription dollars, ad revenue, talent, and data and technology capabilities. And they’re not just competing with each other. They’re competing against some of the world’s largest technology platforms — and the armies of creators that they enable, not to mention the ever-proliferating competitors fighting for attention like video games, music, and even sports betting and AI chatbots. While box office or TV ratings used to be the competitive unit, it’s become clear that the minute is now the competitive unit. Every platform is bidding for the next minute of someone’s attention. The affinity war is on. The Impact on Content So what does consolidation mean for how media companies think about IP? The instinct after consolidation is to assume fewer titles and fewer bets. But technology and AI are simultaneously driving the economics of content creation in the opposite direction. The Paramount-Warner Bros. merger could eventually lead to more content, not less. But that requires a broader view of content, one that extends beyond traditional film and television programming. It’s far past time to stop thinking of content as just “shows” and “movies,” and acknowledge that today’s franchises have ongoing relationships with their fans. Consumers are increasingly moving between long-form video, short-form video, gaming, social communities, merchandise and live experiences. Recent Accenture research found that 55% of consumers want social features within streaming services, while 58% say user-generated video can be just as entertaining as traditional media. The next media battle won’t be held over who has the biggest content library. It’ll be about who’s developed the deepest fan relationship. This is equally appliable in film and TV studios as it is in newsroom, in broadcast trucks outside a sporting event, in record labels and music platforms, social video sites, sports betting apps and AI chatbots. In the affinity war, the future of content may be fewer isolated titles, but infinitely more experiences around the titles and brands that matter. The Audience Is Consuming Everything Streaming is no longer the industry’s organizing idea. The battle has expanded to every channel competing for consumer attention. Audience fragmentation is the new reality, and consumer attention is scattered. Accenture research shows that the number of media types consumers choose most across 10 different entertainment occasions has expanded from just two in 2022 to six in 2025. Streaming remains the dominant source for television content, as it now accounts for almost half of television usage according to Nielsen. Even so, while streaming was once the destination, it’s now just one stop along the way. You Can’t Consolidate Your Way Out of Disruption A merger can make you bigger overnight, but it can’t reinvent you overnight. Accenture research suggests the industry faces a steep challenge: more than nine in 10 media executives expect GenAI and new entrants to significantly reshape the industry within just two years. Meanwhile, 88% of media executives cite rigid technology stacks as a major transformation barrier, and legacy media companies spend roughly 6% of revenue on IT versus 9%-10% for media businesses within diversified technology companies. M&A can create scale, but scale is only valuable if it funds reinvention. The critical question is whether companies will use that financial flexibility to invest in AI, technology, advertising, personalization, new experiences and new business model innovation. The real dividend from consolidation isn’t cost reduction. It’s the ability to build the next generation of media businesses. So the strategic question isn’t “Are we big enough?” It’s “Are we different enough, and can we change fast enough?” The Future of M&A in Media and Entertainment M&A is likely to remain an important part of the industry’s strategic toolkit, although the nature of the transactions may evolve. There is an obvious economic logic to additional consolidation where companies can achieve scale, eliminate duplication or strengthen distribution. However, in the affinity war with audiences fragmenting away from media’s legacy and streaming offerings, scale without reinvention is, sadly, merely increasing the size of the lifeboat drifting helplessly towards the coming waterfall. As the newly named Skydance’s transaction marches toward an increasingly inevitable closure, everyone will naturally ask which big media company will merge next. However, the industry may be asking the wrong M&A question. The key item to consider is which capabilities are media companies missing. For the forward-looking, the next phase of M&A is likely to focus less on scale, and more on acquiring capabilities that create differentiation. In capability-driven M&A, companies are seeking to add AI, advertising, gaming, creator, commerce or data capabilities that can create new growth opportunities and strengthen their ability to compete for audience attention. Roku’s multiyear history of acquiring ad tech fits this model — as does Fox Corp.’s planned acquisition of Roku, which adds not just ad inventory but ad tech, platform and CTV operating-system capabilities. Similarly, Netflix’s recent acquisition of Ben Affleck’s InterPositive accelerates the postproduction AI capabilities they can offer to creatives. Indeed, Accenture research found that 80% of deals that outperformed sector averages saw dealmakers place significant emphasis on technology transformation and technology capability acquisition. The most capable acquirers also get better with every deal. The strongest deals will add something the company lacks. Some of the most important transactions may therefore be smaller acquisitions that bring media companies new skills or technologies. In the war for affinity, legacy brands like Golf Channel and the New York Times are showing what growth and diversification become possible with segment-specific, affinity-targeted acquisition strategies. The rallying cry in corporate development offices across Hollywood should be to stop buying more of yesterday’s media business. Instead, buy the capabilities you need for tomorrow’s. The industry’s future will depend on how effectively media companies turn their portfolios and capabilities into better products, stronger audience relationships, and more engagement experiences. John Peters is Accenture’s global and U.S. media & entertainment industry lead, advising leading media, entertainment and sports organizations on growth, transformation and innovation. Based in Los Angeles, he works with clients across the industry on navigating disruption, harnessing emerging technologies and building new sources of value and competitive advantage. articles.title: Peruvian Filmmaker Sami Hawka Explores Polyamory, Indigenous Rights and Resistance in ‘While Everything Falls’: ’Power Can Oppress People in Different Ways’
articles.full_text: Oct 12, 2026 11:15am PT Peruvian Filmmaker Sami Hawka Explores Polyamory, Indigenous Rights and Resistance in ‘While Everything Falls’: ’Power Can Oppress People in Different Ways’ Selected for VIFF’s Business Hub Co-Productions Forum and the Queer Palm Lab, the film explores marginalized communities and political resistance under a fictionalized dictatorship By Katherine Brodsky Plus Icon Katherine Brodsky Latest Peruvian Filmmaker Sami Hawka Explores Polyamory, Indigenous Rights and Resistance in ‘While Everything Falls’: ’Power Can Oppress People in Different Ways’ 31 minutes ago Beyond ‘Hollywood North’: How Vancouver’s Indie Film Scene Is Building Its Own Ecosystem 3 days ago Jeissy Trompiz’s ‘Three Houses’ Explores a Venezuela Where Afro and Indigenous Communities Sit on the ‘Periphery of the Periphery’ 3 days ago See All Sami Hawka Courtesy of Sami Hawka What happens when the right to love who you want becomes an act of resistance? Peruvian filmmaker Sami Hawka is developing a feature, “While Everything Falls” (Afuera Todo Arde), which explores the fight for personal freedom under a fictionalized dictatorship in contemporary Peru. The story takes place in a conservative rural community where two members of a polyamorous triad marry to keep up appearances. But when their relationship is exposed by their third lover, they flee to the capital, where they become involved in a rebellion against the dictatorship and discover that their fight for personal freedom is inseparable from the struggle for Indigenous rights, the rights of other marginalized communities and economic equality. Related Stories 'Star Trek: Starfleet Academy' Season 2 Adds Bill Nighy, Rosemarie DeWitt in Guest Roles Jason Blum on How ‘Other Mommy’ Got That Controversial Title, Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ and More From Blumhouse at NYCC The Madrid-based filmmaker’s project is gaining momentum after being selected for the Vancouver International Film Festival’s Business Hub Co-Productions Forum and the Queer Palm Lab, an LGBTQ-focused development program associated with the Cannes Film Festival. Hawka is now pursuing international co-production partners and funding for the feature. Popular on Variety “The film follows these characters who are in their bubble,” Hawka tells Variety . “But when they break [out of] the bubble, they start realizing that they have other forms of oppression” beyond queerness and polyamory, and that they share those experiences with other marginalized groups. “In this rebellion, there are also a lot of Indigenous people and Indigenous movements that need vindication of their rights,” Hawka says, connecting the story to Peru’s colonial history and its enduring consequences. “When we as a culture experienced that…It had a very strong impact on our culture and on the lives that we had here.” Peru developed into a country that’s fractured, they explain. “These people still need some sort of citizenship in this new order that’s not organized to fit their needs, or was built on inequality.” For Hawka, the story is also an extension of their own experiences as a nonbinary person with Indigenous roots. They spent a significant part of their childhood in Cusco, in Peru’s Andean highlands, attending an intercultural school where they learned Quechua and developed connections with Indigenous elders and spiritual traditions. Those experiences helped shape both their understanding of gender and their approach to filmmaking. “I think it has helped me situate a place that needs vindication,” they say. “It has helped me look at things from a perspective where rights need to get acknowledged, and where political action needs to start.” Colonialism and cultural erasure, they argue, have also shaped attitudes toward sexuality and gender, leaving a complicated legacy that younger generations are now working to understand and reclaim. “There are documents of many places in the world where societies had more than two genders, and that was sort of erased, and now we are starting to reconnect with that,” they say. In Peru, they point to archaeological ceramics depicting same-sex encounters by shamans in sacred ritual contexts. “Now it’s kind of our work to go back and try to rescue all these things.” For them, reconnecting with Indigenous traditions has also been a way of understanding their own identity. At its core, Hawka says, the film they want to make is about how authoritarian systems restrict people’s ability to determine their own lives. “Power can invisibilize and oppress people in different ways— around class, around gender, around race, around economic privilege,” they say. Eventually, the characters come to recognize that their own experiences of marginalization connect them to a larger struggle. “They realize that they need to join the resistance in order to be free themselves too,” says Hawka. “It’s like a collective thing.” The visual approach will reflect the tensions between the characters’ private lives and the political upheaval around them. Hawka envisions contemplative, quiet scenes in the countryside, with natural light and a documentary-like approach, contrasted with the noise, intense colors, and chaos of the city. They aim to show the “places and spaces inhabited the way they actually ar The film is being developed by Peruvian production company FILMA+ as an international co-production, with casting still open and discussions with potential producers underway. After development had stalled, recently “the project has taken a giant leap,” they say. Ultimately, says Hawka, “While Everything Falls” uses an unconventional love story to explore how people can reclaim the freedom to determine one’s own destiny and fight for what they believe — both individually and collectively — in the face of authoritarianism and oppressive power. Whether it’s about polyamory, or homosexuality — there are a lot of rules that are imposed by power, they say. Social punishment, they note, is also an “exercise of power.” Cynthia Erivo Says ‘Not Enough Credit Is Given to Intimacy Coordinators’: ‘They’re Often Given a Hard Time’ but ‘What They Do Is Important’ Loading comments...

articles.title: How South Africa Rescued Its Rebate and Pulled the Industry Back From the Brink: We’re ‘Back in Business’
articles.full_text: Oct 12, 2026 11:26am PT How South Africa Rescued Its Rebate and Pulled the Industry Back From the Brink: We’re ‘Back in Business’ After more than two years of almost complete paralysis, the country's 25% cash rebate program appears to be back on track By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest How South Africa Rescued Its Rebate and Pulled the Industry Back From the Brink: We’re ‘Back in Business’ 15 minutes ago ‘Mami Wata’ Director C.J. Obasi, ‘Khartoum’ Filmmaker Ibrahim Ahmad and More Take New Projects to Durban FilmMart’s Co-Production Forum 5 days ago Durban FilmMart Head on Why This Year’s Event Is ‘Looking Inward’ as African Screen Industries Strive to ‘Create Solutions’ on Their Own Terms 2 weeks ago See All Courtesy Known Associates Entertainment The long nightmare might be over for South African producers, whose industry has been crippled for more than two years by the paralysis of a rebate program that for all intents and purposes had ceased to function. Speaking this week at the Durban FilmMart , Nelly Molokoane, director of film and television production at the Dept. of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC), insisted that the government body tasked with administering the country’s 25% cash rebate has finally turned a corner. “The department is back in business,” Molokoane said. Related Stories Charlie Brooker's New Netflix Series Gets Title, 'Blackmere,' as Rory Kinnear Joins Cast and First-Look Photos Revealed After months of political pressure from industry bodies that rallied under the banner of the Save SA Film and TV Jobs Coalition, the DTIC is now working through a backlog of applications and rebate claims dating back to 2024, with Molokoane counseling patience as the embattled department attempts to right the ship. Popular on Variety “We know that the industry now is bleeding, but we are doing our best,” she said. The news sparked a collective sigh of relief from the filmmakers and industry groups gathered in Durban, who have locked horns with South African officials over delays in processing rebate claims, bureaucratic bottlenecks, a lack of transparency from their counterparts in government, and overall questions about the future of the once-thriving incentive program. “The worst is over,” said producer Delon Bakker, who serves as chairperson of the Independent Producers Organization. “We’re very confident that we’re now moving in the right direction. We’re not sure at what pace, but we are definitely making progress.” The crisis dealt a devastating blow to a South African industry that was already feeling the squeeze, with the exhibition sector floundering, global streaming networks scaling back their investments in local production and domestic broadcasters — including the struggling public broadcaster, SABC — unable to keep the industry afloat. “We’re talking thousands of jobs. We’re talking hundreds of companies that have suffered losses because of this. We’re talking projects that have made claims that have not been paid two, three, four years later,” said producer Paul Buys, of Rose and Oaks Media. “It’s really pushed everybody to the limits.” The DTIC has made significant strides in paying off most of the nearly 2-billion-rand ($121 million) backlog in unpaid rebate claims and shored up roughly 1.5 billion rand ($91 million) to fund the rebate through 2029. While those producers who spoke to Variety were cautiously optimistic that the industry has finally turned the page, there remains much work to be done. Chief among their concerns is what shape the incentive program will take moving forward, whether it’s a modified version of the existing cash rebate program, a tax credit scheme, or some alternate proposal. Still, after months of often contentious dialogue with government officials, local producers are grateful that both sides have found a way through the impasse. “Ultimately, everyone wants this to work, and ultimately, we want to work with the department,” said Bakker. “We want peace. We want a period of prosperity.” For her part, the polarizing Molokoane — who has faced calls for her resignation from industry bodies — struck a conciliatory tone in Durban. “We’ve been engaging the industry since last year to say, ‘How best can we support this industry?’ And I know maybe the industry has been informed that the DTIC is not on board,” she said. “We are on board…. We would like to work with you in order to ensure that we’ve got a sustainable industry.” For now, local producers are guardedly optimistic that such political goodwill will last, while their foreign counterparts will look for reassurances that the rebate is back on solid footing. “It’s going to take some time to get that certainty back…and build trust internationally,” said Big World Cinema producer Steven Markovitz. In spite of the challenges, South African filmmakers say the rebate crisis has been a wake-up call that has not only galvanized the industry but bolstered their resolve to build a sustainable film and TV business — with or without a functioning incentive program. “There’s a willingness to try and do things in this crisis,” said Markovitz. “I do think that we’re going to come out of it looking at other ways to try and break that dependency on DTI subsidies for every film that we do.” “These obstacles and challenges constantly force us to rethink different ways to do things and different ways to still get our films made and our stories told,” added Yellowbone Entertainment’s Layla Swart. “And I think despite everything, that’s always what we do. We’re fighters and we’re constantly advocating for the things that work with us.” The Durban FilmMart runs Oct. 9 – 12 in Durban, South Africa.
