articles.title: ‘Blade Runner 2099’ Drops New Trailer, Team Teases a Detective Story Set When Replicants Take Over
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Abbey White Plus Icon Abbey White Contributing Writer View All October 10, 2026 5:47pm Blade Runner 2099 Amazon MGM Studios Logo text Prime Video released a new Blade Runner 2099 trailer during the upcoming series’ New York Comic Con panel on Saturday. Michelle Yeoh , Hunter Schafer , Dimitri Abold, Lewis Gribben, Matthew Needham, showrunner Silka Luisa, and executive producers Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson appeared on the Saturday evening panel, where the cast and creative team teased what’s in store for fans of the franchise and how the series will be different than its film installments. At the core of the show is a mystery surrounding Olwen, a replicant Blade Runner who is “supposed to be looking for human insurgents, humans that continue to fight back,” said Luisa. “But… she’s actually here looking for a Blade Runner who’s gone missing, Merrick, one of her colleagues, and that’s the first time that happened,” she teased. Related Stories TV 'Star Trek: Starfleet Academy' Season 2 to Premiere March 2027, Bill Nighy and Rosemarie DeWitt to Guest Star TV Nicolas Cage Teases 'True Detective' Role, Says He "Probably" Won't Work With Prime Video Again After Refusing to Sign AI Waiver for 'Spider-Noir' Speaking to her human character, Schafer shared she is “more or less a fugitive in hiding from LAPD Blade Runners. Her work gets raided, and she’s gotta go on the run and make sure she protects her little brother, and ultimately undergo this mission where she goes undercover as a Blade Runner with LAPD.” Yeoh teased that her character is dying in the limited series: “She knows the time is running out, and she’s a character that doesn’t like to leave things unfinished.” During a clip shown exclusively to the room, Yeoh’s character can be seen with blue-like nail beds, which Luisa explained was inspired by the original Blade Runner film and indicates Yeoh’s character is dying. “It was something early on where we wanted to have a visual signifier… to never forget that she’s dying. She’s so powerful. She’s still so vital, and so there needed to be some marker that she could always look down and remember it’s only days,” she said. “We look to the first film as a reference for how to do it. In that, with Roy Batty, there’s a couple of really, really gnarly shots where you see his hands and his nails, and it makes sense. It’s an extremity, so maybe his heart is shifting, and it’s harder to pump blood there. But we thought that was going to be a really clever way to see the progression over the season as she gets closer to death.” According to the showrunner, Blade Runner 2099 answers what happens when our time as a species ends. “We are 50 years after 2049 , and bad news. The worst has happened. The replicant uprising that has been bubbling up in the films has taken place, and humans have lost,” she teased. “ 2099 is taking place at a junction point when one species is ending and a new one is rising. The first film, something I loved about it was that it was looking at mortality on a micro level. Roy Batty and the other replicants were fighting for more life. This show asked that same question, but on a macro level. Mankind, what happens when we realize our time is running out? Are we going to accept that loss? Can we hold on to our humanity during it?” During the panel, the EPs teased that the limited series will explore how humans and replicants are also both searching for identity. For humans, it’s about finding their identity in a world in which they’re no longer the dominant species, and for replicants, it’s trying to find their identity in a world where they are the dominant species and what that future looks like. “The show is really about a birth,” Luisa continued later on in the panel. “It’s about the birth of a city, of a society, of our characters, and it’s really the dawn of this new era. And in terms of that, when I think of a birth, I think it’s hot, sticky, bright, chaotic, and that’s where the environment came from.” Speaking to how the show’s aesthetic expands upon the films, the showrunner noted that “the first original film actually has a very different aesthetic than 2049, and so 2099 needed to have a third aesthetic. It needed to honor what came before it, but it needed to also introduce audiences to something original [that] still felt foreign.” She later explained how key production design was to delivering that. “So many of the sets are 360. The lighting is built into them. There are monitors with graphics that background actors are interacting with. There are mechanical elements that are moving. It really feels like a functional environment, and it’s a fake world,” she told the NYCC crowd. “It’s not just the creation; it’s also the aging, the weathering, the layering. There are bobbleheads on top of the desks and soda cans that have been left. You really get a sense that people are living here and they’re working here.” In terms of why EP Johnson signed on to this vision of Blade Runner, he pointed to a saying about science fiction. “Great science fiction isn’t actually about the future; it’s about the present. When Silka first came to see us now several years ago, the idea of something replacing humans at the top of the food chain, as it were, and what happens with humanity at that point seemed very resonant to us,” he shared. “Sitting here this evening in October of 2026, as we’re all living in a world with the emergence of artificial intelligence, what does that mean for our future? We’ll let all of you decide about the show, of course. But we think that the themes of the show and the dilemmas for the characters are very relatable.” Added Kosove, it was an “interesting and clever” departure from the existing world of Blade Runner . “It’s someone going undercover, and that dynamic between a human pretending to be a replicant and Owen, whose time is running out, and the impact that they have on one another is at the core of what the show is about,” he said. “I also think, just from the standpoint of a mystery where you’re peeling back the onion and going back and having clues and Easter eggs through both movies — even before the first movie — I thought was a tremendous, exciting thing to explore.” The series offers a completely different spin, according to Yeoh. “We all love the original, but now to go 50 years forward, things have changed tremendously.” For Needham, it’s an exciting thriller and “a great detective story. There is a really exciting, beautiful mystery at the heart of it, and there’s also this huge philosophical debate going on around it that is about being human, and all the mysteries involved in that tied up.” Speaking to what the audience can expect from the mystery of the series, Luisa told the NYCC crowd that the story will be about how “replicants are in control” but don’t have full humanity. “They have agency, but they are made in our likeness. So they still have desires, and they still want more than what they’ve been given. You can’t see much of it, but in that clip, it’s actually the red light district. Instead of selling sex, it sells experiences, human experience,” the showrunner said. “Replicants still can’t get pregnant. They can’t get old. They still want more than what they’ve been given, and they see all these humans out there, and they have they have a life that they still can’t have.” She concluded: “The mystery is asking why Merrick, someone who fought and sacrificed for all this power, is now turning his back and walking away from it. And the question is for what?” THR

articles.title: Justice Department Investigating TV Networks Over Decision to Suspend Press Pool
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 10, 2026 5:54pm The White House Briefing room, on September 19, 2026 in Washington, DC Photo by Graeme Sloan/Getty Images Logo text The U.S. Department of Justice is investigating the television networks that comprise the primary White House television press pool, weighing whether their decision to suspend the pool amid the Trump administrations’s feud with CNN, MS NOW and Politico violates antitrust laws. “Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events,” Department of Justice spokeswoman Emily Covington said in a statement Saturday. “Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.” Related Stories Movies Ava DuVernay Sounds the Alarm Over the "Erosion of Democracy" at '14th' World Premiere: "We Need to Fight" Movies Glen Powell Says He Doesn't Want to Talk Politics, Blames Paramount Marketing Cuts for 'The Running Man' Box Office Performance A network source said that the DOJ reached out on Friday demanding communications related to the decision to suspend the pool. Last month, the White House barred the three news outlets from the White House grounds after President Donald Trump expressed frustration with their coverage. A federal judge subsequently restored access , though the outlets have not had the same level of access they had previously. CNN, MS NOW and Politico also filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration after the White House revoked their press credentials. With CNN and MS NOW suspended, the White House TV press pool suspended operations, with CBS, NBC, ABC and Fox News all showing solidarity with their colleagues. The pool is also responsible for the costs associated with coverage. Still, a federal antitrust investigation represents a sharp escalation, regardless of the legal merits of any case that may come out of it. The White House also launched its own YouTube channel, Trump TV , to pipe live coverage of events to viewers. THR

articles.title: ‘Treasure Island’ Review: David Oyelowo and Hayley Atwell Can Only Breathe So Much Life Into MGM+’s Handsome but Undercooked Pirate Adventure
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All October 10, 2026 8:40pm 'Treasure Island' Cris Rios Bordon/Playground Entertainment/Paramount Global You cannot fault Treasure Island , MGM+’s new take on the Robert Louis Stevenson classic, for a lack of effort. Where some adaptations of beloved literary works might be content to recreate the source material beat for beat, creator Robert Murphy reimagines it wholesale. Characters and plot elements are mixed and matched with abandon. Themes of subjugation and rebellion are brought to the forefront, while real historical events like the Haitian Revolution play out in the background. Treasure Island The Bottom Line Admirably ambitious, disappointingly flat. Airdate: Sunday, Oct. 11 (MGM+) Cast: Tom Sweet, David Oyelowo, Hayley Atwell, Jack Huston, Tomer Capote, Tristan Sturrock, Craige Els, Neil Pendleton, Mayen Mehta, George Frost, Tadghe Murphy Creator: Robert Murphy The main cast is strong ( David Oyelowo , playing the famed pirate Long John Silver, proves particularly adept at doing a lot with a little) and the detailed settings appealingly solid. In its intention to dazzle you with swashbuckling thrills in the moment, and leave you with deeper ideas to chew on in the aftermath, Treasure Island shows admirable ambition. It’s the execution, flat and repetitive and ultimately rather dreary, that lets it down. Related Stories Movies 'The Basics of Philosophy' Review: Paul Schrader Does Some Deep -- and Discomfiting -- Thinking About a College Professor's Guilt Movies Paul Schrader Says He Can't Stop Writing About Guilt: "You Don't Outrun Your Childhood" It takes a while to reveal its shortcomings, however. Initially, there’s plenty to be intrigued by. Our hero to come of age is Jim Hawkins (Tom Sweet), a sweet-natured fellow with the height of a man, the acne-spotted cheeks of a teenager, the wide-eyed innocence of a boy and, most importantly to the plot, the eidetic memory of almost no one of any age. Jim and his widowed mother, Bess ( Hayley Atwell ), are barely scraping by running a bustling tavern, even with the occasional extra coin they pull in by having drunkards bet on Jim’s gift for perfect recall. Then hopes of a better life suddenly wash up ashore in the form of Billy Bones ( The Boys ’ Tomer Capone ), a shipwrecked pirate telling a wild tale of buried treasure and toting the cryptic map to prove it. Unfortunately for Billy but fortunately, in theory, for Treasure Island ’s ability to craft a rip-roaring adventure, he’s not the only one after this legendary trove. As Jim and Bess race to the Caribbean on a ship chartered by a wealthy merchant, Graham ( Jack Huston ), they find themselves unwelcomely accompanied by Long John Silver, who was none too pleased when his former crewmate Billy absconded with that map. The first few of Treasure Island ‘s six hour-long chapters manage to stay afloat thanks to some helpful assets. One is that it is generally quite handsome, in a polished if not especially inventive way. From baroque European manors to endless blue seas to overgrown jungles, the world looks expansive and lived-in — no small thing at a time when big series like this so often look overrun with green screen. It’s easy to want to keep looking at this show. More crucially, it benefits from a few performers capable of popping through the screen on sheer power of their charisma. The most compelling figure is Long John Silver, whose every glare or sneer or smirk Oyelowo imbues with a whole spectrum of feeling — the fury of a formerly enslaved man who’s had to fight tooth and nail for every scrap he’s ever gotten, the icy calculation of one clever and tough enough to have won all those battles, the flashes of decency still buried somewhere deep within. The most fun is Bess, a scheming single mom whose ability to manipulate lovelorn men is akin to a superpower. Atwell makes her slyly funny and unapologetically mercenary — I laughed at how little she bothers to hide her delight when Huston’s Graham speaks of being lonely after his wife’s passing — and she’s never more appealing than when she’s paired with Capone, who gives off his own louche pan-Continental sex appeal. When they’re talking low and close, Treasure Island flirts with transitioning, incongruously but amusingly, into an overheated bodice-ripper. Atwell and Oyelowo are working so hard, in fact, that it’s initially easy to overlook how thin the writing really is. The dynamics between the characters are complicated in the sense that they’re nearly all informed by ulterior motives and mutable loyalties. Everyone’s forever making false promises, or planning mutinies, or framing one another for murder, such that keeping up with their crisscrossing alliances becomes a head-spinning challenge. Emotionally, however, the experience feels empty, not least because most of these characters are defined and driven only by their desire for gold. You might as well be watching computers outwit each other at chess. Once again, the flatness does not entirely seem to be for lack of trying. Treasure Island likes and understands Bess well enough to give her a chance to explain that, as a woman in a man’s world, “I am all I have to trade” — can you blame her for deploying her feminine wiles to get ahead? It’s curious enough about Silver to grant Oyelowo a brief but bitter monologue recounting his youth spent in bondage, and all the horrors he endured therein — the pirate-infested seas may be “no place for an honest man,” but doesn’t it contain a few antiheroes worth rooting for anyway? But then, having raised these ideas, Treasure Island simply leaves them hanging in the air, unconnected to much of anything else. They’re serious but simplistic motivations, and ones all the harder to trust because when everyone is so duplicitous it’s nearly impossible to tell if anyone means anything they’re saying. Even the one clearly earnest bond in the ensemble, between Bess and Jim, lacks a meaningful sense of history or nuance — I couldn’t begin to guess how such a cunning woman raised such a naïve kid, or what lessons he’s learned or rejected under her guidance. While it doesn’t help that young Sweet is outmatched by his more experienced costars, it’s hard to place the blame on him when there’s such scant evidence of depth anywhere else either. When the parent-child bond is fractured, the show barely bothers to give Jim a moment of reflection or regret before it simply barrels ahead to the next plot point. In the series’ defense, those plot points involve objectively exciting things like an armed revolution, an aristocratic dinner party, a trek through the jungle, an active volcano and more guns held to temples and knives held to throats than any human could reasonably be expected to keep track of. (Not much graphic violence, though, give or take an upsetting shot of a murdered cat.) You can see why Jim and his companions would want to rush headlong toward them. It’s just that in the absence of any reason to care all that much about the fates of these characters, even a raucous bar fight or a daring escape turns out to be a slog. If it’s a cliché that the real treasure is the friends we made along the way, it’s one Treasure Island proves true via the negative: Without anyone to feel for, even the most glittering cache of ill-gotten jewels might be rendered dull and mundane. THR

articles.title: ‘SNL’: Shane Gillis Shares “Gas Station Egg” Nickname From Joe Rogan, Pete Hegseth Celebrates USS Lincoln San Diego Homecoming
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 10, 2026 9:00pm Shane Gillis on 'Saturday Night Live.' Screenshot. Logo text Shane Gillis returned for his third Saturday Night Live hosting stint, where he revealed the nickname Joe Rogan and Theo Von came up for him (“gas station egg”) and his gripes with his “Adolf Hitler haircut.” The comedian started his monologue by talking about how he wanted to lose weight: “I gotta lose weight. It’s a bummer, you know what I mean? When you finally get so fat, you’re like, alright, hit that fat rock bottom.” Gillis shared a story about how hiking wasn’t for him, and then explained his contention with public gyms. “Going to the public gym as a fat guy, especially in New York, is a nightmare, dude. It’s just the hottest gay guys you’ve ever seen. They’re jacked and they look at me, like, ‘Yeah, right.’ ‘I know, dude,’” he said. Related Stories TV Taylor Swift Crashes Dakota Johnson's 'Saturday Night Live' Hosting Stint: "My Literal Therapist!" TV 'SNL UK' Season 2: All the Hosts and Musical Guests “Also, I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now,” Gillis said. “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial vape-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look, you’re not allowed to look!” Gillis then raved about Rogan’s own gym that is equipped with a sauna. He said, “The other day I was in the sauna, I’m sitting there, I’m by myself, no one’s around, so I figured I’ll get comfortable. I take my shirt off, I’m in my underwear. About five minutes in, there’s a knock on the glass door of the sauna that scared me. I thought I was alone. I look over and it was Theo Von and Joe, and they opened the door, and Joe just goes, ‘Hey, Theo said you looked like a gas station egg.'” “The thing that hurt the most was when he closed the glass door, I saw my own reflection and I looked exactly like a gas station egg,” he added. “That’s one of the meanest things anyone’s told me: ‘You look like a wet, bagged, hard boiled egg.'” Gillis said he was used to receiving insults growing up having two older sisters, who he called “big, fat-bitch sisters.” He went on to note that “the thing that I’m really bothered by is I’ve balded directly into an Adolf Hitler haircut.” He added, “And it’s not good, because I give a lot of speeches and the front falls down a lot, and there’s no way to adjust it without looking exactly like [Hitler]. It’s the only way. I’m not going to [move it], that’s gay. That’s it: You’re either gay or you’re Hitler, and isn’t that where we’re at as a country?” Later in the episode, Gillis accidentally said the F-word live on-air during a Dr. Seuss sketch where his character was stressing that his father didn’t want to eat green eggs and ham. “Bro, it’s a non-starter. He said he doesn’t fucking,” Gillis said, catching himself swiftly, continuing, “Jeez! Like ’em.” At the end of the night, the comedian seemingly apologized for the slip-up. “Sorry about earlier,” Gillis said during his final remarks to close out the show. Shane Gillis’ monologue! pic.twitter.com/ky6fVtWBx9 — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) October 11, 2026 SNL ’s cold open got the episode started with a greeting from Colin Jost’s Pete Hegseth welcoming the USS Abraham Lincoln home after being deployed for over 300 days. “After seven months of war, you’re back home safe in sunny San Diego, which the president just asked Iran to blow up. I couldn’t be more proud of you,” he said. “Only eight of you attempted suicide, two of you since I started talking. You executed over 3,000 combat missions and you did it with zero casualties, zero flight mishaps, and zero working toilets.” This week, President Trump defended the Iran war at a campaign rally in Nebraska, calling it a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe” and “keeping our country safe.” He then said Iran could “take out” a city in the United States if a nuclear weapon was developed. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego,” Trump said. Elsewhere in the skit, Jost’s Hegseth pointed out the Department of War’s new logo. “I also unveiled a new logo for the Department of War. Yeah, pretty sick, right?” “Sorry, is that a Nazi eagle?” a sailor asked, prompting him to respond, “It’s an American eagle with a Nazi vibe.” Defense Secretary Hegseth addresses crew of USS Lincoln before their deployment ends pic.twitter.com/KnC3fMeUup — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) October 11, 2026 Saturday night’s episode marked Gillis’ third time hosting SNL ; he made his debut in February 2024, and returned again in March 2025. He notoriously was cast as a featured player and quickly fired when a video resurfaced of him using a racial slur. Rosalia was the night’s musical guest, marking her second time on the show. So far on season 52, Jalen Brunson and Dakota Johnson have hosted the late night series. After Gillis, Inde Navarrette will next made her hosting debut for the special Halloween episode, alongside Gracie Abrams as musical guest. THR

articles.title: ‘New Girl’ Stars Reunite — in a Slightly Different Way Than Max Greenfield Claimed
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All October 10, 2026 9:40pm Jake Johnson, Zooey Deschanel, Hannah Simone, Lamorne Morris, Max Greenfield and Damon Wayans Jr. attend the 2026 Chrysalis Butterfly Ball on Oct. 10 in Los Angeles. Monica Schipper/Getty Images Zooey Deschanel , Max Greenfield , Jake Johnson , Lamorne Morris , Hannah Simone and Damon Wayans Jr. had a New Girl reunion on Saturday night — in a different way than fans may have imagined. The stars came together at the Chrysalis Butterfly Ball in Los Angeles, where together they received the Rising Phoenix Award and Greenfield served as the evening’s host. The event was put on in support of Southern California nonprofit Chrysalis, which helps individuals navigate obstacles on their path to meaningful employment. The group’s night out came on the heels of a renewed push for an on-screen New Girl reunion, fueled by Greenfield fibbing in a Today appearance that creator Liz Meriwether had written “amazing” scripts for a revival. This set off a series of jokes between Meriwether and the cast, along with confirmation that there are no real plans for a reunion at this time. Related Stories Movies Ava DuVernay Sounds the Alarm Over the "Erosion of Democracy" at '14th' World Premiere: "We Need to Fight" Lifestyle See Inside Jake Johnson's Pasadena Home (With Creative Studio) as Actor Lists Property for $3.29M Greenfield’s viral moment was a hot topic of conversation at the event, as Deschanel teased while the group accepted their award, “We especially would like to thank Max, who while organizing this announced that an actual New Girl reunion was happening and he made our lives so very annoying.” “Now is probably not the most appropriate time to apologize for this but yes, that’s something that happened and I am sorry. It did, however, bring a lot of attention to Chrysalis and what we are doing here tonight, accidentally,” Greenfield responded. “When the six of us reunite — six actors, none of whom graduated college except apparently Hannah, which does make a lot of sense; Jake says he did graduate college, which no one believes — but when we come together, remarkably people pay attention and people show up, and we are so grateful that you showed up tonight.” Jake Johnson, Zooey Deschanel, Hannah Simone, Lamorne Morris, Max Greenfield and Damon Wayans Jr. have a #NewGirl reunion at the Chrysalis Butterfly Ball charity event pic.twitter.com/ZLMyOyuMrU — The Hollywood Reporter (@THR) October 11, 2026 On the carpet, Greenfield, who organized the big moment via the stars’ group chat, teased to The Hollywood Reporter that instead of making such a public declaration on national television, “I probably should have just said there is a New Girl reunion and it’s happening on Oct. 10 in support of Chrysalis. I got excited and then we found an opportunity for a fun pivot and said, ‘Actually, it’s this.'” Johnson, though, wasn’t letting him off the hook that easily, declaring, “He did such a bad job it was unbelievable.” The actor noted how he and Morris play a game where they “talk shit to each other via interviews — Max didn’t get the memo and sincerely said he read scripts and they were great, with no joke or insult. Then Liz had to step in and say, ‘My lawyer wrote me, you idiot.’ So that is Max being Max,” teasing, “there was zero strategy. He texted me after and said, ‘I think I did a bad job.’ And he did.” The Butterfly Ball — held at The Beehive — also honored Jared Wolff, chairman and CEO of Banc of California, with the Corporate Trailblazer Award; Guadalupe Rios, a former Chrysalis participant and current Caltrans employee, received the John Dillon Award. THR

articles.title: Netflix Has Used AI on About 300 Titles, but “Human Touch Is Critical,” Exec Says in Busan
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All October 10, 2026 10:12pm From left: Film critic and moderator Yun Sung-eun; Sung Q Lee, Senior Director, APAC Production, Netflix; Kimball Thurston, CTO, Wētā FX; and director Kang Yun-sung Netflix Netflix has already used AI in various capacities on about 300 titles, one of its senior production executives said Saturday during an industry discussion at the Busan International Film Festival . Sung Q Lee, Netflix’s senior director of production for Asia-Pacific, said the technology was being deployed across the filmmaking process, but stressed the importance of preserving human creativity. “[AI] is being used in previsualization, production design, working out set-dressing concepts ahead of time, in editing and of course in VFX,” Lee said. “But the question that matters to me isn’t, ‘How much AI can we put into this title?’ but, ‘What more can this title do with AI’s help?’” Related Stories Movies Ava DuVernay Sounds the Alarm Over the "Erosion of Democracy" at '14th' World Premiere: "We Need to Fight" Movies Oscars: U.K. Selects Iran Doc 'Rehearsals for a Revolution' as Best International Feature Entry Lee was speaking at Netflix’s annual Creative Asia event, presented in partnership with the Busan International Film Festival. The panel, co-hosted with the Motion Picture Association, also featured Korean filmmaker Kang Yun-sung, the director of The Outlaws and an enthusiastic adopter of AI tools, and Kimball Thurston, chief technology officer at Wētā FX. Much of the discussion focused on the opportunities AI could create for filmmakers working with limited budgets, although the speakers repeatedly emphasized the need to preserve human creative judgment. The occasion also highlighted just how differently the Hollywood creative community and Asian content sector tend to perceive the potential perils and promise of the technology, with the former profoundly wary and the latter seeing it mostly as an opportunity . Kang partnered with self-described AI filmmaker Kwon Han-seul last year to co-direct Run to the West , billed as Korea’s first fully AI-assisted feature. The project struggled at the box office amid bad buzz over its AI visuals, earning about $100,000. Kang said the pace of AI’s advancement meant the film already looked somewhat dated by the time of its release, but he remains undeterred about the technology’s potential for screen storytelling. The director is now in production on an action film called The Gulf of Aden , which heavily utilizes generative AI tools from China’s Kling AI. He said the technology has enabled him to realize myriad scenes that otherwise wouldn’t have been possible due to the budgetary constraints “that have held the Korean industry back from growing to its full potential.” Kang estimated that the AI-assisted approach could reduce the film’s production costs by around 40 percent. “When we calculated how much we’d save on The Gulf of Aden for financing, it came to a reduction of around 40 percent,” Kang said. “That’s not just from replacing CG and VFX. The shoot itself was streamlined, and that cut down our production time to some extent.” He added: “What has been buried due to budgetary issues was able to be put back on the table.” Netflix’s Sung tried to place AI within the context of the constant technological revolutions that have characterized the film industry since its earliest days. “Technological changes and new tools have helped a great deal with the ‘how,’ or how we make what we make better,” he said. “But they never decided the ‘why’ — why we have to tell this story.” “But when it comes to conveying emotion,” he later added, “ultimately, a human has to touch it. AI can get many jobs done, but does it touch human emotion? The human touch is critical and necessary.” Thurston similarly described Wētā FX’s use of the technology, so far, as “assistive AI,” rather than something that’s “allowed to change the creative intent in any way.” “It provides us — very fast — with the visual images and visualization. So from the director’s perspective or the cinematographer’s perspective, it’s very easy to identify the errors and correct them,” he explained. “Our goal is to reduce simple, repetitive tasks,” he added. THR

articles.title: ‘Wildwood’ Review: Laika’s Ambitious Stop-Motion Epic Is Both a Technical and Emotional Triumph
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All October 11, 2026 6:15am 'Wildwood' Courtesy of Laika “I don’t know whether this is terrifying or adorable,” the central character in Laika ’s new stop-motion animation film observes at one point. The answer is both, with Wildwood representing a staggering achievement from the company that has given us such superb efforts as Coraline and Kubo and the Two Strings . This breathtaking fantasy adventure runs 132 minutes, setting a record as the longest stop-motion movie, but it manages to be enthralling from first moment to last. Based on Colin Meloy’s 2011 bestselling fantasy novel of the same name featuring illustrations by Carson Ellis, the expansive storyline revolves around teenage girl Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee), who lives in the Portland, Oregon, area with her loving parents ( Jake Johnson , Maya Erskine ) and baby brother Mac (Arthur Knight). Despite her folks’ strict instructions that Mac not leave the house, Prue takes advantage of their temporary absence to take him on a joy ride through Portland, winding up in a playground where he is suddenly abducted by a murder of crows in a scene that proves just as frightening as anything in Hitchcock’s The Birds (the film deserves its PG-13 rating). Related Stories TV 'New Girl' Stars Reunite -- in a Slightly Different Way Than Max Greenfield Claimed Movies 'Ray Gunn' Review: Sam Rockwell and Scarlett Johansson in Brad Bird's Forgettable Netflix Animated Neo-Noir Wildwood The Bottom Line Stupendous in every respect. Release date : Friday, October 23 Cast : Peyton Elizabeth Lee, Jacob Tremblay, Carey Mulligan, Mahershala Ali, Angela Bassett, Awkwafina, Maya Erskine, Jake Johnson, Charlie Day, Tom Waits, Richard E. Grant, Amandla Stenberg, Tantoo Cardinal, Len Cariou, Marc Evan Jackson Director : Travis Knight Screenwriter : Chris Butler Rated PG-13, 2 hours 12 minutes Accompanied by her nerdy friend Curtis ( Jacob Tremblay ), who clearly has a crush on her, Prue desperately pursues the birds into the mysterious Impassible Wilderness located nearby and inhabited by talking animals, including coyotes in red military uniforms. They’re in the service of the dowager governess Alexandra ( Carey Mulligan ), who once ruled the kingdom but has become unhinged with grief after the accidental death of her 12-year-old son. We eventually learn that she has orchestrated Mac’s kidnapping as part of a nefarious pact involving black magic. Trying to find her brother, Prue — aided by Curtis, who reveals previously unseen pluck and ingenuity — encounters a variety of colorful animal and human characters as both friends and foes. They include, among others, the General ( Angela Bassett ), the giant eagle leader of the Avian Principality; Brendan the Bandit King ( Mahershala Ali ), who becomes a strong ally; Septima (Awkwafina), a brave rat with whom Curtis forms a tight connection; and Iphigenia (Tantoo Cardinal), a wise, elderly sage who acts as a sort of Yoda stand-in for the story. The narrative and visual imagination on display is truly stunning, but they’re overshadowed by the genuine feeling in the screenplay crafted by director and Laika CEO Travis Knight and writer Chris Butler ( ParaNorman , Missing Link ). Alexandra is far from a cartoon villain, her motivation stemming from the traumatic loss of a son whom she vainly tried to replace with a mechanical replica. The tender family bonds between Prue and her parents and infant brother provide beautiful grace notes, as does Prue’s growing respect and affection for her classmate Curtis, whom she once considered a “loser.” There’s plenty of humor as well, stemming from the colorful characters and situations. At one point Prue finds herself meeting with Owl Rex (a delightful Richard E. Grant ), a leader in the Avian Principality, in her efforts to find her brother. She tells him that she doesn’t believe in magic. “And here you are, talking to an owl in a waistcoat,” he tartly observes. And, of course, action abounds, culminating in an elaborate climactic battle sequence in which Alexandra’s coyote forces are commanded by the rabidly loyal Maksim, memorably voiced by Tom Waits . With Caleb Deschanel behind the camera (it’s the six-time Oscar nominated cinematographer’s stop-motion debut, although he previously shot Jon Favreau’s photorealistic animated remake of The Lion King ), Wildwood looks gorgeous throughout. But what’s truly astonishing is the sheer scope of the effort involved in the gargantuan stop-motion production that involved some 200 practical puppets and 130 practical sets to bring the elaborate story to life. Not to mention how the puppet characters, both animal and human, feel so thoroughly lifelike throughout, completely involving us in the emotion-packed storyline. Much credit should also go to the voice performers — who also include such notable actors as Amandla Stenberg, Blythe Danner, Rob Delaney and Jemaine Clement — who give varied, complex performances rather than merely delivering the jokey asides permeating so many animated films. Laika’s most ambitious effort to date, Wildwood may also be the company’s masterpiece. Full credits Production: Laika Distributor: Fathom Entertainment Cast: Peyton Elizabeth Lee, Jacob Tremblay, Carey Mulligan, Mahershala Ali, Angela Bassett, Awkwafina, Maya Erskine, Jake Johnson, Charlie Day, Tom Waits, Richard E. Grant, Amandla Stenberg, Tantoo Cardinal, Len Cariou, Marc Evan Jackson Director: Travis Knight Screenwriter: Chris Butler Producers: Travis Knight, Sam Wilson Director of photography: Caleb Deschanel Production designer: Nelson Lowery Editor: Christopher Murrie-Green Composer: Dario Marianelli Costume designer: Deborah Cook Casting: Allison Jones, Ben Harris Rated PG-13, 2 hours 12 minutes THR

articles.title: John Malkovich Says an Oscars Campaign “Is the Only Way to Get People to Go to the Theaters Now”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 11, 2026 6:55am John Malkovich at the BFI London Film Festival on Oct. 9, 2026 Courtesy of Getty John Malkovich is well aware of his current awards momentum, even if the “onslaught” of attention doesn’t quite suit his “native personality.” The U.S. star has hit the festival circuit with Martin McDonagh’s tragicomedy Wild Horse Nine , his performance in which is being hailed as potentially the best of his career and almost certainly an Oscar nomination lock. It isn’t the first Academy Award nod he’ll have earned — he’s been recognized before in 1985 and 1994 for Places in the Heart and In the Line of Fire , respectively — but at a BFI London Film Festival talk on Sunday afternoo n, the actor conceded the awards campaign is an entirely different beast in 2026. Related Stories Business Netflix Has Used AI on About 300 Titles, but "Human Touch Is Critical," Exec Says in Busan Movies Oscars: U.K. Selects Iran Doc 'Rehearsals for a Revolution' as Best International Feature Entry “[I feel] probably different [about awards consideration] than I did [when In the Line of Fire came out] because the movie business existed [and] it maintained, undeservedly in my opinion, a very high position in the culture. And when I say undeserved, [I] mean there weren’t that many Chinatown s or Godfather s or Godfather II s,” he began. “Now, [the awards trail] is the only way to get people to go to the theaters, the whole thing, and that’s months and months and months.” He recalled being nominated for Places in the Heart and going to his first and only Oscars in 1985. He was in the car and asked his “a little bit bossy” manager, Phyllis, if he could go in through a side door. “‘Honey, it’s the Oscars,'” she clicked in his face. “There is no side door!” The entire room of attendees burst into laughter at Malkovich’s story. “So that’s my native personality in the face of that onslaught,” he said about embarking on another campaign for Wild Horse Nine . “But also, I’m a grown-up. It’s a part of the business now.” He remembered that his early films made their money even before the big Oscar night. “Now, [winning an Oscar] seems to be the only way you get people to actually go to a theater.” When asked if it broke his heart after Malkovich admitted he’s unsure his daughter would consider going to the theater these days, Malkovich simply said: “No, because I’m 72 years old. Things change. I don’t really like thinking, ‘Things aren’t what they used to be.’ They just change, and you either change with them or die. And I prefer to change with them.” Wild Horse Nine stars Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as Chris and Lee, longtime CIA partners stationed in Santiago, Chile who are dispatched to Easter Island by their bureau chief (Steve Buscemi). Against the surreal backdrop of the island’s monumental Moai statues, the pair begin reckoning with their murky shared past. At the same time, Chris forms an unexpected bond with two rebellious Chilean students, played by Mariana di Girolamo and Ailín Salas — an encounter that threatens to unravel the agents’ friendship and the conspiracy in which they have become entangled. The BFI London Film Festival premiere of the film took place on Friday night , where Malkovich, Rockwell and McDonagh made an appearance at the glitzy red carpet event. Naturally, Malkovich was asked about a running theme in many of his movies — the Kennedy assassination — particularly because his character in Wild Horse Nine is implied to have played a major part in the death of the former U.S. President. When asked about his personal opinion on the matter, the actor replied: “I know what didn’t happen is what they said happened.” Malkovich described McDonagh as a “great writer” and a “direct, kind” filmmaker. “He can give great notes,” he continued. “He told me about one of the scenes with big heads… He just came over and said, ‘More David Attenborough,’ which I just thought was one of the greatest notes, and which I didn’t do very well.” He likened his co-star Rockwell to “a trainer at SeaWorld feeding fish to a shark.” Confused chuckles from the audience had Malkovich explaining: “If you watch him 20 times, you get a good idea of how good he is at that… He’s such a great colleague, such a wonderful actor, and so fantastic in this, everything he does is perfect, and he can go any which way at any second.” Malkovich confessed he is “not a political person,” but said Wild Horse Nine is wildly existential and evocative when it comes to themes of grief and mortality. He covered the milestones of a vast and vibrant career across Sunday’s session, from Dangerous Liaisons and working with Clint Eastwood to the West End and how he came to star in 1999’s Being John Malkovich , a set on which Malkovich admitted to “having a moment” and “being an asshole” when filming on a particularly hot day. He even discussed a little of his ancestry — Malkovich recently discovered he is 43 percent Romanian — and the rarity of reading a genuinely brilliant script. “It’s so rare to read a great screenplay and make a really excellent film. And you can work as hard as you like. You can give a really interesting performance, and if the film isn’t very good, it’s absolutely meaningless,” said Malkovich. “It doesn’t mean anything. It’s totally waste of your time in the public.” To end, Malkovich was probed on his film set to be released next century, 100 Years , from director Robert Rodriguez. To his knowledge, the movie currently sits behind bulletproof glass in a vault and will open in the year 2115. “I have tickets,” the actor joked. “I don’t think I’ll be at the opening night. You know, my grandchildren won’t even be here as well.” The 70th BFI London Film Festival runs Oct. 7-18. THR

articles.title: Javier Bardem on Declining ‘Skyfall’ Role, Pitching to Sam Mendes: “What If He Wants to Have Sex With Mr. Bond?”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 11, 2026 7:27am Bardem at the BFI London Film Festival on Oct. 11, 2026 Courtesy of Getty Spanish star Javier Bardem thanked a BFI London Film Festival crowd for getting out early on Sunday morning to attend a Screen Talk session with him. Bardem, whose other half, Penelope Cruz, is also enjoying some time in the spotlight this year (thanks to a trifecta of buzzy films: La Bola Negra, The Invite and Bunker ), is in the British capital promoting his and Cruz’s Bunker as well as The Beloved , in which he co-stars with Victoria Luengo. During the talk, Bardem reflected on a glittering career, from his early life growing up in one of Spain’s most prestigious acting families to winning an Oscar and, this year, finally conquering his fear of the stage. Related Stories Movies John Malkovich Says an Oscars Campaign "Is the Only Way to Get People to Go to the Theaters Now" Business Netflix Has Used AI on About 300 Titles, but "Human Touch Is Critical," Exec Says in Busan In one of the session’s lighter moments, Bardem, known for roles in Vicky Cristina Barcelona (2008), Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales (2017) and the Dune franchise, spoke about initially declining one of his most iconic roles, as the villainous but sexually magnetic former agent of Judi Dench’s M, Raoul Silva, in 2012’s Skyfall . The actor said about turning down the part at first: “I guess I was nervous. Like, ‘What am I doing in the James Bond movie? What can I do?’ But then we sat down. Sam Mendes is a genius, and we went through the reading of it, and he was so open to what I was proposing, which had to do with the sexuality of the guy.” Bardem was thinking outside the box when it came to his depiction of Silva, and pitched this to the filmmaker. “I said, ‘Listen, all the villains have done everything to destroy the world, but what about becoming personal? What about something besides destroying the world? [Like] he wants to have sex with Mr. Bond?’ And [Mendes] said, ‘I’ll talk to the studio and get back to you,'” said Bardem, erupting into laughter, before referencing one of the movie’s standout scenes where Bardem’s character suggestively strokes the thighs of a tied-up Daniel Craig. Daniel Craig and Javier Bardem in ‘Skyfall’ Everett “The studio was very brave,” continued Bardem. “And I think that scene lasts in the memory of the audience… Because we went a little bit further with it. It’s a way to say, ‘Okay, how do you really put Mr. Bond out of his place with a situation that he hasn’t been there before?’ And the way he comes out of it is brilliant.” Bardem expressed his disbelief, to this day, that he shared the screen with Dame Judi Dench, and even confessed to forgetting his lines when Mendes first called action because he realized where he was. “[Mendes] said, ‘Cut! Javier, what’s going on?’ [I said], ‘Well, sorry, I just realized that I’m in a James Bond movie. Excuse me, I just saw Judi Dench and James Bond looking at me and said, ‘Fuck! I’m in a James Bond movie! Sorry, let’s do it again.’ I was absolutely taken by the joy of it.” Unfortunately, the Bond franchise star was not probed on who he thinks would make a good Bond for Denis Villeneuve’s upcoming movie for Amazon MGM Studios, as rumors continue to swirl around who might next don the tuxedo of Ian Fleming’s beloved spy. Bardem took the crowd through a prolific filmography, particularly some impressive Spanish-language projects such as Jamón jamón (1992) and Biutiful (2010). When the discussion came to his Oscar-winning turn in the Coen brothers’ No Country for Old Men (2007), the audience was shown the nail-biting coin toss scene between Bardem’s terrifying killer Anton Chigurh and supporting actor Gene Jones. “Half of the Oscar I have is his,” said Bardem about Jones, who only appears in that single, four-minute scene. “Because he plays fear, the insecurity and uncertainty so beautifully that he makes the scene,” explained the star. “I do my part, but he does the horror. He’s fantastic. That’s what I mean: You are not working alone. You need your partners. You need to create a moment of commonality.” Toward the end of the session, when Bardem was asked about what advice he has for aspiring actors just making their start in the industry, he joked: “Choose another job. Why would you do that to yourself?” He then continued: “No, it’s a great profession. And in this world of AI, where many other professions are going to go, unfortunately, down, to be able to be a person who shows emotions and has a connection with the audience, it’s an important job to have and to preserve, because it creates a connection between us.” Florian Zeller’s Bunker , also starring Stephen Graham, Paul Dano and Patrick Schwarzenegger, follows a renowned architect offered the chance to secretly design a survival bunker for a billionaire who is convinced that the end of the world is near. As he lets himself be seduced by this morally ambiguous project, his wife begins to question their marriage. Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s The Beloved , meanwhile, stars Bardem as a two-time Oscar-winning filmmaker who casts his estranged daughter in his new period piece. The 70th BFI London Film Festival runs Oct. 7-18. THR

articles.title: R.L. Stine’s ‘The Babysitter’ Adaptation Coming to Tubi in 2027 (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Abbey White Plus Icon Abbey White Contributing Writer View All October 11, 2026 8:15am 'The Babysitter' Tubi Logo text Tubi ’s next Final Girl is here. The streamer is set to release a live action adaptation of The Babysitter , based on the popular series of R.L. Stine novels first published in 1989, in 2027. The film’s announcement comes just two days after the Oct. 9 release of Pumpkinhead 2 , and ahead of the streamer’s New York Comic Con panel, where Stine appeared alongside Tubi’s Chief Content Officer Adam Lewinson, Pumpkinhead writer-director Jem Garrard, and RuPaul’s Drag Race All Stars’ contestant and Afraid of Clowns star Jimbo. Related Stories TV Buffalo Bills' Long-Suffering Fans to Be Focus of Documentary 'Just One Before I Die' (Exclusive) Movies 'R.L. Stine's Pumpkinhead 2' Trailer Teases Cassandra Peterson's New Role and the Curse's Return (Exclusive) The film follows a 16-year-old babysitter, Jenny, who is so desperate to earn enough money for a prestigious writing program that she takes the job despite a prowler terrorizing girls across town. But when she starts receiving threatening phone calls and a dangerous fugitive surfaces in town, Jenny’s suspicion of those around her grows. Meanwhile, danger begins closing in. Produced by Blue Ice, Garrard will write and executive produce the film, which Trevor Calverleya will direct. The Babysitter will be executive produced by Lance Samuels, Joan Waricha, Jane Stine and Garrard. Producers include Dan Bernard, Yvonne Bernard, Tebogo Maila, Darren Cameron and Adam Friedlander. “R.L. Stine has an incredible ability to tell stories that are scary, fun and endlessly entertaining, and that combination continues to connect with Tubi viewers,” said Adam Lewinson, Chief Content Officer, Tubi. “With The Babysitter , one of R.L. Stine’s most iconic novels, we’re delivering a fresh, fun thrill ride for longtime fans and a whole new generation.” The Babysitter not only marks the fourth film in an ongoing partnership between the streamer and the prolific children’s horror author, but also the first not based on a short from Stine’s Nightmare Hour or Haunting Hour anthologies. Check out the teaser, which The Hollywood Reporter can exclusively share, below. First published in 1989, The Babysitter and its three sequels — The Babysitter II (1991), The Babysitter III (1993), and The Babysitter IV (1995) — were pivotal in defining Stine as a preeminent horror and children’s author. The original book followed the same 16-year-old Jenny, who begins receiving threatening calls and notes after taking on a babysitting gig, before she discovers the threat is coming from inside the house. The second and fourth books follow Jenny as she attempts to recover in the immediate aftermath of the first book’s events, and years later as she faces her disturbing past and another terrorizing babysitting experience. The third installment pivots slightly, focusing more on the experiences of Debra, who is haunted and hunted in the same way as her cousin, Jenny. Tubi also recently announced a third Stine adaptation, Afraid of Clowns , based on The Nightmare Hour short and previously developed as a Haunting Hour (2010) episode. Written and directed by Garrard, the film, also set to release in 2027, stars Frankie Honey, Ava Ferrer, Azriel Dalman, Joe Moore and RuPaul’s Drag Race All Stars winner Jimbo, and is teased at the end of Pumpkinhead 2 . The next entry in the Redhaven saga, Afraid of Clowns, sees the arrival of a mysterious clown troupe led by Ringmaster Rollo. A young resident, Frankie, begins to suspect they’re connected to the disappearance of a child years earlier, and in an effort to protect her brother, works to convince her friends to help stop the clowns before her sibling vanishes forever. Pumpkinhead 2 is currently streaming on Tubi. THR

articles.title: ‘Between Two Lovers’ Review: Nanako Hirose’s Contentious Family Drama Examines an Ill-Fated Throuple
articles.full_text: Oct 11, 2026 2:38am PT ‘Between Two Lovers’ Review: Nanako Hirose’s Contentious Family Drama Examines an Ill-Fated Throuple Masami Nagasawa is applaudably unlikable as an adulterous author with a resistance to motherhood, who invites her husband and girlfriend to conceive a child together in a tantalizing proposition that pulls too many of its punches. By James Marsh Plus Icon James Marsh Latest ‘Satoko Always’ Review: A Trio of Women Find Their Inner Voice in Shuichi Okita’s Delightful Celebration of the Art of Writing 4 days ago ‘The Table: Day and Night’ Review: Café-Based Korean Romance With Kim Min-ha and Han Sun-hwa Is All Froth, No Kick 5 days ago See All Busan International Film Festival The sophomore feature from Hirokazu Kore-eda protégé Nanako Hirose , “ Between Two Lovers ” tackles a variety of potential hot-button issues, from polyamorous relationships to same-sex parenting, in its contemporary Japanese setting. The film stars Masami Nagasawa as a free-spirited children’s author who invites her doting husband and secret girlfriend to enter into a three-way relationship of convenience, when both partners simultaneously express their desire to start a family. But what begins as a bold and daring attempt to broach progressive issues in a notoriously conservative society ultimately loses its nerve, acquiescing to a number of eyebrow-raising narrative compromises. Internationally recognizable talent both above and below the line should ensure that “Between Two Lovers” travels far beyond its debut in Competition at the Busan Film Festival , but more progressive audiences may be left frustrated by where Hirose leaves them. Related Stories 'Star Trek: The Next Generation' Star Gates McFadden to Write Dr. Crusher Comic Book Series (EXCLUSIVE) Ben Stiller to Moderate Conversation With William Shatner at New York Comic-Con 'Star Trek' Panel (EXCLUSIVE) Uta (Nagasawa) has built a comfortable life for herself and her husband Morio (Tasuku Emoto), thanks to the popularity of her “Little Miss Mushroom” series of picture books. While her work regularly brings her into close proximity with children, Uta has little interest in starting a family of her own. Conversely, Morio is desperate to have kids, but any effort to discuss the topic with his wife is quickly dismissed. Popular on Variety Little does he know, Uta has also been involved in a passionate six-year affair with her female editor, Junna (Shizuka Ishibashi), and happily flits back and forth between her two homes, beds, and lovers. Junna is eager to become a mother, although several legal barriers prevent her from accessing sperm donations or fertility treatment. She also wants Uta to accept her sexuality and get a divorce, so that they can live together openly. Everything comes to a head when Morio invites Junna over for dinner, under the misapprehension that he is extending an olive branch to the colleague who demands so much of his wife’s time. The compounding frustrations of this situation, fueled by too much alcohol, finally expose Uta’s double life. However, desperate to enjoy all the benefits of her unconventional and self-serving situation, without shouldering any of the blame, Uta proposes that Morio be the donor for Junna’s child, and that all three of them move in together. Hirose, who also writes and edits, has constructed a brilliantly volatile scenario, vulnerable to any number of potentially explosive and destructive dramatic developments. Disappointingly, her screenplay proceeds to unfold in a procession of frustrating get-outs and compromises, repeatedly choosing the least interesting or challenging direction to take this would-be throuple. The archaic legal restrictions restricting same-sex couples or unmarried women, for example, are acknowledged and adhered to, rather than being openly challenged or criticized. The film certainly expresses an interest in the shifting dynamics of this unconventional unit, especially once Junna does fall pregnant and moves into the family home. Morio, already a tender and delicate soul, becomes increasingly protective of the woman carrying his child. At the same time, Junna finds herself sliding into a more conventional role, at once maternal but also spousal. The ever-precocious Uta, meanwhile, feels more and more ostracized within the group, as the supposedly idyllic threesome she conceived to feed her own compulsive nature relegates her to a sulking adolescent. For good or ill, the film also refrains from forcing Uta to ever clarify her sexuality or choose one partner over the other. With the influence of Kore-eda on full display, Hirose raises several legitimate questions about what constitutes a real family, as well as the perceived role of women in society and the guardrails that continue to exist so as to limit and enforce these outdated expectations. While it could be argued that the very fact “Between Two Lovers” addresses these issues at all, and does so this explicitly, is already a bold stride in the right direction, much of that intention is undone in how they are resolved and acquiesced to on screen. Performances across the board are strong, even if the characterizations themselves are more difficult to embrace. Uta is frustratingly selfish and naive, but Nagasawa willfully throws herself into the role, in a manner that makes her unlikable to a degree we have rarely seen her. Ishibashi makes for a resilient and empathetic Junna, even as her character inevitably bears the brunt of much of the film’s divisive moralizing, while Emoto’s Morio is a quivering wreck of fragility and good intentions. Technical contributions are polished, with particular kudos to Ryo Sugimoto’s production design, which creates a pair of equally warm, yet subtly contrasting, living spaces in the married couple’s suburban home and the women’s more illicit love nest, deftly reflecting Uta’s dual existence. HIMI’s score is also employed sparingly yet effectively, but these aesthetic elements fade quickly from memory, overshadowed by the film’s more contentious narrative choices. ‘Between Two Lovers’ Review: Nanako Hirose’s Contentious Family Drama Examines an Ill-Fated Throuple Reviewed at Busan Film Festival (Competition), Oct. 11, 2026. articles.title: Keanu Reeves-Voiced Stop-Motion Samurai Film ‘Hidari’ Looks for New Partner After U.S. Talks Stall
articles.full_text: Oct 11, 2026 3:10am PT Keanu Reeves-Voiced Stop-Motion Samurai Film ‘Hidari’ Looks for New Partner After U.S. Talks Stall By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ Overtakes ‘Avatar: The Way of Water’ as Korea’s Biggest International Film of All Time (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Keanu Reeves-Voiced Stop-Motion Samurai Film ‘Hidari’ Looks for New Partner After U.S. Talks Stall 4 hours ago Korean and Italian Producers Sign Co-Production Pact at Busan Market 7 hours ago See All c: Hidari Inc, Japan’s Dwarf Studios is looking for a new partner for “ Hidari ,” the stop-motion samurai film voiced by Keanu Reeves, after talks with a U.S. company that offered to fund the entire budget in exchange for all rights stalled, producer Matsumoto Noriko told an audience at the Busan International Film Festival ‘s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) on Sunday. Dwarf Studios co-founder and head producer Matsumoto was speaking at “Co-Producing with Japan: Opportunities and Challenges,” a Producer Hub session co-hosted by VIPO. Japan is the Producer Hub’s focus country this year. She was joined by Questry CEO Ibe Tomonobu and Knockonwood founder Yamaguchi Shin, with VIPO’s Tanimoto Hiroyuki moderating. Kawamura Masashi directs “Hidari,” produced by Dwarf, Whatever and Tecarat. Related Stories 'Wildwood' Review: Laika's Most Ambitious Feature to Date Is a Richly Textured, Transportive Fairytale Epic 'The Social Reckoning' Review: Aaron Sorkin's 'Social Network' Follow-Up Is Missing More Than Just David Fincher Dwarf’s “Hidari” pitch was a highlight of the Annecy Animation Showcase at Cannes and at Annecy itself earlier this year. A U.S. company’s offer to fund it came with a condition: it would take all the rights. Matsumoto said the company respected Dwarf’s creativity and was prepared to pay enough, but full funding would have left the studio with no control over a highly original project. Dwarf wanted to hold on to half the rights and asked Ibe to find the Japanese share. Before the talks could go further, the people Matsumoto had been negotiating with lost their jobs amid upheaval in Hollywood, and Dwarf is now looking for a new partner. Popular on Variety “Even with Keanu, we cannot stop the fire,” Matsumoto said. Questry has set up a special purpose company for “Hidari” so that overseas and local investors can put money into the film side by side. Ibe said the project shows why development money matters. Dwarf made a pilot short in 2023 at its own risk, partly through crowdfunding, and the pilot traveled far enough to bring Reeves aboard. Questry now wants to back pilots and development-stage work, which in Japan studios and creators usually pay for themselves. The film could not have been financed in Japan alone, Ibe said, and the reason lies in how Japanese film and anime are usually funded. Ibe spent 11 years at Goldman Sachs before founding Questry about four years ago. His presentation put the share of Japanese anime and films backed by production committees, or seisaku iinkai, at more than 90%, citing industry estimates. Publishers, labels, broadcasters, streamers, toy companies and ad agencies each put in a share, mainly to win a “window” – the right to exploit the title in their own business. Window fees are deducted first, so members often make more from their window than from their stake. Studios, meanwhile, are typically hired for a fee and see little upside. In Korea, by contrast, investors, distributors and producers play separate roles, and Ibe said producers often take around 40% of profit after recoupment. “How you raise money decides how you share it,” he said. Ibe’s presentation described the committee as a well-built system that works very well for titles made in Japan for Japan. It can still serve titles sold worldwide if overseas rights are planned from day one, he said, but the fit gets worse the more global a project is. A co-production with few Japanese windows to sell gives Japanese companies little reason to invest, and only Japanese companies can sit on a committee. Overseas sales made up 56% of anime industry revenue in 2024, up from 20% in 2014, he noted. “If the world needs a project, we want to put money into it, even if the Japanese market can’t see it yet,” Ibe said. Yamaguchi, who said he has wrestled with financing for more than 20 years, has made the committee work for an international film. Fukada Koji’s “Love on Trial,” which Knockonwood joined in 2017, drew 60% of its budget from a Toho-led committee, 29% from the government’s JLOX subsidy and 11% from presales through MK2 Films and French distributor Art House. Yamaguchi kept the committee to Toho, Knockonwood and one music company. The French money went in through Knockonwood’s share, backed by a separate contract giving the French partner full sight of the numbers – an arrangement he said still sits in a gray zone. The film world premiered at Cannes and had its Asian premiere in Busan last year. Hikari’s “Rental Family,” starring Brendan Fraser, took a different route. U.S. partner Sight Unseen put in seed money in 2020 and later connected the project to Searchlight Pictures, which signed on in 2023. Searchlight covered 90% of the budget and a JLOX location incentive the other 10%. The film world premiered in Toronto in 2025 and was released in 73 countries. Yamaguchi has worked with Hikari for 15 years. His third case, Eddie Cahyono’s “Ibuku,” plays in competition at Busan this year. Indonesia’s Talenta Media and Yasa Buana Films hold 80% and Knockonwood 15%. The last 5% came from Thailand’s White Light gap fund, released after the project won the White Light Asian Project Award at BICM. Christine Hakim stars in the 16mm film, which first won a prize at Busan’s Asian Project Market in 2015. Knockonwood came aboard nearly a decade later through Cinema at Sea. “Independent filmmakers and producers never give up because we have to find the new ways,” Yamaguchi said. Japan has started opening up to co-production over the past two years, he added, though it remains behind other countries on language, legal and accounting fronts. Japan has co-production treaties only with China and Italy, and Yamaguchi said neither works well for the Japanese side. Tanimoto said the government subsidy behind “Love on Trial” and “Rental Family” has been upgraded this year into a new program, IP360, with higher minimum budgets for production and post-production. Pre-production support remains, and applicants need a Japanese producer partner. The Agency for Cultural Affairs also offers a co-production subsidy covering 20%, subject to caps. Stop-motion brings its own problems, Matsumoto said. A co-production typically requires 20% to 30% of the budget to be spent outside Japan, which is hard when the shoot cannot easily be split. Dwarf, which co-owns NHK mascot Domo-kun, has still found partners abroad. Its feature “Komaneko” drew more than 250,000 moviegoers in France, over 10 times its ticket sales at home, and “Mogu & Perol” is being developed as a series with French and Taiwanese partners. Dwarf is also adapting Matsumoto Taiyo’s autobiographical manga “Sunny.” Matsumoto, meanwhile, is developing “Moritō,” drawn from an art exhibition by Shibata Keiko, creator of the picture book “Pan Dorobou.” “Even if I give up co-production, I don’t give up finding collaborators,” Matsumoto said. articles.title: ‘12.12: The Day’ Director Kim Sung-soo Says AI ‘Shows What’s in Your Imagination’
articles.full_text: Oct 11, 2026 3:18am PT ‘12.12: The Day’ Director Kim Sung-soo Says AI ‘Shows What’s in Your Imagination’ By Ophélie Surcouf Plus Icon Ophélie Surcouf Latest Sci-Fi Thriller ‘Overstake’ Gets Generative AI Rebuild, Boarded by Cappu Films at Busan Market (EXCLUSIVE) 9 hours ago Slamdance Alzheimer’s Drama ‘Banr’ From ‘Fox Hunt’ Writer Erica Xia-Hou Heads to Busan Market (EXCLUSIVE) 12 hours ago ‘Decision to Leave’ Cinematographer Kim Ji-yong on Chasing Natural Light for Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’: ‘This Is the One Where We Worried, Debated and Planned the Most’ 1 day ago See All Ophélie Surcouf Kim Sung-soo, director of Korean box office hit “12.12: The Day,” once saw AI as a destroyer of the film industry. Speaking Sunday at a session hosted by Kling AI at the Busan International Film Festival ‘s Asian Contents & Film Market, he described how it has instead become part of his craft. His turning point was “Worm Train,” an eight-minute short he first gave up on because AI couldn’t render its key scene, a giant insect colliding with a packed train crowd. Months later, the technology had caught up. “Technology doesn’t replace creativity. It shows what’s in your imagination,” Kim said. The project changed how he imagines and collaborates, he added: “I’ll never go back to the way I used to make films.” Related Stories 'Avatar: Seven Havens' Renewed for Seasons 3 and 4 at Paramount+ Eminem Teams With NERDS Clothing for Original Video Game, New Streetwear Collab Out of New York Comic Con (EXCLUSIVE) He did not make it alone. Kim assembled a nine-person team, including an animation art director and a music director. Though the short could have been made entirely with AI, he said, they chose to generate only part of it and handle the rest with conventional filmmaking methods. He plans a similar hybrid approach for a seven-part drama series he is developing. Its nearly 15-minute opening chase on the Gyeongin Expressway, which he said would require “enormous financial resources” to shoot conventionally, will first be generated with AI, then used to decide which shots need actors on set and where traditional VFX come in. Popular on Variety Kim was joined by Harry Hyun, director and CEO of AI production company MooAm; Chinese animation director Li Wei, co-director of “Jiang Ziya”; and Lee Sangwook, producer and team manager at MBC C&I’s AI Contents Lab. Li made a similar case for animation. Presenting a trailer for “Born of the Tide,” a 105-minute AI-animated feature about China’s boat-dwelling Tanka community, he said the technology works best at the trial-and-error stage: concept designs that once took enormous time to draw by hand can now be visualized quickly and shared with the team. “AI can generate many things, but the choice and the details all come down to the director,” he said. Hyun agreed that filmmaking skill is what makes the difference. “Faces look identical, sets look identical, lighting looks identical,” she said of AI output made without it. That is why MooAm looks for AI artists who have directed at least one live-action short. Otherwise, she said, AI production is not fundamentally different from a conventional shoot, only more efficient. What changes is the crew. Her directing team now includes an “AI coordinator,” who decides which cuts will be generated, keeps a continuity script for them and checks with AI artists that everything cuts together. Even assistant directors need a basic grasp of AI, as gray screens marked with tracking points replace green screens. Building those skills is also a priority for Lee, whose lab is producing “Rendering Love,” a short-form K-pop romantic comedy about a virtual idol group, with “Parasite” producer Barunson E&A developing the story. “If even one or two individuals lag on the learning curve, overall quality can suffer,” he said of keeping pace as models update. Mastering the tools won’t settle every question, though. Kim argued that rules on commercial use and permissions should be settled before the industry sets any technical standards. “Whenever I generate outputs, I scrutinize the results closely to ensure they do not infringe upon existing works or violate anyone’s publicity rights,” he said. “In the future, we won’t call AI movies ‘AI movies,’ just as we no longer call films ‘color movies,’” Kim said. articles.title: AI-Native Studios Can Create Original IP While Traditional Studios Keep Their Edge, VFX Veteran Hong Jae Cheol Says at Busan
articles.full_text: Oct 11, 2026 3:33am PT AI-Native Studios Can Create Original IP While Traditional Studios Keep Their Edge, VFX Veteran Hong Jae Cheol Says at Busan By Lin Ying-Hsuan Plus Icon Lin Ying-Hsuan Latest AI-Native Studios Can Create Original IP While Traditional Studios Keep Their Edge, VFX Veteran Hong Jae Cheol Says at Busan 5 hours ago ‘Squid Game’ Producer Reads Founding Declaration as Asian Independent Producers Form Cross-Border Alliance at Busan 7 hours ago Hollywood Executives See Growing Market for Asian Stories, but ‘Every Movie Is Still a Fight’ 1 day ago See All Lin Ying-Hsuan Small, AI -native companies running automated pipelines can develop their own intellectual property, while traditional studios hold on to their advantages in established franchises, production infrastructure, talent and distribution, according to VFX veteran Hong Jae Cheol. Hong, a producer-director at Viscode who began his career at Industrial Light & Magic and worked on films including “Iron Man,” “Transformers” and “Pirates of the Caribbean,” laid out that vision at the InnoAsia AI Creators Camp, held Sunday at the Busan International Film Festival ‘s Asian Contents & Film Market in Busan. “We are moving from using AI to generate individual images toward using AI as part of a complete production workflow,” he said. Related Stories 'Children of Blood and Bone' Author Tomi Adeyemi Quietly Cancels New York Comic Con Panel Ben Stiller to Moderate Conversation With William Shatner at New York Comic-Con 'Star Trek' Panel (EXCLUSIVE) AI is changing the production model, Hong argued, while traditional visual effects remain essential to making generated material usable on screen. He framed the future as a hybrid, and a partnership between AI and human creativity, rather than a wholesale replacement of existing studios. Popular on Variety Hong contrasted a conventional live-action and VFX process, involving 3D assets, animation, rendering and compositing, with an AI-assisted approach. In the latter, actors perform on a controlled set; AI generates environments and visual elements; and VFX artists handle tracking, integration and finishing. He also outlined current AI applications across VFX, animation and filmmaking, including rotoscoping, cleanup, previs, character design, camera tests and environment creation. Mark Wachholz, chief creative director of Berlin-based Dreamkite Studios, whose AI films “The Cinema That Never Was” and “Céremony” have won top prizes at AI film festivals, approached the shift from the creative side. He described AI co-creation as an invitation to give up some control and allow for surprise, framing the process as “exploring instead of controlling” and “finding instead of knowing.” He also argued that new tools require new ways of thinking, rather than simply applying old methods to new technology. Director Ahn Jaehong of Climax Studio, who turned to AI filmmaking after arm injuries ended his work behind the camera, brought the discussion back to directing and production. He mapped a workflow from prompts and camera information to scene context, shot lists, storyboards, character and prop sheets, locations and keyframes. The sequence reinforced a point shared by the speakers: AI can assist across multiple stages, but filmmakers still need to shape the story, visual design and final result. Hong summed up the distinction: “AI is just a tool; film is a sequence.” The discussion centered on how that tool might become part of a connected filmmaking process, with human direction and VFX expertise still determining how its images fit together. articles.title: Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ Overtakes ‘Avatar: The Way of Water’ as Korea’s Biggest International Film of All Time (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Oct 11, 2026 6:00am PT Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ Overtakes ‘Avatar: The Way of Water’ as Korea’s Biggest International Film of All Time (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ Overtakes ‘Avatar: The Way of Water’ as Korea’s Biggest International Film of All Time (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Keanu Reeves-Voiced Stop-Motion Samurai Film ‘Hidari’ Looks for New Partner After U.S. Talks Stall 5 hours ago Korean and Italian Producers Sign Co-Production Pact at Busan Market 8 hours ago See All Getty Images Christopher Nolan ’s “ The Odyssey ” has overtaken “Avatar: The Way of Water” in local-currency terms to become the highest-grossing international release in Korean box office history, with a cumulative KRW139.2 billion ($101.5 million) as of Oct. 11. The Universal release now ranks as the top Hollywood title ever in the territory. Only two Korean films have earned more. Jang Hang-jun’s “The King’s Warden” took the all-time record this year with KRW153.2 billion ($111.7 million), while Lee Byeong-heon’s 2019 comedy “Extreme Job” sits just ahead of “The Odyssey” on KRW139.6 billion ($101.8 million). Related Stories ‘Helluva Boss’ Actor Lashes Out at NYCC Heckler: ‘I’m Going to Jump Over This Fence and End You’ Amazon Viking Drama ‘Bloodaxe’ Sets Release Date, Debuts Fierce New Trailer at New York Comic Con Admissions for “The Odyssey” stand at 12 million, equivalent to about 24% of the country’s population. No other international film has passed 10 million admissions this year. “The Odyssey” also held the No. 1 spot for seven straight weekends, the longest such streak for an international title in Korea . Popular on Variety It is now Nolan’s biggest film in Korea, as well as the biggest Universal title there. It holds the Imax record too, a total that continues to grow as the film plays into its 10th week on the format’s screens. No film released in Korea has drawn more admissions on Imax and Dolby Cinema screens, and Imax shows sold out continuously through the fifth week of release, the longest run of sellouts on record. The film crossed 10 million admissions in 33 days, faster than any non-franchise international title. It was the first international film carrying a 15+ rating to reach that level, and the first August release of any kind to do so. The result makes Nolan the first director with two non-franchise international films above 10 million admissions in Korea. Demand built well before opening. “The Odyssey” posted the year’s highest advance ticket sales and led Korean presales for 43 consecutive days through Sept. 14, the longest such run this year. As of Sept. 13, it had been the top international film at the box office for 40 days in a row, also a record. The Korean promotional tour set several post-pandemic marks. A Seoul press conference drew 209 members of the media, the biggest turnout for such a tour since the pandemic. A premiere event hosted by CGV attracted 32,411 applications, a 463-to-1 ratio and the highest participation the exhibitor has recorded for a Korea premiere. The visiting delegation made 11 appearances across Korean TV programs and online content, and the tour’s Cine21 Master Talk passed 1 million views, the most in the series’ history. Jungkook of BTS, TXT’s Soobin and members of Riize were among the Korean stars who recommended the film of their own accord, fueling conversation on social media. Content created voluntarily by influencers and YouTubers generated an estimated KRW1.27 billion (about $1 million) in earned media value, while sales of books linked to “The Odyssey” rose 30-fold after release. Nolan also became the first international film director to appear on Korea’s non-drama buzzworthiness chart, a ranking usually filled by local television personalities and entertainers.
