articles.title: Prime Video Takes Global on Turkish AI-Generated Movie ‘Çukur:Vartolu,’ a Spin-Off From the Hit Series Known Internationally as ‘The Pit’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Oct 10, 2026 6:25am PT Prime Video Takes Global on Turkish AI-Generated Movie ‘Çukur:Vartolu,’ a Spin-Off From the Hit Series Known Internationally as ‘The Pit’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Prime Video Takes Global on Turkish AI-Generated Movie ‘Çukur:Vartolu,’ a Spin-Off From the Hit Series Known Internationally as ‘The Pit’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Margherita Ferrari on Working With Paolo Sorrentino on Directorial Debut ‘Föa — Once Upon a Future’: ‘He Helped Me Pursue and Protect My Vision’ 1 day ago ‘Elsinore’ Producer Andrea Occhipinti on Bringing Ian Charleson’s Story to the Screen and His Personal Connection to the AIDS Crisis: ‘I Lost a Lot of Friends’ 2 days ago See All Çukur:Vartolu Courtesy AI Yapim Prime Video has taken global rights to Turkish TV powerhouse Ay Yapim’s AI movie “Çukur: Vartolu,” a spin-off from its hit series “Çukur,” known internationally as “The Pit.” “Çukur: Vartolu” is produced by Ay Yapim under its Singapore-based artificial intelligence studio AI Yapim that in August launched the AI-generated historical drama “Castle Walls” also on Prime Video, in what was touted as the first show made end-to-end with AI to bow on a major global streamer. Related Stories Taylor Swift Crashes Dakota Johnson's 'SNL' Monologue as Her Breakup Therapist, Shows Travis Kelce Love with Cleveland Shoutout Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Music Video, Starring Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell, to Debut at VMAs With “Çukur: Vartolu,” AI Yapım takes the AI-native production approach behind “Castle Walls” – which comprised two 15-minute episodes – “from an original story to an established drama franchise,” the company said in a statement. Popular on Variety Ay Yapim is best known for the International Emmy-winning “Endless Love,” “Fatmagul,” “Ezel” and “Forbidden Love,” among other global hit series. The “Çukur,” which is known as “The Pit” in international markets, has aired on free-to-air television in 105 countries since its 2017 premiere, according to Ay Yapim. The company underlined that the show’s official YouTube channel has surpassed 6.4 billion cumulative views. “Rather than revisiting the series, the film opens a new chapter in its world, built around Vartolu’s origins and drawing on Ay Yapim’s catalogue. AI Yapım’s creative team leads the film, with artificial intelligence at the core of its production,” the statement noted. While the original “Çukur” follows the Koçovalı family and the Istanbul neighborhood under its control, where family loyalty intersects with the criminal world, the spin-off turns to the childhood and choices that shaped Vartolu Sadettin, who is the Koçovalı family’s illegitimate son. “After losing his mother and grandfather, a boy grows up on the streets, waiting for his father to find him,” says the film’s synopsis. “When that hope gives way to revenge, Salih becomes Vartolu. Moving between his childhood in Doğubeyazıt, eastern Türkiye, and a confrontation years later in Istanbul, the film traces the losses, love and violence behind that transformation,” it goes on to add. “A teacher’s kindness and the possibility of a life with the woman he loves offer Salih another path. Yet his desire to settle the past shapes decisions whose consequences reach beyond him. The film connects a child’s need for a family with the reckoning that follows in the next generation,” it continues, and concludes: “The film carries the tagline “No one is more dangerous than a man with nothing left to lose.” “Every frame of the film was generated with AI, from the characters’ faces to every setting,” the Ay Yapim statement said. However, “The acting is human: actors performed the scenes, and AI generated the characters over their movement, timing and expression. All dialogue was recorded by human voice actors,” it added. It will be interesting to see how viewers of “Çukur,” a regular live action show that did not use AI, will react to its AI-generated spin off film “Çukur:Vartolu.” As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year New York Comic Con Unveils 2026 Professional Schedule Lineup, Including ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ Author-NBCUniversal TV Panel (EXCLUSIVE) Jason Blum on How ‘Other Mommy’ Got That Controversial Title, Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ and More From Blumhouse at NYCC Why Gary Vaynerchuk Is Putting Everything Into Collectibles Brand ‘VeeFriends’: ‘It Could Be the Biggest Business I Ever Build in My Life’ Blumhouse Atomic Monster Inks Short Film Development Deal with Horror Creator Heidi Wong Marvel’s ‘VisionQuest’ Surprise Premieres at NYCC and Earns Glowing First Reactions: ‘A Worthy Successor’ to ‘WandaVision’ Loading comments...

articles.title: ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s Latest Animated Feature Is a Giddy Retro-Futurist Noir With More Energy Than Charm
articles.full_text: Oct 10, 2026 6:45am PT ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s Latest Animated Feature Is a Giddy Retro-Futurist Noir With More Energy Than Charm Freely borrowing from past films including ‘Who Framed Roger Rabbit?,’ ‘Blade Runner’ and ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ this Netflix outing impresses technically, but it’s short on laughs and heart. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s Latest Animated Feature Is a Giddy Retro-Futurist Noir With More Energy Than Charm 1 hour ago ‘Animals’ Review: Ben Affleck Returns to the Director’s Chair for a Nasty, Compulsive Kidnapping Thriller 2 days ago ‘Krux’ Review: A Potently Bleak Portrait of German Village Life at the Bitter End of WWII 3 days ago See All Skydance Animation/Netflix “Welcome to the future,” we hear several times in “ Ray Gunn ” — not that the brave new world it presents is all that welcoming. Or, for that matter, particularly brave or new. The good news is we finally have flying cars and superpowered jetpacks; in other respects, though, we haven’t come a long way at all. Co-existence with extraterrestrials has seen humans revert to old habits of prejudice and apartheid; crime and corruption are rampant as ever; pop-up ads now irksomely manifest as holograms in your personal space. Still, at least the future looks good. The fifth animated feature from Brad Bird is a handsome return to the retro-futurism he previously practiced in “The Incredibles” and his live-action oddity “Tomorrowland”: in this case, a vision of an impossible 21st-century metropolis as might have been dreamed in 1939. Related Stories How to Stream the 2026 MTV VMAs Live Online Taylor Swift to Be Honored at 2026 MTV VMAs With Inaugural Artist-Director Award The world-building — indeed, even just the building-building — is the principal ongoing thrill of “Ray Gun,” as it zips restlessly between gorgeous Art Deco skyscrapers, smokily lit Old Hollywood nightclubs and vividly kitsch rent-a-rooms, all rendered in chic, clashing scarlets and lilacs and burgundies, in vehicles that may be futuristically engineered, but have the luxurious, elongated curves of pre-WWII automobiles. Like “Blade Runner,” Bird’s film sits in the genre-melding realm of sci-fi noir; unlike “Blade Runner,” with its seamy, rain-sodden transformation of Los Angeles, this lighter, brighter detective story is not willing to sacrifice much gleam. Popular on Variety And fair enough: “Ray Gunn” is a caper first and foremost, with all its gumshoe antics safely in the PG-rated zone, though one suspects many of today’s kids may be entirely bewildered by it. (After all, Robert Zemeckis’ peerless “Who Framed Roger Rabbit?” — the original and best repurposing of noir tropes for family entertainment, and a clear creative touchstone here — is now very nearly as old as the 1940s classics it was spoofing.) Bird’s mystery zigs and zags breathlessly as it probes multiple murders connected to a femme fatale -styled starlet in the imaginary city of Metropia; it’s consistently nifty, even when it feels less than original. But it it’s never quite as funny as it should be, while its characters — in particular the eponymous hero, a smooth-talking P.I. voiced by Sam Rockwell — want for texture and soul. Audiences should happily speed along with them on their adventures, but after a fairly long two hours in their company, we don’t feel terribly attached to them. These aren’t fatal shortfalls: There are more than enough visual and sonic delights here to compensate. But they are surprising ones from Bird, whose animated work has been marked by zingy, non-snarky but adult-favoring wit and carefully seeded personal stakes. In “Ray Gunn,” the titular pun — the protagonist’s name, but also his preferred weapon — is typical of the script’s quippery, getting more nods and smiles than outright giggles. The only character dynamic worth a damn, meanwhile, is that between Ray and his weary partner Eye-Ra (Tom Waits, the film’s most inspired casting coup, yielding its most affecting voice performance), who run a down-at-heel “discreet investigations” business from a creaky office being gradually stripped bare by repo men. Business is bad for Ray, in part because Eye-Ra is an alien cyclops, and human-alien collaboration is frowned upon in this world. (We never learn how the two species came to occupy the same planet, but the law regarding their separation is entrenched: Eye-Ra is barred from human hospitals, while aliens can only enter certain clubs as serving staff.) It’s a heavy racial allegory to throw into an otherwise breezy enterprise, and the tone hiccups here and there as a result. With more than a nod to the identity politics that underpinned last year’s “KPop Demon Hunters,” however, it does eventually figure into the principal storyline — which, after a couple too many introductory false starts, kicks off when Ray is hired by Arnold (Bobby Cannavale), the lunkhead fourth husband of tempestuous pop megastar Venus Nova ( Scarlett Johansson ) — to spy on her, though his motivations, of course, aren’t entirely what they seem. When people start showing up inconveniently dead and she’s thrust into scandal on the eve of her new album launch, Ray finds himself effectively babysitting her whilst carrying out his own snooping. But she’s a hard woman to pin down, in multiple senses; the more he knows about her, the less he knows about her, and naturally something sparks between them. It’s an odd, perhaps youth-pandering detail that Venus, with her wasp-waisted silhouette and Veronica Lake hairdo, isn’t a Hollywood siren but a Dua Lipa-style electropop artist. (Her original songs are in fact written by Grammy winner Kimbra, of “Somebody That I Used to Know” fame, and they aren’t much in dialogue with Michael Giacchino’s wonderfully busy, brassy score, which makes no secret of its preferred era.) Nova’s particular brand of celebrity doesn’t really fit the film’s 2039-by-way-of-1939 mission statement, though it does allow Johansson a standout torch number in a more anti-period-appropriate vein — when Venus shows her true colors. Turns out she, like Bird, wants everything old to be new again, or everything new to be old again, or whatever the case may be. She has a suitable partner on that front in the analog-inclined, trenchcoat-sporting Ray, but his image, too, doesn’t entirely add up: Rockwell voices him with jaded slyness, but he has the unlined face and swooshy hair of a Disney prince, rather than any stubbly Bogart gruffness. It’s just one reason why we can’t altogether warm to him — and why he doesn’t light up the center of Bird’s beautifully rendered dark-pastel dystopia. Rather like the man himself, “Ray Gunn” has slick, boundless energy and resourcefulness to spare, but that doesn’t quite amount to charm. ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s Latest Animated Feature Is a Giddy Retro-Futurist Noir With More Energy Than Charm Reviewed at Soho Screening Rooms, London, Oct. 8, 2026. In London Film Festival (Galas). MPA Rating: PG. Running time: 119 MIN. Production: (Animated — U.S.) A Netflix, Skydance Animation presentation of a Skydance Animation production. Producers: John Lasseter, Brad Bird, Lisa Beroud, David Ellison, Dana Goldberg. Crew: Director: Brad Bird. Screenplay: Bird, Matthew Robbins, from a story by Bird. Camera: Erik Smitt. Editors: Darren Holmes, Karl Armstrong. Music: Michael Giacchino. With: Sam Rockwell, Scarlett Johansson, Tom Waits, Bobby Cannavale, Alan Tudyk, Matt Berry, Michelle Rodriguez, Kathryn Hunter, Brad Bird. articles.title: Six-Armed, Two-Legged Spider Princess Tale ‘Migali’ Unpacked by Its Director Ahead of MipJunior World Premiere
articles.full_text: Oct 10, 2026 6:45am PT Six-Armed, Two-Legged Spider Princess Tale ‘Migali’ Unpacked by Its Director Ahead of MipJunior World Premiere Ahead of the premiere, Director Cédric Frémeaux shared his memories of the journey that has been bringing this loveable character from page to screen in an ambitious 52x11-minute series, premiering this fall on TF1, RTBF, Ketnet and RTS. By Kevin Giraud Plus Icon Kevin Giraud Latest ‘The Smurfs’ Season 4 Gets First Look as Peyo Productions Reunites With Nickelodeon, RTBF, Ketnet, KiKA and TF1 (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago In a Groundbreaking Premium Drama, ‘R91’ Brings a Murder Mystery Aboard Flagship French Aircraft Carrier 3 days ago BBC, Bobby Prod, Folivari, Gao Shan Pictures Honored by Europe’s Animation Industry at Cartoon Forum 3 weeks ago See All 'Migali,' a spider princess with heart. Credits Easy Peasy Entertainment, Bardaf! Productions, TF1, RTBF, VRT, RTS At MIPJunior , it’s not often that a little creeper gets put out on center-stage. But on Oct. 10, as “ Migali ” makes its world premiere in front of buyers from all across the globe, a tiny spider princess seems to be set on weaving webs of laughter and fun at the unmissable Cannes children’s TV market. Produced by Adelaïde Terme ( Easy Peasy Entertainment , the production/licensing arm of French Auzou Publishing Group) along with Bardaf! Productions in co-production with RTBF , Ketnet , RTS and TF1 , “Migali” is a 52x11minute series centered on six-year-old Migali, a spider princess determined to become queen. Related Stories As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year Credits Easy Peasy Entertainment, Bardaf! Productions, TF1, RTBF, VRT, RTS As she heads to the Royal Academy, where princes and princesses of all kingdoms learn to control their abilities, Migali brings her boundless energy and extraodinary web-weaving skills to the school, meeting a gallery of other quirky characters from all size and shapes. Facing (and, more often than not, provoking) chaos in her daily life, Migali stays happy, merry and positive, meeting each challenge as a new, fun adventure. Popular on Variety An adaptation of the eponymous comic book series by Alexandre Arlène and Fabien Ockö Lambert, “Migali” is directed by Cédric Frémeaux (“50/50 Heroes”). Ahead of the premiere, Frémeaux spoke with Variety about the smooth journey that has been bringing this loveable, quirky spider princess from page to screen. “I’ve always loved animated series,” recalls the storyboard artist-turned director. “As a kid, I woke every morning eager to discover ‘Dexter’s Laboratory,’ ‘Dragonball,’ and many others. I was captivated by these worlds. Growing up, it quickly became clear to me that I wanted to work in that industry someday.” During high school, Frémeaux found his way as an intern at Ankama, the French multimedia giant behind videogame hit “Dofus,” subsequent animated series “Wakfu” and manga hit “Radiant.” After studying animation at LISAA in Paris, he started his career as a storyboard artist, dabbling with editing and directing on trailers and teasers. “Migali” is his second series, a match made possible by Terme, who reached out to Frémeaux for this adaptation. “She presented me Auzou’s line-up, and I immediately connected with ‘Migali,’ which turned out to be her own pick for our collaboration. What struck me with this character is how radiant and fun she was, as a heroin. With our target audience [kids 5-8], it’s very important to connect with a protagonist. And with Migali, they definitely can as she faces the sames challenges that they do.” Migali, who Frémeaux frames as “Spiderman’s young cousin living in a world of unicorns, dragons and potions,” was brought to screen in close connection with the author duo and Terme, who saw the potential for an animated series even before the first comic was published. Since then, Migali’s books have sold more than 150,000 copies in France, and boasts nine volumes already. This success fueled Frémeaux’s enthusiasm even more, as he prepared himself for the challenge of bringing this character to the screen. “What I also love about ‘Migali’ is its humor, which doesn’t shy away from deeper topics that really connect with kids. Children from this age are much smart than we think, and if you’re lazy in your writing, they will see it instantly. Today, they have access to so much content. They know these narratives, and they know how it works. Instead of fighting for their attention span with fast-paced, frantic content, we chose to craft something that both takes them seriously and makes them laugh. And I think that’s key to succeeding in retaining kids’ attention today.” Credits Easy Peasy Entertainment, Bardaf! Productions, TF1, RTBF, VRT, RTS Yet, as Frémeaux continued, the challenge of producing 52 episodes of 11 minutes (or as he put it, a nine-hour movie) was a huge undertaking. “Once storyboard was locked, we had to deliver a full episode’s animatic every week. And to do that, there’s only way I know: surrounding yourself with talented people who understand the project.” Frémeaux goes even further: “My role as a director is to find people who are better than me at they own field of expertise. Once I managed to achieve that, every piece fell right into place, and the production was very smooth.” A production that was split between Caribara studios in Annecy, Paris, and Caribara Belgian subsidiary Waoooh. “The key is these large European co-productions is to communicate constantly, and maintain overall cohesiveness throughout the whole pipeline. Animation is, at its heart, a collaborative art, and I strongly believe ‘Migali’ benefits from this collective effort. It would be a far less interesting product if I had created it alone with AI tools.” “Migali” is AI-free, as the teams received strict instructions during this creative process. While aknowledging its uses, Frémeaux views AI technology as a tool that can’t be part of creating something. “Technology has always been part of the animation industry, which faced similar issues with the introduction of 3D, and other tools that revolutionized the medium over and over. But creativity has to remain at the center of this process, and tools can’t replace artists. Our show is made by people who asked themselves a lot of questions, who made choices in framing, staging, and poured their craft and soul in this series. And that is something that AI can’t do.” Credits Easy Peasy Entertainment, Bardaf! Productions, TF1, RTBF, VRT, RTS As “Migali” premieres this afternoon, Frémeaux is eager to present this colorful, quirky character to the world. “Much like in our show, Migali is about to discover a whole new world, and I can’t wait to introduce her to global audiences. The series has a lot of potential, and we’ve only scratched the surface of Migali’s universe. There are many more paths and characters we can explore, to build beyond the Royal Academy and introduce children to this loveable IP.” “Migali” premieres today at MipJunior, subsequently airing on TF1 and other partner broadcasters in the following months. The series is distributed internationally by Moon-Keys International Content. articles.title: Brad Bird on Why He Took ‘Ray Gunn’ to Skydance Instead of Pixar: Making Animated Films for Teens and Adults ‘Shouldn’t Be a Controversial Decision’
articles.full_text: Oct 10, 2026 6:55am PT Brad Bird on Why He Took ‘Ray Gunn’ to Skydance Instead of Pixar: Making Animated Films for Teens and Adults ‘Shouldn’t Be a Controversial Decision’ Skydance Animation's 'Ray Gunn,' directed by Brad Bird, will premiere on Netflix By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest Brad Bird on Why He Took ‘Ray Gunn’ to Skydance Instead of Pixar: Making Animated Films for Teens and Adults ‘Shouldn’t Be a Controversial Decision’ 1 hour ago Shari Redstone-Backed Sipur Studios Opens London Office, Sets Out International Strategy Including Boarding Olivier Dahan’s ‘Nana’ (EXCLUSIVE) 18 hours ago Skydance-Owned Channel 5 Profits Dropped by $32 Million Last Year Due to Ad Market and Inward Streaming Investment 1 day ago See All Â©2026 Skydance Animation On a balmy April afternoon at Abbey Road Studios in London, a 74-piece orchestra comprised of violinists, cellists, flautists and even an organ-payer, is packed into Studio One. The iconic room, which has hosted musical legends from Edward Elgar to Harry Styles, is painted “Toy Story” blue, a fitting color given the reason everyone is here today is to record the score for “Ray Gunn,” a new feature animation from Pixar legend Brad Bird , the brains behind “Ratatouille” and “The Incredibles.” Related Stories As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year The film, which has been gestating inside Bird’s mind for three decades, is not a Pixar or Disney project, however (more on which later), but a Skydance Animation production which will hit Netflix on Dec. 18 (it premieres at the BFI London Film Festival on Oct. 10). Popular on Variety Directing the orchestra at Abbey Road is Bird’s longtime collaborator, composer Michael Giacchino . “ Ray Gunn ” is the duo’s sixth project together since first teaming up for “The Incredibles” in 2004 and it’s one Giacchino (who won an Oscar for Pixar’s “Up” in 2010) has had more than two decades to prepare for. “We talked about this movie during ‘The Incredibles,’” the composer reveals, when we speak a few months later. “I’ve known about this for a very long time.” Fittingly, given the key role of music in the film , Bird first conceived the idea for “Ray Gunn” – a noir detective caper set in a “Jetsons”-style retro future – after hearing The B-52s’ song “Planet Claire.” To Bird, the tune sounded like a mash-up between the theme song to 1960s detective series “Peter Gunn” and “a ’50s monster sci-fi movie,” Bird says in an interview a day before the film’s premiere. “I went, ‘This is not “Peter Gunn.” What is this?’ And then I went, ‘It’s Ray-Gun.’ And then I went, ‘ Ray Gunn : It’s a guy’s name. He’s a detective, but it’s in the future.’” Michael Giacchino and Brad Bird (courtesy of Netflix) Courtesy of Netflix But the idea got shelved as other projects got in the way: there was his sophomore Pixar project “Ratatouille” followed by “The Incredibles 2” and, in between, live action fare “Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol” and “Tomorrowland” as well as an abandoned attempt to adapt Will Eisner’s comic “The Spirit.” Bird, who describes his mind as a “big shop floor,” would come back and “tinker” with “Ray Gunn” every now and again, biding his time until he could bring it to life (the film fell through at other studios including Warner Bros.) It was “Mission: Impossible” that finally paved the way for what had effectively become Bird’s real-life mission: impossible. “It was [Skydance’s] second film and everybody was happy with how it turned out,” Bird says of his turn at the helm of the Tom Cruise franchise. So when the opportunity arose to pitch the studio on another idea, “Ray Gunn” was the obvious choice. (The move also reunited Bird with Pixar co-founder John Lasseter, now the head of Skydance Animation .) “I never pitched it at Pixar because I felt like it wasn’t in Pixar’s wheelhouse exactly,” Bird explains, referring to the studio’s reputation for catering to younger audiences than the one he’s aiming at with “Ray Gunn.” “If you put a Pixar label on it people would go, ‘Oh well, it’s meant for the same audience that these other films were meant for,’ and inevitably some of them would go, ‘Well, my little Jimmy would be unhappy at this.’” Bird expands on the theme, pointing out there are “10 billion animated films” for children and far fewer for teenagers and adults, despite them comprising the majority of the movie-going audience. Making animated films for them “shouldn’t be a controversial decision,” Bird says, “and yet it was always treated that way by the ministers of resource allocation [at Pixar].” (He is returning to Pixar for his next project, a third “Incredibles” movie.) Skydance had a different take. “My thought when [they] got involved was that that they’ll go with me on this slightly different audience tangent,” Bird says. “And here it is.” Skydance CEO David Ellison is a producer on “Ray Gunn”: was that in name only or was he fairly hands-on? “Well, he was more involved in the earlier days,” Bird says. “But he got — you know, his plate became very full.” The director is obliquely referring to Ellison’s recent battle to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery . Bird won’t be drawn on whether he thinks Ellison will stick to his promise, made as part of his bid, that Skydance will produce at least 30 theatrical films a year . “All that stuff is beyond my pay grade,” he says, sidestepping the question. While Skydance may have become the latest lightning rod in an increasingly polarised and under pressure Hollywood, Bird is a pragmatist. Later in our conversation, he notes that after making “The Iron Giant” he took his nascent idea for “The Incredibles” to Pixar. “The crew from ‘Iron Giant,’ a lot of them were mad at me initially because they felt like I was leaving hand-drawn [animation] and going to the sexy new CG,” Bird recalls. “And I said I don’t really care about the technology part. I’m going up to Pixar because they protect storytelling.” “Ray Gunn” Netflix As it happens, protecting — versus exploiting — art is one of the themes of “Ray Gunn,” which follows the eponymous private detective (voiced by Sam Rockwell) as he uncovers a dastardly plot involving Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson), a superstar singer with a huge secret. For Giacchino, the trick to scoring a film filled with so much intrigue is keeping the viewer guessing. “Probably the second toughest thing was just making sure everything was always in alignment thematically, so that I didn’t give the audience something that they shouldn’t be thinking about,” he notes. (The actual toughest, he says, was an intimate scene between Gunn and Nova when they’re first opening up to each other. “It needed to really hit every single emotional beat in this perfect way,” he explains.) Bird may have written “Ray Gunn” almost three decades ago but it’s themes of art, technology and corporate greed resonate now as much as they did in the late 1990s. He says the screenplay changed “less than you’d think” between that first draft and the finished movie. “A lot of the things that people are saying that [the film] is dealing with that are contemporary right now in the headlines were in there 30 years ago,” Bird notes. “People are people and greed is greed and the flaws of people make good subject material for films. If that’s what’s driving the story, then the story’s not going to age because it’s about eternal things rather than things that were in the news last week.” New York Comic Con Unveils 2026 Professional Schedule Lineup, Including ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ Author-NBCUniversal TV Panel (EXCLUSIVE) Amazon Viking Drama ‘Bloodaxe’ Sets Release Date, Debuts Fierce New Trailer at New York Comic Con Chase Infiniti to Star in Dylan Clark’s ‘Portrait of God’ at Lionsgate With Sam Raimi and Jordan Peele Producing Blumhouse Atomic Monster Inks Short Film Development Deal with Horror Creator Heidi Wong ‘Helluva Boss’ Actor Lashes Out at NYCC Heckler: ‘I’m Going to Jump Over This Fence and End You’ As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year Loading comments...

articles.title: Kleber Mendonça Filho, Wagner Moura and More Brazilian Academy Members Release Open Letter Expressing ‘Concern’ Over Brazil’s Presidential Elections (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Oct 10, 2026 7:25am PT Kleber Mendonça Filho, Wagner Moura and More Brazilian Academy Members Release Open Letter Expressing ‘Concern’ Over Brazil’s Presidential Elections (EXCLUSIVE) 'I'm Still Here' producer Rodrigo Teixeira, Alice Braga, Fernando Meirelles and Petra Costa are amongst signatories pleading for 'close international attention' to the upcoming second round in the polls between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Rodrigo Santoro and Camila Pitanga to Star in Marcelo Gomes’ ‘Garota da Urca’ From a Script by Luciana Paes and Leonardo Moreira (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Prime Video’s ‘Marília Mendonça – Sentimento Louco’ Offers Unparalleled Access to Brazil’s Most Popular Singer Five Years After Tragic Plane Crash 3 days ago Brazilian Cinema at Risk: A Report From Watching the Presidential Elections From the Rio Film Festival 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Cannes Film Festival Several Brazilian members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, including Oscar nominees Kleber Mendonça Filho , Wagner Moura , Emilie Lesclaux, Fernando Meirelles, Alê Abreu and Petra Costa, and Oscar-winning producer Rodrigo Teixeira (“I’m Still Here”), have released an open letter calling international attention to the upcoming second round of Brazil ‘s presidential elections. The polls will open Oct. 25 and see current president Luis Inácio Lula da Silva face far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Flávio is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year and three-month sentence under house arrest for plotting a coup d’état after losing the 2022 presidential election. Earlier this week, Variety published an in-depth report detailing how Jair Bolsonaro dismantled Brazil’s audiovisual sector, alerting to a similar future ahead if Flávio Bolsonaro wins the upcoming elections . Related Stories As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year Other high-profile signatories include Alice Braga (“City of God”), Karim Aïnouz (“The Invisible Life of Eurídice Gusmão”), Sônia Braga (“Aquarius”), Gabriel Mascaro (“The Blue Trail”), Carolina Markowicz (“Charcoal”), Anita Rocha da Silveira (“Medusa”), Anna Muylaert (“The Second Mother”), Laís Bodanzky (“Brainstorm”) and Rio Film Festival director Ilda Santiago. Popular on Variety The letter calls for “close international attention” to the elections, detailing how Flávio Bolsonaro has recently pledged “to rewrite Brazil’s 1988 Constitution” and noting an alleged U.S. intervention in the first round of the elections, reported by The Guardian in an investigation on how the “United States government allocated approximately US$1 million from a State Department human rights fund to a program called ‘Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil.’” “We see the developments unfolding in Brazil as part of a broader pattern of alleged electoral interference across Latin America,” says the letter, which can be read in full below: An Open Letter from Brazilian Members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences to Our Colleagues in the Film Industry and the International Press We, Brazilian film professionals and members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in Hollywood, wish to express our concern over the current political climate in Brazil and call for close international attention to the second round of the presidential election on October 25. The margin between the two candidates in the first round was just 1.87 percentage points. Brazil is therefore a deeply divided country. We are nonetheless witnessing troubling signs of disregard for democratic norms, including allegations of possible foreign interference in Brazil that warrant transparent investigation and international scrutiny. The Guardian has reported that the United States government allocated approximately US$1 million from a State Department human rights fund to a program called “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil.” At the same time, media observers have raised concerns about possible distortions in the reach of political content on Meta platforms and have called for an investigation. Among the cases cited are the Instagram accounts of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, which have reportedly experienced declines in reach, difficulties with access and visibility in search results, as well as an inability to promote posts through paid advertising. Another case involves a US-based website promoting the purchase of advertisements in support of candidate Flávio Bolsonaro in exchange for cryptocurrency tokens, under the promise of helping underprivileged children in Uganda. Brazil’s Federal Police are also investigating suspicions of cash payments to voters in rural areas. Several of Flávio Bolsonaro’s proposals also warrant close scrutiny, including his pledge to rewrite Brazil’s 1988 Constitution, which marked the end of military dictatorship and the restoration of democracy in the country. According to the candidate, a new constitution would be drafted by a Congress dominated by a far-right majority. This statement is particularly troubling in light of the attempted coup attributed to former president Jair Bolsonaro, the candidate’s father. The plot included plans to assassinate the current president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his vice president, Geraldo Alckmin. Jair Bolsonaro is imprisoned in connection with this case, while his son has pledged to grant him amnesty as his first act in office. Our concern is compounded by the way much of Brazil’s mainstream media has normalized these developments, failing to address with the seriousness they deserve the allegations against Flávio Bolsonaro and the crimes attributed to his father. In addition to the attempted coup, Jair Bolsonaro was the subject of a complaint filed with the International Criminal Court in The Hague over the more than 600,000 COVID-19 deaths recorded in Brazil during the pandemic, amid actions and omissions by his administration. The complaint argues that more than half of those deaths could have been prevented. His administration was also associated with Brazil’s return to the United Nations’ Hunger Map. Now, his son is promising cuts to social security spending modeled on the austerity policies of Javier Milei’s government in Argentina. The omission or downplaying of these facts contributes to public misinformation and undermines the defense of democracy. As cultural professionals, we understand the cost these austerity policies can impose on our sector. Under the previous administration, Brazil’s audiovisual industry suffered from the closure of the Ministry of Culture, the suspension of the Audiovisual Sector Fund, the weakening of cultural institutions, and allegations of censorship. We fear a return to that scenario. Protecting freedom of expression and ensuring the long-term sustainability of Brazil’s audiovisual industry are inseparable from defending democracy. We see the developments unfolding in Brazil as part of a broader pattern of alleged electoral interference across Latin America. The defense of Brazilian democracy must therefore rest not only with the Brazilian people, through free, fair and transparent elections, but also with the vigilance and engagement of the international community. We call on the international press to cover this electoral process rigorously, on the international audiovisual community to amplify the debate, and on the relevant institutions to investigate these allegations independently. The single-player sci-fi adventure game is set in the year 2945, as the United Empire of Earth is threatened by outlaws and hostile aliens alike. Players enlist as a rookie in the UEE Navy and embark on a dangerous journey through the galactic war. Aboard a massive capital ship, players work alongside a dynamic crew to earn their rank. The CIG team has been developing “Star Citizen” simultaneously with “Squadron 42,” which follows a focused single-player narrative adventure rather than a multiplayer game style. Much of the technology and game systems utilized in “Star Citizen” is repurposed for “Squadron 42,” game designer and CIG founder Chris Roberts told Variety in May . The independent studio was co-founded in 2012 by game designer Roberts, the mind behind the ‘90s PC game “Wing Commander,” alongside wife Sandi Roberts. “Squadron 42” is slated for release in Q2 2027. articles.title: ‘The Social Reckoning’ Breakout Portia Doubleday on Playing ‘White Girl Wasted’ Conspiracy Theorist: ‘I Knew People Who Were Radicalized’
articles.full_text: Oct 10, 2026 8:00am PT ‘The Social Reckoning’ Breakout Portia Doubleday on Playing ‘White Girl Wasted’ Conspiracy Theorist: ‘I Knew People Who Were Radicalized’ By Daniel D'Addario Plus Icon Daniel D'Addario Chief Correspondent DPD_ Latest Aaron Sorkin and Mikey Madison on ‘The Social Reckoning’: Getting Inside a Whistleblower’s Mind, Jeremy Strong’s ‘Antihero’ Zuckerberg and Why Trump is the Movie’s Voldemort 2 days ago ‘A Few Good Men’ on Broadway: Aaron Sorkin, Bradley Whitford and Team Behind Revival on Why It’s ’So Fucking Relevant’ in Trump Era 1 week ago ‘Adults’ Heartthrob Jack Innanen Reveals All: From Wildest Fan DMs to His Love for ‘Heated Rivalry’ to Whether He’d Shave His Iconic Mustache 1 week ago See All Leah Gallo SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for “ The Social Reckoning ,” now playing in theaters. Aaron Sorkin’s new film “The Social Reckoning” begins with a vignette about the impact of social media that’s as chilling as any statistic about the dangers of social media. And Portia Doubleday sits at its center, portraying the human toll of Facebook. In the first chapter of the new film, entitled “White Girl Wasted,” we see Doubleday’s character, Kaylee, standing by her stalled car on the side of the road. When two police officers (Sierra Capri and Michael Braugher) pull over and approach her, she tells them that AAA is on their way to assist her; she’s also visibly impaired, slurring her speech and combating them at every turn, even as her face is buried in her phone. Related Stories As New York Comic Con Turns 20, Organizer Teases Coney Island Team-Up, After 3 p.m. Ticket and Possibility of Expanding to Five Days Next Year Even as it seems the cops have nothing to go on — as she’s within her rights under California law to refuse to cooperate with their requests, they tell her they’re going to let her slide — Kaylee insists on intensifying the interaction, spewing racist and misogynistic invective at the cops and then capturing the consequences on video, declaring in a screeching monologue that she is “being treated like a fucking immigrant” and broadcasting it to subscribers of the “Voice of Reason” channel online. Popular on Variety This interaction, one that will feel unfortunately familiar to any viewer who’s spent time online this decade, sits at the heart of “The Social Reckoning.” Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network,” the 2010 film he wrote about the earliest days of Facebook, “Reckoning” confronts the world Mark Zuckerberg has brought into being. Kaylee is a person whose particular brand of rage could only exist in a post-social media world. After all, we learn she’s something of a changeling: Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) knew Kaylee as a bleeding-heart leftist. By the film’s end, Frances has been so moved by Kaylee’s trajectory that she decides to spill the secrets of Facebook’s indifference to the harm it causes. Kaylee, meanwhile, joins the Jan. 6 insurrection. Doubleday may be best known for her work on USA’s Emmy-winning drama “Mr. Robot,” in which she played a conflicted employee at the series’ central villainous tech concern, E Corp. As she tells Variety , on the week of “The Social Reckoning’s” release, the way technology affects our cognition is a live concern for her, and has had direct consequences in her own life. When you first read the script, did you have a vision for Kaylee? Did she remind you of anyone or anything that you thought you might draw on? I live in Los Angeles, and I know what’s going on in the world. And I actually have known a couple of people who were radicalized, and they actually came to mind. During COVID, I was actually pre-med for like three seconds. Whoa! What? Yeah, there was nothing to do. But that’s a big thing to do. It was actually really difficult — cell bio is just excruciating. But I actually knew a couple people that were in the pre-med track and who were radicalized. And to know them so well and find that out was … I didn’t really understand. I think I still don’t quite understand how that happens. How can you understand the organelles of a human cell and understand what the scientific method is and how important facts are, and yet still believe that COVID can come from a 5G tower? I remember they were showing me these videos, and I couldn’t make sense of it. And so that’s kind of where I started with my own personal experience of what happens to a person. Repeated exposure can start to make extreme ideas feel normal. I kept thinking, “They’re in an echo chamber, and they’re seeing these really bizarre videos that look like they’re made in a basement, and they’re seeing them so often that I think they just have acclimated to the fact that there are these possibilities that they want to be in on.” They want to be cracking the conspiracy or these other truths that are not being examined. So I started there, and built from that place. I started to better understand how does a seemingly normal person turn out to be the one that you see in the beginning of the movie. What is that process like? That’s an interesting perspective, and one that I think is important in contemporary life and for this movie — that the radicalized are not some strange, naive other people, but people like you or I who fell prey to incredibly powerful technology. I think it’s the important perspective to have, because often I think that people see these videos and they think, “Oh, that’s a very faraway person. Something is wrong with them. They were raised and born that way.” That’s how I viewed it. You know, I viewed it as really away from me, and that’s not what happened. And so, having close relationships with people who were lovely and finding this out about believing in Pizzagate, I was really interested in the social science perspective of that. You know, what does gaslighting look like in human form? And I think that that’s also what [Kaylee] is in the movie, right? She’s the human component. What happens up close when one human is affected by this huge company’s massive influence? Or what can happen when you have that much power to influence the way that people think, especially when you’re giving them repeated exposure to certain ways of thinking? I interviewed Aaron Sorkin for a different story, and he mentioned that he’d had conversations with Frances Haugen, and that the character you play is drawn from a real story from Frances’ life. What were the conversations you had with him about Kaylee like? I think Aaron wanted it to be really grounded. That was really important, especially because — and we talked about this a lot — we didn’t want the moment to be about being under the influence, [as if] that is why this person is acting this way, but that this is actually how she feels. So we spent a lot of time grounding it and making sure that you saw what Frances saw with her friend, what we see online, and what my experience was with people that I’ve met that have just fallen into QAnon radicalization. It was really important that it felt real. A couple of things are happening that I think are easy to see: the entitlement and the victimization. Like she’s the victim in that moment; she feels perpetrated. And why is that? To dumb it down to “She’s a racist” would be reductive of what’s going on. That’s not really what that moment’s about. It’s: How do people, over time, change — especially with repeated exposure and influence? I remember watching these videos and thinking there’s something so emotional about it. It’s almost like an emotional addiction, and you become a part of a group, or you become a part of some way to vindicate yourself from your own pain or your own victimization by making somebody else the enemy to sort of justify the anger that you have within yourself. Those are the things that I brainstormed with him about because I was concerned [that it might] fall into this trap of “Oh, this drunk girl that’s just super erratic.” I want to talk about the nuts and bolts of acting the scene. Sorkin writes very rhythmic dialogue that is meant to be delivered note-perfect down to the comma. And, in the scene, you’re slurring your words. Did this present a special challenge? I was scared about that, actually. I remember Aaron sort of said this when we were rehearsing. He was like, “Just trust the words. They’ll save you.” Trust that you can land on them — and that is true. I don’t know how to explain it, but there is something unbelievably comforting, and I knew it when I read it, when I first got it … It infects your body, that rhythm. If you can get that rhythm in your body, it just feels like molasses. It just sort of runs together because he’s so brilliant. It affords the actor, actually, the ability to live within the constraints of words that you know are going to catch you. So instead of feeling like you might have to add or create a beat or figure out how to pull your truth out of a moment, he makes that process unbelievably effortless. We actually shot it in two days, which was lovely, because it was a pretty heavy scene, you know. How did you feel at the halfway mark, walking into night two? When the stakes feel this high when you’re working with someone, I just let myself feel. Because I trust him to know how to direct me, and he’s approachable and really funny and really warm, and what a joy to feel like “Hey, this lands.” I felt like I had the liberty to play a little bit. It was more about finding the level that he wanted. Where does that escalation begin, and why? Like, where is the moment where this person decides that they’re going to turn this night into what you saw? And I think that there is that moment where she’s sort of calculating; there’s like a moment where it turns, and I think he was really specific about that. I’m always nervous, but thankfully, he’s a great director, so that gave me the liberty to try different levels and see what worked and what didn’t. I’ve been comparing your work here to Rooney Mara’s at the start of “The Social Network”: It’s a one-scene performance, but it defines everything that follows, and we briefly glimpse each character again. In your case, you had to act as Kaylee storming the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. How did that feel to shoot? I remember Jan. 6 and how I felt that day, and … I never thought that I would be doing this. I never thought I would actually have to put myself in those shoes. And it made me really, really sad. I don’t want to get too emotional. It just made me really sad, because I had some space from it — especially given how loud things are, and there’s constant stuff going on every single day. But to actually be in that, there’s just something so tragic. That’s why I appreciated playing this character so much — because she’s a human consequence. She is the one who would be there. Behind amplifying extremism and misinformation and Facebook’s hand in this: What is this doing to one person that ends up being there? I was grateful to examine someone who has been part of what I’ve criticized — but it was really challenging. I had mixed feelings about it. Even that day, [Sorkin] kept saying, “Turn around and take in where you are, and [take in] that those people really believed it.” That’s what’s so gut-wrenching: [they’re] really believing that they’re doing the right thing. And that is what produces, for me, the anger and the rage and the sadness. That they feel how I feel when I’m standing up for something that I believe in. It’s the same. I first saw you on “Mr. Robot,” which was a show all about how the digital world is not separate from our real lives — it’s hopelessly intertwined with them, redefining reality. “The Social Reckoning” has similar concerns. Do you spend a lot of time thinking about these issues? Yeah, of course. I don’t really share too much online. I just talk to myself about how angry I am about things that are going on. And it’s interesting how people feel about AI, because watching this film, you see this person who may have had a good idea to connect people, and the consequences of it being this massive, and having this much influence and the ability to radicalize small groups of people who can actually cause a lot of harm. Where we’re at with AI, I feel like it’s really comparable. I don’t really think we fully understand the implications of what this is going to do to the world, and we’re sort of at the precipice. As a ’90s child, I’m just like, what is happening? The entire world is just going to massively change, and there’s going to be huge consequences to these changes. And who’s thinking about that? You know, like who’s ensuring that we’re actually going to be OK? That’s what I’ve been thinking about the most after “Robot.” I spend time concerned about it — I’m sure you do too. A lot of people do. Look what happened at Facebook. So what’s going to happen now with OpenAI? What is our future going to look like? We could discuss that for hours, and I think we’d emerge pretty dispirited. But I wanted to close the loop: What ended up happening with your pre-med studies? It was like the most incredible experience I’ve ever had. To be honest, taking the bio classes I took opened my brain to a whole different world. But I just was like, I still want to be an actress, and I don’t know if I can make a 20-year commitment . You know what I mean? I don’t know. Can I go 16 hours and just eat Top Ramen? I still think about it, though. It took me 20 years to finish my degree because my parents didn’t want me to become an actor. My dad was all about, you know, “If you’re stupid, you’re going to be evil, and you have to be smart.” And so it took me 20 years, but I got my B.A. — I took a little pre-med journey, and I finished! I’m not actually pre-med. But who knows what will happen? articles.title: Siân Heder & The ‘Being Heumann’ Crew On Creating An Inclusive Film & Production Environment — Contenders London
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Siân Heder & The ‘Being Heumann’ Crew On Creating An Inclusive Film & Production Environment — Contenders London Mike Leigh, Marion Bailey & Kate O’Flynn On The Close Collaboration Behind ‘Tender Loving Care’ — Contenders London Society of Composers & Lyricists Opens First International Chapter In London View All October 10, 2026 4:34am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kevin J. Walsh, Sian Heder, Ruth Madeley, Adam Caldwell and Bernard Telsey at Deadline Contenders Film: London held at the Ham Yard Hotel on October 10, 2026 in London, England. Scott Garfitt/Deadline “I think we created history,” Being Heumann producer Kevin Walsh concluded this morning during a Q&A session at Deadline’s Contenders London . The veteran producer wasn’t speaking specifically about the feature film, but the accessible environment he and director Siân Heder created on the film’s set. “We are as proud of that as we are of the movie,” Walsh continued. The Apple Original Films title tells the true story of disability-rights advocate Judy Heumann, played by Doctor Who alum Ruth Madeley . Based on Heumann’s memoir, it centers on the year 1977, when Heumann led more than 100 disabled people to take over the San Francisco Federal Building, kicking off a 28-day sit-in — the longest occupation of a federal building in U.S. history. Related Stories News Mike Leigh, Marion Bailey & Kate O'Flynn On The Close Collaboration Behind 'Tender Loving Care' -- Contenders London News Brad Bird Talks Long-Gestating Passion Project 'Ray Gunn' & Portraying "Characters Who Are Desperate" In Utopia -- Contenders London The protesters form a tightly bound community, refusing to leave until the government enforces Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which required all federal spaces to become accessible. Watch on Deadline “We really approached this film with the same kind of relentlessness that Judy approached her life,” Walsh said. “We had 10 disabled leads. It took a lot of detail to make it accessible. Making ramps that were accessible with trailers, retrofitting hair and makeup trailers for disabled actors to be able to use. It took a company like Apple to really support us.” Discussing the origins of the project, Heder said a friend who worked on the Sundance documentary Crip Camp , which starred the late Judy Heumann, tipped her off about Heumann’s life story. “A friend of mine was the accessibility coordinator for Crip Camp at Sundance, and she sent me a text message and said, I’m hanging out with this woman, Judy Heumann. She’s the coolest woman on the planet, and someone should make a movie about her,” Heder explained. “I’d had a very profound experience on Coda , entering the deaf community and really understanding how many of these stories aren’t told. There are so many of these incredible stories within the disability community, and they are just never represented.” Heder said she later saw Crip Camp and read Heumann’s memoir, which introduced her to the story of the 504 protests. “I was just really intrigued by Judy because she’s so funny. She was this little woman with this Brooklyn accent. She was so self-possessed and so hilariously in command of everybody,” Heder said. Being Heumann debuted last month at TIFF and screens this week in London as one of the London Film Festival headline galas. The film will debut in select theaters on November 6 before dropping on Apple TV on November 13. ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell & Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie & Bacall ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $27.5M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted ‘Newlyweds’ Showrunner Gail Lerner Fired Ahead Of NBC Sitcom’s Premiere Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Guy Nattiv & Carrie Coon On Finding Empathy In ‘The Liberation’: “Who Are We To Say What Is Required For Someone To Move On?” — Contenders London
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Guy Nattiv & Carrie Coon On Finding Empathy In ‘The Liberation’: “Who Are We To Say What Is Required For Someone To Move On?” — Contenders London Brad Bird Talks Long-Gestating Passion Project ‘Ray Gunn’ & Portraying “Characters Who Are Desperate” In Utopia — Contenders London Oscars: Democratic Republic Of Congo Selects ‘Rumba Royale’ For Best International Feature Film Race; The Fally Ipupa Starrer Is Country’s Second Ever Submission View All October 10, 2026 4:41am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Guy Nattiv and Carrie Coon on the panel for "The Liberation" at Deadline Contenders Film: London held at the Ham Yard Hotel on October 10, 2026 in London, England. Vianney Le Caer Writer-director Guy Nattiv and actress Carrie Coon joined Deadline’s Contenders London event today where the pair discussed making The Liberation , a very personal story inspired by real events from Nattiv’s own grandmother. The film, which Bleecker Street is releasing in in the U.S. in January, is set in the early 1980s where Rita, a depressed New Jersey bank worker and Holocaust survivor (Coon), is lured into an all-female woodland commune by a charismatic leader (Lily James), while her daughters attempt a rescue. “I was only eight when my family took me to seminars to see my grandmother and participate with her in those meetings,” said Nattiv. “I didn’t know what it meant. It was like dancing with people in the dark. I heard horrific stories from people, and my grandmother crying, it was so weird to me. But no one told me what it was exactly, and I didn’t know until I became a teenager when my family had basically broken in front of my eyes, and my grandmother left my grandfather, left our family, and just joined this. Now, we know it was a cult but at the time we didn’t know what it was.” Related Stories News Siân Heder & The 'Being Heumann' Crew On Creating An Inclusive Film & Production Environment -- Contenders London News 'Wildwood Director' Travis Knight On LAIKA's Stop-Motion Fantasy Epic: "It Took Us 16 Years To Make This Movie" - Contenders London Nattiv said that when he was older and was processing these events as a film student, he started asking a lot of questions but didn’t get a lot of answers. It was a decade ago that he decided to take his camera and visit the cult after his grandmother had passed away. “I asked questions and I got answers…ish.” Watch on Deadline He entered the process with “a lot of empathy” and found that the cult “tried to free her” from her trauma of being a Holocaust survivor. “She had the courage to do something very uncommon: To leave your family, say goodbye to your daughters and your husband and go into the unknown and try to save yourself.” Coon admitted she was “absolutely fascinated by the story” and said she watched “hours and hours” of footage from Yad Vashem and from Shoah Foundation testimonies, “particularly women from Poland,” to help her research for the role of Rita. “There’s something very specific about the way the recounting of those unspeakable things is held in the body,” said Coon. “And also, the stories themselves, the myriad forms of trauma that were inflicted upon people. But then also that they were resilient enough to survive was also very fascinating and people had a find a way to survive and Rita had a very particular idea about what that looked like for herself…who are we to say what is required for someone to move on?” Coon continued that it was helpful for her to view the story as “a love story.” “What I became very fascinated by with reading is the idea that these social rules we are living by are tacit agreements,” she said. “There’s nothing written down. We wake up in the morning and we’re a wife and a mother and we follow all of these rules. But it’s all made up. We could essentially walk away from our lives at any time, but we don’t do it. And we did [in this film]. I just find that brave and shocking.” Check back on Monday for the panel video. ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell And Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie And Bacall ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $27.5M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted ‘Newlyweds’ Showrunner Gail Lerner Fired Ahead Of NBC Sitcom’s Premiere Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Léa Seydoux & Marie Kreutzer On The “Earthquake” At The Heart Of ‘Gentle Monster’ — Contenders London
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Léa Seydoux & Marie Kreutzer On The “Earthquake” At The Heart Of ‘Gentle Monster’ — Contenders London Danny Boyle On The Challenges Of Rupert Murdoch & ‘The Sun’ Film ‘Ink’: “We Had A Siege Mentality While Making It” — Contenders London Craig Ferguson & Megyn Price Starring In Addiction Dramedy Series ‘Quitters’ For Angel View All October 10, 2026 4:57am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Léa Seydoux and Marie Kreutzer at Deadline's Contenders London Deadline/Scott Garfitt Gentle Monster writer-director Marie Kreutzer and star Léa Seydoux took to the stage at Deadline’s Contenders London event to discuss the journey behind their Cannes drama. Seydoux plays Lucy, an experimental pianist who moves with her beloved but panic attack-liable husband Philip (Laurence Rupp) and young son to a rural farmhouse in Bavaria. Life seems swell until a special unit of big-city police led by Detective Kühn (Jella Haase) swoop in and seize one of Philip’s devices. As expected, they find and seize thousands of images of child pornography — and his double life is exposed. Catherine Deneuve plays Lucy’s mother in the feature. Related Stories News 'Project Hail Mary' DoP Greig Fraser Says The Film Was The "Most Complicated" He's Ever Shot -- Contenders London News Penélope Cruz On Working With Javier Bardem In Florian Zeller's "Bunker": "We Knew Florian Was Never Going To Manipulate Anything From Our Real Relationship" -- Contenders London The project has a striking resonance for Kreutzer. In 2022, the Austrian director released Corsage , starring Vicky Krieps and Florian Teichtmeister. The following year, Teichtmeister was arrested and pleaded guilty to possession of child pornography: 76,000 files spread over 22 devices. He received a suspended sentence, which outraged many Austrians horrified by the crime committed by a prominent cultural figure. Inevitably, Kreutzer’s film was tarnished by association and even withdrawn from some cinemas. Watch on Deadline How did that experience shape Gentle Monster ? Kreutzer explained today that she “started working on Gentle Monster in 2020, after reading an article in a German newspaper about a ring of criminals being uncovered in Germany. So when all that happened with the actor, I knew so much about the issue, and it was a very disturbing coincidence. I thought, ‘I can’t make the film anymore’, because it will always be connected to an actor, but sometime later, I realized it’s maybe more of a reason to make the film and to confront it and not run away from it.” Seydoux described why she was drawn to the film: “I loved the script. I thought it was well written and and very subtle, because the subject is obviously a tough subject, and it’s not that easy to make a film about a subject like this one. I love the fact that it was told through the woman’s perspective, and that it’s through her eyes that the the story formed. It’s not through the victim’s perspective or through the perpetrator’s perspective. I thought that was extremely interesting because I was able to to express very contradictory feelings and a large range of different emotions.” She described the revelation at the heart of the movie as “a horrible thing” that creates “an earthquake inside” her character. The actress said that among the most challenging practical aspects of the film were speaking German and the concert scenes where she has to play the piano. Kreutzer agreed that the concert scene was among the most difficult to capture: “The big concert scene was a really hard thing for for both Lea and me because she’s a very intuitive actress, which I love, and I’m a very intuitive director, and less technical. I know what I need to know, but I don’t want any marks for the actors, I want them to move freely, so don’t plan shots in millimeters. That’s not how I do it. And so when you’re shooting a scene like that, you have to do that. It was a day where I felt like it was out of my hands and I can’t really do anything and everyone’s really stressed.” Kreutzer also described a “wild day” when Seydoux, who doesn’t drive, had to drive a car in reverse with a child in the back seat. Netflix acquired the film as Cannes was wrapping up in May and opens it October 30 in limited release before it starts streaming on November 18. articles.title: Penélope Cruz On Working With Javier Bardem In Florian Zeller’s “Bunker”: “We Knew Florian Was Never Going To Manipulate Anything From Our Real Relationship” — Contenders London
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Guy Nattiv & Carrie Coon On Finding Empathy In ‘The Liberation’: “Who Are We To Say What Is Required For Someone To Move On?” — Contenders London Brad Bird Talks Long-Gestating Passion Project ‘Ray Gunn’ & Portraying “Characters Who Are Desperate” In Utopia — Contenders London Oscars: Democratic Republic Of Congo Selects ‘Rumba Royale’ For Best International Feature Film Race; The Fally Ipupa Starrer Is Country’s Second Ever Submission View All October 10, 2026 5:36am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Florian Zeller and Penélope Cruz on the panel for "Bunker" at Deadline Contenders Film: London held at the Ham Yard Hotel on October 10, 2026 in London, England. Vianney Le Caer Florian Zeller and Penélope Cruz stepped into Deadline’s Contenders event in London where the duo discussed their upcoming psychological thriller, Bunker . The film, which Zeller wrote, produced and directed, sees Cruz star as the wife of her real-life husband Javier Bardem as their characters face emotional and moral challenges in an increasingly uncertain world. Bardem plays Miguel, a successful London architect, who considers a prestigious offer to build a survivalist bunker for a tech billionaire. The project causes his wife Sofia (Cruz) to question their relationship of 17 years as they are drawn deeper into a life of extreme wealth, paranoia and fear. The intrusion of an unsettling neighbor becomes another source of anxiety. Related Stories News Guy Nattiv & Carrie Coon On Finding Empathy In 'The Liberation': "Who Are We To Say What Is Required For Someone To Move On?" -- Contenders London News Siân Heder & The 'Being Heumann' Crew On Creating An Inclusive Film & Production Environment -- Contenders London Zeller says that it was “a dream” of his to work with Bardem and Cruz. “I was interested in working with them together because I thought it would be an opportunity to explore something unique as a couple in life and also, to question what it is to be together and to explore love, to explore forgiveness in a long-term relationship through these extraordinary talents.” Watch on Deadline Cruz admitted that making the step to play a fictional couple in a feature film was a big one for her and Bardem, as the pair had made the decision “not to work together very often.” “We thought about it a little bit because, of course, the temptation was huge because we both love Florian,” said Cruz. “We love his work so much, but we always said we were not going to work together very often because it is a way to protect the relationship. I think it would be too risky to work together to often. But when we read it, and when we spoke to him, we looked at each other and really didn’t see any reason to say no. We both wanted to do it, and we knew that Florian was never going to manipulate anything or try to force anything from our real relationship into the movie.” Cruz added that a week before their “big fight” scene in the film, which was shot across three days, “things started to happen and I started to feel weird.” “Of course, it was because that scene was coming,” she said. “But I always said to myself, ‘that’s not possible, it cannot be because that scene is coming.’ We are old enough to not let that affect us, but it did affect us.” Cruz added: “But it’s just a natural process to find some truth.” Zeller noted that the fight scene, which is an almost 11-minute scene, is somewhat “the core of the film.” “It encapsulates thematically and emotionally everything the film is about. For a long period of time during the film, Penelope’s character is going through a crisis, but you don’t really know exactly what it is. Something is missing but she cannot exactly know what it is until that moment comes when she starts to become very vocal about it. So that’s a moment that is very key emotionally in the film.” Additional cast in Bunker include Stephen Graham, Paul Dano and Patrick Schwarzenegger. The French-Spanish co-production is produced by Federica Sainte-Rose and Zeller for Blue Morning Pictures, Fernando Bovaria and Simon de Santiago of MOD Producciones and Alice Dawson. Pathé’s Ardavan Safaee and Mediawan’s Pierre-Antoine Capton serve as co-producers. Check back on Monday for the panel video. articles.title: ‘Project Hail Mary’ DoP Greig Fraser Says The Film Was The “Most Complicated” He’s Ever Shot — Contenders London
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Léa Seydoux & Marie Kreutzer On The “Earthquake” At The Heart Of ‘Gentle Monster’ — Contenders London Danny Boyle On The Challenges Of Rupert Murdoch & ‘The Sun’ Film ‘Ink’: “We Had A Siege Mentality While Making It” — Contenders London Craig Ferguson & Megyn Price Starring In Addiction Dramedy Series ‘Quitters’ For Angel View All October 10, 2026 5:51am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Greig Fraser and Charles Wood at Contenders London Deadline Oscar-winning DoP Greig Fraser knows a thing or two about working on challenging movies, from Dune to The Batman , Rogue One to Zero Dark Thirty . At Deadline’s Contenders London event today, the in-demand cinematographer revealed that none were as challenging as Phil Lord and Christopher Miller’s space hit Project Hail Mary : “This was the most complicated film I’ve shot,” the Australian native disclosed. “Every day was the most complicated day,” he explained. “How do you capture a puppet without a face in a rolling circle with no gravity. Then there are stairs and steps to factor in. Everything was a challenge, but an awesome challenge.” Related Stories News Penélope Cruz On Working With Javier Bardem In Florian Zeller's "Bunker": "We Knew Florian Was Never Going To Manipulate Anything From Our Real Relationship" -- Contenders London News Guy Nattiv & Carrie Coon On Finding Empathy In 'The Liberation': "Who Are We To Say What Is Required For Someone To Move On?" -- Contenders London In the film, Ryan Gosling plays science teacher Ryland Grace “who wakes up on a spaceship light years from home with no recollection of who he is or how he got there. As his memory returns, he begins to uncover his mission: solve the riddle of the mysterious substance causing the sun to die out. He must call on his scientific knowledge and unorthodox ideas to save everything on Earth from extinction…on the journey, an unexpected friendship means he may not have to do it alone.” Watch on Deadline Sandra Hüller, Lionel Boyce, Ken Leung, Milana Vayntrub co-star in the Amazon MGM crowd-pleaser, which took $684.5M at the global box office. Fraser and the film’s production designer Charles Wood, also known for his work on blockbusters including Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the Avengers and Guardians Of The Galaxy franchise, talked about how the film was grounded in authenticity and not overly saturated in VFX. Wood explained: “A lot of the sets were eight to 10 foot in diameter. So the camera was on everything. Greg’s camera was on everything. I needed to make sure that whatever was in front of the camera really gave the audience a feeling that you were really in this ship with this man going to eternity.” Fraser added: “There was an authenticity to the rationale of how things operated. There wasn’t anything created for the sake of visual pleasure. It started in a place of honesty from a science perspective, which is how the book’s written.” That desire for authenticity included the puppetry work behind the film’s memorable alien character Rocky. Wood commented: “I didn’t realize coming onto the film that this would all be essentially live action. Working with a team of puppeteers on a set of a certain diameter was a real challenge. I wasn’t even sure how it was all going to play out, but it’s extraordinary how the puppet team did their work. It shines through in the film. You feel this creature really did exist.” Fraser said he recognized the film’s comparison with E.T. , another film celebrated for for relying on practical effects and animatronics rather than computer-generated imagery (CGI). “The times there are VFX, they’re stunningly, authentically appropriate for that particular part of the film. I think that the the directors have found that same through-line with this film. They’re used for an absolutely good reason.” As part of their research Wood described how the team met NASA astronauts and heard about their experiences, including how one was so overwhelmed by seeing the earth from space that he would cry but his tears wouldn’t fall due to gravity, meaning he often had a blurred vision of the planet from his ship. Fraser and Wood were both asked about the potential for a sequel or follow-on movie given that the book’s writer Andy Weir has spoken about writing another novel connected to the story. “That’s the first I’m hearing about it”, Fraser said. The movie is produced by Amy Pascal, Gosling, Lord, Miller, Weir, Aditya Sood and Rachel O’Connor. articles.title: Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo On Directing Rwanda’s Oscar Submission ‘Ben’Imana’: “We Need To Understand What Happened” – Contenders London
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon ‘Wildwood Director’ Travis Knight On LAIKA’s Stop-Motion Fantasy Epic: “It Took Us 16 Years To Make This Movie” – Contenders London Deadline’s Contenders Film: London Kicks Off With A Dozen Buzzy Awards-Season Movies John Leguizamo Boards Colombian Cycling Documentary ‘Cyclovia’ As EP View All October 10, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo on a panel for 'Ben'Imana’ Deadline It’s been a good year for Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo; after directing the first Rwandan feature to be accepted into the official selection by the Cannes film festival, where she was awarded the Camera d’Or, her film Ben’Imana was recently nominated as the country’s first ever Oscar submission. Set in 2012, 18 years after the genocide against the Tutsi, the film unfolds in a Rwandan village where survivors and perpetrators are grappling with the process of reconciliation. Speaking at Deadline’s Contenders London event, Dusabejambo, who was seven at the time of the genocide, revealed that she had turned to cinema after studying mathematics and physics. Several short films ensued, but the idea for Ben’Imana came after the second, in 2013. “I think it was my destiny, but it was a film that was still trying to find expression in me. I needed time to understand, to feel, to read, to hear… There’s a point in time where in every generation needs to understand what happened, where we came from, what happened, and what people decided to do in their time within their own means to be able to continue.” Related Stories News Oscars: Rwanda Makes History As 'Ben'Imana' Becomes First Official Entry; Alexander Set U.S. & UK Release News Indie Media Outfit Alexander Opens Film Arm With Kevin Chan, Hamish Moseley On Board And 'Ben'imana' Set As First Release It was important, she said, to break through the myths and preconceptions that have sprung up around the genocide. “I wanted to be more authentic to the history,” she said, “and I also wanted to not judge the people, the generation, that came before us, and what they did. I didn’t really want to fall into the stereotype of the victim and the perpetrator. All of this was about turning our lives around, making peace, being able to create a future and put a mirror to my community.” Watch on Deadline In wrapping up, Dusabejambo praised her crew and mostly non-professional cast for bringing her story so vividly to life. “I love that the film looks like a million dollars,” she said, “but [it didn’t cost] a million dollars. The million dollars comes from the love and the art and the will of the people who worked with me to tell the story… There were many times when the fictional elements of the story were meeting the reality, because it’s 100% made by Rwandans. All of us, we are connected to this story.” Check back Monday for the panel video. When he died September 14 at Desert Regional Medical Center in Palm Springs, the official cause of death was ruled as the pneumonia. articles.title: ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell And Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie And Bacall In Brad Bird’s Nifty Sci-Fi/Film Noir Mashup – London Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Animals’ Review: Ben Affleck And Kerry Washington Fight A Lot In Netflix Kidnap Thriller That Is Stretched Too Thin ‘The Social Reckoning’ Review: Jeremy Allen White And Mikey Madison Expose Facebook In Aaron Sorkin’s Stirring Journalistic Thriller Sequel ‘Artificial’ Review: Andrew Garfield Is Chilling As Sam Altman In Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI Origin Story That Should Make You Very Afraid – New York Film Festival View All October 10, 2026 6:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Ray Gunn' Skydance Animation If David Ellison wants a ticket to the Oscars this year it most likely won’t be with anything from Paramount or even (so far) from Warner Bros, but if you said Netflix you might be on the right track. Ray Gunn , from Oscar-winning filmmaker Brad Bird ( Ratatouille, The Incredibles ) , comes out of Skydance Animation ‘s original deal with the streamer, counts Ellison among its producers, and is the kind of smart, visually sumptuous and clever ‘toon that is ripe for the Best Animated Feature category. Having its world premiere Saturday at the London Film Festival, Ray Gunn is a throwback to Bogart-style film noir detective classics like The Maltese Falcon, The Big Sleep and other ’40s gems of the Dashiell Hammett, Raymond Chandler and Sam Spade mode. Throw in a little Chinatown via Jack Nicholson or Altman’s The Long Goodbye, or Robert Mitchum in Farewell My Lovely, and you get the idea, and then think elements of The Jetsons or Who Framed Roger Rabbit animated hits, marry them with Blade Runner, and then toss in a bit of Madonna in Dick Tracy, take a visit to the Star Wars bar, stir them all together and you have something approximating the world Bird has cooked up here. In other words it is a love letter to the movies past and futuristic. They call its main setting, Metropia, an “alternate future” channeling 1939, and that seems about right. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Brad Bird On The 30-Year Journey To Bring ‘Ray Gunn’ To The Big Screen — London Film Festival Culture The 30 Highest-Grossing Animated Films Of All Time At The Global Box Office No matter what the inspirations, and there were clearly many, they all come from cinema and that’s a delicious thing here. Bird, who also wrote the nifty script with Matthew Robbins, has been blessed to collect a sensational voice cast to match an intriguing bunch of characters who make up this mashup. Chief among them is Sam Rockwell ‘s Ray Gunn, an analog private dick in a digital planet.
