articles.title: Steven Spielberg Returns to ‘Transformers’ Franchise, Michael Bay in Talks to Direct for Paramount
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 6, 2026 8:30am Mark Wahlberg in 'Transformers: Age of Extinction.' Industrial Light & Magic/Paramount Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Steven Spielberg is returning to Paramount ’s cult Transformers franchise alongside longtime producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura and with Michael Bay, long a master of mayhem, in talks to possibly direct the next tentpole for fanboys of vehicles. Spielberg will focus on all creative aspects of the next live-action film based on a Hasbro line of toys. He will also executive produce the eighth live-action installment as Paramount looks to build out the Transformers universe. Bay directed the first five films in the Transformers franchise as he and his team of creators allowed the titans and other techno-creatures to clash amid action sequences spectacularly conceived and executed. Related Stories Business Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant TV 'East of Eden' Star Mike Faist on Male Ego, Love Triangles and Still Learning from Steven Spielberg Bay directed Transformers (2007), Revenge of the Fallen (2009), Dark of the Moon (2011), Age of Extinction (2014) and The Last Knight (2017). Travis Knight helmed the 2018, 1980s-set prequel Bumblebee . It’s understood Transformers headliner Shia LaBeouf will not return for the eighth installment, and there’s no word on a storyline and other possible casting. LaBeouf played a young Sam Witwicky, a teenager who bought his first car but never expected it to come to life, in the first Transformers movie, and returned for sequels. Spielberg met with Paramount Pictures co-chairs Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg in August 2025, ahead of the studio having now completed a merger with Warner Bros Discovery. Transformers 8 will be based on a script set in the modern day by Jason Fuchs, with Di Bonventura helping develop and Spielberg reading and signing off. Spielberg held creative roles for the first two Transformers films that launched the franchise and generated over $5.4 billion in global box office revenue as Hasbro’s toy brand gained a worldwide following. Di Bonaventura, Mark Vahradian, Don Murphy, Tom DeSanto and Hasbro will produce. THR

articles.title: Skydance’s $80 Billion Debt Bomb: How Will Warner Bros. and Paramount’s New Owner Make It Work?
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close On a frigid but bright December morning, David Ellison, his top legal chief Makan Delrahim and coterie of executives took over a subterranean space in the New York City office of investment bank UBS. Just a few dozen feet away, on the other side of the corporate lunch buffet of roast chicken and farro salad, UBS was hosting its Global Media and Communications Conference. Among the speakers on the agenda: Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters, fresh off their deal to buy the Warner Bros. Studio and HBO Max streaming business. Ellison was not on the line up, but he nonetheless took advantage of the location, quietly ushering investors, portfolio managers and analysts into the corner that Paramount secured, where they made their pitch clear: Netflix should not be the home for Warners. We should be. Ellison, one attendee of those meetings told The Hollywood Reporter at the time, was a “man on a mission.” Nearly a year later, Ellison’s mission is complete. In the span of less than a year and a half, he closed deals to secure two of Hollywood’s storied film studios, Paramount and Warner Bros., and brought together two of the industry’s more formidable streaming services in Paramount+ and HBO Max. Ellison, and his consolidated Hollywood giant Skydance , is now an entertainment juggernaut that rivals only Netflix and Disney for scale. Now comes the hard part. The deal is done. The WBD shareholders (and David Zaslav) have been paid, and two companies have become one. What now? The combined company now has the scale of the Netflixes and Disneys of the world, but it also has a debt load big enough ($80 billion!) that there is little room for error, and that debt will need to be serviced sooner rather than later. Services will merge, studios will merge, org structures will be set, the future of CBS News and CNN will be determined, and sports rights will be unified. Streaming prices will likely keep rising (maybe HBO becomes an add-on to Paramount+?), and, yes, more movies will be made, both existing projects like the Days of Thunder sequel and the Game of Thrones film, and new ideas yet to be born. Thousands of layoffs are expected as the companies consolidate, and Ellison and his team are set to lay out the go-forward strategy, with streaming and theatrical films top of mind. Mattel Ynon Kreiz has been tapped to lead Skydance. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images That may be why Ellison persuaded Ynon Kreiz, the CEO of Mattel, to depart the toy giant for a job as co-CEO. When Kreiz, a media veteran (he previously led Maker Studios and Endemol), joined Mattel as its CEO in early 2018, he promised a “transformation” of the company. Just a few months later, he launched an expansive overhaul, slashing 22 percent of its workforce and restructuring it for a tech-forward future. At Paramount, insiders expect him to operate with similar speed, with Ellison and his investors targeting $6 billion in synergies. Kreiz will be the one to lead that effort. “We will embrace the opportunities AI provides to expand what our creatives can imagine and to make our businesses even more productive,” Kreiz and Ellison wrote in a companywide email to staff titled “ Day 1, ” outlining priorities. “The opportunities ahead are enormous, and we intend to seize them. But one principle will never change: technology must serve the art – never the other way around.” RedBird investor Gerry Cardinale will be instrumental in navigating what’s next at Skydance. Giuseppe Maffia/NurPhoto via Getty Images Gerry Cardinale, the founder of RedBird Capital and Ellison’s operating partner in the deal, told a conference last week that the “notion that $6 billion of cost-related synergies means you’re firing all these people is just completely antiquated.” Cardinale insists that much of the cost savings can come from things like combining tech stacks, more efficient marketing spend, and simplifying the vendors it works with.And in their joint letter, Ellison and Kreiz wrote about going “further than traditional synergies. By embracing the most advanced technologies available and embedding them into how we operate, we will work smarter, move faster and unlock efficiencies the merger alone could not deliver.” But everyone knows that significant layoffs are coming as the two companies combine. Paramount, after all, cut about 10 percent of its workforce in 2025 in conjunction with the Skydance deal. “Wake up Hollywood, you’re going to need to rationalize costs,” one industry veteran familiar with leadership’s thinking said. “That’s not a bad thing. That’s called Darwinian evolution.” The real estate footprint of the company will shrink (though the two L.A. studio lots are safe), particularly in New York, where it will have Paramount’s Times Square HQ, the CBS Broadcast Center and Ed Sullivan Theater as well as WBD’s Union Square HQ (home of the Food Network Test Kitchen) as well as CNN’s newsroom and studios in Hudson Yards. According to Bank of America analyst Jessica Reif Ehrlich, the promised savings would “provide a meaningful tailwind to profitability, free cash flow generation and deleveraging over time. “However, history suggests realizing synergies of this magnitude in media is rarely linear, and we anticipate the benefits to be offset by integration costs, execution risk and elevated leverage in the near term,” she continued in a Sep. 24 note. Still, it is likely the only path forward for Skydance. “There’s a virtue to consolidation here, because that is the only way you’re going to level the playing field, and it’s the only way Hollywood is going to put themselves in a position where it balances out the balance of power,” the industry veteran adds, noting the technological disintermediation that threatens Hollywood. “Don’t forget, AI is only valuable with the data that feeds it.” It is also why one of Ellison’s first orders of business was securing the talent of Casey Bloys, the HBO Max chief who will run streaming for the combined company. Going forward, streaming will be the economic engine of the company, and Bloys, who not only shepherded HBO but managed to expand the brand in populist directions via shows like The Pitt and The Penguin , is being given wide leeway to bring that ethos to the combined service. It is an approach that will only become more important once Taylor Sheridan decamps for NBCUniversal in a couple years. An executive at a competing media company said that, among all the executives at Warners, Bloys was the one that they “had to keep.” “If he left, I’m not sure they could have kept HBO intact,” they added. The brand would have existed, of course, but the connective tissue would have been broken. With Pamela Abdy and Mike De Luca on the way out (but James Gunn and Peter Safran still in), the studios will need to stabilize under their new Paramount leadership of Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg. After all, Ellison has promised to release at least 32 movies per year beginning in 2029, and to produce some 170 TV shows. DC, meanwhile, appears to be elevated in the new world order, no longer having to be subservient to the larger WB brand. Skydance’s news leaders: Mark Thompson will continue running CNN while Bari Weiss leads CBS News. And CBS News and CNN remain a particularly hot-button topic, given the chaos that has enveloped CBS since Ellison appointed Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief. Ellison is said to genuinely admire Weiss and her vision, which is premised on appealing to a silent majority of Americans who are not far left or far right, and being somewhat contrarian or against the grain. “She operates with the idea that if every other place is taking one approach or angle to a story, there might be room to do something different, even if the underlying facts are the facts,” one TV news veteran said. But it is far from obvious that she will get any oversight over CNN, in fact one executive at a competing news operation said that it would be “crazy” to do so. That is why the official news that Thompson had inked a deal to remain chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN such a relief to veterans of the news brand. The issue is that, while CBS News is seen as a breakeven or barely profitable endeavor, one primarily about brand-building, CNN is an actual profit center. CNN is projected to have $1.8 billion in revenue in 2026, according to disclosures from Warner Bros. Discovery, rising to $1.9 billion in 2027, $2 billion in 2028 and $2.2 billion by 2030. CNN’s adjusted EBITDA in 2026 is estimated to be about $600 million, before falling to $500 million in 2027 and remaining flat at $600 million through 2030. While CNN’s revenue is relatively modest compared to the rest of the WBD cable portfolio ($9.9 billion in 2026) its EBITDA is strong, with every other channel in its portfolio combining for $3.8 billion and expected to fall to $1.9 billion through 2030. CNN, by contrast, is expected to be flat in EBITDA in that same period. But there will be challenges. Given the debt load, the combined company will need to keep those profits flowing, and combining CBS News and CNN is seen as an obvious source of cost savings, but it is not clear how that can happen with both Weiss and Thompson in the building. And all eyes will be on CNN’s editorial independence board: Who will be on it, what power they will have, and if it salves concerns from viewers and politicos. George Cheeks will become, for all intents and purposes, the most powerful executive in linear TV. His purview will include CBS, and more cable channels than any other company by far, spanning sports, entertainment, news and more. But most observers recognize that those channels will be milked for cash, with wide cuts expected as the company seeks to harvest the revenue from carriage fees and redistribute to other priorities, like streaming, and paying down that pesky debt. CBS Sports will become a juggernaut, with the NFL, all of March Madness, college football, MLB, NHL, UFC, The Masters, international soccer rights and much more. JB Perrette, a WBD holdover, will be responsible for the business of TV and streaming, letting Bloys and Cheeks cook on content, balancing declining linear TV and growing streaming. And the company will also have what an executive at a competitor called a “secret weapon”: Warner Bros. Games. The game studio is the home of Mortal Kombat , and has produced hit games based on IP like Batman , Harry Potter and Game of Thrones . Earlier this year Ellison launched a new gaming studio within Paramount, and the combined game studio will be formidable, with a vast library of IP to mine (including from outside partners like Disney, which has worked with both studios). While all eyes will be on the film and TV output, the competing executive speculated that the game studio could become a bigger part of the business than Hollywood expects. Still, as Morgan Stanley’s Sean Diffley noted Sep. 22, this is ultimately about creating an intellectual property behemoth that only has one true rival in Disney (Netflix and YouTube are streaming giants, but not IP giants). “While in many ways the hard part begins now (and we are fully sympathetic to the complexity of integrating large media assets), the risk of not getting the asset was significantly greater and we believe scale and IP are important in an ever increasingly fragmented media ecosystem,” Diffley wrote. But first, they have that $80 billion in debt to reduce. House of brands: All of the studios, channels and assets in the combined Skydance empire. THR

articles.title: How David Ellison Won the Battle: Timeline of Paramount’s Rocky Road to Acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery
articles.full_text: Breaking News Paramount-Warner Bros. $111 Billion Merger Officially Closes Illustration: Variety; Elements: Getty Images It’s been a hell of a ride. David Ellison’s quest to control two iconic Hollywood studios has finally been completed — added a rollicking new chapter to the storied recent history of Hollywood megamergers. On the morning of Tuesday, Oct. 6, the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger officially closed . The new company, Skydance Corp., brings together film and TV assets into one big company, which is weighed down by some $80 billion in debt . The storyline’s arc features appearances by such colorful subjects as President Donald Trump, 12 blue-state attorneys general, Netflix, Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds, the Block the Merger coalition, Mark Ruffalo, David Zaslav and so much more. Here’s a timeline of how it all happened. Related Stories MasterClass Launches Podcast ‘Other People’s Business' With Martha Stewart as First Guest Skydance's High-Wire Act Begins: Wall Street Scrutinizes Strategy for Juggling $80 Billion in Debt and a Three-Year Runway to Chop It Down 2025 Aug. 7, 2025: Skydance Media completes its $8 billion acquisition of Paramount Global after a tumultuous yearlong closing process. Popular on Variety David Zaslav, CEO and President of Warner Bros. Discovery Getty Images September 2025: First rumblings surface of David Ellison’s overtures to David Zaslav and the Warner Bros. Discovery board of directors Oct. 21, 2025: Warner Bros. Discovery formally initiates sale process “in light of unsolicited interest” the company has received from “multiple parties.” November 2025: Netflix, Comcast and Skydance Media submit offers for all or portions of Warner Bros. Discovery. Getty Images Dec. 5, 2025: Netflix wins the auction process as Warner Bros. Discovery announces it has set an $82.7 billion cash and stock acquisition agreement to sell Warner Bros. and HBO (but not CNN, TNT and other cable channels) to the streaming giant. Dec. 8, 2025: Paramount Skydance ups the ante, launching a tender offer for Warner Bros. Discovery shares and a campaign to convince WBD shareholders to back its bid. “Our proposal is superior to Netflix’s in every dimension,” David Ellison tells Wall Street analysts on a conference call. Dec. 17, 2025: Warner Bros. Discovery board unanimously recommends shareholders reject Paramount’s tender offer. Dec. 22, 2025: Warner Bros. Discovery receives amended tender offer from Paramount 2026 Jan. 7: WBD board unanimously recommends shareholders reject latest Paramount tender offer. Jan. 20: Netflix agrees to revise its deal to acquire Warner Bros. and HBO to all cash, in a bid to counter the pressure from Paramount’s repeated offers. Feb. 10: Paramount adds a “ticking fee” to its offer that promises to pay WBD shareholders $650 million per quarter that the transaction is not closed after Dec. 31, 2026. Feb. 17: WBD sets March 20 for special meeting of shareholders to vote on Netflix transaction. At the same time, WBD opens a 10-day negotiating window with Paramount to address the latest offer. Feb. 24: WBD confirms receipt of a new offer from Paramount Skydance. Later that day WBD issues a statement acknowledging that it could “reasonably be expected to lead to a ‘Company Superior Proposal’” as spelled out in its Netflix sale agreement. Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos Getty Images Feb. 26: Netflix formally bows out of the WBD chase, declining to match the higher Paramount offer. “The deal is no longer financially attractive,” Netflix told investors. Rob Bonta, California’s Attorney General, gives the first indication of the antitrust suit to come by promising to begin a “vigorous review” of the transaction. Feb. 27: Paramount formally seals its $110 billion all-cash agreement to acquire all of Warner Bros. Discovery. The final terms amend the ticking fee to kick in as of Oct. 1. April 13: A group of 1,000 industry creatives sign the open letter calling on officials to “Block the Merger,” including Ben Stiller, Kristen Stewart, Joaquin Phoenix, Adam McKay, Alan Cumming, Alyssa Milano, Boots Riley, Bryan Cranston, Cynthia Nixon, Damon Lindelof, David Fincher and Denis Villeneuve. Ten days later it had 4,000 signatures. April 16: AMC Theatres CEO Adam Aron endorses the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger on the cusp of the CinemaCon gathering in Las Vegas. April 23: WBD shareholders vote to approve the sale to Paramount. Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman and Chairman of the Saudi Public Investment Fund, an investor in the combined Warner Bros. and Paramount Studios Getty Images April 27: Paramount discloses in a regulatory filing that about 38.5% of the equity in the new company will be held by the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. June 12: The Justice Department closes its investigation into the merger, without imposing any conditions or divestitures. California Attorney General Rob Bonta Getty Images July 13: Twelve state attorneys general — including California’s Rob Bonta and New York’s Leticia James — file suit to block the Paramount-WBD transaction on antitrust grounds. July 14: The Writers Guild of America sues to block the merger on antitrust grounds. July 20: A federal judge puts a 14-day hold on the merger as the states seek a temporary injunction. July 22: European Commission approves the transaction. The SAG-AFTRA building in Los Angeles Variety via Getty Images July 27: SAG-AFTRA issues a statement against the merger, calling for it to be blocked unless “enforceable safeguards” are implemented. July 29: Regal Cinemas CEO Eduardo Acuna announces its support of merger July 31: Paramount asks for a November start date for the states’ antitrust trial. The states and the WGA seek an April 2027 start date. Aug. 4: Judge sets March 2, 2027, as the start date for states’ antitrust trial. Getty Images Aug. 5: David Ellison tells senior Paramount execs that he will move the company out of California as of Oct. 1 if the state AGs don’t drop their antitrust lawsuit aimed at blocking the merger. Aug. 6: Paramount secures approval from U.K. Competition and Markets Authority. Aug. 12: The Directors Guild of America and IATSE sent a letter to California attorney general Rob Bonta and David Ellison calling on them to reach a settlement or jointly push for a faster timeline for the trial, for the sake of both studios. The letter outlines 10 conditions that could help alleviate antitrust concerns. Aug. 14: Mexico clears the transaction. Aug. 17: Paramount asks the court to order the states to put up a $1.88 billion bond to cover the costs of the ticking fee it will owe Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders if Paramount prevails in the lawsuit. Aug. 18: Cinemark exhibition chain announces its support for the merger. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass Variety via Getty Images Aug. 20: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass urges Rob Bonta to settle with Paramount. Aug. 21: David Ellison holds private meeting with state AGs to agree on date for settlement talks. Aug. 23: Rob Bonta cancels planned Aug. 24 meeting for settlement talks after word of the meeting leaks to media outlets. Sept. 11: Paramount argues in a motion that the states’ case is “a series of attempted shortcuts and assumptions that collapse under scrutiny.” Jessica J. articles.title: France Boosts Oscar Campaign Support as Industry Sounds Alarm Over Declining Exports
articles.full_text: Breaking News Paramount-Warner Bros. $111 Billion Merger Officially Closes Oct 6, 2026 7:17am PT France Boosts Oscar Campaign Support as Industry Sounds Alarm Over Declining Exports By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest France Boosts Oscar Campaign Support as Industry Sounds Alarm Over Declining Exports 1 hour ago Dominga Sotomayor’s Cannes’ Directors Fortnight Film ‘La Perra’ Sells Internationally 1 day ago France’s Canal+ Threatens to Pull $1.1 Billion Cinema Deal Over French Tax Hike 1 day ago See All Courtesy of MK2 Films France’s National Film Board ( CNC ) has rolled out a new strategy to boost the profile of French movies and talent navigating the Oscar race. Unveiled during a conference on film and TV exports held at the CNC on Monday, the new strategy will see the government-backed organization double the financial aid granted to campaigns. The CNC has also appointed Sébastien Cauchon as its “Academy Awards” liaison. Under this newly created role, Cauchon will spearhead the campaign for “Minotaur.” Related Stories Judge Questions Legal Points of Paramount's Settlement With States at Hearing, Says a Ruling Will Come in 'Due Course' Block the Merger Coalition Files Legal Request to Oppose Paramount-Warner Bros. Deal France has not won the international feature prize since Régis Wargnier’s “Indochine” took the honor in 1993, despite boasting a record 43 nominations, more than any other country. Popular on Variety The exec, who recently founded the Paris-based consultancy Cinema Collectors, comes into the role fresh off the Oscar-winning campaign for Natalie Musteata and Alexandre Singh’s “Two People Exchanging Saliva.” His other awards work includes serving as a consultant and international publicist on Mubi’s campaign for Coralie Fargeat’s “The Substance,” as well as a longstanding collaboration with Florian Zeller that included “The Father,” which won two Oscars. Speaking at Monday’s conference, Cauchon said France has been relatively slow to embrace the kind of specialized awards strategy. “An awards strategist is a profession that isn’t very widespread in France, or even in Europe,” Cauchon said, describing the job as combining publicity, marketing and influence to make sure films and talent are seen by Academy members and stay on voters’ radar throughout the race. For the CNC, the broader goal is also to move beyond France’s traditional focus on the international feature category and better coordinate campaigns across directing, acting, screenplay and craft categories. “In France, we sometimes focus a lot on the best international film category,” Cauchon said. “But we have such a diversity of productions and talent that we’re represented much more broadly across all the categories.” Case in point, many French movies that thrived in the awards season in recent years, from Coralie Fargeat’s “The Substance” to Florian Zeller’s “The Father,” Gints Zilbalodis’s “Flow,” and Justine Triet’s “Anatomy of a Fall,” did not represent France in the Oscar race. This year, Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Cannes Grand Prize winner “Minotaur” (Mubi) will represent France, but other films that were shortlisted by the French committee could turn up in nominations, notably Marine Atlan’s Cannes Critics Week winner “La Gradiva” (1 2 Special), Louis Clichy’s animated feature “Iron Boy” (SPC) which won a prize at Cannes’ Un Certain Regard, and Antonin Baudry’s “De Gaulle” (Samuel Goldwyn Films). There’s also Lea Seydoux with two movies, “The Unknown” by Arthur Harari (Neon), and “Gentle Monster” by Marie Kreutzer (Netflix). The CNC’s new approach will aim at pooling resources earlier in the process and working alongside U.S. distributors. That tension between France’s cultural standing and the increasingly competitive global marketplace ran through Monday’s conference, where French film and TV figures warned that the country’s international position can no longer be taken for granted. Figures compiled by the CNC and unveiled last month during Unifrance ‘s event in Le Havre showed that international sales of French audiovisual programs dropped 21.6% to €164.3 million ($190.8 million) — the lowest level in a decade. CNC president Gaëtan Bruel pointed out France still remained in 2025 the third most represented country after the U.S. and U.K. in terms of content broadcast on linear TV worldwide, but the country has so far failed to achieve the same level of success on streaming platforms. “We’ve spent years, rightly, celebrating the fact that we fill the top 100 fiction rankings on television, without seeing that we were losing the streaming battle,” Bruel said. He noted the contrasting performances of countries such as Spain and South Korea, where local programming commands a much larger share of streaming consumption. “To put it clearly, Spanish Netflix subscribers watch Spanish series first, ahead of American ones,” Bruel said. “French subscribers watch American series first, and then more Spanish and Korean series than French ones.” Speaking of Korea and Spain, he said there were “smaller markets that were forced to think internationally from the outset because their domestic industries could not sustain production on their own.” France, on the other hand, has relied on its own market for a long time thanks to its “unusually robust internal system of financing, production and distribution.” “That’s an immense strength and there is obviously no question of abandoning it. But I think that strength explains why we have had less need than others to think internationally from the very beginning of projects. That is what now has to evolve, because the world has changed,” Bruel said. UniFrance president Gilles Pélisson similarly warned that the rise of tech giants, streaming platforms and AI had fundamentally reshaped the balance of power facing European content producers. “The tech giants, which are now publishers — more or less, depending on the company — are taking power,” Pélisson said. “And all of this is happening in the context of the evolution of AI, which is impacting absolutely every sector.” Pélisson, who works alongside Unifrance’s well-respected managing director Daniel Elstner, called for France to revamp export support schemes, including funds for film, television and shorts, on top of assistance for foreign distributors who release French movies. “We have to think more broadly than our French territory,” he said. “Foreign distributors are obviously allies. How do we continue supporting them? We probably need to think about creating new forms of support.” For Pélisson, one of the industry’s most pressing battles is over data. Streamers’ reluctance to share detailed viewing data, he argued, is directly tied to the economic value of the works they carry. “Data today is the underlying key to the value of works. And that’s why, strangely enough, the platforms have so much difficulty sharing data. Of course they do — it’s exactly what determines the value of our works and the value of your works.” French sales agents, meanwhile, said France already boasts one of the strongest networks of international sellers in the world who are handling major non-French festival titles, for instance MK2 Films with “Minotaur,” Goodfellas with “La Bola Negra” and “Fjord,” and Charades with “Club Kid.” “We have in France the best, densest and most effective export network. Producers from all over the world come to France to have their films sold,” said Pierre Mazars, co-founder of Charades which sold “Club Kid” to A24 at Cannes, among other films. Yet, Mazars, who also co-presides over the French exporters association ADEF, warned that those companies need to be incentivized to take risks on French movies. “The reality, and we have to say it, is that for exporters it is often more attractive within the ecosystem to sell a foreign film than a French film. The system isn’t sufficiently incentivizing for us to sell French films,” Mazars. French sellers, he said, are increasingly being asked to put up sizable minimum guarantees while international competitors, such as in the U.K., are introducing schemes aimed at reducing those risks. Mazars also called on France to explore ways of attracting private equity into film financing, citing MK2’s partnership with IPR.VC, a Helsinki and London-based fund manager, as one possible model. “I think there is work to be done between exporters, the CNC and perhaps Bpifrance to bring private equity funds into French cinema. We all know the difficulties producers have financing their films,“ he said. Clara Flageollet Schmit, sales manager at SND and ADEF’s co-president, said the role of international sales agents themselves has changed dramatically as they take on more financial exposure at ever earlier stages of production. “We’re no longer simply intermediaries. Today we’re real financiers of cinema, and particularly French cinema. We’re getting involved earlier and earlier in projects, sometimes from the development stage,” she said. “We also participate in casting, and we’re putting up increasingly substantial minimum guarantees, often on first and second films.” While preliminary UniFrance figures suggest French films should reach around 42.5 million admissions and €272 million in international box office revenue in 2025, Flageollet Schmit said the sector remains roughly 26% below pre-pandemic levels while the cost of doing business has soared. “It’s becoming increasingly complicated to accompany films abroad, particularly French films, where we’re investing more and more,” she said. “Supporting risk means supporting investment, and supporting investment means supporting international growth.” New York Knicks’ Jalen Brunson Steams His Jersey in Emmys Opening With Super Fan Mariska Hargitay Anne Hathaway Would Rather Have Another Knicks Championship Over a Second Oscar Jeremy Irons, Keke Palmer, Regina Hall and More Attached to Projects Launching at Toronto Market Here’s Where to Buy New York Knicks Home Opener Tickets at Madison Square Garden Online Jay-Z Brings Out Lauryn Hill and Wyclef at ‘Jay-Z30’ London Concert Jay-Z Brings Justin Timberlake Onstage in Paris Loading comments...

articles.title: Paul Mescal Boards Irish Psychological Thriller ‘Mary Is Missing’ as Exec Producer (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Breaking News Paramount-Warner Bros. $111 Billion Merger Officially Closes Oct 6, 2026 7:46am PT Paul Mescal Boards Irish Psychological Thriller ‘Mary Is Missing’ as Exec Producer (EXCLUSIVE) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Paul Mescal Boards Irish Psychological Thriller ‘Mary Is Missing’ as Exec Producer (EXCLUSIVE) 44 minutes ago London Film Festival Director on Why the Event Has Become Awards Season’s Unofficial Starter Gun: ‘The Whole World Is Here’ 2 hours ago Hammer Films Boss John Gore on Resurrecting the British Horror Icon, Plans to Remake the Classics and Why Christopher Lee Was the ‘Greatest Dracula’ 23 hours ago See All Credit: Christian Tierney Alongside playing Paul McCartney in The Beatles films and juggling the occasional Bond rumor, Paul Mescal has lent his support to a short film from his home town. The Oscar nominee has become exec producer on the Oscar-qualifying short “Mary Is Missing,” an Irish psychological thriller directed by Aisling Byrne and produced by Killian Coyle for Run of the Mill and Arcade Film and created through a collaborative writers’ room with learning-disabled artists. The film was made in Maynooth, where Mescal grew up. Related Stories Jon Stewart’s ‘Daily Show’ Skips David Ellison-Skydance News to Take on AI ‘Coven Academy’ Star Malina Weissman Unpacks Briar’s Backstory, Her Take on the Love Triangle and Her Hopes for Season 2 “There are films that remind you just how exciting cinema can be when it opens itself up to new voices. For me, ‘Mary is Missing ‘is one of those films. It’s bold, surprising and unlike anything else I’ve seen, and what stayed with me most when I first saw it was the collaborative spirit behind it,” said Mescal. “The film has been shaped through the imagination and lived experience of artists with intellectual disabilities, and that originality is there in every frame. Knowing it was created in Maynooth, where I grew up, makes it feel especially close to home.” Popular on Variety Mescal added that in coming on board as executive producer, he wanted to help bring the film to the “widest possible audience and championing such a distinctive piece of Irish filmmaking.” “Mary is Missing” follows care worker Mary, who vanishes without a trace from the Yellow Tree Day Service. When Garda Foley arrives to investigate, the attendees who were among the last people to see Mary become key witnesses. But as their accounts begin to contradict one another and take increasingly fantastical turns, Foley must determine whether they are telling the truth, protecting Mary, protecting themselves, or whether the reality is something far more complicated. The film’s ensemble includes Mark Smith, alongside Derek McSweeney, Eoghan Ashe, Ella-Jane Moore, Jackie O’Hagan, John Egan, Keith Foley, Maurice Coll, Neil Coffey, Teresa Flood, Wesley Fairbrother, Lucy Smith and Conor Begley. Lloyd Cooney plays Garda Foley, alongside care workers Lauren Larkin and Craig Connolly, with Danny O’Connor, Clare Monnelly and Kamilla Fenger also featuring. Thirteen of the 19 cast members are artists with intellectual disabilities, with the story developed through a 12-week writers’ room hosted by Run of the Mill. The ensemble contributed ideas around characters, themes and storytelling. For Byrne and Coyle, “Mary is Missing” marks their third Oscar-qualifying short as a filmmaking team, following “Headspace” and “Turnaround.” “Headspace” won the Grand Prix Irish Short at the Cork International Film Festival and became Ireland’s short film candidate for the 2023 European Film Awards, while “Turnaround” won qualifying awards at both Galway Film Fleadh and Foyle Film Festival. Byrne’s subsequent short “Misread,” an RTÉ/Ardan commission, won Best Irish Short at Catalyst International Film Festival, while “Turnaround” was nominated for an IFTA and later acquired by Disney+. Byrne, Coyle and Arcade Film are currently developing her debut feature, which is among the final 10 projects selected for Screen Ireland’s Perspectives scheme. articles.title: Music Industry Moves: Thomas Rhett Strikes Label Partnership With Hybe’s Blue Highway Records
articles.full_text: Breaking News Paramount-Warner Bros. $111 Billion Merger Officially Closes Oct 6, 2026 8:00am PT Music Industry Moves: Thomas Rhett Strikes Label Partnership With Hybe’s Blue Highway Records By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Music Industry Moves: Thomas Rhett Strikes Label Partnership With Hybe’s Blue Highway Records 33 minutes ago A$AP Rocky Announces Four-Year Full-Tuition Roc Nation School Scholarship 3 hours ago ‘Bowie80’ to Celebrate David Bowie’s 80th Birthday With Events, Exhibits, Releases and More Throughout 2027 1 day ago See All Country star T homas Rhett and Hybe Americas’ Nashville-based label Blue Highway Records have announced a new partnership, Fifty-One/Forty-Nine Records . Described as “artist-led,” the partnership offers “an innovative approach to the artist-label relationship,” according to the announcement. following more than a decade of shared success. (Pictured above, L-R: Blue Highway CEO Jake Basden, Rhett and G Major Mgmt’s Virginia Bunetta.) “When we started talking about what the next chapter could look like, I knew I didn’t simply want to make another deal. I wanted to build something that reflected the legacy and shaped the future of my music,” Rhett said. “From my initial conversations with Jake and the leadership team at Blue Highway, it was clear they, too, were thinking differently about what a record company can be for an artist today. This allows me the opportunity to own the body of work I’ve spent my entire career creating, while still having an ambitious team and global infrastructure around me for my future recordings.” Popular on Variety Related Stories Skydance to Fully Reorganize International; Kevin MacLellan Will Not Lead Key Group Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ to Compete as Comedy at Golden Globes (EXCLUSIVE) Blue Highway CEO Jake Basden said, “ Thomas Rhett has always been an artist, a songwriter, a performer who brings the best of what being a progressive country artist is today: someone who is willing to explore how other genres merge with Nashville without losing his roots, without sounding calculated or forced. Having watched Thomas Rhett come into his own and then achieve major success, I am honored to be his partner going forward.” + Grammy and Latin Grammy-winning Puerto Rican rapper-producer Wisin has signed with WME for representation in all areas. The move comes a month after the September launch of “La Universidad del Perreo,” his new 12-track album and six months after his guest appearance with Karol G at Coachella. Over the years he has also collaborated with Daddy Yankee, Jennifer Lopez, Pitbull, J Balvin, Ricky Martin, Maluma, Rosalía, and more. Wisin is managed by Chris Duque of D27 Entertainment. + Willard Ahdritz , founder of Kobalt Music Group, has launched Ahdritz Capital Partners , a music and media technology investment firm, and announced that Isabel Keulen , most recently CEO of SSE Ventures and SSE Business, has joined as an investment partner, based in Stockholm and working in association with the New York-based Ahdritz and investment partner Stephen Langer . Ahdritz founded Kobalt in 2000 and led it for more than two decades as CEO and then chairman, building one of the largest independent music companies in the world. He also co-founded the digital collection society AMRA. Ahdritz stepped down from Kobalt when it was acquired by Primary Wave in July 2026. “Music is global, yet the capital and networks founders need have been concentrated in a few cities,” said Ahdritz. “We want to support founders and innovation not only in those markets, but also in other parts of the world too.” + Artist House , the independent label-publisher-management-studio company founded by Grammy-winning songwriter-producer Gregg Wattenberg and Steve Lerner, has named Jim Cooperman chief operating officer. He will oversee business and legal affairs, operations and publishing for the New York-based music company. Cooperman joins after 14 years at Madison Square Garden Entertainment, where he served as SVP and associate general counsel of legal and business affairs and played a key role in structuring deals for events at Sphere in Las Vegas, including residencies by U2, Phish, Dead & Company and the Eagles. Previously, he held senior roles at Wind-up Entertainment, BMG, RED, Relativity, Loud and RCA Records. “I’ve had the privilege of working alongside Jim over the years, and I’m thrilled that he has joined the Artist House team,” said Lerner. “We’ve created something meaningful in a remarkably short time, and Jim’s talent, experience, and integrity will be an important part of our continued growth.” + Los Angeles-based band Lo Moon has signed with [PIAS] and will release their first single for the label on Wednesday, “Satellite.” The track was written by frontman Matt Lowell and produced by Alex Farrar (MJ Lenderman, Hotline TNT, Wednesday); the band recently completed dates supporting the War on Drugs. + Floating Leaf Entertainment , the artist management company founded by Jeb Hurt based in Austin, Texas, has joined Red Light Management , bringing its roster — including multi-platinum artist Koe Wetzel, Kolby Cooper, Fox & Vead and others — into the management company founded by Coran Capshaw. “This is about taking what we’ve built at Floating Leaf and giving it an even bigger runway,” said Hurt. “We’ve always been incredibly focused on the artist — who they are, what makes them different and how we can help build a career around that. Red Light has an incredible history of doing the same thing at a global level.” “Jeb has built something special at Floating Leaf,” said Ben Kline of Red Light Management. “He has an incredible instinct for artists and has earned the kind of trust that you can’t manufacture. Koe, Kolby, Fox & Vead and the rest of the roster are a reflection of that.” + The Beggars Group of Labels (4AD, Matador Records, Rough Trade Records, XL Recordings and Young) has added four new staff members and a brand-new department: Max Datner, Ariana Mamnoon, Rrita Hashani and Molly McGuffin . Datner and Mamnoon will comprise the radio and music discovery department, while Hashani and McGuffin join the marketing team. The announcement reads, “As phrases like ‘marketing’ and ‘radio’ have evolved over the last couple of years, we have found it beneficial to redefine what those kinds of roles mean for us in today’s music industry. As we embark on massive album campaigns for Queens of the Stone Age, Erykah Badu, Fontaines D.C., Julia Jacklin and more, this is the perfect time to expand with new roles that dedicated to identifying modern and creative ways to champion both established and new artists.” + Warner Music Group has announced an expansion of its Middle East and North Africa (MENA) leadership: Ahmed Nureni has been promoted to Managing Director, MENA, reporting to President of EMEA, Recorded Music, Guillermo Gonzalez; while Ahmad Alghawanmeh joins the company as General Manager, MENA, reporting directly to Nureni. Nureni will oversee Warner Music’s MENA’s overarching vision, corporate development, strategic joint ventures, and catalog expansion across all markets. Alghawanmeh joins WMG from Sony Music Entertainment and will lead commercial growth, business development, market expansion initiatives, and multi-territory operational delivery for the region. Gonzalez said, “MENA continues to be one of the fastest-growing music markets in the world, and Warner Music is committed to staying at the forefront of that momentum. Ahmed has done an outstanding job building our presence in the region over the last several years, and will develop this further in his new role, while, in Ahmad we are adding an executive with sharp commercial instincts, deep regional relationships, and a proven track record in digital strategy.” + Activist Artists Management has announced the addition of Chelsea Fodero and Mak Symmonds as Artist Managers. articles.title: Skydance CEOs Acknowledge Layoffs Will Be Coming After Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger: Read the Full Memo
articles.full_text: Breaking News Paramount-Warner Bros. $111 Billion Merger Officially Closes Oct 6, 2026 8:32am PT Skydance CEOs Acknowledge Layoffs Will Be Coming After Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger: Read the Full Memo David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz say there will be 'difficult decisions that affect our workforce' By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Skydance CEOs Acknowledge Layoffs Will Be Coming After Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger: Read the Full Memo 16 minutes ago Paramount-Warner Bros. $111 Billion Merger Officially Closes: ‘Today Is a Historic Day, Not Just for Skydance but for Our Entire Industry,’ David Ellison Says 3 hours ago David Zaslav Bids Farewell to Warner Bros. Employees in Video on Eve of Skydance Merger Close: ‘It’s Been a Great Honor to Be Alongside All of You’ 20 hours ago See All Getty Images Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery have officially merged into Skydance Corp. And the top leaders have notified the new company’s staffers that layoffs are in the offing. David Ellison , chairman and CEO, and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz (formerly chief exec of Mattel) sent a memo to employees at the combined company Tuesday morning around 9:40 a.m. ET after the deal closed outlining the operating philosophy of Skydance — and its goals in the years ahead. Related Stories Casey Bloys Poised to Run HBO and Paramount+ as Cindy Holland Confirms Her Exit From Studio on Eve of Merger Closing Paramount, Warner Bros. Insiders Were Stunned by the Settlement With State AGs. Now They're Girding for Inevitable Mass Layoffs The duo acknowledged that layoffs will be part of the process in the memo, a copy of which was obtained by Variety . “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce,” the execs wrote. “We are committed to handling this process thoughtfully and respectfully.” Popular on Variety Paramount execs have said they are shooting to achieve more than $6 billion in annualized cost savings over three years — and part of that will come from layoffs. The company has not revealed at this point the extent of the job cuts it expects. According to a report issued by Los Angeles County in August, the merger could result in the loss of some 4,500 film and TV jobs over three years in L.A. alone. However, overall, Ellison and Kreiz sounded an upbeat note, telling the troops that together they will “build the next-generation media and entertainment company, powered by creativity and technology. The goal was never simply to add more production capacity, brands or IP. It was to unite the talent, resources and capabilities of these companies into a stronger competitor, one with the scale to take on the biggest players in our industry.” “Together, we will give these iconic studios the opportunity to win for generations to come,” the execs wrote in the 1,705-word memo, which has the subject line “Day 1.” Here’s the full memo: Team, Today we begin an exciting new chapter as Skydance. Getting here has been quite a journey. Over the past year and beyond, it has taken hard work, perseverance and commitment with many challenges along the way – but we did it! To everyone at both companies who helped get us to this moment: thank you. Thank you for your patience, your resilience and, above all, your belief in what we could accomplish together. Bringing Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery together fulfills a vision that began with Skydance’s acquisition of Paramount: to build the next-generation media and entertainment company, powered by creativity and technology. The goal was never simply to add more production capacity, brands or IP. It was to unite the talent, resources and capabilities of these companies into a stronger competitor, one with the scale to take on the biggest players in our industry. Together, we will give these iconic studios the opportunity to win for generations to come. Built for What’s Ahead As all of you know, our industry is in a period of profound change. Audiences have more choices than ever, technology is reshaping how stories are created, distributed and experienced, and competition for people’s time and attention has never been greater. We don’t just want to succeed in this environment – we want to win and help shape the future of the industry. We want to lead. And that starts with what we’re building together: a company that tells great stories in every genre, for audiences everywhere, on every platform. A company that can compete in a crowded market and win at global scale, create enduring value for all stakeholders, and strengthen the industry as a whole. As owner-operators, we’re in this for the long term, committed to building Skydance for the future – not simply optimizing for the next quarter or the next year, but creating a company built to endure, evolve and remain relevant. That means being creative-first, audience-focused, tech-forward and globally scaled – building a thriving ecosystem where stories and worlds are imagined, brought to life and experienced by audiences of all ages, everywhere. At the center of it all is a clear purpose: to entertain, inspire and inform the world through extraordinary storytelling. And we’ll be guided every step of the way by shared priorities that shape how we intend to operate, how we make decisions, how we work together and how we show up for our audiences, our partners and one another. Our Top Priorities To bring that mission to life, these are the priority areas where we will concentrate our energy: Win in Storytelling Great stories remain at the heart of everything we do. We will invest in the ideas, creators, franchises and experiences that captivate audiences around the world and create lasting cultural impact. On the big screen, we are committed to making at least 30 movies a year, pairing original stories from today’s most exciting filmmakers with beloved franchises like Harry Potter, Mission: Impossible, The Lord of the Rings, DC, Transformers and Star Trek. On television and streaming, it means storytelling like Game of Thrones, Landman, NCIS, Tracker and SpongeBob SquarePants. In games, it means worlds like Hogwarts Legacy and Mortal Kombat; and in live sports, it means the NFL on CBS, the UFC, UEFA and March Madness, just to name a few. Become the Most Technologically Capable Media Company Technology is fundamentally reshaping our industry, and we intend to be at the forefront. We will use technology, data and emerging capabilities to improve how we create, distribute and monetize content, from new production tools to personalization and entirely new ways for fans to engage with the stories they love. We will embrace the opportunities AI provides to expand what our creatives can imagine and to make our businesses even more productive. The opportunities ahead are enormous, and we intend to seize them. But one principle will never change: technology must serve the art – never the other way around. Lead in a Crowded Market We came together to create another major competitor in the industry. And with our combined scale, assets and global reach, we are positioned to take on some of the largest technology and media companies in the world and to lead in an evolving entertainment landscape. We will use that strength to drive synergies, operate with discipline and invest in the long-term growth of our business. And we will go further than traditional synergies. By embracing the most advanced technologies available and embedding them into how we operate, we will work smarter, move faster and unlock efficiencies the merger alone could not deliver. Earn Trust Every Day Trust is foundational to everything we do. And we are committed to earning it every day by communicating directly, following through on our commitments and listening closely to those we serve and work alongside. That is essential to our reputation and our long-term success. As we work toward these goals, we must never lose sight of what matters most: our people. We will build a culture where people feel respected, empowered, supported and proud of the work they do. And we will extend that same commitment, with reliability and responsibility, to our creators, audiences, consumers, advertisers and partners. None of what we accomplish happens in a vacuum. It reflects everyone joining forces to unlock the full potential of our assets: an unmatched portfolio of brands, franchises, libraries, IP and creative talent, with decades of history and, in many cases, decades of opportunity still ahead. Together, we can reach audiences across platforms, markets, and generations in ways neither Paramount nor WBD could have achieved alone. With the talent, scale, relationships and resources to build on, we can create something truly distinctive. For audiences, it means more choice and more ways to experience the stories they love. For creators, it means a partner with the scale and capabilities to help their best ideas reach the widest possible audience. For our partners, it means a broader, more powerful platform to build on. And for the broader creative community, it means an enduring commitment to storytelling and the people who make it possible. That is the foundation of Skydance. And it’s why this combination matters so much. Honoring an Extraordinary Legacy The union of these two iconic companies represents an exciting future. But, just as important as what we build together is preserving what has made them iconic in the first place. Paramount and Warner Bros. each have a distinct identity and extraordinary legacy that deserves to stand on its own. In choosing our corporate brand, we never wanted to diminish, alter or overshadow any of the assets that have global recognition and have withstood the test of time. Both studios will continue to operate under their own names, and audiences will still see the Paramount mountain and the Warner Bros. shield before the films and shows they love. Warner Bros. is woven into the history of modern entertainment, from film and television to journalism, sports, unscripted programming and some of the world’s most recognizable characters and franchises. Paramount has an equally extraordinary legacy, with more than a century of storytelling that helped define the American film industry and shape entertainment across every medium. We realized early on that simply combining the two names – WarnerParamount, ParaWarner or ParamountWarner – accomplished none of what we wanted. Every variation somehow made two giants feel smaller, not greater. It asked each to give something up rather than allowing us to create something new. This isn’t a merger of convenience. It’s the beginning of a new era in entertainment, and we wanted a name that looks forward rather than one that simply splices together the past. That brought us to Skydance – a name that obviously has special meaning to David, who chose it for his own studio 20 years ago. It evokes possibility: scale and ambition, creativity and imagination, artistry and innovation. Most importantly, it doesn’t compete with either legacy. It gives the new company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. – and all our extraordinary brands – to remain in the spotlight. Because ultimately, what we are bringing together is much more than brands and libraries. It is the creative spirit, ambition and craftsmanship that have kept these companies culturally relevant for generations. That spirit will continue to be a core part of who we are at Skydance. And who we are will also be defined by what we strive to accomplish – not just for our company, but for the industry at large. That means looking ahead to the forces that are reshaping entertainment and finding ways to harness them to expand what’s possible – for creators, for audiences and for the business itself. Financial Strength We’re building a diversified company with the financial strength to compete aggressively and the discipline to create sustainable value. That’s not just important to our investors – it’s important to all of us. A financially strong, well-run company gives us the freedom to take creative risks, invest in our people and our technology, and pursue the kind of opportunities that set us apart. In concrete terms, we are together one of the largest media and entertainment companies in the world, with nearly $70 billion in revenue. As we have said publicly, we are also targeting at least $6 billion in synergies, which will make us leaner and more nimble and free up capital to invest in the stories, creators and technology that matter most. Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce. We are committed to handling this process thoughtfully and respectfully. The Road Ahead Today is Day One. We have an incredible collection of assets. Extraordinary creative talent. Global scale. The technology to lead. And most important, we have the people who bring it all to life every day. We have everything we need to win, and that is our goal: to build a next-generation global media and entertainment company that puts audiences first, empowers creators, embraces innovation and creates lasting value for generations to come. But none of this happens without you. Thank you for everything you’ve brought to this moment. We’re proud to write this next chapter with you. Now the real work begins. Let’s go! articles.title: David Zaslav’s Farewell: Warner Bros. Discovery CEO Signs Off In Message To Staff
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News $110B Merger Of Paramount & Warner Bros Discovery Officially Closes Read the full story By Jill Goldsmith , Dade Hayes October 5, 2026 1:29pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc David Zaslav Getty/Dominic Patten/Deadline David Zaslav , Warner Bros Discovery’s CEO (for a few more hours, anyway), has started his goodbyes, thanking employees in a video posted Monday on the company’s internal portal. “It’s been a great honor to be alongside all of you,” says Zaslav, speaking from Warner Bros. Studios’ Ranch facility in Burbank. “I hope you take pride in what you’ve built, what you’ve created, and the role you’ve played in shaping an extraordinary history.” Related Stories News New Skydance Sets Top Executive Structure As Paramount-WBD Merger Set To Close Executives Ynon Kreiz Anointed Co-CEO Of New Paramount-WBD; David Ellison Says Mega-Studio Is “Transformational Moment For Our Industry” A rep from WBD declined to share a link to the video, explaining that it is intended for employees only, but Deadline has obtained a transcript. (Read it below.) The three-minute video features Zaslav sitting in a stiff-backed chair on the Warner lot, with shots of him giving remarks eventually transitioning to a series of still photographs. Multiple employees told Deadline that the photos are weighted toward award shows, red carpets and the movie and TV stars Zaslav interacted with during his tenure. Watch on Deadline The CEO, who became an unexpected (and ultimately controversial) Hollywood kingpin with the acquisition of WarnerMedia from AT&T by the much smaller Discovery in April 2022, is exiting with a large gold parachute. The Paramount -WBD deal is due to close Tuesday, less than eight months after Zaslav and the WBD board inked a deal to sell the company to David Ellison’s studio. After taking the helm, Zaslav bought an L.A. home, had Jack Warner’s old desk moved into his office on the Burbank lot and set about paring down the company’s massive debt of more than $50 billion. A substantial amount of the debt remains and will be absorbed by the new Skydance , whose debt load of $80 billion leaves little room for error as it looks to cut costs and boost streaming profits. WBD had previously planned to split in half, separating studios and streaming from cable networks, and the company later agreed to sell the former to Netflix. Ellison continued to bid for the combined company and was ultimately able to elbow his way in and seal the deal, which is valued at $110 billion. It was a rich transaction for WBD stockholders, who will get a $31-a-share payout. (WBD finished its last day as a publicly traded stock at $30.95.) Zaslav in particular stands to reap hundreds of millions from his shepherding of the deal, with the official figure to be disclosed in SEC filings over the coming days.

articles.title: Clockwork, Warner Bros’ New Specialty Label, Is Making Jump To Skydance – The Dish
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News $110B Merger Of Paramount & Warner Bros Discovery Officially Closes Read the full story By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony ‘Verity’ Lures 2nd Best Opening For Colleen Hoover Pic With $62M+ WW; ‘Digger’ DOA At $20M WW – Top 10 Global Box Office Update Clockwork, Warner Bros’ New Specialty Label, Is Making Jump To Skydance – The Dish ‘The Batman Part II’ Production Paused As Matt Reeves Steps Away For Personal Reasons View All October 5, 2026 2:23pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc Warner Bros./Getty Images EXCLUSIVE: Warner Bros’ new Christian Parkes -led contemporary film label Clockwork , which we first told you about in December , will be making the segue to the newly merged Paramount-Warner Bros company now known as Skydance . Clockwork was on an internal list of Warner Bros labels shown in-house at Paramount. In addition, we’ve heard from reliable sources that all Warner Bros label heads (i.e., James Gunn and Peter Safran at DC, Richard Brener at New Line, etc) will stay in charge of their domains at the new conglomerate. As previously reported, all film label heads roll up and report to Paramount Pictures co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein . Related Stories Executives James Gunn & Peter Safran To Stay At DC Studios After Paramount-Warner Bros Merger Executives New Line Boss Richard Brener Poised To Jump To Merged Paramount-Warner Bros – The Dish Clockwork’s first theatrical release is due October 16 with the unearthed 1971 Ken Russell-directed spicy Catholic taboo pic The Devils, which will be screened in a 4K restoration. The whole idea why former Warner Bros Motion Picture bosses Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy launched the label with former Neon Chief Marketing Officer Parkes was to give the studio some A24-like mojo shots in the arm. Clockwork is an entry point for edgy filmmakers and their pics with moderate-sized budgets. The label’s original output was for two-to-three films annually. Watch on Deadline When the label was first announced in December (the name followed at CinemaCon), there was some in town who wondered whether the new indie division would make the transition in any Warner Bros. merger. Paramount currently sees Clockwork as a blooming rose. Clockwork, we understand, will co-exist with Paramount’s current global acquisition division and Republic Pictures, led by Wicker producer Lia Buman. That Melrose lot department made a big purchase out of Cannes with StudioCanal’s Midnight Library for $36 million (which includes domestic and a bulk of foreign). In addition, Republic Pictures is the label responsible for the 2024 Oscar-nominated Munich Olympics thriller September 5. Projects coming into Paramount from Clockwork include the next movie from Anora Oscar winner Sean Baker, Ti Amo! (financed by FilmNation). There’s also Clockwork’s mid-teen millions North American pick-up out of the Cannes market, Park Chan-Wook’s western The Brigands of Rattlecreek starring Matthew McConaughey , Austin Butler , Pedro Pascal and Chinese star Tang Wei ( Decision to Leave ). Also in the Clockwork portfolio is the Sean Penn-directed feature about the January 6th Capitol riots. Let’s also not forget the Mary Bronstein directed Nasty starring Jenna Ortega and Rose Byrne from producers LuckyChap; that project now in prep. Paramount didn’t return request for comment. articles.title: WBD’s JB Perrette Makes The Leap To Skydance: Here Is Why Zaslav's Lieutenant Ended Up In Ellison's…
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News $110B Merger Of Paramount & Warner Bros Discovery Officially Closes Read the full story By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Skydancing At Last: $110B Merger Of Paramount And Warner Bros Discovery Officially Closes ESPN & HBO Vet Bomani Jones Teams With Playmaker For Long-Running Podcast ‘The Right Time’ WBD’s JB Perrette Makes The Leap To Skydance: Here Is Why Zaslav’s Lieutenant Ended Up In Ellison’s Executive Suite View All October 5, 2026 4:11pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc JB Perrette, newly appointed Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance TV and Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance DTC Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for Warner Bros. Discovery When Skydance confirmed the company’s executive leadership team Monday, most industry reaction centered on elevated roles for content execs such as Casey Bloys, Channing Dungey and George Cheeks. But another exec in a key new post is JB Perrette , a veteran of streaming since its earliest days and a close associate of Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav . He not only is making the leap to the new company from a top position at WBD — something of a surprise given that execs at the company being acquired generally head for the exits — but his turf also is expanding in some intriguing ways. Related Stories News Post-Merger Skydance Keeping Both HBO Max & Paramount+ Streaming Brands Executives David Zaslav’s Farewell: Warner Bros. Discovery CEO Signs Off In Message To Staff Skydance is due to close the deal Tuesday morning, and Perrette will join Co-CEOs David Ellison , Ynon Kreiz and others at a press conference later that afternoon on the Paramount lot. Watch on Deadline Upon the close of the $110 billion deal, Perrette will be Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance DTC and Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance TV. He will have direct global oversight of distribution, advertising sales, content sales, DTC strategy, marketing and business operations. Perrette is poised to benefit handsomely from the merger. An SEC filing in March said he would receive $142 million in various deal-related proceeds, though some portion of that could be deferred given his post in the new company. One source cited the massive payday as a potential motivating factor. “He certainly didn’t need the money,” the person said. “He obviously felt compelled by the opportunity.”

articles.title: Skydancing At Last: $110B Merger Of Paramount And Warner Bros Discovery Officially Closes
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News $110B Merger Of Paramount & Warner Bros Discovery Officially Closes Read the full story By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Skydancing At Last: $110B Merger Of Paramount And Warner Bros Discovery Officially Closes ESPN & HBO Vet Bomani Jones Teams With Playmaker For Long-Running Podcast ‘The Right Time’ WBD’s JB Perrette Makes The Leap To Skydance: Here Is Why Zaslav’s Lieutenant Ended Up In Ellison’s Executive Suite View All October 6, 2026 5:59am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc The long-gestating merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery officially closed Tuesday, yielding a new major player in media. Shares in the combined company, Skydance , will start trading later in the day on the New York Stock Exchange. Shares of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery have been discontinued on the Nasdaq. Related Stories News New Skydance Sets Top Executive Structure As Paramount-WBD Merger Set To Close Executives Ynon Kreiz Anointed Co-CEO Of New Paramount-WBD; David Ellison Says Mega-Studio Is “Transformational Moment For Our Industry” The closing brings to an end a year-long saga over who would control two century-old movie studios along with a pedigreed stable of TV studios, streaming services and networks including HBO and CNN. Now, attention will turn to the difficult economics faced by the new company. It starts off with some $80 billion in debt and an ambitious plan to convert a traditional media company into a tech-oriented operation capable of measuring up to Netflix, Amazon and Disney. Larry Ellison, the billionaire co-founder of Oracle, is a key backer of Skydance. His son, David Ellison , an actor-turned-producer who has made a dramatic entrance to the Hollywood corporate scene at just 43 years old, is running the company as chairman and CEO. Watch on Deadline “Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” David Ellison said in a statement. “From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality. We’re grateful to everyone who made this possible – the employees, creative talent, and production teams of both companies, who worked tirelessly to get us here and inspire audiences around the world every day, as well as the advisors and partners who guided this transaction to completion. Our focus now turns to the future: building a company that empowers creatives, entertains audiences and rewards shareholders. We couldn’t be more excited to get to work.” Gerry Cardinale, a Skydance board member and key financier via his firm, RedBird Capital, called the merger close “a defining moment for the industry. By applying our owner-operator model to Paramount and WBD ’s unmatched portfolio of iconic franchises, premium original programming, and live sports rights, we can protect that legacy while building for a media landscape that’s undergoing transformational change.” The merger was set in motion about a year ago when Paramount, soon after combining with the previous incarnation of Skydance, made an unsolicited offer to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery. The overture was rebuffed multiple times, and it took more than a dozen attempts for the board of WBD to finally warm up to the deal. Along the way, a bid was accepted from Netflix to acquire just the streaming and studio side of the company. Ultimately, that proposal fell by the wayside when Paramount made its sweetened pitch to buy all of WBD. The transaction sailed through regulatory approval, only to hit a major road block in July when the attorneys general of 12 states filed a lawsuit seeking to block the deal on antitrust grounds. The Writers Guild of America filed a similar suit . Thousands of actors, writers, producers and others in the creative community signed a petition opposing the deal. It will likely remain a talking point, especially for high-profile opponents like Mark Ruffalo , who stars in HBO series Task . L-R: California AG Rob Bonta, New York AG Leticia James and David Ellison Getty Images Initially, it appeared that legal and industry objections could have a chance to derail the combination, or at least result in a shrinking of its scale. In the end, though, the AGs agreed to settle the lawsuit with only so-called “behavioral remedies” required under a 5-year consent decree . Skydance agreed to negotiate pay-TV deals for Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery as though they were still separate companies as well as supplying a minimum number of theatrical movie releases, among other concessions. Ties between the Ellisons and President Donald Trump have long been scrutinized over the course of the year-long quest for WBD by Paramount, as well as Skydance’s $8.4 billion purchase of Paramount in 2025. While Skydance has steadfastly denied it has gone out of its way to appease Trump, critics have questioned the motives behind a series of moves by David Ellison and his senior leadership team. The company, which acquired rights to the UFC mixed-martial-arts circuit last year, broadcast a live match from the White House lawn over the summer. It also acquired the Free Press, a right-leaning digital news outlet, and installed its co-founder, Bari Weiss, as editor-in-chief of CBS News despite her lack of TV experience. Paramount, during the lead-up to the deal, hosted Trump during the White House Correspondents Dinner, and Ellison also paid a visit to his compound in Mar-a-Lago. Democratic members of Congress have voiced concerns about the future of CNN, though the consent decree agreed to with the state AGs calls for an editorial oversight board to be installed.
