articles.title: ‘SNL’s Weekend Update Tackles Cornell Controversy & Return Of ‘Glee’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lynette Rice Lynette Rice Senior TV Writer @LynetteRice More Stories By Lynette ‘SNL’s Weekend Update Tackles Cornell Controversy & Return Of ‘Glee’ Taylor Swift Joins ‘SNL’ Host Dakota Johnson During Opening Monologue Jeremy Strong Says He Cares What Mark Zuckerberg Thinks About ‘The Social Reckoning’ View All October 3, 2026 9:48pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kam Patterson on 'SNL' NBC After cracks about Pete Hegseth, Kristi Noem and President Donald Trump’s vendetta against CNN, Michael Che on Saturday Night Live ‘s Weekend Update touched on the ongoing controversy at Cornell University and Ryan Murphy’s decision to bring back Glee . Che first served up a serious note by referencing the sexual assault case at Cornell and how “obviously we don’t want to make light of anything that happened, but it is a good time to talk about men holding other men accountable.” Related Stories Late Night TV ‘SNL’ Cold Open Goes Full MAGA Midterms Desperation With Hegseth’s “Schlong Donkeys”, Trump’s Rambles & A Sad VP Late Night TV Taylor Swift Joins ‘SNL’ Host Dakota Johnson During Opening Monologue As the camera panned toward to a silent Colin Jost , Che said, “Look, we all have that one friend that seems like a nice guy, but they’re definitely not. It could be someone you’re close to, or someone you work with. Maybe you can’t prove anything. You can just look at him and tell those weird, privileged Ivy League types always got some messed up stuff going on.” Che then turned to Jost and said, “Is there anything you want to add, Colin?” “Stop cutting to me,” Jost responded. Watch on Deadline Later, cast member Kam Patterson joined the desk to show his enthusiasm for the reboot of Glee . (Ryan Murphy recently said that he “just finished” a Glee reboot script). Che was a bit skeptical that Patterson is a true Gleek, despite Patterson claiming he was eager to find out if Rachel was still on Broadway and if Kurt and Blaine were still together. But Che wasn’t convinced. “Look, I know you man. You don’t have to say yes to every day that a white writer pitches to you …. Look Kam. I’ve worked here, what, 30, 35 years. I know what this is. Two white writers came up to you in suits, pitched you an idea about Glee , and now you’re out here saying a bunch of names you’ve never heard before, right?” Patterson admits he hasn’t and feels “pretty bad” that he “just did jazz hands on national television.” Weekend Update with Colin Jost and Michael Che! pic.twitter.com/xyQ5MjizyT — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) October 4, 2026 Taylor Swift Crashes Dakota Johnson’s Monologue; Cold Open Goes Full MAGA ‘Verity’ Solid $33M+ Start; ‘Digger’ At $8M Lowest Cruise Open In 19 Years Skydance Putting All 3 TV Studios Under George Cheeks: WBTV, CBS Studios, PTVS What’s Next For De Luca, Abdy; Top Film Jobs To Greenstein, Goldberg Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Tinashe Wants to Challenge the Pop Star Label
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Tinashe. Paris Helena “The Popstar universe has been building in my mind for a while now,” Tinashe says. The 33-year-old, one of pop’s most forward-thinking acts, is speaking about her latest album, Popstar , which dropped on Sept. 25 and features sixteen tracks. It’s the type of album that Tinashe, who’s been working in the entertainment industry since she was a child, could only make now. “I’ve just reached a place in my life, personally and professionally, where I feel very self-assured and confident in my position,” she tells The Hollywood Reporter on a Zoom, pacing around what appears to be an outdoor patio as she excitedly talks about this next chapter. “Both in the industry and just I guess as an individual.” Related Stories News Wynonna Judd Says Rosie O'Donnell's Claims That She's a Trump Supporter Are a "Complete Assumption" Music Jesse Jo Stark and Deadly Doll Sign With BMG Tinashe wanted Popstar to feel “real and raw and empowered.” The singer left the major label system in 2019, finding success in pursuing the music and creative she wants. It’s been a journey of growth and learning, she admits, but it’s been seven years, so growth is to be expected. Realizing she was able to do this on her own restored the confidence in creativity that she felt she had been losing. Despite the album’s name, she wasn’t trying to box herself into a genre. She’s never wanted to limit herself to one of anything, and she feels her music has always been reflective of that. “The categorization was definitely probably the biggest hindrance to how I think I was perceived to the public and the world,” Tinashe says. Letting go of genre might sound confusing when the album’s named Popstar , but to Tinashe, a pop star is so much more than a genre label. “It’s an energy, it’s an embodiment, it’s an ownership of a space that I want to take up in the world,” she says. Tinashe wants to expand what people think of what it really means to be a pop star. From a technical genre perspective, she’s hoping that pop can continue to feel more expansive. “People, when they think of the genre of pop, they have a very watered down and narrow-minded point of view of what that sounds like and looks like,” she says. “I hope to challenge that.” *** How does DJing fit into the equation for you? There’s a couple ways that I feel like I’ve really connected with DJing. One is just dance music, dance culture, dancing. I really enjoy that. It’s really important, maybe now more than ever, for us to have community. To have connection and these points of connection — whether it be live shows, live spaces or places where people can listen to music together, I think is really important. I really want to continue to bring that energy to as many people as possible, whether it be from my live shows or smaller venues or after parties. It’s just fun. The other element is just the exploration of the genre. I’ve dabbled and explored that genre a lot over the years and that led me to more collaborations in the space and working in the space. That just opens your mind to — again, in the spirit of blending these worlds and blending these genres — I feel like we need more women in this space. We need more Black women in the space. We need more conversation. We need to bring all of these different things that are inspiring to me together and not have them be so in their own lane. To that point, do you see yourself as a DJ separate to how you see yourself as a pop star? Yes, I do. In the same way, but different. When I think of myself as a pop star, it’s an additional skill, an additional tool to my tool belt, versus an entirely separate thing. But that’s what a pop star is to me. You can dance, you sing, you can DJ, you can create music, you can write music, you’re the muse. That’s what it’s all about. Do you find it frustrating ever, for pop music in particular, there’s this idea that it’s something made in a factory and it’s just given to artists? In reality, all of the women like yourself that are in this space are actively involved in creating the music . One hundred percent. That’s one of the things that I’m exploring visually in concept with this album, poking fun at the machine of it all or the perfection. We obviously know the cliches that are involved with being a pop star and being a part of that machine. But I also think people can see behind the curtain now a bit more, and that’s another layer to me of what this album means. By embodying what a pop star is, I can both lean into the spectacle and the show of it all, and I can also reject it and be like, “Fuck you, I am who I am. I might not fit this mold or expectation, but this is still what a pop star is because I said so.” Does it feel nice to be able to take that back into your own hands to decide? A million percent. That was really important for me, just where I am in my life, because when I wanted to write this new project, I really wanted to embody that energy. That was the North star of how the creative came together in my mind. How do you feel about social media these days? It’s played an interesting role in your career. I have a good relationship with social media right now. Sometimes that hasn’t always been the case over the years, but I think now I see it in the same way as this whole album concept. There’s an element of performance that is, I guess, a through line. It’s both known and used as a tool. I think about social media as the performance and about how I’m able to tell the story of this album through the performance of it via social media. That’s how I’ve changed my perspective on it. I find that I have a lot more fun doing that. Whereas, I felt [at times] in the past, there was just way more pressure to, who knows, post more or do whatever. Would you call yourself online or more offline? I’m definitely online. So you’re seeing things? Yeah, I’m online a lot. I think, in terms of my own self-perception of the internet or my place on the internet, I more so enjoy now being a part of conversation for the sake of conversation. And being a part of discourse for the sake of discourse. I think that’s important, whereas, obviously, it’s never fun to be the subject of negative discourse, but I think being a part of conversations is fun. It’s fine, it’s good. How do you feel about the industry now versus when you were first getting started? It’s changed a lot. I think, to be fair, I’m very optimistic about it at this point because I’ve seen how many iterations there are of it. And that leads me to believe that whatever’s happening now will not remain the same. That’s exciting in a way. Where music is going, and how people are going to continue to experiment and try new things, I think that’s really fun. I can’t predict it, and being part of that conversation is fun. Obviously, there’s bad things about it all, but there’s always bad things about it. It’s like, it’s the music industry, man. It’s the wild, wild west. THR

articles.title: Sean “Diddy” Combs Reportedly Ran Fort Dix Prison Cell Like a Luxury Suite With Paid Staff
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All October 2, 2026 3:22pm Sean "Diddy" Combs Shareif Ziyadat/Getty Images for Sean "Diddy" Combs Sean “Diddy” Combs may not be getting out of prison as soon as expected after a Dateline segment this week detailed the luxe lifestyle the rap mogul has allegedly built behind bars, complete with a team of fellow inmates treated like his personal staff. Since arriving at Fort Dix in October 2025 after more than a year at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, Combs has seen his projected release date bounce around the front half of the 2028 calendar, shifting several times between January and June. It now stands at Jan. 21, 2028. In that time, he has entered a drug rehabilitation program at the New Jersey facility, has been involved in a fight with another inmate, and violated several prison rules while serving a 50-month sentence for Mann Act violations . Related Stories News Tupac Murder Trial Highlights a Persistent Diddy Conspiracy Theory Music Tupac's Murder Case Heads to Trial, 30 Years After Rap Icon's Death A report from NBC News’ Dateline this week indicated that the former near-billionaire Bad Boy founder had extended his luxurious lifestyle to his prison cell, where a crew of incarcerated men has been receiving funds in their commissary accounts in exchange for doing basic chores like making the rapper’s bed, cleaning his toilet and shower, and giving him massages. Some inmates also reportedly cooked him meals outside of the prison’s daily menu. Dateline ‘s reporter said she spoke with several inmate sources inside Fort Dix. One inmate at the federal facility showed NBC News an Instagram account that Combs allegedly had been using to communicate with contacts outside the prison. The profile has no profile picture, but it is followed by Combs’ PR representative. Despite his stint in prison rehab, Combs reportedly has had regular access to alcohol, the antidepressant Remeron, a cell phone, and a tablet, none of which inmates are permitted to have without authorization. The Bureau of Prisons has a policy of not commenting on current inmates. After an eight-week trial over the summer of 2025, Combs was convicted of two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution and acquitted of the more serious racketeering conspiracy and sex trafficking charges. After a sentencing hearing in a New York federal courtroom in which his life was laid bare, he was handed 50 months. He and his attorneys are awaiting a decision on their appeal of the sentence. But their client hasn’t been making a case for himself from the inside. TMZ reported on July 24 that Combs was allegedly involved in a fight with another inmate over an insult and was then placed in solitary confinement. The skirmish reportedly pushed his release date back about a month, to Feb. 20, 2028. Combs’ rep did not respond to a request from The Hollywood Reporter on Friday for comment on the Dateline story. Asked about the solitary confinement reports, the rep said he is unable to confirm Combs’ movement out of the general population at Fort Dix and into “the hole,” telling THR , “I can’t know where he is. BOP doesn’t keep us apprised.” THR

articles.title: Rick Devens on How ‘Survivor’ Prepped Him to Win ‘Big Brother,’ Canceling on James Gunn’s ‘Superman 2’ Cameo and If He’d do ‘Traitors’: “I’m Open”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 2, 2026 3:31pm Rick Devens wins 'Big Brother' season 28. Matthew Taplinger/CBS Logo text On Big Brother , Rick Devens was labeled a reality television icon. After winning season 28 on Thursday night, he definitely has entered “icon” status, becoming the first Survivor player to win Big Brother . His casting was part of a larger twist for season 28 that saw three former reality TV players join a pool of new contestants ; competing alongside Devens was his fellow Survivor 50 opponent and season 45 winner Dee Valladares and Big Brother season 26 alum Angela Murray. Devens himself competed on season 38 and 50 of Survivor . Related Stories Movies James Gunn, Peter Safran to Stay at DC Studios as Brand Takes Key Position at Skydance News Kennedy Center Honors 2026 Sets Date, New Venue The show labeled them icons after they entered the Big Brother house, and the name stuck. So did their strong three-person alliance, which through strategic gameplay and season-long dominance ensured at least one of them would have a real shot at winning the game. Devens ultimately won Big Brother in a vote of six to one from the jury, beating out runner-up Taylor Brown. Plus, the audience also took to Devens, awarding him the title of America’s Favorite Houseguest, which fans vote upon at the end of each season. He’s also the most-winning player from a single season, earning $750,000 from winning the show; the $50,000 prize for America’s Favorite Houseguest; and an extra $10,000 he pocketed during a competition while filming. Below, Devens breaks down why he wasn’t sure if would have won Big Brother if Drew Campbell made it to the final two, his thoughts on season 28 houseguests asserting that the icons had “privileges and advantages” this season, James Gunn revealing he was supposed to make a cameo in Man of Tomorrow , and what competitive reality shows he’d do next ( Survivor part three? Big Brother All-Winners? The Traitors ?). *** After you won the final HOH, you decided to evict Drew. Do you really think that Taylor would have had enough time to flip Lala and tell her, “We’re going to vote for Drew to win”? I really don’t think it would have taken much time. I think if Taylor walked out on stage and said, “Lala, we’re voting for Drew,” Lala would have gone, “Okay. You’ll explain to me later.” I think that’s all it would have taken, because those two were so tight. I was legitimately very concerned about it. Now that the show is over and you potentially had time to talk to everybody, if there was a scenario where Drew was in the final two with you, did the jury tell you they would have voted you to win? No, I didn’t. I haven’t had those conversations. I now know that Drew and Taylor, neither of them were gonna take me to the final two, so that makes me feel better about it. But I haven’t had any conversations about how a Drew, Devens vote would have gone. Wow! So do you really still think that Melody [Morris] and Barrett [Pfeiffer] would have voted for Drew? I think it’s very possible. I think Drew’s and my game was super similar, very intertwined. A lot of the moves we made, we made together. We’d won about the same number of comps. He dragged me to the final three. I would have dragged him to the final two. So I think that they had every right to vote however they wanted. I would be shocked if Melody hadn’t gone for Drew, and then Barrett would have been the deciding vote. And that’s a little closer than a six-one vote. I had to do what I had to do, unfortunately. Rick Devens after winning ‘Big Brother’ season 28. Matthew Taplinger/CBS Let’s go back to when you made it to final three. If there would have been a scenario where it would have been you choosing if Drew or Dee would have moved forward, do you think you would have taken her with you? I don’t. I think I would have cut Dee at final three to not sit next to her, and I think Dee would have cut me at final three to not sit next to me. Two Survivor players: We know each other too well. What elements of gameplay that you learned on Survivor do you think served you best for Big Brother ? On Survivor , everything is so much faster, so you turn a vote at the last second almost out of necessity. Dee and I came on here, and I think a lot of Big Brother is you set your vote, you decide what you’re going to do, and then you just wait ‘til the live show. Whereas her and I would go, “I think we can still flip this. Let’s go work on this.” Even sometimes, to our own detriment, we were just bored and were like, We can flip this. Let’s do it. Why not? Also, I learned on Survivor that there’s no shame in going home early or making a dumb move and getting voted out. Great players do that all the time, so you can’t be afraid of that. On this season of Big Brother , I would make a pitch to someone, and they’d be like, “No.” I think a lot of other houseguests would have gone, Oh, that didn’t go well, not doing that again . Whereas I’m like, I got all week, I’m going to make that same pitch to him tonight, and then I’ll pitch it to him again tomorrow morning . And by the end of the week, so many times they were like, “Okay, I get it, let’s do it.” I think just not being embarrassed and not being scared of going home early is a huge power in games like these. Why do you ultimately think these Big Brother players did not opt to get the icons out at the very beginning of the game? Obviously that was a mistake. Yeah, and then they blame that we had all these privileges and advantages. It’s like, you guys had week two through 11 to come together. There’s 14 of you, there’s three of us. You could have gotten us out at any time, and you didn’t do it. Don’t blame our privilege now. Like, come on. I think some of them made a really good move; the [players] that we were working with, they realized that we were valuable to them, that we were good shields for them, and that’s what we sold them. Others, I think, just didn’t want to make a big splash, didn’t want to put a target on themselves, and that’s obviously something that we weren’t worried about. We made big moves every chance we got, so I don’t know. I’m annoyed that they want to blame us having all this special stuff when they outnumbered us 14 to three, and they had 11 weeks to get us out. I feel like if you wanted us out, you could have gotten us out. Get it together, newbies. What advantage do you think they thought y’all had? Because as somebody who loves reality TV, I would want to get y’all out because you have that knowledge of gameplay, and you have targets on your back coming in. That’s what I feel like. I think they’re like, “You were automatically a three-person alliance,” and it’s like, okay, so all it takes [to vote one of us out] is a four-person alliance. And by the way, if it had been Rachel [Reilly] there instead of Dee, I don’t think we’d be [an] automatic [group of three working together]. I don’t think Angela and Rachel were going to work together. I don’t know if Rachel and I were going to work together. I do think we had an advantage in getting into the BB Time Capsule. [ Writer’s note: Viewers voted which players to send into the BB Time Capsule, where they could earn a punishment or advantage .] But even then, it’s a 50/50 chance of what you’re [going to get]. Actually, a lot of people thought it was random: I’m sure that I saw a pattern in there. I [looked] at the button for five minutes, saw the pattern, and got a power. Three newbies went in there, and two of them came out with punishments. That’s not because we came in with a privilege. I think if anything, we were at a disadvantage. I thought half the house was going to be returning players or players from other shows. Oh, really? Yeah. Why did you think that? Because I thought that would be fair. Give us a chance. You know, half newbies and half returnees. That’s even. Angela Murray, Devens and Dee Valladares at the ‘Big Brother’ season 28 finale. Matthew Taplinger/CBS When did this opportunity or conversation for you to go on Big Brother start? Did it come out of you being on Survivor 50 ? I think it might have, but I don’t know the details, and I don’t think I’m even allowed to talk [about it]. But I think probably if I hadn’t done well or I hadn’t made a splash on 50 , I’d never be here. When you were approached about doing Big Brother , were you game on immediately, or were you like, I don’t know, maybe, maybe not ? I was really hesitant about it. I had always said the one [show] I’m not going to do is Big Brother , because it’s so long. And then it comes up, and I’m like, well, maybe I want to do it, but I was like, I can’t do this to my wife. And I went home to my wife Becca and was like, “Hey, this thing came up. I’m not saying I want to do it,” and she said, “You have to do it. You’re never gonna get this opportunity again.” And I was like, “Wait, what?” So it’s all credit to her that I ended up going into that house and winning the game. You have been away from your phones and the outside world. Something that picked up once you got into the house was James Gunn said that you were supposed to do a cameo for Superman , but you canceled last minute because of Big Brother . Have you spoken with him since you’ve won? I haven’t, not since I won, but I cannot wait. I shouted him out in the house. I was so upset that I couldn’t be there on the set of Superman 2 . My whole family still went, and he apparently treated them amazingly and made it such a special experience for them. He was filming in Macon, [Georgia,] where I’m from. That’s why it was all going to work out. But now, I’m like: James, I will go wherever you are. Let me visit whatever set you’re on. I’m so excited to hopefully meet him and be able to talk some Big Brother and Superman with him. I’m a huge James Gunn fan, even bigger now that he’s shown what a great dude he is. What former Survivor player do you think should go on Big Brother next? I’ve got two. They were both on 50. Rizo [Velovic] and Tiffany [Nicole Ervin] would be absolutely incredible at Big Brother . Both of them would just knock it out of the box. They probably have even bigger targets now because the three Survivor players that have been on have done pretty well. But if anyone could pull it off, it would be those two. Which player from this season of Big Brother should cross over and do Survivor ? It’s got to be Kamu [Kirk]. He’s got the physical to do those rough challenges. He has an amazing social game, and unlike a lot of the houseguests in there, I think he would actually thrive being out in the elements and going through all the suffering. Which show between Survivor and Big Brother would you be more ready to do another season of? Just because of how long it is, it’d be harder to come back to Big Brother until my kids were a little bit older. I don’t want to give up another summer while they’re 12 and nine years old. Whereas Survivor ‘s a little shorter, so I’d probably be more ready to go back to Survivor just because of that. What if the Big Brother team came to you next year and was like, “We’re doing All-Winners.” Would you do that? I’d say, “Can you do it [for] season 33. Can Drew stand in for his dad?” Maybe, yeah. But that would be a tough one to say no to for sure. But the kids made a big sacrifice letting me go, and I made a big sacrifice leaving them behind. So I don’t know that Becca would be as supportive this time. What were those first conversations like with your family when you ran off stage and reunited with them? It was so funny. They were so proud of me, even the kids. It wasn’t like, “Hey, we’re rich. What are we gonna get?” It was like, “You did it! We can’t believe it.” And then they were very emotional, and it turns out the reason they were emotional is because they were upset for Drew. They love Drew, their big brother, and they were not happy with me for cutting Drew. I have a lot to answer for with the Drew thing. They told me some of the funny things that happened with Big Brother while I was gone, that I missed some of their fun social posts, and then immediately it was like we were back in regular life, and they’re just telling me about the latest YouTube video they watched or what video game they’re playing. It’s like Big Brother ‘s a thing of the past already. The cast of ‘Big Brother’ season 28. Matthew Taplinger/CBS If your children came to you one day and said, “I want to play Big Brother or Survivor ,” what would you say? I would say, “Heck yeah! Let me get on the phone with Julie [Chen Moonves]. Let me get on the phone with Jeff [Probst]. We’re gonna try to work this thing out. We have a lot to talk about to prepare you mentally and emotionally before you go in this.” Always need to be prepared that it could not go well, but I think they’d be great. I’d love to see them play. Which one would you suggest or push them to take on first? I’d get them to follow their hearts, but I can tell you this: They both really wanted to play Survivor . And now they’ve watched Big Brother , and they saw all the costumes, they saw that we got fed and that there was a bed, and I think they might both be leaning towards Big Brother now. You have a huge name now in the reality TV space as the first Survivor player to win Big Brother . Would you do any other competitive reality TV shows? One that could definitely be in your future would have to be The Traitors . That’s the next big one, right? I’m open to all invitations. I would love to take Becca on The Amazing Race . I think that we would be maybe not this successful, but very entertaining. I just love playing these games. I feel so much gratitude that I get to play these goofy games that I know people would kill to go and play, and I’ve gotten to do it three times. So if I get to do something else, I’m all ears. *** Season 28 of Big Brother is available to stream on Paramount+. THR

articles.title: Ouster Rumors and a Tense Phone Call: Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy’s Final Weeks at Warners
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Borys Kit , Mia Galuppo , Aaron Couch October 2, 2026 3:40pm Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy at the premiere of 'Weapons' Gilbert Flores/Variety/Getty Images Mike De Luca began hearing the rumor over a month ago: He and his Warner Bros. film co-head Pam Abdy were on the chopping block. The source of the rumor was not David Ellison, whom the duo had met months earlier and seemed to indicate they would stay on in a post-merger world. No, De Luca was hearing that this was coming from Josh Greenstein, co-chair of Paramount Pictures. Greenstein, according to sources familiar with the meeting, told other executives in a cross-town engagement that he wanted to get rid of Abdy and De Luca. Other sources, also with direct knowledge of the conversation, countered the remark was directed toward the general stability of Warner Bros., and was made in the context of Greenstein vying for a project and peacocking Paramount’s own superior stability and executives. Regardless, De Luca, never one to sit on his hands, decided to go head on and called Greenstein. “Are you seriously saying this?” He demanded to know, according to sources familiar with the conversation. Greenstein denied the accusations and blamed it on a bad game of telephone. Because the deal was still in limbo given the antitrust suit, he was not legally allowed to make personnel decisions. But on Friday, that conversation feels prescient in hindsight as Abdy and De Luca are exiting the studio they have run since 2022. They learned that Greenstein and his co-chief Dana Goldberg would be taking control of both film divisions — and that they were out of a job – just before a Puck report broke the news late Thursday night. It was the end of four years of highs and lows, during which the duo has been the subject of the Hollywood rumor mill, with constant questions about potential ousters and contract renewals, in almost equal measure. They have faced accusations of overspending on movies with limited commercial prospects, like this weekend’s Tom Cruise bomb Digger , and have been hailed as cinema heroes thanks to major box office wins like Sinners and Weapons, and for bringing home best picture for One Battle After Another . For months leading up to the merger, De Luca and Abdy believed they were safe after a meeting with Ellison, in which he suggested they would stay, according to a high-level Warners source. They told people they believed there could be a friendly rivalry between themselves and Greenstein and Goldberg, given that they all had their own relationships with talent and filmmakers. Maybe the competition could even inspire each other to be better. “Clearly a lot has changed since then,” says the Warners source. Now, De Luca and Abdy are left to plot their next moves. A year ago, they signed a five-year contract renewal through 2030, which they will be paid for. They have told associates they could go to Netflix, and De Luca is said to have grown close with Netflix mogul Ted Sarandos during a series of conversations they had when the streaming giant was tipped to buy Warner Bros. late last year. Could they help Netflix move more into the theatrical space? Could they bring their auteur-driven philosophy to the streamer, which counts middle of the road movies like Carry-On and Red Notice as among its most viewed movies ever? “All of their relationships are theatrical relationships. You aren’t going to convince those filmmakers to go make their big streaming movie,” cautions one source who has business with both Warners and Netflix. “If I were Ted, I’d say, ‘Come over, I’ll give you a sweetheart deal, and help us think through what theatrical could look like.” Netflix showed a willingness to get into the theatrical business when it was going to acquire Warner Bros., and is giving its longest theatrical window ever for its Cannes acquisition La Bola Negra as it hunts for an elusive best picture Oscar. “Netflix’s audience taste is more down the middle. It would be interesting to have them and their more filmmaker-driven approach at Netflix,” says one observer with business at Warners. “I just don’t know if the Netflix audience wants that. They want Red Notice , not May December or Roma or Lost Daughter .” In the weeks since California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced that a settlement with Paramount Skydance would clear the way for a merger, reps and studio execs across the industry expressed doubt that a single executive team could lead the 30-film slate that was laid out in the settlement. Per the agreement, the combined studios must release 30 films for two years and then 32 for the next three years. There are penalties if this threshold isn’t met. For every movie that Skydance falls short of, the studio must pay $30 million to health and pension funds, split among the guilds. Additionally, a judge can force it to sell or spin out Miramax, which was behind the 2026 Paramount Skydance hit Scary Movie. Of course, Goldberg and Greenstein are not completely alone in the oversight of the combined Paramount and Warners film slate, with studio labels actively run by veteran executives. DC Studios, which is still in the middle of a turnaround and coming off of an unfortunate showing with Supergirl , will continue to be led by James Gunn and Peter Safran, while it is believed that Richard Brener is safe for the time being at New Line, home of lucrative franchises like The Conjuring and The Lord of the Rings. And then there is Warner’s newest studio label, Clockwork, the boutique outfit run by a trio of former Neon executives. Clockwork is readying for its first big theatrical release, a remastering of the 1971 British film The Devils , out Oct. 16, and has proved a player at festival markets, landing upcoming film from Sean Baker and Park Chan-Wook. It’s also looking to get into the low-budget genre game. “At the end of the day, you can’t have four chairmen,” says the Warners insider, assessing the notion of De Luca, Abdy, Greenstein and Goldberg all working together. “You can’t share marketing and distribution. You can’t have people fighting over who gets Memorial Day, who gets the Super Bowl ads, and who gets the big spend.” Greenstein and Goldberg’s mandate at Skydance is meat and potatoes and franchise movies, rather than the swings of De Luca and Abdy, known for offering a studio home and big budgets to filmmakers like Paul Thomas Anderson, Ryan Coogler, Alejandro Iñárritu and Emerald Fennell, to varying degrees of commercial success. In this way, De Luca and Abdy’s Warners filled the void left behind when Megan Ellison’s Annapurna, once the place where filmmakers like Anderson could find patronage and distribution, paused its film operations. (Annapurna began reopening its doors for at least some business earlier this year.) And while Neon and A24 have certainly taken up the auteur mantle in the past half-decade, these studios can offer low-to-mid-level budgets, a far cry from the $100 million-plus that De Luca and Abdy greenlit. It is these big swings from name brand directors that will mark De Luca and Abdy’s time at Warner Bros., for better and for worse. There was Sinners , Coogler’s vampire movie that delivered $370 million in ticket sales and Academy Awards glory. Coogler, who took home the original screenplay Oscar , repeatedly credited De Luca and Abdy’s support during the awards campaign, including in his Oscars speech. On the other end of the spectrum, there were films like Maggie Gyllenhaal’s The Bride! ($23.9 million on a $90 million budget), and Cruise starrer Digger , which is tracking to open this weekend to a dismal $8 million to $15 million on a $125 million-plus budget. The detractors categorized the chiefs as overzealous with budgets to the detriment of the larger studio slate, while champions heralded them as Medici-esque in their commitment to ensuring that some of the best films of the past couple of years made it in front of audiences. Hollywood, a town that has never particularly enjoyed any shade of gray, is likely to continue arguing along this binary. Ultimately, it is these strong filmmaker relationships, as well as those with their powerful reps (they are known to be close to CAA’s Bryan Lourd), that De Luca and Abdy will carry with them into their next act. Alex Weprin contributed to this story. THR

articles.title: ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Hints at Soulful Depths, but the Drama Keeps Stalling in Tony Gilroy’s Wan Character Study of a Virtuoso Cellist
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All October 2, 2026 5:00pm Pedro Pascal in 'Behemoth!' Justin Lubin/Searchlight Pictures Tony Gilroy returns to features after 14 years’ absence — the last three of them spent in the Star Wars TV trenches as creator, showrunner and head writer on Andor — with a movie that makes itself hard to love. Hampered by a fussy hopscotching time structure that too often halts the dramatic momentum and by a central character whose passivity fights against the warmth and magnetism of Pedro Pascal in the role, Behemoth! is an odd duck, alternately intriguing and frustrating. What it does have going for it is a series of thrilling sequences observing the workings of an orchestra employed on Hollywood’s scoring stages. Related Stories Movies 'Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall' Review: Paul Thomas Anderson's Effectively Austere Concert Doc Puts You Right in the Room Movies Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes Documentary Holds a Raucous and Revealing NYFF Screening That rarely glimpsed milieu and a virtuoso cellist protagonist might make Gilroy’s film sound like Maestro meets Tár . But the story’s internal engine seldom revs hard enough to stand up to either of those comparisons, despite its capable ensemble cast and polished craftsmanship. Behemoth! The Bottom Line Adagio when it needs to be agitato. Venue : New York Film Festival (Centerpiece — Main Slate) Release date : Friday, Dec. 4 Cast : Pedro Pascal, Olivia Wilde, Eva Victor, Alexa Swinton, Kaya Ralls, Erik Griffin, JoBeth Williams, Margarita Levieva, Hank Azaria, Will Arnett Director-screenwriter : Tony Gilroy 2 hours 7 minutes One issue is that the script by Gilroy (an Oscar nominee for screenwriting and direction on Michael Clayton ) gives insufficient dimension to Pascal’s character, Alex Serian, for someone meant to carry a film. He’s a sideliner in his own life, which may well be the result of living in the shadow of a family of narcissists, but that is not enough to make him interesting. Nor does it help that Alex’s failed relationships seem less a symptom of his own damage than his poor choice of partners. The women characters generally are not drawn kindly, especially Carol Spedding ( Olivia Wilde ), a wealthy, married arts patron whose ferocious pursuit of Alex when he ends their affair makes her seem like a soul sister to Glenn Close in Fatal Attraction . Maybe Carol’s $6 million gift to the Chicago Symphony during Alex’s tenure there enables her to feel some kind of ownership, though that’s more implied than explored. “I bleed for you and you shun me?” screeches the manic drama queen after he blocks her calls. Alex’s flight from scary Carol lands him back in his hometown, Los Angeles, after 20 years of playing in other cities, looking to get back into session work recording orchestral film scores. It’s in those scenes on studio lots — including the Barbra Streisand Scoring Studio at Sony — that the movie is most dynamic. That’s in large part due to the staggering range of ravishing original film music we see being performed — from dark drama to suspense to action to soaring romance — written by an assembly of nine respected composers billed as “The Behemoth! Collective.” They include Michael Abels, Emily Bear, Lukas Frank, Michael Giacchino, James Newton Howard, Henry Jackman, Nami Melumad, Brandan Roberts and Alan Silvestri. Much of their work also plays over scenes elsewhere in the movie, including an art rock song, a requiem, a cartoon theme tune, a harp concerto and cello etudes. For anyone who loves movies, being prompted to think about the experiential role that a great score plays is fascinating, but while Behemoth! feints toward being a celebration of film music, it never fully commits. It seems a missed opportunity that we don’t get to watch music being matched to specific beats on the screen, beyond background shots of fuzzy footage on a monitor. Alex’s relationship with his parents was defined by their need to outshine their children. We see video of Alex playing Bach at age 6 on Johnny Carson’s show, but the film seems to suggest their nurturing of their sons’ musical gifts was just another way to burnish their own reputations. His self-absorbed brother Andy ( Will Arnett , who’s in a different movie) became something of a black sheep when he turned his back on classical viola to form a briefly successful rock band in the ‘90s. He now hosts a podcast about the TV and movie themes of their late father Peter ( Hank Azaria , in a video cameo). Their mother Ginnie (an unrecognizable JoBeth Williams ) was a renowned harpist, fading fast with dementia when Alex stays with her upon first returning to L.A. She once said of her husband, “He was a Peter who really wanted to be a Pierre.” But those glimmers of insight fail to coalesce into a fleshed-out family mythology — though we do learn that Alex and Andy’s grandfather died from a stroke, immedicately after hitting a high C while playing trumpet on the same MGM stage where Alex now works. There’s simply not enough meat on the bones of the parental background or in Alex and Andy’s conversations about them to give much shape to the supposedly chaotic upbringing that formed them. The movie is more engaged in Alex’s reflections on his own life in the two decades since he left, jumping between fizzled relationships and elite orchestra positions in Boston, Dallas and Chicago. The one woman he appears to have loved is brilliant violinist Nadia ( Eva Victor ), who bailed to marry a billionaire businessman (Matthew Lillard). Victor ( Sorry, Baby ) is a vivid screen presence, but Nadia isn’t around long enough to leave much of an impression before Alex’s memories jump to her funeral six years later. It’s on that solemn occasion that he first sees Nadia’s prodigiously gifted daughter Viviana when she plays an original piano composition of astonishing maturity. That piques Alex’s curiosity about the possibility that he might be the girl’s father; his paternity sleuthing gives the movie a much-needed kick. While Alex’s romantic past is too thinly outlined to be compelling, Pascal’s internalized performance becomes more affecting once the character’s paternal instincts emerge. This happens first with Bronte (Kaya Ralls), a bright young cellist he coaches for an audition with the prestigious San Francisco Symphony. (Professional musician Ralls is a natural in her first acting role.) But it’s when he starts following Viviana’s success as a composer and musician across multiple genres that the film finally gains some emotional heft. An interlude during which their professional paths cross, when 15-year-old Viviana (Alexa Swinton, terrific) is hired to take over scoring duties on a major movie from a temperamental Euro-diva (Thomas Kretschmann, amusingly playing a male Lydia Tár), is lovely. But it comes too late in a movie that gives us few reasons to care about its opaque central character. Behemoth! is handsomely shot by Damián García, who previously worked with Gilroy on Andor , but in the end it’s satisfying only as a sensory experience in which music acquires physical form, an aspect greatly enhanced by the advanced sound technology of Dolby Atmos. Full credits Venue: New York Film Festival (Centerpiece — Main Slate) Release date: Friday, Dec. 4 Production company: Searchlight Pictures Distribution: Searchlight Pictures Cast: Pedro Pascal, Olivia Wilde, Eva Victor, Alexa Swinton, Kaya Ralls, Erik Griffin, JoBeth Williams, Margarita Levieva, Hank Azaria, Will Arnett, Alia Shawcat, Thomas Kretschmann, Matthew Lillard, Zlatko Burić, Stephanie Sigman, Kate Lyn Sheil Director-screenwriter: Tony Gilroy Producers: Tony Gilroy, Sanne Wohlenberg, John Gilroy Executive producer: Jeremy Reitz Director of photography: Damián García Production designer: Jade Healy Costume designer: Mary Zophres Music: The Behemoth! Collective Editor: John Gilroy Sound: Steven A. Morrow Casting: Carmen Cuba 2 hours 7 minutes THR

articles.title: George Cheeks May Level Up in David Ellison’s TV Empire
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 2, 2026 6:02pm George Cheeks Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images The last surviving Paramount Global co-CEO is likely to ascend in a new chapter of the company. George Cheeks , who currently oversees the CBS Studios portfolio and Paramount’s linear TV channels, is said to be poised to add oversight of Skydance ‘s television studios, including Warner Bros. TV studios and Paramount TV studios, when the deal closes next week. In November of last year, Paramount Skydance reworked its linear TV business under Cheeks, adding cable outlets BET, Comedy Central, MTV and Nickelodeon to the exec’s portfolio alongside CBS. In the previous Shari Redstone regime, Cheeks was part of a trio titled “the office of the CEO” along with Brian Robbins and Chris McCarthy on an interim basis after CEO Bob Bakish was ousted amid a sale process that ultimately went in the direction of David Ellison’s Skydance Media. Cheeks’ goal will now be stability, reorganization and to milk those titles for cash, with wide cuts expected across the company as it seeks to harvest the revenue from carriage fees and redistribute to other priorities, like streaming, and paying down debt. The combined company, notably, also will have to abide by a consent decree negotiated with the 12 states that sued Ellison’s team. That includes having the Paramount and Warners cable channels (Comedy Central-MTV-BET-Nick and HGTV-Food Network-TNT-CNN-Discovery, respectively) negotiate affiliate agreements separately. On Friday, after Ellison shared on X that once Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery combine they will take on the name Skydance , it was also reported Warner Bros. film chiefs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy were exiting . Deadline first reported Cheeks’ elevation. THR

articles.title: “Good Heavens”: Kathleen Turner Reacts to Michael Douglas’ Bombshell About Their Secret Romance During ‘Romancing the Stone’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 2, 2026 6:21pm Kathleen Turner and Michael Douglas. Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images for AFI Michael Douglas revealed in a new excerpt from his memoir One Helluva Ride that he and Kathleen Turner had a secret romantic relationship while filming 1984’s Romancing the Stone , and the actress is responding to his revelation. The Fatal Attraction actor shared an exclusive excerpt from his new memoir with People Thursday, writing that he and his then-wife, Diandra Douglas, were separated and “were both having extramarital affairs.” He wrote that “Kathleen and I fell hard for each other and began a relationship,” and vowed to keep their romance private. Related Stories Movies Michael Douglas, Willem Dafoe Reunite with Oliver Stone for Drama 'White Lies' Movies 'Basic Instinct' Writer Joe Eszterhas to Pen Reboot Movie for Amazon MGM Studios “The chemistry I had with Kathleen Turner was so strong, audiences have been certain for years that we were in a relationship together while making the film. We both denied it through Romancing The Stone, Jewel of the Nile, War of the Roses , and even while doing press a few years ago for The Kominsky Method ,” he said, noting four projects they’ve worked on together. “The official story went as follows: Yes, we confessed, we had amazing chemistry. Yes, we were both, as Kathleen said, ‘terrible flirts,’ and yes, we were both tempted, but nothing ever happened between us,” Douglas wrote, per the excerpt. “That was a lie.” Turner responded to Douglas’ admission on Friday. “Good heavens what a fuss about something 40 years ago!” the actress wrote in a statement shared with People . “I love Michael and I look forward to enjoying the book.” Elsewhere in his excerpt, the two-time Oscar winner said they lied about their romance for 40 years “to protect my wife and son.” He said they kept things so under wraps that director Bob Zemeckis and their co-star Danny DeVito “were unaware.” “The truth is that during the production of Romancing the Stone , Kathleen and I fell hard for each other and began a relationship,” Douglas wrote. “It wasn’t a fly-by night affair; it grew naturally from how closely we were working together, how much pressure we were under, how much we respected and cared for one another, and how attracted we were to each other. Like every other guy in the world at the time, I was knocked sideways by Kathleen….” Douglas wrote that during a set visit, Diandra “grew suspicious,” and spoke with Turner and “made it clear to her that we were still married.” “Her view of the terms of our separation was different from mine. This gave Kathleen pause. She didn’t want to interfere,” he wrote. “After that visit, Kathleen and I ended things, and I went back to Diandra.” THR

articles.title: How a 100-Year-Old Indie Movie Theater Stays In Business
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 3, 2026 5:01am Doreen Sayegh completed new renovations to reopen the Cranford Theater in Nov. 2019 — and then the pandemic hit. Courtesy Doreen Sayegh’s Cranford Theater, the last indie and family-run cinema in Union County, New Jersey, is about to turn 100. Sayegh, who owns the five-screen cinema in Cranford, near to New York City, will mark the centennial with a throwback screening of Padlocked, the silent film that opened the theater’s doors on November 29, 1926, with an accompanying organ player. But while honoring the legacy of her family in the exhibition business since the 1980s, Sayegh is just as committed to transforming the Cranford Theater with new programming and experiences to keep bringing customers through the door for the foreseeable future. “I want us to honor this incredible history while continuing to evolve and ask, what can the next 100 years look like?” Sayegh tells The Hollywood Reporter . As a child, she learned the cinema business alongside her father, Jesse Y. Sayegh. He ran an independent chain of movie theaters in New Jersey during the 1990s — when cinemas had far less competition for customers — and purchased the twin-screen Cranford Theater in 1997 from Cineplex Odeon and a year later reopened the indie cinema as a five-screen venue. “I sold my first popcorn at 8 years old, I could barely see over the concession counter,” she recalled, and sold her first movie tickets at age 11, before moving up the ranks as an usher, a box office cashier and eventually as a theater manager. Sayegh’s father, while retaining ownership of the building, sold the indie theater business in 2010, and she remained with the new owner, Bud Mayo’s Digiplex Destinations. But in 2019, after two other operators after Digiplex ran the theater, Sayegh, while showing a potential new tenant around the building, realized she wanted to make a go as its latest theater operator. “I was standing on the roof, looking out at the [Cranford] downtown and, I thought, ‘You know what? I want to do this. This is the right place for me,’” she recalled. So, with her father’s support, Sayegh completed new renovations to reopen the cinema complex in Nov. 2019, in time for the Christmas holidays. It wasn’t long, however, before the COVID-19 pandemic undid her best-laid plans. “By the time we got to March, the night before we closed down, we had maybe seven people in the building, and four of them were employees,” Sayegh recalls of that dark time. But, determined, she insists the pandemic was never to write the end of the story for the Cranford Theater. Instead, Sayegh got creative by, for example, handing through car doors fresh popcorn and candy to families pulling up at her front door to be consumed at home. And she transformed a parking lot she rented into a drive-in theater. “I was worried. You don’t know what’s going to happen,” she recounted of the new venture, which included an alert on her cellphone that sounded every time a ticket was sold. “I remember the day I was in the parking lot, in the heat and my phone started dinging as soon as the tickets went on sale. And then it just stopped,” Sayegh added. Suddenly, she feared only a couple of tickets had been sold, and her drive-in was a bust. So Sayegh rang her web hosting company to ask what had happened, only to be told surging ticket demand had crashed their servers. “You’re sold out. You sold out in 90 seconds, for three nights,” the report came back. The drive-in theater soon went to six nights a week of featuring classic movies on its outdoor screen. “That was so special to me because it really was such a terrifying time. And because the tickets were selling themselves, I didn’t have to worry about selling them. I focused my energy and our efforts on donations, fundraising and the community. Because at the beginning of the pandemic, I found myself in this position of ‘How do I help?’ I just couldn’t sit back and do nothing,” Sayegh recalled. Her creative efforts for the drive in included a 2020 showing of Willy Wonka and Chocolate Factory where golden tickets were hidden at local Cranford businesses and those that nabbed them earned free admission to the screening. Of course, amid the rise of streaming movies in the home coming out of the pandemic, followed by the 2023 Los Angeles writers and actors strikes, getting film lovers back into the Cranford Theater remained a challenge. “That was definitely a tough time, because our goal is to get people off their couches and into our seats to enjoy movies together on the big screen,” she remembered. To accomplish that, Sayegh knew the years of just opening the doors of a cinema and selling drinks and popcorn as people bought tickets were long past her industry. So she continued to think outside the box for new business opportunities. “That’s what we do here, try to create events around a lot of our films or classic films, and create ways for people to get excited and off their couches and into our theater to watch movies together and experience that together,” she explains of diversified programming like comedy shows, piano recitals, film festivals and indie film screenings. And just when that effort was paying dividends, Sayegh faced another major setback in April 2025 when part of the ceiling in her theater collapsed. Luckily, the building had few people in it at the time, and everyone was safely evacuated. “No one was hurt,” Sayegh recounted about that fateful night. “That was most important to me, because that would have changed the whole story. And the fact that no one was hurt meant I knew I was going to rebuild.” Doreen Sayegh renovated and reopened the Cranford Theater in Union County, New Jersey. Courtesy of Doreen Sayegh (2) After a seven-month closure, the now 99-year-old movie house reopened on Nov. 26, 2025 with marquee lights lit up and neon signage glowing. And among recent film offerings are movie shot locally as the Garden State enjoys a Hollywood production boom underpinned by film tax credits and other state incentives and local hires. Sayegh has shown New Jersey-shot pics like an advance screening for Steven Spielberg’s Disclosure Day , Steven Soderbergh’s supernatural thriller Presence, which was shot in Cranford, another thriller, Mother’s Instinct, starring Anne Hathway and Jessica Chastain, and Maybe I Do , featuring the late Diane Keaton and William H. Macy. “I love it when you have new visitors to our town, cast and crew coming in and they go out into our community and they grab a cup of coffee and a bite to eat,” she explains. Sayegh is also excited about upcoming Thanksgiving dates in her theater for another New Jersey-shot picture, Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky . That drama recounts the making of the 1976 Sylvester Stallone-starrer Rocky , a triumph-of-the-underdog saga that for Sayegh echoes the story of the Cranford Theater and recent efforts to keep the lights on the marquee lit up during the pandemic and a ceiling collapse. “The story of Rocky is so rooted in perseverance, resilience and continuing to fight when the odds are against you, and in many ways those themes resonate with the Cranford Theater’s own story and everything it has survived over the course of 100 years,” she said. Sayegh also puts her staying power down to her father’s influence, which instilled core values like honoring deals, treating people with respect and booking movies based on audience demand and not personal taste. And she looks forward to carrying on the legacy of a family-owned indie cinema business. “My father represents where it all started. I’m carrying that forward today, and now my five-year-old daughter, Natalia, is growing up in the theater much the same way I did. She is already watching and learning what it means to welcome people, take care of a theater and, most importantly, serve a community. I would love to see her running the show one day, although ultimately that will be her story to write,” Sayegh added. THR

articles.title: Will ‘The Shards’ Return? FX Show Tests Ryan Murphy’s Sway In Disney Empire
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All October 3, 2026 6:02am Kaia Gerber and Homer Gere in FX's 'The Shards.' Everett Logo text As The Shards hit screens in early August, Ryan Murphy spoke about how he and author Bret Easton Ellis saw the series potentially running for several seasons. It will have to get to season two first — and on that front, The Shards remains in limbo. Three-plus weeks out from the season finale, which ended on a sizable cliffhanger, there’s been no word from FX on the show’s status. That’s not necessarily a bad sign: The Disney-owned outlet has been known to take its time on renewal decisions. Pickups for Adults and The Lowdown , to name two recent critically acclaimed shows, came months after their first seasons ended. FX and Murphy also seem to have an understanding that when he’s ready with an idea, they’re ready to back it. Two-plus years passed between the last season of American Horror Story and the one that premiered Sept. 24. There was a nearly seven -year gap between seasons one and two of Feud . Those are anthology series, however, and one season doesn’t necessarily flow directly from the previous one (the large pile-up of AHS lore aside). The Shards is intended as an ongoing show, following the same set of characters over a long time. Murphy has also spoken about how much he personally connected to The Shards, even though Ellis’ novel — about a group of L.A. prep school kids in the early ’80s and a possible serial killer in their midst — is semi-autobiographical (not the serial killer parts, obviously). “My pitch to him was that 1981, the year the book is set, was the most important year of my life in many ways,” Murphy told The Hollywood Reporter about how he sold Ellis on working together. “That was the year I turned 16. That was my first date. My first driving lesson. I lost my virginity. On and on and on. I really understood those kids, and particularly, the Bret character.” Compounding the mystery is the fact that no one outside of Disney really knows how well The Shards performed for FX and Hulu. Linear ratings were small — an average of 237,000 viewers for initial airings on FX — but that’s par for the course for a scripted cable series now. A great majority of the show’s audience will come from streaming, but The Shards never made Nielsen’s streaming top 10s and FX hasn’t released any of its own data. Neither of those facts is out of the ordinary either: Most FX shows don’t break into the streaming charts, and the outlet rarely does ratings PR. The Shards is also the second Murphy-produced FX show this year to end on a cliffhanger and not (as yet) be picked up. The Beauty wrapped its season in early March with a lot of loose threads; in July, the show’s cast was released. ( Love Story , which FX did point to as a ratings success, also hasn’t been renewed, but it may fall under the aforementioned “when the right idea hits” plan for Murphy’s anthologies.) Murphy has a big overall deal with Disney’s 20th Television and a long working relationship with both the studio and FX — even when he was based at Netflix, his 20th-produced shows continued to churn out new seasons. If The Shards does get a second season, it may be a testament to those relationships more so than the validation of a big hit. THR

articles.title: Denver Film Festival Unveils Lineup and Honorees
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 3, 2026 7:00am Anthony Ippolito stars as Sylvester Stallone in I Play Rocky Claire Folger/Amazon Content Services This year’s Denver Film Festival has fallen into view. Denver Film today unveiled the roster of movies and boldfaced name honorees that will make up the 49th edition of the Colorado capital city’s marquee film event, which is scheduled for Oct. 22-Nov. 1. In all, 129 features, documentaries and shorts will hit screens inside the Sie FilmCenter, Ellie Caulkins Opera House, MCA Denver at the Holiday Theater, and the Denver Museum of Nature & Science. The fest will open with Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky starring Anthony Ippolito (as Sylvester Stallone) at Ellie Caulkins Opera House (with writer Peter Gamble in attendance and participating in a later conversation), and close with James Gray ‘s Paper Tiger starring Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller at the MCA Denver at the Holiday Theater. Centerpiece picks in between include Danny Boyle’s Ink starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy, and Tony Gilroy ‘s Behemoth! starring Pedro Pascal as a gifted cellist. Related Stories Movies 'Avengers: Endgame' Powers $26M Return at Crowded Box Office Movies James Gray on Broader Takeaways From Personal Film 'Paper Tiger': "What Connects Us Is What Matters" Paper Tiger Cannes Film Festival The special presentations section features many standout films from the fall festival circuit and beyond. Those selections include (in alphabetical order) Stephanie Ahn’s Bedford Park , Siân Heder’s Being Heumann , Pedro Almodóvar’s Bitter Christmas , Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid , Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut , Simon Stone’s Elsinore , Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster , Beth de Araújo’s Josephine , Guy Nattiv’s The Liberation , Andrew Haigh’s A Long Winter, Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , Brad Bird’s animated Ray Gunn , Liz Sargent’s Take Me Home , Anton Corbijn’s A Talent for Murder , Leah Nelson’s animated Tangles , Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fisher’s Wicker , and Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine. Club Kid A24 It’s worth noting that the showings of Josephine and Take Me Home are being co-presented with the Sundance Film Festival, which is heading to Denver Film Festival’s backyard in Boulder, Colorado in 2027. Also notable: Other picks include standout international films like TIFF’s People Choice Award winner La Bola Negra from Netflix, Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s All of a Sudden , and Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur which won a Grand Prix in Cannes. Speaking of awards, Denver Film will dole out a few during the fest’s run. Carrie Coon has been tapped to receive an excellence in acting award for her thus far critically acclaimed work in The Liberation as a woman who stuns her family by joining a cult led by Lily James. John Cho will be feted with an Outlaw Award for work opposite Mahershala Ali in Y our Mother Your Mother Your Mother. Sargent will take a spin in the spotlight as breakthrough director for Take Me Home , which was based on her short film of the same name about a woman caring for her aging parents. Fred Hechinger, who broke out in The White Lotus and Gladiator II , will receive a rising star prize after a screening of his latest, A Long Winter. Others set to receive awards include Benedetta Porcaroli with a Maglione Italian Film Award for The Kidnapping of Arabella , David Acord with an excellence in sound design for Behemoth!, and experimental filmmaker Michael Gitlin will accept an annual Stan Brakhage Award, presented along with a retrospective of his work. Carrie Coon in The Liberation Courtesy Bleecker Street Some other notable titles among this year’s selections are Ron Howard’s Avedon , Nanette Burstein’s Carl Sagan: We Are Made of Star Stuff , Lukas Dhont’s Coward , Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , Petra Volpe’s Frank & Louis , Rachel J. Morrison’s Joybubbles , Ken Russell’s The Devils , Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love , Markus Schleinzer’s Rose starring Sandra Hüller, Mike Leigh’s Tender Loving Care, Barbara Kopple’s Union Town, Dawn Porter’s When a Witness Recants , and Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fisher’s Wicker . “This year’s program highlights the remarkable ways cinema captures human connection and resilience, and it delivers a lineup that is as entertaining as it is thought-provoking,” explained Denver Film Festival artistic director Matthew Campbell. “From sharp, high-altitude Colorado comedies to award-winning festival circuit fare, captivating documentaries and stories born here in our own community, these films demonstrate the pure joy and impact of great storytelling. We’re looking forward to welcoming our audiences to experience this dynamic mix of bold international cinema, new voices and brilliant local talent.” Added Denver Film CEO Kevin Smith: “Forty-nine years in, the Denver Film Festival is still driven by what has always mattered most: bringing our community together around great movies and the people who make them. We’re incredibly proud to be a long-standing part of Denver’s vibrant arts and cultural landscape and I can’t imagine a better way to open our 49th Festival than with I Play Rocky , an underdog story that captures the determination, creativity and spirit of independent film we celebrate every year.” The film festival is funded by the Colorado Office of Film and Television, Bonfils Stanton Foundation, Denver Arts & Venues and SCFD (Scientific and Cultural Facilities District) with media sponsors CBS Colorado, Axios, City Cast Denver, Colorado Public Radio, Denverse, Metromode, Rocky Mountain Public Media, and marquee sponsors William LaBahn, Epicurean, Next50, Amazon, AOR, Halcyon, Sheila K. O’Brien, Crusonia Wealth Advisors, Dormer Harpring, LLC, Anna and John Sie Foundation, Betsy Mordecai Heyman and Gareth Heyman, Julie Mordecai, Mercedes-Benz of Denver, and HW Home. The full lineup — including documentaries, shorts and more — can be found here , including intel on tickets. Fun fact: The Denver Arts & Venues and the 2026 Arts Complex Creates grant program makes it so that all three public screenings at the Ellie Caulkins Opera House will be offered with an allotment of sliding-scale “Pay-What-You-Can” admissions. Pedro Pascal in Behemoth! Courtesy of Searchlight Pictures THR

articles.title: 17 Best New Movies Streaming in October: ’The Invite,’ ‘Disclosure Day,’ ‘Evil Dead Burn’ and More
articles.full_text: Oct 2, 2026 2:26pm PT 17 Best New Movies Streaming in October: ’The Invite,’ ‘Disclosure Day,’ ‘Evil Dead Burn’ and More By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest Ed Sheeran Told U2 He Didn’t Want to ‘Get Into Politics’ on Song About Ukraine’s War With Russia, Says Bono 2 days ago Nicolas Cage Says the Marvel Cinematic Universe ‘Is Becoming a Well-Funded and Glorified WWE’ With 50-Plus Year Olds in ‘Ridiculous Outfits’ 3 days ago Florence Pugh Says ‘Instagram Censored Me’ Over Cornell 7 Posts Addressing Sexual Assault Case: ‘Another Shock That Women Are Censored’ 3 days ago See All Courtesy Everett Collection / ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection / Â©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection October is Halloween movie season, so it’s the perfect time for two of the year’s high-profile horror releases to debut on streaming platforms. “Evil Dead Burn,” the extremely grotesque ninth installment in the long-running franchise, premieres on HBO Max this month and should prove to be a big home viewing hit. For the indie horror lovers, Jane Schoenbrun’s instant cult classic “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” arrives to on Mubi to stream after a buzzy summer run that kicked off at the Cannes Film Festival in May. For non horror lovers, summer movie season tentpoles “Disclosure Day” and “Minions and Monsters” are both arriving on Peacock this October. Neither movie set the box office on fire, but streaming should prove a popular destination to watch the latest Steven Spielberg alien blockbuster and the latest entry in the uber-popular “Despicable Me” franchise. A24’s “The Invite” was a huge success in theaters, meanwhile, and should keep the Oscar buzz when it debuts on HBO Max this month. Check out a full rundown below of the biggest movies hitting streaming this month. The Invite (Oct. 23 on HBO Max) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection Olivia Wilde’s acclaimed comedy “The Invite” arrives on HBO Max after earning a sturdy $58 million worldwide at the summer box office. Wilde stars opposite Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton in this story of two couples whose uproarious dinner party exposes the cracks in their relationships. Variety named “The Invite” one of the best movies of 2026 so far, calling it a “bravura dinner-party dramedy that’s like ‘Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?’ remade by the Woody Allen of ‘Husbands and Wives.’” Disclosure Day (Oct. 9 on Peacock) Image Credit: ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day” arrives on Peacock after a $241 million run in theaters worldwide over the summer. Heavily touted as the Oscar-winning legend’s return to alien-centric science fiction (he is the master who gave us “E.T.” and “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” after all), the chase thriller casts Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt as a cybersecurity analyst and meteorologist who set out on a mission to disclose the existence of alien life to the world. Colin Firth, Eve Hewson and Colman Domingo co-star. The Death of Robin Hood (Oct. 16 on HBO Max) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection “The Death of Robin Hood,” from “Pig” and “A Quiet Place: Day One” director Michael Sarnoski, casts Hugh Jackman as an aged and battle-weary version of the title character, who now lives in self-imposed exile and is tormented by his past. Robin Hood gets a shot at redemption after befriending an orphaned girl. Jodie Comer, Bill Skarsgård, Murray Bartlett and Noah Jupe also star in the A24 release. Evil Dead Burn (Oct. 2 on HBO Max) Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection “Evil Dead Burn” arrives on HBO Max just in time for Halloween movie season. The third movie since the “Evil Dead” series reboot in 2013 (and sixth film in the franchise overall) is directed by Sébastien Vaniček and stars Souheila Yacoub (“Dune: Part Two”) as a woman looking for comfort from her in-laws after her husband’s death. Their gathering at a secluded house quickly turns into a hellish reunion as the family members turn into Deadites. Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (Oct. 2 on Mubi) Image Credit: ©Mubi/Courtesy Everett Collection “We’re All Going to the World’s Fair” and “I Saw the TV Glow” director Jane Schoenbrun returned bigger and better than ever this year with the Mubi-backed meta slasher dark comedy “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.” Hannah Einbinder plays a filmmaker tasked with rebooting a horror movie franchise who gets in over her head when she seeks out the franchise’s original star, played with seductive wit by Gillian Anderson. The movie rocked Cannes in May before earning $8 million worldwide over the summer, making it Schoenbrun’s highest-grossing movie yet. Minions & Monsters (Oct. 28 on Peacock) Image Credit: ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection “Minions & Monsters” is coming to Peacock after an underwhelming summer box office run with $523 million, putting it on the lower end of movies set in the “Despicable Me” franchise. However, family audiences are sure to turn out in force for the movie’s streaming debut. Pierre Coffin, the series co-creator and voice of the Minions, and Patrick Delage directed the film, which is set in 1920s Hollywood and follows the Minions as silent movie stars who struggle to adapt to talking pictures. Naturally, chaos ensues when the yellow creatures accidentally release monsters out into Los Angeles. Animals (Oct. 9 on Netflix) Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection Ben Affleck directs, co-writes and stars in “Animals,” a Netflix original crime thriller that could continue the Oscar winner’s streaming luck after “The Rip” became one of Netflix’s biggest movies of the year. The synopsis reads: “When their son is kidnapped, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate and his wife find themselves drawn into a web of deception. As they scramble to raise the ransom payment, they’re forced to make choices – and reveal secrets – that could tear their world apart.” The cast also includes Kerry Washington, Gillian Anderson, Adriana Paz, Ray Fisher and Steven Yeun. Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger (Oct. 9 on Disney+ and Hulu) Noel and Liam Gallagher get reflective, philosophical and foul-mouthed in “Don’t Look Back in Anger,” the acclaimed documentary that chronicles the brothers’ highly-publicized reunion and comeback tour in 2025. Cameras were given access to rehearsals, backstage and onstage, while the documentary also includes the first joint interview with the brothers in over 25 years. Sacrifice (Oct. 16 on Netflix) Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection Netflix’s “Sacrifice,” starring the high-profile pairing of Chris Evans and Anya Taylor-Joy, marks the English-language debut of “Athena” director Romain Gavras. Evans plays a movie star trying to launch a Hollywood comeback after a viral meltdown. Taylor-Joy stars as the leader of a group of environmentalist radicals, who crash a black tie gala attended by Evans’ actor. This hostage situation quickly goes haywire. Vincent Cassel and Salma Hayek Pinault also star. Love of Your Life (Oct. 14 on Prime Video) Image Credit: ©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection Rachel Morrison’s romantic drama “Love of Your Life” earned strong reviews after its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival last month. Margaret Qualley stars as Maya, whose chance encounter with Charlie (Gabriel Basso) “sets in motion a sweeping romance and a future beyond anything she had imagined. When that future is suddenly upended, Maya is sent hurtling toward an unexpected new life — one that will force her to reckon with who she is, what she wants, and how to love again,” reads the synopsis from Amazon MGM. Masterplan (Oct. 16 on Prime Video) Stanley Tucci gets a star vehicle in Prime Video’s original heist movie “Masterplan.” The actor plays “a legendary thief who sets his sights on the Mona Lisa, recruiting two young strangers to help him — Chiara, a sharp Italian cybercrime expert, and Jay, a swaggering French explosives specialist — before revealing they are long-lost siblings… and oh yes, by the way, he is their father,” the synopsis reads from Amazon MGM. The supporting cast includes “The White Lotus” Season 2 favorite Simona Tabasco and Victor Belmondo. V/H/S Mixtape (Oct. 9 on Shudder) “V/H/S Mixtape” is the ninth installment in the long-running horror anthology series and features segments from Ernest Dickerson (“Tales From the Crypt: Demon Knight”), RZA (“The Man With the Iron Fists”), David Moreau (“Mads”) and Renee Zhan (“O Black Hole!”). Musician and director Flying Lotus (“Ash”) contributes music video interludes to the film, and debut filmmaker Tobias Forge contributes a music video. Heavy metal icons GWAR also make a featured appearance. The Housemaid (Oct. 9 on HBO Max) Image Credit: ©Lions Gate/Courtesy Everett Collection Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfried powered “The Housemaid” to a hugely impressive $400 million at the worldwide box office this past winter. The success launched a new film franchise, with “The Housemaid’s Secret” now on the way for a December 2027 release. Sweeney is returning alongside director Paul Feig. New cast members include Kirsten Dunst and Paul Anthony Kelly. Tenzing (Oct. 16 on Apple TV) Image Credit: ©Apple TV/Courtesy Everett Collection Jennifer Peedom directs “Tenzing,” the Apple Original Films thriller starring Genden Phuntsok, Tom Hiddleston, Willem Dafoe and Caitríona Balfe. The synopsis reads: “Based on true events, ‘Tenzing’ chronicles the little-known story of Tenzing Norgay (Genden Phuntsok), a gifted Himalayan climber who, alongside New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary (Hiddleston), became the first to summit Mount Everest. Encouraged by his wife Dawa (Thinley Lhamo), Tenzing finds an ally in expedition secretary Jill Henderson (Balfe). Together, they persuade Colonel John Hunt (Dafoe) that Tenzing belongs on the British climbing team, rather than merely serving it.” Hokum (Oct. 10 on Hulu) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection “Hokum” stars Adam Scott as the alcoholic author Ohm Bauman, who becomes an unlikely detective trying to solve the mystery of a haunted hotel in a remote Irish town. As answers get closer, Ohm is forced to confront the darkness that has made him such a curmudgeon. From Variety’s review : “Irish filmmaker Damian McCarthy enlists Scott to play a bitter American writer who grapples with his own trauma while fending off supernatural occurrences in this unnerving spine-chiller.” Doing Life (Oct. 2 on Netflix) Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection Tyler Perry’s latest Netflix original movie is “Doing Life,” the synopsis for which reads: “A single mother fighting to survive and a reformed ex-con with untapped talent find in each other an unlikely second chance.” The cast features Naomi Baker, Jay Reeves, Tamberla Perry, Karen Obilom, Jasmine Sargent, Lucky Johnson and Danielle Moné Truitt. Lorne (Oct. 5 on Netflix) Image Credit: ©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection Directed by Oscar winner Morgan Neville, “Lorne” is a behind-the-scenes portrait of the comedy icon and “SNL” creator Lorne Michaels. The documentary traces Michaels’ journey from a young Canadian writer to the force behind “Saturday Night Live,” the late-night sketch show that has shaped American comedy and pop culture for more than five decades. The film draws on exclusive archival material, plus candid interviews with Michaels and the comedians he turned into superstars.
